en: First Chapter:

Having bowed to Śiva, who is established in the digit of the supreme reality, who is uniquely vibrant with the nectar of knowledge, whose form is the Supreme Self, who pacifies the diseases of passion and the like, who is the subduer of Smara, who eternally bears the moon, and whose nature consists of the three qualities (guṇas). 1.
The Dialogue between Ātreya and Hārīta:
On the northern shore of the Himavat, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, there was a peaceful place filled with herds of deer and adorned with various trees. 2.
Residing there, endowed with ascetic power, possessing the brilliance of the rising sun, as white as pure crystal, his body adorned with sacred ashes;
dwelling at the base of the forest of matted locks, he wore bright earrings.
To Ātreya, who was resplendent with many disciples and endowed with ascetic power,
the disciple Hārīta asked about this great, all-encompassing knowledge.
Hārīta said:
O you who are the receptacle of a multitude of virtues, the best among those who know Āyurveda,
O bull among sages, I, though lacking discipline, ask you out of humility:
how does the origin of disease arise, and once arisen, how is it recognized?
"How do ritual practice and conduct lead to success?
O Great Sage, explain this thorough knowledge correctly.
Thus was the Great Teacher questioned by the high-souled Hārīta.
The sage, with eyes wide open in joy, laughed and replied to his son.
Ātreya said:
"Listen, my son, O highly wise one, you who are proficient in all the scriptures."

O son, how can there be a complete understanding in a short time of this Ayurveda— which is skilled in the science of medicine, expert in the knowledge of physicians, and consists of a hundred thousand verses— without limit?

These men born in the Kali age are short-lived, speak little, are experts in only a few scriptures, and are capable of protecting only a small number of people. This Kali Yuga is brief and serves as a cause for the affliction of mankind.
"O son, how shall I explain the traditional teaching to you in detail?
O dear son, the time for its hearing is passing away;
therefore, I shall speak even in brief—listen now."
The first compendium was spoken by me as consisting of twenty-four thousand [verses],
and likewise the second compendium is considered to consist of twelve thousand. The third consists of six thousand, and the fourth consists of three thousand.
The fifth direction is said to consist of five hundred [verses], and five compendiums (*saṃhitā*) are mentioned therein;
therefore, I shall speak even with fewer words—listen, O son!
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes a knower of the Vedas and their commentaries.
O expert in what is of little substance, what is the use of much speaking in this matter?
One should perform that action by which there arises righteousness, wealth, and happiness—that by which prosperity is born, as well as fame and great bliss. (17–18)
That action which brings joy to people is most certainly to be accomplished.

There is but one scripture—whether medical or spiritual—and but one happiness—whether the bliss of pleasure or the bliss of austerity; there is but one venerable person—whether a king or an ascetic; and there is but one deed—whether for the sake of ultimate good or for the sake of fame. (19–20)
In this world, it is through service that one gains more of the essence, the birth of great happinesses, and the increase of blessings;

moreover, her form of radiant fame is free from all impurity, for indeed no crookedness of hers is heard of by the masses of people. (21) This Āyurveda should not be given properly to just anyone. (22)

It should not be given to one who is not devoted, nor to one who is not tranquil, nor to a fool, nor to a base person; it should not be given to the base, and under no circumstances to one who is destitute. (23) It should be given to one who is most righteous, whose mind is free from hypocrisy, who is tranquil, pure, of purified intellect, steadfast, fearless, whose heart is the essence of discernment, and who shines with the splendor of learning.

The wise physician, skilled in the movement of the multitude of diseases, free from greed, and always maintaining contentment—thus, as a mine of all virtues, the knower of disease is always to be honored by the king and his people.

(24) Just as the leader of an elephant herd, seeing the lord of beasts, flees to the forest with an agitated mind, leaving behind his temples where the drops of ichor have dried up; even so, the elephant of disease, upon seeing the physician, departs. (25)
Just as the sun, with its rays, quickly brings light to this entire world which was shrouded in darkness,

so too does a skilled physician, having diagnosed a disease, swiftly bring about the destruction of that ailment for the patient, relieving him of the burden of illness. (26) One who is greedy, cruel, deceitful, gluttonous, a drunkard, lazy, undisciplined, timid, distressed in heart, deficient in action, and dull-witted regarding wealth— [such a person is unfit].
Even if he is learned in the scriptures, a physician who is ignorant of the nature of diseases and who upholds heretical views should be avoided from afar by kings of great intelligence.
(27) The method for studying the science of medicine:
[One should study] in a manner that is wonderful yet free from doubt, neither too high nor too low.
Whoever recites the scripture in this manner attains mastery of the scripture. Furthermore,
the reciter should avoid chewing, swallowing, trembling, panting, as well as speaking too loudly or too softly, and should maintain a deep tone.

The study of the scripture is not prescribed during periods of suspension (*anadhyāya*), nor during festivals, nor during sacrificial rites, nor at the birth of a child, nor during the period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*). Likewise, [it is forbidden] on the fourteenth, eighth, new moon, first day of the lunar fortnight, and full moon days.
These five occasions for avoiding the recitation have been proclaimed by the sages:
during untimely weather, on a cloudy day, during thunder, when the quarters of the sky appear aflame, and during an earthquake;
likewise, the recitation of the scriptures is to be avoided during lunar and solar eclipses. 31–32.
These twelve occasions for the suspension of study have been declared; listen, my son:
when there is suffering to the guru, or when the king is oppressed, or during a battle, or when there is a gathering of living beings, or again at the time of dusk.
When there is suffering in the kingdom, one should not engage in the recitation of the scriptures.

(34) The scripture recited by these [people] does not accomplish success for one's own purpose; it leads neither to spiritual welfare, nor to auspiciousness, nor to benefit, nor does it bring happiness. (35)
Knowing this, the skillful person who studies this treasury of medical science shall daily attain his desired goals;
for him there will be fame, supreme happiness, and the praise of the world.
"He indeed becomes constantly worthy of honor by kings, and the accomplishment of his own purpose is attained.
36. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for Studying the Treatise on the Qualities and Defects of Physicians," in the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Two.
In the *Cikitsāsaṃgraha*,
Ātreya said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the compendium of this treatise."
O best of physicians, I shall describe in brief the origin of Āyurveda, which contains the summary of the meaning of all sciences, as well as the eight medical treatments that reside therein,
and those treatments individually.
I shall proclaim the Compendium (Saṃgraha): first is food and drink; the second shall be on elixirs (ariṣṭa); the third is therapeutics (cikitsita);
the fourth is declared to be the ritual procedures (kalpa); and the Sūtrasthāna is the fifth.
And the authors of Āyurveda maintain that there should be a sixth branch here:

surgery (śalya), the treatment of diseases of the head and neck (śālākya), internal medicine (kāya), pediatrics (bālacikitsita), toxicology (agada), the science of poisons (viṣatantra), demonology (bhūtavidyā), and rejuvenation therapy (rasāyana).
Thus, the treatment known as *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy) is recorded as one of the eightfold branches of medicine;
this great and supreme [branch] is proclaimed in all medical scriptures,
and likewise, those who know the Vedas declare that there are eight [branches] in the science of healing.
The application of mechanical instruments, surgery, fire, and alkali, as well as medicine, wholesome diet, fomentation, and massage—these are declared to be the beneficial auxiliaries;
by means of these, the essence of the medical science is realized in its entirety. (7–8)

In the medical tradition (vaidyakāgama), that which extracts the foreign body (śalya) by means of the principles of the science of instruments (yantraśāstra) and their application is called the *Śalyatantra*.
For one whose limbs have been pierced there by iron arrows, barbed shafts, crescent-headed arrows, spears, and javelins,
as well as by stones or fire, the extraction of the embedded fragments and so forth constitutes the treatment for those wounds; and that is the science of surgery (शल्यचिकित्सितम्).

Likewise, one should recognize as a *śalya* (foreign body) grass, dust, insects, hair, blood, a fleshy mass (*peśī*), pus, and whatever else remains within; as well as objects split by clods of earth or wood. (11–12)
Śālākya deals specifically with diseases of the head, diseases of the eyes, diseases of the ears, and those diseases that indeed arise in the eyebrows, throat, temples, and the neck. 13.
Their remedial treatments consist of non-unidirectional enemas (*nasya*), collyriums (*añjana*), massage (*abhyaṅga*), and the practice of mouth-rinses (*mukha-gaṇḍūṣa*); this is known as *śālākya*.
Thus ends the section on *śālākya*.
Internal medicine consists of decoctions, powders, and pills; the five purificatory procedures, and the therapeutic actions that pacify diseases of the digestive tract—this is internal medicine. 15.

The treatment for diseases of the rectum, the alleviation of bladder pain, enemas that promote growth, as well as non-unctuous enemas (āsthāpana) and unctuous enemas (anuvāsana), and that which is called the "antidote" (agada)— these constitute the chapter on the medical treatment of children (bālacikitsā). 16.

The consciousness of the embryo's commencement, the commencement of birth, and the pacification of diseases in infants— this procedure is known as *Bālacikitsita* (Pediatrics), and it is called the *Viṣatantra* (Toxicology). 17.
That practice which neutralizes the poison of snakes, scorpions, and spiders is called *viṣatantra* by the wise; it is also known as *bhūtavidyā*. 18.
*Bhūtavidyā*.
The planets, spirits, piśācas, śākinīs, ḍākinīs, and grahas—the thorough subjugation of these is declared to be the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā). 19.
Aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa).

That which nourishes those who are emaciated and of little vigor, increases strength, and provides satiation for those with balanced bodily constituents is called *vājīkaraṇa*. (20) This is the section on *rasāyana* therapy.
That which consists of the strengthening of the body, the senses, and the teeth, as well as the practice for the removal of wrinkles, graying hair, and baldness,
is called *rasāyana* as formulated by physicians in ancient times. (21-22)
The treatment for minor injuries— namely those that are severed, split, fractured, wounded, or crushed— and the remedies for their burns are declared to be known as *upāṅga-cikitsā*. 23.
Having thoroughly studied this *Vaidyakasarvasva*, the ornament of the scriptures on therapeutics, the wise person shall attain union with success.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Compendium of Therapeutics," in the *Vaidyakasarvasva*.
The Third Chapter:
The Prescription for the Training of Physicians. Now I shall explain the method of treatment for diseases, as well as [the training].
The wise man who understands correctly is honored by the best of kings.
Having understood the origin of diseases and the methods for treating them,
and having determined the remedy, the physician should apply the appropriate cure.
Having observed the place, time, age, digestive fire, suitability, constitution, medicine, body, mental state, and the strength of the disease, one should perform the treatment.
Through the proper attendance of the patient, there shall be the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure.

When he does not practice [the remedy], then his own destruction occurs. The thorough knowledge of the nature of the disease and the suppression of the sensation—this is the physician's status as a physician; the physician is not the master of life.

Treatment for diseases is of two kinds: palliative and provocative; having understood this, the wise and discerning physician should apply the appropriate action. Furthermore, the physician is to be known as twofold, according to his mastery over the signs of disease and the diseases themselves.

The physician is said to be of two kinds: one who knows proper conduct (*upacāra*) and improper conduct (*apacāra*). Knowing that [diseases] are pacified by proper conduct and provoked by improper conduct, a skilled physician should perform the treatment for pacification.
Disease is declared by physicians who are virtuous and learned in the scriptures to be of four kinds: curable, incurable, manageable, and difficult to cure.
Those diseases which are curable through treatment may nevertheless become manageable.
O son, those diseases which are palliable become incurable; even great diseases that are difficult to cure may arise and indeed lead to death through arduous treatment.
Having thus understood the fourfold nature of disease, one should perform the appropriate action.
The complications caused by improper treatment become difficult and reach a state of palliation;
those that are merely palliable turn into curable conditions, and what was once easily curable certainly becomes difficult to treat.
However, a patient who is healthy may quickly become easily curable through the skillful applications of wise physicians.

Having understood the thorough knowledge of what is curable and incurable, one should likewise proceed with treatment. When a disease has become curable, one should not allow a remnant of the *doṣas* to remain;
for even a remnant of the *doṣas* may cause suffering, therefore one should eradicate it with effort. (13–14)
For just as food may be spoiled by time, or as a minute spark from a fire may seem small, so too a disease that has reached its full manifestation becomes most terrible;
yet, when only a remnant of the *doṣa* remains, it can be pacified with little effort.
When, by fate, it turns toward wickedness, it becomes like a fire that is violently provoked.
Just as a most terrible fire, having reached a heap of wood from afar, becomes even more fierce,
so too does a disease become more terrible through the association with unwholesome things.
When all treatments— decoctions, fruits, powders, boluses, electuaries, and oil enemas— are utterly futile and the disease does not subside,
the physician should always understand the cause for the pacification of the illness.

The wise physician, having ascertained the strength of the humors (doṣas), should administer fasting therapies (laṅghana) by means of the appropriate application of the sense of duty, so that the disease may be pacified; when the humors are present,
even many fastings will not lead to harm.
One should first digest the food; when the food is exhausted, the *doṣas* [are digested];
when the *doṣas* are exhausted, the digestive fire [digests] the tissues (*dhātus*); and when the tissues are exhausted, it consumes the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Having understood the strength or weakness of the disease, as well as whether it is with or without residual humors (*sāma* or *nirāma*), one should act accordingly.
Then, when there is *sāma* (undigested matter), there should be digestive treatment; when *nirāma* (free from undigested matter), there should be a transition to wholesome diet.

Having correctly observed whether the condition is with or without *sāma*, and having observed the destruction of the pain, this [treatment] becomes the essence of the entire medical science. Indeed, such a physician bestows both longevity and strength. 22–23.
No physician is capable of bestowing either happiness or suffering upon a living being; rather, it is the ripening of one's own karma alone that leads to happiness or suffering in this world.
Therefore, he alone is capable here of destroying the ailments that are the cause of human suffering.
The physician is the abode of the treasure of wisdom, while the other is clever merely by name.
He who possesses a thorough understanding of diseases, knows how to suppress the humors (*doṣa*), and recognizes what is incurable as well as what is curable—he shall be a true physician. (24–25)

Whether an ascetic or a brahmin, a woman or likewise a child, one who is wretched or even weak, or one who is wise or a scholar; whether a high-souled man, a learned priest, a virtuous person, or one who is helpless and bereft of kinsmen—(all these must be protected). 26.
One should especially treat these who are seized by disease:

the king, the wealthy man, the provincial governor, and the commander of forces; for their well-being will bring about the accomplishment of one's aims, and wealth may be taken from them without fear.
The middling army consists of merchants, while the priestly force includes Brāhmaṇas and others, as well as the Bhaṭṭas and the courtesans; however, physicians are especially important.
When these [members] are afflicted by disease, medical treatment brings them renown. (29)
A hunter, a thief, a barbarian, an arsonist, a fisherman, one full of hatred, a village traitor, an unchaste woman, and a seller of meat—
one should never perform medical treatment for these people who are afflicted by disease. (30–31)
From these [patients], there is no accomplishment of one's own purpose, nor is there benefit, welfare, or auspiciousness for them;
the physician who lives off them becomes a partaker in their faults.
Having understood this, the good physician should then apply the remedy.
The attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as fame, prevails in the world.

(33) Thus, he who even for a moment maintains in his heart this investigation of medical science, endowed with many methods, becomes capable of destroying the multitude of diseases; possessing pure and renowned fame, he is honored by kings. (34)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Regulation of Medical Training," in the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Four:
Now, [the discussion of] the strength and weakness of place, time, and power.
Now I shall fully explain the strength and weakness of place and time, as well as suitability, the constitution of the body, and the specific characteristics of the digestive fires (agni).
Place is to be known as threefold: namely, the marshy (anūpa) and the arid (jāṅgala).
These common characteristics should be specifically understood by the wise:

[a place] where there are many auspicious rivers nourished with beautiful waters, endowed with lakes and ponds, and ground rich with lush grass; where the fields of rice are delightful with green *kuśa* grass and water, and where the people long for the brilliance of the sun's rays.
The sugarcane shines, rich with its intensely sweet juice and always moist; the broths of rice and wheat display various colors.

Through the consumption of sweet flavors, the phlegm and wind of men become provoked; such is the nature of that coastal region (anūpadeśa). The mountains there are rugged, harsh, and vast, and are covered with thorns.
In every direction there are mirages; the trees have withered leaves;
the earth is filled with dust from the exceedingly harsh rays of the sun; the lake is devoid of moisture; and the excellence lies only in the water of the wells. 5.
Thereafter, cows and buffaloes will consume crops that lack flavor; there will be an abundance of meat and fat, yet a state of dryness (rūkṣatā) will prevail.
Furthermore, the winter rains will bring rice crops but not sugarcane, and blood and bile will quickly fall into a state of agitation.
Or, if the land possesses both qualities in equal measure—neither excessively dry nor too oily, neither too rough nor abundant in thorns on all sides—[the results will be mixed].
Know that when it is covered with water, being neither too cold nor too hot, and endowed with a balanced nature, it is the "common" (sādhāraṇa) time.
Time is to be known as threefold: the past, the future, and the third, the present; listen as I describe its characteristics.
Time impels the world; Time impels the universe;
Time impels the entire cosmos; therefore, Time is ordained as the sovereign. All gods, sages, perfected beings, and kinnaras are subject to the power of Time.
Time is indeed the Blessed Lord, he is the Supreme Sovereign manifest;
he is the protector and the destroyer of serpents. That Time is equal toward all things; by Time the universe is driven, and by him Time is ordained.
By which origination arises, by which indeed the parts are fashioned, and by which Time becomes possessed of essence— the Time that is the cause of the world's production—
He who perceives all actions as they proceed in their excellence.

He too should be known as the initiator; time is that which brings about the dissolution of what has been created. He who brings one under the power of death and by whom all is withdrawn should also be understood as the Destroyer—time, devoted to the act of reckoning.
Time creates all beings; Time destroys all creatures. Time sleeps and Time is awake; indeed, Time is insurmountable.
In due time, even the gods perish; in due time, asuras and serpents likewise pass away.
All kings and all living beings perish in due time. Beyond the three periods of time, he is to be known as the adventitious one whose activity has ceased;
though subtle, he is omnipresent, more manifest than the manifest and unmanifest, and auspicious.
Likewise, these three seasons known as the rainy, the cold, and the hot are recognized; furthermore, three others should also be understood as rising, midday, and setting.
[18] These are the rainy season, autumn, early winter, late winter, and spring.
Summer is to be known as passing away; thus the six seasons are traditionally taught.
I shall describe them individually according to the specific movements of the sun.
Having understood the provocation and pacification [of the humors], the two solstices (ayana) are recognized by the wise.
One [half-year] would be the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and the second the northern course (uttarāyaṇa).
The rainy season, autumn, and winter are situated within the southern course;
the cool season, spring, and summer would be in the northern course.
When the sun's course is in the south, the earth possesses the qualities of the moon;
there, water produced from cool sources becomes cold,
and substances that are strong, sweet, bitter, and especially astringent prevail.
The incomparable wholesomeness of living beings, the potency of medicinal herbs, the moisture of the mountains, and the extreme coolness of the directions—
therefore, the entire earth is moist, damp, and frothy.

How should one treat pitta so that its provocation is dissolved? Therefore, through treatment that is contrary [to its nature], it is pacified. When the sun’s course is in the north, then the Sun is the lord of water. 25–26.
Therefore, intense heating qualities arise that cause a burning sensation;
by the masses of rays from the harsh sun, the forest groves are dried up. The entire earth becomes parched, as do the directions and the essences of water and other things.
Strong sour, pungent, and alkaline substances produce a burning sensation;
therefore, the pitta becomes agitated and becomes combined with the blood, as do dried medicinal juices and the milks of the cow species. 28–29.
The strength of living beings is slight, and the manifestation of phlegm occurs only occasionally;
it is seen in the springtime and subsides by itself. Knowing this, the wise person should properly perform every remedial treatment. (30–31)

The quarters and intermediate directions were filled with the downpours of dense clouds and brimming with excellent water as if they were entirely full; the earth, teeming with joyful worms and insects, was made fragrant by the intoxicated winds.
The ground, radiant and green with dark crops, was bent low, its small irrigation channels flooded with water. 32.
The excellent earth, adorned with mud and graced by *indragopaka* insects, shines;
the mountain, with its bursting mango sprouts, is resplendent, as is the sweet-sounding forest where bees hum.
All living beings, including the peacocks, gain strength at the roar of the rain-cloud. 33–34.
The peacock cries out in the forest, the lake is filled with clear water,
the swans return to Lake Mānasa, and the lotuses reach their full bloom;
meanwhile, the earth is dark green, covered with crops, and resounds with the thundering of great clouds from the mountain caves and ravines.
Thus, the rainy season, which provokes the wind, shines forth as most auspicious (35).
There may be some emergence of crops from their internal germs and the attainment of firmness;
the earth, filled with water, shall repeatedly yield abundant harvests during the autumn (36).
The rivers have their banks eroded by full waters, and the trees on the slopes are shattered;
from the canals and springs, water flows in every direction.
The clouds, bearing abundant water, possess many trees and emit deep roars.
Thus, the rainy season is characterized by these qualities according to those skilled in the seasons.
Therefore, wind and phlegm become excessively aggravated in men;
knowing this, the best of physicians should administer the appropriate remedy during that time. (38–39)
Fomentation, massage, staying in a windless place, delighting in white flowers and gardens, and the practice of physical exercise and prowess are recommended;
pungent, sour, alkaline, and savory tastes, which remove wind and phlegm, should be consumed. 40.
In this context, the application of nirūha-basti (non-unctuous enema) removes diseases caused by kapha and vāta.
The clouds possess a luster like that of sun-stones, emit little rain, and produce little sound; the beautiful lotus pond is adorned with rows of swans and clusters of water-born flowers.

The moonlight of the Kaumudī night, with its intensely cool and pure rays, is delightful; the lotus pond is clear, and the water is as delicious as it is ripened by the summer heat. Therein, for one whose bile and blood have been provoked, the application of that which has reached a state of coldness and maturity is appropriate. 42.
In this condition, the wholesome regimen for a man is seen to be, somehow or other, that which arises from the three [cooling factors]:
boiled milk with sugar, the enjoyment of moonlight at night, and delighting in dark gardens; and in the morning, pure curd is recommended. 43–44.

One exhausted by the bliss of embracing a beloved woman should resort to sandalwood and the like, which have cool sprouts; for it is observed that in autumn, even that which is provocative becomes pacifying—thus is pacification observed in the provocation of pitta in autumn. 45.
In this season, the wind is very cold and light, the days are short, the sun possesses little brilliance, and the quarters of the sky are shrouded in smoke;
yet the earth is vast with rice fields and radiant with dark grain. 46.
Thus endowed with these qualities, the winter season (haimantī) comes to be.
Therein, the humors of wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha) are seen to be greatly aggravated;
the consumption of fire [warmth] is wholesome, as is the use of pungent, alkaline, and sour substances. 47–48.
Devotion to white flowers and gardens is recommended, and physical exercise is likewise praised;
in this way, the humors arising from phlegm and wind are pacified.
In the winter season, for those who are strong, the wind becomes powerful due to the suppression of cold.
With little fuel, stirred by the wind, it may even cook the bodily elements (dhātus).
Therefore, during this winter, one should consume tastes that are sweet, sour, and salty;
for then the nights become long, and one becomes hungry at the very break of dawn.
One should perform that which has been prescribed as the "impossible task" (akārya) after considering it; one should practice this according to the instructions.
Having eaten in the morning, one should consume substances such as arka, nyagrodha, khadira, karañja, and kakubha, as well as those that are sweet, astringent, pungent, and bitter. 52–53.
This earth has abundant cool breezes and its crops have slightly emerged; it is parched by ripened grain.
Yet, somehow there might be frost, or perhaps some specific omen.
In the winter season, disorders of wind and phlegm arise (54).
Women with fair complexions take great delight [in men], and one should wear excessively red garments;
bitter, pungent, and salty foods should be consumed, as indeed mostly sour ones as well.
One should perform this daily sudation and massage where wind and phlegm diseases have been properly eliminated; for where could there be their provocation?
(55) [The forest] resounds with the joyful warbling of cuckoos and is adorned by *kiṃśuka* trees that signal the arrival of the god of love.

This entire world is truly joyful—the mountains are suffused with the fragrance of flowers, and they are filled with the longing hum of intoxicated bees; it is crowded with the arrows of the god whose banner is the makara.
Indeed, the spring season, accompanied by the Malaya breeze, possesses the quality of heat and produces phlegm. 56–57.
The soothing treatment that destroys the provoked *kapha* consists of emesis, nasal therapy (*nasya*), and the use of drying substances (58). Various forms of sexual pleasure, agitation,
and the suppression of exertion and fatigue cause the mind to rest when it is weary (59).
Pungent, alkaline, and sour substances should be consumed to dry up that which arises from phlegm;
by thus completing the course of treatment, a person will quickly become happy.
[The world] is long-lasting, intensely hot, and filled with garlands of flames.
In every direction there will be mirages, and the dust shall become intensely hot. The wind from the southwest will be harsh, the trees will have withered leaves,
the forests will be filled with scorched grass, and all directions will be crowded with forest fires.
Such, indeed, is the characteristic of summer: bile and blood are provoked;
therefore, the physician should apply remedial treatment and pacification. Water-sports, daytime sleep, and the enjoyment of comforts are the means for relief.
The dark garden-pleasure is praised, with filaments cool within its groves;
there is the breeze from fans that dispels fatigue, accompanied by the petals of blue lotuses, ketaki flowers fragrant with scent, and cooled by sandalwood and uśīra. 64–65.
Anointing with cooling substances, dwelling properly in a fountain-house, and thus completing these activities brings comfort to the limbs during the summer.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Seasonal Regimen," as spoken by Ātreya. 4.66.
The Fifth Chapter:
Now, therefore, the knowledge of age shall be explained.
Age is said to be of four kinds: superior, inferior, and intermediate.
The inferior [regimen] for the fourth day has been declared; I shall now describe those [regimens].
Child, youth, old age, and likewise middle age—these four stages of life will be correctly explained in brief.
One who is weary on the road, one whose strength is exhausted by fatigue, a child, a woman, and one who is delicate— among these, the middle category is designated in the medical tradition.
A man is considered a child until the age of sixteen, and a youth until the age of twenty-five.

Up to seventy years is considered middle age, and beyond that, one is called old. Likewise, those who are delicate and so forth are designated as being in the middle stage; and the time when there is an increase of sixteen years [in age] constitutes the period [of middle age].
Having reached twenty years of age, he possesses a slender body;
women have reached their full maturity, as well as their middle and declining ages. A man who has passed twenty-five years and reached up to fifty years [is considered mature].
A woman is seen to be firm in her duties and in the prime of her youth;
from twenty-seven years upward until she reaches fifty, and likewise for one who possesses the growth of a child [in vigor], this is considered the best age. 7–8.
One who is stout, very tall, and firm, as well as a woman with a large abdomen, should be known as having excellent limbs; such a person is the highest of the high (the *uttamottama*).
From the age of sixty upwards until eighty, one has reached a stage of life characterized by diminished strength.
Beyond that, the sequence of age should be understood as progressively inferior and more inferior.
One who is exhausted by a long journey, distressed, likewise afflicted by disease, parched, and excessively emaciated—this is declared to be the natural state of the young (bāla-sātmya). 10–11.

One who is delicate, extremely timid, has a medium-sized body, or is even a woman, should be known as having a moderate constitution (*madhya-sātmya*); likewise, one whose age is moderate is to be understood as such. A child is considered to be up to five years of age, and the period of childhood extends to six years.
A girl is considered *bālā* (young) up to twelve years; she is *mugdhā* (innocent) until the age of seven;
*prauḍhā* (mature) for nine years; *pragalbhā* (bold) for thirteen years;
and from twenty-four years onwards until thirty-seven, she is *madhyagā* (middle-aged).

When women have reached full maturity, this is considered their prime of life. A man who is of moderate constitution, stout, strong, and endowed with mental vigor (sattva) should also be regarded as being in his prime; one should treat such a person with measures appropriate for those in their prime.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme knowledge of constitutions (prakṛti):
the windy (vātika), the bilious (paittika), the phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika), and the combined (sānnipātika).
He who is black in complexion, restless, very thin, has sparse and rough hair, yet is strong and enduring—[this is the wind-constitution].
One with subtle teeth that bite excessively, with growing nails, a long voice, and capable of long-distance walking;

one with long strides, greedy, of diminished strength, and likewise desiring sour-tasting food; such a man, being of windy temperament (*vātalā*), attains comfort through sweating rather than through massage. (17–18)

Fair-complexioned yet very tawny, with a delicate form, he is joyful in the cool season; his eyes are honey-tawny, and though sharp, he is somehow momentarily fragile and fearful. His body is soft and hairless (19). He is fond of greed, enjoys bitter flavors, is hostile toward the sharp, and consumes fresh and hot things.

That man who is fond of praise, possesses teeth of pure color, and is of a bilious (pitta) temperament; who has a very glossy complexion, white eyes, a dark (śyāma) hue, beautiful hair, long nails and body hair, a deep voice, and is fond of learning, sacred scriptures, sleep, and sloth; and who eats bitter, pungent, and hot food—such a person is born with a bilious nature. 20–21.

A person who is fleshy, fond of unctuous and juicy foods, accompanied by song and instrumental music, extremely tolerant of cold, habituated to physical exercise, and longing for sexual pleasure, is one whose constitution is dominated by *kapha*.
(22) One who has a mixed complexion, very radiant limbs, profound and steady intellect, and thick body hair [is of a mixed constitution].
It is dear to women, capable of bearing burdens, very dark, endowed with enjoyment, and equal by nature.
23. Now I shall speak of the intermediate directions—the east, as well as the west, south, and north;
listen as I describe their qualities and their respective defects and disturbances one by one. 24.
Cold and possessing the quality of extreme sweetness, it aggravates vāta and especially bestows strength;

however, for those with a predominance of vāta and for those suffering from swelling of wounds, the wind blowing from the east is not recommended. Slightly bitter and endowed with sweetness, kapha causes diseases arising from vāta.
Extremely cool, it is recommended for those with swellings and for wounds; it is neither fiery nor windy.
Bitter, astringent, and very mildly sweet, it is preeminent due to its fragrant and cooling qualities.
They call it "Malaya breeze," for it captivates the hearts of the most excellent women.
The wind arising from the mind (manobhava) is of the nature of wind (vātika); that which arises from phlegm (kapha) is a covering (pravāra).
The wind originating in the south is neither too cold nor too hot, and it is auspicious.
The wind that brings about pacification is dry and hot; it causes the aggravation of the humors (doṣas), specifically bile (pitta) and blood (asṛj), through pungent and sour qualities.

The wind associated with phlegm (kapha), belonging to the southwest (naiṛta) direction, dries up the strength of the body. However, the extremely subtle wind that has indeed set in from the western direction is beneficial; likewise, the wind that rises from the north aggravates blood and bile (raktapitta), yet it is praised for those suffering from wounds or swelling caused by phlegm.
The wind born of the northwest (Vāyavya) is praised; it is clear, possessing the qualities of being astringent and parching.

It brings men under the power of the wind (vāta), is recommended for those with swellings from wounds, and is neither censurable nor praiseworthy [in all cases]. The wind proceeding from the direction of Kubera (the north) is sweet and astringent, yet it provokes phlegm (kapha).

The arrival of clouds brings rain that is cool, neither hot nor blameworthy; this is verse 32. Rain proceeding from the northeast direction is excessively cold and very bitter; it provokes phlegm and wind, and is not recommended for those with wounds, swellings, coughs, nor for those suffering from disorders of asthma (verse 33).

Various kinds of cloth, leather, bamboo, palm-leaf fans, uśīra root, and peacock feathers— each of these possesses excellent qualities. However, among those items made of cloth, wind is not recommended for those suffering from wounds and swellings.
One should especially avoid [food] produced from red cloth;
it provokes phlegm and blood, causes many diseases, and excessively induces fatigue, exhaustion, thirst, drowsiness, and sleep. (35–36)
A fan made of bamboo causes drowsiness and sleep; it is dry and has an extremely astringent taste, yet it does not provoke vāta. A bell-metal vessel, wind, and dry things that are warm pacify vāta.
The fan made from the leaf of the *tālapattraka* plantain is cooling, sweet, and exceedingly effective at removing fatigue;
however, due to its moisture, it provokes *kapha*. (38–39)

A fan fashioned from the roots of *uśīra* grass and peacock feathers induces sleep, brings delight, removes the disturbances of grief and disease, destroys burning sensations, bile, fatigue, and exhaustion, and pacifies dizziness. (40)
By means of a fan, it becomes fragrant and possesses the qualities of being gentle and cool;
thus, the fivefold wind is rendered by this method for men as a destroyer of exhaustion, fainting, dizziness, emaciation, erysipelas, poison, and pride. 41–42.
In the dewy season (śiśira), the wind from the east prevails; in the late winter (hemanta), the wind from the southeast;

in spring (vasanta), the southern wind; and likewise in summer (grīṣma), the wind from the southwest. In the rainy season (varṣā), the western wind is known to blow, and in autumn (śarad), the wind from the northwest.
In the seasons of Śiśira and Hemanta, the northern wind is said to blow;

the experts declare that it is the rainy season (Varṣā) in the afternoon, while at midnight in that same period, it is said to be Autumn (Śarad); thereafter comes the season of Śiśira, and then the winter season (Hima-ṛtu), preceding sunrise.
And at midday, the experts likewise say that it is the summer season (grīṣma);
thereafter, the spring season (vāsanta) is always declared by the sages during the forenoon and afternoon.
[This applies] in the months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, Māgha, or the one named Āṣāḍha.
And during the transition between seasons, in the winter, the wind may become poisonous.
Wherever—in a city, a region, a village, or even a non-village—this fierce wind touches cows, humans, elephants, or horses, [it brings misfortune]. 46–47.
One should recognize *tilaka* in cows and consumption (*yakṣman*) in humans;
one should know *pāvaka* in elephants, while in horses it is said to be *vedya*.
Bile (*pitta*) must always be protected in the elephant, and phlegm (*śleṣman*) in horses.

This wind generally protects human beings at all times. (49) The wind becomes aggravated internally during the rains; in autumn, the wind remains latent and becomes aggravated in bile-related diseases; the bile remains latent in the cold season; and likewise, it accumulates in the winter or in the thicket of phlegm. (50)

The disease of phlegm (kapha) becomes aggravated in spring; therefore, its pacification occurs in the heat [of summer]. Bile (pitta) reaches a state of aggravation during the summer season; having observed this, its pacification occurs in the rainy season.
[Aggravation occurs] due to the suppression of downward wind, urine, and feces, as well as from astringent foods, excessive cold, and staying awake at night.
Furthermore, from sexual intercourse, or from the fatigue of a day's journey, from overeating, from loud speaking, or generally from excessive fear;

52 from dry, excessively alkaline, bitter, and pungent substances; likewise, from riding in vehicles, swings, on horses, camels, chariots, donkeys, or elephants; or from climbing a palace, or from fasting—there may arise the provocation of the wind (vāyu). 53

In cold weather, on cloudy days, after bathing and drinking, in the afternoon, during a night vigil, or even during the day in the rainy season, the wind-affected [wind disorder] becomes aggravated; it subsides when food has been digested. Lentils, peas, flat beans, large white beans, and clean barley should be used.

Large beans, black varieties, and those prescribed for colds; *kaṅgu*, *nīvāra*, red *śāli* rice, as well as *koradūṣaka* and *śyāmāka*—with these, one may prepare boiled rice (*odana*) or boiled gruel (*yavāgū*).
Also, *kaliṅga*, *vāstūka*, *cillī*, *kapūtī*, onion (*palāṇḍu*), as well as *gṛñjana* and bulbous vegetables (*kanda-śāka*). 55–56.
When these [doshas] are excessively indulged, they fall into provocation; thus has been described the origin of *surāsambhava* (alcohol-induced disorders).
Therefore, if you desire well-being and the constant pacification of disease, men must protect themselves with great effort from it.
[It is provoked] by very hot, pungent, sour, and dry foods, by burning sensations (*vidāha*), by the consumption of *sīdhu* and *surā* liquors, and by fasting.
Pitta moves through heat, anger, sweating, or sexual intercourse, and it becomes provoked (58).

A soup made from kulittha, āḍhakī, mūlaka, śigru, śaṭhī, sarṣapa, and rājikā, as well as leafy vegetables, provoke it through staying awake at night, battle, or physical exertion; its provocation is declared to occur at the end of the rainy season and in the autumn (59).

The aggravation of the Pitta-type fever is declared by learned experts to occur through sour substances, or during the hot season, or intensely in autumn, or at midday, or at midnight, or when the previous meal has been digested, or immediately after eating;
it may also arise from staying awake at night, excessive sleep during the day, the consumption of very cold water, or exposure to cold.

The provocation of *kapha* in the springtime is declared to result from the constant consumption of milk, the nectar of sugarcane juice, sesame seeds, as well as *gṛñjana* bulbs, leafy vegetables, vāstuka greens, tiny fish, curd that is thick with whey, black gram, wine, and heavy foods;
and by the excessive intake of very unctuous substances in one's diet. (61–62)

If a man’s provocation [of the humors] is predicted at the end of the day, at dawn, or at the end of the night, yet he does not eat until what was previously eaten is digested, the wise and learned declare that this very condition is a disease; know it to be a painful manifestation arising from phlegm (kapha). Or, if the provocation is predicted for a person during cold weather or the winter season at the end of the night, even after eating...
The wise have declared that when the force of a disease has subsided, it is the cause of *kapha*; thus it has been stated by the learned.

(64) When the season has undergone a change and one indulges in that which was prescribed as provocative for that [disease], a disease called "dual-origin" (*dvandvaja*), which causes disorder, shall afflict that person. (65)

If a person indulges in things that aggravate phlegm during the season when the agitation of wind has been described, then there will be an aggravation of both phlegm and wind for him. Likewise, if one indulges in those factors that cause the provocation of bile during the season when wind is provoked, [the same result follows].
Or else, there may be a reversal regarding the seasons and grains; then that [disease] arises from pitta and vāta.
(67) When the time has shifted into its opposite and the tastes are consumed in a contrary manner, then indeed a sannipāta occurs, which causes diseases and complications. (68)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Provocation of the Doṣas," in the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya. Now,
therefore, I shall fully explain the qualities and defects of the tastes.
By which mere consciousness one may become a knower of the qualities of tastes:
sweet, astringent, bitter, sour, alkaline, and pungent—these are the names of the six tastes.
They say that two by two they provoke wind and phlegm, and likewise two produce bile.
Alkaline (kṣāra) and astringent (kaṣāya) tastes increase wind (vāta); sweet (madhura) and bitter (tikta) provoke phlegm (kapha);
pungent (kaṭu) and sour (amla) cause disorders of bile (pitta). Pungent and sour tastes are prescribed as pacifiers of wind;
sweet and bitter tastes destroy bile; pungent and astringent tastes are pacifiers of phlegm.
Those possessed by an increase of mutual defects say to one another that this is a means of pacification;
sweet and pungent flavors act as mutual intensifiers, while the salty is said to be distinct from them, following the specific nature of the other tastes.
Likewise, when combined with bitter substances, the unmodified astringent taste becomes exceedingly light and sweet; it is indeed excellent and produces a superior quality.
(5) Bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes aggravate the wind (vāyu);
pungent, sour, and salty tastes aggravate the bile (pitta); and sweet, sour, and salty tastes aggravate the phlegm (kapha). (6)
In the case of Vāta, pungent, bitter, and astringent [substances] should not be given;
in Pitta, pungent, sour, and salty; in Kapha, sweet, sour, and salty;
and in Vāta, sweet, sour, and salty, or bitter, sweet, and astringent.
In cases of pitta and kapha, one should employ bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes.

That which is sweet removes fatigue and wasting, bestows strength and virility, provides nourishment, and produces a sense of refreshment upon the tongue; subsequently, it increases the phlegm (śleṣman).
Sweet honey indeed subdues bile, pacifies fatigue, and is aphrodisiac for men; it destroys the ailments of those who are emaciated, as well as wounds, jaundice, and eye diseases.
That which is bitter destroys phlegm and wind, and removes disorders such as skin diseases (kuṣṭha).

It is cooling, removes all diseases, alleviates vertigo, is appetizing, and does not cause excessive moisture; it destroys cracks of the tongue and is beneficial for those who are emaciated or wounded; it brings radiance to the mouth and is highly praised as a preparation that imparts the flavor of the *nimba* group of herbs. 10.
It causes the eyes to water, burns the mouth, brings heat to the ears,
produces loathsomeness, distorts the face, and provokes the derangement of bile and blood;
it consumes the stomach fire for a moment and causes a burning sensation upon digestion— it is not recommended when old.
The extremely fierce pungent [taste] destroys wind and phlegm and causes a burning sensation;
it produces salivation of the tongue as well as the closing of the eyes or a loathsome state, yet it always removes diseases of the wind.

Sour [substances] cause itching, skin diseases, and pain from wounds; they are not beneficial for those with swelling (*śopha*). They are said to pacify Vāyu but provoke the blood (*asṛj*). The one called *grāhaka* (astringent) excessively dries the tongue and throat; it cures diarrhea and pacifies diseases of Kapha. It removes asthma and cough, thoroughly alleviates hiccup and colic, and acts as a purifier of ulcers. This excellent decoction (*kāṣāya*) is said to possess superior qualities. (12–13)

Alkaline (kṣāra) produces moisture in the mouth; it is unpalatable, hot, and causes a burning sensation. It removes colic, phlegm, and anorexia, and it dries up thirst, dysuria, and [excess fluids]. Furthermore, while it generates undigested food (āma), it also kindles the digestive fire. Indeed, it is declared to be the best among tastes, as it is suitable for all purposes.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Six Tastes."
The Seventh Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the various types of water; listen briefly to their qualities and the contrary effects of those qualities. 1.
Water is said to be of two kinds: atmospheric and terrestrial.
Atmospheric water, moreover, is of two kinds: the water of the Ganges and the water of the ocean. Likewise, that which originates from the atmosphere is said to be of four kinds.
That [water] which has fallen upon the ground becomes eightfold;
I shall now explain the knowledge of the waters of the Ganges and the ocean.
By whichever vessel it is held, it is perceived as being of that same nature.
A washed, pure, white cloth measuring four cubits [in length] and three cubits [in width] for the staff should be tied at its four corners. Then,
one should examine that water in a pure vessel made of silver.
Having placed it in a bronze vessel, the excellent physician should examine it;
or else, a ball of pure cotton-wool or of white śāli rice,
when thrown into that [fluid], becomes white once again.

The white, stainless *piṇḍī* is pure and stainless water; that which comes from the Gaṅgā destroys all defects when taken in a fine vessel. A wise man should preserve it, for it is strengthening, purifying, and a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).

The rain of the Ganges water destroys fatigue, exhaustion, and thirst; it wards off the defects of itching, is light, and eliminates fainting, thirst, vomiting, and retention of urine. This may be seen occurring during the day.
That which is turbid, impure, blue, thick, or even yellow, salty, and slimy is called *sāmudra* (sea-salt).
It is dense, increases *kapha*, and causes itching and elephantiasis (*ślīpada*).
Water accompanied by wind should be known as the cause of suffering from blood disorders (raktadoṣa).
Water is said to be of two kinds, and likewise I shall describe it as being of four kinds:
that which falls at night, that which falls during the day, that which falls on a cloudy day, and that which arises at an improper time.
Night water produces phlegm and is characterized by qualities of density and cold;
it should be known as equal to ocean water and provocative of wind (vāta).
As for that water which clouds rain during the day, heated by the rays of the sun—

It destroys phlegm and thirst, is light, and aggravates wind (vāta). During a cloudy day, the onset of rain, or when the atmosphere is filled with wind, it increases phlegm, cures wasting, provides nourishment, and provokes the bodily humors (doṣas). 15–16.
Likewise, rain that falls only momentarily causes harm and disease to men;
water that produces itching and the three humors (doṣas) is not recommended.
For the clouds vomit forth whatever water they hold, including that which comes from mountains, forests, and groves.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, it is censurable if the sun rains down water from its rays upon the earth.
(18) Water from the clouds is thick, produces phlegm, and aggravates wind;
it pacifies bile diseases but is sweet and causes disorders of the blood. (19)
That which arises under the constellation Citrā is dry, increases bile, and is sour; it causes abdominal tumors and blood disorders, is harsh, and harms the crops.
That which arises from rain during the month of Kārttika is cooled by the heat of Svāti.

It destroys the three humors (doṣas), promotes the growth of all crops, is cooling, strength-giving, aphrodisiac, and cures fever caused by burning sensations. In a certain very holy region, it rains during the month of Mādhava in autumn.

For the destruction of fever caused by bile (pitta) and for the sake of the successful growth of crops, the nectar born of the Svāti constellation is always wholesome when situated in the sky; likewise, rainwater from the heavens that has been collected in a vessel destroys the three humors (tridoṣa). 23.

It is strengthening, an elixir, and improves the intellect; beyond that, it depends on the source [of the water]. However, when clouds release water that is not seasonal, that which has fallen is detrimental to the three humors (doṣas) of all embodied beings.
Rain that falls out of season, arising from the heat [of drought], produces disorders;
it is especially not recommended as a cause for diseases of phlegm (kapha).
Likewise, rain that falls continuously, in torrents, as frost, or during the winter months [is similarly unsuitable].
The fourfold [classification] has been indicated; I shall now state their merits and defects.
(27) O Great-minded One, I shall explain the fourfold *dhāra* and the *kāra*, for the benefit of the illustrious and the highly wise, and for the pacification of disease. (28)
By the cold wind of the celestial river, the water— once thick with the thundering of clouds—
becomes solid through the frost and turns into stone;
yet later, due to the heat of the brilliant sun, that water melts slightly.
The clouds pour forth what is considered cool fragments of water;
it is praised for its cooling qualities, for allaying fatigue, for destroying thirst and pain,
for curing fainting, delusion, and headache, and for warding off hiccup and vomiting.

For those with swellings and ulcers, they praise the alleviation of the humors as beneficial for conditions of a pitta-nature, being preeminent in its qualities; therefore, it has not been kept far away from daily use.
It is cooling, light, removes fatigue, and provides relief from the affliction of pitta.
It pacifies the humors, alleviates distress from water, and is the supreme destroyer of all diseases;
it removes leprosy, elephantiasis, scabies, and poisons, and cures ringworm and erysipelas;
beneficial for those who are emaciated or suffering from wasting due to chest wounds, it is to be consumed by men. 32

Water originating from snow is immediately golden, dense, sweet, and characterized by phlegm (kapha); it pacifies fainting, exhaustion, and pain, destroys vertigo, soothes bile and blood disorders, sustains the blood, and brings about tranquility.
However, water that falls upon the earth as a stream becomes differentiated by various qualities according to the place where it is produced.

They say that water, having arisen properly through various distinct qualities, is of eight kinds: 34. spring-water, water from a natural source, water from a cascade, water from a well, water from a pond, water from a lake, and water from a large tank; the wise declare these, and here they speak of water in brief. 35.
That water which is prescribed for the illustrious lords of the earth as being most worthy of use— sweet, light, parching, warm, and a pacifier of wind—
is to be consumed during the arrival of winter or the cold season, as it kindles the digestive fire and destroys grain. (36)
This is always prescribed by physicians as providing strength and being wholesome for men.
(37) Sprouts from the earth are hot, light, and alleviate Vata; they increase Pitta and destroy thirst and fever.
They are recommended for skin diseases, ulcers, and those suffering from exhaustion and wasting, yet they do not possess the qualities of an alkali. (38)

Hot, astringent, and arising from a spring, it removes phlegm (śleṣman), cures abdominal tumors (gulma) and heart disease, and causes itching, erysipelas (visarpa), and consumption (kṣaya); it produces various accumulations of the humors (doṣas).
They say that salt water is heavy, composed of phlegm, and a cause of disorders. (39)
It certainly causes hiccups, fever, colic, and loss of appetite, as well as skin diseases arising from the humors (doṣas).

Water from wells is declared to be dry, kapha-destroying, salty, digestive-stimulant, pitta-producing, light, and hot; it subdues wind (vāta) and is said to be beneficial, yet not recommended in the autumn season. 40–41.

Water from a pond that is thick and astringent is sweet when digested; likewise, it is recommended in autumn, though it increases *kapha* along with wind (*vāta*). The wise do not declare it beneficial in summer.
Alkaline water that is thick aggravates wind and phlegm, causes skin diseases, and is pungent yet digestive.
It is said that water from a lake causes delusion and emaciation in its digestion and does not bring happiness;

it is alkaline, slightly warm, destroys diseases of phlegm and wind, increases bile, and is pungent. It is always recommended for those with bile disorders, whereas they say water from a pond is not recommended in autumn. 43–44.
Thus, the eight types of water have been described by the best of physicians.

Now I shall explain the water that is not fit for drinking (*anādeya*), such as that from the ocean, rivers, streams, and lakes, as well as those flowing from the east, the mountains, and others following the west. 45.
O best of virtuous ones, I shall describe their qualities and defects in brief:
those with sand, those with stones, and those carrying water—thus rivers are of four kinds, consisting of wind, bile, and phlegm. 46–47.
Water that flows constantly, or that is heated by the sun's rays, pacifies wind and phlegm; such water is especially beneficial in the spring, but never during the onset of winter.
[48] It is frothy from the splashing against thick, clear rocks, and proud with the agitation of its many waves covered in water.
Now, water that is light, pleasant, cool, not excessively warm, and dense properly removes wind and bile while producing phlegm (49).
However, the flow from a sandy bank does not possess dense, pure water; it lacks lightness and, while producing phlegm, destroys bile.
Thus, it becomes sweet, somewhat warm, and astringent; it provokes wind (vāta) yet destroys dehydration and fainting. 50.
The rivers originating from the Himalayas are meritorious, frequented by divine sages (devarṣi), carrying thick stones and sand, and possessing pure water. 51.

Water destroys wind and phlegm and cures exhaustion and wasting; it slightly increases bile, yet water [in general] pacifies the three humors. Rivers originating from the Malaya mountains have cool waters comparable to nectar.
They destroy wind and bile, and remove consumption, dizziness, and fatigue. (53) The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Śoṇa, Yamunā, Sarayū, Śacī, Veṇā, Śarāvatī, Nīlā, and the Uttarāpūrvavāhinī— (54)
For these rivers originate from the Himalayas; cool with the snow-born waters, they are equal in all their qualities and remove wind and phlegm for men.
The wise have declared that the Gaṅgā is joined by nine hundred of these.
Likewise, the Carmmaṇvatī, Vetravatī, and Pārāvatī; the Kṣiprā, Mahāpadī, Pītā, Mutsakā, and Manasvinī;
the Śevatī and the Śaivalinīs—all these rivers flow into the ocean, joined with the Sindhu. 56–57.
Water flowing toward the northern direction is considered supreme for removing wind and bile, destroying the three *doṣas*, alleviating fatigue and exhaustion, being aphrodisiac, and cooling;
it is known as Tāpī, Tāpā, Golomī, Gomatī, Salilā, and Mahī. 58.
The rivers joined by the Sarasvatī and those following the Narmadā to the west—
69— their thick water, when drunk, destroys bile (pitta), increases phlegm (kapha),
removes disorders of wind (vāta), is pleasing to the heart, and destroys itching and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 60.

The Gautamī, arising from the western mountain, is a source of merit and cultivation; its cool water alleviates disorders of phlegm and wind, increases bile, is pacifying, strengthening, and cures disorders of the urinary tract. 61
The Pūrṇā, Payasvinī, Vetrā, the fair-faced Praṇītā,
Droṇā, Govardhanī, and whichever other [rivers] follow the Gautamī— 62—
the water of these is abundant and does not cause disorders of wind or phlegm.
And there are nine hundred rivers flowing to the eastern ocean:
the Kāverī, the Vīrakāntā, the Bhīmā, the Payasvinī, the Vibhāvarī, the Viśālā, the Govindī, and the Madanasvasā.
Pārvatī and these other rivers flowing toward the southern direction— one should not worship them individually, nor separately from those already mentioned;
the total number of all these is twenty-one hundred.
Every *krośa* there should be a canal, and every *yojana* a river;
a river two *yojanas* wide is to be known by the wise as a "great-water" river (66).
The earth is to be known as fivefold: black, red, and likewise white.
Another may be yellow or blue; their qualities have been proclaimed [as follows]:
the black variety is sweet, dry, and astringent; the yellow-colored one is bitter; the red one is sweet and sour; and the white one is known to be sweet. 67–68.

That which is blue is known to be pungent; those who know [the science] understand the water of the soil portion to be thick and sweet when it rests upon black earth. That resting on yellow earth is astringent, while that of red earth is alkaline and sweet. (69)
One should discern the sour and sweet [tastes] in white soil by means of its specific characteristics.
Likewise, O wise one, listen as I describe the four kinds of water:
the water of sin, the water of disease, the water of impurity, and the water of health.
One who commits sin and sinful deeds likewise causes aversion;
[the water] becomes mixed with excrement, constipating, infested with worms and insects, impure, covered with blue moss, and as foul as the roar of a sinner. 72.
It is not recommended for men or horses for bathing or drinking;
by bathing, it causes skin diseases such as itching, leprosy, and erysipelas,
and by drinking, it produces phlegm, abdominal tumors, and worms born from excellent food.

It causes various diseases; therefore, one should avoid it. (74) A well or a lake in the shade of a grove of many trees and creepers is likewise inexhaustible, even if its bottom is covered with worms and moss. (75)

One should recognize "disease-water" (rogodaka) as being moist, slimy, black, situated at the base of a tree, surrounded by many trees and leaves, and foul-smelling like the scent of urine; it causes various severe diseases. (76)
Indeed, when consumed, it causes colic, leprosy, and itching.
It is hot, thick, frothy, and mixed with feces, urine, grass, and *nīlikā* poison;
it cannot be held by the teeth, lacks its natural color, is watery, foul-smelling, and originates from algae.
One should never drink water that is mixed with various living organisms, heavy, turbid with a mass of leaves and mud, or obscured by the rays of the moon and sun, for it is always full of defects;
such water causes abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, anemia, or even dropsy.

Heated by the rays of the sun during the day and cooled by the rays of the moon at night, it is known as *aṃśūdaka* (sun-moon water); it wards off all diseases, destroys phlegm, fat, and wind, stimulates the digestive fire, and cleanses the bladder. (80)

Water boiled down to one-quarter of its original volume is known as *ārogya-jala* (health-giving water); it removes cough and dyspnea, is beneficial for the eyes, cures eye diseases, is wholesome, and subdues the deranged wind (*māruta*). 81–82.

It quickly removes fever immediately, destroys phlegm along with fat, ripens catarrh, and cures colic, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids; it stimulates the digestive fire and removes anemia, edema, and abdominal enlargements. 83.
Undigested food is quickly digested when warm water is drunk at night (84).
Furthermore, in diseases arising from the consumption of alcohol accompanied by pitta,
as well as those originating from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta), cold water is beneficial (85).
In autumn and likewise in summer, one should boil it until a quarter remains;
in winter and spring, one should prepare it until half remains.
(86) In the opposite season, having ground it, during the rainy season, one should take a third part. (87)
When it has been boiled until it is free from agitation, free from foam, and clear,
and remains as half its original quantity, that is called hot water (uṣṇodaka). When reduced by one-quarter, it subdues wind (vāta), and when reduced by half, it conquers disorders of bile (pitta).
Water boiled down to one-quarter its original volume destroys phlegm, is light, and promotes digestion (89).
Water poured in a continuous stream causes constipation, is difficult to digest, and subdues wind.
Water that has been boiled and then cooled destroys the three doṣas, alleviates phlegm, and removes dizziness; it is cooling (90).
Water boiled during the day should be avoided at night because it becomes heavy;
however, water boiled at night attains heaviness during the day.
[This applies] in cases of alcoholism (madātyaya), with burning sensations (sadāha), internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and upward-moving blood disorders (ūrdhvaga). 91.
In cases of blood-dysuria (raktameha), warm water is especially not recommended.
[It is contraindicated] in pain in the flanks, catarrh, wind-diseases, throat-obstruction, abdominal distension,
a lethargic digestive tract, after immediate purification, and in acute fever.
Likewise, cold water is not beneficial in cases of indigestion, cough, catarrh, excessive salivation, fever, skin diseases, ulcers, swelling,
eye diseases, weak digestion, and wasting. (94)
In cases of women who have recently given birth, those who have not yet given birth, excessive discharge of blood, and loss of appetite—
those desiring success in these conditions should consume water only in small amounts;
for if it is drunk when the previous meal is digested and hunger has returned, it destroys the digestive fire of the stomach.

Water drunk while one is fatigued causes abdominal tumors (gulma) or colic (śūla); therefore, water destroys the digestive fire when drunk on an empty stomach, whereas water is a medicine when drunk after a meal.
Water drunk at the end of a meal is praised for its beneficial qualities.

Water drunk by one exhausted from travel, overcome by hunger, afflicted by thirst or anger, or seated in an uneven posture, causes pain. Therefore, one should drink water slowly when the mind is tranquil. (98–99)

If one drinks water at the beginning of a meal, it burns like fire; if drunk in the middle, it acts as an elixir; but if drunk at the end, that water becomes difficult to digest. By drinking water before a meal, there occurs a suppression of the digestive fire and emaciation of the body.
It produces coarseness [of the body] and increases phlegm above the stomach (āmāśaya).
101 Thus ends the procedure for drinking water;
thus concludes the seventh chapter, titled "The Section on Water. 7
The Eighth Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the group of milks (kṣīravarga), as well as the curd, clarified butter, fat, and buttermilk, along with all their respective qualities and defects. 1.
Whatever essence is produced from food that follows the milk-carrying vessels,
as well as the water and the consumed food,
are heated by the digestive fire and become condensed together with the *pitta*.
O son, when that which is being cooked reaches the vessels, it is mixed with milk and water;
thus it is known as "kṣīra" (milk), a liquid whose nature is like fire.
It is considered the nectar of all beings, their life-sustainer, and the provider of strength.
Hārīta, overcome with doubt, questioned his father again:
"O Lord, how does the perfection of the rasa occur, and how is it accumulated? How is milk said to be produced from the white [element] in the formation of blood?"
"How could it not be so for those who are barren maidens?
Thus questioned, the Great Hero, the bull among sages, replied:
"Listen, O son of great wisdom, to what was said by the ancient seers."
Milk is unctuous, and likewise blood, when transformed by bile, attains whiteness;
thus milk becomes white.
How can there be a milk-duct in young girls and in barren women?
Because the strength of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) is diminished, milk is not produced. In barren women, however, the milk-ducts are filled with wind (*vāta*);
therefore, milk does not arise, and because the menstrual blood (*ārtava*) is excessive. (9–10)
When women have given birth, [the woman] gives birth along with the *bala* (afterbirth);
by that, there shall be purification of the channels and milk will flow forth quickly.
Therefore, in one who has recently given birth, phlegmatic (*ślaiṣmika*) milk is produced.
Because of that, it becomes hard; therefore, one should avoid it.
(12) Milk clarifies the channels, provides strength, destroys defects, pacifies the three doṣas, is aphrodisiac, and increases the digestive fire. (13)

The black variety is aphrodisiac, subdues wind (vāta), and its milk is preeminent; the white variety produces phlegm (śleṣman) and increases wind, while the milk of the raktikā is a pacifier of bile (pitta) and its milk is especially distinguished. 14.
The yellow variety pacifies bile, and its milk is preeminent.

Black [lines] are associated with blood and bile; white [lines] possess the qualities of phlegm (kapha). Yellow [lines] are based on phlegm and wind (vāta), while red [lines] are endowed with the qualities of wind. Whatever the colors and qualities may be, they should be understood by one of great soul. 15–16.

Cow’s milk is recommended when fresh from the udder; buffalo’s milk is best when cooled after being drawn; sheep’s milk is wholesome when boiled and warmed; and goat’s milk is beneficial when boiled and cooled.
Cow’s milk is purifying, a rejuvenative elixir, wholesome, pleasing to the heart, and bestows strength and nourishment.
It bestows longevity and destroys blood disorders, pitta, the three doṣas, heart disease, and poison (18).
Goat's milk is astringent, sweet, cooling, constipating, light, and removes the depletion of pitta;
it is beneficial for cough, fever, and bleeding diarrhea, and conquers the three doṣas (19).
Mutton is sweet, dry, hot, and removes wind and phlegm;
it is not recommended for those with blood-bile (raktapitta), but it is beneficial for those with wind disorders (vātika).
It is unctuous, alleviates wind and cold, induces drowsiness and sleep, is highly aphrodisiac, and destroys fatigue.
Buffalo milk is said to bestow strength, promote nourishment, and revitalize the *kapha*.

Camel’s milk is dry, hot, and salty; it wards off *kapha*, removes disorders of wind (*vāta*), is light, and is praised as beneficial for worms, swellings, and hemorrhoids. It is pungent and wholesome. 21–22.
Woman’s milk is vitalizing, nourishing, wholesome, satiating, and a remover of eye diseases; it destroys pitta and blood, and is praised as an excellent unctuous substance.
It is cooled by the night and the moon, and it follows upon sleep, lassitude, and fatigue.
Milk collected at dawn is thick and increases cold and phlegm (kapha).
During the day, milk becomes hot immediately due to the sun's heat; it conquers phlegm and wind (vāta).
When very cold, it is beneficial for pacifying bile (pitta) when consumed as food at night.

For those who drink little water, engage in physical exercise, and consume pungent and bitter foods, [the diet] is light; however, for those who eat oil-cakes and sour substances, it is heavy, obstructive, and cold.
This applies likewise to those who are emaciated, weak, or afflicted by chronic fever.

The drinking of milk is prescribed for those with a blazing digestive fire, for those who are unwearied, for those suffering from disorders of exhaustion and emaciation, for those who are habituated to sexual intercourse, for those with scant semen, for those with labored breathing, for those with irregular digestion, and likewise for those afflicted by pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman). 27–28.
Milk mixed with salt or with sour substances is not recommended;
it causes skin diseases and leprosy, and therefore is considered not beneficial.
[However, milk] that has a sour-sweet taste is astringent, heavy, hot, and a conqueror of wind-related diseases.
Cow’s curd produces fat, semen, strength, phlegm, blood, bile, digestive fire, and swelling;
it is unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect, appetizing, strength-promoting, a subduer of Vata, purifying, and a reliever of pain. (30–31)
Goat’s curd, when warm, destroys wasting diseases and disorders of Vāta;
it is beneficial for hemorrhoids, dyspnea, and cough, stimulates the digestive fire, is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), aphrodisiac, and clarifies the blood and Pitta. 32.
The morning milk is declared to be wholesome and is said to subdue wind (vāta) and bile (pitta).
Buffalo milk is described as thick and sweet; it causes blood disorders, removes phlegm (kapha) and swelling, is beneficial for those in good health, increases bile, and aggravates wind.

Camel’s curd is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), alkaline, heavy, and purgative; it destroys wind-disorders, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, worms, and is especially effective against abdominal ailments.
[35] Cow’s milk curd is unctuous, sweet in its post-digestive effect, strengthening, nourishing, and beneficial.
Curd for women is beneficial to the eyes, nourishing, and destroys the [three] humors (doṣas), possessing the highest qualities.
(36) Sheep's curd aggravates kapha and vāta and is used for hemorrhoids; it is digestive, beneficial to the eyes, produces pallor, and increases wind (vāta). (37)
It is dry, hot, and astringent; it causes excessive secretions and aggravates the *doṣas*.
It is sweet in taste and in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*), yet astringent and increases skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*).
The autumnal variety (*vārṣika*) generates *pitta*, pacifies *vāta*, and provokes *kapha*.

Autumnal curd is heavy and sour; it is not recommended for those suffering from gulma, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, or internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). It increases raktapitta and causes irregular fever (viṣamajvara) in those afflicted by swelling, thirst, and fever. 39–40.
Winter rice is heavy, unctuous, very sweet, increases phlegm, and enhances strength;
it is aphrodisiac, promotes intellect, provides nourishment, and bestows contentment and growth.
It is aphrodisiac, increases strength, is beneficial for those with pitta, and is the supreme remover of fatigue.
The winter [season] is characterized by being thick, sour, slimy, and heavy;
it increases wind, is sweet, unctuous, slightly sour, and dominated by phlegm.
It is said to bestow strength and virility, yet it is not recommended in the spring.

Curd that is light and sour is suitable for summer, but that which is excessively hot produces blood-bile (raktapitta), causes emaciation, vertigo, and thirst; therefore, curd is said not to be [recommended] in the summer season. In autumn, summer, and spring, it creates imbalances of the humors and is not beneficial.
One should not eat curd at night, nor should one eat it without ghee and sugar.
One may eat curd with salt, and one may even eat it with water; indeed, curd combined with salt and water is certainly recommended for consumption at night. 45–46.
For those suffering from fever, internal hemorrhage, erysipelas, leprosy, anemia, and jaundice, and especially for those with edema (47),
as well as for those with pulmonary consumption, epilepsy, and chronic rhinitis.

For those suffering from catarrh or facial paralysis, curd is not beneficial in their diet. However, for those with hiccups, asthma, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, diarrhea, or fistula-in-ano, curd is said to be recommended when it has been processed by being mixed with salt.
Cow’s milk pacifies the three doṣas; it is said to be the best among wholesome foods, digestive, appetizing, intellect-promoting, and a conqueror of hemorrhoids and abdominal diseases.
Buffalo’s milk produces phlegm, is somewhat thickening, and causes swelling in men.

The meat of the goat is recommended for those suffering from splenic disorders, hemorrhoids, and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī-doṣa), as well as for those with diarrhea. It is light, easily digestible, an excellent pacifier of the three doṣas,
and a destroyer of abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, colic, and anemia.

And likewise, three types of *takra* (buttermilk) are described; listen, my son, to how each is recommended for which patients through its specific application: that from which the ghee has been entirely removed, and that from which half the ghee has been removed. (53)

And another type is clarified butter that has not been skimmed; thus, this [clarified butter] is considered to be of three kinds. All of it is light, wholesome, and supreme in pacifying the three doṣas.
Beyond that, it is declared to be increasingly aphrodisiac in successive order.
One should know that clarified butter (ghṛta) that has not been removed from the milk is thick, heavy, and characterized by phlegm (kapha).
It bestows strength upon those who are emaciated, yet it causes undigested matter (āma), swelling, and diarrhea.
It is [contraindicated] in cases of artificial poison, piles, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), and those afflicted by fever.

In cases of retention of feces and urine, as well as in splenic disorders and urinary disorders (meha), [medicines that are] nourishing, strengthening, and antagonistic to pitta and blood are beneficial. Sweet [substances] destroy pitta and blood, while those that are extremely hot produce pitta and blood.
That which contains much water is digestive-stimulant and provokes *rakta-pitta*;
it is said here that it is not recommended for chronic rhinitis, asthma, and cough.
