*Udaśvit* should contain half water, while *takra* is provided with one-quarter water.
Water with added whey (udaśvit) removes severe wind and phlegm, though it itself increases phlegm.
Water churned by the hand is considered to satisfy living beings,
bestow strength, remove fatigue, be unctuous, and cure disorders of the digestive tract, hemorrhoids, and diarrhea.
Except in cases of swelling, in those who are emaciated, during the hot season, in autumn, or when there is fainting,
vertigo, or thirst; likewise, it is not recommended for blood disorders associated with pitta, as the drinking of buttermilk produces various diseases.

Buttermilk is declared to be beneficial during the cold season, in cases of weak digestion, disorders characterized by the aggravation of phlegm (kapha), obstruction of the channels, impaired digestive fire, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, and similar ailments; it is said to be always wholesome for these conditions.

Fresh butter, prepared at all times with the addition of ajāji and salt, is wholesome; it is pleasing to the heart, stimulates the appetite, and cures consumption, anorexia, splenic disorders, malabsorption syndrome, and hemorrhoids. (64–65)

It is beneficial for the eyes, cooling, unctuous, aphrodisiac, life-sustaining, and nourishing; in cases of emaciation, it is liquid, cold, constipating, and cures hemorrhagic disorders and eye diseases (66);
it increases memory, wind, fire, semen, vitality, phlegm, and fat.

The froth of the milk of black cows, horses, and goats is praised for removing insanity caused by wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as swelling, misfortune, and fever; it pacifies all the humors (doṣas) and is cold, sweet in both taste and post-digestive effect. 67.
For those with weak digestion, for the emaciated, and especially for those suffering from diarrhea (68),
[this] when stirred with milk is an energizer, a digestive stimulant, strengthening, sweet, a subduer of Vāta, and provides immediate strength (69).

For one whose fever and diarrhea have subsided, yet who still has residual *āma*, and for those with irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*) or weak digestion (*mandāgni*), the froth of milk is recommended when it is based on an excess of *kapha*.
Cow's milk, the froth of cow's milk, or even buttermilk is indeed beneficial in these cases.
Or even by eating ripe mangoes, his chronic diarrhea (grahaṇī) is destroyed.
A person should not consume betel leaf after drinking milk; it is recommended that he wait until that milk has been digested, or even until the end of the meal. 71–72.

Cow’s ghee possesses the highest qualities: it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), aphrodisiac, and removes wind, bile, and phlegm; it is beneficial for the eyes, strength-promoting, and clarifies the intellect.
Clarified butter (ājya) is digestive-stimulant, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength.

Buffalo ghee is beneficial for cough, dyspnea, and consumption; it pacifies vāta and pitta upon digestion and removes kapha. It is very cooling, sweet, heavy, constipating, strengthening, and endowed with excellent qualities. (74–75)

Camel ghee is pungent in its post-digestive effect (pāka), cures consumption, worms, and poisons; it stimulates digestion, subdues kapha and vāta, and removes skin diseases, abdominal tumors, and enlargement of the abdomen.
Sheep's ghee is light in digestion and cures all diseases and poisons.
It indeed promotes the growth of bones and removes urinary calculi and gravel (77).
Horse milk increases the digestive fire of the body, destroys poison,
is beneficial for the eyes, stimulates the fire, and wards off disorders of wind (vāta) (78).
Ghee made from milk promotes the growth of bones and is declared to be a destroyer of poison; it is a nourishing agent that cures eye diseases and removes burning sensations.
Matured ghee is used for kindling the digestive fire and for treating fainting, leprosy, insanity, and pain in the ears and eyes.
Thus, aged ghee is recommended for men in cases of swelling, hemorrhoids, disorders of the female reproductive tract, and ulcers (80).
It is beneficial for diseases caused by kapha and vāta, as well as for disorders of the female reproductive tract; it is good for the eyes and, when taken by women, is like nectar (81).

The wise declare that fresh ghee is indicated in cases of loss of strength, during satiation meals, in exhaustion, in pitta-blood disorders, when dust has entered the eyes, in ophthalmia, in jaundice and anemia, and in wasting; likewise, it is used when fever,
constipation, choleraic diarrhea, or anorexia have been pacified, as well as when the digestive fire is suppressed.
In cases of alcoholism or excessive intoxication, the wise do not highly regard ghee as beneficial.
(83) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Group of Milks," in the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Nine.
The Group of Urines:
Cow, goat, sheep, buffalo, elephant, horse, camel, donkey, and human urine—listen now to a summary of their qualities. 1.
Sharp, hot, alkaline, and similarly astringent, it is strengthening, promotes intelligence, subdues phlegm and wind, acts as a purgative,

pacifies internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and removes the afflictions of abdominal tumors, constipation, and pride. It also cures diseases of the eyebrows, temples, jaw, throat, and mouth, as well as abdominal tumors, diarrhea, and ailments of the anus, wind, and eyes.
Even a single dose of cow’s urine, taken together with kuṣṭha, destroys cough, abdominal ailments, and the network of intestinal worms within days.
Goat’s urine is sharp, hot, and astringent; it should be used for drinking to destroy the pain of colic and abdominal tumors (gulma).
They say this is the best remedy for cough, asthma, jaundice, anemia, and hemorrhoids.

Sheep urine is alkaline, pungent, and sharp; it subdues Vata, destroys hemorrhoids and abdominal colic, and purifies skin diseases and urinary disorders. It is substantial, bitter, pungent, and astringent; it is a laxative and brings about the pacification of Vata.
It constantly provokes pitta and destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (arśas), anemia (pāṇḍu), abdominal enlargement (udara), and colic (śūla).
Elephant urine is extremely bitter, salty, a purgative, subdues vāta, aggravates kapha,
and destroys ringworm (maṇḍala) and skin diseases.
Camel meat removes cough and phlegm, destroys vomiting, worms, and skin diseases;
it is digestive, pungent, sharp, and hot, and cures disorders of wind and phlegm.
(8) It removes phlegm, is dry, and destroys worms and cutaneous sores.

The urine of a donkey is excellent for curing skin diseases (kuṣṭha), abdominal enlargements (udara), insanity (unmāda), consumption (śoṣa), hemorrhoids (arśas), worms (krimi), and disorders of wind (vāta).
Donkey urine may sometimes be used mixed with oil;
when combined with alkali (kṣāra) and bitter or pungent substances, it cures insanity and skin diseases.
Human urine is said to be alkaline, pungent, sweet, and light;
it cures eye diseases, is strengthening, stimulates digestion, and destroys phlegm (kapha).
The urine of a woman who has not yet given birth is thick, while that of one who has given birth is thin and light.
There would be no distinction in quality between the equality of their ripening and potency.
However, the urine of a bull is praised when it is thick and dense;
that of castrated bulls is considered slightly lighter.
Bull urine destroys swelling, eliminates worms and disorders, cures jaundice, malabsorption syndrome, and anemia, and stimulates the digestive fire.
The best of physicians recommends the urine of goats and sheep for drinking.
Sheep’s fat, buffalo fat, and horse fat are prescribed for cooking oil;
an ointment with elephant urine removes itching, scabies, and erysipelas.
Alternatively, camel fat or donkey urine may be applied as an oil for nasal administration.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Group of Urines," in the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya. Now,
therefore, I shall fully explain the group of sugarcane varieties, which are preeminent in their qualities.
It is the best of elixirs, strengthening, and the supreme warder-off of disease;
it is unctuous, satiating, nourishing, and life-sustaining.
It pacifies both Vāta and Pitta, is likewise aphrodisiac, yet causes internal burning and increases Kapha—such is the dark sugarcane.
Similarly, *sukṛṣṇa* is aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*), nourishing, and a destroyer of burning sensations (*dāha*).

Alkali (*kṣāra*) is slightly sweet in taste, removes dryness (*śoṣa*), and causes swelling of ulcers (*vraṇa-śopha*). Juice extracted by pressing with a machine (*yantra-pīḍita-rasa*) is boiled, heavy, aphrodisiac, produces phlegm (*kapha*), and is very cooling.
When cooked, it causes burning and increases strength; when well-consumed, it is very beautiful and destroys the afflictions of blood and bile.
The juice squeezed out with the teeth is appetizing, heavy, nourishing, strength-giving, and increases phlegm;
it destroys wind-disorders, causes constipation, and likewise destroys all defects of blood and bile, as well as vomiting and consumption.

When it has stood overnight, it is undesirable; it is heavy, hot, and produces a single-minded effect [in digestion], increases phlegm and bile, causes emaciation, is laxative, or else it is diuretic.
When cooked, it is very heavy, unctuous, slightly sharp, and destroys phlegm and wind.
It specifically destroys pitta and cures abdominal tumors (gulma), diarrhea, and cough.
Molasses (phāṇita) is heavy, causes internal secretions (abhiṣyandi), is nourishing, and increases semen;
it also destroys pitta, removes fatigue, and eliminates blood disorders.

It is strengthening, aphrodisiac, heavy, unctuous, subdues Vata, and cleanses the urine; when old, its qualities are even greater, and it cures abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and anorexia. It is beneficial in wasting diseases, cough, emaciation from chest wounds, anemia, and loss of blood.
Sugar (guḍa) is considered most wholesome when consumed by one who is fit for it.
Granulated sugar (khaṇḍa), white sugar (sita), and honey-sugar are sweet, destroy wind and bile, possess a slight cooling quality, and are strengthening, aphrodisiac, and a promoter of appetite.
Sugar candy (khaṇḍa) is said to alleviate wind and bile, be cooling, unctuous, strengthening, pleasant to the mouth, beneficial for the eyes, and increases phlegm; it is considered most aphrodisiac.
White sugar (sitā) is declared to be very sweet, aphrodisiac, and an increaser of semen.

Sugar-candy (śarkarā) is a destroyer of bile, sweet, strengthening, and beneficial for men who drink it. Another type of sugar-candy is very cooling; it is beneficial for those suffering from cough and pain arising from [bile], for bilious hemorrhage, and for consumption; it removes fainting, vertigo, and intoxication.

In cases of hemorrhoids, jaundice, consumption, urinary disorders, abdominal tumors, anemia, and halimaka, as well as in vāta associated with pitta and blood, and in rājayakṣman, jaggery (guḍa) is heavy yet provides appetite; it is beneficial in cough and consumption, and is considered wholesome in other conditions as well. 16.
Jaggery is not desired in [certain] coughs and consumption, though it is held to be beneficial elsewhere.
Indeed, one who is disciplined in yoga is beneficial in all circumstances and is a repository of a multitude of virtues.
[This applies] to those suffering from emaciation, wounds, pain, dyspnea, fainting, and other ailments;
and to those afflicted by fatigue from travel, exhaustion, intoxication, poisoning, urinary distress, and urinary calculi.
It destroys all diseases in cases of chronic fever, emaciation, poison, and contagious ailments; in the provocation of *rakta-pitta*, thirst, burning sensations, consumption, and blood disorders.
(19) Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Group of Sugarcane," in the first section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Eleven:
Rice-water (taṇḍulodaka) is cooling, sweet, and a destroyer of severe diarrhea; it is very palatable, cooling, and nourishing. 1.

Tuṣodaka (fermented rice-water) alleviates vāta and pitta; it cures raktapitta, acts as a laxative, is digestive, promotes digestion, destroys worms, and overcomes indigestion. It is pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka). Yavāmla (sour barley-liquor) is pungent in its post-digestive effect, removes vāta, and subdues kapha along with blood.

The decoction (kaṣāya) produced from wheat causes the provocation of pitta, is laxative, and is a purifier of the blood and pitta-related diseases. It is digestive-stimulant, relieves colic, promotes appetite,
is carminative, destroys kapha, and even more so than that, it removes disorders of vāyu.
When drunk, it digests food; when applied externally, it removes the fatigue caused by heat and exertion.
Combined with oil, it destroys leprosy and itching, and subdues the wind (vāta).
Sour Yugaṃdhara destroys phlegm (kapha) and wind, and acts as a digestive for diseases characterized by colic.

Sharp and sour, it is considered beneficial for blood and for those suffering from urinary disorders and hemorrhoids, as it destroys the defects caused by fatigue. However, *kāñjika* (fermented rice water) is not recommended for those afflicted by consumption, fainting, fever, vertigo, the effects of potent poisons, skin diseases, or bleeding disorders.

For a person suffering from jaundice, pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā), or edema, as well as for one emaciated by chest wounds, exhausted from travel, or afflicted by mild fever, fermented gruel (kāñjika) is said to be not at all beneficial, as it provokes the bodily humors. 8
For those afflicted by colic and wind, as well as for those suffering from chronic constipation, sour [substances] are declared to be the best; they possess superior qualities for human beings.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Group of Fermented Gruels," in the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 11.
Chapter Twelve:
The Group of Mandas.
The *dhāmyamanda* removes pitta, destroys fatigue, and cures urinary calculi.
The scum (maṇḍa) produced from red rice is excellent for increasing wind, pacifying blood, being astringent, and stimulating digestion; it is sweet, astringent, and cooling,
destroys urinary disorders (prameha) and stones, increases wind, and is best for removing bile.
White rice (śvetataṇḍula) is sweet, cooling, slightly increases phlegm, cures emaciation, and alleviates urinary calculi, urinary disorders, vomiting, and wind disorders.
Barley gruel (yavamaṇḍa) is astringent, constipating, and undergoes a hot post-digestive transformation.
Similarly, that which is produced from wheat is sweet and wards off pitta. The scum (maṇḍa) of other minor grains is known to alleviate vāta.
Kodrava grain is considered immediately harmful, as it causes exhaustion and fainting.
And likewise, sour gruel made from small grains increases wind (vāta) and produces bile (pitta);
it causes elephantiasis (ślīpada), abdominal tumors (gulma), and provokes catarrh (pratiśyāya) and other ailments.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Group of Sours," in the Hārīta-uttara spoken by Ātreya. 12.
Chapter Thirteen:
Kulattha soup is sweet and astringent; it destroys blood and phlegm, cures large stones, piles, and obesity, stimulates digestion, and dries up urinary disorders. 1.
A soup made from *āḍhakī* is sweet, drying, wind-dispelling, phlegm-removing, and bile-alleviating; it separately cures various fevers and is a formidable destroyer of worms.
A soup of mung beans is cooling and sweet, and it conquers disorders of bile.
That is said to remove wind and is the supreme pacifier of fevers.
The soup of chickpeas is declared to be astringent, pungent, and hot; it subdues wind, increases the kapha humor, and quickly stops internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). 3–4.

Thick bean soup with its broth generates phlegm, while that which is sour and has stood overnight generates bile; however, it is recommended for use in the cooking of oils. Other types are also praised, as are horse-gram (kulattha) that has been kept overnight.
Masūra, tripuṭā, and varieties such as kalāya are strengthening, while others are to be avoided.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Group of Soups," in the Hārīta-uttara spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Fourteen.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the qualities and defects of oils;
that should be understood in brief, as is appropriate and according to the rules:
it has an astringent aftertaste, is sweet, subtle, hot, and pervasive.
Wise men know that sesame oil increases bile, pacifies wind, and increases phlegm-related diseases;
it is slightly appetizing, wholesome, a remover of itching and skin diseases,
an aphrodisiac, and known to dispel fatigue.

In cases of wounds that are cut, pierced, dislocated, rubbed, or fractured, as well as in burns from fire, in cases of wind-disorders (vāta), excessive lacrimation (abhiṣyanda), and cracking of the skin, sesame oil is used for massage. It is also used for poison, and for massage or immersion baths following a bite by a predatory animal, a dog, a snake, or a frog.
Sesame oil is prescribed for use in drinks, enemas, and in cases of *balāśa* (phlegm);
sesame oil should be employed for the prevention of all diseases. It is pungent, bitter, astringent, hot, and it subdues phlegm and wind.
Sesame oil that has been strained is a purifier for worms and itching, yet it generates pitta.
It is used for ear diseases, worm infestations, wind disorders (vātāmayas), itching, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and conditions characterized by the qualities of phlegm (kapha) and fat (medas).
Mustard oil is indeed praiseworthy for the alleviation of diseases;
however, it is not recommended for the administration of enemas (basti), as it greatly increases pitta and causes burning sensations.
Oil derived from linseed (alasī) is thick, sweet, and slimy.
In its post-digestive effect, it is hot in potency and wards off wind and phlegm.
Castor oil derived from the *eraṇḍa* plant is also known to be cooling and mild;
it alleviates pain in the heart, bladder, calves, waist, and thighs, as well as abdominal distension and constipation.
It destroys abdominal tumors, piles, wind-disorders, blood disorders, splenic enlargement, upward movement of gases (udāvarta), and colic;
it should be administered for the pacification of all wind-related disorders.
Thus, as many fixed fats as have been described in brief, [they are all included herein].

All the qualities of oil should be known as such, and all of them destroy Vāta. Among all oils here, sesame oil is praised above all others. Castor oil is strengthening, heavy, hot, and likewise sweet.
Castor oil is sharp, hot, slimy, and foul-smelling;
safflower oil is hot, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), heavy, causes a burning sensation, and especially aggravates all the bodily humors (doṣas). 15–16.
Having understood the qualities and actions of whichever oils for increasing *kapha* have been mentioned, one should prescribe those that increase *kapha* and *vāta*.
Sahakāra oil is slightly bitter, extremely fragrant, subdues *vāta* and *kapha*, and is subtle.
Likewise, that which is sweet and astringent does not cause excessive redness and does not produce pitta.
[18] That which originates from the heartwood of sauvarcala, iṅgudī, pīlu, and śiṃśapā, as well as that which originates from trees such as sarala, aguru, and devadāru; [19]
That which arises from *tamburu*, from *karañja*, and likewise from *jyotiṣmatī* destroys hemorrhoids, skin diseases, worms, phlegm, semen, fat, and wind.
One should prescribe *karañja-ariṣṭaka*, which is bitter and not excessively hot. 20–21.
The juice derived from *accha*, *atimuktaka*, *acchoḍa*, coconut, and *madhūka* is astringent, sweet, and bitter; it promotes healing, cleanses wounds, and is cooling.
[Likewise is that] derived from cucumber, gourd, pumpkin, *śleṣmātaka*, and *pīlu*. (22)

[The meat] derived from the Śrīparṇī and Kiṃśuka destroys wind, bile, heart disease, and hemorrhoids; it increases phlegm, is heavy, and is cooling. (23-24) Fat, when consumed in excess, destroys wind and bestows strength, bile, and phlegm. (25)
The fat of the pig and the buffalo increases wind (vāta) and increases phlegm (śleṣman).
[Verse 25] The fat of the snake, the mongoose, and the iguana, when used as an ointment, destroys wounds and skin diseases (kuṣṭha);
the fat of fish, the porpoise, the crocodile, the grāha, and others is likewise [effective].
It is curative of erysipelas, pleasing to the heart, and a destroyer of the disease of leprosy (kuṣṭha). 26.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Group of Oils and Fats," in the first section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Fifteen.
The section on grains: red rice (raktaśāli), great rice (mahāśāli), kalama rice, sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika), the other [varieties], khañjarīṭa, apasāhī, jīraka, and ākapiñjalā.
Saugandhī, śūkalā, another called bilavāsī, kacorakā, garuḍā, rukmavantī, and another called kalamā, as well as bilvajā, māgadhī, and pītā— these are the eighteen types of śāli rice.

Red *śāli* rice destroys the three *doṣas*, is beneficial for the eyes, and cures urinary diseases; *mahāśāli* is heavy, aphrodisiac, beneficial for the eyes, and increases strength. (3) The other *ṣaṣṭika* variety is cooling, heavy, destroys the three *doṣas*, and is sweet. (4)
Jīraka destroys vāta and pitta; kalamā destroys kapha and pitta; kapiñjalā is kapha-increasing; māgadhī increases kapha and vāta;
bilavāsī is heavy, destroys pitta, and increases semen.
Śūkalā destroys pitta and vāta; kacorā destroys pitta.
Another variety, garuḍā, overcomes falling [diseases], removes disorders of pitta and urine, and is considered light, promoting appetite, strength, and nourishment. (6–7)
The *kālā* variety is light and wholesome, while that produced from the *bilva* tree increases wind and phlegm;
the *māgadhī* variety, when drunk, possesses qualities similar to those [other types],
yet it creates appetite, bestows strength, cures urinary disorders, and removes fatigue.

Rice grown on hills where villages have been burnt is light to digest, wholesome, constipating and diuretic, dry, and it reduces phlegm (śleṣman). Trees originating from irrigated fields destroy wind (vāta) and bile (pitta). 9–10.
They cure disorders of blood and bile, increase wind (vāta), and produce phlegm (kapha);
one should observe that their names vary from region to region.
One should know that all of them, when grown in their respective lands, possess equal qualities.
Śāli rice and chinnarohā are diuretic, increase vāta, and are cooling.
Śyāmāka, kodrava, kaṇḍū, markaṭī, and kapikacchu—these are declared to be minor grains; listen, my son, as I shall now describe them. (13–14)
Śyāmāka is drying, parching, dry, increases Vāta, and wards off Kapha.
Kodrava is dry, constipating, and dries up Śyāva (blackish) blood and Pitta.
It is said not to increase Kapha excessively; it is proclaimed to be appetizing and sweet. 15–16.
I shall describe the foods made from split grains; listen, my son, in due order:
barley, wheat, chickpeas, black gram, green gram, and pigeon pea (17), as well as makuṣṭaka, horse gram, lentils, and tripuṭa.
Niṣpāvaka and kalāya are proclaimed to be split-grains (vidalānna).
Barley is dry, cold, heavy, sweet, and astringent; it is aphrodisiac, constipating, and destroys phlegm, while also curing pitta, asthma, and cough. (18-19)
Wheat is sweet, heavy, constipating, aphrodisiac, strengthening, nourishing, slightly astringent, and a destroyer of the three doṣas.
Sesame is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), most strengthening, unctuous, and is said to be wholesome as an application for wounds.
Black sesame is strengthening, stimulates the intellect, is excellent, removes disorders of the urine, and is heavy (21).
Among all types of sesame, the black is preeminent; the white is middling, while the others are inferior (22).
[It is indicated] in cases of blood [disorders], phlegm, chronic rhinitis, throat ailments, diseases of the gullet, and wind-pitta disorders.
Chickpeas (caṇaka), whether dry or fresh, are excellent; they are cooling and destroy catarrh and worms.

Furthermore, black gram (māṣa) is known by men to be unctuous, aphrodisiac, sweet, strengthening, and a nourisher of wind and phlegm; it is sour and hot during digestion, yet cold in its natural state, and is considered heart-pleasing.

Mudga is cool, astringent, sweet, light, laxative, and removes the defects of pitta and blood; it is primarily pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and another variety is described as being likewise pleasant.
It is mild and astringent, and it destroys raktapitta, vāta, and kapha, as well as mouth ulcers.
Āḍhakī cures abdominal tumors, fever, loss of appetite, cough, vomiting, heart disease, and hemorrhoids;
it destroys blood-bile, phlegm, and wind, and is declared to be hot, astringent, and sweet.
Makuṣṭaka is constipating, very cooling, and cures abdominal tumors caused by wind; it destroys all diseases.
This *kulattha* is hot; it conquers wind (*vāta*), swelling, cough, catarrh, obstructions, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*).
When accompanied by blood, it destroys hiccup, phlegm (*balāśa*), and bile, as well as fat.
It is declared to be dry, desiccating, and sweet; it strengthens the sinews and the bones.
They cause colic, constipation, vertigo, swelling, burning sensations, hemorrhoids, and heart diseases.

Slightly astringent and sweet, they are prescribed as strengthening agents that bring about the pacification of blood; resembling the *mudga* bean in form, *kalāya* beans slightly subdue both wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*). 29–30.

The lentil (*masūra*) is declared to be dry, parching, and sweet; it causes colic, pain, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), and increases wind-related diseases. It is astringent and removes *pitta* and blood disorders. Thus ends the section on various grains, only a portion being given for fear of excessive length in this treatise.
"Indeed, whatever things are most well-known in the world, their qualities are declared to be the most excellent.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Group of Grains," in the first section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Sixteen.
Vegetables are said to be of four kinds: leaf, flower, fruit, and also bulb; these shall be described individually.
Vegetables are indicated as being of two types, and one should know the latter to be heavy.
Generally, all leafy vegetables (śāka) are constipating, heavy, dry, increase feces, and promote the passage of stool and flatus.
Jīvantī is beneficial for the eyes, cures all diseases, is sweet, and cooling.

Taṇḍulīyaka is sweet in digestion, destroys blood, bile, and poison, and is beneficial for various types of wind (vāta), constipation, urine, wind, and phlegm (kapha). It is sweet, subdues kapha and vāta, is digestive, and cleanses the throat.
The *kāsamardaka* is said to be especially a subduer of *pitta*.
Similarly, *jayantī* increases *vāta* and *kapha* while pacifying *pitta*;
*kākamācī* pacifies the three *doṣas*, is an aphrodisiac, and is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
Vāstuka is sweet, pleasing to the heart, and beneficial for disorders of wind, bile, and hemorrhoids;
likewise, cillī should be known as such for those suffering from disorders of wind and bile.
Ketakī increases wind, is aphrodisiac, and is considered to cause drowsiness and sleep.
Methikā pacifies Vāta and is considered to be Vājikaraṇa (aphrodisiac) and Vātalā (Vāta-aggravating).
Sarṣapa destroys the three Doṣas, stimulates the appetite, and increases the digestive fire.
Śatapuṣpā destroys the three Doṣas, is beneficial for the intellect, wholesome, and provides a relish for food.
Jarātrī is called Siṃhikā; it is recommended in cases of diarrhea.
Kusumbha improves the appetite, destroys Vāta, is strengthening, and provides relish. It slightly increases Vāta, is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and removes Kapha.
That which is slightly sour and alkaline is recommended for weak digestion (agnimāndya).
[The fruit] is emollient, dry, sweet, and astringent, and it greatly increases vāta.
Hot, astringent, and sweet, caṅgerī stimulates the digestive fire.

Kaphādanī, as well as phaṇjī, tilaparṇī, siṃhikā, and what others call cakramardana— these are difficult to digest and aggravate vāta. Piṇḍāluka, balā, bhiṇḍī, and another variety called ciñcukā are also balādanī.
These leafy vegetables (śāka) increase phlegm (śleṣman), aggravate wind (vāta), and pacify the digestive fire (agni).
All leafy vegetables impair vision due to their potency; however, this is not the case for *taṇḍulīyaka*, nor for *śatapuṣpā*, *jayantī*, and *kāsamardaka*.
Ālūṣaka, vetāgra, guḍūcī,
apāmārga, and tila seeds combined with kirātatikta are considered pacifiers of pitta.
Kūṣmāṇḍa, āliṅga, cirbhaṭa, paṭola, and likewise the flower of tuṇḍī [are also such].

The seeds are those of the karkoṭaka, kāravella, kośātakī, and velli; and likewise the fruits of the kūṣmāṇḍa are known to be of three kinds: young, middle, and superior. The young variety destroys wind (vāta) and is appetizing; the middle variety alleviates all three doṣas. 17–18.

It destroys swelling and the deranged *vāta* and *kapha*, and it eradicates *rakta-pitta*. (19) *Kaliṅga* increases *kapha*, produces *vāta*, and destroys *pitta*. (20) *Kāravella* destroys *vāta*, destroys *kapha*, and generates *pitta*.
It is said to be hot and appetizing, yet it causes blood disorders in men.
Both the flower and the *cirbhaṭa* fruit are known to aggravate all three *doṣas*;
when unripe, they increase *kapha*, while when ripe, they are slightly superior.
Tuṇḍīra stimulates the appetite and alleviates vāta and pitta;
karkoṭaka destroys the three doṣas, stimulates the appetite, and is likewise sweet.
The fruit of kośātakī is palatable, sweet, and subdues vāta and pitta.
In its post-digestive effect (vipāka), it destroys kapha; it is prescribed as highly recommended for fever. 24.

The wise declare that the leaf of paṭola subdues pitta, its stalk destroys kapha, and its fruit certainly brings about the pacification of all three doṣas; it is beneficial for those suffering from fever. 25.
The fruit of the *bṛhatī* is heavy, induces sleep, and provides pleasure; it is associated with wind (*vāta*) and causes disorders of cough.
It is excellent for long-term use, increases phlegm (*kapha*), and aggravates asthma, cough, and loss of appetite.
Likewise, the fruit of the *bṛhatī* alone is recommended as a digestive stimulant that destroys phlegm and wind.
They say this is recommended for itching, erysipelas, fever, jaundice, as well as for loss of appetite.
(27) I shall describe the bulbous vegetables; listen, my son, to each one separately:
suraṇa, piṇḍālū, piṇḍālu, palāṇḍu, and likewise gṛñjana. (28)
*Tāmbūlaparṇa*, *kanda*, and another called *hastikanda*, as well as *varāhakanda*— these others are known as bulbous vegetables (*kandaśāka*).
Surana is digestive, appetizing, subdues *kapha*, is clarifying, and light.
It is especially beneficial for all [the bodily constituents], and it destroys splenic enlargement and abdominal tumors (30).
The bulbous root of *āmlikā* is considered light and beneficial for the digestive tract and hemorrhoids (31).
The *piṇḍaka* fruit increases wind and phlegm, is constipating, aphrodisiac, and very heavy.
Piṇḍāluka increases phlegm, promotes the increase of semen, and is soft.
(32) Palāṇḍu destroys wind and phlegm, is spermatogenic, and cures colic and abdominal tumors.
Tāmbūlaparṇa-kanda is spermatogenic, clear, and light. (33)
The *hastikanda* is considered heavy, constipating, and a promoter of semen;
the *varāhakanda* destroys hemorrhoids and wards off wind-related abdominal tumors (vātagulma).
O sinless one, those others which have unknown tubers have not been described by me.
Among all bulbous roots and vegetables, sūraṇa is said to be the best (35).
It is a digestive stimulant and destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, worms, and splenic disorders;
however, it is not recommended for ringworm, bleeding disorders, or skin diseases (36).
These bulbous roots have been fully described, O best of physicians, for they are indeed glorious.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, named "The Group of Pot-herbs," in the first section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Seventeen.
Mango, rose-apple, jujube, pomegranate, and likewise emblic myrobalan;
dates, parūṣaka, citron, and that which comes from the piyāla tree;
ginger, vālimkā, grapes, and karamardaka.
The *kṣīrikā* and sweet fruits are proclaimed in the category of fruits. Unripe mango fruit is indeed praised for its constipating properties, yet it aggravates bile and blood;
likewise, when fully ripe, it is sweet and sour, laxative, and a destroyer of bile-related diseases.

The *jambu* fruit is astringent, destroys sweet phlegm (*kapha*), improves the appetite, and removes wind (*vāta*). The *kola* is sour and sweet, increases phlegm, is astringent, and is highly recommended.
The pomegranate (*dāḍima*) is excellent for curing diseases caused by wind and other humors; it is said to destroy ailments, and the *rājādana* is likewise declared to be sweet and delicious.

The fruits of *parūṣaka*, *karahā*, *pīluka*, *piyāla*, *siṃhī*, and *karamardaka* destroy urinary disorders (*meha*), pacify *pitta*, and cure all diseases of the joints and *vāta*. *Mātuluṅga* destroys *kapha* and *vāta*, kills worms, and cures abdominal diseases.
Mātuluṅga is declared to be an appetizer that pacifies disorders of blood and pitta,
removes colic, cures dyspnea, cough, and anorexia, alleviates thirst, reduces swelling of the throat,
and is light and palatable.
The bark is bitter, difficult to digest, and beneficial for those under the influence of Tiṣya; it removes worms, wind, and phlegm.
The fruit is sweet, cold, heavy, and unctuous; the Karaha variety conquers wind and bile.
The middle variety of Śleṣmātaka destroys vomiting, phlegm, and loss of appetite.
Keśara is digestive, light, and constipating; it destroys abdominal tumors (gulma) and hemorrhoids (arśas).
Baddhakeśara removes pitta and vāta, yet increases vāta and pitta; it is beneficial for the heart, improves the complexion, stimulates the appetite, and bestows blood, muscle, and strength.
Its juice is prescribed for colic, indigestion, incompatible foods, weak digestion, disorders of phlegm and wind, loss of appetite, asthma, and cough;
the juice is extremely sweet, heart-pleasing, and its potency subdues pitta and vāta.
The rind of the citron (*mātuluṅga*) increases phlegm and is difficult to digest; it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (*pāka*).
Because it captivates the mind, it is described as having a distinct and extreme pungency.
It causes heart disease, flatulence, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), asthma, and phlegm, yet it is a destroyer [of these] during the summer season.
Vīryakṛt is considered to cure hemorrhoids and heart disease; likewise, Puṣpa and Bīja are thought to destroy worms. Furthermore, Tiktam destroys abdominal tumors (gulma).
Nimbūka destroys swarms of worms, is sharp and hot, and removes abdominal pain.
The sages declare that this is beneficial for those suffering from pain caused by vāta, pitta, and kapha; it is a supreme purifier for those who have lost their appetite for grain;

it is beneficial for those afflicted by acute fever arising from the three doṣas, for those whose doṣas are localized, and for those with watery discharges; and it is also beneficial in cases of constipation, intestinal obstruction, and cholera. 15–16.
The sweet orange is endowed with excellent qualities; it is digestive, appetizing, and destroys hemorrhoids.

It removes the three *doṣas*, subdues colic and worms, and alleviates weak digestion, cough, and asthma. However, the sour variety, when unripe, produces blood-bile (*raktapitta*), causes diarrhea, and is burning to the system.

Ripe grapes are highly recommended for diseases of wind (vāta) and for the ailment of colic; likewise, when endowed with cooling properties, they are beneficial. Sweet, sour, and astringent, and combined with alkali, they quickly destroy pitta, wind, and phlegm. They are excellent for curing blood disorders, burning sensations, emaciation, fainting, fever, asthma, and cough. 18–19.
Grapes destroy the *kaṣāya* humors, are beneficial in their post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and are wholesome for *kapha*.
(20) Coconut is very sweet, heavy, unctuous, and cold;
it is pleasing to the heart, nourishing, a cleanser of the bladder, and a subduer of *rakta-pitta*. (21)
The wise know that the coconut fruit is constipating when ripe; when unripe, it is heavy with phlegm. It is nourishing, cooling, and aphrodisiac.
It is pleasing to the heart, delightful, increases phlegm, is soothing, satiating, and strengthening. (22)

The plantain fruit always destroys blood, bile, dyspnea, and burning sensations in men. (23) The unripe fruit is astringent, cooling, and astringent-tasting; it increases wind and phlegm, causes constipation, and is strengthening, heavy, and difficult to digest. The wild plantain fruit is exactly like that. (24)
The wood-apple (kapittha) is sour, sweet, astringent, clear, heavy, and it removes cough, diarrhea, heart disease, vomiting, and diseases caused by phlegm (25).
The wood-apple is also sweet, cooling, astringent, constipating, and light (26).
Unripe dates are considered to pacify the three doṣas;
however, only the ripe ones are beneficial, excellent, and supremely effective at pacifying the three doṣas.
Betel nut is astringent-sweet, laxative, and removes pitta and kapha. (27–28)
Betel leaf is pleasing to the heart, fragrant, and conquers phlegm and wind (29).
Khadira destroys phlegm and bile, is beneficial for the throat, and eradicates skin diseases (30).
Betel nut powder removes bile, is sharp, and betel [prepared with it] conquers phlegm and wind (31).
Through its combination, it becomes delicious and sweet, removing the distaste in the mouth, strengthening the teeth, and bringing peace to ailments such as dryness and chronic catarrh;
it is considered to produce clarity in disease, purification, and to bestow a beautiful voice and luster. 32.
It is beneficial for the throat, pleasing to the taste, and good for the chest when combined with *phala* and camphor.
(33) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Group of Fruits," in the first section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Eighteen.

Therefore, O son, I shall speak of honey; listen to its three types: *bhrāmara*, *sāragha*, and *kṣaudra*. I shall now describe their qualities and defects. It is cooling, astringent, sweet, light, digestive-stimulant, and is highly recommended as a demulcent.

It acts as a purifier and cleanser of ulcers, promotes healing, is most heart-pleasing, and provides strength; it destroys the three *doṣas*, brings about nourishment, and is beneficial in cases of cough, wasting, or injury-induced consumption,
as well as in vomiting, hiccup, vertigo, emaciation, chronic rhinitis, hematuria, and diarrhea caused by *sarala*.

It is recommended for dysentery with blood, for blood mixed with bile, and even for thirst, delusion, and diseases of the heart and flanks; it is also praised for eye diseases or disorders of the *grahaṇī*, and for poison. That which is collected by bees (*bhrāmara*) is thick, very heavy, and predominantly sweet.

Honey should be known especially as cooling, light, and a substance for licking (lehana). Honey from the *sāragha* bee is even lighter and drier than that, though not excessively cold; it is recommended for cough and wasting (kṣaya), and it destroys jaundice and hemorrhoids.
It is considered neither too cold nor dry, an appetizer, and strength-promoting;

it is beneficial in cases of diarrhea, eye disease, or wounds, whether traumatic or born of vitiated blood (kṣataja). Honey from bees (*bhrāmara*) is found on the trunk of a tree, while that from *sāragha* bees is found on the branches.
Honey is recommended for use in a cavity or even within a hollow.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Honey," in the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Nineteen.
Gauḍī, Mādhvī, Paiṣṭī, and Niryāsā are declared as another; thus, these four types of liquor (surā) should be known, along with their sub-varieties.
By further division, twelve types of liquor are proclaimed, including Sauvīraka and Āsava.
Sīdhu, gauḍī, and matsyaṇḍī—these three arise from molasses (guḍa).
Mādhvīka, madhuka, and mādhva—these liquors are prepared with honey (madhu). Paiṣṭī and those produced from ariṣṭa, as well as those arising from rice—these are the three [types of liquor].
That which is produced from the juice of grapes, or arising from the juice of *tāḍa* and *māḍa*, should be known as *niryāsa*; I shall now describe its qualities and defects.
*Sīdhu* is astringent, sour, or sweet; it is digestive, promotes digestion, and subdues impurities.

It destroys diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āmātisāra*), disorders of wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*), colic, diseases of phlegm (*kapha*), hemorrhoids, and ailments of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*).

Gauḍī liquor is astringent, sweet, sour, and cold; it stimulates digestion, removes colic and waste, is pleasing to the heart, pacifies the three *doṣas*, cures indigestion, anemia, hemorrhoids, and asthma.
This [mādhvīka] removes impurities, is digestive, treats *pāṇḍu* and urinary disorders (*prameha*), is light, sweet, and very cooling, improves the appetite, and destroys *pitta*.
When drunk in excessive sourness, it digests everything; it also destroys asthma, blood disorders, cough, and jaundice (*kāmalā*).
Likewise, *mādhvīka* that is cold, sour, and sweet, yet also astringent and warm, destroys diseases of *pitta*, hemorrhoids (*arśas*), asthma, as well as diarrhea and urinary disorders (*prameha*).

It destroys colic, abdominal tumors, and piles; it digests everything and stimulates the digestive fire and its suitability. Therefore, it also cures vāta and āma-vāta, as well as vomiting, and all diseases.
(8) Wine that is astringent, sweet, and sour is considered a stimulant of digestion;
it destroys cough, hemorrhoids, malabsorption syndrome, disorders of breast milk, and urinary diseases. (9)

The flour-based (paiṣṭī) [alcohol] is considered to be many-fold: it is digestive, appetizing, increases phlegm, destroys wind, increases bile, and causes diseases of the spleen (pāṇḍuroga). It generates wind and bile, is parching, astringent, clear, and heavy.
The *tāḍamaṇḍikā* increases phlegm, is laxative, constipating, relieves dysuria and headache, increases *vāta*, promotes virility, increases phlegm,
and destroys cough and nausea. (11-12)
Surā (fermented liquor) prepared with astringents and *pitta*-pacifying ingredients is beneficial when combined with medicinal formulations;
it removes many morbid humors (*doṣas*) and is especially useful in diseases of *śleṣman* (phlegm).
It is also beneficial for those afflicted by fever from over-exertion, consumption (*śoṣa*), edema, anemia (*pāṇḍu-āmaya*), and wasting (*kṣaya*). 13.
Vāruṇī wine is considered unsuitable for those suffering from wounds, exhaustion, epilepsy, consumption, or vertigo;
likewise, it is not beneficial for the weary, those who have ingested poison, those bitten by snakes, nor for those with ascites, hemoptysis, or asthma. (14–15)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Section on Intoxicants," in the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty:
Those with horns, those with hooves, those with claws, and others are now proclaimed.
Beasts of prey, other birds, various fish, and reptiles; creatures that move in water, those supported by water, those dwelling in villages and forests,
those of marshy lands, those of arid lands, as well as others that are common to both.
Those with variegated bodies like the *mṛgaruru*, as well as the *gaṇḍa*, wild oxen, buffaloes, boars,
and others who possess various colors, including those that dwell in villages; and whatever horned creatures there are, such as wild elephants and those found in villages and the like.

Pigs, porcupines, and the like, as well as lions and others, are known as the Amas; the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, cats and others that have claws as weapons, and those such as snakes and fish, are to be understood as the Sarīsṛpas. 4–5.

Fish such as the *matsya*, *maṅkuraka*, and others; tortoises such as the *durjara* and others; and birds such as the *haṃsa*, *sārasa*, *cakravāka*, *kapiñjala*, and *kumudaka*—these are to be known as marsh-dwellers (*ānūpa*), which increase *śleṣman* (phlegm) and aggravate *vāta* (wind).
The hare, the quail, the vātāṭa, the iguana, the deer, the kūṭaka, the chikkara and others, as well as the partridge and other kūrcakas,
the bhāradvājas, the hawks, the mice, and the excellent elephants.
These are the forest-dwelling creatures that exist without water:
wild boars, deer, antelopes, and the like; crocodiles and other such beings who resort to aquatic habitats; as well as gaṇḍakas, gavayas, and others. 9–10.
Buffaloes and others of that kind are considered to be common to all; so too are the osprey, the crane, the crocodile, the heron, the sparrow, the monkey, the bee, the crane,
the āḍi, the dātyūha, the swan, the water-bird, the karaṭika, the piṅkaṭa, the ṭiṭṭibha, and others.
The water-dwelling birds are the *khañjarīṭas* and the *bhāsakas*; these are the creatures born of water. Those that move on land are the land-dwellers:
elephants, horses, camels, buffaloes, cattle, and goats.
Donkeys, pigs, rams, dogs, cats, and mice—these are to be known as the domestic animals that dwell in villages;
as well as cocks, sparrows, pigeons, and doves. (14–15)
I shall now speak of the qualities and defects of birds that frequent villages.

Among horned animals, the deer is the best; it is strengthening, a promoter of the digestive fire (rocanadīpana), a destroyer of the three humors (tridoṣaghna), light in digestion, sweet, and beneficial for those suffering from fever.
The meat of the ena deer brings comfort to those suffering from wounds, consumption, hemorrhoids, anemia, loss of appetite, cough, and asthma.
The citrāṅga is considered to pacify vāta, to be nourishing, and to increase strength.
The meat of the śleshmala (the musk deer) is said to be difficult to digest, increases fat, and is heavy;
however, the chikkara is light, nourishing, sweet, and a destroyer of the [three] doshas.
It is equal to the meat of the hariṇa (antelope) and is highly recommended even in cases of fever.
The Rohita fish is nourishing, causes constipation, is difficult to digest, and is dense;
it terrifies those suffering from fever, irregular digestion, and diarrhea.
Likewise, the Gaṇḍa, Gavaya, buffalo, camel, and horse [are similar].
Fatty, heavy, and unctuous foods are prescribed for wind-induced lethargy (22).
Pork is said to subdue Vata, improve appetite, act as an aphrodisiac, be difficult to digest, and alleviate fatigue;
it pacifies Pitta, stimulates the sense of taste, and increases the bodily tissues (23).
The hare is considered the best of the Jāṅgala animals; it is light, aphrodisiac, digestive, appetizing, nourishing, strengthening, and a pacifier of the three doṣas.
It is indicated in cases of fever, anemia, consumption, cough, and anal diseases. (24)
It is beneficial for those suffering from pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), anemia (pāṇḍu), and diarrhea.

The Śallakī is nourishing, strengthening, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and improves the appetite; it alleviates Vāta and Kapha, is pleasing to the heart, sweet, and increases the bodily tissues (dhātus). 25–26.
The porcupine (śalyaka) is nourishing, strengthening, unctuous, aphrodisiac, and provides relish;
it increases wind slightly, promotes the growth of the bodily tissues (dhātus), and is sweet and dense.
It alleviates blood-bile (raktapitta), is aphrodisiac, unctuous, sweet, and cooling.
The iguana is said to cure asthma and cough, while the monitor lizard is beneficial for hemorrhoids.
The mouse is unctuous, strength-promoting, aphrodisiac, sweet, light, and it destroys piles, worms, and humoral disorders while removing wind.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Section on the Meat of Quadrupeds," in the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-one:
Among birds, the quail (*lāvaka*), born of the wild (*jāṅgala*) class, is the most excellent.
The astringent taste is said to be astringent, digestive-stimulant, sweet, and light;
likewise, it is sweet in its post-digestive effect (vipāka) and is highly esteemed in cases of the three humors combined (sannipāta).
Similarly, the partridge increases virility and enhances intellect, digestive fire, and strength.
The crane removes all defects and is strengthening; it is equal to the quail in its qualities.
The eggplant is clarifying and aphrodisiac, just like the common quail.
Among the various species of partridge, both black and white, the white one is the best.
The third type of partridge is also similar in its general characteristics;
it is cooling, provides great strength, is dense, acts somewhat as a rejuvenative (rasāyana), increases intelligence, and clears the bodily channels. The peacock, however, causes their dilation.
The first *mayūraka* is slightly *vāta*-alleviating, provides great strength, is dense, and acts as a mild rejuvenative (*rasāyana*).
The second type of *mayūraka* is very unctuous, increases *śleṣman*, is aphrodisiac, increases semen, promotes the growth of muscle tissue, and is strengthening. 6–7.
Likewise, the meat of the cock (kaukkuṭa) should be known as sweet and possessed of excellent qualities.
The meat of the pigeon (kāpota) is nourishing, strengthening, and a destroyer of wind and bile;
it is satiating, generates semen, is beneficial for men, and provides a relish for food.

Likewise, the pigeon (pārāvata) should be known to increase wind and phlegm, and it is heavy, strengthening, aphrodisiac, and appetizing; the same is considered true for the haritaka. So too are the potakī, the bhaṅgikā, the kṣudrā, and the kunaṭī.
These should be known as having equal qualities, being light and removing wind (vāta). The *kṛkara* should be known as light and a great increaser of the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*).
Likewise, the *kāṣṭhakūṭa* is light, removes wind, and increases the digestive fire.

The *vātā* (Cakora) is known to have a predominance of wind and phlegm (*vāta-śleṣmādhika*), it is cooling, increases semen, is clear (*viśada*), promotes strength, and is beneficial for digestion. The *śārī* (Śarī bird) is likewise equalized in its humors (*sama-doṣa*) with respect to both virtues and defects.
The curlew (krauñca) is aphrodisiac, highly appetizing, and constantly destroys urinary calculi;
it removes consumption and fainting, is aphrodisiac, and cures cough and loss of appetite.
The cuckoo (kokila) should be known as increasing phlegm and is considered a pacifier of bile.
The Vaivṛtākṣa bird destroys the three doṣas, is strengthening, and increases semen (18).
The domestic sparrow is aphrodisiac, increases strength and semen,
removes all doṣas, stimulates digestion, and promotes the growth of flesh (19).
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Section on the Meat of Land-Animals," in the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-Two:
The swan (*haṃsa*) increases phlegm, provides great strength and relish, is aphrodisiac, heavy, and cooling.

Similarly, the *sārasaka* (crane) is known to produce itching, numbness, and semen; it is aphrodisiac, highly palatable, and soft. It is said to alleviate *kapha* and *vāta*, and is aphrodisiac and heavy.
Likewise, the *kaṅka* and the *bhāsaka* are aphrodisiac, increase virility, and remove *kapha*.
The *āḍī* bird cures disorders of wind (*vāta*) and cough; it is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and digestive.
The *krauñca* and *cāsuri* birds destroy defects of the semen, as does the *karkaṭa*.
The *dātyūha* destroys wind, is aphrodisiac, strengthening, and increases the semen.

Likewise, the crocodile (makara) among fish is the best; it pacifies fatigue, bestows semen, and subdues wind (vāta). It is digestive, destroys wind, provides relish, produces semen, and cures the disorder of urinary stones (aśmarī).

Śṛṅgī is considered to destroy wind (vāta), stimulate the appetite, act as an aphrodisiac, and subdue phlegm (kapha); therefore, Rohitaka is beneficial, bestows strength, and is characterized by wind and phlegm. Sapharī, however, produces phlegm, while Nalamīna is characterized by phlegm.
The *śakulī* and the *viśālā* should be known as being composed of wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*);
the *bila* fish, excluding the *vimatsya*, should be known as producing wind, bile (*pitta*), and phlegm.
The tortoise is considered sweet, savory, and an increaser of semen (*śukra*).
The crab generates wind and phlegm, is nourishing, and indeed dry;
it is extremely strengthening, aphrodisiac, and destroys anemia and wasting.
It is beneficial for those with edema, diarrhea, and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), for the elderly, and for women.
The *makara* is digestive, pleasing to the heart, astringent, and removes disorders caused by heat; it pacifies urinary calculi and destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and dysentery.
As for the crane, crow, heron, white porpoise, boar, donkey, camel, horse, and so forth, as well as the bear, predatory beasts, and those beginning with the bull— [these are likewise described].
And other living beings of men;
frogs and the various classes of reptiles and the like; owls; and those which are the Kalingas, crows, cranes, mynas, and parrots—these are not recommended as food.
(9) House-sparrows, cakoras, those of the crow species, hawks, cuckoos, parrots, maghas, saris, bhringadatyūhas, and mangas [are likewise forbidden].
The water-fowl (*jalakaraṭa*), the dove (*kapota*), the female dove (*poṭakī*), the wagtail (*khañjarīṭa*), the *kukuramagha*, the *maliṅga*, the *yūkapiṅga*, and so forth—these are not to be eaten;
nor are those that are undesirable, nor any other egg-born creatures whose names are unknown, nor any other censurable beasts of prey; all such are excluded here from being eaten. (10–11)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Section on Meat," in the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-three:
*Maṇḍa*, *Parisrava*, *Bhakta*, and *Tarpaṇa* destroy wind (*vāta*).
It is considered to destroy urinary disorders and wind, to stimulate the appetite, and to increase urine. Fresh *maṇḍa* (scum) is astringent, sweet, or increases *kapha*;
it is nourishing, cures the disorder of wasting (*kṣaya*), and is excellent for increasing semen.
Yugandhara rice, when not processed with other ingredients, is thick, clear, and sweet;
it is said to pacify kapha and the three *doṣas*, and it is traditionally considered effective for cough and dyspnea.
A gruel (*yavāgū*) that is digestive-stimulant and sudorific promotes the digestion of the *doṣas*, impurities, and diseases.
This nourishing preparation is beneficial for the tissues, strength, and sense organs, and it is recommended for those suffering from fever.
One part [of the ingredients] should be taken, and one should add water equal to two parts;
[the powder contains] *citraka*, long pepper root, long pepper, *cavya*, and ginger.
Having ground equal parts of coriander, white rice, and black rice,
that well-purified, slightly loose gruel is called *yavāgū*.
A person consuming *yavāgū* should not practice aversion toward it.
Gruel prepared with vegetables, mung beans, and fruits is difficult to digest (7).
Furthermore, scum (maṇḍa) combined with the five spices (pañcakola), coriander,
and rāsnā pacifies the three doṣas and is the best for maturing fevers (8).
Milk-rice (pāyasa) is heavy, causes constipation, increases phlegm and wind,
pacifies bile, is strengthening, aphrodisiac, excellent, and a supreme elixir (rasāyana). It is traditionally known to be heavy, causing constipation, and producing wind and phlegm.
It pacifies pitta, is strengthening, aphrodisiac, and bestows fruitfulness.
When mixed with rice, or again with masha-rice, it possesses the qualities of grain; thus it is observed by the best of physicians. (10-11)
A preparation of sesame seeds is pleasing to the heart and increases the nourishment of the bodily tissues (dhātus);
however, it is heavy, causes constipation, produces impurities, is difficult to digest, and provokes phlegm (kapha).
Soup made with sesame is said to destroy the three doṣas when seasoned with clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
It is excellent for nourishing the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), is nourishing, and increases strength (13).
*Khalaka* produces wind and phlegm, is beneficial for the heart, and promotes strength (14).
Sour pomegranate (*dāḍimāmlaka*) removes phlegm and wind, is beneficial for the heart, and stimulates digestion (15).
Parpaṭa, when fried in oil, removes the humors and fevers;
it promotes appetite, bestows strength, and alleviates burning sensations, emaciation, and thirst. Saṇḍākī is heavy, unctuous, difficult to digest, and extremely cold.

The *śikhariṇī*—delightful with jaggery and curd—is beneficial for men; it increases bile and phlegm, is strengthening, provides nourishment to the bodily tissues (*dhātus*), is difficult to digest, sweet, and appetizing, being prepared with black gram (*māṣa*) and other ingredients. (17–18)
It increases the bodily elements (*dhātu*), acts as an aphrodisiac, and destroys *vāta* and *pitta*.
It is cooling, pacifies *pitta*, and removes dizziness, fainting, and thirst.
When combined with sugar it is excellent; when mixed with ghee and containing more water, it is superior. (19–20)
Barley flour mixed with clarified butter, saturated with cold water,
neither too liquid nor too thick, is called *mantha*.
*Mantha* immediately destroys fatigue, vomiting, thirst, and burning sensations, and bestows strength.
Fatty substances mixed with sour [flavors] and jaggery are a remedy for dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
Meat prepared with vesavāra is strengthening, excellent, delicious, and digestive;
it pacifies the three doṣas, is heavy, salty, oily, difficult to digest, and is known to stimulate the appetite.
Indeed, there is nothing else equal to meat for increasing the bulk of the body;
the flesh of a meat-eater is distinguished by its own meat, because it is nourished by meat. When cooked with charcoal, it is digestive and destroys phlegm.
Maṇḍaka that is strengthening, combined with fats, thick, and possessing the qualities of density is wholesome; moreover,
it is lighter and more beneficial in successive stages,
and likewise removes pain in the three vital regions (trika), pain in the flanks (pārśva), and disorders of digestion (pariṇāma).
It subdues thirst, wind, and vomiting, and likewise produces the *āmāśaya* (undigested matter).
That which is cooked in a heated pan (*taptakarpara*) is nourishing, sweet, and dense;
it increases phlegm, is strengthening, and brings about an increase in bile and blood.
Pūrikā, filled with ghee, is the supreme pacifier of the three doṣas;
it is aphrodisiac, nourishing, sweet, and prevents chest wounds and consumption. It should be known as heavy, hot, difficult to digest, and increases vāta and śleṣman. (28)
Pūpaka is demulcent, pleasing to the heart, aphrodisiac, and it facilitates the downward movement of wind (vāta).
Somaalikā is dense, sweet, appetizing, and increases strength;
it is considered difficult to digest, pacifies the humors (doṣas), and acts as an aphrodisiac. 29–30.
Phenikā is considered nourishing, a destroyer of vāta and pitta, wholesome, and very light; it is appetizing, strengthening, and provides strength to all the bodily tissues (dhātus).
Viṣṭambhī is sweet, pleasing to the heart, dense, and characterized by the nature of vāta and kapha.
It is bitter, destroys the three doṣas, and becomes difficult to digest again.
When undigested, it is considered difficult to digest, strengthening, and causes heaviness and thirst;
being sharp, it causes constipation and becomes difficult to digest again. (32–33)
Sweetmeats (*modaka*) of many colors, which are pungent, nourishing, strengthening, difficult to digest, and dehydrating, are not recommended for those with weak digestion;
this is due to the specific quality of their ingredients or their savory taste. (34)
Polikā is said to be strengthening, considered to increase the kapha humor, aphrodisiac, bestowing virility, known to be slightly aggravating to the humors, and increasing vitality.
It is prepared from split grains using a shallow pan.
One may discern all the defects by means of one's preference for a particular type of food;
O Mahāmati, other foods and drinks have not been mentioned here, as people fear excessive prolixity in the text and are unable to describe them all. (36–37)

If a man consumes food or drink while fatigued, fever will arise for him, or vomiting may occur at that very moment. Likewise, if one immediately engages in physical exercise or sexual intercourse after eating, [the same result follows]. (38)
Whichever limb one uses [for such acts], misfortune will certainly befall that very limb.
(39) One should not eat food that is excessively cold; it is beneficial to eat food that is not too hot. Cold food aggravates wind and phlegm, while hot food promotes digestion. (40)
One should not eat when fatigued, nor when distressed by physical exertion;
one should not eat on an uneven seat, for that produces various diseases. At the beginning of the meal, one should eat fruits, with the exception of the karkaṭī.
One should not eat curd at night, nor should one rinse the mouth while eating. (42) By sitting while eating, one gains stoutness; by lying on one's back, strength;
by resting on the left hip, longevity; and for one who runs, death pursues. (43)
At the beginning of a meal, water should be drunk; one should take a drink during the meal. One should eat with half the stomach empty, and a third part should be for condiments.
A fourth part should be for drinking water; thus a full meal is properly produced. 44–45.
After eating, one should walk slowly for a hundred steps;
thereafter, lying on one's back, one should sleep for a moment on the left side. Having sipped water after the meal, one should wipe [the mouth] with the right hand.
Furthermore, the wise person should rub the abdomen with the right hand;
one should expel the upward-moving wind (udgāra), but not suppress it. One should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, running, and drinking [alcohol].
One who has eaten at the moment of the *kṣaṇa* should avoid battle, singing, and recitation (49).
One should not engage in reading, walking, or riding a vehicle immediately after drinking; nor should one engage in dispute (50).
One should not sleep during the day, nor should one rest immediately after eating.
From sleeping at improper times, phlegm, catarrh, chronic rhinitis, consumption, swelling, and headache arise, as well as a loss of digestive fire. 51–52.

In those who have drunk alcohol, those who are exhausted, and those afflicted by hiccup or asthma; in those distressed by fear, grief, or hunger; through recitation [of this], as well as through sexual intercourse (53);
likewise in the elderly, children, those overcome by heavy burdens, and the sick.
In cases of diarrhea, swelling, thirst, and even in pānātyaya (intoxication from excessive drinking),

as well as during the summer, in childhood, and for those exhausted by the night, sleeping during the day is beneficial. Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Section on Food and Drink," spoken by Ātreya in the *Hārītottara*.
The first section is completed.
Chapter One.
Ātreya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the second section, which is supreme:
auspicious and inauspicious dreams, health, and fatal signs among humans.
Listen, my son, in brief, O child, as it is revealed. 1–2.
Hārīta said:
"O one of great wisdom, I have understood the excellence of food and drink;
now I wish to understand the knowledge of diseases regarding diseases. (3)
"O high-minded one, tell me of those diseases that are born of karma.
Ātreya said: "Indeed, all diseases of embodied beings are born of karma."
All these [afflictions] take the form of hells; they may be curable or incurable. (5) Whatever sin has been committed unknowingly, one should later perform a *kṛcchra* penance;
even by the power of such expiation (*prāyaścitta*), a disease that was incurable may become curable. (6)
If one acts with a known form [of transgression], one should later perform a *kṛcchra* penance;
for at the end, a disease becomes difficult to cure even through such expiation.
(7) A killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a cow, a slayer of a king, one who destroys groves or water-reservoirs, and one who commits adultery with another's wife—[these are the great sinners].
One who approaches the wife of a master, a female ascetic, a teacher’s wife, or one born of a noble family— these thirteen types of men are "tender" (prabāla) yet are like clubs (gada).
Leucoderma, leprosy, consumption, diarrhea, urinary disorders, dysuria, urinary stones, strangury, colic, asthma, cough, swelling, and ulcers— these defects manifest in men as the forms of sin.
Fever, indigestion, vomiting, vertigo, delusion, and weak digestion;
as well as liver disease, splenic enlargement, hemorrhoids, and consumption—these are indeed the complications (upadūṣakas).
Furthermore, there are ulcer pain, headache, and upward-moving internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta).
"O one of great wisdom, these diseases indeed arise from curses;
other diseases as well are born in many ways from the [three] humors (doṣa).
Therefore, O high-minded one, I shall speak of them in brief; listen to me."
One who kills a Brahmin is born pale; one who kills a cow becomes afflicted with leprosy;

one who kills a king suffers from pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman); and one who causes injury to another through diarrhea suffers from dysentery. Indeed, by approaching the wife of one's master, urinary disorders arise.
Through sexual union with the wife of one's guru, urinary disease and the ailment of stones (aśmarī) arise; through union with a woman born of one's own family, fistula-in-ano (bhagandara) occurs;
from causing pain to others, one becomes afflicted with colic; and from backbiting, one suffers from asthma and cough.
Those who create obstacles on the path become afflicted with diseases of the feet;
through a curse, sores arise, or even liver disease may occur.
Furthermore, he who causes a rain of excrement upon a temple or in water [suffers these consequences].
For such a person, diseases of the stomach arise that are sinful in nature and extremely terrible (17).
Furthermore, great fevers arise for those who cause pain to others and to the twice-born; indigestion also arises from creating obstacles for the food of others (18).

One who gives poison shall suffer from vomiting; likewise, one who causes the loss of eight feet [or limbs] shall suffer from epilepsy. One who gives bad food shall have indigestion (agnimāndya), and from the sin of destroying an embryo, one shall suffer from diseases of the liver and spleen.

From causing distress or injury to others, one suffers from wounds, colic, and headaches; one who is addicted to drinking what should not be drunk becomes afflicted with *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic fever),
and he who sets forest fires is born with *visarpa* (erysipelas).
The cutting down of many trees results in many wounds; from the theft of another's property, the disease of *grahaṇī* arises.
From the stealing of gold, the birth of one with deformed nails occurs.
From stealing silver one suffers from variegated leprosy; from stealing copper, one gets cracked feet (vipādika).

The thief of tin becomes afflicted with skin spots (sidhma) and mouth diseases; the stealer of lead becomes a barbarian (varvara). The thief of iron becomes [deformed], and the thief of alkali suffers from excessive urination.
A stealer of ghee suffers from intestinal disease; a stealer of oil suffers from severe itching.
Through these transgressions, one becomes one-eyed, crooked in speech, and squint-eyed (25).
One who steals sesame becomes afflicted with defects, has black teeth, foul speech, and is marred by leprosy.
One who tastes [forbidden] flavors suffers from diseases of the tongue, and one who destroys a lineage suffers from sores caused by spiders.
These indeed are great defects; therefore, I shall describe the expiation by which these diseases, which take the form of sin, are cured through the Kṛcchra penance.
Having performed the gift of a cow, the gift of land, the gift of gold, and the worship of the gods,
one should thereafter perform an expiation for the pacification of the sins of Pāṇḍu;
in the case of great sins, one's entire property should be given, or half of that in the case of minor offenses.
The strength or weakness of the disease should be determined from the sixth part of the [number] sixty;
for the pacification of the disease of leprosy (kuṣṭha), one should perform rites according to the sixty-ninth [part],
as well as the gift of cows and gold, and the feeding of others with sweet food.

Having given these four kinds of gifts, one should perform a remedial rite; perhaps then, success may be achieved regarding longevity and the restoration of strength. In cases of urinary disorders, one should give gold, and likewise for colic, asthma, and fistula-in-ano.
By the gift of a horse or an ox, one is liberated from asthma and cough (32).
In the case of fever, one should perform worship of Īśvara and practice the recitation of the Rudra-mantra;
for one afflicted by vertigo, there should be the gift of food and the gift of weapons (33).

An *agnihoma* sacrifice is performed for sluggish digestion (*agnimāndya*), and the gift of a maiden (*kanyādāna*) is given for the destruction of *gulma*, urinary disorders (*meha*), and stones (*aśmarī*); salt is also administered [for these].
(34) By the giving of abundant food, one is liberated from the disease of colic (*śūla*).

In cases of high fever (mahājvara), one should perform a propitiatory rite (śāntika) and bathe [the patient] with a thousand auspicious medicinal balls (gaṇḍuka); through this, success will be achieved and one is liberated from the disease of fever. By the offering of ghee and honey, the disorder of blood and bile (raktapitta) is pacified.
By watering a *vanaspati* tree one is liberated from erysipelas (*visarpa*),
and by watering a shrub (*viṭapa*), one who suffers from many ulcers no longer goes there; furthermore, the disease of *grahaṇī* can be cured by the fourfold gift.

By the gift of gold, one with deformed nails or discolored teeth shall become happy. (38) By the gift of silver, even incurable leprosy (*citrakuṣṭha*) is declared to be cured. For one afflicted with *sidhma* (leucoderma), the gift of tin is prescribed, and for one with *barbara* (a type of skin disease), the gift of iron. (39)
One should give the gift of an elephant for a mouth ulcer, the gift of a cow for a disease called *bahupunnaka*,
ghee for eye disease, and fragrant substances for a disease of the nose; one should give oil for itching and the gift of meat for a disease of the tongue.
By offering a dark-colored goat, the honoring of the gods is performed;
likewise, in cases of lip disease and spider-bite, one should give cows. Furthermore, I shall describe other [remedies] for diseases affecting the bodies of human beings.
One who is ashamed of censuring others becomes one-eyed from the sun;
one who cuts hooves has a crooked nose; by striking with the wings, one loses their wings; by praising oneself, one becomes a dwarf; and by hating others, one becomes excessively tawny.
One becomes a performer of deeds for another and is born with a distorted nature;
these and other great diseases arise from the occurrence of evil.
Or else, if one does not succeed here, there will be no higher state.
Therefore, the best of physicians should indeed cause an expiation (prāyaścitta) to be performed;
for as long as one suffers from disease due to sin in another birth, that sin persists, but once the expiation has been performed, it does not arise again in existence. 45–46.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Counteraction of the Faults of Sin," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Two.
Ātreya said:
Listen, my son, in brief: just as it is revealed, O child, so shall the thorough knowledge of fatal signs (ariṣṭa) and its remedy be fully declared.
[These arise] from wind (vāta), from bile (pitta), from fear, and also from diminished strength.
One should avoid [consulting] when there is urine, feces, or bile present, as well as during the six forbidden times; for a dream seen at night bears fruit within a year,
while one seen in the first watch of the night yields auspicious results immediately.

It may take half a year or even more than a watch; furthermore, it becomes fruit-bearing in the second month, and in the third month they say it yields some result at the end of the night for a human being over a period of ten days.
The wise declare that [omens] occurring on the first day of the month portend peace; those occurring at midday are prescribed as lasting for six months.
Among dreams, the wise consider white objects to be auspicious; yet, having excluded all these, [dreams of] cotton, ashes, bones, skulls, and spears bring misfortune or disease to men.

All black objects seen in dreams are censured, for they bring about misfortune or disease for men; however, these are exceptions: a cow, a horse, a king, a brahmin, an elephant, a fish, a mirror, a flower, a horn, an ornament, a parasol, or a banner.
Curd, fruit, or cloth; food, betel, and clothing;
a lotus, a water-pot, and a conch; and ornaments of gold—all these bring about complete welfare for those who are ill.
One crosses the mandala of the moon, the lord of the night, which is like a cluster of blooming lotuses; or one crosses a full lotus pond, or the far shore of a great river within the mass of waters.
The attainment of abundant happiness and prosperity, and liberation from diseases;
or if a god, a brahmin, ancestors, or a king speak words in dreams exactly as they are,
then for that person there shall be nothing else— whether it be happiness, calamities, or illnesses.
A man who is ill, or afflicted by disease, who sees in his dreams cows, horses, elephants, kings, and flowers praised by the wise, will find happiness and the destruction of his ailments.
Even one who is bound will, at that very moment, be released from bondage if he sees an ornament, a temple, a maiden, curd, a young fish,
or a tree laden with flowers, creepers, and fruit; or if he sees these while healthy, it leads to the acquisition of wealth and the destruction of disease.
In a dream, drinking milk is highly auspicious; likewise, drinking liquor, eating goat meat, or consuming ghee, gruel, *kṛsara*, boiled rice, or milk-rice (*kṣaireyika*) leads to happiness.
If a white snake bites the hand-tip or any part of the body of a sleeping man, it is favorable.
One may announce the birth of a son or the acquisition of wealth, or it may bring about the destruction of wealth or the onset of disease before long.

(13) That man who embraces a beautiful woman dressed in white garments in a dream will experience supreme happiness and prosperity, obtain an excellent son, and suffer the destruction of his ailments. (14)

The acquisition of a heap of grain—sesame, rice, wheat, white mustard, barley, and so forth—is a cause for the destruction of disease; in dreams, it brings swift happiness to a person. When the [planets] are fruitful and radiant, there is an abundance of wealth and the destruction of illness.
When [the tree] is in bloom, happiness is to be known; when it is fully laden with fruit, one's desired object is attained.

(16) Or if one sees one's own body being devoured by crows, herons, young camels, snakes, boars, owls, vultures, jackals, wolves, donkeys, buffaloes, hyenas, dogs, tigers, crocodiles, sea-monsters, or monkeys;
The wise declare that for such a person, the onset of disease occurs swiftly; therefore, one should skillfully perform the prescribed remedy.
[One should avoid] a woman wearing red or black garments, with disheveled hair, who is spreading about.
If one sees her standing in the south, weeping or singing;
or if one sees her calling out in anger, embracing, or chewing [something], he who sees this shall become happy, but if he is diseased, he meets with death.
He in whose dream the extraction of teeth or their falling out is seen, or whose hair and body hair wither away, shall become happy and overcome misfortune.
(22) He whose bed breaks apart due to the impact of a spear or similar weapon [shall likewise attain prosperity].
If blood is seen on the body, one who was previously healthy will fall ill.
(23) The man who sees an empty house, or sees a palace devoid of its deity, and perceives the heat of trees in bloom during the month of Caitra, shall quickly meet with an undesirable death. (24)

A man might see a god shattered, or a jar broken, or a tree with its branches snapped, or a temple fallen into ruin; yet he might perceive these and remain happy, while encountering a mass of disease, he would soon die, seized by agony.
(25) If the ancestors call out to a man from the southern direction, taking hold of him, they swiftly bring about his death.
He who sees one with a trident, a staff, or a raised noose in hand calling out to him quickly meets death and spreads great suffering.

(26) If one should see cotton, ashes, bones, a skull, a trident, a discus, or a noose in a dream, it portends calamity or the loss of wealth; or if the person is ill, it spreads extreme suffering or even death. (27)

Thus have those auspicious rites been prescribed; O high-minded one, having understood them quickly—especially since they must be performed while mankind sleeps during the nights—perform the mantra for the destruction of Gada.
Perform likewise the ritual bathing, charity, worship of the gods, and fire-oblations according to the rules for securing good fortune.
"Among these [dreams], a bad dream goes to destruction, and it quickly spreads auspiciousness and happiness.
(29) Thus ends the second chapter, named the Chapter on Dreams, in the second section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Three.
Ātreya said: Listen, O son of great wisdom, to the essence of the science of medicine, which accomplishes all the purposes of the body regarding both health and fatal signs in human beings.
If a wise man does not clearly see the fixed golden line,
his death will surely occur within six months. Furthermore,
if a person does not see the second white line of snow, he shall suffer the loss of his teeth.
Upon reaching three months,
the life-force of one who does not hear the ringing in the ears, and from whom dead lice fall away despite their abundance, shall swiftly depart for the world of Yama.
One who hears sounds in a contrary manner abandons the life-force upon reaching two months.
He whose body is healthy yet breathes through the mouth, whose eyes are bloodshot and his face is sallow,
whose tongue is withered and teeth are black— even if he is currently well, he will soon go to the realm of Yama.
He who experiences a headache at dawn and perceives a halo around the lamp [is likewise fated].
