He who perceives a film or dust upon [the sun] will indeed meet death; his life is not long.
He who, looking at the solar disc, sees the moon within it without a halo, or perceives the orb of the sun shrouded in smoke, shall go quickly to death.
He who sees a rainbow in a clear, cloudless sky across the cardinal and intermediate directions,

or likewise sees one before his very eyes, will soon depart for the realm of Yama. He who, even when his eyes are closed, perceives a flickering light before him or a hole in his ear— [shall likewise go to the world of death].
Then, when sound has ceased, a person cannot hear it in any way;
nor does he perceive even the mere tasting of bitter and other flavors by the tongue; furthermore, the human beholds his own return to the terrible realm of Vaivasvata.

That man whose body is excessively hot or conversely cold, whose breath is turbid or not cold, and who does not experience horripilation when sprinkled with cold water; he who does not become a king by the stroke of a staff—such a person does not attain a beautiful state of health in this world, for he is destined for the realm of the God of the Ancestors (Yama) to behold the worlds. Know that he who does not see his own reflection in oil, water, a mirror, or ghee, as if it were another’s eye, is one who has departed to the other world and is indeed bereft of life.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Signs of Health and Fatal Omens," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Four.
Ātreya said:
O child, listen with one-pointed mind to those diseases which, though nourished by complications, are warded off by means such as *rasāyana*:
wind-disease (*vātavyādhi*), urinary disorder (*prameha*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*).
Stone (aśmarī), retained fetus (mūḍhagarbha), and likewise abdominal enlargement (udara) as the eighth—
these eight great diseases are by their very nature difficult to treat,
especially when accompanied by wasting of strength and flesh, dyspnea, thirst, emaciation, vomiting, and fever.
Furthermore, those afflicted by these complications— fainting, diarrhea, and hiccups—
should be especially avoided by a physician desiring success.
This applies to one whose tongue becomes excessively parched, or turns yellow, or takes on a bluish appearance.
The breath becomes exceedingly hot and the body is marked with horripilation;
when the eyes are blue-black or reddish-yellow and the throat makes a rattling sound,
one afflicted by fever does not live if his symptoms are such as these.

He whose breath issues from the mouth, whose row of teeth has become dark, whose eyes are fixed, and who is forcibly afflicted by fever, does not live at all. One who passes urine frequently, breathes heavily, is emaciated, and is tormented by loss of appetite [does not survive].
And he whose senses have lost their luster perishes quickly;
he in whose mouth blood is found, in whom headache is seen,
and who has internal burning with external coldness— such a fever leads to death.
The man who faints, loses consciousness, or lies prostrate,

who is afflicted by cold externally while burning with heat within, dies of fever. He whose hair stands on end, whose eyes are bloodshot, and who suffers from a piercing pain in the chest [is likewise fated].
When the breath is constantly forced through the mouth, that fever kills the man.
Fever destroys the man who is afflicted by hiccup, dyspnea, and thirst, who is delirious with wandering eyes, breathing incessantly, and emaciated.

Fever destroys a man whose eyes are turbid, who is fainting, who is excessively overcome by drowsiness, and whose blood and flesh are greatly wasted; likewise, it destroys one with thick expectoration, clouded vision, and suffering from anorexia. 14. [Also one with] copious salivation and eyes afflicted by watering and loss of appetite.

Internal burning and a black tongue—such a fever destroys quickly. Moreover, if a fever afflicted by a single complication does not subside, and other terrible complications appear, it is mostly characterized by many forms. 15–16.

Because of that, the cruel one falls under the power of death and does not attain success. Furthermore, he in whom diarrhea is first observed, as well as other symptoms such as labored breathing and emaciation, shall also quickly go to his death.

Diarrhea will especially destroy an old man who is afflicted by dyspnea, colic, thirst, emaciation, and fever. He for whom there is diarrhea and swelling, accompanied by anorexia and colic, [shall perish].
Even he meets death quickly despite many remedial treatments.
(20) In a child, an elderly person, or a man who is physically impaired, swelling arises in all the limbs; such a person suffering from swelling will certainly die. (21)
He who exhibits flatulence, colic, dyspnea, thirst, fainting,
and headache shall meet his death. Furthermore, that man whose teeth and nails are pale, and whose eyes are pale, [shall likewise perish].
One who has a pale complexion and suffers from jaundice perishes;
likewise, one whose skin, eyes, and urine become pale, and who has a pale complexion, perishes as a victim of jaundice. 23–24.
Consumption (yakṣmā) kills the man in this world who has white eyes, who loathes food, who is oppressed by upward-breathing, and who voids much urine with difficulty; likewise,
he whose bodily constituents are depleted and who is afflicted by swelling and asthma.
One who eats excessively, is full of loathing, and suffers from consumption (rājayakṣmā) perishes.
(26) He for whom the *huṃkāra* sound is cold and the *phūtkāra* breath is hot, whose pulse is rapid and unstable, quickly goes to the abode of Yama. (27)

Trembling of the limbs, a breaking of the gait, or the face having the luster of saffron, and if wind arises during defecation, he goes to the abode of Yama. One who has long suffered from a chronic disease becomes incapable even of eating.
One should disregard even a physician who has broken limbs and lacks secret knowledge; having recognized such a man, the wise provide treatment [only] in this manner.
(29) Due to the destruction of the rectum, dyspnea, swelling, and likewise from the affliction of fever—
His chest becomes deep and dense, and it consumes the man.
For one suffering from gulma who is destined for death, there occurs dyspnea, piercing pain, thirst, distress, aversion, hardness of the bowels, stupor, and weakness. (30–31)
He whose eyes and lips are red, or who vomits blood,
who has bloody urine and bloody excrement, and who suffers from *rakta-pitta*, perishes. Furthermore, he who repeatedly vomits blood and has reddened eyes [is likewise lost].

One who sees the directions as red and suffers from blood-bile perishes. (33) He whose face becomes swollen, who is afflicted by vertigo and loss of appetite, and who suffers from constipation and abdominal pain, perishes at sunrise. (34)

A person afflicted by abdominal distension, constipation, and lack of movement, accompanied by vomiting, hiccups, and pain, and overcome by labored breathing, will be destroyed by internal abscess (vidradhi).
This is also true for one who experiences severe thirst, burning sensations, or vomiting.
A man who is overcome by delusion does not live.
(36) O highly wise one, if a woman afflicted by fever should experience menstruation before the day is complete, she will not live, for such is her *sāraṇa*. (37)
The man who suffers from swelling accompanied by dyspnea, thirst, and colic,
and who is afflicted by jaundice and anemia, perishes.
Worms [are found] in his flatus, urine, feces, and even his semen.
One should avoid treating a patient from whose anus there is a discharge;

likewise, one afflicted with urinary obstruction, accompanied by pain, and having a flower-like umbilicus and testicles, is quickly destroyed by gravel and stone (aśmarī) associated with sand-like particles (sikatā). 39–40.

When the fetus has entered the womb and become obstructed at the birth canal, it kills the woman during a "confused delivery" (mūḍhagarbha), along with the complications already mentioned. [The woman] is afflicted by pain in the sides, aversion to food, swelling, and diarrhea. 41.1–2.

Apasmāra (epilepsy) destroys one who frequently loses consciousness, whose strength is wasted, whose eyebrows are knitted, who exhibits convulsions with the eyes, and who suffers from sharp pain, numbness of the skin, broken limbs, and oppression by flatulence. 42-43.
Vāta-vyādhi destroys a man who is afflicted with pain;
likewise, prameha kills a person who is beset by the aforementioned complications, excessively discharging urine, and severely tormented by carbuncles (piḍakā). 44–45.
One whose body is cracked and oozing, whose eyes are red, whose voice is impaired,
and who has transcended the five therapeutic measures— such a leper afflicted with *kuṣṭha* perishes here.
Furthermore, one who lies with face downward or upward, and whose flesh and strength are excessively diminished, [is likewise lost].
But one who remains vigilant, without doubt, is not destroyed by insanity.
47. Thus ends the fourth chapter, named "Signs of Death from Disease," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Five.
Ātreya said:

He who is virtuous yet succumbs to anger, and he who possesses anger yet maintains the quality of virtue—both of these, O knower of the rules, bring death upon themselves; the stout man perishes more quickly than the lean-bodied one.
If a sinner here who is of a wicked nature should become virtuous and devoted to dharma,
he quickly becomes one who partakes of death in this world; as does he who undergoes a transformation of his natural state—
whether it be one who is fair-complexioned and turns black, or one who is black and attains extreme fairness.
Likewise, a man dies according to his nature; through a transformation, he meets with separation. He who perceives sound perversely upon hearing it, or does not hear it at all, quickly beholds death.
He who does not see his own shadow cast upon the ground, indeed sees death approaching.
He who is afflicted by the senses falls into emaciation;
he who is stout yet possesses a body devoid of luster should foresee death; and he who perceives neither the foul odor nor the taste of anything anywhere [should likewise foresee it].
That man indeed experiences the most beloved death,
whose mouth-odor the blue flies frequent;
whether it be from his nose or his body, he alone goes to the realm of Yama.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Disorders of the Five Senses," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Six.
Ātreya said:

Now, I shall describe the curable, incurable, and manageable diseases that arise through the conjunction with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); listen, O son! Maghā joined with the Sun, Viśākhā joined with the Moon, and Ārdrā joined with Mars— [The rest of the verse follows: ...these are the combinations that bring about disease. Listen further, O son, as I explain which are curable, which incurable, and which merely manageable. Maghā conjoined with the Sun, Viśākhā conjoined with the Moon, and Ārdrā conjoined with Mars [are such].
The wise declare these to be the Yamaghaṇṭa yogas: Mūla with a woken Jupiter, Kṛttikā with Venus, Rohiṇī with Saturn, and Hasta with Mercury;
if a man afflicted by disease encounters such a meritorious conjunction.
How could he live when [the sun] is scorched by the terrible mechanism of Ghanadatta? How could there be happiness?
When the Sun is in Anurādhā, the Moon is conjoined with Uttarā, Mars is joined with Pitṛīśa (Mūla), and Mercury is joined with Turagī (Aśvinī)—this is not happiness.

Therefore, the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) joined with Jīva (Mercury) in Mṛgaśiras, or joined with Āśleṣā, or joined with the asterism named Hasta—though one learned in the scriptures might declare these yogas auspicious—they do not speak of them as such. (4) The Sun joined with the rays of the Moon (the Moon), or Mars joined with Mercury in Aśvinī, or Mercury in Anurādhā, Jupiter in Puṣya, Revatī on Friday, or Rohiṇī joined with the son of the Sun (Saturn)—these are the causes of happiness. (5)
If it occurs during the Śūla, Vajra, Atigaṇḍa, Vyāghāta, or Vyatīpāta yogas, or when the moon is in conjunction with the Viṣkambha yoga, or under a nak�ṣatra presided over by a malefic deity—
by these conditions, fever-patients become incurable; therefore, one should examine these yogas.
If a cruel [planetary] influence has arisen during the yoga, the asterism, or the day, one does not live.
Siddhi, Śukla, Śubha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhaga, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, and Harṣa— these are remembered as the [yogas] easily accomplished with auspicious results.

Maghā, Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, as well as Ārdrā, Mūla, Kṛttikā, Hasta, and Tiṣya—these are not auspicious, so the sages declare; they must be considered according to the sequence of the days of the week. Even one afflicted by fever [should avoid] Maghā, Bharaṇī, Hasta, or Mūla.
Even he meets his death; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Jyeṣṭhā, and Punarvasu—these are to be known as the Sādhya constellations, especially for those suffering from fever.

The three *pūrva*s, Svāti, Citrā, as well as the three [nakṣatras] Ārdrā, Śravaṇa, and Dhaniṣṭhā, Mūla, Viśākhā along with Kṛttikā, Sārpa (Āśleṣā), Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā—these, together with their respective *kāṣṭhās*, bring about the pacification of a man’s suffering from disease. 12. Tiṣya (Puṣya) makes it easily curable.
Therefore, having understood this correctly, the wise should strive for the destruction of disease through medical treatment.
In Aśvinī, death is seen after one night;
in Bharaṇī, after nine nights; and in Kṛttikā, after three days; while in Rohiṇī, it occurs after three days.
If the deer is caught under Ārdrā, there will be great suffering;
under Punarvasu and Puṣya, it is afflicted for seven nights;
likewise, under Āśleṣā and Maghā, it goes to the abode of Yama after nine nights. (15)
The *pūrvā* [nakṣatras] are to be known for three months each, and the *uttarā* for three sets of five [months].
Wise men should know that the three divisions (*aṃśas*) of the three *pūrvās* are auspicious;
however, if illness occurs at the end of the fourth [division] of these, then death follows. 16–17.
Happiness is obtained by hand during Citrā for fifteen days;
Svātī lasts for sixteen nights, Viśākhā for twenty nights, Anurādhā for one fortnight, and Jyeṣṭhā for ten days. (18)
If [the moon] is in Mūla, one meets death; in Āṣāḍhā, fifteen days;
in Uttarā, twenty nights; in Śravaṇa, two months;
in Dhaniṣṭhā, two months; and in Śatabhiṣaj, twenty days.
The *Pūrvā* [Phalgunī] constellation lasts for nine nights; the three sets of five [days] belong to the *Uttarā* [Phalgunī];
and *Revatī* lasts for ten days. After that, one is freed from the affliction of disease. Under *Kṛttikā*, there is a severe fever and a bilious (paittika) illness occurs.
One should prescribe ten days for the first quarter;
ten days for the second part, and five days for the third.
For Rohiṇī, nine nights are proclaimed for the first portion.
In the second [portion] it is said to be double, and in the third, ten nights;
indeed, suffering certainly arises when the moon is in a lunar mansion presided over by the Moon deity (Mṛgaśiras).
In the first portion, it lasts five nights; in the middle, twelve days.

Likewise, it should be known that death occurs after one month in the third portion. If [the moon] is in a lunar mansion presided over by Rudra, death will occur in the first portion for a fortnight, in the second for twelve days, and in the third portion he does not live.
In the first quarter of Punarvasu, one should know that fever lasts for three fortnights;
in the middle [quarter], for seven days; and in the third, for twenty-five days.
In the first quarter of Puṣya, it lasts for seven days; in the second, for twenty days.
Likewise, one should know that in the third quarter there are twenty-one days; and for the person whose fever arises under the constellation Āśleṣā,
that man lives through three months with difficulty in its first quarter.
In the second and third [periods], there is certainly death, without a doubt;
for one in whom disease arises under a lunar mansion presided over by the ancestors (Pitṛ-daivata),
[the duration] is seven nights in the first division and equal to the number of the asterism in the second.
One is afflicted for twenty-three days by the power of karma (31).
For one whose fever arises under the lunar mansion presided over by Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī),
[the duration is] five nights in the first part and twelve days in the middle (32).
Likewise, in the third portion, death should be known to occur after one month (33).
In the first part of Uttarā, [death occurs] after fourteen days;
in the second, after seven nights; and in the third, after nine days (34).
If there is a disease in the hand, one should know that death will occur after seven nights in the first [case],
four days in the second, and five days in the third;
likewise for one whose fever belongs to Tvāṣṭra in the east.
In the second portion, for three months, there will be a severe illness (36).
Likewise, in the third portion, it should be known that there is a wind-related affliction for thirteen [months].
In the northwest, [the duration is] seventeen [months] in the first [portion], and twenty-one [months] in the second (37).
One should indeed predict death in the third quarter of this very [nakṣatra].
In the first quarter of Viśākhā, sixteen [nāḍīs] are recorded as being tripled;
in the second, twelve are declared, and likewise in the third.

O Great Sage, one should indicate seven days in the first third of Maitra, a fortnight in the second, and sixty-four days in the third; in the first two-thirds of the first Āindra, it is a fortnight, and sixteen days in the third. 40–41.
In the first third of the base portion, it should be known by the wise that there is indeed a fortnight;
in the first [third], three months [are added], and in the middle, sixteen days. In the second third of the base portion, it should be known by the wise that there is indeed a fortnight.
Furthermore, O great sage, death occurs again in the third part after twelve nights;
in the first fortnight of the Viśva-part, it is said that twelve nights pass in the middle, and twenty days in the third part. 43–44.
In the first part of the listening [to the teachings], it is considered to be seven days; in the middle part, twenty days;
and in the third part, sixteen days—I speak this truth. In the eastern direction under Indra, it is twenty days; in the middle, two months.
The third month is to be understood by astrologers as having been declared [in this manner].
In the Vāruṇa [dasa], there is a severe illness during the first portion for three fortnights; in the second, however, it lasts for six months; and in the third, for sixteen days. 46–47.

In the constellation Ahibudhnya (Śleṣā), one should indicate suffering for twenty-eight days at the beginning of the fortnight, for the entire month in the middle, and it should be known that there is affliction at the end during sinful deeds.
In Revatī, there are eight days of suffering in the first half, and sixteen in the second half.
Thus, thirty days have been declared by the ancient masters for the duration prior [to the full effect].
One day is proclaimed for the first part of Aśvinī,
five nights for the second, and likewise seven for the third.
In the first quarter of Bharaṇī, there is indeed a period of seven days; in the middle, death occurs, and at the end, illness for a duration of three months.
Having understood this, the wise person should properly perform rites of pacification.
"Three divisions of the constellations were elucidated by Ātreya.
(52) Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Knowledge of the Constellations," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Seven.
Ātreya said:
Arka, khadira, pālāśa, badarī, pāribhadraka, dūrvā, śamī, kuśa, kāśa, pippala, and the banyan tree (vaṭa). 1.
Jambu, āmra, karahāṭa, somavṛkṣa,
kalidruma, raktasāra, candana, jayantī, guruvṛkṣaka, sahacarī, sitā, varṣā, and the pair of all-healing herbs (sarvauṣadhi) and niśā.
The entire section on fuel-sticks (*samid-varga*) has been explained as part of the *samid*-oblation.

[The following are the fragrant substances: sandalwood, red sandalwood, *gorocanā*, turmeric, red ochre, *nimba*, *bilva*, *kadamba*, musk mixed with saffron, camphor, *śrīparṇa*, deodar, yellow sandalwood, *padmaka*, the two types of turmeric, *kālīyaka*, agallochum, *śiṃśapā*, red *gorocanā*, and *palāśa*. [The flowers are: lotus, *bilva*, *surasā*, *dūrvā*, *kuśa*, *jayantī*, *śamī* leaves, *arka*, *kiṃśuka*, *karṇikāra*, *girikarṇikā*, *sahacara*, *ālūṣa* flowers, the sprouts of *jambū* and mango, *kāñcanāra*, *pāṭala*, and *varvarī*.

Having prepared the Vāstumaṇḍala adorned with incense, lamps, and other ornaments—such as Agastya, Kākakāhlārī, and Aśoka flowers—one should worship the Nakṣatramaṇḍala in the sequence starting from the northeast (Īśāna) direction. Having worshipped the planets, beginning with Āditya, in the center of that maṇḍala, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) in their proper order. Furthermore, one should offer oblations with fuel sticks smeared with curds, honey, and ghee, following the sequence beginning with Aśvinī.

With the verse *ākṛṣṇena*, one should offer fuel-sticks of *arka* to Aśvinī; with *viṣṇorarāṭamasi*, fuel-sticks of *palāśa* to Bharaṇī; with *madhumādhvī*, fuel-sticks of *badarī* to Kṛttikā; and with *kāṇḍātkāṇḍāt*, fuel-sticks of *pāribhadraka* and *kuśa* to Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Punarvasu, and the others; thus one should perform the oblation.

One should offer oblations during the constellation Puṣya with *pippala* wood fuel-sticks while reciting "idaṃ deva," during Citrā with mango (*cūta*) wood fuel-sticks while reciting the *Agnimantreṇa*, and during Maghā with rose-apple (*jambū*) wood fuel-sticks while reciting "agni-mūrdhā. One should offer oblations during the first three [asterisms] with *karahāṭaka* wood fuel-sticks while reciting the *Sadyojāta* mantras. One should offer oblations during the next three [asterisms] with moon-creeper (*somavallī*) wood fuel-sticks while reciting "tatpuruṣāya vidmahe. One should offer oblations during Hasta with *vibhītaka* wood fuel-sticks while reciting "namo ghorāya. One should offer oblations during Citrā with red *sārasa* wood fuel-sticks while reciting "namo jyotiṣpataye."

One should perform a fire offering for Svāti with *candana* fuel-sticks, reciting "Namo devāya namo jyeṣṭhāya. One should offer oblations for Viśākhā with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* and *jayantī*. One should offer oblations for Anurādhā with fuel-sticks of the *guruvṛkṣaka* tree, reciting "Bṛhate yadupataye. One should offer oblations for Jyeṣṭhā with fuel-sticks of the *etajjyotis* plant; and with fuel-sticks of *śatāvarī*, reciting "Kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt," one praises the desired root.

One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *niśāyuga* under the asterism Pūrvāṣāḍhā; with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* under Uttarāṣāḍhā while reciting "madhu vātā"; with fuel-sticks of *bilva* under Śravaṇa while reciting "tryambakaṃ yajāmahe"; and one should offer oblations for the asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā (Vāsava). One should give a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) of clarified butter. One should perform the installation of the nine planets within a square sacrificial pit (*homakuṇḍa*). Thereafter, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*abhiṣeka*). Having dressed the patient in white garments along with a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one should bestow blessings with the Vedas and so forth, and then make gifts of cows, land, clothing, gold, and other items.
When this procedure is performed correctly, peace is attained. 4
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Homa," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Eight.
Ātreya said:
Now, therefore, O best of physicians, the auspicious or inauspicious signs regarding messengers for those seized by disease shall be briefly explained.
A messenger goes to the physician’s house for the sake of assisting the patient.
An examination of him must be performed by which the disease may be discerned— whether he be lame, blind, mute, deaf, or afflicted by pain; or whether he be a child,
a woman, one who is deformed, thirsty, or aged.
Those who know the Vedas declare that a messenger who is exhausted, afflicted by hunger, wandering, or miserable is not auspicious here;
likewise, one wearing saffron, black, or wet garments, or one whose head is covered by a cloth, [is inauspicious].
Those with eyes overflowing with tears, or likewise with shaven heads; those with monkey-like eyes, hair standing erect on their heads, or who are dwarfish, stunted, or have a cut nose—
wise lords of sages do not praise these as messengers of men, for they lead to the destruction of one's life.

One who is harsh, wrathful, carries a noose in hand, is a reviler of physicians, and is shrouded in darkness—these are not commended; the wise declare that such messengers increase the patient's affliction.
He who carries a staff in hand, holds a raised noose, and likewise weeps with piteous words like one who is afflicted; [such a messenger is not auspicious].
A messenger with watery eyes, though eager to depart, should be rejected; one afflicted by disease brings ill fortune.
A messenger who arrives quickly from the southern direction with a rope in hand or a raised noose in his grasp, or who speaks forcefully and angrily, likewise brings misfortune.
He stands with a staff grasped in his hand and his feet turned inward;
therefore, one who speaks in such a confused manner is not recommended for medical treatments.
He walks quickly along the path, and having entered [the patient], he becomes agitated and faints.
Stretching out his feet, he enters [the body] and places his hand upon the head;
he splits iron, wood, or grass, and sometimes he bursts [them apart];
he touches these things, or again he touches his own nose or breast.
He who scratches the ground with his foot,
or draws a line, or falls asleep, is a messenger who brings about undesirable results. One who has hands full of white cloth, and whose mouth is filled with betel, is auspicious.
Likewise, the twice-born youth Suśīla, who is preeminent in wisdom, invokes [the deity] for the sake of happiness—
[the deity] whose face is like a mirror of flowers, and who always possesses the lotus of his feet blooming with exertion and the blossoms of its filaments.

A messenger who has excellent garments in his palms, carries flowers, betel nuts, and unguents in his hands, and brings happiness— having arrived from the north or the east, or taking recourse in the western or northern directions— is indeed peaceful. 14.

Seeing the physician, he speaks with a smile—skillfully, neither too humbly nor too loftily: "Rise up, O Wind, and show favor! Such words of comfort spread joy; for the wise, the acquisition of a physician brings about the supreme benefit and the medicine that cures the suffering of the sick. 15.
Having approached the eastern direction, being tranquil and speaking with a peaceful voice,
he speaks to the physician for the sake of gain and to bring happiness to the sick. (16) And whoever, having arrived and sat down, recites a verse or a well-spoken word—
He speaks with peaceful words for the sake of gain and peace;
furthermore, he who asks after the welfare of a physician worthy of salutation bestows fruit or flowers that bring happiness to the sick. (17–18)
The messengers know this: for whom there is happiness, for him there is the accomplishment of bliss;
what is the use of much speaking here? The messenger brings happiness to men. (19) Therefore, one should avoid that which is not beneficial, namely, [a messenger] who is neither female nor male.
The physician who knows this attains success, happiness, and prosperity.
(20) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Examination of the Messenger," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Nine.
Ātreya said: Now, my son, I shall describe all the auspicious and inauspicious omens occurring at the time of leaving or entering a house.
A king, an elephant, a twice-born man, a peacock, a wagtail, a blue jay, a bird, a washerman, one dressed in white garments,
a young woman accompanied by her sons, and a maiden— these bring prosperity.
They indicate happiness and renown.
The *laṭvā*, hawk, vulture, green pigeon, ruddy goose, *bhāradvāja*, *chikkara*, and that known as the *chāga*—
these are the most excellent for the physician’s entry on the right or left side, and for his departure, they lead to prosperity.

The snake, owl, monkey, boar, iguana, bear, chameleon, and rabbit— these are auspicious omens at the time of departure or entry, in one's undertakings, and in providing assistance during calamities. Furthermore, either a deer or a yellow-brown animal is always praised when appearing on the right side.
Whether departing or entering, a deer on the right side is a bringer of auspiciousness.
At the time of good fortune for men, one, three, five, seven, or nine deer may pass by in a clockwise direction.

The peacock, the house-lizard, the donkey, the *bhṛṅgarāja*, the cuckoo, the *bhaṣaṇa* bird, the pigeon, the *potakī*, the sow, the crane, the king of birds (*garuḍa*), the *dīrghakaṇṭha*, and others [are auspicious].
The knower of omens says that if these appear on the left during departure—
the partridge, the *krakara*, the crane, the *sārasa*, the *abhāsa*, the boar,
the bird *kirīṭin*, or the crow— they are always considered most auspicious. (7–8)
And these [sounds] occur at the time of departure for the accomplishment of all undertakings.
(9) A crow on the right is excellent during departure, bestowing auspiciousness; the black crow is declared excellent on the left during entry. (10)
The owl, the hare, the monkey, and the chanting [of their names] are said to bring neither happiness nor even fame;
nor indeed is the sight of snakes, lizards, chameleons, and cats auspicious. However, they declare that the sight of the wagtail, the swan, and the chikkara bird is beneficial.
By name, the woodpecker, the crane, and the parrot are said to bring auspiciousness; 12.
for the accomplishment of various tasks upon their departure, [one should observe] the bhringaraja bird, silver, milk, water, fish, meat, blood, a corpse, a washed garment, a mirror, or a lid. 13.
Cats, snakes, lizards, or even monitor lizards may cut across the path; at the entrance, one should not take even a single step forward.
The tops of their feet stumble, or their garments slip away.
Upon hearing a cry for help, one should not fail to go even a single step.
Seeing fire in houses, one should break a water-filled jar;
and seeing trees falling, one should not remain standing still.
Having heard abusive words and likewise the cries of cats,
and having seen the quarreling of household folk, one should not even walk about.
A golden bracelet is indeed an ornament, as are flowers with fruit and the wine of vāruṇī.
Then, for those suffering from fever, the fruit of the Aśoka tree brings relief; indeed, the physician is always a bringer of well-being.
Having thus understood the supreme expertise regarding the potency of drinks, foods, and the like, as well as their qualities, their provocative nature, and the intensity of their provocation—
Furthermore, the wise physician who understands the accumulation and the treatment of provocation becomes honored in his dwelling by kings and the world.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of Omens," in the second section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 9.
The second section is completed.
Chapter One.
Ātreya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the causes of the confusion of diseases:
from fatigue, from the suppression of physical exertion, or even from anxiety, grief, and fear;
from anger, from the smell of medicinal herbs, and especially from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Having stirred up the digestive fire from its seat and likewise the blood and bile externally, it then combines with that which is located in the skin; therefore, it indeed produces fever.
Furthermore, due to the aforementioned causes, even an existing fever may become a mild fever.
It should be known that [the disease] is mild or very mild due to the consumption of excessive sour [substances];
from that arises *kāmalā*, and when it has fully developed, it becomes *halīmaka*. From *halīmaka* one becomes *pāṇḍu* (anemic), for which reason these [stages] have been proclaimed.
From *yakṣman* (consumption) swelling arises, and from swelling, abdominal enlargement (*udara*).

From that, *gulma* (abdominal tumors) such as those caused by *vāta* and other humors arise; from *gulma*, dyspnea and colic pain; from that, weak digestion (*mandāgni*); and from that, hoarseness of voice and obstruction of the respiratory passages.
The origin of all these diseases is indeed through fever;
death is to be known as occurring through fever, for there can be no death without fever.
Listen, O knower of medicines and diseases, to the second [topic]: the combination of diseases.
In humans, there occurs a mild fever, followed by diarrhea and then fever;
from that, hiccups, emaciation, delusion, vertigo, and loss of appetite arise.
Death results from swelling in these cases; now the third [type] is described.
Or, due to defects such as sleeping during the day, catarrh (pratiśyāya) arises;

from that, cough (kāsa) is declared to emerge, and from cough, nasal congestion (pīnasa) likewise. From that, consumption (kṣaya) arises; from consumption, swelling (śopha); and by means of swelling, one may even meet death.
Fever, consumption, tuberculosis, leprosy, abdominal tumors,
hemorrhoids, urinary gravel, urinary disorders, insanity, epilepsy, and fistula-in-ano—
these most terrible diseases render a man merely manageable (palliable).
All diseases arise from the humors (doṣas), such as wind (vāta) and bile (pitta), as well as those originating from phlegm (śleṣman); I shall now describe their treatment.
Wind [causes symptoms] after seven days, and bile after three nights.
O best of physicians, phlegm (śleṣman) may take even one and a half days to digest;
a fever born of two humors (dvandvaja), such as wind and bile (vātapitta), is digested in nine nights;
phlegm and wind (śleṣmavāta) in ten days; and bile and phlegm (pittaślaiṣmika) in five days.
For the pacification of dual disorders (*dvandva*), there is likewise digestion (*pācana*) on the fourth day;
for the terrible three-fold disorder (*tridoṣa*), digestion occurs on the twelfth day (16);
and the combined disorder (*sannipāta*) is digested even after fourteen days.

Having ascertained that the strength of the doshas has ripened, a digestive (pācana) treatment should therefore be administered; once the etiological factors have been addressed, a pacifying (saṃśamana) therapy should follow. Even impurities located within the seven bodily tissues (dhātus) may take up to seven days to ripen.
For even after a long time, the humors (malas) in a sannipāta fever are digested;
therefore, a remission is said to occur, and the fever generally ceases on the eighth day.
On the seventh day, however, the cause for remission does not yet exist.
Having deliberated, the wise physician should administer medicine even in cases of indigestion;
for when the digestive fire is extremely weak, it will not digest the medicine.
When all the humors have subsided, digestive therapy and fasting are prescribed.
There are the *laṅghita*, the *madhyalaṅghita*, and the *atilaṅghita* types;
listen now as I describe their characteristics for these men:
freedom from fatigue, absence of aversion or languor, and clarity of the sense faculties.
In the case of excessive fasting (laṅghana), there is the maturation of the humors (doṣapāka);

however, the signs of properly performed fasting are slight fatigue, loss of appetite, malaise, discoloration of the sense organs, excessive thirst, slight emaciation, and exhaustion, O best of physicians. (23–24)

Some slight unctuousness in the body, a lack of relish for food, and excessive binding of the bowels, along with indigestion in the middle of the process, are the signs of moderate fasting. A state of debility, drowsiness, diarrhea, and sleeplessness arise [from excessive fasting].
Trembling, headache, emaciation from hunger, and colic; a darkened face, watering of the eyes, and being afflicted by fainting, delusion, and exhaustion—
one should recognize these as the symptoms of one who has excessively practiced fasting (atilaṅghita).
In cases of fever occurring at specific times (velājvara), fever caused by spirits (bhūtajvara), as well as fever arising from bile (pittajvara),
or that born of exhaustion, anger, fear, or passion— the best of physicians should never prescribe fasting for these. (28–29)

One should never prescribe fasting for a child, an elderly person, one who is emaciated, one with diminished strength, one suffering from diarrhea or ulcers, a pregnant woman, or one who is delicate; likewise,
it is contraindicated in cases of fever with undigested matter (āmaja), mild fever, severe fever, loss of appetite, or constipation.
In the case of indigestion (ajīrṇa), fasting administered in the proper measure is recommended.
Excessive unctuousness of the limbs, a rumbling sound in the abdomen, headache, abdominal distension, a burning sensation, and a gurgling sound in the throat [are the signs]. 31–32.

Recognizing a person who suffers from anorexia, yellowish urine, drowsiness, lethargy, and fever caused by undigested matter (āmaja-jvara), the best of physicians should administer fasting (laṅghana) through methods such as fasting,
emesis, purgation, bloodletting, or the drinking of hot water. (33)
Six types of fasting (laṅghana) are described along with the procedure for sudation (svedana):
[34] emaciation from hunger, exhaustion and lassitude, the onset of vertigo and fever, internal burning heat, blood in the urine, and the symptoms of remittent fever (virāmajvara). [35]
One with a vāta constitution should undergo six days of fasting, while one with a pitta constitution should fast for three days;
kapha takes seven days to digest, so one should observe fasting upon seeing [the signs of] kapha. One with a disorder of all three doṣas (tridoṣa) digests over ten nights through such fastings.

When the fifteenth day arrives, the *sānnipātika* fever ripens; it may release the patient, kill him, or become a chronic intermittent fever (*viṣamajvara*). In childhood, the humors consist primarily of blood, followed by phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*).
When the sixteenth year is reached, diseases arising from the three doṣas occur;
when the twenty-fifth year is reached, fever indeed becomes of the sannipātika type, produced by vāta, pitta, and kapha through their accumulation in the rasa and rakta. 39.
When a fever has been properly ripened, one should administer a decoction (kvātha).
Decoctions are said to be of seven types: digestive (pācana), pacifying (śamana), appetizing (dīpana), moistening (kledana), drying (śoṣī), and specifically nourishing (santarpaṇa). 40–41.

A wise person should administer a digestive (pācana) medicine to a man during the nights; a pacifying (śamana) medicine should be given in the forenoon, while a digestive-stimulant (dīpana) is prescribed for the afternoon. A nourishing (santarpaṇa) and a breaking (bhedana) medicine should be administered for drinking in the morning.
A decoction for consumption is also prescribed for drinking at dawn.
The first watch of the night is proclaimed as *bhūtavelā*; they say the second watch is *niśi*, and that which follows is *niśītha*. 43–44.
Thereafter, one should know the "multi-night" (gaṇarātra) period, which consists of times when the [planetary] signs have not yet reached their full duration;
these include the forenoon, afternoon, midday, the latter half of the day, and the remainder of the day.
Furthermore, at the end of the day, there is the commencement of the administration of medicines. 45–46.

The decoction (kvātha) is traditionally said to be of seven types: digestive (pācana), appetizing (dīpanīya), purifying (śodhana), pacifying (śamana), nourishing (tarpaṇa), moistening (kledana), and drying (śoṣī).
A digestive decoction should be reduced to one-half [of its original volume], while a purifying one should be reduced to one-twelfth.
The varieties of decoctions (kvātha) are proclaimed as follows: the moistening (kledana) is four parts; the pacifying (śamana), eight parts remaining;
the kindling (dīpanīya) is ten parts; the satiating (tarpaṇa) is equal parts;
and the drying (viśoṣī) is sixteen parts. 48–49.
The digestive (pācana) digests the humors; the appetizer (dīpana) kindles the fire;
the purifier (śodhana) purifies the waste; the pacifier (śamana) pacifies diseases. The nourisher (tarpaṇa) nourishes the tissues; the moistener (kledī) produces moisture in the heart.
The drying [quality] brings about emaciation; therefore, one should examine the decoction. Having recognized whether it is moistening or drying, one should cause the person to undergo emesis.
One should not skip the decoction, nor should one disturb the internal [doshas]. 51–52.
One should not dry it again; it should be kept [in its vessel] and not displayed in an impure place. Furthermore, that decoction is not recommended, as it causes a mixture of diseases.
One should not dry the decoction again, nor should one leave it on the ground.
These [decoctions] are praised for the pacification of the *doṣas* in the treatment of disease (54). However, when a person undergoes tearing, falling, or bursting due to a decoction,
these decoctions are undesirable and do not serve to pacify the *doṣas* (55).
Having observed that the decoction is devoid of these characteristics, one should examine it further:
that which is black, blue, thick, red, slimy, or thin; and that which is burnt, smells like a corpse, or has a raw-flesh odor—one should reject such. (56–57)
One should know that a patient is incurable by these [symptoms]; there is no doubt about this.
By describing the qualities of substances, one should indicate the scent of the substance;
likewise, it should be pure, well-colored, astringent, and like nectar.
In vāta-fever, after administering fasting (laṅghana) and giving food,
a digestive medicine (pācana) should be given at night, having ascertained the strength or weakness of the doṣas;
it should be given on the third day in pitta-type fever, and on the first day in kapha-type fever.
One should not administer digestive therapy (pācana) when the disorder is unknown;
for the limit [of the fever's duration] is recognized by the fever itself after seven nights.
Therefore, in acute fever (navajvara), what is drunk [as medicine] produces disorder rather than removing it.
Therefore, first a digestive (pācana) medicine should be administered for three days, and thereafter a palliative (śamanīya) medicine should be given for five nights;
then one should administer a purificatory (śodhana) and digestive-stimulant (dīpanīya) medicine for one night. 62–63.
When exhaustion, fainting, and mental distress are observed during the drinking of decoctions,
or when emesis occurs, or even when a pacifying (śamana) diet has been prescribed,
a wholesome regimen (pathya) must always be administered; he does not achieve success through unwholesome practices.
By the best of physicians, [a patient] may be cured through wholesome regimens even without medicine;
however, without wholesome regimen, one cannot be cured even by hundreds of medicines.
One suffering from fever should eat what is beneficial, even if a lack of appetite should arise.
By not eating at the proper times for meals, one wastes away or even dies;
being emaciated, one falls into a state of suffering and reaches a condition that is truly incurable.
Therefore, one should protect the strength of men, for life itself depends upon the preservation of strength.
When the digestive fire has been suppressed and when there is a disorder, one should practice the drinking of gruel (yavāgū).
Indeed, they say that soup made from *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and mung beans is recommended;
likewise, gruel prepared with the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*) is for one whose digestion is moderately suppressed.
Constant nourishment is always beneficial for him;
goat’s milk mixed with jaggery should be drunk for the pacification of fever.
By this, exhaustion shall be destroyed and he will quickly attain comfort. 70–71.
One should have him sit facing either the north or the east,
administer a decoction to drink, and perform the recitation by Brāhmaṇas; then,
placing the drinking vessel beneath him, he should lie down and cultivate knowledge alone.
Even if afflicted by thirst, one should not make him drink water for even a moment after he has drunk;
rather, when seeing that the man’s exhaustion has departed, then happiness is attained.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Method for the Knowledge of Medicines," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
The second chapter.
Ātreya said:
What is the use of studying the treatises for one who is ignorant of medical practice?
Just as straw devoid of seeds is useless,
it would be better to drink the venom of a poisonous snake or molten copper,
or even to eat iron balls heated by a fierce fire.
But it is not right for those learned in the scriptures, even while wearing their formal attire, to accept food, drink, or wealth from one who has come for refuge and is afflicted by disease;
that alone is a proper medicine which results in health.
And he alone is the best of physicians who can liberate one from diseases.
Therefore, with every effort for the purpose of warding off disease, this compendium (Saṃhitā) should be studied, joined with its etiological signs and endowed with the means of treatment.
One should study this work in brief for the sake of understanding the medical compendium (*saṃhitā*);
having understood the remedy for a disease, one should then apply the treatment. Without correctly diagnosing the ailment, one undertakes treatments out of delusion.
If one knows the ritual procedure but does not know the treatises, success will not arise. However,
for one who acts after having understood the diagnosis, the recognition of diseases, and the merits and defects of medicines, success is not far off.
At the very outset, the wise physician should ascertain the knowledge of diseases— whether they are curable, incurable, or palliable—
and likewise [the nature] of all ailments; thereafter, he should administer the remedy,
taking into account the place, time, age, digestive fire, suitability, constitution, and the medicine itself.
Having understood this, the skilled physician should then apply the remedy.
There is no disease without the humors (doṣas); the humors are known as vāta and the others.
Diseases such as fever and so forth are recorded [in scripture]; one should correctly observe them.

Through the instruction of authoritative persons and through direct perception—by observing those who are ill and so forth, by touch, and subsequently by inquiries regarding cold and other symptoms—the knowledge of diseases is considered to be threefold: [arising from] seeing, touching, and questioning. (12)

After [examining] the face, eyes, and appearance, and through touch and inquiries regarding cold and other symptoms, a curable disease is said to be of two types, both involving difficult and unpleasant means of treatment.
The incurable type should be known to be of two kinds: the difficult and the most difficult.
Some diseases are palliable by their very nature; some curable diseases become palliable through neglect; some palliable diseases reach a state of incurability likewise. (15)
Furthermore, diseases destroy the vital breaths of men who do not take action against them.
A disease that arises upon an existing disease is called a complication (*upadrava*);
those with complications do not survive, whereas those without complications do survive.
Even a minor disease, once recognized by a physician, must be carefully considered and never neglected; for such a group of ailments can become incurable.
Even a small enemy possesses a nature like that of poison or fire.
An enemy who has attained strength does not reach a state of calm at the [proper] time;
likewise, a powerful disease, having reached another constituent element (*dhātu*), displays its prowess. (18–19)

O knower of the proper method, even if it has been brought to a state of calm through various treatments, a disease that is emaciated yet remains at its root must not be maintained; for even a powerful ailment, though somehow turned back by many wholesome remedies, may [resurface].
For one does not truly pacify a disease by mere childishness.
Just as a small amount of poison is potent, just as a small serpent is dangerous,
and just as even a very small fire is fierce, so too is a subtle enemy of disease.

As long as a disease remains within its location and causes transformation, its remedy lies in abandoning that location, especially when the disease is powerful. Some diseases are born of karma, while others arise from the humors (doṣas).
Others are said to be innate; these three types of diseases are recognized.
Furthermore, those which do not subside despite many treatments are designated as the terrible diseases born of karma. 23–24.
Diseases born of the humors (doṣas) include those of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and so forth; those innate (sahaja) include hunger, thirst, and the like.
Therefore, I shall first describe fever—an incomparable malady—affecting horses, elephants, humans, domestic animals, deer, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, and other such creatures, as well as trees.
This fever, declared to be the snatcher of life for creepers, medicinal herbs, mountains, serpents, birds, and mice, is indeed difficult to ward off in this world.
This incurable disease of fever is most difficult to overcome for cows, buffaloes, horses, and elephants; for humans it is somewhat more arduous, while for others it is a destroyer of life.
Just as a hunter is the most powerful among deer, so this fever is the most potent among diseases;
no other being on earth—whether gods or others—is capable of withstanding it, let alone a human. (28) For by means of his own karma, a human attains the status of a deity in heaven.
And thus, having fallen from heaven, he exists even in the human state.
Therefore, due to his divine nature, he endures the human fever;
all other classes of beings, afflicted by fever, perish.
This fever is the king of diseases, just as the lord of beasts is among animals; just as fire is supreme among those whose nature is burning, so too is this fever superior.
Born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath, it scorches all living beings. 31
It is known as *pātaka* among the serpents, *abhitāpa* among the horses, *īśvara* among the cows, and it is considered *jvara* among human beings;
it is *dāridra* among female buffaloes and *mṛgaroga* among wild animals. (32)
For goats and sheep, it is called *pralāpa*; for camels, it becomes *alasa*. For dogs, it is known as *alarka*; for fish, it is considered *indramata*.
For birds, however, it is *abhighāta*, while for serpents, it is designated as *aikṣita*.
In water, there is generally the *nīlikā* [disease] caused by what is known as saline soil (*ūṣara*);
in trees, however, the *koṭarākṣa* fever is seen everywhere. (35) He has three legs, ashes for weapons, three heads, and a very large belly.
Clad in a tiger skin, his body radiant with the hue of tawny hair,
with reddish-brown eyes, long arms, and shanks like those of an elephant— this powerful man, who is like a fishless [ocean], is known as Jvara for the destruction of the world. (36–37)

Just as fire, having consumed its fuel, or just as poison, having destroyed the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), attains peace once its purpose is fulfilled, so too does fever attain peace after destroying the body.
Therefore, O son, listen as I describe its origin. 38.

That which was fourfold and most terrible became eightfold. (39) For Maheśvara, enraged and distressed by the loss of his beloved, sought to pacify Dakṣa from above; he released a fierce breath, and from that, fever arises in eight ways according to its eightfold origin. (40)

Due to the accumulation of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), phlegm (kapha), and blood, and because of indulgence in food and drink according to one's own whims or due to the reversal of the seasons, the humors (doṣas) move from the receptacle of waste (malāśaya) outside the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni). They cause the falling of the fire that resides in the blood.
Consequently, they receive the established name "fever" (jvara), arising from the production of cold through such causes as physical exertion, anger, and eating.
He was not particularly troubled by incompatible foods, nor by the water from mountain torrents,
nor satisfied with well-water; he endured the fierce rays of the hot-rayed sun,
and through the fragrant breeze, he was freed from the affliction of the bodily humors.
A most terrible disease called fever arises intensely in human beings.

(44) Fatigue, numbness, watering of the eyes, horripilation, a rattling sound in the throat, yawning, discoloration, aversion to food, and dryness of the mouth are the manifest symptoms of fever. (45)
In the wind-disorder (vāta), yawning occurs; from phlegm (kapha) comes dejection and sinking;

from bile (pitta) comes burning pain in the eyes; indeed, all these symptoms appear in the combined disorder (sānnipātika). Therefore, I shall describe the remedy by which well-being may be attained. 46
One should drink at night this warm decoction of vacā, yavānī, dhanikā, and viśvā;

for a person suffering from vātika diseases, rheumatic pains, or fevers that produce such conditions, this will lead to well-being. (47) A decoction of niśā, nimba, mṛtavallikā, dhānyaka, and viśvā, taken with jaggery, [is likewise beneficial].

And at night, a drink mixed with milk and *sakola* fruit serves to digest a fever accompanied by bile (48). A decoction of *vacā*, *yavānī*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), and *viśvā*, taken at night, acts as a digestive for a person suffering from a fever born of phlegm (*kapha*), as well as for disorders involving pain, catarrh, and nasal congestion (49).

A decoction of śaṭhī, vacā, nāgara, kāphala, vatsādanī, and dhanvayavāsaka is beneficial for all types of fever; it acts as a digestive promoter (sampācana) in cases of human fever caused by all three doṣas. For the wise, this should be administered at night with a large quantity of lukewarm water.
Gentle massage of the limbs is beneficial, provided it is free from excessive sleep and physical exertion.

Trembling, irregular feverish paroxysms, emaciation, a bad taste in the throat, palate, and mouth, dryness of the body, distension of the abdomen and bowels, yawning, headache, and insomnia [are the symptoms]. 51–52.

A fever caused by Vāta is characterized by blackness of the nails and teeth, delirious speech, powerful breaking pain in the limbs, a loathsome appearance, and sleeping like one terrified even while awake (verse 53).
Nāgara, Surataru, Dhānyaka, Kuṇḍalī, and Bṛhatī [are used] for two nights.

In the seventh night, it is recommended for fever when the fever has reached its eighth part; indeed, one who possesses [this knowledge] is considered expert. (54) Medicine that is excessively potent, if taken without food, will undoubtedly and swiftly destroy the disease; however, if that same medicine is drunk by children, the elderly, young women, or those of delicate constitution, it quickly leads to extreme exhaustion and loss of strength. (55) It also causes lightness of the sense organs and clarity of the eyes and face.
When there is belching and heat in the stomach, these are the signs that the medicine has been digested (verse 56).
One should recognize that the medicine has been expelled when exhaustion, nausea, malaise, headache, vertigo, and excessive secretions arise (verse 57).

Burning sensations, prostration of the limbs, fainting, headache, exhaustion, dejection, and vertigo— these manifest with particular intensity through sexual passion, taking on the appearance of specific medicinal effects.
Therefore, when only the remnants of the medicine remain, there is never any actual alleviation of the underlying disorder.
The humors (doṣas) provoke various complications; therefore, medicine should not be administered without a digestive agent (pācana).
When covered by food, it undergoes digestion quickly, does not destroy strength, and does not repeatedly exit through the mouth.
This very great medicine should be given to the elderly, children, the timid, and excellent women. (59–60)

A decoction (kaṣāya) prepared by boiling one *kumbha* each of *bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śukanāsa*, *kapāṭalī*, and *kumbhārikā* cleanses the teeth, restrains the wind (*samīra*), and quickly destroys wind-born fever (*marutajvara*) in men.

*Kirāta*, *musta*, *mṛtavallī*, *kraṇāsa*, *vit*, *gokaṇṭaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *udīcya*, and *tiktā*— [Note: This second line appears to be part of a subsequent verse describing another medicinal compound.]
A decoction made by boiling *śāliparṇī* and *kalaśī* together quickly destroys fever caused by Vāta (62).
Furthermore, a decoction of *guḍūcī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *plakṣī*, *rāsnā*, *punarnavā*, and *trāyamāṇaka*,
taken with jaggery, removes Vāta-fever (63).

Fainting, burning sensations, vertigo, intoxication, thirst, forceful diarrhea, drowsiness, lassitude, prostration, vomiting, and a burning sensation in the mouth; sweating, labored breathing, a pungent taste, and agitation or hunger—by these symptoms, fever caused by Pitta indeed arises in a person. (64) Rodhra, utpala, amṛtalatā, kamala, sugar, and sārivā—these indeed, when boiled together for the purpose of digestion, quickly destroy Pitta and bring about the pacification of Pittaja fever in men. (65)
Śakrāhvā boiled with rice-water and combined with kaṭurohiṇī,
or a decoction of yaṣṭīmadhu, is indeed the destroyer of pitta-type fevers (66). [Likewise, decoctions] of durālabhā, vāsaka, parpaṭa, priyaṅgu, nimba, and kaṭurohiṇī [are effective].

Kirātatikta boiled as a decoction and enriched with plenty of sugar is a digestive agent; when prepared thus, it quickly destroys bilious fever accompanied by burning sensations, thirst, giddiness, and wasting disorders. Indeed, even a single Parpaṭaka is the most excellent for the pacification of bilious fevers.
Therefore, it is enriched with nagara and bālaka, like a lion set upon its armor.
Nagara, uśīra, mustā, candana, kaṭurohiṇī, and a decoction of dhānyaka destroy pitta-fever. 69–70.

A decoction of Amṛta, Parpaṭa, and Dhātrī removes Pitta-fever (71). A decoction of Drākṣā, Parpaṭaka, Tiktā, Pathyā, Āragvadha, and Mustaka cures Pitta-fever accompanied by thirst, giddiness, and burning sensations (72).
A plaster made from Vidārī, Rodhra, Dadhittha, Mātuluṅga, and pomegranates,
applied according to their availability, destroys burning sensations, thirst, and fainting.
This should be applied while the patient lies supine on a bronze or copper vessel.

Placing a stream [of water] upon the navel would indeed ward off the burning heat. (74) The embrace of one bent by the weight of the breasts of lovely women in a garden, the drinking of grape juice through desired union, and the use of white lotuses, garments cooled by being sprinkled with sandalwood water, pearl necklaces, pure snow, and the moonlight at the beginning of the night—these constitute cooling service. (75)

By these [remedies], one quickly destroys the bile of humans, as well as burning sensations, emaciation, exhaustion, thirst, vertigo, and fainting. Through these formulations, there arises a complete pacification of the burning of bile; thus, this practice becomes constantly suitable for the illustrious. (76) If a person suffers from the drying up of the tongue, throat, and palate—

The filaments of the citron (mātuluṅga), ground together with honey and rock salt and applied as a plaster on the palate, immediately remove fever caused by pitta. Stiffness, a sweet taste in the mouth, numbness, excessive drowsiness, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, forgetfulness, horripilation, and coldness [are the symptoms].

They know that in Kapha-fever (śleṣmajvara), there is perspiration, obstruction of the ears, paleness of the eyes, and the suppression of stool, urine, and flatus, along with vomiting; 78. However, a paste of Pippalādi is beneficial as a digestive (pācana) remedy for the Kapha-type fever. 79.
Likewise, Vyāghrī, Siṃhī, Rodhra, Kuṣṭha, and Paṭolaka [are beneficial].
This is an excellent digestive (pācana) remedy for fever born of phlegm (kapha).

Vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, paṭolī, śaṭhī, and kaṭukā—this decoction of honey [and these herbs] properly destroys fever caused by phlegm and quickly alleviates diseases characterized by an abundance of phlegm. 80–81.
Āmalakī, abhayā, kṛṣṇā, and ṣaḍgranthā—these three groups of three [drugs] are purgatives, destroyers of phlegm, fever-destroyers, and digestive stimulants.
Pippalī, śṛṅgavera, ṣaḍgranthā, and the fruit of vatsaka [are also such]. 82.
A decoction [of these] mixed with plenty of honey destroys phlegm-fever (83).
One should lick powdered long pepper (pippalī) with honey; it removes phlegm-fever, destroys splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, and poison, and subdues cough, dyspnea, and indigestion (84).
Thirst, fainting, vomiting, and a pungent taste in the mouth; dryness of the body, internal burning, and redness of the eyes;
dryness of the throat, loss of sleep, pain and splitting in the head, breaking pain in the limbs, horripilation, and tamaka—these are the symptoms if it is vātapitta fever. (85)

When the doshas are combined, a proper digestive (vipācana) treatment should be administered for fever caused by pitta, vāta, and jvara; one should drink a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) combined with śālmalī, or a decoction of rāsnā and kirātatiktaka.
[One may also take] the two pañcamūlis together with ginger, along with guḍūcī, bhūnimba, and ghanasāraka.
A paste (kalka) mixed with jaggery is highly recommended during wind disorders; it is the cause for the destruction of fever characterized by pitta and vāta.

(87) A decoction of kirātatikta, āmalakī, śaṭhī, drākṣā, uṣaṇā, nāgaraka, and amṛtā, when well-cooled and combined with jaggery, shall be the cause for the destruction of fever characterized by pitta and vāta. (88)
A decoction of *amṛta*, *mustaka*, *vāsā*, *parpaṭa*, and *viśvā* drunk with water, as well as *bhadramuñja*, destroys fever caused by *pitta* and *vāta*.
Furthermore, it cures sleepiness, heaviness, pain in the joints and head, distress, and the splitting sensation in the joints; here, the eyes exhibit a moderate intensity [of symptoms].

In a fever characterized by phlegm (śleṣma) associated with wind (vāta), there is burning heat, labored breathing, loss of appetite, a dry obstruction in the ears and throat, drowsiness, delusion, anorexia, and vertigo; whereas in a fever characterized by phlegm and bile (pitta), [the symptoms are as follows]. For these, one may use ginger (nāgara), bhadramustā, or guḍūcī and āmalaka.

A decoction of *pāṭhā*, lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*), and *udīcya* is beneficial in fever caused by pitta and kapha; it is digestive, appetizing, and a remedy for the wasting of blood. [91-92] Drākṣā, amṛtā, vāsaka, riṣṭaka, bhūnimba, tiktā, indrayava, and paṭola—[these are also used].

A decoction of mustā and bhārgī, when boiled, destroys fever caused by pitta and kapha. (93) One should prepare a decoction of guḍūcī, nimba leaves, śuṇṭhī, mustā, kustumburu, and candana; this "guḍūcī-ādi" decoction destroys fever arising from kapha, pitta, and vāta. (94)
This [decoction] destroys all fevers, nausea, and other ailments such as anorexia;
it cures catarrh and thirst, and wards off emaciation and burning sensations.
(95) Guḍūcī, nimba, cakravāka, śaṭhī, kirātatikta, and pippalī—these eight [ingredients]... [are used].

A person should drink the decoction of *dārvī* and *paṭola* when afflicted by fever caused by pitta and kapha (96). The group consisting of *paṭolī*, *candana*, *tiktā*, *mūrvā*, *pāṭhā*, and *amṛtā* wards off fever, vomiting, burning sensations, and itching caused by pitta and śleṣman (97).
This decoction, prepared from the roots of *paṭola*, *vāsā*, and *picumanda*, along with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and *ghanā*, is recommended for fever arising from phlegm and bile;
it is likewise an appetizer and beneficial for fevers characterized by both bile and phlegm, as well as those arising from bile and blood. 98.
In fever, a decoction prepared from *paṭola* and coriander (*dhānyāka*) is excellent for breaking up the impurities (*malas*). 99.

Coldness, shivering, breaking pain in the joints, vomiting, numbness in the limbs, dullness of sensation, mild heat, loss of appetite, constipation, roughness of the skin, cough, darkness of vision, and colic—these are the symptoms [of this fever].

Drowsiness, moaning, self-indulgence, or else a sense of stiffness, yawning, loss of appetite, perspiration, and retention of stool and urine—these are the symptoms of fever caused by Kapha and Vata. 100.
Aragvadha, Tiktarohini, Haritaki, Pippali-root, and Musta [are the remedies].
This paste, having been decocted, is beneficial for fever associated with *kapha* and *vāta* and accompanied by colic; it is wholesome and promotes digestion.
(101) A decoction of *kṣudrā*, *guḍūcī*, *nāgara*, *vāsā*, water, *parpaṭaka*, *pathyā*, *mustā*, and *duḥsparśā*, when drunk, is beneficial for fever arising from *vāta* and *kapha*. (102)

A decoction of parpaṭa, nāgāhvaya, vacā, tantuka, kaṭphala, elā, abhayā, viśva, and bhūtika, combined with hiṅgu and honey, is indeed effective for diseases of kapha and vāta accompanied by hiccup, as well as for galagraha (throat obstruction).
(103) A decoction of the two pañcamūlas (the ten roots), impregnated with the powder of kaṇā (pippalī), [is likewise used].
It should be administered in cases of pain arising from *vāta* and *kapha*, as well as in fever, asthma, and chronic rhinitis (104).
Drowsiness, laziness, sweetness in the mouth, spitting, dryness of the throat, loss of sleep, labored breathing, fainting, anxiety, numbness of the tongue, or roughness,
or perhaps pain in the back and head, or an internal burning sensation— if these occur— [then this remedy is indicated].
Know this to be the disorder of the three humors (tridoṣa). Having observed the terrible fever born of the three humors which robs one of life,
therefore, the drying up of this phlegm (kapha) is prescribed first.
One should not perform treatments that pacify pitta if one desires one's own reputation;
for [such treatments] immediately kill a strong patient afflicted by pain caused by kapha and vāta.
In cases arising from all three doṣas (tridoṣaja), fasting, subduing [the doṣas], or spitting [expectoration therapy] should be employed. 107.
Fasting for three nights, five nights, or even seven nights is prescribed after assessing the relative strength and weakness of the bodily humors (doṣas);
once the phlegm (kapha) is known to have been dried up, one should then proceed to alleviate the wind (vāta).
Having recognized that pitta has been provoked, one should perform treatments to pacify pitta;
however, while vāta and kapha should be dried up, one must not destroy the pitta. Thirst, pain, emaciation, labored breathing, and insomnia [occur] during the days.

Drowsiness, delusion, and dryness occur, as does inflammation of the nose, tongue, and lips; one spits out what has been consumed, becomes emaciated in body, and circular spots appear on the skin; there is darkening of the eyes, lips, and face, along with intoxication, perspiration, flatulence, and wasting. 111
Loss of appetite, dizziness, as well as the shaking of the head,
headache, obstruction of the channels, vomiting, or being constricted by a rumbling and piercing pain in the throat—
by these symptoms manifested, it arises in men as the condition known as *sannipāta*.
Fever is the most rapid-onset of diseases and causes extreme suffering for horses or elephants.
(112) In a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta-jvara*), one should first apply treatments that remove wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*);
subsequently, when the phlegm has been diminished and the disease is free from undigested matter (*nirāma*), one should treat the bile (*pitta*) and wind. (113)
Having exerted effort in the treatment of *sannipāta* fever, one should conquer excessive drowsiness (*tandrā*),
which is the most difficult complication among all fevers, especially in those patients who have been administered wholesome food while their bodies were filled with *kapha*. (114)
That alone would be his enemy, not wholesome food nor medicine.
Śaṭhī, the two groups of five roots (pañcamūla), durālabhā, koṭaja, paṭola, pauṣkara, and likewise bhārgavī combined with pippalī—[these are the remedies]. 115–116.
The ten-ingredient compound (daśāṅga) [of] bhūnimba, dāru, daśamūla, mahauṣadha, abdatikta, indrabīja, dhanika, bhadrakaṇṭaka, and kaṇā destroys the fire of *sānnipātika* fever on the first day.

117 Furthermore, a decoction (kaṣāya) of bhūnimba, dāru, daśamūla, mahauṣadha, abdatikta, indrabīja, dhanika, bhadrakaṇṭaka, and kaṇā quickly destroys fever accompanied by drowsiness, delirium, vertigo, thirst, loss of appetite, burning sensations, delusion, dyspnea, and weak digestion. 118

A paste (kalka) made from equal parts of śaṇṭhī, ghanā, agaja, kaṇā, suradāru, dhānyāka, tiktā, kaliṅga, and daśamūla is excellent for destroying fevers born of the three doṣas, and it cures dyspnea, vertigo, anorexia, constipation, and diseases of the heart.
Mustā, uśīra, niśā, viśāla, madhuka, pāṭhā, balā, and rohiṇī... [119]
A decoction made from equal parts of nīlī, dhanvayavāsa, kaṭvarā, śaṭhī, śuṇṭhī, samaṅgā, vivṛt,
yaṣṭīmadhu, pippalīmūla, parpaṭa, phalā, pippalyaka, dāru, śyāmā, hemā, and guḍūcī, along with milk, is known as the ender of fever (jvarānta). 120
The two types of *bṛhatī*, *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, *kirāta*, *kaṭurohiṇī*,
*paṭola*, *pauṣkara*, *bhārṅgī*, *vatsaka*, and *durālabhā* (121)—
this is the *bṛhatyādika* digestive decoction (*kāthana*), which destroys complications such as cough.
This quickly destroys fever caused by the simultaneous derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) and is praised for alleviating pain, distress, and drowsiness. 122.
Śaṭhī, kirāta, kaṭukā, viśālā, guḍūcī, bhṛṅgī, the two types of bṛhatī, mahauṣadha, pauṣkara, dhanvayāsa, rāsnā, surāhvā, and gajapippalī. 123.
This yellow decoction, prepared from the fourteen ingredients beginning with *śaṭhī*, is beneficial for men;
it destroys drowsiness, labored breathing, headache, and stiffness, and swiftly cures fever accompanied by pain.
[124] *Bhūnimba*, *suradāru*, *nāgara*, *ghana*, *tikta*, and *kaliṅga*...
Similarly, a decoction prepared with five groups of drugs beginning with Hastikarṇa is beneficial;
when drunk, it brings about the destruction of all diseases, destroys *sannipāta* fever, and swiftly eliminates asthma, emaciation, pain in the chest, and drowsiness. 125

A decoction prepared from equal parts of *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, *ghanaparpaṭaka*, *paṭolī*, *bhūnimba*, *vatsaka*, *śaṭhī*, *nāgara*, *tiktā*, *surāhvā*, *gajapippalī*, *māgadhikā*, *yavāsa*, *vāsā*, *balā*,
and *gajabalā* destroys diseases arising from Vāta, as well as asthma, cough, abdominal pain, and cholera. (126)
This is the best for men on earth in cases of *sannipāta* fever or diseases caused by *kapha* and *vāyu*.

127 A decoction of *rāsnā*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *śatamūlī*, *bhārgī*, *puṣkara*, *ghanā*, *suradāru*, and *dhānyaka* is beneficial for all fevers born of *vāyu*, even those arising from *sannipāta* that are extremely severe. 128

A decoction of trivṛt, viśālā, surāhva, māragvadha, and tiktakarohiṇī acts as a purgative for the removal of impurities and destroys the fear of vāta-śūla. For external application, a powder made from vacā, yavānī, and mahauṣadha should be used when dry.
They declare this to be excellent; it truly brings about the pacification of the fever’s heat and acts as a massage. 130.

A powder consisting of *māgadhī*, *suradāru*, *viśvaka*, *tiktā*, and *dīpyaka* is highly recommended for anointing the body; it wards off perspiration from the body and one will surely and quickly become cool-bodied. 131.

Madhūka-sāra (the heartwood of Madhūka) ground with mahauṣadha, vacā, uṣaṇā, and saindhava, along with either urine or warm water, [is used] for the awakening of lost consciousness. [Likewise,] the juice of the root of śobhāñjanaka combined with marica [is used]. 132.
For those suffering from fainting, nasal medication (nasya) should be administered to quickly awaken the patient.
A single powder consisting of *bṛhatī*, fruit-pippalī, and ginger is highly recommended; when blown into the nostrils, the resulting sneeze restores consciousness and movement. (133–134)

Śirīṣa seed, marica, and upakulyā, rubbed with cow’s urine along with rock salt, should serve as an eye-salve for men; it restores consciousness to those whose perception has been lost. (135) Likewise, trikaṭu, karañja seeds, triphalā, suradāru, and rock salt [are used similarly].
An ointment made from *tulasī* and eye-salve (*añjana*) destroys drowsiness of the eyes.
(136) Having prepared a mixture of *kesara*, *mātuluṅga*, *śṛṅgavera*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), one should wear it in the mouth up to the throat. (137)
The wise man should rub his teeth, tongue, mouth, and palate;
he should spit out everything according to the prescribed rule, doing so repeatedly.
By this, there will be purification of the throat, and it draws away the phlegm.
The sharpness of the tongue, loss of appetite, and labored breathing are pacified.
(139) A powder made of *kaṭuka*, *cavya*, and *kāpathyā*, combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), should be used to rub the teeth as well as the tongue and the impurities of the palate. (140)
Spitting out [the phlegm] cleanses the throat, induces a desire for food, and destroys the kapha;
nausea comes to an end and sharpness of the senses is greatly restored.
Or, if the body is cold, then sudation (sveda) is prescribed. 141.
Thirteen types of sudation (sveda) should be known, along with the causes for preventing sudation:
saṅkara, prastuta, nāḍīpariṣeka, apagāhana, ātaṅka, asmayana, karṣa, kūṭī, and bhūkumbhī. (142–143)
The pit (kūpa), the oven (holāka)— these thirteen methods cause perspiration.
One should apply Kālasveda, Ghaṭīsveda, and Vālukāsveda to the patient's hands, feet, and likewise to the head.
Thus there is no peace for us; or rather, he might burn [us] with an iron probe.
If the feet are not cooled when burned, he might likewise burn the base of the big toes, the wrist, the heart, or even the head. (145–146)

If a man afflicted by cold has perspiration on his forehead, or if that perspiration remains sticky upon his throat even though he is chilled and does not reach his chest, he will surely go to the house of Death within seven days, ten days, or again, twelve days. 147.5–6.
On the thirteenth or fifteenth day, it either subsides or kills [the patient]. Or else, on the fifteenth day, it kills or protects the man;
this is the most terrible fever of *sannipāta*, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.

O best of physicians, this is the boundary of the three *doṣas* for both liberation and destruction; when a person suffers from internal burning (*antardāha*) due to the *sannipāta* disorder, he who sprinkles that man with cold water [performs a grave error]. 150.
How could a patient survive by any means, and how could that physician not be worthy of honor?
(151) What indeed has not been accomplished by that physician who rescues a man fallen into the ocean of *sannipāta*?
Endowed with righteousness, fame, and discipline, what kind of worship would such a physician not receive upon the surface of the earth? (152)
That fever which is joined with the three—wind, bile, and phlegm—is likewise born of the three doṣas; and when that is further combined with blood, it becomes a sānnipātika fever.
Know that there is indeed no sānnipātika fever without blood.
In a person, the humors (doṣas) are pacified by digestive decoctions;
therefore, when the humor has been pacified, the blood does not liquefy,
and by that very [fact], a severe swelling arises at the base of the ear.

Therefore, one should provide its remedy by means of bloodletting using leeches, a gourd, or *bhṛṅga*; thereafter, an ointment is beneficial, consisting of the roots of *bījapūraka* and likewise *agnimantha*. 156.
This ointment for the root of the ear is a destroyer [of disease].

Having ground together house-soot, turmeric, the great medicinal herb (mahauṣadha), white mustard, rock salt, and *vacā* with milk, this applied paste effects the destruction of blood and brings relief to swelling and ulcers in the ear of a person. (157–158)
When suppuration occurs, a remedy must be applied there:

an ointment made from the bark of Dhava, Arjuna, and Kadamba promotes wound healing (verse 159). An ointment consisting of the roots of Nimba and Āragvadha combined with Niśā [turmeric] is also used for application.

It causes the drainage of pus-like odors and promotes the healing of wounds. One should avoid sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, excessive water, cold water, staying awake at night, physical exercise, and likewise grief. (160–161)

One should avoid from afar mung beans, barley, wheat, sesame, parṇīka, lentils, and tripuṭā, as well as oil; one should also abstain from sexual intercourse for one month and from overeating for one fortnight. 162.
One should avoid [food] at the base of the ear, for by that one attains happiness.
Old *ṣaṣṭika* rice, or *bālya*, or likewise *āḍhakī*, as well as soup made of *kulattha* or mung beans, is recommended for the meal. 164
One should abandon eggplant, onions, and bulbous vegetables;
by this, one attains comfort and is quickly liberated from disease.
When, at the end, the bile remains within while phlegm and wind are on the outside, [one should act accordingly].
Then there will be internal burning and dryness, while externally there is perspiration and coldness.

To this patient, one should quickly administer a decoction of *amṛtā* with water, combined with honey and long pepper (*pippalī*); thus he shall indeed be liberated from the fever caused by the combination of all three humors (*sānnipātika*).
Alternatively, a decoction of ativiṣā, vālaka, nāgara, ghana, and parpaṭa, mixed with sugar, serves to pacify internal burning sensations (antardāha).
This should be used when pitta is located externally, or when kapha and vāta are situated internally. (168)
Therefore, heat arises in the body at first, and coldness arises at the end.
For one who suffers from deceitfulness and the like, one should administer a decoction that subdues *kapha*.
This applies to one in whose upper body there is *vāta* and *kapha*, and in whose lower body there is *pitta*.
