Consequently, one half of the body becomes cool while the other half becomes hot.
For such a person, one should administer a warm decoction of rāsnā and other herbs.
This applies to one in whom blood and bile are present in the upper part, while both wind and phlegm are located in the middle.
Above that, heat arises, and below, cold is produced. 173.
The best of physicians should administer a decoction of ginger and other such drugs for one whose heat is observed to be diminished and whose digestive power has become weak. 174.
One who understands [the disease] should recognize it as having an external onset; such a fever is curable. 175.
That fever at the end of which heat, thirst, a burning sensation, and headache arise, one should know as having a deep-seated onset; it is difficult to cure even for men. 176.
One should apply the eighteenfold yoga as a remedy for that condition in men.
When pitta remains at the extremities of the body while both vāta and kapha reside within,
it causes coldness in the body and heat in the hands and feet.
For that [condition], a decoction of rāsnā and other such herbs mixed with pippalī should be administered.
When pitta resides in the body while both vāta and kapha remain at the extremities,
heat arises in the body and coldness occurs in the hands and feet.
A decoction of grapes and other such fruits, mixed with jaggery, should be applied [as a poultice]. Wherever there is a sensation of coldness, fomentation (sveda) should be administered;
however, a wise practitioner should not perform fomentation when the fever is excessively hot. 181–182.
By means of *kapha* and *pitta*, the wind (*anila*) always becomes motionless;
from that very wind, diseases such as fever and others arise. [The symptoms are:
dizziness, coldness, exhaustion, trembling, diarrhea, and fatigue. (183)
Fatigue, perspiration, and talkativeness occur at the time of fever's release (184).

Furthermore, there is perspiration, itching, and fullness of the vessels; likewise, sneezing, lightness, a desire for food, and the expansion of the sense organs; the person is free from exhaustion and free from pain (185).

For even in one who has been liberated [from fever], heaviness of the head does not leave him; know that he is not yet freed, for the fever returns to him. (186) This occurs if the fever residing in the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) has indeed entered the body.
One should recognize irregular fever (viṣamajvara), and it is to be known as being of four types:
the quotidian (ekāhika), the tertian (dvyāhika), the quartan (tryāhika), and furthermore, the wise physician should identify the fourth as the periodic fever (velājvara). 187–188.

If a fever is cold first and subsequently becomes hot, it is declared in the case of a human being to be curable; it is quickly cured by medicines. Furthermore, if one subsequently experiences a burning sensation, the fever becomes severe.
Even that fever which causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) is not quickly released [from the patient].

(190) Pain in the three corners [of the head] and the waist, as well as vāta and pitta, occurs; there is pitta in the head and vertigo, while on the back it produces thinness and pain from phlegm (śleṣman). That is the threefold characteristic of the tertian fever (tridhā tṛtīyajvara). (191)

The tertian fever (tṛtīyaka) is of three types: that which seizes the sacrum due to kapha and pitta; that which arises from vāta and kapha and seizes the back; and that which arises from vāta and pitta and seizes the head. The quartan fever (caturtha) should be known as being of two types, consisting of vāta and śleṣman (kapha).
The fever known as *śleṣmaka* arises from the calves, while that originating from *anila* (vāta) arises in the head;
having understood this, a skilled physician should apply the appropriate remedy.
Thus, *velājvara* occurs when [the humor] has reached the *rasa* (plasma), and likewise, *ekāhika* (quotidian) fever occurs when it has reached the blood.
The third [type] resides in the flesh, the fourth is dependent on the bones;
it should be known as pervading all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and when aged, it causes the depletion of those constituents.
(195) In the case of a disease born of the elements (*bhūta-ja*), there should be the science of spirits (*bhūtavidyā*); one should administer pacification and beating.
For one whose fever arises from a curse, the remedy is pacification (196). In a fever born of desire, one should treat it with bile-inducing remedies and beneficial breath-control (197).
In a fever born of anger or bile, one should pacify it with virtuous words.
One should induce a state of intoxication with medicinal herbs and fragrant substances; such consumption is beneficial.

(198) One should drink a decoction of *nidigdhikā*, *nāgarika*, and *amṛtā*, mixed with *pippalī*, for chronic fever, loss of appetite, cough, colic, dyspnea, weak digestion, facial paralysis, and catarrh. (199)

For those suffering from cough, indigestion, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, weak digestive fire, jaundice, and loss of appetite, long pepper (pippalī) taken with jaggery is recommended; it quickly destroys chronic fever in men.
A decoction of the light five roots (laghupañcamūlī) boiled together with long pepper and chinnodbhavā [is likewise beneficial].
For chronic fever, this decoction destroys dyspnea and disorders of phlegm, and cures weak digestion, colic, anorexia, and catarrh:
201 A decoction of *paṭola*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), *vatsaka*, *nimba*, *mokṣā*, *drākṣā*, *amṛtā*, *candana*, and *nāgara* serves to destroy long-standing fever. 202
One should eat jīraka with jaggery, or *harītakī* with jaggery,
or sesame seeds with jaggery, in the case of a fever following a chronic (viṣama) course.
Alternatively, one may consume ginger with jaggery, or a decoction of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) with jaggery.
A decoction [prepared] from Vāsā, Dhātrī-phala, Dāru, Pathyā, and Nāgara is also a destroyer of irregular fevers (viṣamajvara);
when combined with honey, this decoction wards off quartan fever (cāturthika). 204–205.

Agasti leaves, when administered as a nasal drop (nasya) with their own expressed juices, destroy even the most violent quartan fever (cāturthika), as well as cough, giddiness, and headache; indeed, this nasal treatment is beneficial for men. (206) One who is afflicted by irregular fever (viṣamajvara) should daily consume a paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil.
He is liberated from intermittent fevers (viṣamajvara) as well as from diseases of wind (vātāmaya) of most terrible form.
(207) One pala each of neem leaves, kuṣṭha, vacā, jaggery, guggulu, mustard seeds, and harītakī, combined with clarified butter—this incense is indeed the destroyer of intermittent fevers. (208)
The root of *surasā*, tied to the hand on an auspicious day,
destroys *velājvara* and other fevers, acting as a warder-off of fever caused by malevolent spirits (209). *Mustā*, *amṛtā*, *āmalakī*, *nāgara*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*—

A decoction combined with powdered *kaṇā* (Pippalī) and likewise mixed with honey, dispels fever occurring every day (*ekāhika*) or at specific times (*velā-ādi*). Furthermore, having removed the seeds of *rasona* (garlic) and cut it into pieces during the nights... [210-211]

Having cast it into buttermilk and consumed it at dawn mixed with ghee, it destroys fevers such as those caused by irregular timing (velājvara) that have entered the bodily tissues. One should also drink milk according to the *pippalī-vardhamāna* method as a rejuvenative elixir (*rasāyana*).

One should drink the great medicine *nāgara*, *dhānyaka*, and *candana-vāluka*, along with *guḍūcī* and milk, which removes tertian fever; likewise, the root of *apāmārga* or even the root of *nīlī*. 214–215.
Having tied a red thread from the navel up to the crown of the head around the left ear and the waist, it destroys tertian fever;
[this is] the divine Vānarendra-mukha, possessing the splendor of the rising sun. 216.
A terrible quotidian fever (jvara) perishes at that very moment.
Listen further: having drawn the form of a monkey with chalk, the best of physicians worship it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and incense. 217–218.

Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ! To Sugrīva, possessed of great strength and prowess, son of the Sun, of immeasurable splendor; [to you who are invoked] against the fevers that occur every day, every two days, every three days, every four days, the great fevers, the fevers caused by spirits, the fear of fever, the fever of anger, the fever of time, and so forth—burn, burn! Cook, cook! Protect, protect! O King of Monkeys, bind, bind the fevers!
Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā! There is no fever. One is protected from fever by this mantra capable of removing fever. 219.
Furthermore, I shall here describe the forms and characteristics of fevers:
appearing like molten gold, with a radiance equal to fire, wearing a sacred thread that seems to float upward, he is fierce and takes the form of a Brahmin. 220–221.

Resembling a hibiscus flower, endowed with fierce fangs, sword in hand, and extremely terrible—such is the Kṣatriya known as Māhendra. Adorned with ornaments of refined gold that shine like the five-fold blossoms [of the *pañcaka*], he is thus described. (222)
The Vaiśya is considered the Lord of Fever (Jvareśvara), holding a staff in his hand and possessing moderate speed.
Likewise, Kāla is considered the Śūdra; he has the appearance of a black cloud or collyrium, possesses sharp fangs and a blazing face, has three eyes, and is radiant like fire. 223–224.
One possessed of sharp impulses, afflicted by hunger, pure, hateful, fond of vows,
with urine resembling the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers, habituated to recitation, excessively talkative,
suffering from frequent breathlessness, overcome by thirst, and oppressed by fierce brahmins. 225.
By performing bathing, recitation, and fire-offerings for him, peace is attained.
(226) One afflicted by a sharp fever, excessive thirst, and passing blood in the urine, who speaks of war and rises up with physical distress— (227)
With burning eyes and heavy breathing, likewise afflicted by hunger,
with honey-scented sweat upon his face, he was oppressed by the Māhendraka Kṣatriya.
At the outset, being pure, one should perform the fire-oblation for the planets and the praise of the deities.
Through activities such as charity and recitation, one attains union with the Siddhas.
(229) One of moderate impulse has a yellowish body, is prone to sleep, and likewise lacks appetite;
he finds heat pleasant when it is cold and windy, has perspiration on the throat, and is extremely agitated. (230)
One who passes urine frequently, is endowed with devotion, observes silence, has yellowish inner eyes,
is not excessively afflicted by thirst, and is gentle— such a person should be known as the Lord of Fever (Jvareśvara).
In that case, one should perform rites for well-being, hospitality, and the worship of the twice-born and the deities.
All rites such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblations (*homa*) should be performed for the sake of pacification.

One who suffers from heart-pain or dysentery should apply a plaster of *matsyagandhā* to the limbs; likewise one who is insane, whose eyes are excessively fixed, or whose organs are impaired during sexual intercourse [should do so]. (232–233)
One who is attached to the path and fearful of it does not desire even a morsel of food;
even for such a Śūdra, with the water-pot of time [as his only wealth], success is not born.
Bathing, charity, recitation, the rite of worshiping the gods, fire-offerings, and the like—[these lead to] satisfaction.
Then, by means of various offerings to the spirits (bhūtas), one should bring about their satisfaction;
through the ritual gift of cows, land, gold, food, and drink, there shall be peace for all, and those who observe the vow of truth proclaim that this is the destruction of all diseases. 235

Just as poison, having gained momentum, dissolves within the internal seat and its power becomes exceedingly aggravated at the proper time, so too does the bodily humor (*doṣa*) act like poison. [One should prescribe] the soup of *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, along with *mudga* and *āḍhakī* beans.
Indeed, the previously mentioned leafy vegetables (śāka) are wind-alleviating (vātaghna).
Śatapuṣpā, jīvantī, taṇḍulīyaka, vāstuka, and bhājikā prepared with ghee—these are the leaves used as vegetables. 237–238.

For one who is ill, one should employ the meat of the common quail (*lāva*) and the partridge (*tittira*), as well as eggplant (*vārttāka*); likewise, the meat of wild animals such as the *mṛgachikkarikā* and other forest-dwelling species should be used.
*Kośātakī*, *paṭola*, and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) are also beneficial. (239)

The best of physicians should avoid split grains, foods that cause burning sensations, and heavy foods (240). Likewise, he should avoid slimy oils as well as sour substances, curd-whey, large quantities of *viśālā*, and small-quantity foods (241).
Having abandoned excessive water, betel, ghee, or even liquor, as well as anger and grief, one indeed always enjoys happiness;
one should not keep a vigil at night and should avoid sleeping during the day. 242–243.

A wise person, who is a treasury for performing auspicious deeds, should always strictly avoid riding in chariots, on horses, or on elephants when suffering from fever; instead, he should quickly eat wholesome food as it becomes available. Furthermore, one should avoid physical exertion, sexual intercourse, eating, and staying awake at night. 244.
One who has been freed from fever should not [indulge in] those [activities]; then he attains well-being.
(245) Thus ends the second chapter, named "The Treatment of Fever," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Three.
Ātreya said:
Now, my dear son, listen to the diagnosis and treatment of diarrhea; the diarrhea born of fever and its treatment are now being taught. 1.

Certain substances are considered to pacify the *doṣas*, certain ones to vitiate the *dhātus*, and certain others are intended for the maintenance of health (*svasthavṛtti*); thus, substance is said to be threefold.
Furthermore, it is based on the path of destiny (*daivapatha*), the path of reasoning (*yuktipatha*), and the conquest of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*).

Recourse to the path of the divine (*daivapatha*) consists of mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, auspicious marks, offerings, oblations, burnt sacrifices (*homa*), observances (*niyama*), expiations (*prāyaścitta*), fasting, rites for well-being (*svastyayana*), and prayers (*praṇidhāna*). Recourse to the path of reason (*yuktipatha*) consists of the application of food, conduct, and medicinal substances. And the conquest of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*) consists of the restraint of the mind from harmful objects.
[Furthermore, one should avoid] food that is oily, excessively cold, heavy, chilled, or slimy, as well as corrupted food, excessive or irregular eating and drinking, and unwholesome edibles.

One may suffer indigestion due to grief, poisons, or fears; or, through the adverse effects of milk spoiled by grief and pain, weakness arises from irregular eating. When this impurity is dissolved in the waters, the fire destroys the indigestion;
yet for that person, diarrhea is born, which, having destroyed the digestive fire of the belly, results in diarrhea. 4–5.

That [fever], moreover, becomes thickened by impurity and is described as being of five types by the sages who know the rules. Briefly stated, its destruction occurs through the application of decoctions and other digestive (pācanaka) remedies for one whose pain has intensified.
When fever and diarrhea arise simultaneously in a person, [it is a grave condition].
This terrible fever accompanied by diarrhea is difficult to cure even for the wise.
Listen, my son: that [diarrhea] does not arise without pitta;
furthermore, fasting is not prescribed for that condition, whether it be fever or diarrhea.
Suvarcala with ativiṣā, hiṅgu, pathyā, and kaliṅgaka, along with śuṇṭhī, destroys diarrhea caused by vāta, cures colic, is constipating, and promotes digestion.
(9) [A preparation] combined with pathyā, dāru, vacā, mustā, nāgara, and ativiṣā...
To destroy diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āmātisāra*), a person should drink a decoction made of these [ingredients]:
blue lotus (*utpala*), coriander (*dhānyaka*), dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *pṛśniparṇī*, and *balā*.
One should then grind young *bilva* fruit together with very warm cow's buttermilk (*takra*). 10–11.
Therefore, having brought and administered cooled parched-rice gruel,

it pacifies fever and diarrhea and bestows strength upon the digestive fire. A decoction of ginger, *viṣā*, *taladhara*, *amṛtā*, *vatsaka*, *tiktāhvaya*, *kanaka*, and *śītalaka* [is likewise beneficial].
Now, for the treatment of fever and diarrhea, this prepared decoction should always be administered.
A decoction of pāṭhā, indrabhū (musta), nimba, ghana (musta), amṛtā, and parpaṭaka is highly recommended here;
it quickly conquers diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āma), as well as that associated with fever, even when severe and chronic. 13–14.
Dry ginger, *bālaka*, *mustā*, *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, *viṣā*, and coriander constitute a digestive formulation for loss of appetite; it destroys vomiting, fever, and diarrhea.
(15) *Vatsaka*, *suradāru*, *rohiṇī*, coriander, *bilva*, *magadhā*, and *trikaṇṭaka* [are likewise used].
A decoction of nimba seeds, gajapippalī, and vṛkī is likewise a medicine for diarrhea (16).
A preparation boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, bilva, guḍūcī, musta, nāgara, pāṭhā, bhūnimba, hrīvera, and the bark and fruit of kuṭaja [is also effective] (17).
Thus, it destroys all types of diarrhea, vomiting, dyspnea, fever, and those afflicted by pain, as well as the terrible diseases caused by Asuras;
furthermore, the five minor roots, which are generally similar, should be employed when pitta is predominant.
The great five roots (mahatī pañcamūlī) are beneficial in fever caused by vāta and kapha.
Blue lotus (utpala), pomegranate bark, saffron, honey, lotus stalk (padmaka), and emblic myrobalan (dhātrī),
ground with rice-water, act as a digestive (pācana) remedy that cures fever and diarrhea.
Uśīra, dhānyaka, musta, bilva, bālaka, balā,
and likewise dhātakī flowers are recommended for a decoction that pacifies fever and diarrhea accompanied by blood and pitta. (21)
It destroys all types of swelling, stimulates the appetite, and acts as a digestive.
22. Aralu, processed by the *puṭapāka* method and taken with honey, pacifies chronic diarrhea that has been long-standing, accompanied by blood, and excessively increased. 23.

One should always prepare a powder from these: Jambū, Vaṭa, Udumbara, Plakṣaka, Nāga, Prapauṇḍarika, Śamī, Gundra, Cūta, and Ambudajīvikā. One should drink two *prasthas* of this until a specific improvement occurs. 24.
Furthermore, one should cook it properly in a cauldron with a paste of dārvī and its own juice until [the consistency is right];
having removed it from the fire, the best of physicians should certainly mix it with honey, and it cures diarrhea.
Thus has Kākamācī been highly praised by Hārīta.
Having consulted numerous treatises, even Ātreya honored [this method]:
having boiled the bark of the *jambū* tree and the inner bark of *vatsaka* in water until one-fourth remains, one should remove it from the fire and then strain it through a cloth. 27–28.
Furthermore, one should cook it properly in a cauldron with a paste of dārvī until its own juice remains;

having removed it while still warm and mixed with honey, when licked, it removes even severe diarrhea. When the sides, the abdomen, the chest, the region of the navel, and the upper part of the body are constantly constricted, [this remedy should be used].
Obstruction of flatus and occasional breaking pain occur in all types of diarrhea.

Those who know the truth declare that in Vata-type diarrhea, the stool is frothy, slimy, dry, scanty, accompanied by the sound of undigested matter and colic, black in color, and involves convulsive movements of the limbs. (30–31)
In the beginning, one should administer fasting alone, or if the condition is mild, no fasting at all; therefore, a decoction should be given,
as well as drinks and food made with the paste of *udīcyadhānya* (coriander) and water, which is beneficial when drunk to pacify diarrhea.

This [decoction] removes thirst, destroys burning sensations, and acts as a destroyer of colic and hiccups. (33) This very decoction—prepared with water and combined with two parts of *bālaka*, one part of *mocā*, and *harītakī* and *parpaṭa*—quickly brings about the cessation of diarrhea and the relief of [abnormal] stools. (34)
Śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, bṛhatī, kaṇṭakārikā, bālā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva fruits, pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka (35)—
this is beneficial when combined with food for all those suffering from diarrhea.
Having taken the bark of *tinduka* wrapped in the leaves of *kāśmarī*,
the physician should coat it with clay according to the prescribed method and burn it over a gentle fire; having extracted the juice and mixed it with honey, this drink cures all types of diarrhea.

Then, having crushed and extracted the juice of *Ārdra-girimallikā* weighing one *tulā*, one should prepare it; once purified, one should add one *pala* of the powder, having ground it together with *śālmalī*.
[The ingredients are: *pāṭhā*, *samaṅgā*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *bilva*, and the flowers of *dhātakī*. 38.
Having added these, one should cook it further until a paste forms on the ladle and its own juice is extracted.
This [medicine], when drunk with water, rice-gruel (maṇḍa), or goat's milk by one who knows the proper time,
destroys all severe types of diarrhea— whether black, white, red, or yellow.

This *Kuṭajāṣṭaka* formulation certainly destroys various disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), as well as hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*), blood-stained hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi saśoṇitāni*), and even incurable forms of menorrhagia (*asṛgdara*). [It is contraindicated] by heat, by eating hot food, and by the consumption of water heated by the sun's heat.
Through grief, heat, or anger, it becomes pungent; through alkaline substances, it extracts the essence of bile and blood.
42. Because of that, [the stool] is reddish, yellow, or very dark blue, accompanied by foul odor, dryness, fever, and jaundice;
along with giddiness, pain, fainting, thirst, and burning in the limbs—these are the symptoms of Pitta-type diarrhea. 43.
A decoction prepared with *śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *balā*, and *bilva*, acidified with pomegranate juice, is beneficial as a drink for the pacification of *pitta*-type diarrhea (44).
[One may also use] water from the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and sugarcane, along with the waters of *śālīna* and *labha*.
The decoction of the roots [of the five grains] is recommended for those suffering from pitta-type diarrhea (45).
The decoction of the roots of the five grains (dhānyapañcaka) is also for those with pitta-type diarrhea (46).
Furthermore, the bark of the root of the śālmalī tree, ground together with jaggery and milk, [is beneficial].
This drink pacifies an excess of *pitta* and removes blood-related burning sensations and emaciation.

(47) Diarrhea caused by *kapha* arises from bad dreams and the like, from fatigue, from innate sluggishness, from exposure to cold, from consuming unctuous food in excessive quantities, from sesame seeds, flour, jaggery, sugarcane pieces, and heavy foods;
and it is produced by an addiction to cold baths, by drinking milk, and by the consumption of food combined with curd.
When the digestive fire in the stomach fails to digest food, it results in the suppression of hunger;

by that, one should know that there arises a thick, foul-smelling, and cold phlegm (śleṣmā), accompanied by loss of appetite, heaviness, horripilation, weak digestion, diminished motility, and a state of lethargy—this is the specific essence arising from kapha. 48–49.
At the outset, having assessed the strength and weakness of the body, fasting (laṅghana) is prescribed;
furthermore, O best of physicians, a digestive (pācana) treatment beginning with the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) should be administered.
Tryūṣaṇa, abhayā, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, rucaka, and vacā [constitute this formulation].
This linctus, taken with honey, would even stop the flow of the river Gaṅgā for men.
(51) A paste made of kāliṅga, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, balā, uśīra, mustā, marica, and śuṇṭhī, mixed with jaggery and honey, is highly recommended for the alleviation of blood-diarrhea caused by kapha. (52)
Vatsaka, ativiṣā, bilva, mustaka, and vālaka, taken together with water as a decoction to be drunk,
destroy excessive colic, blood, and pus in cases of diarrhea accompanied by fever (53).
However, if one observes that the stool is pure, there is purging, and there is excessive drying, burning, and discharge;
This should be known as *raktātisāra* (bloody diarrhea) by physicians of great intelligence.
A decoction consisting of *dhānyaka*, *nāgara*, *mustā*, *vālaka*, *bālabilvaka*, *balā*, and *nāgabalā* is for those suffering from bloody diarrhea.
Having ground pomegranate, wood-apple, Pathyā, rose-apple, and mango sprouts,
they should be administered with whey to ward off bloody diarrhea.
Wood-apple cooked with jaggery should be given to one suffering from bloody diarrhea.

For a person, Pathyā mixed with honey or with curd cures bloody diarrhea (raktātisāra). Furthermore, a paste of Vatsaka, Ativishā, Nāgara, and Abhayā combined with whey (mastu) is recommended as a linctus with honey; it effectively stops even excessive bleeding from the vessels. 57–58.
The powder of *kuṭaja* bark, *pāṭhā*, *viśva*, *bilva*, and *dhātakī*,

when administered with honey, destroys bloody diarrhea (59). [Blood that is] like the color of a boar, like the color of *vāsā*, like the luster of sesame seeds, or resembling the wash-water of meat— [these are the types it cures].
The *sannipāta* [fever] of those suffering from diarrhea resembles a ripe *jambu* fruit.

One should take the juice of fresh *girimallikā*, having crushed it, boiled it, and strained it; when that liquid has been well-purified and measured at one *pala*, one should add [the other ingredients] after grinding them together with *śālmali*. 60–61.

Having added pāṭhā, samaṅgā, ativiṣā, mustā, bilva, and the flowers of dhātakī, one should boil them further until they form a paste as thick as dārvī; this should then be drunk with water, gruel, or honey at the appropriate time. 62.

This *Kuṭajāṣṭaka* formulation certainly destroys all severe and violent disorders—whether black, white, red, or yellow—as well as various defects of the *grahaṇī*, blood, and bile; it also overcomes hemorrhoids accompanied by bleeding and even menstrual disorders that appear incurable. (63–64)
A decoction of *pathyā* and the five roots (*pañcamūla*) is boiled down until one-fourth remains;
into that decoction, one should then add the following medicinal powders: ginger, lac, long pepper, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and so forth.
One should crush the powder of pomegranate rind, dārvī, vatsaka, and viṣa (66), as well as the powders of āṭarūṣaka, and mix them together;
then one should add goat’s milk equal to half that amount and ghee consisting of one-eighth part (67).
Knowing it has been smeared with *dārvī*, sixteen *palas* of jaggery mixed therein should be given before breakfast; this cures severe diarrhea arising from the aggravation of all three *doṣas*. 68.
It is a digestive agent for colic, fainting, vertigo, flatulence, and jaundice (69).
This "Amṛta-vaṭa" is beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds, emaciation, and wasting diseases (70).
It consists of the powder of one part each of bilva, aguru, and rodhra, combined with honey and other ingredients.
This pacifies bloody diarrhea in children whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are depleted. When the secret [discharge] is expelled, then one should perform this treatment:
the juice of *sahacārī* and *balā*, and furthermore, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be taken. 71–72.
An application of cooked ghee is recommended for this;
or a decoction of the sprouts of the *araṇī* tree may be used, or a clod of earth mixed with sandalwood.
Alternatively, having extinguished a clod of earth that has been heated until it resembles fire with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should apply it in the same manner.
One should properly administer an enema for comfort; it is praised when the anus is positioned centrally and secured with a firm bandage.

(74) One should avoid diarrhea that has the smell of garlic or a corpse, or the smell of pus, or is thick like minced meat and water, or resembles ripe jambu fruit, or resembles ghee, honey, or milk, or is dark like oil or algae, or has the color of thick curd. (75)

May that true Creator, who has never been seen, keep far away from him those afflicted by delusion, intoxication, emaciation, colic, fainting, burning sensations, labored breathing, extreme discoloration, vomiting, and thirst; and those suffering excessively from physical impairment,
swelling, fever, and pain— [and likewise] swelling, colic, fever, thirst, dyspnea, cough, and loss of appetite.

One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea upon seeing vomiting, fainting, and hiccups (77). Likewise, one should abandon a patient afflicted by swelling, flatulence, hiccups, vomiting, anorexia, and jaundice, as well as one who suffers from both jaundice and diarrhea (78).
When even the slightest amount of impurity, constantly consumed in small doses, reaches the seat of the genitals and,

having abandoned the internal fire, causes a disorder in a person, they call that by the name *grahaṇī*. Once the diarrhea has ceased, it further extinguishes the digestive heat, even though it is provoked by the humors (*doṣas*).

Having consumed food that contains impure portions and having accumulated it incessantly over many days, it emerges; repeatedly seizing that which is innate, crooked, ripening, or dense, this terrible disease of a formidable form causes pain to a person—such is *grahaṇī*. 80.
One should observe diarrhea and recognize it as *grahaṇī-gada* (malabsorption syndrome),
which may be of the *vātika*, *paittika*, *śleṣmika*, or *sānnipātika* type; indeed, the disease of *grahaṇī* does not arise from a single *doṣa* alone.
By that, the body is emaciated and internal burning arises as its maturation.

[The pitta is increased] by those who consume bitter, astringent, pungent, sour, and burning foods, and by those who are dry, eat little, or follow a cold diet; and by physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and the running of elephants, chariots, or horses while carrying heavy loads on the road; and by the suppression of the provoked wind (vāyu) and the forceful retention of fire (analavega). 82–83.
Therefore, when that [wind] is cut by the wind and joined with blood, it undergoes maturation;

thus a third type of disease arises in a person known as *gulma*, and that became fivefold: enlargement of the spleen (*plīhā*), enlargement of the liver (*yakṛt*), abdominal itching (*jaṭhara-kaṇḍu*), obstruction of waste (*malabandha*), and the stone-like growth (*aṣṭhīlā*) caused by worms (*krimi*); then the sixth is the arising of abdominal diseases (*jaṭhararoga*).
These are the transformations of *grahaṇī* that become terrible and cause suffering in a person’s mind:

dryness of the throat, darkness before the eyes, pain in the sides, extreme emaciation in the navel, severe choleric vomiting (*ativiṣūcikā*), ringing in the ears, excessive vomiting, exhaustion, pain, delusion, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*) due to dyspnea—know these indeed to be its symptoms. 85–86.
The wise know that one who possesses these symptoms has *gulma*; now I shall describe the characteristics of that which is called *grahaṇī*, which is curable.
In this condition, one voids stool that is varied in color and accompanied by sound; there is swelling, and the wind makes the stool exceedingly dry.
Accompanied by labored breathing and physical debility, there is discharge from the *grahaṇī* due to the provocation of Vāyu (88).
When the stool is mixed, burning, decomposed, painful, afflicted with thirst, and foul-smelling, yellow, reddish, blue, or black, it is known as *grahaṇī* arising from Pitta (89).

Heartburn, vomiting, labored breathing, swelling, coughing, numbness, coldness, a bad taste in the mouth, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and stiffness of the temples and retention of feces—
these are declared to be the symptoms when [the doshas] are combined in groups of three; or alternatively, sweetness in the mouth may indicate the provocation of this [disease].
Burning sensation, fainting, labored breathing, and numbness—this is the disease of *sannipāta-grahaṇī*.
(91) Dāru, nāgara, niśā, vāsaka, kuṇḍalī, māgadhajā, śaṭhī, ghana, rāsnā, bhārṅgī, saralā, and puṣkara constitute a digestive (*pācana*) formulation for the seizure caused by *vāta*. (92)

The root of *nalaveṇu*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and *ikṣu*, taken as a decoction, is beneficial for this patient; it is a digestive aid in cases of *pittaja* seizure (93). [Likewise,] *vyāghrī*, *granthika*, *cavya*, *surasā*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *dāḍima* [are also used].
Rajanī and ghanacitraka likewise destroy hiccup, kapha, and disorders of the grahaṇī.

(94) Furthermore, one should employ a powder of śuṇṭhī, kaṇā, dvirajanī, and ghanasatva, along with prativiṣā, triphalā, viḍaṅga, rock salt, citraka, the three pungents (trikaṭu), and the three aromatics (trisugandhi); this powder, combined with jaggery and mixed with ghee, [is effective]. (95)

Having prepared it in the measure of a cat's footprint, one should eat it along with modakas; it cures even water-retention in cases of *grahaṇī*, as well as hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, loss of appetite, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, colic, stones, worms, and old age.
It removes anemia (pāṇḍu) and is the best elixir (*rasāyana*); it destroys debility, acts as an aphrodisiac, bestows strength, and cures the defect of extreme emaciation.
It always bestows excellence of complexion, strength of the senses, and complete luster; it destroys disease and removes leprosy and vertigo.

(97) A wise person, knowing the proper procedure, should cook five hundred *harītakī* fruits with one *droṇa* of cow urine over a gentle fire until the urine is entirely consumed. Once the urine has been fully digested, [the physician] skilled in the rules should proceed according to the injunctions. (98)

Having extinguished [the fire], dried it in powder, and once cooled, having split the seeds after they have been dried in the shade, one should take the powder along with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *magadhā*, *viṣā*, fragrant *mūrvā*, and *cavikā*. Having boiled these as a paste of *kuṭaja* until it becomes thick enough to coat the stirring ladle. 99.
Having churned jaggery with half that amount [of the liquid], one should add milk with half of that again, or goat's milk;

having cooled it and placed it in a vessel of ghee, one should then mix it with a powder of rock salt, the three fiery spices (trikaṭu), and the three aromatics (trisugandhi), along with more jaggery and blended with ghee. 100–101.
By means of that powder, there is the immediate destruction of all disorders of the *grahaṇī*, jaundice, consumption, urinary calculi, worms, abdominal tumors, and diarrhea;
as well as splenic enlargement, liver disease, asthma, cholera, chronic catarrh, and pain in the head in human beings;
likewise, it destroys fevers and the exhaustion of strength caused by the fatigue of travel or abdominal ailments.
This electuary, beginning with *abhayā*, destroys fevers such as those occurring every day; for men, it is like nectar.
Thus ends the *Abhayādyo'valeha*.
Having cooked grapes with milk until it becomes thick and can be smeared by a ladle, [it is prepared].
Having seen [the symptoms], the wise physician should then mix these medicinal herbs:
104 parpaṭa, ativiṣā, mūrvā, paṭola, ghana, and vālaka;
likewise, he should add a powder of abhayā together with an equal amount of sugar. 105
Having combined that with milk and the bulb of the vidārī plant, one should then form a bolus with ghee and fresh butter and consume it;
this removes bile disorders, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, jaundice, affliction, and thirst. (106)

It certainly and quickly destroys vertigo, fainting, hiccups, fainting (tamas), insanity, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, hemorrhaging, and skin diseases. Thus ends the *Drākṣādikṣīra* (Milk with Grapes, etc.).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diarrhea," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Four.
Ātreya said:
Listen, my son, I shall explain the characteristics of the abdominal tumors (gulma), as well as their remedies and specific medicinal treatments. These five types of tumors arise within the abdomen.
The heart, the belly, the navel, the bladder, and the fifth is said to be the middle [of the body].
That which resides in the heart is named *yakṛt*; that which is in the belly is called *aṣṭhīlaka*; in the middle it is designated as *plīhā*; and in the bladder it is the *caṇḍavivṛddhaka*.
A distinct knot is perceived at the navel in these [diseases], each one separate from the others;
therefore, I shall describe their provocation by which they cause affliction.
When arising from pitta and blood due to their own nature, [the disease is provoked] by the consumption of sour and burning substances.
Through the excessive consumption of hot or alkaline liquor, or by the overuse of warm drinks; likewise, through grief, fatigue from travel, dehydration, and agitation;
and by loud speaking, singing, and the drawing of bowstrings—(5–6).
Blood is dried up in the heart by being struck with a fist, by a blow to the chest, or even by lifting heavy weights;
because of that, the condition known as *raktapittaja-gulma* arises.
Sometimes its occurrence is seen to arise from three doshas:
impelled by vāta, thickened by kapha, and brought to a state of ripening by pitta; thus it is a combination of all three doshas in the liver (yakṛt). 8–9.
I shall describe its symptoms by which it is recognized, and that by which a person quickly meets death through exhaustion:
vomiting, fatigue, belching, nausea, labored breathing, and dizziness. (10)
Burning sensation, loss of appetite, thirst, fainting, burning in the throat, headache,
pain in the heart, catarrh, spitting along with bitter tastes, piercing pain in the chest, loss of sleep, and delirium [are the symptoms]. 11–12.
One should recognize [the disease] located within the chest cavity of the liver by these signs: there is a sense of hardness in the heart, and the abdomen rumbles excessively.
If one takes Trikaṭu, Kuṣṭha, Pañcamūla, and Yavānī directly—
One should consume a fine powder of the sixth [ingredient] mixed with *sindhūttha* (rock salt) along with asafoetida; thereafter, one should drink buttermilk or drink water boiled and then acidified.
This, or *sauvīraka* (sour gruel), quickly destroys liver disorders, abdominal enlargement, colic, and cough. (14)

This powder of ginger and other ingredients (śuṇṬhyādi-cūrṇa) quickly destroys cholera, indigestion, diseases of phlegm, the pain of piles, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Alkali (kṣāra) made from *muṣkaka*, *kiṃśuka*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, *apāmārga*, *rambhā*, sesame, *jīvantī*, *kanakāhvaya*, and turmeric likewise acts swiftly.

Likewise, the *kūṣmāṇḍa* creeper, as well as *vāsā* and *sūraṇa*, should be set ablaze with a fierce fire and reduced to ashes; having consumed this with water, one should then drink quieted milk to treat liver disease (*yakṛt*). 16.

Likewise, it conquers diseases born of phlegm such as colic, abdominal distension, and constipation; it overcomes jaundice, abscesses, heart pain, anemia, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), edema, and hemorrhoids; as well as chronic rhinitis, weak digestion, indigestion, worms, lassitude, prolapse of the rectum, and fainting. Furthermore, by this [treatment], vomiting characterized by a burning sensation and pain, accompanied by a foul-smelling, excessively putrid discharge resembling pus, falls away from the chest. 17. Phlegm that resembles pus, having a putrid odor and being very offensive, falls out.
There, appearing reddish, he voids blood repeatedly;
likewise, he suffers from bloody diarrhea, his strength wanes, and his body is emaciated. Blood flows through his limbs, and it has spread to his liver and chest.
Dyspnea, thirst, vomiting, delusion, swelling of the hands and feet, loss of appetite, and diarrhea—these occur in Yakṛddūṣa; one should abandon such a patient.
(20) Therefore, I shall describe the remedy by which well-being is attained.
For that [condition], first fasting alone is prescribed, and immediately thereafter, digestive treatment (pācana).

A decoction or paste of ginger (śuṇṭhī), long pepper (upakulyā), black pepper (timira), costus (śaṭhī), yavānikā, abhīru, and harītakī is recommended as a digestive remedy for abdominal distension, gulma-pain, and choleraic disorders (viṣūcikā). 21–22.

Bhadra, upakulyā, abhayā, śṛṅgavera, and tribhāgā, with kaṇā as the fourth part (23)—this powder, combined with hiṅgu, is beneficial for that patient; it should not be given to one suffering from chest wounds, consumption, liver disease, or those who have fasted, but rather serves as a digestive aid. (24)

A decoction of nimba, nīpa, vetasa, niśā, kāśmarī, tulasī, and siṃhikā indeed removes heart disease, quickly alleviates colic, and destroys liver ailments. Saurāṣṭrī, sīsa, mahauṣadha, durālabhā, jāti, and pravālaka— these [are likewise used].
A decoction of dārvī, yavānī, kakubha, and samaṅgā, taken with ghee, quickly destroys [the disease]; 26.
Having boiled dhava, arjuna, kadamba, śirīṣa, and badarī, drinking this destroys undigested matter (āmadoṣa) and wards off colic in viṣūcī. 27.
Taking either the alkali of plantain or the alkali of conch shell,
one should drink it with water mixed with asafoetida and sauvarcala salt;
this quickly removes undigested matter (āma) when it has been expelled and swiftly subdues colic pain.
It pacifies cholera and even digests indigestion.
One should take the juice of *mātuluṅga* with double the amount of sour gruel (*kāñjika*), combined with asafoetida and *sauvarcala* salt; this drink destroys cholera. 29–30.

One should cook alkaline water over a fire for drinking; it quickly destroys pain and flatulence and stimulates the digestive fire. In cases of undigested matter (āma), one should administer emetics, and once the matter has been digested, fasting (laṅghana) should be performed.
Specialized sudation is beneficial for sleep; purgation is indicated when there is residual rasa.
Day-sleep is beneficial in cases of insanity, diarrhea, those afflicted by vomiting and anger, indigestion, and viṣūcī fever. (32-33)
One should avoid daytime sleep when there is an excess of phlegm (śleṣman), heart disease, headache, nausea, or catarrh.
One should likewise avoid the three fruits (triphalā), the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), karañja seeds, meat broth, pomegranate, and citron.
A wick made from these ground together with *niśā* (turmeric) and used as an ointment destroys *viṣūcikā*.
35 *Rāsnā*, *viśālā*, fragrant *kuṣṭha*, *śigru*, *vacā*, *nāgaraka*, *śatāhvā*, *āgneyī*, *piṣṭā*, *ahapuṣā*, and *vidārī*, when ground together, ward off *khallī* and *viṣūcī*. 36
Sudation should be applied to the patient using a single pot filled with warm water and covered with a cloth;
likewise, pouring warm water over the hands will conquer cholera (visūcī) and diseases of the stomach.
Sulfur, rock salt, and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), rubbed together with lime juice, [should be used].
The afflicted person should quickly consume this remedy for the alleviation of *viṣūcī*.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gulma," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Five.
Ātreya said:
"Worms are said to be of two kinds, arising externally and internally. The external ones are well known as lice (*yūka*), while the internal ones are the *kiñcaka*s."
The external [impurity] is of seven kinds, while that which arises internally is of six kinds;
I shall describe the production of these among men, both external and internal.
[It arises] from dryness, excessive impurity, perspiration, anxiety, and even from grief.
Indeed, lice arise from the phlegm constituent (kapha-dhātu). There are sharp lice; some are black, others white, and the third kind resides in the skin.
Subtle, extremely deformed, and rough, they are called carmabhā; the one that stays on the skin is the carmayūki.
The fourth is named Bindukī, round and born from urine; the fifth is Matkuṇā, who causes external afflictions. Yūkā resides on the head; she is white and dwells upon the head.
Leather-lice [arise] on the eyelids; a stick-like growth occurs on fine body hair.

[These are caused] by dry food, barley-based meals, wheat flour, or molasses; by the absence of milk products, by sleeping during the day, by oily substances, by heat, and by the consumption of heated water.
By that [process], a swarm of worms is generated in the seats of impurity, causing disorders within the digestive tract.
They are declared to be of six types; I shall describe their characteristics.
The seat of phlegm (kapha) is the receptacle for waste; they crawl through the digestive tract like serpents.
Some have broad heads, some resemble jackets, some resemble grain-sprouts, and some are subtle and atomic in size;
they should be known as needle-mouthed, for they pierce the intestines.
I shall describe their characteristics and their treatment; listen to me.
Fever, heart disease, colic, vomiting, moisture in the heart, vertigo, loss of appetite, discoloration, and frothy diarrhea [are the symptoms]. 12.

In one afflicted by *kiñcuka* [poison], rumbling occurs in the abdomen, weak digestion arises, and there is thirst; the eyes become yellowish, the intestines are pricked as if by needles, and blood is discharged in diarrhea. (13)
Others may eat the liver, or vomit blood profusely;
a discharge from the mouth, loss of appetite, numbness, weak digestion, trembling, hunger, thirst, and fever are to be known as the symptoms of the pain caused by *sūcīmukha* worms. (14–15)
And as for those sprouts of grain, I shall now describe their characteristics:
worms residing in the seat of impurity devour that impurity excessively;
by them, the body is afflicted with emaciation, abscesses, various skin diseases, and roughness.
By that [wind], pain in the limbs, moistening of the heart, and barley-shaped worms are produced.
Hārīta, overcome with doubt, grasped [the sage’s] feet and asked:
"How is it that in the body of a human being there is a reservoir for impurities, urine, and fluids?"

How do they first come into being, and how do they increase again? And when the essence of food has decayed through the consumption of various kinds of food, by what means are worms produced—whether they be subtle or those that move downwards? (19)
"The fire does not burn various kinds of raw and cooked foods;
how is it that those worms are not burned at the end by the internal fire?
Thus questioned, the great teacher, the bull among sages, replied.
Ātreya said:
Listen, O mighty-armed son, to the cause of the origin of worms; by the juices of incompatible foods, my son, his blood becomes provoked. 22
By means of *kapha* it passes for one day, and by means of *śukra* it goes to its source;
in this body composed of the five elements, those [semen and blood] have arisen as sentient beings.
They are not consumed by the digestive fire of the stomach, nor do they decay, for they are the essence.
Just as a worm born within poison does not meet death by that poison,
so too that which has arisen from fire is not consumed by fire.
I shall now declare the remedy by which even they indeed cross over.
They either fall out or become pacified; listen to my [remedy].

(26) Vaca, ajamoda, krimijit, palāśa seeds, śaṭhī, rāmaṭha, and trivṛt—having ground these together with warm water, one should drink it; they will quickly fall out by the hundreds, rendering the teeth sound. (27)
Having ground together śaṭī, yavānī, picumanda, putrā, viḍaṅga, kṛṣṇā, and ativiṣā with the juice [of these] and with urine, combined with trivṛt, it is the destroyer of all worms and diseases.
(28) Marica, pippalīmūla, viḍaṅga, śigruja, vānikā, and trivṛt...
Ground with cow urine, this should be drunk; it quickly destroys worms.
(29) A paste of mustā, viśālā, triphalā, suparṇī, śigru, and surāhvā taken with water, along with the powder of kṛṣṇā and krimiśatru, is a destroyer of all worms and their afflictions. (30)

Surasā, suradāru, māgadhī, viḍaṅga, kampilla, dantinī, trivṛt, tāla, and rasonaka, when consumed with water, remove worms and heart disease (31). The roots of mātuluṅga, rasona, krimijit, and trivṛt [likewise act as vermifuges].
One should grind ajamodā and nimba leaves with cow’s urine;
this drink is praised for warding off the affliction of worms.
One should also administer the wholesome diets prescribed for fever in cases of worm-infestation.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, named "The Treatment of Worms," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Six.
Ātreya said:

Fire is said to be of four types: balanced (*sama*), irregular (*viṣama*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), and dull (*manda*); now hear their characteristics. Due to the equilibrium of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, the fire becomes balanced (*sama*).
When these [humors] become thus imbalanced, a discordant fire arises:
through the predominance of sharp pitta, the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) becomes intense;
through the predominance of vāta and śleṣman, it becomes known as weak (manda).
That which, being situated in its natural state, digests the mass of food, is called "equal" (sama); it is faultless and increases all the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Sometimes it digests food only slightly, and at other times it leaves it undigested.
He does not suffer from irregularity of wind, nor even from cholera;
by nature he bathes excessively, yet finds no satisfaction;
his eyes are always burning and yellow, and his sharp [digestive fire] indeed causes the destruction of strength.

That which one is unable to eat at all, due to the predominance of the strength of phlegm (śleṣman), is also known as *mandānala*; it is considered primarily characterized by abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and enlargement of the abdomen (*udararoga*).
When [the humors] are equal, there is equilibrium in the body through the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), strength, and the sense organs.

The man remains joyful, with his limbs fully restored and active. However, in the case of an imbalance, disorders such as those caused by Vāta and the other humors, chronic diarrhea (grahaṇī), dysentery (atisāra), splenic enlargement,
abdominal tumors (gulma), cholera-like illness (viṣūcī), and conditions known as colic (śūla) and upward-moving wind (udāvarta) may arise.
Due to the irregular digestive fire (viṣamāgni), constipation and sluggishness of movement arise;
both vāta and kapha become depleted, while pitta becomes intense.
One finds pleasure in eating, and what has been eaten is indeed digested. 10.

By that [cause], the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) arises with the designation of "ash-maker" (*bhasmaka*). Furthermore, there occur anemia (*pāṇḍu*), bilious diarrhea (*pittātisāra*), consumption (*rājayakṣmā*),
chlorosis (*halīmaka*), vertigo (*bhrama*), exhaustion (*klama*), extreme debility, enlargement of the liver (*yakṛt*), and urinary disorders (*prameha*).
Pain in the vital organs, fainting, internal hemorrhaging, acidic bile, and difficulty in urination occur;
by these his body is emaciated and a craving for food arises.
Wooden sticks and stones, when eaten, are digested within the body of that person.
Thus has been declared the etiology that provokes the digestive fire (agni) in a person;
although it could have been described in many ways, it has not been stated here for fear of excessive length.
Therefore, I shall now describe the remedies individually and concisely.
It is indeed digestive, pacifying, and furthermore, an appetizer. 16.

A powder made of rāsnā, śaṭhī, prativiṣā, surasā, śuṇṭhī, rock salt (sindhūttha), asafoetida (hiṅgu), pippalī (magadhā), and suvarcalā, when consumed as a sweetmeat with jaggery, equalizes the irregular digestive fire caused by vāta. 17.
In cases of colic, indigestion, irregular digestion, and cholera, this [decoction] of Vāta and the other humors shall destroy all types of abdominal tumors (gulma).
One should drink it lukewarm immediately after eating; likewise, it is excellent when followed by a meal containing all six tastes. 18.
Drākṣā, Abhayā, Tiktarohiṇī, Vidārī, Candana, and Vāsaka— [The above constitutes the first group of drugs.]
Mustā, paṭola, kirātatikta, pippalī, balā, vikacā,

viṣāṇā, palāla, vaṅgāla, padmaka, bhṛṅgī, and dhanikā— these should be combined in equal parts as a powder and mixed with dates and sugar, along with an amount of ghee equal to half the weight of the medicinal herbs. 19–20.
A person should consume it with milk in the morning; having prepared it as a decoction, it should be taken with ghee.

It acts like a powerful digestive fire, certainly bestows nourishment upon the emaciated, and indeed destroys fatigue, dizziness, and wasting, while pacifying thirst and excessive greed. 21. It serves to eliminate exhaustion, vertigo, and consumption, and brings about the quelling of thirst and voracious appetite.
Blood-bile (raktapitta), wasting disease (kṣaya), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), jaundice (halīmaka), and jaundice (kāmalā) will quickly perish.
For the wise, having roasted two parts of red śāli rice and finely grinding them, they should be mixed with half as much sesame. 22–23.
Having fried mung beans equal in amount to that [rice] and combined them together, one should cook them properly;
once the *kṛśara* is prepared, one should serve it with ghee. For one who eats this with a single day's interval between meals, even a severe digestive fire is extinguished. 24–25.

Harītakī possesses six qualities equal to those of Hari and Hara; when combined with four parts of twenty-four large pippalīs, along with citraka, asafoetida, and rock salt, this elixir kindles the digestive fire like that of King Kuru. Having increased the portions of ajamoda, citraka, harītakī, and viḍaṅga respectively, they should be used as a powder.
Take one *karṣa* each of extremely sour vetasa, kola, pomegranate, and tamarind (27);
and these others in equal parts: *jājī*, *varāṅga*, and *suvarcala* in portions of one *karṣa* each, along with one hundred *kaṇās* (long pepper) and half that amount of black pepper (28).
Having finely powdered four *palas* of sugar, one should rub it on the abdomen and then eat it; this produces appetite, overcomes constipation, splenic pain, and cough (29),
destroys asthma, cures heart disease, and serves to purify disorders of the tongue and throat.

This powder, known as *yavānikākhaṇḍavikā*, is indeed an inflamer for those with disorders of the seizing-grasper (*grāhagrahaṇī*) and hemorrhoids, and for those with weak digestive fire (30). It is highly praised as a pacifier for various types of anorexia (31).
[One should also take] a gruel (*yavāgū*) of the five spices (*pañcakola*), along with horse-gram (*kulattha*), *āḍhakī* beans, and *pūṣaka*.
A proper meal of cooked grains with mung bean soup is beneficial;
likewise, a side dish enriched with asafoetida and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) is highly recommended, being as excellent as agasti-ghee even for those suffering from a loss of appetite.
Kāravella, paṭola, onion, sūraṇa, śaṭhī, salt, coriander, and the excellent praleha made from the three pungents (kaṭutrika);
śaṭhī, mustard, vāstuka, śatapuṣpā, and kāñcanamācikā.

The leafy vegetable made from the roots of *tuṇḍīraka* is praised as the best; likewise, wheat cakes fried over glowing coals are excellent for one suffering from loss of appetite. Furthermore, the most eminent physician should prescribe the meat of wild animals for such a patient.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Weak Digestive Fire," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Seven.
Ātreya said:
Through physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, staying awake at night, sexual intercourse, grief, excessive carrying of loads, walking, running, and the fatigue thereof;
through irregular drinking and sleeping, and through cold food, the Vāyu becomes aggravated and produces strength [in its deranged state]. [The following grains cause obstruction:
Viṣṭambhin, Rūkṣa, barley (yava), black gram (māṣa), horse gram (kalāya), green gram (mudga), niṣpāva, kārpāsa-seed, kodrava, and masūra.
Due to the consumption of wheat, small quantities of phlegm-inducing foods, and dry meals, as well as by the obstruction of excrement and the retention of urine,
the wind (vāyu), having ascended its downward path and reaching its root, becomes characterized by wind and possesses internal fire;
thus, being provoked by this intensity, it causes pain in the forearm even when the anal passage is obstructed.
O Great-minded One, even on the body of a man afflicted by the pain of wind (vāta), there occurs a cessation of pricking sensations, yet he remains stained and extremely wretched;
this arises from the causes of anger, heat, and exposure to fire, as well as from grief, fear, affliction, running, and engagement in unwholesome practices,
along with alkaline substances, acids, wine, pungents, hot things, burning agents, dry foods, pickles, dried meat, scratching, and black mustard.
Stirred by the wind (vāyu), that pitta becomes agitated and causes intense pain in the abdomen of the person;
by it, there arises burning of the limbs, loss of appetite, fever, thirst, distress, and fainting, while the humor burns within the navel and the mouth turns yellowish.
This occurs through lack of exercise, consumption of ununctuous food, and through greed for food such as sugarcane, oil, and milk.
By means of these practices— eating little, sleeping, and indulging in [these] things— one aggravates the phlegm (śleṣman).
When excessively consumed with black gram (māṣa), very cold milk, curd, very cold fish, and the flesh of marshy animals,
the phlegm quickly pacifies the digestive fire (anala) and produces a violent disorder in the person's abdominal cavity (koṣṭha), causing colic (śūla).
Nausea, cough, vomiting, lassitude, heaviness of the head, a sense of numbness, coldness of the body, and looseness of the joints;
salivation after eating, a sweet taste in the mouth, and likewise a pleasant, glossy face—he in whom these appear has a disorder of *kapha*.
Indeed, when these symptoms occur, it is *śleṣmā* (phlegm), and that [condition] is accompanied by pain.
Those people say that when one's [symptoms] are as if associated with pitta, even during indigestion (ajīrṇa),
there is pain in the heart, throat, and flanks; however, kapha associated with pitta causes pain in the region between the heart and the navel,
while that which moves restlessly in the bladder, the navel, and the region of the lower abdomen arises from vāta and pitta.
Even a single [dosa] is easily curable; a combination of two is cured with difficulty; but that which arises from all three dosas is incurable, being accompanied by many complications.
Provoked by its etiological factors, the Vayu moves within the abdomen.
Thus, the designation "ten" is proclaimed for the types of *śūla*.
Three are to be known as arising from Vāta and the other [doshas] individually, while three more arise from combinations of two (*dvandvaja*).
Furthermore, there are two—*sāmānya* and *nirāmaka*—and these eight are remembered as the types of *śūla*. (13–14)
The ninth is said to be caused by indigestion (ajīrṇa), and the tenth arises from the transformation of food (pariṇāma);
thus, colic occurs in ten ways in human beings.
That which occurs after eating should also be known as being of the nature of phlegm (kapha).
That which occurs when food has been digested should be known as arising from the transformation (pariṇāmaja).

One who knows the procedure recognizes that distension, upward obstruction, yawning, trembling, cleansing [of the mouth], vomiting, a greasy mouth, excessive salivation, and pain due to wind (vāta) are experienced. (16–17)

Burning sensation, delusion, thirst, painful urination, a bitter taste in the mouth, excessive perspiration, and parchedness of the face— these the wise declare to be the symptoms of that which is of the nature of *pitta*.
(18) Likewise, vomiting, cough, dyspnea, delusion, laziness, drowsiness, stupor, and extreme coldness [are the signs of *kapha*].

O best of physicians, that which is of the nature of *kapha* is known as the colic born of two humors (*dvaṃdvaja*). When caused by all three humors, it is *tridoṣaja*. Thus, including that caused by blood, eleven types have been described.
Those for whom symptoms of the *pitta*-nature arise, and for whom there is vomiting of blood—[these are the signs]. 19–20.
Emaciation, thirst, burning sensation, as well as cough, dyspnea, hemorrhage, and excessive pain—21.
There is no pain without vāta, no vertigo without pitta, no vomiting without kapha, and no darkness (fainting) without rakta. 22.
Thus, I shall now describe the thorough knowledge of colic and its medicinal treatment,
by which the sufferer of colic pain attains relief through the pacification of that pain.
Upon observing colic, one should administer fasting, digestive stimulants, purgation, emesis, or sudation.
One should administer alkaline powder for the relief of pain through drinking or massage in a person suffering from cough and flatulence (24).

A decoction of hiṅgu, nāgara, śaṭhī, suvarcala, dāru, pauṣkara, ghana, and apunarnavā is beneficial for those with colic, as it is both digestive and helpful for those suffering from abdominal enlargement and gulma (25).
Likewise, a decoction of asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), lotus stalks (*pauṣkara*), *śaṭhī*, and *suvarcala* is beneficial for those suffering from colic;
it is praised for alleviating Vata-type colic and is declared to be a digestive stimulant (*pācana*).

(26) A powder made by grinding rock salt (*sindhūttha*), asafoetida, black salt (*rucaka*), *śaṭhī*, *yavānī*, and chebulic myrobalan (*pathyā*) in equal parts with alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*) [is also recommended].
This should be administered lukewarm; it destroys colic of a Vata-nature, or even other types of colic, before long.
(27) Hingu, sauvarcala salt, pathyā, yavānī, punarnavā, balā, eraṇḍa, the two types of bṛhatī, tuvara, and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) combined [should be used]. (28)
A decoction or a powder containing kṣāra and sauvarcala salt immediately destroys colic caused by vāta and acute viṣūcikā; likewise,
[a powder of] tumburu, pauṣkara, hiṅgu, yavānī, and tryūṣaṇa, combined with three times the amount of bṛhatī.

This powder of the eight salts (lavaṇāṣṭaka-cūrṇa) is rightly capable of warding off colic. A decoction of castor root, ginger, suvarcalā, and asafoetida destroys the mass of colic arising from Vāta. Indeed, asafoetida combined with harītakī, vacā, indrayava, ginger, water, and suvarcalā destroys colic. 30–31.
Asafoetida, ginger, vacha, yavani, both types of haritaki, trivrit, vidanga,
devadaru, chavya, tumburu, kushtha, mustaka,
hapusha, kalashi, rasna, vatsaka, and durala-bha. (32)

One should mix together in equal parts white sugar, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *lāṅgalī*, the five kinds of *jīraka*, *puṣkara*, *tintiḍīka*, *vṛkṣāmla*, *amlavetasa*, the two types of alkali (*kṣāra*), and the five salts. (33–34)
Having given one application of impregnation with urine and dried in the shade,
one should then impregnate it with the juice of *bījapūraka* for three days;
one should administer a dose the size of a cat's paw for the alleviation of colic.

A decoction of triphalā mixed with sugar, taken with wine, is recommended for diseases of phlegm (kapha) when accompanied by wind (vāta), as well as for colic, abdominal distension, constipation, weak digestion, abdominal tumors (gulma),
and abscesses (vidradhi). (36–37)
It destroys the accumulation of bodily humors in those suffering from splenic enlargement, anemia, and especially fever, just as a wind disperses a mass of clouds.
(38) Having processed equal parts of *dhātrī* fruit, iron powder, *pathyā*, and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) together, one should [use it].
Or, in the case of colic accompanied by bile (pitta-śūla), one should administer the powder of pomegranate and citron enriched with sugar (verse 39).
One should prepare a powder of *biḍālaka*, pomegranate, *pūtanā*, and *dhātrī*;
having impregnated it with the juice of citron, one should consume it to alleviate colic associated with bile (verse 40).
One should drink *jīvantī* with ghee, or milk mixed with sugar;

purgation should be administered daily to alleviate bile-induced colic (41). One should immerse oneself in cool, refreshing water, apply sandalwood paste to the center of the forehead, and sleep during the nights.
Gold, silver, bell-metal, lotus, gold, and snow— prepared according to the prescribed method for the root cause of a Pitta-type fever (42)—
along with parched rice from white *śāli* grain, milk mixed with sugar and honey,
immediately destroys burning sensations, Pitta-fever, vomiting, and colic pain (43).
Meat from wild animals is recommended for food; ghee and milk mixed with sweet substances are praised for those suffering from pitta-type colic (pitta-śūla).
For those suffering from kapha-type colic (kapha-śūla), fasting, emesis, and digestive stimulants are indicated.
One should not consume very thick or excessively sweet foods, nor should one indulge in excessive sleep.

(45) A decoction made from equal parts of bilva, agnimantha, vṛṣa, citraka, nāgara, eraṇḍa, hiṅgu, and rock salt (saindhava) instantly destroys colic arising from kapha and immediately increases the digestive fire. (46)
The juice of *mātuluṅga*, the juice of *dhātrī* combined with rock salt (*saindhava*),
and the juice of the root of *śobhāñjanaka* mixed with black pepper (47), when combined with alkali and honey, is a remedy for phlegmatic colic (*śleṣma-śūla*).
It undoubtedly destroys cough arising from the destruction of [vitiated] tissues (kṣaya). 48.
A powder consisting of Tuvaraka, Granthika, Eraṇḍa, Vyōṣa, Pathyā, and Ajamōdaka, combined with alkali and salt, is used for pain caused by Kapha. 49.

A decoction made from castor root, bilva, the two types of bṛhatī, mātuluṅga, pāṣāṇabheda, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), and radish, mixed with alkali, vermilion, salt, and oil, should be applied to the hips, thighs, penis, heart, breasts, and abdomen. [50] Also, the leaves of paṭola and ariṣṭa combined with triphalā.
A drink consisting of a decoction mixed with honey is beneficial for pain caused by Pitta and Vāta;
it wards off Pitta-fever, thirst, burning sensations, and Raktapitta. Durālabhā, Parpaṭaka, Viśvā, Paṭola, Nimba, Ambuda, and Tintiḍīka [are used for this purpose].
This paste, mixed with sugar, should be administered for the pacification of colic arising from pitta and vāta.

(53) This powder, consisting of *sauvarcala* salt, *śaṭī*, and *nāgara*, when drunk with water boiled with *śuṇṭhī*, destroys colic associated with vāta and kapha; it is highly recommended for severe pain in the flanks, abdominal disorders, impaired digestion, and heart disease. (54)

A decoction of *dāru*, *nāgaraka*, *vāsā*, *hiṅgu*, and *sauvarcala* salt is used for pain caused by *vāta* and *kapha*, as well as for indigestion (*āma*), chronic digestive disorders (*jīrṇa*), and constipation (*vibandha*).
[55] [The same applies to a decoction of] *palāśa*, *kadalī*, *vāsā*, *pāmārga*, and *kokilāhvaya*.

That [preparation], boiled with cow's urine and combined with asafoetida and ginger, is beneficial for colic born of the three doṣas, as well as for jaundice and constipation; it pacifies abdominal tumors and abdominal enlargements, and restores the digestive fire in those with weak digestion. (56–57)
Even a single *kuberākṣa* alone removes all colic;
how much more so when it is combined with the three— *pathyā*, *arucikara*, and *āmaṭha* (58)— along with conch-ash, salt, asafoetida, and the three pungents (*vyoṣa*).
That [mixture], when drunk with warm water, destroys colic born of the three doṣas.
Lightening therapy, emesis, purgation, unctuous enema, and decoction enema—
these are the applications of basti-karma for colic arising from the three doṣas in its stage of digestion.
The wise person should prepare boluses (modakas) from equal parts of *citraka*, *trivṛtā*, *dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), mixed with jaggery;
one should eat them upon rising in the morning and afterwards drink warm water.
It destroys colic arising from the transformation of food (pariṇāma-śūla) and the colic of a man.
Yavānī, hiṅgu, rock salt, kṣāra, sauvarcala,
and abhayā should be drunk with wine from a liquor-jar in cases of colic born of the three doṣas (tridoṣaja).
Asafoetida, the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, long pepper), *vacā*, *ajamoda*, *hapuṣā*, *pathyā*,
*yavānī*, *śaṭhī*, cumin, long pepper root, pomegranate, *vṛkī*, *cavya*, *agnika*, tamarind, sour *suvarcalā*, as well as barley-alkali and *sarjikā*.

Sindhūttha (rock salt) and powdered viḍa salt, taken in equal parts and mixed with the juice of bījapūra, should be made into pills the size of a jujube fruit. Administering this to those suffering from disorders of vāta cures colic, hemorrhoids, and splenic enlargement. Alternatively, it may be given as a paste.
This formulation, known as Hiṅgvādi, quickly destroys cough, abdominal distension, urinary disorders, and pain in the heart; it is the destroyer of all types of colic and pain,
the subduer of all vāta disorders, and the preventer of all wasting diseases.
Diarrhea, thirst, fainting, constipation, heaviness, loss of appetite,
dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and hiccups— these ten are the complications of colic (śūla). A physician should abandon from afar a patient with colic accompanied by these complications and thirst.
This was declared by Śrī to the physicians who desire success regarding that which is free from affliction:
one suffering from colic should avoid double-seeded pulses, as well as thick, cold, and slimy substances; likewise, one should avoid curd and sleeping during the day. (68–69)
O best of physicians, rice, *ṣaṣṭika* grain, rock salt, asafoetida, and *sauvīraka* alkali, as well as wine, jaggery, or ginger, are excellent for drinking (70).
*Śatapuṣpā* and *vāstuka* are also declared to be beneficial and are highly praised (71).
The meat of the ena deer, the partridge, the quail, the curlew, the hare, and the crane—these are declared by the best of physicians to be recommended.
(72) Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Colic," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (7)
The Eighth Chapter.
Ātreya said:
Listen, my son, I shall explain the great disease known as pāṇḍuroga (anemia).
There are exactly five types of anemia that arise here among human beings:
the Vātika, the Paittika, the Ślaiṣmika, the Sānnipātika, and the fifth is called Rūkṣaṇa; I shall now describe their origin.
O man, this paleness arises in one who is afflicted by a long journey, or by fever, or afflicted by a hemorrhage or a wound, or through anxiety, exhaustion, and weeping;

likewise for one who consumes alkaline substances, acids, *kalya*, and *maireya* liquors; or due to lack of exercise, excessive sexual indulgence, lack of sleep, or excessive sleep during the day—by these practices and by eating clay.

When the body is weakened on the road or afflicted by disease, through the excessive and constant consumption of salty, pungent, astringent, and sour substances, or by the overuse of clay, it leads to the drying up of the blood; by that, indeed, jaundice (pāṇḍuroga) arises.
Consequently, swelling occurs in the eye-sockets, yellowness comes to the body, and the urine becomes yellow.

He spits, and his skin becomes cracked; these are the premonitory symptoms that arise for him. Pricking pain, roughness, heaviness of the head, and yellowness of the skin, urine, eyes, and nails—know this to be the wind-natured (vātika) anemia in a person, characterized by these signs of anilapāṇḍuroga.
Indeed, that which causes greenish-yellow discoloration in the world brings about emaciation and a bitter taste in the mouth;
mild fever, thirst, delusion, and swelling—this jaundice (pāṇḍu) born of pitta has a yellowish complexion.
Furthermore, one afflicted by kaphaja jaundice experiences drowsiness, swelling, cough, as well as laziness, perspiration, and heaviness.
In that man, this disorder characterized by paleness arises from the nature of phlegm (kapha):
drowsiness, laziness, swelling, vomiting, cough, nausea, emaciation, diarrhea, lethargy, rough eyes, fever, and indeed affliction by hunger.

If a physician observes that a person quickly develops delusion, thirst, and exhaustion from even a slight distance away, he should immediately abandon that case of anemia arising from *sannipāta* (the simultaneous derangement of all three humors).
Now listen, my son, to how the great disease of anemia may arise from eating clay; though it is a most severe malady, it causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). 10–11.
By eating earth and by scattering filth over their channels, they are indeed satisfied with clay;
for that very reason, they do not transform the blood, nor do they nourish the body with its essence.
Through the drinking of alkaline, astringent, and sweet substances, that clay within a man quickly becomes provoked.
Due to the provocation of phlegm (*śleṣman*), clay produces sweetness; when not eaten, it would not be beneficial.
Indeed, the three humors—wind (*māruta*) and the others—when aggravated, are most powerful and quickly destroy luster, strength, and life.
In this way, the body becomes deficient in *pāṇḍuroga*, and through the eating of clay, it destroys the digestive fire (*jaṭharavahni*).
(14) A wise person should place iron in cow’s urine for seven nights;
from that, a powder mixed with honey should be administered to remove the disease of *pāṇḍu*. (15)
Take equal parts of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), the three myrobalans (triphalā), mustā, viḍaṅga, and citraka;
add one part of iron powder and macerate it with sugarcane juice for seven days. Even if it has been stored, when ground in a mortar, it will once again become most excellent.
When consumed with honey and ghee, it removes anemia and heart disease, and destroys jaundice, hemorrhoids, and chlorosis; thus it has been declared by wise and learned men.
(18) [One should take] the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), along with the three myrobalans (triphalā), citraka, musta, cavya, suradāru, and honey.
One should add granthika, śikhī, and bhṛṅgarāja, each in a portion of one pala;
furthermore, one should add iron powder, which has the luster of collyrium, twice the amount of the powdered ingredients.
Prepared with eight parts of urine and cooked again, it bestows strength. (19–20)
One should employ strength and likewise appropriate therapeutic measures; this combined treatment here is excellent.
It destroys *kaphaja* jaundice, worms, anemia, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and *halīmaka*.
[The formulation consists of] *punarnavā*, the three acrids (*tryūṣaṇa*), *trivṛt*, *surāhvaya*, *niśāhvaya*, *cavya*, and the three fruits (*phalatraya*). 21.
One should mix equal parts of ghanā, yava, and tiktarohiṇī with two parts of iron filings.
Having added double the amount of cow’s milk and applied a paste of dārvī, the wise man should let it dry in the shade and form pills; these should be consumed with honey and cow urine. 22–23.

Having understood the strength of the disease and the strength of the man, [one should act] regarding jaundice, all types of urinary disorders (prameha), abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, indigestion, choleraic dysentery, edema, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome, constipation, colic, worms, and the causes of hemorrhoids. 24.

Take the five pungents (*pañcakolaka*), the three aromatics (*kaṭutrika*), *ghana*, *devadāru*, *kṛmiśatru*, and *kolaka*; having separated these into their respective portions, one should then mix them with iron powder.
This should be cooked in eight times its amount of urine, by which it becomes a medicinal ointment (*lepikā*). 25.
Furthermore, one should prepare a paste the size of a jujube fruit with its own shade; this should be ground and dried.

When mixed with well-scented buttermilk, it forms a drink that pacifies jaundice, anemia, hemorrhoids, diarrhea, loss of appetite, consumption, urinary disorders, anal fistula, and even worms. (26–27)

One *prastha* of the juice of *dhātrī* fruits, one *prastha* of sugarcane juice, one *prastha* of *kūṣmāṇḍa* juice, and one *prastha* of *arka* juice should be prepared; having combined these, they should be cooked over a gentle fire until only a small residue remains. 28.
One should mix this collection of medicinal substances and subsequently boil them in a quantity of exactly one *pala*. [The ingredients are:

*bhṛṅgī*, *surāhva* (devadāru), *śatapuṣpa*, *dhānyaka*, fragrant *śuṇṭhī*, *madhuka*, *viśālā*, along with *pippalī*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *viḍaṅga*, *mustā*, *hapuṣā*, and *dalā*. 29–30.
A powder of bhūri, haridrā, kaṭurohiṇī, durālabhā, pauṣkara, vatsaka, kuṣṭha, ajamodā, and surasā leaves should be prepared;
two parts of old jaggery and one part of cow’s ghee should be mixed in the middle to form pills. 31.

By consuming it, one overcomes jaundice, hemorrhoids, anemia, and most severe fevers; it destroys edema, emaciation, and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), as well as wind-disorders, diarrhea, consumption, cough, and abdominal tumors (gulma).
It should be taken with wheat, *śāli* rice, barley, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, black gram (*śyāmā*), and *āḍhakī*, combined with ghee, milk, and buttermilk.
Furthermore, the gāṇḍīvavāstuka, śatapuṣpā, vartā, and pathyā are declared beneficial for a person suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍu).
34. Meat from wild animals is also recommended for consumption.
35. Bitter, dry, pungent, sharp, and burning substances, as well as sour gruel (kāñjikā), are likewise advised.
Wine, sour gruel, fermented rice-water, citron, and oils should be avoided in cases of *pāṇḍuroga* (anemia/jaundice).
36. Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Pāṇḍuroga*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Nine.
Ātreya said:

Listen, O best of physicians; there is a terrible disease among men that arises from prescribed activities for those whose nature is dominated by *vāta*. This disease, which causes long-term accumulation [of humors] and brings about humiliation here through the ripening of one's natural past actions, is the destruction of the human being.
That man who brings about the destruction of the gods, or the torment of an embryo, the killing of cows, the earth, mountains, Brahmins, or children, the devastation of gardens,
or the ruin of his own dwelling, commits the murder of women.
