By these heavy deeds of his, there arises a great disease that consumes the body and its wealth:
it robs one of divinity by burning the wealth of the gods and by causing the destruction of an embryo; it robs one of divinity by administering poison and by destroying a grove.
By that very rule, it indeed arises among men as a severe pain that causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus); it is a terrible destroyer of the person's life-force.
Furthermore, this wasting disease (kṣaya) should be understood by the best of physicians to be of ten types.
Due to fatigue or heavy burdens, sleeping on uneven beds, long journeys, indigestion, or excessive indulgence in sexual pleasure;
or due to fever resulting from irregular sleep and very cold things, the phlegm (*śleṣman*) perishes within the bodies, as do wind (*pavana*) and bile (*pitta*).
This occurs when one is overcome by disease or by irregular sleep following a mild fever.
Phlegm, bile, and wind, or the wasting away of the body;
likewise, the depletion of plasma, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen— thus, ten types of wasting (kṣaya) are to be known as occurring in the bodies of men.
Furthermore, their characteristics will be stated again; listen to them.
Due to excessive sweating, extreme heat, anxiety, emaciation, fear, and so forth, as well as by the provocation of wind and other humors, the depletion of *māruta* (vital air) arises. 8.

From that depletion of vāta, there arises drowsiness, burning in the limbs, thirst, loss of appetite, trembling, darkness before the eyes, exhaustion, and vertigo. Therefore, one should consume foods from marshy regions, meat broths, and minced meats.
One should also consume a paste of garlic and other such ingredients to destroy Vata.
When Pitta is diminished, sluggishness of the digestive fire arises, as well as loss of appetite, lethargy, cough, nausea, swelling, and a lack of physical vigor.
One should employ sudation, oil massage, and digestive stimulants for food and drink;
one should consume the meat juices and foods of wild animals when there is a depletion caused by pitta.
[This occurs] through physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and the consumption of dry foods.
From excessive heat and anger, the phlegm-born [fever] arises.
By that, there occurs burning, or pallor, swelling, labored breathing, vertigo, sleeplessness, hunger, thirst, and one even finds pleasure in sexual union with women. (13–14)
For him, the consumption of cool food and drink, along with the juices of tubers and vegetables, or with marshy products, curd, and milk, is desired.
For when the three *doṣas* have reached a state of depletion, death is then certain.
O Mahāmati, its treatment should be applied according to general principles.

Now I shall describe the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus); listen, O Hārīta, to this at once. [I shall explain] the symptoms of the depletion of each: chyle, blood, flesh, and fat. 16–17.
Upon the depletion of rasa (plasma), excessive emaciation, weak digestion, trembling, headache, sluggishness of movement, and exhaustion and vertigo arise.
Upon the depletion of rakta (blood), a person becomes pale, emaciated, and sluggish in movement.
Dyspnea, spitting, emaciation, and weak digestion arise;

with the wasting of muscle, there is extreme leanness, restlessness, and a breaking sensation in the limbs; loss of sleep or excessive sleep, loss of consciousness, and diminished vigor occur. (19–20)

Upon the depletion of fat (medas), there is diminished strength, loss of consciousness, breaking pain in the limbs, a harsh gait, dyspnea, excessive coughing, anorexia, and weak digestion; by this, a parched state arises, leading to the emaciation of the body.
In the depletion of bone (asthi), there is extreme sluggishness of movement and diminished vitality; such is the case in the depletion of fat.
Loss of consciousness, emaciation, trembling, breaking pain in the limbs, vomiting, and roughness; 22.

dryness, the affliction of exhaustion, and swelling, as well as convulsions, wasting, and irritability arise—O best of physicians, you should thoroughly understand these symptoms when there is a depletion of the marrow, or even just trembling. 23.

Dizziness, exhaustion, extremely sluggish movement, swelling, staying awake at night, drowsiness, mild fever, emaciation, and impaired bodily functions occur in a person during the depletion of semen; likewise, dryness, vertigo, trembling, wasting, anger, aversion toward women, and so forth [occur in the depletion of ojas]. 24.
Deformity, impairment, and wasting occurring at the joints—
now I shall duly explain the medicinal treatments, namely oleation, drying, and likewise beneficial depletion. 25–26.
One should consume the meat of wild animals and various foods, along with water boiled with *guḍūcī*, ginger, and *yavānī*.
Milk boiled with black pepper is recommended for drinking at night. (27)
By that, there shall be an increase of the *rasas*, and one is quickly liberated from [disease]. 28.
The best of physicians have declared that the means for increasing the *rasas* are wheat, barley, and *śāli* rice, and especially the meat of wild animals (*jāṅgala*). 29.
Clarified butter, milk, sugar, honey, black pepper, and long pepper—
this drink is highly recommended for humans as a supreme means of increasing blood.
One should also prepare dishes of marshy grains and those known as light [digesting].
One should consume wholesome substances such as ghee and milk, as well as sweet things (verse 31).
O best of physicians, the juices of wild animals should also be used for consumption (verse 32).
[Furthermore, one may take] a powder of sugar-candy and other ingredients, goat’s milk, and *kolaka* (verse 33).
Wholesome drinks during the period of depletion, as well as [medicines] taken at dawn and before breakfast;
various cooked milks praised with ghee, sandalwood, and powders of grapes and other fruits—these, O best of physicians, [are prescribed]. 33–34.
O son, all meats from the arid (jāṅgala) regions should be consumed,
and one should employ all sweet foods; specifically, when there is a deficiency of semen, one should use soups and meat broths that are well-cooked.
One should likewise consume fresh butter, milk, and sweet substances (36).
Drinking the juice of karkaṭī roots with milk, along with vidārīkanda, śālmalī, and plenty of sugar, is beneficial; sweet substances are also recommended (37).
Now, powders that cause the depletion or increase of semen shall be described.

(38) One should employ *balā*, *vidārī*, the five minor roots (*laghupañcamūlī*), and the bark of the five milky trees; likewise, *punarnavā* combined with *megha* and *tugākṣīrī*, along with equal parts of the *sañjīvanīya* group and *madhuka*. (39)

All these [ingredients] should be equal in measure to one *akṣa*; having ground them all together into a powder, one should mix into it hundreds of *kaṇā* (long pepper) seeds, as well as barley, wheat, and barley-flour, with an amount of *tugākṣīrī* equal to [the other ingredients], and white rice; this [mixture] should then be combined with *subhṛṅgāraka*.
It should be separated by half a *karṣa* or even by a whole portion; the white [substance] is to be employed.

41 One should process it three times with the juice of *āmalaka*; having processed it with cow’s milk, it should then again be processed with all [the ingredients], including sugar and clarified butter. 42

One should consume half a *pala* of that [medicine] mixed with honey; once it has been digested, one should eat food avoiding pungent and sour items, along with milk, ghee, white sugar, or foods made of barley, wheat, and *śāli* rice.
Having ascertained the digestive fire within the person's stomach, those who know the procedure should administer this for the pacification of the disease of consumption (*kṣaya*).
It is recommended as a strengthener for those whose digestive fire has been exhausted, for those afflicted by long-standing fatigue and heat, and likewise for those suffering from headaches (44);
for those afflicted by pitta, those with depleted blood, those oppressed by exhaustion and travel, those with jaundice, those suffering from asthma,
those with diabetes, and those with impaired senses (45).
For the woman by whom a fetus has been conceived, the powder of *balā* and other herbs is indeed recommended.
(46) Thus ends the *balādi-cūrṇa*. [The ingredients are:
*bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śoṇāka*, *kāśmarī*, and likewise *pāṭalī*.
Śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, śvadaṃṣṭrā, the two types of bṛhatī (47),
bhṛṅgī, śītā, āmalakī, jayantī, and that which is called puṣkara;
drākṣā, abhayā, amṛtā, medā, candana, aguru, and padmaka (48).
Two parts each of balā (also known as karṇa), both jīvaka and ṛṣabha,
kākolī, kṣīrakākolī, and the fleshy root-tuber of vidārī—
each of these should be taken in a measure of one pala; this is how the best of physicians should prepare it.
Five hundred *dhātrī* fruits, combined with their well-ripened juice,
should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth; having thus decocted them, the wise man should remove the impurities.
One should grind that decoction into a paste until it reaches the consistency of a coating for a ladle;
then, having cooked *āmalaka* fruits with oil and clarified butter,
all of them should be ground into a powder and combined with an equal amount of sugar.

The best of physicians should add four *pala* of *tugākṣīrī*; furthermore, one thousand *pippalī* fruits, as well as cinnamon, cardamom, and cinnamon leaves—the most excellent practitioner should place two *pala* of each of these therein. (53–54)
One should carefully add all the aforementioned powders to the previously described linctus and lick it with equal devotion; this is a rejuvenative (rasāyana) for men that dries up asthma,
cough, consumption, anemia, and jaundice.
It protects the bodies of children and the elderly who are emaciated and wounded;
it removes hoarseness of voice, thirst, heart disease, bile-blood disorders, seminal defects, severe headaches, and chronic catarrh. (56–57)

It destroys chronic fever, weak digestion, skin diseases, malignant fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, painful micturition, and stones; likewise, it is a purifier and a subduer [of humors], and it undoubtedly eliminates heart disease, colic, and abdominal distension.
It brings about the birth of sons for barren women and increases the scanty semen of the elderly; even a eunuch becomes a supreme man capable of procreation at all times;
and it certainly and swiftly increases intelligence, memory, and splendor. 59–60.

Beholding happiness and good fortune, even an old man becomes like a youth; for the destruction of the disease of consumption, this great Cyavanaprāśana has been proclaimed by Atri, as expounded by Kṛṣṇa Ātreya. 61–62.
Thus ends the electuary named Cyavanaprāśana.
[The ingredients are: Bhārgī, Puṣkaramūla, Citraka, Kaṇāmūla, Gajāhvā, Śaṭhī, Śaṅkhāhvā, Daśamūla, Citraka, Balā, Yāsā, and Ātmaguptā.

The best of physicians has declared that two palas of these [drugs] should be boiled with one hundred myrobalans (*pathyā*) in five *āḍhakas* of water over a low fire, continuously and for a long time. Having cooled it and extracted the pure liquid, one should then take out the hundred myrobalans.
When it has dried completely, this excellent decoction of *subhavana* should be cooled;

then, having added one *tulā* of aged jaggery (*guḍa*) and one *kuḍava* of honey, along with half that amount of ghee as the oily medium, one should add five hundred and ten *akṣas* of *magadhā* (long pepper). 64.
One should place the powder therein and once again triturate it thoroughly; taken with honey, these two *pathya* powders provide great benefit, cutting through all diseases:
jaundice, cough, *halīmaka*, ailments of the anus, heart disease, hiccup, and vertigo.

It destroys chronic rhinitis, urinary disorders, bile, blood disorders, skin diseases, and ailments of the digestive tract (grahaṇī). It increases the menstrual flow and alleviates swelling, wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, pain, consumption, urinary disorders, flatulence, and constipation; it is beneficial for those with impaired senses. Equal to a submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), it pacifies weak digestion and cures loss of appetite.

Or, *abhayā* prepared by Dāgasti bestows bodily happiness and brings about destruction [of disease]. (66) A decoction of *balā* (also known as *gokṣuraka*), the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇā*, mixed with honey and abundant sugar and drunk with milk,
is beneficial and destroys jaundice or consumption.
It destroys the underlying cause of thirst in cases of urinary disorders (meha) and bestows strength upon those whose sense organs have declined.
(67) One should prepare an increasing dose of long pepper (pippalī) with milk and ghee, starting with five, then seven, and then nine, in successive order. (68)
The eleventh, the thirteenth, the fifteenth, as well as the seventeenth, the nineteenth,
and the twenty-first are recorded respectively;
in this manner there should be an increase in sequence, extending up to one hundred.
Then, gradually thereafter, one should feed the remaining five-fold portion of sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika) combined with mung beans and ghee; in this way,
both the young and the old man shall possess the strength of an elephant.
The *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen is recommended when fever has become chronic, as well as for weak digestion or hemorrhoids; it should be consumed as described.
Thus ends the *pippalī-vardhamāna*.
Two *pala*s each of *mārkava*, *dhātu*, *mākṣika*,
*punarnavā*, *tugā*, *pṛkkā*, *śāliparṇī*, *vāsaka*, and *durālabhā* (73) should be combined with half that amount of powder, along with the three aromatics (*trigandha*) and black peppers.
One part each of tālīsa and māgadha, half that amount of śilodbhava (realgar),
and half that amount of śilābheda (bitumen)— all these should be mixed together with an equal portion of sesame powder and combined with an amount of sugar equal to the whole. 74–75.
One should consume it with milk or, preferably, combined with ghee;
by this, consumption (kṣaya), pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā), and jaundice (kāmalā) are destroyed.
It quickly overcomes epilepsy (apasmāra), and one becomes endowed with increased strength and virility. 76.
Great diseases are pacified, and the man becomes rich in semen.
Thus ends the powder of *śilājatu*.
[One should take] *jīvantī*, *vatsaka*, *yaṣṭikā*, along with *pauṣkara*, *gokṣuraka*, and the two types of *bala*.
Nīlotpala, āmalakī, yavāsa, satrāyamāṇā, māgadhā, and kuṣṭha [are the ingredients].

(78) One *prastha* of the juice of grapes and *āmalakī*, two *prasthas* of goat’s milk, and one *prastha* of curd—having cooked ghee with these, it is highly recommended for consumption and in food for those suffering from *vahnivāta*. (79)

One should employ it as a nasal drop (nasya) and also in enemas (basti); by this, consumption (rājayakṣmā), jaundice (halīmaka), jaundice (kāmalā), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), fainting (mūrchā), vertigo (bhrama), tremors, headache, and pain quickly come to an end.
Furthermore, even great urinary calculi (mahāśmarī), hemorrhoids (gudakīla), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), and diseases located in the head shall perish.
By the administration of that [medicine] deprived of its liquid portion, anemia (pāṇḍvāmaya) and consumption (rājayakṣmā) go to destruction and pacification;

likewise, jaundice (halīmaka) is cured by the administration of enemas (basti), and diseases arising from the rectum reach destruction in men through the sprinkling of erysipelas (visarpa) and boils (visphoṭaka). 81–82.
One should cook equal parts of *kaṇā*, *palāśa*, five times the amount of milk, and fresh ghee;
this is recommended for drinking or with food for the purpose of destroying consumption caused by royal [affliction].
Furthermore, one may take the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*), the tip of barley, milk, curd, and ghee.
Bhārgī, kuṣṭha, and pauṣkara should be added in equal parts;
one hundred fruits of harītakī should be placed in four times as much water, and the three decoctions should be combined and boiled over a gentle fire. 84–85.

Ghee prepared with mild cooking, when administered through drinking, nasal drops, and enemas, brings about a great increase in the qualities of men in cases of anemia (pāṇḍuroga), chlorosis (halīmaka), pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), and wasting (kṣaya); thus it is praised and declared by the best of physicians. (86–87)

Equal parts of yaṣṭīmadhu, balā, guḍūcī, and the five roots (pañcamūla) are boiled; to this decoction, an equal amount of āmalaka juice, as well as sugarcane juice and the juice of vidārī, along with an equal portion of ghee, are added. 88.
In this case, milk should be equal to curd, and fresh butter (navanīta) should likewise be equal to that;
one should add grapes and tālīsa as available. This prepared ghee should be administered for drinking, as nasal drops (nasya), or via enema (basti). 89–90.
It conquers consumption (rājayakṣmā), the most dreadful anemia (pāṇḍuroga), jaundice (halīmaka), and hemorrhoids; it is a remedy for bleeding disorders (raktapitta).
When applied as a paste, it destroys malignant erysipelas (duṣṭavaisarpa), bilious fevers, and burns from wounds. 91–92.
Having prepared a decoction of *balā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *parṇī*, *gokṣuraka*, *sthirā*,
the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba*, *musta*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *durālabhā*,
one should apply this powder once the remaining liquid has been strained.

A decoction made from grapes (*drākṣā*), *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *dhātrī*, and *tamālakī* should be prepared with an equal amount of milk (94). Fresh butter (*navanītaka*) should be added to this ghee, using half as much butter as ghee.
This prepared ghee is to be used for drinking, as well as for enemas (*basti*), nasal drops (*nasya*), massage, and in food (95).

It is recommended for chronic cough, consumption, and jaundice; for those whose strength and senses have declined due to royal affliction (rājayakṣmā); and in cases of swelling and ulcers numbering in the hundreds. It destroys headaches, pain in the flanks, and diseases of the anus. (96) Sandalwood, Sarala, Devadāru, liquorice, cardamom, Vetivera, and Śaṭhī— [Note: The verse continues with further medicinal herbs.]
Nalada, śaileyaka, pṛkkā, padmaka, vanakesara (97), kaṅkolaka, murā, māṃsī, śairīya, the two types of harītakī,
reṇukā, tvak, kuṅkuma, the two types of sārivā, tiktā, and aguru (98).
Likewise, well-strained decoction of grapes, oil, and curd-whey, along with parched grain flour in equal parts, should be cooked over a gentle fire;
this prepared oil is used for drinking and in enemas. 99.
The excellent physician should employ it for both nasal administration and as an external ointment;
it destroys anemia and consumption, cough, and acts as a demon-destroyer while promoting strength and complexion; furthermore, it removes chronic fever, epilepsy, leprosy, and scabies. (100–101)
It is said to produce strength, nourishment, vigor, and to increase intelligence, wisdom, and longevity; it bestows beauty and good fortune, and brings glory to all beings.
(102) [This is attained] through approaching the wife of one's master or from longing for the wife of one's guru.
From stealing gold belonging to a king, the disease of consumption (rājayakṣmā) may arise;
or else, it is born from a malignant disease—listen, O son! Now hear how consumption arises from four causes. 103–104.

This great disease arises in a human being from the affliction of the limbs caused by physical exertion, travel, sexual intercourse, or movement; or from a body emaciated by the pain of wounds; or from excessive anger, grief, fasting, fear, and the observance of vows of abstinence;
or that which results from old age, or from excessively drawing a bow with a heavy string, or from carrying an excessive burden, or from slaughter, calamity, and captivity in battle. 105.

From excessive distension of the abdomen, from the consumption of unwholesome food, from anxiety, and from over-indulgence in sexual intercourse, there arises the disease known as *rājayakṣma*, which affects the strength and heart of man.

(106) It may also arise from chest wounds, wasting, exhaustion, or even from sudden affliction, as well as from excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse and the habitual use of parching substances. (107)
By that, the body is emaciated and a mild fever arises;
at the end of the fever, swelling occurs, as do foul-smelling excrement and excessive urination. Diarrhea also occurs, and one suffers from overeating. 108.
One who coughs excessively, spits, and suffers extreme emaciation;
who has an intense longing for women and a constant aversion to food—this disease is to be known as Rājayakṣmā (kingly consumption), and it is incurable. 109–110.
If both feet become numb, if one considers a morsel of food to be much,
and if there is clarity in speech, the consumption of *rājayakṣmā* does not subside. Whatever food, whatever diet, and in whatever manner one begs for it—
To him, sweet and substantial food should be given (112).
Whatever food a person afflicted by *rājayakṣman* desires, by obtaining that very thing, his bodily tissues (*dhātavaḥ*) are restored. (113)
When the swellings become reddened and reach a state of suppuration in the person, then a decoction of *punarnavā* with *leśa* is prescribed.
One who takes it will live for four months, or six months if endowed with great strength. (114)
With the most excellent remedies, one may live for a thousand days;
beyond a thousand days, there is no life remaining for one afflicted by *rājayakṣman*.
His breath, vitality, and vigor have departed; he is emaciated and his sense faculties are impaired.
If there is no further improvement and he is released from a chronic disease,
yet becomes exhausted by that effort, then a most terrible consumption (rājayakṣmā) may arise, which will take away his life. 117.
In three months, six months, or again in three years,
one should prepare [the medicine] with a *prastha* of the juice of *śatamūlī*, a *prastha* of *guḍūcī* paste,
a hundred *harītakī* fruits, and a *tulā* of *kuṭaja* bark.
Having decocted [the ingredients] separately, one should mix the *pūtanā* with them together;
then, having applied a paste of *dārvī*, [one should prepare] five hundred balls of jaggery (*guḍa*),
along with sugar, *āmalakī* powder, cinnamon, cardamom, *citraka*, and *śaṭhī*.

Grapes, kuṣṭha, śilājatu, and śilābheda (realgar), as well as tālaka, should be added there in the measure of one akṣa; one should consume this with purified ghee, drink milk over it, and thereafter take food. 121–122.

One suffering from consumption (rājayakṣman) shall obtain happiness; one shall conquer anemia (pāṇḍu) and jaundice (kāmalā); diarrhea is destroyed, and one's strength becomes equal to that of an elephant. 123 Tālaka, śilābheda, and likewise śilājatu—
The two types of *kṣīraka*, *samaṅgā*, *kuṣṭha*, *nāgabalā*, and *balā*; 124.
*elā*, *patra*, *tālīsa*, *tamāla*, yellow *candana*, *mustā*, *drākṣā*, *rāsnā*, *muṇḍī*, *śaileyaka*, and *pura*. 125.
One should combine *surasā* with black sesame seeds in a two-part proportion;
one should employ this fine powder joined with jaggery and honey.
Afterwards, there should be the drinking of cow’s milk, and meals should be taken together with milk.

For those who are emaciated by diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣman), those afflicted by malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and those whose bodily constituents and strength are depleted— one should administer this medicine copiously;
even an old man, having become young again, delights in women.
Even a barren woman obtains a son, and even a eunuch acts as a man, by means of this preparation called Tālakāmrātaka, as expounded by Kṛṣṇātreyas:
guḍūcī, the two types of balā, dhātrī, and marica. (129)

This powder, combined with jaggery, destroys pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā) in men. One should consume śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, wheat, vāstuka greens, and the meat of wild animals; likewise, mung beans, cow's milk, and the flesh of rabbits, eṇa deer, and kuraṅga deer.
The flesh and other parts of the partridge, curlew, quail, eggplant, peacock, and goat are indeed prescribed as medicinal plasters in this world; furthermore,
one should feed milk and ghee to a patient suffering from consumption or pulmonary tuberculosis.

Alkaline, sour, pungent, and sharp substances, oil, fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), liquor (*surā*), and mustard seeds— these should be avoided in cases of consumption (*kṣaya*) or pulmonary tuberculosis (*rājayakṣman*).
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Consumption Disease," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Tenth Chapter: Due to excessive heat, or from the consumption of pungent, hot, and acrid substances, or from the consumption of alkaline and sour substances, or from the consumption of wine and similar intoxicants. (1)
Due to excessive sexual indulgence, coldness, and the consumption of dried vegetables and similar foods,
the *pitta* humor becomes aggravated by these factors and merges with the blood.
Then the son, fallen into doubt, questioned his father once again.
Hārīta said:
How does the *pitta* become aggravated, or by what is it set in motion? Likewise, for what reason does the blood (*rakta*) become aggravated? 4.
"By whom is it seen simultaneously, and how does it proceed?
Thus questioned, the Great Teacher, the bull among sages, replied.
Ātreya said:
Listen, O wise one of great splendor, you who have reached the further shore of the medical scriptures:

by whatever [cause] the *pitta* becomes aggravated, by that very same [cause] the blood becomes aggravated. When the *pitta* is thus provoked within the abdominal cavity (*koṣṭha*), the *vāyu* tears it apart violently.
The *prāṇa* leads [the breath] upward, while the *apāna* drives it downward;
in the middle, the *samāna* causes the provocation of blood and bile.
Thus, the pitta simultaneously becomes provoked together with the blood.

Anger is seen to be of four kinds, and its course is considered to be twofold. When blood flows from the upper part of the body, mixed with phlegm, from the nostrils, the mouth, and the ear canals, it is curable by one who desires victory.
When it is mixed with downward-moving [doshas], it also flows through the anus;
that is to be known as Rakta-pitta (hemorrhagic disease), which seeks success only with great difficulty.
When both wind and phlegm move through both the upper and lower [channels], [it is likewise difficult]. 10–11.
One should know that [the disease] is incurable by means of *tamas* (darkness/dark humor), or if it is cured only with great difficulty;

however, *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) that has arisen from the force of a single path or from the *nābhi-vega* (navel-pulse) may be curable even with ease, provided it is free from complications.

Rakta-pitta associated with a single doṣa is curable, while that involving two doṣas is said to be palliable; however, when it proceeds from all three doṣas, it is incurable. In cases of upward-moving rakta-pitta, the wise physician should administer purgation.
When blood has moved to the lower part of the body, then emesis is beneficial for him.

In one whose disease has been exhausted, yet whose complexion is unimpaired, whose body is diminished in strength, or who has weak digestion, or suffers from sneezing, pallor, burning sensations, or dryness;

Thirst, vomiting, labored breathing, restlessness, aversion to food, delusion, cardiac pain, and dizziness— these eighteen complications are said to arise from the affliction of *rakta-pitta*. 16.16.18.

A disease is curable when it is without complications, whereas it is incurable when accompanied by complications (verse 17). One who suffers from spitting blood, has bloodshot eyes, is afflicted by vertigo,
and passes bloody urine— such a person who vomits blood and has bloody urine does not survive (verse 18).
Thus has the meaning of the etiology been declared; next, I shall describe the treatment for *raktapitta* that brings ease, endowed with excellent characteristics:
that which is reddish and accompanied by froth from wind, as well as excessively black or yellow like safflower, is due to pitta. (19)
The wise declare that [purgative] which is produced from bile to be "bilious" (pittaja), while that which is thick, pale, excessively produced, and dense is "phlegmatic" (kaphaja).
One should not administer strong purgation to one whose flesh is wasted, who is emaciated, or who is aged, young, or afflicted by fever, nor to one suffering from consumption, fainting, or vertigo.
One should extract the essence of *vāsā* by pressing it, and take it as a drink combined with honey and sugar;
blood flowing from the nose, mouth, ears, or eyes will quickly be pacified.
[The same result is achieved with] a decoction of *vāsā*, blue lotus, clay, *priyaṅgu*, *rodhra*, collyrium, and the filaments of a lotus.
Having drunk this, it should be administered with honey and sugar; thus, even an acute aggravation of Pitta located in the chest is quickly pacified.

(23) When a man is suffering from bleeding disorders, wasting, cough, dyspnea, or consumption, and is treated with a cotton-wool swab soaked [in this remedy], how could he suffer? Why do physicians not treat the patient with this? (24)
If a physician or the mother of physicians performs the prescribed treatment at the outset,
it will grant success in cases of hemoptysis, consumption,
and cough, provided that there remains hope for life while the *vāsā* plant is available. (25)

Why should one suffering from *raktapitta*, consumption, or cough despair? (26) A powder of *tālīśa* mixed with the juice of *vṛṣa* leaves should be drunk; beginning this treatment, it destroys *kapha*-and-*pitta*-induced cough, dizziness, and the distress arising from the combination of asthma and cough, and quickly provides relief for broken voice. (27)

A decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*, mixed with sugar and enriched with honey, wards off asthma, cough, and *rakta-pitta* (hemoptysis). Alternatively, goat's milk or cow's milk, four times the quantity of water, along with a medicinal paste (*kalka*), [may be used]. 28.
This drink with sugar is recommended; it quickly destroys raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).
Milk boiled with balā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, āmalakī fruits, drākṣā, madhūka, and madhuyaṣṭikā is beneficial as a drink for the pacification of raktapitta in a person. 29–30.
One should lick the powder of the flowers of khadira, priyaṅgu, kovidāra, and śālmali with honey; may you have good health.
[This powder] has been processed seven times with the juice of āṭarūṣaka and dried again.
Abhayā combined with pippalī and honey conquers even the most difficult-to-overcome raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders).

(32) Equal parts of elā-phala, padmaka, nāgakeśara, drākṣā, ghanā, madhuka, and pippalikā, mixed with an equal amount of white sugar and used as a linctus, completely destroys raktapitta along with kharjūrikā. (33)
It destroys burning sensations, the distress of fever, labored breathing, delusion, thirst, and fainting, as well as the discharge of blood and semen.
(34) If blood should begin to flow from the nose, then one should grind *āmalakī* fruits with ghee and water and apply it as a paste to the head; that will quickly arrest the *raktapitta*. (35)

In cases of raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders), one should administer grape juice enriched with ghee and sugar, or water enriched with sugar; likewise, barley-based food and sugarcane juice enriched with sugar destroy wasting (kṣaya), cough, and hemorrhage from chest wounds.
One should also apply nasal drops (nasya) made from the juice of haritālī or from lac juice.

Nasal therapy (nasya) with the juice produced from the blossoms of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*) may be used even when there is bleeding from the nose. Nasal therapy rich in sugar derived from mango stones and *jambu* fruit, combined with white sugar, is beneficial for fevers;
it stops blood flowing from the nose and overcomes hiccup, vomiting, and labored breathing. (37–38)

One should administer as a nasal drop (nasya) a preparation of onion leaf extract mixed with liquorice and honey, which reaches the tip of the nose; this subsequently conquers hemorrhage from the nose.
A wise person, having prepared a decoction of vāsā leaves, should likewise employ these following [remedies].

This digestive powder, consisting of *rodhra*, blue lotus (*utpala*), clay (*mṛttikā*), *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, and *priyaṅgu*, when prepared with flower-nectar, is beneficial for disorders located in the *pitta* humor; it alleviates cough, jaundice, anemia, chest wounds, dyspnea, and colic. (40)
The juice of pomegranate flowers, likewise the juice of the filaments of a blue lotus,
or lac-resin, when used as a nasal drop with milk, stops blood flowing from the nose. (41) If blood flows from the mouth, the prescribed remedy for that shall be set forth for a human being.

Among humans, blood disorders are not easily cured; however, that which flows from the female genital tract is incurable. Here, honey, madhuka, uśīra, the filaments of the lotus, and the juice of dūrvā grass, when drunk together with the fruit of the pomegranate;
or sandalwood, white kuṣṭha, padmaka, and tender leaves; or honey, madhuka, tender leaves, and the two types of kodrava—all these taken together [are effective].
Alternatively, one may wash rice with fragrant water; when thoroughly washed, it should be combined with a fourth part [of its weight] of clarified butter.

Even if it is very light, once washed and cooked over the fire, it becomes perfectly prepared. Its drinking should be done while the mouth is red. (44) Furthermore, if blood has issued from the ears or the nose, then even if it was prescribed, there should be filling of the ears and the nose.
It stops bleeding, quickly heals wounds or dyspnea, and cures vomiting of blood, urinary disorders, and insanity (45).

When [blood] flows from the nose, nasal drops should be administered; when from the mouth, drinking [medicated liquids] should be prescribed; for the ears and eyes, filling [with medicated oils] is required; and for the anal passage, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is indicated (46).
One should lick either the powder of pomegranate rind mixed with sugar, or again, the powder of lotus filaments mixed with sugar;
this quickly stops bleeding from the mouth, as well as vomiting and exhaustion. (47)

This is certain: it quickly destroys labored breathing, emaciation, vertigo, and thirst. (48) The tender leaves of the Jambu and Amra trees, combined with Harītakī and mixed with honey and sugar, are a remedy for blood from the mouth. (49)
A linctus made with honey from whichever is available— of the *vaṭa*, *prabāla*, *arjuna*, *vṛkṣaka*, *kadamba*, *jambū*, *āmra*, or even *khadira*— instantly stops the flow of saliva from the mouth.
(50) Likewise, *śatāvarī*, *madhuka*, *balā*, sugar, *kākolikā*, and pomegranate [are effective].

Meda, kṣīravidārī, phalinī, tintiḍīka, and balā, prepared with cow’s milk and clarified butter—this is beneficial for drinking as well as for enemas; it stops bleeding from the vagina, penis, and anus, and cures cough and consumption. 51
raisins, licorice, vidārī, vasudhā, indigo, samaṅgā-phala,
the two types of kākoli, the pair of bṛhatīs, vṛṣa, mahāmedā, black sandalwood,
jasmine buds, paṭola, śyāmā, amṛtā, sañjīvaka, and abhayā.

Take two parts each of *medā*, *kucandana*, *madhurasā*, and *śyāmā*; having cooked these in equal proportions with cow's milk according to the purified procedure until one-fourth remains, add *matsyaṇḍī* and *madhuka*. If this preparation is thus perfected, its consumption is highly recommended for men.

It also destroys the blood that is beneficial to women; when it occurs in the anus, the penis, or the path of the pores, it destroys the menstrual flow. This ghee known as Drākṣāghṛta is prescribed for internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), fever, gout (vātāsra), vaginal pain, vertigo, intoxication, insanity, urinary disorders with blood, bilious acidity, severe skin diseases (kuṣṭha), wasting due to injury, blood disorders, consumption (rājayakṣma), and anemia (pāṇḍu). It is declared by Ātreya to be beneficial for men when used as a drink, an enema, or an errhine.
Having removed the skin, one should cut the pumpkin into pieces;
these should be quickly washed with *kāñjika* and then again with water. Afterwards, they should be ground into a paste in a *prastha* measure of milk.
One should cook this once again with ghee according to the proper method (56).
When the substances have become like honey, one should then place them together with sugar and add these medicinal ingredients (57).

Take two palas each of pippalī and śṛṅgavera, along with marica, the two types of jīraka, dhātrī, tvak, elā, and patrakam; one should add a powder made from half a pala of these ingredients to that [mixture]. 58.
One should stir it with a wooden ladle until it becomes thick like molasses;
then, having assessed one's strength and weakness, one should lick it with honey and ghee.
It cures hemorrhaging (raktapitta), consumption (kṣaya), cough, jaundice, chronic fever, and vertigo.
It cures vomiting, thirst, fever, dyspnea, anemia, chest wounds, consumption,
epilepsy, headache,
and severe pain in the female reproductive tract; it also treats chronic blood discharge from the womb and afflictions of mild fever.

Even an old man becomes young and lustful, and a barren woman becomes possessed of sons. A man who lacks virility attains vigor and becomes beloved by women. This linctus of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* is a remedy for all diseases.

The wise physician should take fifty palas of very succulent pieces of kūṣmāṇḍaka and fifty palas of white sugar; having added water, he should cook it until it is thoroughly cooked with one *prastha* of ghee. Once it is known to be cooked, he should then mix it with a decoction of vāsā.
One should cook it until it sticks to the ladle; then, having understood this, one should again add these:
āmalakī, ghanā, bhārṅgī, and the three fragrant substances (sugandhatraya)—all of these together in a measure of one karṣa.
Furthermore, punarnavā, nāgara, and dhānyaka—these are declared to be measured at one pala in total quantity. 65–66.

One should prepare this powder of the eight drugs beginning with Śyāmā; having thoroughly mixed it all together once more with a ladle, one should administer it in equal parts combined with honey. It destroys all diseases and quickly subdues cough, fever, and hemorrhage from chest wounds, as well as hiccups (67), heart disease, blood disorders, consumption, chronic catarrh, acid dyspepsia due to pitta, asthma, and fainting.
This is beneficial for women, excellent for children and the elderly, and bestows the destruction of all diseases.
(68) Śatāvarī, muṇḍitikā, amṛtā, the fruit and bark [of puṣkara], puṣkaramūla, bhārṅgī, vṛṣa, the two types of bṛhatī, khadira, and māṃsī—each taken individually in a measure of five palas. (69)

Having quickly removed the decoction once it is cooked, the wise one should then place the remaining pure liquid therein, along with twelve palas of honey and an equal amount of powdered iron stirred together with candied sugar and ghee. 70.

One who knows the procedure should cook sixteen palas [of the drug] in an iron vessel; it should be given along with an equal amount of jaggery (guḍa). As long as the tugā, viḍaṅga, māgadhā, śuṇṭhī, the two types of jīraka, kaṇṭaka, the three myrobalans (triphalā), bhṛṅga, dhānyamarica, and kesara [are present], it remains radiant. 71–72.
One should prepare the powder separately with sugar; having placed this well-mixed powder in a ghee-smeared pan, one should administer it in a dose of one karṣa.
At dawn, one should drink lake water and avoid heavy, sour, or wind-increasing foods.
This preparation cures fistula-in-ano and other swellings, as well as blood-acidosis (raktāmlaka) and consumption (yakṣman).
It is prescribed as a desiccant for skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and pains, a remedy for abdominal tumors (gulma), a provider of strength, and the most potent aphrodisiac.
It suddenly destroys hemoptysis (raktapitta), disorders of the female reproductive tract (yoni), and vaginal bleeding with pain.

This [preparation], when applied to the penis and bladder of men suffering from bloody diarrhea or blood-urinary disorder (raktaprameha), is declared to bestow good fortune and luster; it generates splendor, vitality, nourishment, and strength.
It should also be employed in cases of bloody diarrhea that is painful and characterized by a burning sensation.
The three fruits (triphalā), viṣā, samaṅgā, and parpaṭaka, along with dāḍima and dhātakī— this powder, combined with honey and sugar, or likewise with curd, ghee, and linctus,
[cures] bloody diarrhea, continuous discharge of blood, and [menorrhagia] in women.

It quickly wards off what is harmful to men and is suitable for the pacification of diarrhea in children. (79) In cases of vaginal discharge, a paste made of madhuka, samaṅgā, leaves of elā, leaves of nimba, pathyā, mustā, viśālā, and kaṭurohiṇī, combined with sugar, is beneficial. (80)

One should also check the discharge from the vagina (yoni-pravāha) as well as vaginal pain, inflammation, and thirst with a decoction prepared from equal parts of ela, samaṅgā, śālmalī, harītakī, and māgadhikā;
when this decoction is mixed with sugar and honey, it likewise checks the discharge from the vagina. 81–82.

At the end of the summer heat, for the benefit of a person suffering from raktapitta (hemorrhagic disorders), one should avoid foods that are burning, sour, sauvīraka, pungent, astringent, alkaline, or liquor;
instead, vāstūka, cillī, suniṣaṇṇaka, jīvantikā, or śatapuṣpikā [should be consumed]. 83.
Leafy vegetables are beneficial for blood disorders, as are mung beans and red rice when pitta is involved (84).
Barley, wheat, chickpeas, kośātakī, and paṭola are also helpful;
furthermore, mung beans and black gram are beneficial for the alleviation of raktapitta (85).

The flesh of the deer, hare, partridge, francolin, quail, peacock, curlew, and pigeon is indeed beneficial for increasing wind and bile; it provides strength that is not in vain, as well as vitality, splendor, and beauty. (86)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktapitta," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Eleven.
Ātreya said:
Now, my son, the treatment for hemorrhoids shall be explained;
listen to the characteristics of those which are said to be of six types,
arising from all three humors— wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth.
The fourth occurs from the combination [of all three humors], and the fifth arises from blood;
the sixth is to be known as innate (*sahaja*). Thus, the sixfold origin of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) is produced in these six ways. (2–3)

Through fasting, the consumption of light and dry food, or the use of pungent, salty, and burning substances, the wind (vāta) becomes obstructed; due to this constant and repeated suppression, the wind becomes agitated, and from its force, hemorrhoids (arśas) arise, characterized by a deficiency of excrement and urine.
This occurs when one remains seated in fasting, resulting in the retention of feces and urine.

Even by the excessive use of cold things, the hemorrhoids (gudaja) become aggravated. Through the consumption of salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter substances, as well as by eating food that is unmeasured, too light, or cold, the wind (vāyu) becomes provoked; it then produces impure blood in the anal passages and wind in the channels of the anus.
Through the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, hot, burning, and heavy foods with wind (air) or water, or due to fatigue, the affliction of physical exercise,
or the defects of travel and sexual intercourse, hemorrhoids arise from the derangement of pitta. (7)
From a lack of physical exercise, from constant coldness, from exposure to other winds,
from greed for excessively sour food, and from the accumulation of oil and fat, hemorrhoids arise from the disorder of phlegm (śleṣma).
[Verse 8] Coldness, piercing pain, roughness, insomnia, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, prostate-like growths, and choleraic dysentery [arise].
Swelling in both eyes and black nails are the signs of hemorrhoids arising from Vata (9).
Burning sensations, vertigo, fever, thirst, fainting, loss of appetite, and yellowness of the eyes, teeth, and face, along with diarrhea, are the symptoms of hemorrhoids produced by Pitta (10).

O knower of medicines, anal diseases arising from *śleṣman* (phlegm) indeed consist of drowsiness, dullness, wealth, slow digestion, pain, swelling, colic, excessive abdominal tumors, fissures in the anus, constipation, piercing pain, loss of appetite, and slowness of movement. Furthermore, there are colic, flatulence, loss of appetite, cough, nausea, and a burning sensation in the mouth.
Indeed, all types of hemorrhoids arise from the dullness (jaḍatā) of the two *dhātus*.

I shall now describe the symptoms of hemorrhoids (*arśas*): due to *vāta*, hemorrhoids are considered to be characterized by itching, discharge of blood, roughness, irregularity, and elongation. (12–13)

Hemorrhoids caused by *pitta* are characterized by burning sensations, being variegated in color, yellowish, or appearing blue; they discharge hot, reddish blood. Those which are accompanied by burning and are hard are subject to suppuration and constipation.
Hemorrhoids caused by *kapha* are considered to be cold, itchy, and thick;

those arising from both itch and blood (*kaṇḍvāsṛgbhava*) are accompanied by burning, pain, and a dark discoloration, with itching and desiccation occurring, and they constantly discharge blood. (15–16)
Worms resembling grains of rice sprouts arise, and hemorrhoids (gudaja) manifest with symptoms similar to those of wind (vāta) and constipation.
Some [worms] are curved, sharp, and have split mouths, resembling long bimba fruits; some resemble mustard seeds, and others have the appearance of black dates.
Some [hemorrhoids] have the appearance of jujube fruits, some are like *kalambaka* flowers, or like lotus seeds; and this is the origin of hemorrhoids caused by wind (*vāyu*).

(18) In the anus, the nostrils, the ear-cavities, the mouth, or likewise in the eyelids, the corners of the eyes, and the middle of the vagina—these diseases that arise in men are incurable; they cannot be easily treated, though effort and medical action may be applied. (19)
One should know that there are indeed three locations for hemorrhoids (arśas): within the three folds of the anus, in the middle, and externally.
That which is external is easily curable; that which is in the middle is cured with difficulty.
O best of physicians, hemorrhoids born from internal seeds are incurable; however, those located externally are most effectively cured by medicinal pastes, suppositories, and fomentations.
Those in the middle region are treated with surgical instruments, while those born internally are treated with internal medicines.
Therefore, O son, an action must be performed with effort by one who understands,
so that there may be protection for the afflicted and so that the disease may be turned back.
For if swelling, emaciation, and fever should occur in men on the hands, feet, or face, or at the navel, the penis, or the anus—
Dyspnea, vomiting, fainting, pain in the heart and flanks, emaciation, anorexia, constipation, and diarrhea are the complications (upasarga) that arise from hemorrhoids.
Thus, twelve complications indeed occur in cases of hemorrhoids; those without complications are curable, while those with many complications are incurable. 24–25.

One afflicted by colic, loss of appetite, and thirst, who passes excessively bloody stools and suffers from pain, swelling, and diarrhea— such a person suffering from hemorrhoids certainly does not survive.
Therefore, O best of physicians, I shall now describe the treatment for hemorrhoids, including pills, alkalis, and surgical instruments, by which success is achieved.
27–28. These treatments for hemorrhoids have been described as being easy to perform, curative of hemorrhoids, strength-promoting,
pacifiers of pitta and blood, and not aggravators of vāta.
At the outset, cooking [the medicine] is best; thereafter, one should take the remedy: a decoction of *pathyā*, *amṛtā*, and *dhanikā* mixed with jaggery for drinking. [Also recommended are:
*dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, *magadhā*, coriander, *bhallātaka*, jaggery, sesame, and *kuṣṭha*.
This paste, when mixed with milk and drunk, destroys hemorrhoids and other diseases.
This paste— consisting of ginger, long pepper, bilva, viḍaṅga, dantī, śaṭī, abhayā, and trivṛt— taken with jaggery as a drink, brings about the destruction of hemorrhoids in men.
A decoction of patra, kesaras, śuṇṭhī, ela, tumburu, dhānya, viḍaṅga, and sesame seeds,
when drunk with harītakī, ghee, and jaggery, destroys diseases of the rectum. Furthermore,
if a person eats long pepper and abhayā mixed with jaggery every morning, [the same result follows].

It quickly destroys hemorrhoids (gudakīlaka), as well as the entire range of diseases such as jaundice (kāmalā) and anemia (pāṇḍu). (33) The water of a well-steamed eggplant (*vārtāka*), when drunk with curd, sugar-candy (*sitāhvā*), and water boiled with *amṛtā*, should be administered for hemorrhoids; it kills worms and the diseases born of worms. (34)
A powder of *bhallātaka*, black sesame seeds, and *pathyā* (chebulic myrobalan) should be consumed by a person with jaggery;
it destroys hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, colic, and cough when drunk.
Furthermore, a *sūraṇa* tuber wrapped in *arka* leaves and smeared with mud [is likewise effective]. 35.

That milk, heated until it takes on the color of fire and mixed with rock salt and oil, should be consumed for the purpose of destroying hemorrhoids; even for a person free from disorders of wind (vāta), this is beneficial.
To these [preparations], sesame seeds should be added in equal parts with *citraka*, *puṣkaramūla*, and *śaṭhī*.
One should place pieces of *sūraṇa* tuber together with those [other ingredients] and add equal amounts of *agni* (citraka) fruit; 38.
having added four times as much rock salt (*saindhava*) and everything soaked in *arka* leaves, one should place it in a jar of ghee and cook it over a fire of wild cow-dung. 39.

This milk, cooked with salt and ghee and mixed with buttermilk, when administered as a drink, destroys even hemorrhoids; it also cures cholera, fistula-in-ano, jaundice, anemia, abdominal distension, intestinal obstruction, abdominal tumors, and loss of appetite. (40)
This is the "Auspicious Saindhava" (Bhadrakasaindhava), which destroys urinary disorders, throat ailments, itching, and worms.

(41) One should take equal parts of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *magadhā* (long pepper), the roots of *citraka*, and the three aromatics (*trigandha*). To these, an equal amount of *bhallātaka* should be added. Having thoroughly powdered all these together, one should then add treacle (*guḍa*) weighing twice the total weight of the aforementioned ingredients. (42)
Having thoroughly crushed it all and placed it in a greasy vessel, wise men should consume it daily in a dose the size of an eye;
it cures hemorrhoids, abdominal diseases, colic, tumors, and worms, while it destroys the "mare's fire" (excessive digestive heat), as well as anemia and consumption. 43
One should employ three palas each of nāgara and triphalā, four palas of marica, two palas of pippalī, and one pala of cavya; these should be added there by the best of physicians. (44)
One and a half *pala* of *tālīśa* should be given, along with half a *pala* of *padmaka*.
The dose of *jīraka* is equal [to that], and an equal amount of *guḍa* (molasses) should be weighed together.
The well-cooked, thick, dark-colored preparation contains three hundred *pippalī*s. (45–46)
Having ground [the ingredients] in a mortar, one should hold them with a greased vessel.
A pill the size of an axle (akṣa) should be administered to men every morning; it destroys all diseases and cures hemorrhoids, anemia, chlorosis, jaundice, and vertigo.

This life-bestowing *modaka* is beneficial for those suffering from abdominal tumors (*gulma*), diarrhea with blood and bile (*raktapitta*), consumption (*kṣaya*), chest wounds (*kṣata*), wasting diseases (*yakṣmā*), chronic fever, loss of appetite, and catarrh (*pīnasa*).
[It contains] two *palas* each of *jājī*, long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), jujube (*kola*), *magadhā*, *pathyā*, *agnika*, ginger (*nāgara*), and small cardamom (*sūkṣmailā*). 49.

Having gradually prepared five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits with an equal amount of rock salt (*saindhava*) in *palas*, one should then add an equal amount of old jaggery (*guḍa*). Having crushed this entire mixture into a paste the size of a *vaṭaka* pill, a specific benefit arises from this preparation: it wards off hemorrhoids, cures consumption (*kṣaya*), and likewise bestows nourishment and a radiant complexion.

It stimulates the weak digestive fire like a submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), removes dizziness, and cures heart disease, anemia, colic, abdominal distension, fistula-in-ano, and fear; it is the banisher of malignant pain.
Even though this formulation was prepared by the wise sage Kāṅkāyana, who was endowed with yogic skill, for the sake of [curing] disorders, one who desires happiness should employ it. 51–52.

Drink the best salt (lavaṇottama) combined with citraka, kaliṅga, vacā, cirabilva, and great picumanda for seven days, well-churned, if you wish to rub away all ailments of the anus. [53] Take viśva, upakulyā, marica, kesara, patra, lavaṅga, elā, and vṛddhi.

This powder, mixed with sugar, is beneficial for hemorrhoids and for the alleviation of abdominal pain. (54) A bolus made of ginger, *puṣkaramūla*, *vṛddhadāraka*, jaggery, and fresh *dāruharidrā* acts as a destroyer of the disease known as *durnāma* (hemorrhoids); it suddenly makes even a severe case disappear as if it were a child. (55)
One should prepare a powder of the three pungents (trikaṭuka), abhayā, puṣkaramūla, and citraka, along with one *tila* measure of *kṛmiripu* (viḍaṅga).
A person who eats one bolus (*vaṭaka*) of this with jaggery at dawn is freed from anal diseases and increases the digestive fire.
(56) Crush black pepper, ginger, and citraka together with an additional portion of *sūraṇa*.
One should consume a bolus (modaka) the size of a bilva fruit, made from equal parts of all [the aforementioned ingredients] combined with jaggery;
it subdues the disorders of pitta in humans and brings about nourishment of the body.
A wise person should take a surana tuber that possesses a red color and is composed of three equal parts.

Even though it has been divided into six parts, sixteen dry portions [of the drug] should be weighed; half of that amount of *citraka* and ginger should be added there, along with one portion of black pepper. This bolus (*modaka*), bound together with jaggery, should be consumed by men. 58–59.

Indeed, when consumed, this virtuous [preparation] swiftly destroys all diseases of the bowels and is said to stimulate the digestive fire; it also cures abdominal tumors (gulma) and pains of the stomach.
[It consists of] equal parts of the three myrobalans (triphalā), roots of Pippalī, Tālīsapatra, Viḍaṅga, Magadhā (Pippalī), and Puṣkaramūla.

One part of black pepper, one part of ginger, and one part of *sūraṇa* root [weighing equal to the total]; combined with *madana*, *capala*, *vṛddhadāra*, *elā*, and *bhṛṅga*, this powder is prepared here. When two parts of refined sugar are added and formed into pills (*vaṭaka*), the person who consumes them quickly and effectively removes abdominal disease. 61–62.

This renowned "King of Formulas" (Yogarāja) cures hemorrhoids, blood disorders, bile, cough, weak digestion, colic, consumption, fever, jaundice, and worms; it bestows strength and nourishment, quickly clears the channels, and kindles the digestive fire.
One should employ this Yogarāja, even by merely remembering Agastya.
By the application of this yoga, even Bhima became a great eater. [The recipe consists of:
chavya, pāṭhā, trikaṭu, magadhā, mūlaka, tumburu, bilva, ajājī, rajanī, surasā, pathyā, and saindhava.
Having ground these together with equal parts of cow’s ghee, one should cook it well; when used for drinking or as an ointment, it removes hemorrhoids, wind diseases, and urinary stones.

(65) Having ground Śyāmā, Kuṣṭha, Madhuka, Madana, Puṣpaka, Citraka, Bilva, Dāru, Prativiṣā, Śatāhvā, Kaliṅga, and Aśaṭhī, one should cook oil with twice the amount of milk; this is beneficial for both enemas and massage for the purpose of destroying anal diseases. (66)

This oil is excellent for wind-diseases, ear-discharge, and bleeding; for earache, urinary stones, and pain in the calves, back, waist, head, and veins; for the piercing pain of Vāta, constipation, suppression of stool, expulsion [of toxins], and difficult delivery; it sustains all accumulated diseases. (67)

Mustā, viśva, viḍaṅga, cavya, kaṭphala, pathyā, tejovatī, dantī, indrayava, and trivṛt—one pala each of these; and from that [mixture], one should add eight palas of puruṣkara and six palas of vṛddhadāru. All this should be boiled until it is completely reduced in sixteen droṇas of water known as sūraṇa-water. Having been prepared, it should be cooked again with three times the amount of jaggery (guḍa). One should then add citraka, trivṛt, tejovatī, and sūraṇa; having extracted [the essence] once more, it becomes a "speaker" (vādin) [of its benefits].

Take equal parts of cardamom, cinnamon leaves, *nāgakeśara*, and cloves; having ground these together, prepare them so that they constitute sixteen parts of the total, and place all of this in a single, oily jar.
At dawn, one should eat a dose the size of a *vata* seed. Once it has been digested, one who possesses great intelligence should drink copious amounts of milk both during and after the meal.
This [medicine] destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, jaundice, colic, constipation, cough, wasting from chest wounds, and consumption.
Two thousand *bhallātaka* fruits should be boiled in one *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains;
into that decoction, one should again cook one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*),
having added five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits— or three *palas*— to it.
One karṣa each of vyoṣa, javānī, ghanasāra, saindhava, elā, lavaṅga, dala, and nāgakeśara should be weighed and combined; having crushed them,
they should be kept in oil or in a vessel of clarified butter, and in the morning, taken in the measure of a vaṭaka pill.
He who eats this jaggery destroys diseases such as fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, worms, consumption, and jaundice;
it cures abdominal tumors, urinary stones, urinary disorders, chlorosis, and blood-bile (raktapitta), and it overcomes malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī).
It produces nourishment, bestows strength, brings about excellence of complexion, and grants happiness. (73–74)
One should take ten *mūlaka* roots, *guḍūcī*, *saṭhī*, *kṣuraka*, along with *citraka*, *bhārgī*, and *phala*;
adding five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits, one should boil them in one *droṇa* of water.
Once the decoction is prepared, one should add one hundred *guḍa* (molasses) that has been aged, and when it has cooled completely, an amount equal to the *melā* (resin).

This entire single formulation consists of *dala*, *kesara*, *bhṛṅga*, and *lavaṅga* made into a powder (76). Having been saturated with ghee for one day, one should place it in a vessel of ghee for seven days;
a person should place this in a smooth jar when administered for the multitude of diseases caused by hemorrhoids (77).

One should consume a single modaka every morning; it destroys hemorrhoids and urinary diseases, cures cough, phlegm disorders, and jaundice, is indeed beneficial, and stimulates the digestive fire—this is the case for that [modaka] which, when cast into cold water, dissolves by the water itself. 78.
The red [substance] goes to the red [substance], and there is a single cooking of molasses (guḍa). 79.
Granthika, citraka, musta, cavika, triphalā, amṛtā, sahadevī, gajakarṇā, apāmārga, and kuṭheraka. 80.
The wise one should grind two thousand *bhallātaka* fruits, each consisting of four parts, along with a paste in a *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-quarter; then,
when the paste has been reduced to one-quarter, one should add half a *tulā* of iron powder.
One should cast two *kuḍava* measures of clarified butter and all [the other ingredients] together into one vessel and stir them thoroughly.
Triphalā, trikaṭu, citraka, the eight salts, and viḍaṅga—all these in equal parts, each weighing one *pala*. (82–83)
Take four palas of vṛddhadāru and four palas of the plant called mūrvā;
take eight palas of powdered dried sūraṇa root. Having combined these, one should taste the powder once it has been removed from the heat and cooled completely.
Having added two *kuḍava*s of honey, this paste should first be administered in the morning on an empty stomach for hemorrhoids (*arśāṃsi*);
it also cures disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), and pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*). (85–86)
It quickly destroys Gulma, worms, urinary calculi, weak digestion, urinary disorders, and blood diseases; it cures consumption and bestows natural vigor upon the body.
It rapidly promotes growth and eliminates wrinkles and graying hair.
Through the application of this elixir (rasāyana), a man shall possess the strength of an elephant. 88.
O son, listen as I describe the treatment for hemorrhoids with blood;
one should consume sesame seeds mixed with fresh butter in the morning. 89.

One should consume fresh butter mixed with sugar, white ginger, and the filaments of the citron; or viḍaṅga combined with sugar; or the honey-syrup of the pumpkin gourd with fresh butter and sugar. (90)
By this, the wise pacify hemorrhoids with blood.
Having ground together *samaṅgā*, *śālmalī* flowers, sandalwood, the bark of the *kakubha* tree, blue lotus, and goat’s milk, they form a drink for blood diseases. 91–92.

Milk boiled with the root and filaments of *kuṭaja*, blue lotus (*utpala*), and the root of *khadira* and *dhātukī*, when drunk or used as an ointment, cures the disorder arising from blood and destroys hemorrhoids. Likewise, the dung of a cock and that of a pigeon [are effective].
Having ground together *grahadhūma*, white mustard seeds, *dhattūra*, and plantain leaves with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should apply the resulting wick to the anus.
A wick made from the tuber of *sūraṇa* should be prepared by coating it with the juice of jasmine and ghee.
It quickly destroys the polyp in the diseased anus, as well as worms born in the rectum.
(95) Turmeric, *mārkava*, costus, soot, and *suvarcala* are ground together with the juice of white mustard and sour gruel. (96)
If a wick mixed with honey is inserted into the rectum,
it quickly effects the destruction of hemorrhoids in men.
(97) One *pala* of *devadālī*, along with the juices of the six groups of digestive spices (*yavānī* etc.), *ṣaḍgranthā*, *picumanda*, water, *kaṇā*, *bhārṅgī*, *śilājatu*, and oil—

Having ground [the ingredients] into a fine paste and combined them with sour gruel (kāñjika), applying this as a plaster on the stone [of the rectum] destroys hemorrhoids (durnāman), as well as anal fistulas (gudaja) and all diseases of diarrhea (atisāra).

(98) The application of instruments, surgical tools, and cauterization has been described; that procedure is as prescribed for the extraction of foreign bodies (śalyaka). There, [the growths] are cut with an instrument, and cauterization should be performed there. (99)
Likewise, having cut out the *carmakīla* (skin-hardening lesion), it should be cauterized with alkali by the wise physician;
when cauterized with alkali, the color is praised as being like that of a ripe jambū fruit.
Alternatively, one may cauterize with the alkali of *sūraṇa*, along with *kadalī*, *jīva*, and *mudga*.

An alkaline solution of *palāśa* and *kokilākṣa*, combined with *apāmārga* and ghee, is recommended for the burning sensation caused by alkali; alternatively, *kuṣṭha*, *pathyā*, nimba leaves, and realgar may be used with fresh butter or ghee. 101–102.

Therefore, one should cast [the mixture] mixed with honey and ghee onto smokeless embers and fumigate the end of the anus until comfort is attained. [The ingredients are] realgar, ginger, guggulu, and mustard seeds. 103.
One should fumigate hemorrhoids, anal diseases, and fistula-in-ano with Devadāru, Pauṣkara, Viśalyā, and the juice of Sarjikā, along with ghee;
this destroys malignant catarrh and ulcers emitting a putrid odor.
This incense—consisting of *nirguṇḍī* leaves, *patra*, *haritāla*, mustard powder, and *devāhva* (tagara), combined with ghee, sugar, and honey—is for hemorrhoids and similar ailments;
it destroys painful anal fistulas, ulcers, irregular fevers, malignant skin eruptions (*visarpa*), scabies, chronic catarrh, and cough, and it eradicates the influence of malevolent planets. (106)
Thus the ritual procedure has been declared; now hear from me the wholesome foods:
*śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, horse gram, *āḍhakī*, *vāstuka*, *cillī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *kūṣmāṇḍaka*, and *paṭola*.

Kāravella, tuṇḍīra, sūraṇa, rājika, and arjaka (108), as well as jaggery, buttermilk, and ghee—these are always recommended for hemorrhoids. Furthermore, the meat of a boar, a porcupine, an iguana, a rat, or a reptile [is beneficial]. (109)
The flesh of the common quail (*lāva*), the partridge (*tittira*), and the eggplant (*vārttāka*), as well as boiled meat, are declared [unfit].
110 Dried meat (*vallūra*), fish, curd, slimy oil, and food consisting of *bilva* and eggplant must be strictly avoided.
One should also carefully avoid unnatural postures, sleeping at night or during the day, and that which is cold or excessively cold. 111
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twelve.
Ātreya said:
Now I shall explain the etiology and treatment of coughs; listen, O high-minded son, to the eight types of coughs:
those arising from laughter, excessive laughing, dust, suppression of wind, and food passing through the wrong channel.
Likewise, from the suppression of the urge to sneeze, a cough arises in men at every dwelling place.

From the consumption of sweet and slimy foods, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, and eating curd, sour, salty, and cold things, there arises the *madanataila* type of phlegm, as well as that caused by small bulbs, wine, or even the phlegm accumulated in a previous birth. 2–3.
The *udāna* wind, due to its upward movement being obstructed by *kapha* that has followed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), becomes elongated;
having emerged from the heart, it produces a cough in the throat characterized by *kapha*, and by this means it receives the designation "cough" (*kāsa*).
Eight types of coughs have been fully described, and another, born of injury (*kṣataja*), is proclaimed.
The [fevers] are those caused by vāta, pitta, and śleṣman, as well as that caused by the combination of all three (sānnipātika); 5.
that arising from vāta and pitta, that arising from śleṣman and pitta;
the seventh here is caused by blood, and the eighth arises from wasting (kṣaya). 6.
There is no dyspnea (śvāsa) without vāta, no cough (kāsa) without phlegm (śleṣman), and no hiccup (pikṣa) without blood; likewise, there is no wasting (kṣaya) devoid of pitta.
Thus the origin [of these diseases] has been described; hereafter I shall state their symptoms.
By which [signs] the eightfold supreme cough of men is characterized:

one whose sense organs are wasted, who suffers from pain in the flanks, excessive force, or is enveloped by colic and has a constriction in the throat; a person who is drowsy and has a broken voice—such is the manifestation of cough caused by Vāta. (8–9)
In cough arising from Pitta, there is a burning sensation in the throat, fever, emaciation, fainting, thirst, and giddiness;
the mouth has a pungent taste, and there is pain in the head. One spits out Pitta, and the nails and eyes become yellow.
In cough arising from Kapha, there is stiffness, vomiting, and paleness; one spits out thick phlegm.
In cough arising from *kapha*, there is a lack of appetite for food, a feeling of the body being filled with phlegm, and a thick voice (11). In cough arising from all three *doṣas*,
the patient is afflicted by itching, burning sensations, dyspnea, vomiting, emaciation,
anorexia, headache, swelling, and nausea (12).
Cough, itching, thirst, abdominal pain, insomnia, dry cough, and thirst arise from vāta and pitta;
there is a smell of smoke, yellow discoloration, inflammation of the eyes, and blood-tinged secretions.
13. Kapha [is characterized by]: [the smell of] smoke, yellow color, and inflammation of the eyes accompanied by blood.
Kapha associated with pitta and blood causes thirst and other symptoms;
when kapha is combined with blood due to excessive sexual indulgence, suppression of natural urges, injury, or the exertion of lifting heavy weights, it becomes "kṣataja" (traumatic) kapha. 14–15.
Because of that, there is pain in the heart, he coughs harshly with blood, his breath is exhausted, his body wastes away, and he is dejected, afflicted by mild fever; he trembles,
suffers from a splitting sensation in the joints, and is oppressed by delusion and vertigo.
Thus described by Kṣataja, this [disease] takes away the lives of men.
From a wound that is slight, diminished, or from a sudden impact, and through the occurrence of a fall or a blow, the phlegm (kapha) originating from blood arises. 17–18.
His mouth has a cadaverous odor, he is afflicted by heart-pain, his sense organs are impaired,
he suffers from spitting blood, or he is afflicted by labored breathing and intoxication;
his body constantly wastes away, and delusion and thirst arise.
One should diagnose *raktakāsa* (blood-spitting cough) as being endowed with these characteristics.

Now, the symptoms of cough are observed by inference from wasting (*kṣaya*) in cases of anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), consumption (*yakṣma*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), or chest injury with wasting (*kṣatakṣaya*). 20–21.

In cases of swelling, hemorrhoids, and catarrh, cough necessarily arises; one should carefully diagnose the cough in these instances through inference. In the elderly, blood-cough (raktakāsa) occurs, and that too is declared to be palliable (yāpya).
Cough arises in children due to the deficiency of breast milk.
These coughs have been described by the ten foremost physicians;
their remedial treatment consists of wholesome diet and medicine.
A decoction of *śatamūlikā* boiled and mixed with powdered *kaṇā*, drunk lukewarm,

destroys cough arising from wind (*marut*) along with its pain for men, and acts as a digestive. (25) A linctus combined with the powders of *bhārṅgī*, *śaṭhī*, *gostanī*, *śṛṅgavera*, *śṛṅgī*, and *kaṇā* [is likewise beneficial].
Taken with jaggery and oil, this is beneficial for men and destroys disorders of cough arising from wind (vāta).

(26) A powder consisting of viśvā, duḥsparśā, śṛṅgī, śaṭhī, puṣkaramūla, devadāru, bhārṅgī, kaṇā, musta, and rāsnā, combined with sugar and taken daily, indeed cures cough caused by breath and wind. (27)
One should grind together kaṭphala, kaṭutṛṇa, bhārṅgī, mustā, vacā, dhānyaka, parpaṭa, devadāru, dārvī, viśvā, and uttakarkaṭa;
this paste, when combined with honey, should be drunk by the person. 28.
It acts as a remedy for coughs arising from wind as well as those produced by phlegm;
it quickly destroys wasting, catarrh, throat-obstruction, and dryness caused by wind, as well as phlegm, hiccup, and fever associated with phlegm. (29–30)
An electuary made from one kola each of raisins, *āmalakī* fruits, and long peppers, combined with dates,

destroys hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*), cough, and consumption, as well as jaundice, anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and chlorosis (*halīmaka*). (31) [Likewise,] *vālā*, *bṛhatī*, licorice, *vṛṣa*, as well as *kuṣṭha* and *picumandaka*...
This paste, combined with cow’s milk, is beneficial as a drink in cases of fever caused by pitta and kapha.

(32) A powder made from mustā, āṭarūṣaka, triphalā, devadāru, bhārgī, kaṇṭakārī, along with its flowers, fruits, roots, and leaves, together with rāsnā, viṣā, and madhukasāra, when taken with boiled water, destroys cough. (33)

Alternatively, a pill made from sugar, dates, grapes, parched grain, long pepper, honey, rock salt, and the great medicinal herb (musta) from Magadha, when held in the mouth at night, possesses vast therapeutic qualities; it destroys asthma, consumption, hemorrhage, and cough.
(34) Sugar, dates, grapes, parched grain, long pepper, and honey—[these are used for the same purpose].
A linctus prepared with ghee is beneficial for warding off pitta-type cough.
[The ingredients are: leaves of *āṭarūṣaka*, leaves of *picumanda*, the fresh juice of *tulasī*, *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, and *marīcaka*. (35–36)
One should lick powdered ginger mixed with jaggery in cases of cough caused by phlegm;
one should drink a comfortably warm decoction of bhārgī and nāgapippalī, or the wise person should take the juice of fresh ginger with honey. 37.
In cases of cough, dyspnea, catarrh, and fever arising from phlegm,
the wise have likewise prescribed kaṭphala, bhūtṛṇa, bhārṅgī, śuṇṭhī, parpaṭaka, vacā, and surāhva boiled in water. (38–39)
This drink, combined with honey, is used in cases of cough caused by vāta and kapha,
as well as in dyspnea, hiccup, fever, wasting, and severe chronic cough (40). Tālīśapatra, marica, viśvā, and śyāmā are added in increasing proportions.

One should lick at dawn a paste of cinnamon bark, cloves, cardamom, and long pepper increased eightfold, along with four parts of sugar (41). This destroys respiratory distress, cough, splenic enlargement, loss of appetite, catarrh, vomiting, hiccups, edema, diarrhea,
malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, consumption, and pulmonary tuberculosis (kṣataja-yakṣman) (42).
Tālīsa, triphalā, priyaṅgu, magadhā-bhūla, mustā, śaṭhī, dārvī, lādalana, nāgakeśara, lavaṅga, and likewise nāgara; kṛṣṇā, kola, bālaka, along with cavilā, mūrvā, viṣā, and karkaṭa.

Grapes, kuṣṭha, niśā, agni, vatsaka, vṛṣa, gokaṇṭa, tiktā, as well as vṛkṣāmla, pomegranate, sour karaka juice, and ripe badara fruits— having prepared an equal-part powder of these, one should add an equal amount of sugar.

Half a *pala* [of this] should be administered; it destroys hemorrhagic cough as well as asthma, and is always recommended for those suffering from anemia (*pāṇḍu*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), wasting due to fat (*meda-śoṣa*), anal diseases, and consumption (*yakṣman*).

In cases of cough caused by wasting (*kṣaya-kāsa*) or those arising from the three *doṣas*, [it is used]; in that born of undigested matter (*āma-ja*), there is pain from colic (*śūla-roga*), splitting of the joints, giddiness, and exhaustion.

Emaciation, headache, and discharge from the eyes indicate that [the disease] has entered deep; 45. Furthermore, lockjaw or loss of consciousness, as well as vomiting arising from indigestion—that vomiting is also of two types, being either oily (snigdha) or dry (rūkṣa). 46.
Deep-seated eye pain, vomiting, constipation, flatulence, diarrhea, aching in the limbs, swelling, excessive fainting,
deformity of the body parts, and being afflicted by vertigo such that one perceives the world as spinning; 47.
Headache and extreme trembling, with hands and feet feeling cold as ice—when vomiting is accompanied by these symptoms, one should avoid it from afar;
for that vomiting, even when combined with all other treatments, is incurable if it arises from indigestion, according to the wise. 48–49.

A decoction prepared from the five roots (pañcamūlī) with rock salt (saindhava) and a paste (kalka) of āmalaka, or a decoction mixed with long pepper (pippalī), should be drunk; this wards off wind (vāta) and vomiting.
One should give milk with sugar to a person, for it very quickly destroys vomiting arising from bile (pitta). 50.
Either a powder of grapes or of *kṣīradārvī* taken as a linctus with honey destroys [the disease]; they drink [this] fifty-one times.

One should lick a powder of the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *puṣkaraka*, *vacā*, as well as *abhayā* and rock salt, along with jaggery; drinking this combined with human urine destroys vomiting caused by *kapha*. 51–52.
A powder of śaṭhī, dārvī, abhayā, śuṇṭhī, and māgadhī, combined with ghee and mixed with buttermilk, destroys vomiting caused by the three doṣas.
parched rice grains produced from red śāli rice, when combined with honey and sugar, [likewise cure it].
It is my opinion that this quickly destroys the feverish affliction of a young woman.
(54) Furthermore, sandalwood ground with the juice of *āmalakī* and mixed with honey, taken as a linctus in the measure of one *pala* in pill form, certainly cures vomiting. (55)

The juice of fresh pomegranate mixed with cumin and sugar, or likewise with oil and honey— these four gargles (kavalagraha) destroy the four types of anorexia, as well as those arising from wind and other humors, and those produced by combinations of two. (56–57)

A powder made from equal parts of the three pungents (trikaṭuka), the two types of turmeric (rajanīdvaya), the three fruits (phalatrika), honey, and barley-awn (yāvaśūka), when combined with honey, cures vomiting.
(58) Pomegranate with jaggery, or grapes, or myrobalan (pathyā) combined with ginger and jaggery [are also effective].
Trivṛt or Nāgara, combined with jaggery, induces emesis;
one should cause men to drink a cold decoction of Parpaṭa with jaggery,
which destroys even the most terrible vomiting accompanied by Pitta and vertigo.
A decoction of *kākolī* and *kākamācī* combined with sugar,
or parched rice flour (*lāja*) combined with sugar, cures vomiting caused by *pitta* in men.
Likewise, the juice of *mātuluṅga* combined with *pathyā* and sugar [is effective].

It destroys vomiting arising from bile and quickly subdues it. Upon seeing a severe bilious vomiting accompanied by burning sensations and vertigo, one should [administer] its *āragvadha* leaves combined with honey and sugar. 62–63.
Drinking milk mixed with *mustā* and sugar is recommended; likewise,
drinking the tender sprouts of the *jambu*, mango, pomegranate, and *āmalaka* fruits after being soaked in whey (*mastu*) destroys vomiting caused by *śleṣman* in men.
One should administer a powder of *sarja*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, and *kadamba* mixed with *kolo*, along with *śuṇṭhī*, *dhānyaka*, and jaggery;
this quickly destroys vomiting arising from *śleṣman* (phlegm) in men. Likewise, a linctus composed of *śaṭhī*, *kaṇā*, honey, and *viḍaṅga* also [achieves this].
[66] [A linctus] of *elā*, *lavaṅga*, *gajakesara*, *kola*, *sarja*, parched rice (*lāja*), *priyaṅgu*, *ghana*, *candana*, and *pippalī*...

Having licked powders combined with *mārkava* and sugar, one destroys vomiting born of phlegm, wind, and bile.
