(67) Having licked a powder consisting of equal parts of cardamom leaves, *gajakesara*, cinnamon bark, *ela*, *lāmajjaka*, *dahana*, *ghana*, *priyaṅgu*, sandalwood, and *magadhajā*, one overcomes vomiting caused by the three *doṣas* when mixed with sugar. (68)
When the *doṣa* has moved to the upper part of the body, purgation is recommended;
once that has occurred, even if [the disease] remains in the lower part, emesis certainly pacifies it.
Alternatively, if it has moved to both parts, then *bhārṅgī* and honey should be administered.
Having recognized vomiting caused by worms, one should perform the treatment for pacifying worms.
[One should avoid] that which is hot, nor excessively sour, nor sharp, nor likewise light;
nor the *tandulīyaka* potherb, nor wine, nor even *kāñjika*.
Now listen to me as I describe the wholesome diet prescribed for the disorder caused by *vāta*: meat from marshy regions, cooked *śāli* rice, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vāstuka*;
likewise, *āḍhakī*, mung bean soup, curd, and preparations combined with jaggery and ghee.
Furthermore, charcoal cakes (aṅgāramaṇḍaka) are recommended as wholesome food.

Having observed [the patient] according to their strength, according to the time, according to the disease, and according to the digestive fire, they thus administer the appropriate therapeutic regimen of wholesome foods.

One should employ daytime sleep in cases of vomiting, dyspnea, diarrhea, hiccups, emaciation, indigestion, or again, in cases of nausea and excessive salivation; however, one should neither drink hot water nor consume excessive food.
Neither running nor physical exercise should be performed; one should avoid them when afflicted by vomiting.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vomiting," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirteen.

Ātreya said: [Fever arises] from fear, fatigue, loss of strength, the consumption of split pulses and dry foods, exposure to the sun, or when a chronic fever has subsided, as well as from wasting and blood-injury.
By these [factors], the three humors—vāta, pitta, and kapha—become aggravated.

The fourth type is said to be born from injury (kṣataja), while the fifth is known as born from wasting (kṣayaja). The sixth is declared to arise from indigestion (ajīrṇa), and the seventh from the consumption of dry substances (rūkṣa).

The eighth [type] arises with fever; hear from me its symptoms. Emaciation, a dark-brown complexion, a bad taste in the mouth, and trembling—these, along with thirst, should be recognized by the best of physicians as being caused by Vata. 3-4.
A desire for cold water, along with dizziness, burning sensations, delirium, fainting,
redness of the eyes, and thirst, is considered to arise from pitta (5). Sleepiness, a darkish complexion of the face, lassitude, and a craving for warmth result from kapha (balāsa).
Thickening of the phlegm, dark discoloration of the body, coldness, and thirst arise from kapha (6).
Eye pain, vomiting, burning sensation,
vertigo, headache, shivering, and coldness of the limbs constitute thirst born of the three doṣas (7).
Dryness of the mouth, yawning, headache, heaviness, and pain in the abdomen occur; furthermore, thirst is observed as a disease in a person suffering from indigestion (ajīrṇa).
When there is a depletion of rasa (plasma), thirst arises, as well as intolerance and affliction by hunger.
In cases of wasting due to chest injury (kṣatakṣaya), exhaustion, emaciation, giddiness, dyspnea, and dejection quickly manifest.
The thirst that occurs in these wasting conditions is not accompanied by a desire for food;
this other type of thirst in one afflicted by fever is said to be born from the force of the fever itself.
In cases of diarrhea or colic, thirst should be recognized by the best of physicians as [a complication].
Know that thirst arising from diarrhea, vomiting, burning sensations, fainting, giddiness, and emaciation does not reach satisfaction even with water; recognize that as incurable. 11–12.
Seeing thirst arising from wind (vāta), curd with jaggery is recommended;
or a decoction of *amṛtā* (guḍūcī) with jaggery, when drunk, removes thirst caused by wind. A paste of *śuṇṭhī*, *ajājī*, and *śṛṅgavera* mixed with water and *sauvarcala* salt [is also effective].
One should drink this well-cooled decoction, for it quickly destroys thirst arising from Vāta. 14.
A decoction of Kāśmarya, Padmaka, Uśīra, Drākṣā, Madhuka, Candana, and Vālaka, combined with sugar, removes thirst caused by Pitta. 15.
The banyan tree (*vaṭadruma*), *rodhra*, white sandalwood (*candana*), and pomegranate (*sadāḍima*),
ground with rice-wash water or even with cold water and drunk, remove thirst arising from bile (*pitta*).
[Verse 16] *Kuṣṭha*, blue lotus (*utpala*), parched grain (*lāja*), and the sprouts of the banyan tree (*nyagrodha*);
A pill made from these [drugs] ground together with sugar wards off thirst (17).
Grapes, blue lotus, and liquorice are recommended when consumed with sugarcane juice;
when drunk, they destroy thirst arising from bile as well as burning sensations born of bile (18).
A person should likewise drink milk mixed with sugar up to the throat and then induce vomiting; this destroys thirst accompanied by pitta.
One should also take water heated over a red-hot clod of earth and then allow it to cool.
One should drink water mixed with sandalwood for the destruction of thirst.
Or, one may take the sprouts of the *jambu* and mango trees, along with parched grain and sandalwood;
these, together with the flowers of *dhātakī*, should be ground and combined with the juice of *vāsā*.
This electuary removes phlegm and thirst, and it alleviates burning sensations, fainting, and vertigo; one should also drink a soup of *āḍhakī* mixed with parched rice and sugar (22).
One may drink milk with black pepper, or water mixed with black pepper.
To destroy thirst caused by phlegm, one should drink milk boiled with *kola* fruits (23).
A decoction of *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *priyaṅgu*, the *lodhra* tree, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and *kuṣṭha*,
when well-cooled and mixed with honey and sugar, destroys thirst arising from all three *doṣas* (24).
The sour fruits of the *kāla-dāḍima* tree mixed with *sārivā* and equal parts sugar,
or *pathyā* with the powder of pomegranate and combined with the juice of *mātuluṅga*,
or likewise water properly boiled and cooled in a wooden vessel— [these are beneficial]. 25.
One should cause that water, which has been repeatedly stirred, to be drunk; and in cases of parched palate, the best of physicians should also administer ghee,
for it removes thirst, burning sensations, vertigo, vomiting, emaciation, and fainting.
It certainly and quickly wards off thirst born of wounds or born of wasting.
Pomegranate, *kola*, *cukrīkā*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlavetasa*, along with the juice of *pathyā*, should be used as a plaster for the palate. 28–29.
The pulp of the *mātuluṅga* fruit ground with rice-water quickly prevents dehydration and destroys thirst accompanied by fever.
A plaster of parched honey applied to the palate removes dryness of the mouth.
A coating of honey and sugar on the palate prevents dryness (31).
A cold application of lotus-root boiled in cool water quickly destroys dryness of the palate, as do the tender leaves of the *jambu* and mango trees (32).
If one afflicted by thirst should first eat nimba fruits, or mātuluṅga fruits, or sauvīra, or ginger, a wise person should not give [the medicine] to him;
for upon seeing it, or even from its mere sight, saliva flows profusely from his mouth. 33.133-134ab.
By this, it removes his wasting and also subdues thirst.
(34) Red rice (*raktaśāli*) with curd and sugar is recommended as food; furthermore, alkaline and pungent foods are not advised. (35)

In cases of wasting (śoṣa), vomiting, thirst, exhaustion, alcoholism (pānātyaya), diarrhea, and consumption, sleeping during the day brings relief. (36) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Thirst and Dryness of the Palate," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 13.
Chapter Fourteen.
Ātreya said:
[This condition arises] from the suppression of natural urges, from excessive restraint, from emaciation or physical injury, or even from thirst.
By consuming incompatible foods, the aggravated *doṣas* cause fainting (*mūrcchā*). Attached to each of the five sense organs are twelve [channels],
and the channels associated with all five sense organs together number sixty.
The channels block the gateway; by that, the mind becomes stupefied.
Due to the destruction of perception, a person quickly becomes unconscious and remains so perpetually. Falling swiftly like a piece of wood, this is called the swoon of delusion (mohamūrcchā).
That [fever] is declared to be of six types: arising from wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha), as well as from blood (śoṇita), injury (abhighāta), wine (madya), or poison (viṣa).
Among these, it provokes the bile, while the wind and blood are combined.
Due to the weakness of the humors' proportions, fainting (mūrchā) and delusion (moha) are proclaimed;
I shall describe their symptoms individually in brief.
One sees blue or black darkness and enters into a state of unconsciousness in an instant.
Trembling and softness of these [limbs] returns in an instant.
Fainting occurs due to Vāta, as well as emaciation, distortion of the face,
watering of the eyes, salivation, and momentary flatulence.
The patient enters deeply into darkness that is yellow, blue, or green;
there is burning heat and thirst, and the eyes become red or yellow. Furthermore, the body is covered in sweat, there is exhaustion, and the stools are broken up.
From pitta arises fainting and headache (10);
one sees the quarters of the sky as if filled with smoke and perceives darkness before him;
there is distress in the eyes, weak digestion, and a coldness in the limbs (11).
One awakens after a long time, the throat makes an excessively gurgling sound,
nausea and fainting occur, and there are various symptoms born of phlegm; O best of physicians, epilepsy is seen arising from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta).

If one causes living beings to be killed together with blood, they faint from the smell of that blood; there is fainting, headache, trembling, loss of physical control, muttering, and vomiting again. 13–14.

With a bewildered mind, bloodshot eyes, and a disposition for sleep, he becomes subject to liquor. Furthermore, from the wasting of wounds or from the consumption of *kodrava* grain, another [condition] arises;
through that, delusion and fainting occur, and he sleeps with a troubled mind. 15–16.
From an excess of *pitta* indeed arises fainting (*mūrchā*) for a person; from *pitta* and *vāyu* together, men experience vertigo (*bhrama*).
From *vāta* and *kapha* combined, a person suffers from drowsiness (*tandrā*), while from *kapha*, *vāyu*, and darkness (*tamaḥ*), a man experiences excessive sleep (*nidrā*).
[For the relief of sweat, affliction, and massage, one should use wind; for the pacification of *pitta*, cold food, drink, and the breeze of a fan.]
The drinking of medicinal decoctions (*kaṣāya*) is always praised as being truly effective for alleviating dizziness or fainting arising from an excess of phlegm (*śleṣman*).
One should cause [the patient] to drink a cooled decoction of *triphalā* mixed with sugar, and one should also cause them to drink a decoction of *durālabhā* mixed with sugar. 18–19.

Having ground the kernel of a jujube fruit (*kola*), the marrow of a *kesara* nut, *uśīra*, and sandalwood with cold water, one should drink it in an unbroken draught; this destroys fainting (*vimūrcchita*).
Upon seeing fainting born of blood (*raktajā mūrcchanā*), a cooling regimen must be applied.

In a person who is weak due to consumption (kṣaya), emaciated, suffering from fainting, and has lost all physical movement, the restoration of consciousness is the cause for nourishment. One should press the thumbs together and firmly squeeze the nostrils. 21–22.
One should gently press the body with the teeth or with tongs, or one should apply heat to the forehead, the region of the back, and the crown of the head.
If it is not successful even in this way, then swinging (cāndolana) is beneficial. 23–24.

One should sprinkle a person afflicted by fainting with all cold water and fan them with the feathers of a peacock's tail; indeed, the practice of swinging (dolāyana) removes the delusion of fainting, dizziness, or even alcoholism (madātyaya).
Where there is karañja seed with rock salt and the juice of garlic leaves— 25.
An ointment made by grinding *mārka*, *pathyā*, and *vacā* with water destroys the drowsiness of the day.
(26) An ointment for the eyes consisting of horse saliva, black pepper, and salt is recommended;
it utterly destroys the drowsiness or sleep of a person for a hundred days. (27)

A fragrant decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) prepared with a good amount of astringent, taken with jaggery and fresh ginger in the morning, destroys intoxication, fainting, and insanity caused by sweet substances within seven days;
those who desire to draw out the blood [of the body] for the sake of pacifying delusion and fainting [should use it]. 28.
Therefore, one should attentively administer bloodletting in those [conditions].
In all types of fainting (mūrchā), one should employ cold affusions, immersion baths, sandalwood paste, the breeze of fans, and cool food and drink. (29–30)

A person should overcome fainting due to vāta with syrups made from sugar, sugarcane juice, and grapes; and fainting due to pitta with decoctions of *kāśmarya* and *madhuka*. [One should also take] a boiled decoction of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, clarified butter, or a boiled preparation of *āmalakī* juice.

One should drink the juice mixed with sugar and parched grain (lāja), whether warm or cold. When combined with honey, it destroys fainting (mūrchā), and one should restore consciousness with medicinal plasters.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fainting," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Ātreya said:
One dispels drowsiness and daytime sleep by means of songs, dances, and laughter from those who lead the way.
When there is no sleep at night, then one should perform this rite:
having tied the root and the crest of the *kākamācī* plant, the best of physicians—
having tied the crest with its tip pointing downward— induces sleep during the night.
One who desires sleep should rub the soles of the feet with marrow;
for one who finds no sleep during the day, there shall be sleep at night.
That sleep which does not come at night due to fear, anxiety, or greed— [it shall be attained].
By abandoning that anxiety, sleep arises in an instant.
A decoction made from the roots of *siṃhī*, *vyāghrī*, *siṃhamukhī*, *kākamācī*, *punarnavā*, and *vārttākī* induces sleep in men.

A decoction of *kākajaṅghā*, *cāpāmārga*, *kokilākṣa*, and *suparṇikā* quickly induces sleep; or one should bind the root [of these] upon the crest [of the head]. Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Sleep," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Sixteen.
Ātreya said:
O Lord of Sages, it has been stated that one suffers from separation from those worthy of service—such as disciples and younger brothers—as if from the poison of the Hālāhala snake.
Thirst, vomiting, labored breathing, delusion, burning sensations, and excessive thirst arise, as do the extreme impairment of the sense faculties.
For those wicked men who constantly and excessively consume liquor,
that intoxicant— which causes delusion— is like unwholesome food.
Just as poison is life-taking, yet through the application of yoga it is called nectar,
so too wine may be beneficial when joined with yoga, whereas through the lack of yoga it brings about extreme suffering.
For one afflicted by hunger or overcome by thirst, wine is like food in the absence of food.
There is no intoxication without the depletion of bodily constituents (*dhātus*), nor without food, nor from excessive drinking.
Alcohol consumed during overeating or during indigestion causes disease;
likewise, excessive verbal chatter constitutes the disorder of wind-intoxication (*vāta-madātyaya*).
In pitta-type alcoholism (madātyaya), there is burning sensation, fainting, diarrhea, and fever.
In kapha-type alcoholism, there is vomiting, anorexia, lassitude, drowsiness, a sense of being wrapped in a wet cloth, heaviness, coldness, and coryza.

O best of physicians, that intoxication arising from the three doṣas which is treated with the symptoms of all three being in equilibrium is called *madātyaya*. In such a case, emesis is recommended, as is the indulgence in sleep.
Bathing is beneficial, as is the drinking of milk; for food, curd with jaggery is recommended.
A linctus made of whey, sugar-candy, dates, raisins, sārivā, tamarind, āmalaka, and parūṣaka destroys alcoholism (madātyaya). 9–10.
Alternatively, one may grind [the herbs] with the juice of grapes, *āmalaka*, dates, and *parūṣaka*; that milk-drink is for all types of alcoholism (*madātyaya*).
Milk mixed with a decoction of *pathyā* is also a drink for alcoholism.
In intoxication by areca nut (*pūgīphala*), trembling, delusion, fainting, exhaustion, darkness of vision,
perspiration, agitation, and salivation arise.
One should recognize that being overwhelmed by dizziness and fatigue occurs in one intoxicated by areca nut.
A person who has fainted due to the consumption of betel nut should be recognized by these symptoms.
For him, cold water drunk or an enema (basti) beneficial for the bladder would be appropriate;
or, upon eating sugar, nut-grass (mustā) mixed with sugar should be given.
If fainting occurs from eating *kodrava* grain, very cold milk should be given;
in the case of intoxication by *dhattūra*, curd mixed with sugar should be administered.
Halinī, karavīra, mohinī, and madayantikā [are also used]. 16.
One should also quickly induce emesis with other types of tubers (kanda). One should cause [the patient] to drink milk mixed with sugar, or curd, or sugar.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Alcoholism," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 16.
Chapter Seventeen.
Ātreya said:
When the *samāna* [vāyu] is provoked, it causes even the beautiful pitta located in the skin of a person's body to become intensely burning and even most terrible.
When there is grinding pain in the teeth at the onset of the burning sensation, or when there is suffering from coldness, or even labored breathing,
emaciation, and restlessness— O best of physicians, these symptoms are identical to those of Pitta-fever.
One should begin the treatment for the pacification of the doshas as in the case of pitta-fever.
A decoction of kuśa grass, kāsa, sugarcane root, uśīra, musta, and vālaka,
combined with sugar, alleviates cold and burning sensations.
Parpaṭa boiled with ghanasāraka and uśīra, mixed with sugar and taken as a cold drink, quickly destroys the burning sensation of pitta-fever in men.
An ointment made of lāmajja, candana, and uśīra is for the alleviation of burning heat.
One should fan with palm-leaf fans upon a bed of plantain and lotus leaves.
For burning sensations, an ointment mixed with *kālīyaka* resin is recommended;
cool water is likewise praised for quelling burning heat and thirst.
While he is lying on his back and fast asleep, one should place a bell-metal vessel above his navel; by filling it with streams of cold water,
one should diligently perform sexual union, through which he attains pleasure.
One should also apply hundred-times-washed ghee over the burning sensation; alternatively, an application of *dhātrī* fruit (myrobalan) is for cold-born [fevers],
or for one afflicted by burning and dryness, it may be taken as a linctus to bring comfort.
Having ground the sprouts of the *jambu* and *āmra* trees with the juice of *nimba* and *bījapūra*, one who desires swift relief from burning sensations should apply this as an ointment.
(10) Furthermore, a fountain-house, the cool moonlight of the moon, cooling drinks, a cool breeze, and sandalwood paste [are beneficial].
A lotus, a continuous flow of affection,
as well as embracing and massaging Rāma, white and moist garments on the pair of breasts, milk, sugar, iron chains, and silver are beneficial for the pacification of burning sensations. 11.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Burns," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Eighteen.
Ātreya said:
When pitta, vāyu, and kapha severely aggravate the udāna breath,
and the prāṇa becomes intensely disturbed in the head, it causes a loss of motor function;
it leads the vital breaths toward unconsciousness and blocks the channels of the sense organs.
The patient's mouth becomes dry as if made of wood, and he spits out saliva;
his throat makes a gurgling sound, or he vomits froth;
his hands and feet tremble, and his eyes turn bloodshot.
O best of physicians, the symptoms of apasmāra arise as follows:
the eyes are turned away and sunken; there is darkness, burning sensations, and headache (4).
One afflicted by apasmāra perishes when their radiance, senses, and consciousness are destroyed (5).
For that [condition], a wise person should administer as a drink, collyrium, ointment, massage, or even as a potion, ghee and oil prepared for the treatment of epilepsy; likewise,
*agasti* leaves and black pepper ground with urine [should be used].
When used as a nasal drop (nasya), it is recommended and quickly destroys epilepsy in a person.
Alternatively, the root of *bandhyākarkoṭikā* mixed with ghee and sugar should be administered as a nasal drop for the pacification of epilepsy.
Slices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin) with cooked juices, along with *tryūṣaṇa*, *elā* leaves, and *nāgakeśara*,
together with equal parts of *kumedhikā*, *granthaka*, and *dhānyaka*, mixed with white sugar, *priyaṅgu*, and ghee—
this should be consumed at dawn; it is highly recommended that an unlimited amount of milk be taken over this.
It quickly overcomes the disorder of epilepsy and swiftly destroys disorders of the blood.
(10) A powder made from kūṣmāṇḍa, brāhmī, ṣaḍgranthā, śaṅkhapuṣpī, punarnavā, and surasā, combined with sugar and honey, [achieves this]. (11)
It is beneficial for consumption and indeed wholesome when eaten; it cures epilepsy, insanity, and disorders of bile and blood, and bestows pregnancy upon a barren woman.
[The ingredients are] the roots of rāsnā and māgadhikā, daśamūla, and śatāvarī.
One should add two-pala portions each of *caṇa*, *trivṛt*, and *eraṇḍa*.
[Also add] *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *śatāvarī*, *rāsnā*, *samaṅgā*, *śṛtaka*, the three aromatics (*trisugandha*), and *bhīru*. (13–14)
Excellent physicians should administer this *kuṣṭha* and *dīpaka* ghee;
it destroys epilepsy, insanity, internal hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*), and diseases of the rectum (hemorrhoids).
[This is prepared] with the juices of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*. 15.
Boiled old ghee cures epilepsy (apasmāra).
Mahābalādyataila is recommended for use as a medicinal enema (basti) or nasal drops (nasya); likewise, the Śatāvaryādigaṇa and the Daivata group are also beneficial. 16–17.
Furthermore, the *candanādya* ghee should be administered here by the best physicians;
it is beneficial in cases of epilepsy (*apasmāra*), insanity (*unmāda*), or diseases of wind (*vātaroga*).
[The ingredients are: the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), rock salt (*saindhava*), *kaṭukā*, and *vacā*.
The seeds of *naktamālaka* as well as white mustard seeds (19),
ground with goat's urine and formed into pills dried in the shade—
this collyrium destroys epilepsy and even severe insanity (20).
It destroys the defects of loss of memory, vertigo, and possession by malevolent spirits; it removes fever that occurs on a single day, every second day, or every fourth day.
It also dispels the veil of cataracts, night-blindness, and headaches. 21.
It quickly causes the forgetfulness of the *sannipāta* disorder for those who possess pride.

[One should use] sandalwood, *tagara*, *kuṣṭha*, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, the three fragrant substances (*trisugandha*), *vāsaka*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *abhīru*, *mṛdvīkā*, *pāṭhā*, along with *śyāmā* and *priyaṅgu*. 22–23.
Svayaṃguptā, pīluparṇī, viṣā, rāsnā, gavādanī,
the two types of kākoli, jīraka, the two types of medā, puṣkaramūla, ghanavāluka, vidārī, vāsumantī, vṛddhadantī, and viḍaṅga. (24)
Padmaka, aindravṛkṣa, as well as āragvadha and citraka;
dhānyaka with the five types of jīra, as well as tālīsa leaves, khadira, niryāsa, tagara, and kālīyaka and kaikata. (25–26)
One should grind nāgakesara, parūṣaka, and kharjūra together,
and then saturate them repeatedly with honey and ghee. This linctus is always recommended for severe epilepsy.

In cases of insanity, jaundice, anemia, and chlorosis; in consumption, internal hemorrhaging, and those afflicted by bile-induced diarrhea; in blood-dysentery, wasting diseases, head ailments, and chronic fever—28–29.

This [medicine], which wards off all diseases, should be administered in cases of Tamaka-shwasa, Bhramaka, vomiting, burning sensation, severe dysentery, urinary calculi, urinary disorders (prameha), cough, asthma, and chronic catarrh.
It should be administered to barren women and especially to the elderly;
it is also beneficial for children. Listen now to the authoritative measure for this:
when thus applied in disease, it is considered by the wise to be a "great paste" (mahākalka). 31–32.
Strong and endowed with excellent qualities, this linctus (leha) is declared by physicians to be a bestower of results in this world; it is honored by Kṛṣṇātreya. [The ingredients are:
grapes, devadāru, as well as niśā, madhuka, kṛṣṇā, kaliṅga, trivṛt, yaṣṭīkā, triphalā, viḍaṅga, kaṭukā, saffron, candana, and pomegranate.
Cāturjātaka, nimba, turagī, tālīsapatra, ghana, the two types of medā, suradāru, kuṣṭha, kamala, rodhra, samaṅgā, varī,
bhārṅgī, kola, dāḍima, amla, kāśmarya, śṛṅgāṭaka, kāmbojā, śaṇa, and ghaṇṭikā. (34)
A smaller and milder version contains Rāsnā.

One should lick one Karṣa of this powder, mixed with an equal amount of sugar, honey, ghee, and Kharjūra; it bestows all strength and quickly destroys epilepsy (apasmāra), as well as most dreadful insanity (unmāda), consumption (kṣaya), phthisis (yakṣmā), anemia (pāṇḍu), asthma, cough, blood disorders, urinary disorders (prameha), and hemorrhoids.

What is beneficial for women is praised [in this context]. (36) If happiness is not attained through these [means], one should burn [the offender] with an iron rod on the forehead between the eyebrows, or one should burn the man on the crown of his head. (37)
Those suffering from disorders of blood and bile (raktapitta) should avoid pungent and sour foods;

indeed, wine, betel nut, and astringent decoctions should be especially avoided (verse 38). Furthermore, in cases of epilepsy (apasmāra), substances that cause delusion or fainting should not be consumed (verse 39).
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Apasmāra," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. Chapter Nineteen.

Ātreya said: This mental disorder is known as *unmāda* (insanity). The deranged humors (*doṣas*), having become agitated, ascend upward due to their movement through improper channels. This condition called *unmāda* is difficult to cure even for the best of physicians; it is proclaimed to be of various types: one arising from a single humor, another from a combination of two humors (*dvi-dvandvaja*), another from the conjunction of all three (*sannipāta*), and yet another arising from poison. Furthermore, [it may occur] in an impure place, a deserted path or house, in the middle of a forest, or in a terrifying, dense street or a temple, or perhaps through some sudden fear or apprehension.

One whose mind is distressed and whose heart is agitated should abandon the wrong path and follow the right one (3). The birth of madness in men has been described by the most eminent authorities as arising from anxiety, pain, fear, joy, deliberation, greed, or from the disrespect shown toward gods, guests, brahmins, kings, and teachers, or from excessive love, or from separation from a beloved woman (4). Because of that, a person may become mute, or cry out, or recite things in a distorted manner; they may twitch, vomit, tremble, or laugh (5); they may run about or strike at their own bodies, and likewise their tongue perishes in the heat of their agitation.

If a person who is striving excessively sees wealth and then becomes afflicted, the best of physicians should perform the ritual for epilepsy (apasmāra) for him; I shall explain this specifically and first among the topics of the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā). Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Insanity" (unmāda-nidāna), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty.
Ātreya said:
Eighty-four well-known types of wind (vāta) exist that cause affliction in human beings;
I shall describe their etiology briefly, one by one.
[1] It arises from contradictory thoughts, improper eating, staying awake at night, excessive physical exercise, and being overcome by excessive darkness.
Due to bloodletting, irregular postures, and the forceful retention of prāṇa, apāna, and samāna,
the wind (vāyu) residing within the bodily constituents (dhātus) becomes aggravated even in those whose strength and senses are diminished by travel and ascetic toil—
namely, prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
From the disorder of these [doshas], these wind-related disorders arise individually:
headache, earache, pain in the temples, blood diseases,
and the affliction of hemi-crania (ardhaśīrṣa) which increases daily.
Afflictions of the nose, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), lockjaw (hanugraha),
stiffness of the tongue, pain in the palate, as well as asthma (tamaka), vertigo (bhrama), drowsiness, dyspnea, and throat disorders— these sixteen are located in the head.
Impelled by the provocation of the *prāṇa* [vital breath] together with *pitta*, there arise hiccup,
dyspnea, labored breathing, cough, wasting, pain,
hoarseness, nausea, pain in the heart, and vomiting caused by the liver and wind (*vāta*).
Sneezing, yawning, as well as hoarseness of voice, catarrh, loss of appetite, and coryza— these are said to arise from the *udāna* [vital air].
When the *udāna* is joined with phlegm, it becomes aggravated in the heart due to the bodily humors (*doṣa*).
We shall now describe the condition known as Vyānaka, which is a provocation of the Maruta (Vata);

this Vata, pervading all the limbs, produces a severe disorder of the bodily constituents (dhātus). It should be understood as residing within those constituents, and is thus described individually for each.

In vāta located in the skin, there is horripilation, as well as stiffness of the neck (manyā) and the shoulders (aṃsābhū). When it resides in the flesh, there is swelling and pricking pain; when it is situated in the fat, there is trembling; when it has reached the bones, there is breaking pain; and when it reaches the marrow, falling down occurs.
In the stage of semen (*śukra*), there is swelling of the joints; therefore, the symptoms of Vāta affecting the skin [are described].
One should suppress these Vātas located in the tissues (*dhātu*)—determining them as curable or incurable—by these means.
Vāyu that has abandoned its residence in muscle and fat is cured by medicinal treatments.
Others succeed only with great difficulty, or perhaps not at all.
There arises horripilation, a piercing pain, loss of sleep, lack of appetite, and darkness; the body feels as if pierced by needles, and ants seem to be crawling over it. 14–15.
Roughness of the skin and the face, emaciation of the eyes, and further, the loss of the embryo, menses, and semen, as well as trembling, occur;
there is also a dulling of the digestive fire, and he beholds various dreams. (16)
Loss of sleep agitates the general symptoms of Vāta:

it repeatedly convulses the limbs, causes piercing pain and tearing sensations, and produces high fever; this condition, born from the provocation of Vyāna, is known as Ākṣepaka (convulsive seizure). 17–18.
The body bends like a bow and is repeatedly convulsed;
with eyes moistened or fixed, he coos like a pigeon—him the best of physicians call by the name of apatantraka. 19.
In another school of thought, others say that the *prahva* is considered the *pratānaka*;
thereafter, when half of it has been seized, that wind is known as the *apratānaka*.
That wind, resting upon the *kapha*, torments [the body] like a staff.
That which quickly stiffens the limbs is called *daṇḍāpratānaka*.
That which, residing in the heart, the breasts, the fingers, and the joints of the ankles,
causes the tendons to stretch is called *snāyupratānaka*.
Then, when the wind spreads through the external channels or becomes localized in the waist, it causes a sensation as if there were a splinter;
the wise call that incurable wind-condition *pratānaka*.
There is another fourth type of *ākṣepa* (convulsion) arising from trauma (*abhighāta*). That *pratānaka* which is born from trauma is not curable;
it stretches the body upward and causes the limbs to wither.
That which is caused by the darkness of delusion (mohatamas) is considered to have its bone-joints completely dried up;

it results in half a *karṣa* of difficulty and causes the body to contract into a state of dryness. That which indeed involves the expansion of the back is likewise considered to be "single-limbed" (*ekāṅgika*). 26–27.
There may also be paralysis of one limb; furthermore, if the Vāyu is not cured by all the Vāyu-subduing medicines, it becomes difficult to treat.
Pricking pain, fainting, trembling, convulsions, and insensitivity to touch occur.
That wind which causes the limbs to waste away is called *tūnī*;
furthermore, that which causes trembling, pricking pain, and constriction, and by which one perceives touch, is said to be *pratitūnī*, as it causes the limbs to throb (*pratitūnayati*). (29–30)
Stiffness of the heart, stiffness of the back, and stiffness of the thighs, as well as sciatica (gṛdhrasī), have been described separately; listen further, O wise one.
These sixteen types of diseases are proclaimed to arise from the provocation of the vyāna wind. 31–32.
Colic, abdominal tumors (gulma), upward movement of wind (udāvarta), flatulence, and indeed the upward movement of gas;
indigestion due to transformation (pariṇāma), irregular digestion, and undigested food (ajīrṇa) cause abdominal tumors.
Furthermore, there is excessive moisture, residual chyle, and chyle that carries waste products.
Bandhī, bhedī, and vilāsī—these sixteen are equal [in their effects].

Bhagandara, bladder pain, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, severe skin eruptions (koṭhaka), defects of the male organ, prolapse of the rectum, and likewise other rectal pains [are also included]. 34–35.
Obstruction of urine and obstruction of feces—these sixteen should be primarily understood by the wise as resulting from the provocation of the apāna vāyu.
These disorders have been described; they have also been proclaimed in detail.
Burning sensation, fever, emaciation, and fainting are caused by wind (vāyu) combined with bile (pitta).
Coldness, swelling, loss of appetite, and numbness are caused by wind combined with phlegm (kapha).
O wise one, that which arises from a combination of two [humors] is known as curable wind-disease (māruta).
Even a simple wind disorder (vāta) is considered most difficult to cure.
The face becomes distorted, half the mouth is affected, the neck is twisted, there is a deformity of the eyes, and the patient suffers from pain and loss of joint function.

Those who are experts in the diseases of Vata declare that one who experiences excessive pain in the neck, the cheeks, and the sides of the teeth has Ardita (facial paralysis). Furthermore, salivation, dryness, lockjaw, and loss of taste [are its symptoms].
If one suffers from toothache and is afflicted by Vāta, [the symptoms are as follows];

likewise, when it is born of Pitta, there is yellowing of the limbs, fever, thirst, delusion, and swelling with stiffness; or when it is born of Kapha, or in the case of Ardita (facial paralysis), these same occur. 42–43.
For one who exhibits these signs— the onset of trembling, turbid eyes, exhaustion, unblinking gaze, and incessant, indistinct speech—
even a severe and irregular facial paralysis will be cured.

The throat becomes terrible for the purpose of devouring when the mouth is wide open during yawning; these conditions, including lockjaw (hanustambha), are indeed difficult to cure, occurring from irregular postures, sleeping during the day, or looking with the eyes turned sideways. 45–46.

The bodily wind (vāsanānila), having obstructed the speech-carrying vessel (vāgvādinī-śirā), produces stiffness of the neck; it causes one to look toward the side with great difficulty and may cause paralysis.
Furthermore, the wind residing in the blood, when localized in the vessels of the head, [produces similar effects].
That which causes headache is also an incurable seizure of the head (śirograha).
Therefore, I shall describe the counter-measures by which the wind (māruta) may be cured: oleation, drying, digestive processing, and pacification therapies should be employed. 48–49.

When [the disease] has reached the sinews, joints, and bones, the wise physician should employ fomentation, massage, oil-enemas, unctuous enemas, and purgative enemas; then, using the māṇimantha instrument, he should cause it to burst and subsequently pacify the wind.
In cases of *śukra-ga* (semen-disorder) and *vyāna-ga*, one should treat the patient like one suffering from *bīja-vat* (impotency).
A decoction prepared from *muṇḍī*, *guḍūcī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *rāsnā*, and *samaṅgā*, when mixed with milk, curd, or fresh butter, is beneficial even when combined together. (51–52)
The wise man should cook it over a gentle fire; once prepared, this ghee is indeed an emollient for men.
A dose of one *karṣa* is prescribed for drinking, as well as for massage and with meals.
It is beneficial as an enema (*basti*) for men suffering from disorders of Vāta for a period of seven days. 53–54.

Rāsnā, viḍaṅga, turmeric, dry ginger, along with sour gruel (sauvīraka), surasā, and rock salt—this very drink, taken warm in a dose of one karṣa for five days, serves as a drying agent (virūkṣaṇa) for men;
thereafter, for seven days, it acts as a proper digestive (pācana). 55.
Therefore, one should administer a pacifying treatment once the dosha has been ripened.

I shall now describe [the treatment] for when [the dosha] has reached the nourishing stage and taken refuge in the vessels (dhamanī): through abundant food, sudation, and sprinkling with warm water for seven days, one destroys the vāyu. 56–57.

A decoction of rāsnā, trikaṇṭaka, eraṇḍa, śataparvā, and punarnavā quickly destroys vāta disorders pervading the entire body. [58] A preparation combined with rāsnā, guḍūcī, dāru, nāgara, and eraṇḍa [is likewise effective].
A decoction [of these] is beneficial even in cases of generalized vāta affecting all the bodily constituents (samadhātugata).
59 A decoction of rāsnā, aśvagandhā, kāśīśa, vacā, and kapikacchu, when drunk with eraṇḍa oil, destroys vāta. 60
A decoction of rāsnā, dhānyaka, śuṇṭhī, yavānī, and daśamūla is declared to be a digestive (pācanaka) for men suffering from disorders of vāta;
these drugs beginning with rāsnā are said to be beneficial as purifiers (pāvana). 61–62.

One should consume half a *pala* of garlic every day for one month, combined with asafoetida, rock salt, cumin, black salt, as well as the three pungent spices (*kaṭutrika*), all mixed with clarified butter.
It destroys wind-diseases (*vātaroga*), facial paralysis (*ardita*), and tetanus (*pratānaka*);
it likewise draws away the afflictions of those with localized diseases as well as those with systemic diseases,
and it removes thigh-stiffness (*ūrustambha*), intestinal worms, and sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*).
Half a *pala* and one *pala* of well-minced garlic, along with asafoetida, cumin, rock salt, black salt, and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*),
all these powdered together should be combined with an equal amount of oil.
Just as fire might consume [fuel], one should take this in the morning with the decoction of *ruvuka* as an after-drink;
by using it for one month, one conquers all diseases of Vata,
including those affecting a single limb, those affecting the whole body, *ūrustambha*, and *gṛdhrasī*.
It cures pain localized in the joints of the hips and back, apatantraka, chronic fever that has entered the bodily tissues (dhātugata), and the fever known as saikarahva;
[the remedy consists of] ginger, turmeric, long pepper, cumin, and jasmine.
A man should drink equal parts of vacā, saindhava, rāsnā, and madhuka as a fine powder every day with ghee;
within twenty-one days, he undoubtedly destroys his diseases. (70–71)
One becomes a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*), illustrious, with a voice like the sound of clouds and kettledrums;
this linctus (*leha*) destroys all wind-related disorders (*vātāmaya*) and brings about well-being.
[The ingredients are: *śatāvarī*, *vacā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rāsnā*, *kadara*, and *śallakī*. (72)

The paste of the ten roots (daśamūlī), balā, kiṇva, tumburu, and guḍūcī, when combined with ghee, destroys wind (vāta) that has entered the body. A decoction of the bark of śallakī and cikkaṇī, mixed with oil, will restore a man afflicted by vāta-ardita to health within twenty-one days.
Therefore, an oil massage should be performed using both oils and clarified butter;
furthermore, one should prepare guggulu and garlic according to the prescribed ritual. Eight parts of bala root and four parts of daśamūla [are required].
The decoction should be prepared with four times as much water, or according to the measure of one *droṇa*.
To that, one should add one *āḍhaka* of milk, mix in one *āḍhaka* of curd,
and quickly add one *āḍhaka* of Kulattha pulse soup that has been left to stand overnight.
One *droṇa* of sesame oil should be cooked slowly in a cauldron with *jīvantī*,
*jīvanīya*, the two *kākalyas*, *jīvaka*, *ṛṣabha*,
the two types of *medā*, *sarala*, *dāru*, *śallaka*, and *kucandana*.
Kālīyaka, sarjarasa, mañjiṣṭhā, the three aromatics (trisugandhika), 80, māṃsī, śaileyaka, kuṣṭha, vacā, kālā, aṣṭā, śārivā,
śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā. 81.

One should mix yeast, *surā*, *mustā*, as well as *tālīśapatra*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), and *vālukā* right there; having performed the auspicious recitation (*maṅgalavācana*), one should prepare this excellent preparation which possesses all virtuous qualities. 82.
Having heated it in a vessel made of gold, silver, earthenware, or iron,
it should be administered according to the patient's strength as a drink, an external massage, or as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha-basti). (83–84)
One should administer this in cases of affliction by wind (vāta), or in fractures, or even in ruptures;
it is also for women who are barren, for men with scanty semen,
and for those who are emaciated, weak, or afflicted by chronic fever.
For those afflicted by rheumatism (āmavāta), one should likewise add kañcaṭa;
it should be administered in the morning for dryness of the jaw,
earache, eye pain, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), and pain in the sides.
Oil is as beneficial for all disorders of wind (vāta) as nectar;
it destroys asthma, cough, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and diseases of the digestive tract, and it quickly subdues even the eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). 88.
Planets, spirits, and piśācas, as well as ḍākinīs and śākinīs, flee to distant lands at the mere sight of *balā* oil;
it also drives away defects such as epilepsy and the like from afar. 89–90.
The elderly become young, and even a barren woman obtains a son;
this oil is known as Mahābala, and it is remembered as a great remover of Vāta.
Having added one Āḍhaka of Balā decoction, one should then add one Āḍhaka of curd.
One should cook together one āḍhaka of horse-gram soup and one āḍhaka of sour gruel (sauvīra), and add these medicinal herbs:
śatapuṣpā, devadāru, pippalī, and gajapippalī. 92–93.
One should add the powder of the three aromatics (trisugandhi), surāmāṃsī, kuṣṭha, and daśamūla; once prepared, one should remove it from the heat.
It is to be employed for drinking, as well as for massage, non-unctuous enema (nirūha), and nasal therapy (nasya).
It destroys eighty types of wind disorders and is the best of those possessing manifold qualities.
(95) Just as great medicinal oil is, so too is this [preparation] an increaser of qualities.
(96) [One should take] the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* and likewise the juice of bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*).
One should employ the juice of sauvīraka, a decoction of daśamūla, the broth of fermented māṣa beans, and curd; all these should be used in equal parts, with oil added as half that amount. 97–98.
It should be cooked over a mild fire and removed from the heat once prepared;
it is to be used for massage, but not for drinking or for enema therapy (basti).
It is also used for filling the ears in cases of ear diseases and for severe headaches.
In cases of disorders affecting half the head, pain in the eyebrows, temples, or eyes (100),
a person quickly attains relief through its application;
furthermore, by means of anointment, it destroys leprosy, scabies, and skin diseases (101).
It quickly undergoes destruction; it cures even severe epilepsy, and there is no pain in the bladder, nor fatigue or exhaustion in cases of Vāmavāta (left-side wind).
This is to be known as Āmapākī; one should not administer digestive treatment (*pācana*) for it. 102
Purgation should not be administered; instead, one should perform a stabilizing (stambhana) treatment for him.
There will be pricking pain in the waist, back, and chest region, as well as pain in the bladder, abdominal distension resembling a gulma, and finally, swelling itself. (103–104)
Heaviness in the head occurs and it falls excessively to the left;
that [disease] which pervades all the limbs should also be recognized by the wise one (verse 105).
One should perform digestive treatment for it, and thereafter, purgation.

Another type is proclaimed as being obstructive, causing inflammation of the abdominal tumors (gulma), and affecting all parts of the body. Among these, that which is curable should be recognized; the other two are difficult to treat.
The "unctuous" (snehī) and the "left-sided" (vāma) types are said to bring about the suppression of epilepsy.
Śyonāka, pāṭalā, bilva, tarkārī, pāribhadraka,
aśvagandhā, kaṇṭakārī, prasāriṇī, punarnavā, śvadaṃṣṭrā, and atibalā— these should be taken in equal parts. 108.
One should boil the remaining portion of the decoction in one droṇa of water until it is reduced to one-quarter;
then the best of physicians should add the following medicinal herbs while the liquid is being spoken of:
śatapuṣpā, vacā, māṃsī, dāru, śaileyaka, and varā.
Pataṅga, candana, kuṣṭha, and likewise another, raktacandana;
karañja seeds, aṃśumatī, the three aromatics (trisugandhi), punarnavā, rāsnā, turaṅgagandhā, rock salt (saindhava), and durālabhā. 111–112.
Having made a powder of two *pala*s each of sweet and astringent substances, one should add them therein, along with an *āḍhaka* of lac juice,
the juice of *śatāvarī*, and four times as much goat's milk. (113)
One should employ one āḍhaka of cow’s curd and sesame oil therein;
when it is seen to have been prepared, then the recitation of auspicious mantras (maṅgalavācana) should take place.
Having welcomed him and established him there, this is remembered as the rite for Nārāyaṇa.
It destroys disorders of the wind (vāta), as well as epilepsy and demonic seizures,
diseases of the head, diseases of the ears, and even the eighteen types of leprosy (kuṣṭha).
A barren woman obtains a son, and even a eunuch attains manhood.
A lean man acts like a youth, and a fool becomes intent upon the pursuit of knowledge.
This *Nārāyaṇa* oil was spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya;
one should also employ other medicated ghees and oils here.
By this, happiness is produced and wind-disease (vātaroga) is subdued.
119. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wind-Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-one.
Ātreya said:
Listen, my son, to the symptoms; I shall describe them to you in brief.
[They occur] in one who is sexually active, whose digestive fire is weak, and who is nourished by heavy food and drink.
When raw food is consumed along with bulbs and leafy vegetables, it is driven by the wind (vāyu) into the seat of phlegm (śleṣma-sthāna), where it undergoes putrefaction and gives rise to great pain.
Thus, diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra) occurs, and swelling arises in the joints.

O best of physicians, in Āmavāta there occurs the aging of the limbs, the falling away of strength from the mouth, and when the pain arises in the back and the neck, one sinks down in agony; furthermore, the body undergoes deformity.
For that [patient], oleation (snehana) should not be performed; instead, digestive therapy (pācana) is prescribed.
The wise physician should reduce the undigested matter (āma) by means of the fourfold signs of its classification:
the obstructive (viṣṭambhī), the tumor-forming (gulmakṛt), the diuretic-type (mehī), and the "cooked-undigested" (pakvāma).
Another [type] affects all the limbs; I shall now describe its characteristics as well:
it causes obstruction, heaviness, flatulence, and pain in the bladder.
For this too, digestive treatment (pācana) should be administered, and oleation (snehana) should likewise be performed.
When the abdomen rumbles and is afflicted with a mass-like pain (gulma) in the region of the waist,
accompanied by numbness, one should suspect undigested matter (āmagulma).
For such a patient, after first assessing the strength and weakness of the body, fasting therapies (laṅghana) should be administered at the outset.

One must never administer digestive (pācana) therapy when a gulma is suppurating, for it will lead to fainting. If digestive therapy is applied to a suppurated gulma, death will certainly occur quickly. Furthermore, one who possesses unctuousness in the body, numbness, weak digestion, and strength [should not be treated with such measures].
If one's *āmadoṣa* (undigested morbid matter) is devoid of unctuousness (*sneha*), it is proclaimed as "vāma" (obstructed).

For such a person, oleation therapy (*snehana*) should not be performed; rather, one should administer fasting (*upavāsa*), digestive remedies (*pācana*), and cause the *āma* to be expelled through diarrhea.
One whose face is swollen, who suffers from numbness as well as a distended abdomen, and who has loss of appetite along with diarrhea, is incurable according to the wise;
one must refuse treatment when there is even a doubt regarding his life.
Having recognized that the digestive process (pācana) has been completed, one should then administer powders from that [decoction].

When it is drunk with water, the *śyāmā* [plant] becomes cooked; the undigested matter (*āma*) falls downward, there is no pain in the bladder, and the exhaustion and fatigue caused by *āmavāta* disappear. (14–15)

One should recognize this as *āmapākin* (undigested fever); one should not administer digestive (*pācana*) treatment to it, nor should a purgative (*virecana*) be administered; instead, one should employ a constipating (*stambhana*) treatment.
[In such a case], there is pricking pain in the waist, back, and chest region, accompanied by bladder pain.
From the gulma, abdominal enlargement arises, as well as rumbling in the abdomen and swelling;
heaviness of the head occurs and undigested matter (āma) falls away profusely.
That [gulma] which spreads through all the limbs should also be recognized by the wise. 17–18.
One should administer digestive therapy for that [type], followed by purgation.

Another type is considered obstructive, causing suppuration of the gulma, and affecting all parts of the body. Furthermore, among these, those which are curable should be recognized, while the other two are difficult to cure.
The unripe (āmaja) type is said to be associated with oleation (sneha), while both types are considered difficult to cure (kṛcchrasādhya).
However, the ripened-unripe (pakvāma) type is easily curable; having understood this, one should perform the treatment.
[The decoction consists of] rāsnā, trikaṇṭaka, eraṇḍa, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā.
O best of physicians, when Vāta is located in the left side, a digestive potion (pācana) is recommended.
A man should drink a comfortably warm decoction prepared from rāsnā, śyonāka, kāśmīra, cikkaṇīka, and puṣkara as a digestive agent.
Know this to be the digestive (pācanaka) formulation prescribed for undigested matter (āma) accompanied by vāta.
In the case of āmavāta, one should drink water boiled with daśamūla and mixed with kaṇā;
or one may take the powder of guḍūcī, nāgara, and pathyā combined with jaggery.
Dhānyaka, nāgara, rājāmla, devadāru, vacā,
and abhayā constitute an excellent digestive (pācana) remedy for āmavāta that brings comfort;
likewise, one may drink the powder of kola with warm water.
It destroys rheumatism (āmavāta), weak digestion, colic, and abdominal tumors (gulma).
Having added one āḍhaka of balā decoction, one should add one āḍhaka of curd and one āḍhaka of buttermilk,
as well as one āḍhaka of horse-gram (kulattha) soup and one āḍhaka of sauvīra.
Having combined these together, one should cook them and then add the following medicinal ingredients:
*śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, *pippalī*, *gajapippalī*,
the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), *murā*, *māṃsī*, *kuṣṭha*, and the two sets of five roots (*pañcamūla*).
One should add the powder to it and, once prepared, pour it out. It should be administered internally as a drink or used in the procedure of a non-unctuous enema (nirūha-basti).
It destroys all wind-related diseases (vātāmaya) and is the best provider of a multitude of beneficial qualities.
One should drink castor oil combined with jaggery and milk;
for this is the best purgative for *āmavāta* affecting the entire body.
(31) One part of ginger and two parts of *krimija* [seeds]...

Having added three parts of the powder of *trivṛt* equal in measure to jaggery, one should eat a bolus; then, one should drink hot water and subsequently drink hot milk. By this means, a comfortable purgation is produced from the left side.
The best of physicians should prepare a decoction of viḍaṅga, śuṇṭhī, rāsnā, pathyā, and trikaṭu, reducing it to one-eighth of its original volume.
He should then add milk equal to half the volume of the decoction, as well as oil derived from eraṇḍa seeds in the same proportion.
One *karṣa* should be well-drunk as a purgative followed by a liquid vehicle (35).
One should eat *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, and *pathyā* together with jaggery; for this is the best purgative in cases of *āmavāta* and brings about comfort (36).

Abhayā ground with whey and combined with honey and sugar, as well as guḍa and āmalaka, will arrest acute diarrhea (āmātisāra). One should also administer vatsaka and the two types of jīraka ground with curd.
It pacifies diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra) and alleviates pain in the bladder.
Guggulu, garlic, and asafoetida combined with ginger—
this decoction serves to destroy worms and pacifies Vāta.
Ajamoda, ugragandhā, kuṣṭha, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), śaṭhī, the three fruits (phalatrika), bhārṅgī, puṣkara, the eight salts (lavaṇāṣṭaka),
the two types of jīraka, viḍaṅga, the two types of tumburu, and devadāru. 40.
Likewise, one should prepare fine powders of equal parts of bilva, śilābhedaka, rodhra, vatsaka, vāsaka, dhātakī flowers, śālmalī bark, and pomegranate. 41–42.

Vāta combined with ghee certainly destroys it quickly; likewise, when taken with asafoetida and alkaline water, it destroys the pain of colic, and similarly, it subdues Vāmavāta even with warm water. 43.

In cases of sciatica (gṛdhrasī) and pain in the hips, [one should use] water boiled with the ten roots (daśamūla). In cases of constipation, it is used with castor oil; or even in very severe swelling, combined with cow's urine for abdominal tumors (gulma); and when mixed with jaggery, it conquers anemia (pāṇḍuroga). 44–45.
Combined with honey in cases of urinary disorders (prameha) and with sugar in cases of consumption (yakṣman), it destroys all terrible diseases when administered according to the appropriate method.
One should avoid foods made from split pulses, sour substances, oil, and slimy preparations.
O best of physicians, one should not bathe with cold water during āmavāta;
when the āma-doṣa has been ripened, one should avoid āmavāta [therapies], as well as anything warm, liquid, or especially liquefying. 47–48.
One should also employ those wholesome regimens prescribed for fever in this condition.
(49) Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Āmavāta," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-two.
Ātreya said:
Listen, O high-minded one, to the disorders arising from blood and wind;
intense pain arises in the region between the hips, thighs, and knees. (1)

One should recognize it as *gṛdhrasī*; for that reason, its specific characteristics were not mentioned [separately]. When there is swelling in the middle of the knee accompanied by intense pain arising from *vātarakta*, it should be known as *koṣṭhaśīrṣikā*. 2–3.
When it occurs in the tendons of the arms and back, as well as within the fingers, that [disease] should be recognized by the wise as causing the wasting away of the hands and feet;
moreover, there is a tingling sensation in the feet and horripilation on the soles.
At the conclusion of the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*, there is perspiration of the hands and feet;
at the end of that associated with *pitta* and *vāta*, there is heat in the hands and feet.
For these [conditions], one should then cause the shedding of blood and apply sudation.
For massage, oil that removes Vāta is used; for drinking, Rāsnā-pañcaka, Śatāvarī, the two types of Bala, Pippalī, and Puṣkaramūla—
this powder taken with castor oil (eraṇḍa-taila) eliminates Gṛdhrasī.

The powder beginning with *ajamoda* is proclaimed for *āmavāta*; it should also be applied here as a remedy for *gṛdhrasī*. If comfort is not obtained by these means, one should cauterize [the area] with an iron rod.

In all diseases of the feet, one should apply cauterization transversely two finger-breadths above the two ankles; having examined the foot, one should cauterize the vein. (10) One should also employ the dietary regimens prescribed for diseases of the wind (vāta). (11)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gṛdhrasī," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-three.
Ātreya said:
Blood becomes aggravated in the body by pungent, alkaline, sour, and salty substances,
or through suppression [of natural urges], retention, or the practice of sleeping during the day and so forth; thus,
a simultaneous provocation of the wind (vāyu) is seen in all the limbs of men.
What is known as Vatarakta occurs in the bodies of men;
O best of physicians, it arises in those who are delicate, as well as in women,
and it especially becomes aggravated in those who are corpulent.

One should recognize vātarakta by laziness, itching, the appearance of circular patches (maṇḍala), discoloration, throbbing, swelling, emaciation, burning sensation, softness, and a dark-brown tint of the teeth and blood.
Having observed these contrary symptoms, a remedial treatment must be administered:
one should prescribe purgation, bloodletting, and drinks, ointments, and electuaries; furthermore, one should give him milk combined with coriander and dry ginger.

Having boiled the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba*, combined with honey, this acts as a digestive for those suffering from *vātarakta* (gout/rheumatism) and likewise serves as a pacifier; furthermore, the leaves of *picumanda* should be ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
An ointment is recommended for him to pacify vātarakta (gout/vasculitis):
dūrvā, mūrvā, śaṭhī, śuṇṭhī, dhānyaka, and madhuyaṣṭikā; this application as a plaster with cold water is for vātarakta. 8–9.
One should administer a preparation of one karṣa of coriander and two jīra seeds cooked with jaggery for those suffering from vātarakta, in order to pacify the doṣas.
If no relief is obtained by these means, then bloodletting should be performed.
One should administer those wholesome (pathya) remedies prescribed for fever in this case as well.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktavāta," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-four.
Ātreya said: Due to the consumption of jaggery and sour foods, as indicated by incompatible dietary combinations, the pitta becomes aggravated by the acidity; consequently, the throat is inflamed.
A burning sensation arises in his heart, as well as pain in the head;
sour eructations occur in the throat, and even sour hiccups rush forth.
Listen to the remedy for this: one should quickly induce emesis.
When the *amlapitta* has moved downward, a purgative should also be administered.
A decoction made from the leaves of the *pāribhadra* tree and the fruits of the *āmalakī* should be used for drinking; this dispels *amlapitta*.

A decoction of *paṭola* and *pāṭalā*, combined with coriander and ginger and taken with water, is said to be beneficial for the alleviation of *amlapitta*. [Likewise, a decoction of] *paṭola*, *viśva*, *amṛtavallī*, *tiktā*, *patra*, *nimba*, and *vatsaka* [is also beneficial].

The decoction [of these] destroys *visarpa*, *amlapitta*, *maṇḍalaka*, and *idradū*. At night, a digestive stimulant (*sampācana*) should be administered with a paste of coriander (*dhānya*) and ginger (*nāgara*).
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Amlapitta," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 24.
Chapter Twenty-Five.
Ātreya said:
Swelling occurs when the strength of the body is diminished by the consumption of sour, pungent, and hot substances, resulting in the impairment of the sense organs and the channels of the hair.
Due to coldness, or from the use of clear and slimy substances, or from dryness, injury, falling, or from being retained,

the wind (vāta) that has entered the stomach of a person may rush toward the extremities; consequently, this disorder produces swelling and various morbid changes in the hands and feet, occurring either separately or as a combination of two humors.

Swellings (śopha) that originate internally in a man may be curable when they are localized on the face; however, they are incurable when they spread throughout the entire body, or when they appear on the feet of a woman or on the face of a man. Furthermore, they are incurable in cases of wasting (kṣaya), vāta disorders, abdominal tumors (gulma), consumption (rājayakṣman), or abdominal enlargements (udara).
Even when born from blood, this very swelling occurs in the limbs as a disorder characterized by swelling;
furthermore, other upward-moving swellings arising from phlegm and bile should be known as difficult to cure and accompanied by many complications. 4–5.
When the phlegm reaches the head, swelling arises in the upper part;

when it stays in the middle [part] or has reached the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), the swelling is moderate and located in the lower part. When it resides in the nutrient fluid (rasa), the swellings follow the entire [system], as do the fluids that pervade the whole body.

Swellings affecting all the limbs, as well as those affecting the middle parts of the body, are to be avoided; likewise, swellings occurring in the elderly or the young, those born from injury, those arising from wasting, and those accompanied by vomiting, diarrhea, or dyspnea;
as well as those occurring in a person suffering from vertigo, fever, or emaciation, and any swelling that arises from another pre-existing swelling.
A disease that arises from no other cause than the physician is not curable, O best of physicians; nor is it curable when [the patient] has no other fault.
Pricking pain, dryness, and labored breathing result from Vāta; exhaustion, swelling, and a burning sensation from Pitta;
coldness, heaviness, distress, and itching occur in the Kaphaja type; and in the type born of two humors (Dvandvaja), the symptoms appear according to the characteristics of those two.

Therefore, I declare that for these [conditions], the application of sudation, digestive processing, purification, purgation, and bloodletting is prescribed as the procedure for swelling caused by decoctions (kaṣāya-śopha). Furthermore,
neither oleation nor drying therapy should be performed in this case.

A decoction of *punarnavā*, *magadhajā* (pippalī), the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *nimba*, *abhayā*, *kaṭukā*, *paṭola*, and *dārvī*, boiled until lukewarm, quickly causes the swelling and abdominal enlargement of a man to subside through its digestive action.
[13] *Punarnavā*, *guḍūcī*, and *guggulu* should be taken as an equal paste.

It destroys swelling, humors, abdominal tumors, and this type of kaphaja Udara (ascites). 14. The urine of an elephant, a buffalo, or a bull, as well as parched grain with jaggery, should be employed;
by drinking it, or milk combined with castor oil, the swelling quickly departs. 15.

Furthermore, the act of fomentation (saṃsvedana) should be performed there repeatedly, either with castor leaves or with tamarind leaves, using either sour gruel (kāñjika) or water; likewise for hairy plants and bitter gourd (kaṭutumbī). 16.
And likewise, one should apply fomentation after boiling [the herbs], using that same decoction while it is warm.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Swellings," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-six.
Ātreya said:
Through those treatments that give rise to swelling, the *vāyu* (wind) becomes aggravated;
by means of weak and irregular digestion, a *gulma* (abdominal tumor) is produced in the belly.
One should diagnose Vātagulma when the abdomen rumbles, an irregular digestive fire is observed, and there is piercing pain in the body and colic.
[Furthermore, one should recognize it by] emaciation, restlessness, a yellowish tint, and being afflicted by mild fever.
Darkness, confusion, thirst, pain, and abdominal tumors arising from that [wind] are caused by pitta;
emaciation, numbness, nausea, drowsiness, lethargy with coldness,
weak digestion, and constipation are the symptoms of an abdominal tumor arising from kapha.
Delusion, confusion, dullness, restlessness, hunger, thirst, laziness, sleepiness, and the affliction of abdominal tumors (gulma) arising from phlegm and bile;
as well as excessive sleep, lassitude, burning sensations, swelling, pain, and fever— these are the symptoms.
Discoloration, lack of appetite, dullness, constipation, deformity of the limbs, as well as diarrhea,
fainting, thirst, nausea, trembling, dyspnea, anorexia, indigestion, and abdominal tumors— this is the *sānnipātika* (combined) type.

That which arises from a single doṣa is curable; that arising from two doṣas is cured with difficulty; and that arising from the combination of all three (sannipāta) is incurable. We shall now describe its treatment.
The very same treatment prescribed for liver disease (yakṛt) and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī) is stated here, along with fasting.

In the same manner, splenomegaly (plīhā) has been described, though it was not mentioned again here. Now listen as the treatment for abdominal enlargement (udara) and abdominal tumors (gulma) is being explained:
namely, oleation (snehana), drying (rūkṣaṇa), digestive processing (pācana), and purification (śodhana). 9–10.

Palliative treatment, purgation, enemas, oleation, drying therapy, the drinking of alkali, and medicinal powders are the therapeutic procedures for abdominal tumors (gulma). [The following are the ingredients:
ginger, devadāru, surasā, mūrvā, and the minor five roots (laghu-pañcamūla).
The decoction of this [herb] should be reduced to one-eighth, and an equal amount of milk should be added;
then, an equal amount of curd and an equal amount of ghee should be cooked over a moderate fire until the ghee becomes visible, at which point it is declared ready.
One should cause that [oil] to be administered as a drink, an unguent, or for use in vessels;
since there are seven types of oleaginous substances (sneha), dryness (rūkṣaṇa) is beneficial following them. This should be performed for three days; O learned one, I shall explain this here.
Ginger, black salt, the two types of cumin, and asafoetida—
drinking these with sour gruel (kāñjika) causes drying and pacifies gulma.
In the treatment of gulma, the preparation of alkaline decoction (kṣārapāka) is also employed here.
One should also mix the alkali of *palāśa*, *arjuna*, and *sūraṇa*, as well as the alkali of *yavaśūka*, along with *sauvarcala*, *saindhava*, *udbhida*, or *sāmudra* salt;
having strained the water according to the prescribed method, these should be combined with the medicinal herbs. 17.
A powder consisting of *pathyā*, *agni*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rajanī*, *surāhva*, *kuṣṭha*, *viśālā*, *javānikā*, as well as *ajamodā*, the two types of *jīraka*, *ṣaḍgranthikā*, and *hiṅgu*,
when mixed with alkaline water and drunk, destroys all diseases arising in the digestive tract. 18–19.

It destroys all types of *gulma*, cholera (*viṣūcikā*), sluggish digestion with colic (*mandāgni-śūla*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), abdominal distension (*ānāha*), and constipation (*viḍvibandha*); it cures these three diseases of men. (20) Pathyā, samaṅgā, kalasī, vṛṣa, mahauṣadha, vātiviṣā, and surāhva— The provided text contains a Sanskrit verse followed by a list of medicinal herbs. Here is the translation of the verse: "It destroys all types of *gulma*, cholera (*viṣūcikā*), sluggish digestion with colic (*mandāgni-śūla*), fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), abdominal distension (*ānāha*), and constipation (*viḍvibandha*); it cures these three diseases of men. (Note: The phrase "these three diseases" likely refers to the preceding triad of *gulma*, *viṣūcikā*, and *mandāgni-śūla*, though the commentary might interpret it differently depending on the specific medical context. The subsequent list of herbs is: *pathyā*, *samaṅgā*, *kalasī*, *vṛṣa*, *mahauṣadha*, *vātiviṣā*, and *surāhva*.
Indeed, this [decoction] boiled in water is a digestive stimulant for abdominal tumors (gulma) and serves as a drink. 21.
A decoction of vacā, yavānī, trikaṭu, and daśamūlī is prescribed;
or alternatively, a warm decoction of dhānyaka and nāgara is beneficial for drinking. 22.
In all cases of vāta-gulma and in irregular fevers (viṣama-jvara),
the five-fold formulation beginning with rāsnā, or the digestive (pācana) formulation, is effective for maturing vāta-gulma.
Alternatively, śaṭhī, sauvarcala salt, and śuṇṭhī may be used as a digestive remedy for one suffering from gulma.
Vidula, grapes, kaṭukā, and nimba leaves,
combined with jaggery, should be administered as a digestive (pācana) remedy for a patient suffering from pitta-type gulma.
A paste of āmalakī mixed with sugar is also a digestive for one afflicted by pitta-gulma.
Yavānī, ugragandhā, and likewise the three pungents (kaṭukatraya),
drunk warm at night, act as a digestive aid for a kapha-type gulma.
Nāgara, krimijit, and pathyā, combined with three times the amount of trivṛtā, [are also used].
This powder, combined with jaggery, should be administered as a purgative for vāta-gulma (wind-type abdominal tumors).
Take one part of dantī, two parts of harītakī, three parts of trivṛt, and four parts of śuṇṭhī. (27–28)
Having mixed everything together in one place with an equal amount of jaggery (guḍa), one should eat a bolus (vaṭaka) in the morning and drink water over it;
this decoction leads to purgation and brings about the pacification of vāta-gulma. 29–30.
One should drink castor oil combined with sugar and milk;
this is excellent for inducing purgation in cases of *pitta*-type gulma and brings about comfort. (31) Likewise, one should use the tender leaves and the bark of the *āragvadha* tree.
Having processed it with castor oil, one should wrap it with castor leaves (32). Then, having smeared it with mud, one should place it over glowing coals.
Once well-steamed, that *bharjikā* should be eaten together with sugar (33).
Purgation is beneficial in pitta-type gulma; pure purgative therapy is likewise appropriate.
Having prepared a powder of triphalā, surasā, and śuṇṭhī, one should saturate it once with the latex of snuhī and then mix it with jaggery. (34–35)
Purgation is the destroyer of all abdominal enlargements (udara) in the case of a phlegm-born (śleṣma-ja) tumor (gulma). 36.
A powder of ginger (śuṇṭhī), black salt (sauvarcala), myrobalan (pathyā), viḍaṅga, and punarnavā, as well as apāmārga seeds, should be saturated with the milky sap of snuhī. 37.
One should eat this combined with jaggery and afterwards drink warm water;
this purgative is praised as beneficial and effective for all types of gulma (abdominal tumors). 38. Śuktikā, kṣāra, niśā, viśālā, kadala, sūraṇa, and kokilākṣa— [these are the ingredients].

Having burnt *pālāśa*, *dahanārjuna*, *śaṭhī*, *jayā*, *apāmārga*, and *kūṣmāṇḍaka*, and having cooked them with alkaline water until they are well-extracted, one should add asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and the three pungents (*trikaṭu*). This preparation removes abdominal tumors (*gulma*), distension, constipation, and colic, and is beneficial for all types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*).
[39] *Ajamodā*, *śaṭhī*, *dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, *kuṣṭha*, and *tumburu*...
Triphalā, citraka, śuṇṭhī, karkaṭaśṛṅgikā,
trivṛtā, surāhvā, puṣkara, vṛddhadāruka, as well as amlavetasa, tintiḍīka, and ciñcinī. (40–41)
Equal parts of citron (mātuluṅga) and asafoetida (hiṅgu), combined into one, mixed with a third part of ghee and powdered, is beneficial;
it destroys Vāta-gulma as well as abdominal enlargement accompanied by pain. 42
Asafoetida, the three fruits (trikaṭu), the two types of cumin, citraka, bhārṅgī, kuṣṭha, viḍaṅga, tumburu,
puṣkaramūla, viśva, surāhvā, along with alkali and the five salts— these, for the purpose of destroying vātika gulma, destroy the pain of colic in men. 43–44.
Asafoetida, sauvarcala salt, cumin, ginger, costus, and viḍaṅga,
when drunk with fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), destroy abdominal tumors (gulma) associated with vāta.
Two types of cumin, the three pungents (trikaṭu), śaṭhī, tumburu, citraka, and honey [are also effective].
Linctus is beneficial for a pitta-type gulma and serves to alleviate swelling (46).
A powder of liquorice, nimba leaves, as well as āmalaka fruit,
and sugar, when licked with honey, wards off pitta-gulma (47).
The powder of trikaṭu, triphalā, citraka, and vaṭaka fruit,
when drunk with wine or with a decoction of the fruits,
is beneficial for the destruction of kaphaja gulma and is conducive to well-being. (48–49)
Rodhra, kamala, viśvā, kuṣṭha, and citraka,
combined with nāgara and hiṅgu, this powder mixed with urine destroys phlegmatic gulma and alleviates pain in the abdomen.
One should drink *ugragandhā* (black hellebore) along with black pepper (*marica*) and alkaline powder (*kṣāracūrṇa*), combined with urine; this destroys phlegmatic abdominal tumors (*śleṣmagulma*).
[Likewise, one may take] ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), black salt (*sauvarcala*), *bhārṅgī*, *vatsaka*, and barley-alkali (*yāvaśūka*).
Two parts of jīraka, one part each of cāṭarūṣa, yavānī, hiṅgu, and saindhava salt,
combined with āragvadha and mixed with ghee— this powder brings relief quickly and easily for a gulma arising from vāta and śleṣman. (53–54)

Ugragandhā, the three fruits (triphalā), devadāru, punarnavā, trivṛt, combined with sauvarcala salt and alkaline water— when drunk, this is considered an excellent remedy for providing relief in cases of vāta and kapha-type gulma. 55

If the treatment for *grahaṇī* and abdominal tumors (*gulma*) should be applicable here, it may be employed; furthermore, purgation (*virecana*) should be administered in all cases of swelling and abdominal enlargement (*śopha-udara*).
Abdominal tumors and enlargement, when accompanied by swelling and diarrhea, destroy a man.

For him, the drinking of alkaline water (kṣārodaka) along with powders of bṛhatī, hiṅgu, and so forth, or those beginning with ajamodā, serves to pacify swelling and diarrhea; for although vomiting and diarrhea may also occur in cases of abdominal tumors (gulma). 57–58.
One should understand that the treatment is thus accomplished; however, if the procedure is beneficial, it should be rejected [for the time being].
One should repeatedly administer a mixture of jaggery, pomegranate, and *pathyā* (yellow myrobalan) combined with honey for both vomiting and diarrhea. 59. One should apply this again and again.

A Gulma endowed with all the symptoms is caused by the combination of all three Doshas (Sannipatika). Pricking pain, restlessness, discoloration, accompanied by fainting, diarrhea, vomiting, moisture, and drowsiness— that which arises from the three Doshas is incurable.
Listen now, O son of great wisdom, with a one-pointed mind;
the procedure for the removal of swelling in men shall be explained by me, who am knowledgeable.
(62) Trivṛt, combined with sugar and milk, should then be drunk with lukewarm water.

Therefore, it destroys abdominal enlargement accompanied by swelling, or it eliminates that which is of a bilious (pitta) nature in men. Harītakī, trivṛtā, and ginger, when combined with jaggery, likewise destroy swelling.
A decoction of the two groups of five roots (daśamūla), taken lukewarm with castor oil, removes swelling.
Varuṇa oil combined with cow’s urine is beneficial when drunk; it destroys swelling (śopha).

One should avoid meat from domestic or marshy animals, salt, dried vegetables, fresh grain, molasses-based foods, flour preparations, curd, rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛśara), and food mixed with waterless wine.

One suffering from the disease of swelling (*śvayathu*) should avoid grain, dried meat, food that causes edema, heavy food, unwholesome food, and food that causes a burning sensation; furthermore, one should avoid sleeping at night and sexual intercourse.
(66) An ointment made of *aruṣkara* (marking nut), sesame milk, licorice (*madhuka*), and fresh butter cures swelling.
Alternatively, an ointment made of the clay from the base of that tree, or with plantain leaves and *vīraṇa* grass, [is effective]. (67)

In cases of wasting caused by poison, the pacifying treatment prescribed for poison should be employed— namely, fasting, digestive stimulants, unctuous substances, heat, and the soothing of Vata. However, nourishing food is beneficial for all those suffering from abdominal tumors (gulma) caused by that poison.
One suffering from gulma should not eat dried meat, radish, fish, dried vegetables, pulses, *vāluka*,
