or sweet and bland foods (69–70). However,
in the case of a gulma with blood, digestive stimulants, the drinking of asafoetida, and the massaging of the waist are not prohibited.
Furthermore, fomentation and massage, as well as walking and jumping, are beneficial.

(71) A decoction of rodhra, arjuna, khadira, māgadhikā, and samaṅgā, combined with amlavetasa, honey, and ghee, quickly destroys abdominal tumors even when accompanied by blood; it also dries the moisture of the heart and subdues provoked blood. (72)
Milk mixed with ghee and sauvarcala salt should be administered for the destruction of blood-born gulma, or even for that arising from a wound in the liver (yakṛt). Furthermore,
food combined with asafoetida is wholesome, as are items that are neither hot nor burning.
In cases of gulma born of blood or born of injury, [one should prescribe] the meat of wild animals.
74. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, named "The Treatment of Gulma," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-seven.
Ātreya said:
[The fever arises] from sitting in an uneven posture, or from drinking water [at the wrong time],
or even when one has emerged from exhaustion, travel, or labored breathing, or when one has over-exerted oneself.

The abdomen becomes yellowed in this manner, and from that, *jalodara* (ascites) arises. When the abdomen contains water, it produces a gurgling sound; when the swelling has greatly increased, there is edema in the feet—these are the symptoms of *jalodara*.
One should administer purgation, emesis, and digestive remedies;
furthermore, an application of alkali (kṣāra) and pills (vaṭaka) will alleviate that condition.
Therefore, leaving a space of one finger-breadth from the navel's fold [one should apply the treatment].
Having examined the water-channel, one should wrap it with a blade of kusha grass; then the wise man should insert a castor-oil stalk into it,
drain the water contained within, and then quickly secure the joint.
When that [ointment] no longer adheres, then cauterization (dāha) is recommended;
having strained the powder of the seeds (kaṇakalka), four times as much ghee should be added.
Having cooked it with an equal amount of dry ginger (śuṇṭhī) and aconite (viṣā), this drink and external application are beneficial.
The best of physicians should perform surgical procedures only when they have full knowledge of them.

One should not perform surgery in cases where it is difficult to execute; for in such instances, death is certain if no action is taken, while if action is taken, there remains doubt as to the outcome.
Therefore, one who acts must necessarily have the Lord as witness.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Jalodara (Ascites)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Twenty-Eight.
Ātreya said:

Thus, there are twenty types of *prameha* (urinary disorders) in men; here are their characteristics [arising] from fatigue, sexual excess, and likewise from the consumption of food that is contrary to the heat of summer, or that is sharp and hot.
The lords of sages have declared that the onset of *meha* (urinary disorders) results from the consumption of alcohol or the excessive use of milk and pungent substances.
Urine-melancholy (*jalaprameha*), blood-melancholy (*rudhiraprameha*), pus-melancholy (*pūyaprameha*), salt-melancholy (*lavaṇaprameha*),
buttermilk-melancholy (*takraprameha*), chalk-melancholy (*khaṭikāprameha*), and semen-melancholy (*śukraprameha*) were described previously.
One should distinguish between those with gravel-like urine (śarkarāmeha), fat-like urine (vasāprameha), meat-broth-like urine (rasaprameha),

ghee-like urine (anyaghṛtaprameha), those with bilious urine (pittapramehī), those with phlegmatic urine (kaphamehin), and those with honey-like urine (madhupramehī); for just as their names are, so too are their symptoms and the wasting of strength in the person's body.

The best of physicians should quickly perform treatments for the pacification of the cause. A decoction of dhava, arjuna, sandalwood, and śāla bark is beneficial in cases of urinary disorders involving water (jalaprameha);
in cases of blood-related urinary disorders (raktaprameha), cold milk mixed with grapes, liquorice, and sandalwood is recommended.
Sexual indulgence is also minimal in this condition. For *pūyameha* (pus-like urine), a decoction of *dhava*, *arjuna*, *dūrvā*, *kaseruka*, *kadalī*, and *nalinī* is beneficial.
For *lavaṇameha* (salty urine), a decoction of *kadamba*, *śāla*, *arjuna*, *dīpyaka*, *viḍaṅga*, *dārvī*, *dhava*, and *śallakī* is prescribed.
All these decoctions with honey should be used for the various types of *kapha*-dominant urinary disorders (*kapha-prameha*).
In that same context, *rodhra*, *arjuna*, milk, the leaves of *ariṣṭa*, *dhātrī* fruit, and *candana* are to be used.
For *takra-prameha*, chalk (*khaṭikā*) is beneficial, as is a preparation of decoction, jaggery, and *avaṭa*.
Dūrvā, mūrvā, the roots of kuśa and kāśa, dantī, samaṅgā, and śālmalī— this, boiled with water, is beneficial as a drink in cases of seminal prameha, or likewise in cases of bloody prameha.
(10) Triphalā, the root of āragvadha, mūrvā, the leaves of śobhāñjana and ariṣṭa, and mocā— [these are also used].

Or a decoction prepared with grapes (drākṣā) is for the prevention of *sarpir-prameha*. Likewise, a strongly boiled decoction of *kuṣṭha*, *parpaṭaka*, *tiktā*, and sugar, combined with *mūrvā*, *ariṣṭā*, *pāṭalī*, *durālabhā*, *kiṃśuka*, and *ṭuṇṭuka*, [is used for the same purpose].
And it is always beneficial in cases of *rasaprameha*. 12.

The wise declare that for the alleviation of *pittaprameha*, one should boil blue water-lilies (*nīlotpala*), *arjuna*, *kaliṅga*, *dhava*, *amlīkā*, *dhātrī* fruits, and *picumanda* leaves in water; this, when mixed with sugar, is prescribed for a person’s drink. 13.
A decoction made with water from *viḍaṅga*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *kapittha*, *kadamba*, *rodhra*, *aśana*, and *vṛkṣaka* is beneficial for men; it destroys *kapha*-type urinary disorders (*prameha*).
(14) A decoction prepared with *mustā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *niśā*, *suradāru*, *mūrvā*, *indrā*, and *rodhra* with water [is likewise effective].
It is beneficial when drunk for all types of urinary disorders (meha) and should be administered in all cases of retention of urine (mūtragraha). 15.
Furthermore, a powder of abhayā, iron filings, and nikumbha, combined with sugar, or a linctus of triphalā with honey, is said to be beneficial in all forms of prameha. 16.
In cases of madhumeha (diabetes mellitus), the wise physician should prescribe the drinking of ghee, or milk mixed with sugar, or decoctions and medicinal pills [prepared from the following]:
nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, āragvadha, and ṭuṇṭuka. 17.
Piyāla, kukubha, jambu, kapittha, and āmrātaka (18);
madhuka, yaṣṭimadhuka, rodhra, and pāribhadraka; paṭola, cāriṇī, dantī, and meṣaviṣāṇikā (19).

One should administer a fine powder consisting of equal parts of *citraka*, *karañja*, *śakrāhva*, and *triphalā*, along with *bhallātaka*, the three aromatics (*trigandha*), and the three pungents (*kaṭukatraya*); this formulation beginning with *nyagrodha* is superior in its qualities. (20)
This electuary, combined with honey, destroys madhumeha (diabetes).
Whether as a decoction, an oil preparation, or even a ghee preparation, it is highly recommended for drinking and massage; it truly cures diseases arising from the urine.
This powder, beginning with *nyagrodha* and others, should be drunk mixed with milk; for *madhumeha*, there is no other remedy than this when prepared according to availability.
[23] *Mākṣika*, *dhātumākṣika*, *śilodbheda*, and *śilājatu*.
One should drink sandalwood, red mineral (cinnabar), camphor, long pepper, and bamboo-manna mixed with milk;
this cures honey-like urinary disorders (madhumeha) and one is liberated from diseases of the urine. 24–25.
Now we shall describe the treatment for the carbuncles of prameha:
the decoction of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, badarī, khadira, śiṃśapā, and pāribhadraka should be used for washing the penis. 26.

The bark from within the fruit of *arjuna*, *kadamba*, or *ṭiṇṭukī* is recommended for the purification of pus during the cooking of a medicinal oil for urinary disorders (27). One should take the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* as well as the leaf of *surasā*.
Having ground the leaves of *niṣpāvaka* and *paṭola* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*),
one should apply it as an ointment for wind-tumors (*vātapiṭikā*) and for the penis.
Likewise, [one may use] *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *kuṣṭha*, *candana*, and *raktacandana*.
O best of physicians, a plaster consisting of uśīra, kattṛṇa, red mineral (raktadhātu), and lotus stalk (mṛṇālaka), combined with the cream of milk and prepared according to availability,
pacifies the burning sensation of urinary disorders caused by pitta and blood.
Washing with cold milk, rubbing with fresh butter,
and [using] the grains, the leaves of the kadamba, arjuna, and piṇyāka, as well as those of the pomegranate (32),
the leaves of the khadira tree, and likewise the leaves of the āmalakī.
Having ground it with warm water for use in a *somapāka* preparation during urinary disorders,
or using the powder of *triphalā*, one should perform a wash to remove dried pus with either *kāñjika*, *takra*, or water boiled with husks.
In cases of urinary disorders (mehapāka), one should perform cleansing with very cold water;
furthermore, red śāli rice, ṣaṣṭika rice, āḍhakī, or kulattha pulse,
along with some sweet ghee, is prescribed for the purpose of food.
Alkaline, sour, or pungent substances, as well as sleeping during the day—especially so;
beholding women, sexual intercourse, likewise overeating, as well as physical exertion, running, and the suppression of the urge to urinate. (36–37)

The best of physicians should avoid exposure to wind from clothing, red garments, singing, women, and children, whether in a secluded place or within the house; nor should he wear ornaments or betel, nor should he give way to anger or emaciation. 38.

One who desires the attainment of happiness should avoid these [foods] from afar (39). A decoction of the two types of turmeric, ginger, viḍaṅga, and harītakī, taken with honey, is prescribed for kaphaja prameha (40).

One suffering from the urinary disorder *pītaprameha* should drink a decoction of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *uśīra*, *pathyā*, *āmalaka*, and *mustaka*, mixed with honey. Likewise, one may drink a decoction of *kamala*, *rodhra*, *uśīra*, and *arjuna*.
This decoction prescribed for Pitta-prameha should be taken with honey.
Alternatively, the fresh juice of Āmalaka mixed with honey,
or the powder of Harītakī, prevents all types of urinary disorders.

One should drink the powder of khadira, śarkarā, dāruharidrā, and musta to alleviate all diseases of prameha (urinary disorders). [44] Kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, devadāru, pāṭhā, guḍūcī, triphalā, and musta— [these should be used].
Indeed, the powder of these [drugs], mixed with honey, removes urinary disorders (prameha) and pain. 45.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Disorders," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. Chapter Twenty-Nine.
Ātreya said:
A powder of cardamom, bitumen, long pepper, and rock-pennywort, when drunk with rice-water, certainly cures the disease of urinary disorder (prameha). 1.
A person should drink the decoction of castor root, *pāṣāṇabheda*, *gokṣuraka*, as well as cardamom, *āṭarūṣa*, and long pepper, combined with liquorice and prepared with *śilāditya*.

In cases of urinary calculi (aśmarī) and gravel (śarkarā), two palas of sugar with one karṣa of very cold water removes dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). Iron powder mixed with curd-water is likewise a source of comfort.
One should take the powder of barley-alkali mixed with asafoetida,
and having taken it along with pumpkin and sugar, one should drink it;
for this indeed wards off dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra) arising from the three doṣas.
One should drink the root of śatāvarī mixed with cold water as a powder.
Therefore, for one afflicted by the disease of gravel (śarkarā), one should administer sugar. [The following is used:
āragvadha fruit and root, durālabhā, dhānyaka, and śatāvarī.

This decoction of *pāṣāṇabheda*, *pathyā*, *trivṛtā*, *durālabhā*, *gokṣura*, and *puṣkara* would be beneficial for dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*). Alternatively, a decoction of *elā*, *kuruṇṭaka*, *karkaṭī*, and seeds [of *pāṣāṇabheda*] is effective for severely obstructed urine.

A decoction of *paṭolī* root combined with *kulattha* beans and mixed with *puṣkaramūla*, when administered as a subsequent enema (*pratipāka*), destroys urinary disorders (*prameha*) and stone diseases (*pāṣāṇaroga*).
One who drinks the root of *mātuluṅgikā* with water that has stood overnight [attains similar results].
The pain arising from that sugar dissolves immediately.
One who is afflicted by the disorder of sugar should drink the medicine called Kṣipranāmaka ground with cow's buttermilk, and should consume buttermilk for a long time. 11–12.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Dysuria," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty.
Ātreya said:
One should drink the seeds of *Karkaṭikā* mixed with *Triphalā* and rock salt;
this powder, when drunk with warm water, brings relief from the obstruction of urine.
He who drinks the alkali of sesame stalks mixed with curd and honey [is likewise cured].
That man, having destroyed the obstruction of urine, immediately attains comfort. One should drink the root of the *jāti* flower ground with goat's milk,
since it pacifies burning sensations, urinary distress, and heat.
In cases of urinary obstruction accompanied by intense pain, one should drink the root of the lotus (padminīkanda) mixed with oil and boiled cow’s urine. Furthermore,
[this condition may arise] from substances that aggravate pitta, such as those that are pungent, sour, or colored.
Even by the service of a fair-complexioned woman, or even by [sexual] passion, blood flows forth. Furthermore,
by drinking hot liquor, or by those afflicted by fatigue and physical exertion,
pitta is quickly provoked and causes dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
Because of that, one urinates with difficulty and a hot stream of urine flows;
it obstructs the urinary channels and blood also flows out.
I shall describe the medicine for this, by which well-being is attained. (7)
Yaṣṭīmadhuka, mṛdvīkā, candana, and raktacandana,
when taken with water boiled from red rice, remove the pain of dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
A garland of banyan shoots combined with grapes and sugar [is likewise beneficial].

O best of physicians, this electuary (leha) is a destroyer of dysuria; it is declared to pacify the body when caused by immersion in cold water. Furthermore, in cases of dysuria, a diet consisting of sweet foods is said to be beneficial.

In one who has experienced a break during intercourse while lying on his back, resulting in burning sensations and exhaustion, and suffering from urinary obstruction, *vacā* is excellent; in that case, one should administer obstructing [medicines].
For a man who has not engaged in physical exertion, wholesome food is beneficial, as is immersion in cold water after eating.
When the Vāyu is provoked by these [factors], it obstructs the opening of the urinary passage;
accompanied by Kapha, this most wicked disease is said to be the most difficult to treat.
Listen now to its remedy: a decoction or an oil enema (anuvāsana).

Enema therapy using decoctions for non-unctuous enemas (nirūha) is a beneficial procedure for urinary obstruction, as is all forms of sudation; one should remain in a position like that of a person walking crookedly.
Furthermore, riding horses or carts and running are considered beneficial.

A decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) with equal amounts of jaggery, drunk with milk or meat broth, cures urinary obstructions; or, when caused by pitta, it may be taken with salt and sour substances.
Likewise, pāṭalā, ṭuṇṭukā, nimba, and gokṣuraka [are used for this purpose]. 15–16.
Cardamom bark, as well as cinnamon leaf, combined with a decoction of triphalā and drunk together with jaggery, destroys urinary obstruction (17).
It is also beneficial for men suffering from urinary pain when taken with pomegranate and sour substances.

Triphalā with sugar and a decoction of sugarcane, along with rock salt (saindhava), prevents urinary obstruction; or else, Harītakī combined with jaggery [is effective], or alternatively, sexual intercourse with a woman who causes a pricking sensation [should be practiced]. 18–19.
By this, there shall quickly be relief for women suffering from the affliction of the female genital tract (yonimardana).
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Obstruction," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty-one.
Ātreya said:
The disease of urinary calculi (aśmarī) arises due to defects in the father or mother, from the obstruction of urine, or from the practice of unwholesome habits. 1.
If the parents, overwhelmed by urine, engage in sexual union,
the conception of the embryo falls away along with the urine;
he who possesses a body [in that state] is born there as one of the five types.
It causes the retention of urine and produces a binding obstruction in three ways;
that urinary disease is also incurable, yet it occurs in humans even when slight, and urinary gravel (mūtraśarkarā) becomes curable during youth. 4.
If [the act] is inverted, or if the woman lies on her back while the man is on top, his semen will flow excessively; the woman then extracts that semen.
Furthermore, when the semen is in the urethra or the garment, it is drawn out by the wind along with the blood.
If two [substances] are administered, it reaches the urinary passage and obstructs it;
by that, obstruction of urine occurs along with intense pain.
A gravel-like stone (śarkarā) situated at the joint of the scrotum moves and must be treated with surgical instruments.

Therefore, I shall explain the remedy; listen, O son of great intelligence! A decoction of ginger, *gokṣuraka*, and the bark of *varuṇa*, combined with jaggery and barley-alkali, destroys urinary calculi.
A decoction of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *nala*, bamboo, *agnimantha*, *akṣanṛttaka*,
*śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *moraṭā*, or *pāṣāṇabheda*, mixed with *palāśa* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), combined with jaggery, [is an effective remedy]. 9–10.
When drunk, it destroys urinary calculi and removes pain in the bladder (11).
A decoction of cardamom, long pepper, *vṛṣa*, *tri-kaṇṭaka*, *reṇukā*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, licorice, the three fruits (*phalatrika*),
castor oil, bitumen (*śilājatu*), sugar, and so forth, likewise destroys stones when taken with warm water (12).

A powder made from the seeds of *gokṣuraka* combined with honeyed mineral (*dhātumākṣika*), when drunk with buffalo milk, causes the removal of urinary calculi. The surgical procedure is described in the *Uttaratantra*, and is also recorded in the chapter on clarified butter (*ghṛtādhyāya*) within the *Sūtrasthāna*.
The physician [should prescribe] ancient sixty-day rice, red rice, as well as śyāmāka, kodrava, dāla, markaṭī, and grass-grains (tṛṇadhānyaka);
likewise barley, wheat, horse-gram, and also adhakī.
Vata-alleviating foods should be administered in the diet of those suffering from Vata disorders (16).
Furthermore, the meats of the krauñca and other such birds are wholesome for the destruction of urinary calculi (aśmarī) (17).
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Calculi," in the third section of the Hārīta-uttara as spoken by Ātreya. 31.
The thirty-second chapter.
Ātreya said:
"O best of physicians, hereafter the increase of the embryo (maṇḍa) is observed."
In childhood, due to the fault of the mother or the father, [the disease] arises following the testicles;
furthermore, from indulgence with a wicked wife, the Vata located in the bladder reaches the site of the scrotum and indeed causes its enlargement.
The fourth type is the combination of each [dosha] individually; those arising from pitta-dosha and those from sannipata (the combination of all three) are likewise considered incurable.
O best of physicians, I shall now describe the doshas and their remedies; listen to them.
Fomentation, anointing, decoctions, and drinking are prescribed;
O best of physicians, I shall describe the symptoms of head-draughts (śiro-virecana) for these [conditions]:
trembling occurs from mild wind (vāta), and burning fever from bile (pitta).
Due to *kapha*, there is swelling and dryness, and the testicles become hard;
for the purpose of treating this enlargement of the scrotum (*muṣkavṛddhi*) when accompanied by *vāta*, one should consume a decoction of *rasāla*, *śallakī*, *tarkārī*, and *kaṭutumbikā*.
Immersion in cold water, the application of cold substances,
and likewise cooling ointments are recommended for a pitta-type swelling of the scrotum (uṣka).
[This is done] with a decoction of vacā, salt, kadamba, arjuna, and mustard seeds.

The use of astringent decoctions (kaṣāya) is said to remove the harm caused by phlegm (kapha) in the scrotum. O best among the learned, a decoction of aruṇa, varuṇa, kola, śāliparṇī, and śatāvarī is [prescribed] for pitta-sannipāta and enlargement of the scrotum (muṣkavṛddhi).

The decoction of *varuṇa*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *daśamūlī*, and *śatāvarī* is beneficial when drunk for *muṣkavṛddhi* (scrotal enlargement) caused by *vāta*. By this, well-being is attained; then one should have the medical procedure performed.

One should extract blood from a vein located in the middle of the earlobe (karṇakoṣa). Due to the swelling of the left side of the abdomen, one should extract blood from the right vein; both veins should be pierced by these two methods, or by that [specific] means, it will become comfortable.
Thus has the surgical procedure (caṇḍakriyā) been described, and that indeed [is indicated] for the patient whose condition has been diagnosed.
This concludes the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Scrotal Enlargement," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty-three.

Ātreya said: O best of physicians, when blood and bile (raktapitta) become aggravated by salty, sour, alkaline, and pungent substances, as well as by heat, sweating, and excessive morbidity, it manifests as erysipelas (visarpa).

It is to be understood as sevenfold: [arising] from individual humors, from combinations of two, and the pure [blood-born] type; another is born from all three combined (sannipāta) as the seventh. Furthermore, other names will be declared individually for each.
Ājñeya, Granthika, Ghora, and Kardama are the other types.
Ājñeya arises from vāta and pitta; Granthika from pitta and śleṣman; Kardama is produced by vāta and śleṣman; and Ghora is of the sānnipātika (combined humors) type.
Blood, lymph, skin, and flesh are the corrupted tissues (dūṣya), while the three doṣas are the impurities;
these seven elements should be known as the sources for the origin of visarpa (erysipelas).
A decoction of nyagrodha, bilva, and khadira is beneficial for washing [the affected area].
Washing with sour gruel, with slimy substances, or with the juice of fermented rice-water (sauvīraka),
or even with the juice of citron (mātuluṅga), is for those suffering from wind-type erysipelas (vāta-sarpis).
Washing with milk or cold water is for the pitta-type erysipelas.

For one with spreading phlegm (śleṣmavisarpin), a wash (dhāvana) made of dhava, arjuna, and kadamba is recommended; or for one with spreading [disease] (sarpin), a wash with surā liquor or sauvīraka is praised. Furthermore, such a wash is beneficial for that patient suffering from the spreading type caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta).
A decoction made from *yava*, *agnimantha*, *śaṭhī*, *nyagrodha*,
and *sarṣapa* is beneficial for washing erysipelas (*visarpa*) arising from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta*).
Furthermore, one should grind the five types of *jīraka* and *kapittha* with *kāñjika*.
An ointment made with the juice of *mātuluṅga* is also for one suffering from *vāta-sarpis*.
Likewise, an ointment consisting of *dhava*, *rodhra*, sesame, *caila*, *vidārī*,
and *kaṇṭaka* is used for *pitta-visarpa*, or alternatively, an ointment made with the leaves of *guñjā*.
Ghee cooked with rock salt (saindhava), ariṣṭa, tumbīka, and paṭola leaves is recommended for external application as a remedy for erysipelas (visarpa).
In cases of erysipelas caused by blood (raktaja-visarpa), one should perform bloodletting.
The smoke from a house-fire mixed with *kadamba* flowers is always said to be beneficial for anointing; furthermore, washing with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*) is recommended.
*Kuṭheraka*, *surasā*, *cakramarda*, and the two types of *niśā* (turmeric) [are also used]. 13–14.
Mustard seeds ground even with sour gruel (kāñjika) and applied as an ointment are beneficial.
15. Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Visarpa," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty-four.
Ātreya said: The disorder arising from vātarakta is of four types;
due to the defect of odor, others arise with distinct names for each.

The terrible Antaka is even more minute; or else, there is another called Masūrikā, which appears as eruptions the size of mustard seeds during the springtime. That too is declared to be even more minute, arising from a disorder of bile and blood.
If pustules are seen on a person who is like one whose body has been burnt by fire,
he too will suffer from a highly spreading disease (visarpa) and constant misery. When a person's thick pustules ripen simultaneously due to phlegm (kapha), [it is a sign of severe illness].

Burning sensations, restlessness, and discoloration arise in him immediately. When pustules resembling circular *masūrikā* (lentils) are seen and subside quickly through suppuration, that should be known as *masūrikā*.
O Mahāmati, I shall explain his medicine according to the prescribed rule:
he should maintain a concealed appearance and protect himself well through the application of protective rites;
he must avoid association with or attachment to women and those who are base.
One should very diligently cause a cool and refreshing place to be prepared; here, one should also apply an ointment for the minor affliction [of *kṣudraka*]. [The ingredients are:
*kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, *nyagrodha*, and likewise the bark of *udumbara*.
An ointment is recommended for warding off minor afflictions (kṣudropasarga).
Drinking milk mixed with honey and sugar brings comfort.
Likewise, the ash of jambū and mango sprouts combined with curd and honey [is beneficial]. 9–10.
One should administer this paste—consisting of gokṣura, ativiṣā, karkaṭādyā, and parpaṭaka—to one suffering from minor diarrhea, as it destroys both diarrhea and the loss of digestive fire;
it should be taken in combination with honey and sugar. (11)
Harītakī and the fresh juice of mātuluṅga mixed with sugar (12) prevent vomiting and emaciation caused by the minor affliction;
this same application should also be used as an ointment for the fire-like affliction. (13)
A plaster made of red sandalwood, mañjiṣṭhā, nimba leaves, and arjuna,
mixed with milk and fresh butter, is beneficial; likewise, upon seeing a severe complication, one should avoid fomentation and massage.
The wise do not apply ointments according to their specific requirements.
Washing with forest cow-dung, alkali, and oil is beneficial; one should not perform an oil massage, but rather apply only an ointment. 15–16.
A paste of *candana*, *madhuka*, *rodhra*, *nyagrodha*, *utpala*,
and *sārivā*, combined with honey, removes complications when administered as a drink.
(17) During a complication, a severe fever arises along with blood in the urine.
I shall describe its treatment by which well-being is attained:
a paste made from equal parts of *paṭola*, *parpaṭa*, *śuṇṭhī*, *mustā*, and *khadira*, mixed with honey, is beneficial when drunk and serves to destroy fever. (18–19)
Sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, and puṣkara used as a tooth-cleansing stick,
or taken as a decoction mixed with honey, removes fevers caused by the upasargas;
likewise, pomegranate and kuṭaja are used for vomiting and diarrhea.

A drink combined with honey and curd prevents diarrhea (atisāra). The remaining minor diseases have been described; here, the prescribed treatment should be applied. For *masūrikā* (smallpox), a single treatment should be performed according to the proper method. 21–22.
The wise man should avoid from afar all wind-increasing foods, as well as dry substances, sexual intercourse, and the grief caused by dryness;
furthermore, one should administer those wholesome diets prescribed for fever in this condition. 23.
In this way, within three weeks, a person attains happiness. Then, after performing the recitation of auspicious mantras, the consecration (abhiṣeka) should be performed,
wearing new, fine, and white garments.
Having caused [the patient] to be clothed, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa), and the provision of desired food should be carried out. 26.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Afflictions," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty-Five.
Ātreya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the treatment of wounds;
for wounds are said to be of many kinds, arising from various constituent elements (dhātus). 1.

Furthermore, a severe and malignant ulcer arises from drinking or eating contaminated water or food, or from anger, excessive burden, or addiction; indeed, it is produced by another corruption of the blood,
whether by Vata, Pitta, Kapha, by a combination of two, or by the accumulation of all three Doshas.

Having excited the flesh and scattered the blood, even a malignant ulcer arises that is most terrible. When the humors (doṣas), having become excessively aggravated, affect the skin, blood, and fat while residing in the bones, they gradually produce a severe swelling.
A wound that is reddish-brown, accompanied by piercing pain, throbbing, and tremors,
or one that is dry and painful, should be known as arising from Vāta. Furthermore, a wound that emits a burning sound for seven days but tolerates touch [is also of this nature].
A wound arising from *pitta* is cold, pleasant, and light to digest. A *kapha* wound is hard, circular, severe, yellowish, slightly painful, tolerant of heat, very unctuous, and slow to heal.

One should recognize that which arises from the combination of all [three] doshas by all their symptoms; in that born from two [doshas], however, the signs of two doshas are observed. Those arising from injury (abhighāta) should be known as fourfold.
As for other sinus ulcers that may be accompanied by wind and pain,
listen now to their treatment among the various channels:
first, the draining of pus with a poultice, and second, fomentation is prescribed.
The third stage is declared to be ripening (pācana); once ripened, incision (pāṭana) should likewise be performed, as well as purification (śodhana) and healing (rohaṇa).
Subsequently, the sequence should be applied in that same manner, which is beneficial for ulcers.

Rāsnā, vacā, and likewise śuṇṭhī, along with the juice of mātuluṅga and equal parts of kāñjika, used as a single wash for a vātika wound; [and] with yaṣṭīmadhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, paṭola, and nimba leaves. 12–13.
Milk that has not been boiled, used cold, is for washing a Pitta-type ulcer (14). A decoction of Triphalā, Kadamba, Jambu, and Kapittha,
applied lukewarm, is excellent for washing a Kapha-born ulcer (15).
Mātuluṅga and agnimanthā, or the root [of these] with kāñjika, as well as suradāru and śuṇṭhī— this ointment is beneficial for a wind-wound (vātavraṇa).
Nala, mūrvā, madhuka, candana, and raktacandana.
Ground with rice-water, it destroys bile-born ulcers (17).
Having ground aṅkolaka, rodhra, kadamba, arjuna, vetasa, and the leaves of pāribhadra, one should apply it as an ointment for wounds (18).
When a wound has reached suppuration, or is deep, painful, or even perforated,
the best of physicians should perform purification and irrigation using [decoctions of] karañja,
dhava, nimba, kadamba, arjuna, and vetasa.
When the decoction has been reduced to one-quarter, there should be irrigation of the deep wound with it (20).
Having ground together mañjiṣṭhā, lac-resin, realgar, and the two types of turmeric, and having strained the mixture through cloth, [it should be applied] (21).
Combined with honey, it is a purifier of wounds and beneficial;
Nimba leaves, finely crushed and mixed with honey, purify wounds.
(22) Nimba leaves, sesame, honey, along with Dārvī and Madhuka—these together [are used].

Likewise, a paste of sesame seeds is beneficial for cleansing wounds. (23) Leaves of *tilaka*, neem, and *sītā*, as well as jasmine, and their decoction, are indeed beneficial for the cleansing of wounds. (24)
Having recognized that the wound is purified, one should apply an ointment to that wound;
with ghee it is best, and by that means the wound does not burn.
(25) Jātī, karañja, picumanda, paṭola, madhuyaṣṭī, haridrā, and kaṭurohiṇī [are to be used here].
Equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, utpala, muśīra, karañja seeds, sārivā, trivṛt, and māgadhikā should be taken;

this ghee, when cooked, is indeed beneficial for wounds, highly recommended for those that have become sinus-like, painful, or accompanied by blood, and it destroys spider-bites and erysipelas (visarpa). It heals even deep-seated wounds, those with burning sensations, and those that are hard, and it causes them to heal completely.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wounds," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya, concerning ghee for [diseases such as] fever and other conditions.
Chapter Thirty-six.
Ātreya said: Elephantiasis (ślīpada) arises from the same treatments prescribed for ulcers;
it is cracked by Vāta, dry, and appears dark-colored.
It is seen that [the discharge] is accompanied by burning and suppuration due to pitta, and is associated with fever due to kapha;
it arises as oily, thick, and swollen through the action of kapha.
O best of physicians, all these symptoms arise together through the combination of the three humors (sannipāta).

The *medāśrita* type of *vālmīka* appears like an anthill (*valmīka*). One should observe signs similar to those arising from *vāta*, and one should have the treatments prescribed for wounds performed upon it according to the rules. (3–4)
Ghee prepared from the milk of a cow that has recently calved is recommended, as are various ointments;
furthermore, an application should be made with *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* trees,
as well as the root of *girikarṇikā* and *vṛkṣādanī*.
Having ground [these], an ointment should be applied for *vālmīka-ślīpada*. Having ground a *sūraṇa* tuber with honey and ghee,
this ointment is beneficial and removes *vālmīka-ślīpada*.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Elephantiasis," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty-seven.
Ātreya said:
Furthermore, due to the impact of wind or from a wound,
blood-channels (raktanaḍīs) sprout and likewise obstruct [the flow] again;
by that, the passage of the blood is blocked, and because of that, [disease] arises.
An arbuda is very large and arises from the obstruction of the channels.
The wise should recognize that it is soft and rough due to vāta, dense and cold due to kapha, and characterized by burning, suppuration, and so forth due to pitta.

Through the combination [of humors], a tumor (gaḍuka) may become hard, dense, resembling stone, and increasing in size; that is incurable, O best of physicians. At the outset, one should perform incision on it, avoiding the vital spots (marmasthāna).
One should also apply an ointment of Saindhava salt and ghee. O best of physicians, having burnt the Sūraṇa tuber with ghee and molasses, its application is the destroyer of arbudas.
The remaining treatments for ulcers, which are praised for the pacification of *arbuda*, have been described;
likewise, wind-alleviating diets that are wholesome and sweet are beneficial.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Arbuda*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
The thirty-eighth chapter.
Ātreya said:
Thus has the treatment of wounds been declared in brief by the best of physicians.

Having understood the appropriate application [of treatment], one should employ it correctly. From drinking contaminated water and from the consumption of poor-quality food, there arises a cluster of glandular swellings (*gaṇḍamālā*) produced by worms;
and when a disorder born of phlegm and bile spreads along with wind, the host of defects produced by worms spreads from the glands.
By means of wind (vāta), the symptoms are like those of wind; by means of bile (pitta), there is burning, pain, dryness of the ulcer, and heat;

and by means of phlegm (śleṣman), there is coldness and density. From their combination, there occurs that which is produced by the derangement of all three (sannipāta), characterized by all the symptoms together.
I shall now describe its remedy; listen, my son.
Rohiṇī, Viśadā, Vijayā, Vibhedinī,
Kāntārī, Vajrapuṣpā, and Indrāyudhā—
these are the seven kinds of spiders; hear now about each one individually.
Raktamuṇḍā is red; Rohiṇī is in the place of blood and is bright; Dīrghikā is white-colored in the place of flesh;
and Vijayā is in the middle of the head, yellow in color with the luster of barley.
Bhedinī is located in the fat tissue; Śvetā and Nīlarekhikā are also [found there].
Kāntārī is in the middle of the bladder; Śvetāṅgā and Raktamuṇḍikā are also there.
Vajrapuṣpā is in the middle of the bones; Śvetā and Kṛṣṇā are considered to be the veins (śirā). 8–9.

The *indrāyudhā* is at the tip of the head, while the *dhūmrā* and *kṛṣṇā* veins are considered to be at the head. The *rohiṇī* is the size of a finger-joint; the *viśadā* is equal [in size] to urine; the *vijayā* is shaped like a barley grain, and the *vijayā* is likewise circular.
In men, another [type] should be known as resembling the bristles of the *taṇḍulīya* plant; it is called *rohiṇī*, *vijayā*, or *viṃśā*, and it is found located within the flesh.
Or, in a man, it is seen at the ankle or in a joint of the bone, and it is characterized by splitting [the flesh].
"Know, O son, that Kāntārī resides in the belly, the ears, and the corners of the eyes;
Vajrapuṣpā is on the head; and Indrāyudhā is considered to be at the end of the head. Therefore, I shall speak of the medicine as well; listen, my son, with diligence. (13–14)
They recognize a wound as deep when it exudes thick pus and has a foul odor;
furthermore, it is painful and resembles the color of a ripe jambū fruit.
These characteristics of spider wounds are observed as long as they remain unripened.
Having removed the spider from the joints, vital points, or the site of the wound,
one should then promptly apply a cauterization with hot oil.
[One should also employ] *aṅkola*, liquors, and the leaves of the *pāribhadra*.
House-soot, black cumin, and [black mustard] ground with cow's urine is an excellent ointment,
supreme for the destruction of spiders.
Piṇḍītaka, viḍaṅga, and likewise the root of iṅgudī—
One should grind the roots of the *bījapūraka* and apply them as an ointment;
this quickly destroys even the most terrible *gaṇḍamālā* and *prakaṇṭaka*. One should also apply the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka* to the opening of a spider-bite.
By that means, the insect dies in its midst; of this there is no doubt.
(19) Having ground girikarṇī and sandalwood in equal parts, an ointment should be applied; it destroys even the most dreadful spider-bite. (20)

One should cook *karavīra*, the milky sap of *arka*, as well as *kaṭutumbikā*, the two types of *niśā*, and *jāṅgalikā* in sesame oil. By anointing with this, one destroys spider-bites (*lūtā*) and even severe *gaṇḍamālā*.
One should likewise apply ghee, *jātyādi* [powder],
and other substances prescribed for wounds according to the rules.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Spider Bites and Scrofula," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Thirty-nine.
Ātreya said:
[One should avoid] incompatible drinks, heavy foods, sour substances, and water used for bathing.
From sleeping during the day and failing to remain vigilant at night, the *pitta* residing in the blood becomes aggravated.
When this morbid humor spreads having reached the skin, the wise declare it by the name "leprosy" (*kuṣṭha*).
O knower of the rules, these diseases arise from past sins and manifest intensely in the bodies of men who greatly provoke [the humors].

They say that leprosy (kuṣṭha) is of eighteen types; I shall describe their characteristics individually, as well as which are incurable, which are curable, and those born of karma, those arising from the humors (doṣa), and those congenital. Among these, there is cruelty, harshness, itching, horripilation, and numbness.

Toda (pricking pain) and likewise *saṃvyathana* (aching pain) occurring in the body when located in the skin are the signs arising from *kuṣṭha*. Furthermore, there are *kapālaka*, *udumbara*, *dadrū*, *maṇḍala*, *visarpaka*, *hastibala*, *kiṇa*, *gojihvaka*, and *lohitamaṇḍala*. 4–5.
The Vaipādika, the Carmadala, as well as others, the Visphoṭakas, and then the Bahuvraṇa;
Kaṇḍū, Vicarcī, and another are likewise declared; these diseases established on the skin arise from the differentiation of the bodily constituents (dhātus).
That which has the appearance of a skull and is white in color is called Kapālya by those who know the rules.

The virtuous call that which is oily, affecting all parts of the body, and characterized by itching, *udumbara*. That which resembles *dadrū* (ringworm) is called *dadrū*; they call that circular patch *maṇḍalaka*.
That which spreads is *visarpa*, and another type of it, which extends like an elephant's hide, is likewise called *gajacarma*.
That which is rough, harsh, and hard like a cow's tongue, and is indeed susceptible to splitting;
and those circular patches (maṇḍala) that are yellowish-red, accompanied by itching and joined with ulcers—
this should be known as *lohita-maṇḍala*, arising from blood and dependent upon the blood.
For one afflicted by pain, that [condition] is clearly described as *vipādikā* (cracking feet); it should be treated [as such].

Likewise, when it arises from blood and aggravated *vāta*, it resembles a cluster of pustules; furthermore, it is well known among men by the other name *bahuvraṇa* (many sores) and is characterized by being minute. 10–11.
Itching and skin eruptions (vicarcī) are well-known in this world; when a man’s blood spreads with white, subtle, and pale-red spots, no youth can ever master him.
Śirīṣa flowers, śirīṣa seeds, and a subtle man who has abandoned worldly attachment [are the remedy].
Trembling and horripilation are the signs of [fever] caused by Vāta; by Pitta, there is emaciation, giddiness, burning sensations, and thirst.
When Kapha is the originator, the eyes, nails, and body become hard, cold, and pale, and there is a desire for warmth.

When it arises from a combination [of two humors], the symptoms of those two are present together; when it arises from the Sannipāta (the combination of all three), it is characterized by many symptoms.
One should know that [the swelling] located in the skin is rough, itchy, soft, and cold; that located in the blood is characterized by discharge, burning, and a reddish appearance.
One should indicate that which is located in the flesh as being very unctuous, pricking, and deep-seated. 15.
When located in the fat (medas), there is piercing pain and a sense of constriction, the eyes are very glossy and red;
when located in the bone (asthi), the visarpa is deep-seated and affects the nose and mouth.
When located in the marrow (majjā), the patient becomes incapacitated and a discharge of marrow occurs.
It disintegrates across all its parts; thus it is known as *śukragama*. 17.

Therefore, O best of physicians, I shall explain the counter-treatment (*pratikarma*) in brief: for [the poison] located in the skin, there is sudation (*sveda*), as well as ointment (*ālepa*); and for that which has reached the blood, there is bloodletting (*raktasrāva*). 18.
Purgation is prescribed when [the disease] has reached the muscle tissue, and decoction therapy when it has reached the fat tissue (19).

Now, these same three treatments are likewise applied when they have reached the bone and marrow; in cases of Vātika [disease], sudation is beneficial, while in Pittaja cases, cooling treatment is required (20).
This [fever] arising from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika) is declared difficult to cure or incurable;

having examined the cause of the disease, one should then begin the treatment. One should administer purification (śodhana) and digestive remedies (pācana) every fortnight, and induce purgation (recana) every month.

For the purification of leprosy (kuṣṭha), one should exert oneself for six months, and bloodletting should be performed every sixth month. One should quickly drink a decoction of vāsā, paṭola, phalinī, lavaṇa, vacā, and nimba bark;
this, combined with madana, induces emesis in cases of leprosy. In emetic treatments involving madana, a decoction of pathyā is also used.
O best of physicians, the three fruits (triphalā), trivṛt, and dantī constitute a purgative;
O supreme physician, their decoction should be drunk with warm water.
If there is obstruction of inhalation and exhalation, a vein on the head should be pierced externally.
Then, the meal following the administration of the decoction-unguent should be prepared as follows:

A decoction-ointment (kaṣāyasiddha) prepared with ginger, long pepper, khadira, pāṭalī, paṭolī, mañjiṣṭhā, kṣura, viṣa, bilva, yavānikā, vāsā, and triphalā, when taken as a drink, destroys the disorder of leprosy (kuṣṭha) in a person. 25–26.

A decoction of vāsā, viḍaṅga, picumanda, paṭola, pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, surerindrataru, the roots of the five trees (pañcataru), and pathyā destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) caused by Vāta; this great medicine should be administered for twenty-one days. Furthermore, the powder of chinnodbhavā taken daily along with its decoction [is effective].
When digested, one should drink [the aforementioned medicine] with ghee, and then drink sixty-day rice (ṣāṣṭika) with milk;
this destroys all types of leprosy (kuṣṭha), even those that have reached the seven bodily constituents (dhātu).
Kāśmarya, darada, ghana, kuṣṭha, and the two types of niśā constitute this "Kāñjika-kuṣṭha" formulation.
This plaster is highly commended; it destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha), as well as eczema (vicarcikā) and the disorder of erysipelas (visarpa).
In that regard, these [substances] ground with honey, sour gruel (añjika), and urine, when applied as a plaster, destroy even severe leprosy and eczema.
Furthermore, one should perform the aforementioned washings for the disorder of erysipelas.
Washing with a decoction of sauvīraka salt or with a decoction of triphalā is praised by the wise for vātika kuṣṭha;
likewise, [a paste] of yaṣṭīmadhuka mixed with a decoction of nimba leaves is recommended. 32–33.
Even with cold milk or a decoction of vidārī, one destroys most terrible leprosy; however, washing [the area] is not recommended. (34) Agnimantha, paṭola, and the leaves of mātuluṅga—
A decoction of *śaṭhī* and *parpaṭaka* is a wash for those suffering from diseases of *śleṣman*.
O best of the learned, having washed *vipādikā* with fresh butter and applied heat with the milks of the *arka* plant, one should apply an ointment of honey and oil. (35–36)

One should prepare a decoction by boiling together khadira, nimba, kadambaka, kakubha, pāṭalī, śirīṣa, kuṭaja, kiṃśuka, vāsa, moraṭa, vaṭa, kuṭa, naṭa, pippalī, pīlu, dhava, mudgara, ambu, and vetasa; this is then combined with ghee prepared according to the rules for drinking decoctions. 37.
It becomes the destroyer of all types of leprosy, and the man’s body becomes equal to the moon in luster.
(38) Āragvadha, dhātakī, karṇikāra, dhava, arjuna, sajjaka, and kiṃśuka;
likewise, kadamba, nimba, kuṭaja, āṭarūṣa, along with khadira and mūrvā. (39)

Having properly collected their roots and boiled them down until eight parts remain, this decoction, when mixed with an equal measure of ghee, destroys all diseases born of the body—40—all types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (visarpa), ringworm (dadru), and eczema (vicarcikā); it quickly cures a man. 41

Khadira, kadara, mūrvā, vālaka, karṇikāra, kuṭaja, saptaparṇa, bhadrā, and āragvadha— these, when ground together and boiled down to one-tenth their original quantity, taken as a medicated ghee (sneha-pāna), utterly destroy all the pride of skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and erysipelas (visarpa).
Bhallātaka, tryūṣaṇa, and one akṣa of powdered kuṣṭha, along with guñjā and the five salts...
An ointment prepared by boiling the three fruits (*phalatrika*) in oil destroys ringworm and leprosy. 43.

A powder consisting of the roots of *aśvaghna*, *malina*, *samaṅgā*, the two types of *niśā*, mustard, *citraka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *kuha*, *tumbī*, *kuṣṭha*, *viḍaṅga*, and *magadhā* [is likewise effective]. 44.

This oil of sesame seeds, cooked with the milky sap of *snuhī* and *arka*, when fully matured, certainly destroys ringworm and itching when used as an ointment for a person. (45) [The following ingredients are:
turmeric, *samaṅgā*, *surāhva*, *citraka*, *viḍaṅga*, black pepper, *viśālā*, *ambu*, and *kuṣṭha*.
Likewise, *lāṅgalī*, *cakramarda*, *guñjā*, *viśālā*, and the leaves of *ariṣṭa*—this powder, once prepared and processed, should be cooked with jaggery over a gentle heat;
when applied as an ointment, it very quickly destroys *kuṣṭha*, *pāmā*, and *vicarcī* in a person. 46–47.
Nimba, paṭola, kirātaka, jātī, viśālā, punarnavā, payoda, lākṣārasa, vāsā, trāyantikā, bilva, kuṣṭha, and yaṣṭi— these,
finely powdered and combined with milk, curd, and ghee, should be cooked for use as a medicinal wash. 48.
It cures leprosy, wounds, ringworm, blood disorders, scabies, and eczema, as well as itching (49). Furthermore,
when the Pitta humor becomes diseased and is impelled by Vāta, it becomes aggravated along with the blood and produces a pale complexion (50).
A stiffened mind and deformity are its characteristics;

that leprosy (kuṣṭha) should be understood by the best of physicians as either incurable or curable. That which arises from the derangement of the three humors (sannipāta) becomes slightly red and pale.
That [fever] which is variegated in all its limbs and glossy is indeed incurable;
however, that which has become yellowish, pale, and rough is known to be most easily curable.
For such cases, digestive treatment (pācana), purification (śodhana), purgation (virecana), and bloodletting (raktavimokṣaṇa) are recommended.
A paste made from vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, karañja, paṭola, nimba, arjuna, vetasa,

along with kṛṣṇā and samaṅgā, is beneficial when drunk for the treatment of maṇḍala-type leprosy. (54) [Likewise, a paste] of khadira, vāsaka, nimba, paṭola, dhava, yavāsa, and the three fruits (phalatrika)...
It conquers all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and circular skin lesions (*maṇḍala*), as well as the pallor (*pāṇḍura*) of a person.

(55) Pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, pippalī, devadāru, citraka, the two types of *dadrughna*, the two types of *rātri* (haridrā and dāruharidrā), and likewise *samaṅgā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, and *madhuka*—these, ground with *saindhava* salt and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), or even with urine, blood, or meat-broth, [are used for application]. (56)

Furthermore, when applied as an ointment, this proven remedy destroys ringworm (*kaṇḍukuṣṭha*), eliminates scabies (*vicarcikā*) and itching, and quickly counteracts eruptions and spreading skin diseases. Black sesame seeds, *citraka*, and likewise yellow sandalwood (58),

ground with urine and applied as an ointment, destroys all varieties of *citrakuṣṭha* for one suffering from it; it also cures ringworm (*dadrū*), skin eruptions (*kuṣṭha*), and scabies (*vicarcikā*) (59).

Those which are non-burning, non-sour, and likewise not aggravating to vāta are declared to be wholesome in fever; one should employ them here as well, for they are beneficial for those undergoing treatment for ulcers and patches of leprosy. 60
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Kuṣṭha," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Forty.
Ātreya said:

Due to excessive burdening, excessive application [of pressure], or an excessively sharp and hot state; or due to coldness from a lack of oil massage, and especially due to pitta; or through the affliction of parasites—by these means, a disease of the head arises in men.

They are to be known as arising from wind (vāta), blood, phlegm (kapha), and bile (pitta)— especially from bile— as well as from the combination of all three (sannipāta), and others born of worms (krimija). Furthermore, there is the disorder of half the head (ardhaśīrṣa) which increases day by day.
If there is pain at night caused by Vāta, and the head of the patient also suffers,
he may find relief through fomentation and massage; or if there is pain in the anus and the testicles due to Vāta,
for one whose limbs and head become hot during the heat of day or night, [this applies].

In the case of *balāśa* (kapha), there is a burning sensation from smoke or pungent substances, or one finds relief from cold during the night; or there is comfort from cold, and first there is thirst and intense pain arising from *pitta*,
which occurs at sunrise or at the end of the day, accompanied by dizziness and very intense thirst.
When a disorder of the head is desired [to be diagnosed] as arising from *kapha*, the head becomes drowsy and cold, and certainly a pair of eyes accompanied by perspiration appear similar;
furthermore, when it arises from *rakta* (blood), a web-like discharge issues from the nostrils, and the remaining symptoms include thirst in the mouth.
That [headache] in which the eyes are red and there is pain in the neck and the abdomen is called Raktodbhava-śīrṣaroga (blood-born headache).

That headache which arises from the obstruction of the three doṣas occurs when the yellow [bile] vitiates the middle part [of the head], spreading through it, causing a discharge from the nose, and accompanied by feces, water, numbness, delusion, and labored breathing.
For one who has an excessive goad-like pain on the head, even when the skull is being split open;

where there is a discharge from the nose mixed with blood and pus; and where there is headache accompanied by the emergence of worms—this arises from anger, grief, or other causes such as over-exertion and extreme fatigue. 10.
That headache caused by wind (vāta) occurs in men as well when accompanied by pain; furthermore,
pain born of vāta and rakta arises from excessive writing or reading, as well as from the close inspection of minute objects or from looking at things from a great distance.
He experiences pain in the middle of the nose, and pain occurs in the pair of eyebrows;
he sees blue and black, and there is pain in the head.
Bile does not exist without blood, and blood is moved by bile.
Headache does not arise from pitta alone, for pitta is moved by vāta.
Therefore, I shall describe the treatment; listen to the characteristics of the medicine: fomentation, external application, nasal drops, drinking, massage, and rubbing. 14–15.
Fomentation (svedana) should be applied in cases arising from vāta and kapha, as well as in trauma;
however, one should not perform fomentation for those two [types] when they are caused by pitta or blood.
In the case of blood-born [fever], a vein should be venesected, or likewise in some instances of pitta-born [fever].

One should apply a decoction made from *kokilākhyā*, *tarkārī*, *kaṭukā*, neem leaves (*nimbapatraka*), and the seeds of *śobhāñjanaka*; or one should foment [the area] with that decoction. Furthermore, by applying an ointment of these same substances, relief will arise for him. 17–18.
For a fever born of pitta, cooling applications should be made with cold sprinklings of liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhuka), sandalwood, kesara, and mātuluṅga;
the excellent physician should also use kadamba, arjuna, and sindhu for the purpose of application. 19.
Alternatively, ginger with jaggery, or myrobalan with jaggery;
or separately, as nasal drops (nasya), the juice of jaggery and śobhāñjana, or goat’s urine—by means of these nasal applications, headache is pacified. (20–21)

O best of physicians, for a severe headache arising from phlegm (kapha), one should administer as a nasal drop (nasya) black pepper, myrobalan (pathyā), and katphala, mixed with either urine or warm water; or alternatively, vacā, the essence of madhuka, or the root of girikarṇikā.
In cases of *sannipāta* affecting the head, the administration of nasal drops (*nasya*) as prescribed is indicated.
One should administer a measured amount of the root of *vandhyākarkaṭakī*, ground with warm water, as a nasal drop in cases of head disease caused by worms.
One part of the juice of *mṛṅgarāja*, two parts of *kāñjika* (sour gruel),
and three parts of *śobhāñjana*— one should throw all of these into that [vessel].
[Add] five parts of the juice of *sauvīraka* and six parts of the juice of *tumbikā*.
Dry ginger, rock salt, emblic myrobalan, patola, vāsaka, harītakī, and abhayā, along with *surasā*, should be cooked with oil in one-fourth the quantity;
this should then be administered as a nasal drop (nasya) in six drops.
Likewise, it is beneficial for anointing the head, beneficial for filling the ears,
and likewise beneficial for diseases of the head arising from wind (vāta) and other humors, as well as for headaches caused by worms (krimija).
O wise one, having filtered oil through a pouch made of Karañja seeds and Vibhītaka fruits—
Three drops should be employed in the procedure for nasal administration; this cures leprosy and disorders born of worms.

Having taken *kuṣṭha*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and the juices of *paṭola*, *jātī*, and *surasa*, and having cooked them with fresh butter (*navanītaka*) and ghee, this [mixture] certainly [cures] blood-bile (*raktapitta*). 29–30.
This [milk] from a cow, combined with sugar, should be administered during the day when the aggravation of the *doṣas* has increased.

(31) Lac-resin, sandalwood, liquorice, *paṭola*, *dhātrī* fruit, and sugar—these, along with curd, milk, and fresh butter, are employed in the procedure for nasal administration (*nasya*) after they have been boiled together. (32)
In cases of eye diseases caused by defects of the eyebrows, or from the depletion of blood in the temples, or when the humors (doṣas) increase with the passing of days and so forth,
one should administer as a nasal drop (nasya) saffron, licorice, and costus, mixed in equal parts with sugar, cooked with fresh butter and ghee.

Diseases born of *pitta* perish through the avoidance [of heat] as the days increase, and the affliction of hemi-crania (*ardhaśīrṣa*) quickly comes to rest. Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Head," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 40.

Chapter Forty-one. Ātreya said: In one who is habitually prone to excessive recitation, or due to the observation of subtle objects, or by gazing at distant things, or by heat, the disease of the eyebrows (*bhrū-doṣa*) arises. (1) The morbid humor (*doṣa*), localized in the blood and wind (*rakta-vāta*) and intensified by bile (*pitta*), produces pain in the eyebrows and in the vessels (*sirā*) originating from the bridge of the nose. (2) It throbs during times of heat and especially when cooled; furthermore, one perceives blue and yellow circles in the middle of the eye. (3) For that condition, one should first perform the treatment, and the veins (*sirā*) should be diligently venesected.

The previously mentioned sudation (svedana) should be performed, followed by nasal therapy (nasya) consisting of six drops and so forth. (4) Devadāru, rañjanī, ghana, śaṭī, puṣkara, seeds of kuṭaja, māgadhī, kuṣṭha, rodhra, cavikā, and yavāsaka should be boiled and then filtered again. (5) Into that [filtrate], one should further add guggulu, along with powdered śuṇṭhī, saindhava salt, and the three fruits (triphalā), which are beneficial. This is mixed with curd and milk, cooked, and turned into fresh butter (navanītaka). (6) Once prepared, this should be administered cold and mixed with sugar; it is a beneficial nasal medicine (nasya).

Nasal therapy (*nasyakarma*) applied to the region of the eyebrows, forehead, shoulders, and the roots of the temples removes pain from the head (7). Furthermore, when administered as a simple massage, it wards off diseases of the head, including hemicephalic pain (*ardhaśīrṣaka*), and oil is the supreme remedy for diseases of the head (8). The juice of betel leaf, combined with *viḍaṅga*, rock salt, and asafoetida, ground with jaggery and water, and used as nasal therapy, destroys defects of the eyebrows and temples as well as parasites (9). Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Eyebrow Disorders," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 41.

Chapter Forty-two. Ātreya said: O wise one, nasal disease may be born of worms, of the [humoral] defects (doṣas), or of blood; O best of physicians, hear from me its symptoms. In the case of Vāta, there is headache and swelling; in the Vāta-Pitta type, it is accompanied by the respective defects; in the Kapha type, it is thick and cold; and in the worm-born type, there is the discharge of blood. For nasal suppuration (nāsāpāka), in the Vātika form, a nasal drop (nasya) of jaggery and ginger is prescribed; in the Pittaja form, a nasal drop of sugar, ghee, and liquorice is prescribed; and in the Ślaiṣmika (Kaphaja) form, it is prepared with the juice of *surasā* and *vāsā*.

In cases of worm-infestation, *viḍaṅga*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and *magadhā* are considered beneficial. In diseases of the head arising from blood, bloodletting is the primary treatment. Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Nose," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-three. Ātreya said: Now listen, O Hārīta, to the treatment for hair-destroying diseases (keśaghna). Due to Vāta, it is dry and pale; due to Pitta, it is red and accompanied by a burning sensation. When associated with Kapha, it becomes oily; when arising from blood, it undergoes suppuration. That which arises from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) manifests with symptoms resembling all of them. For hair-destroying disease born of Vāta, washing the head with jaggery, *surasā*, ginger, and the juice of *mātuluṅga* is recommended. Triphalā, *vacā*, and *rohiṇī*, well-ground together with jaggery, [should also be used].

Washing (dhāvana) is recommended for alopecia (aindralupta) arising from phlegm (kapha). For the pitta-type, milk combined with fresh butter is beneficial; likewise, sugar, the fruit of the āmalaka, and liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu) are considered a washing for the pitta-type. One should take the juice of bhṛṅgarāja as well as the juice of ginger (śṛṅgavera), and having ground sesame seeds with the juice of sour gruel (sauvīraka), an ointment should be applied; afterwards, the man should bathe with warm water. A decoction of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, śirīṣa, and also rohita [is used] for head-diseases and scabies (śirodadrū).

One should pacify *indraluptaka* (alopecia) with the flower of the *kurabaka* and the blossom of the *japā*. By rubbing [the area] with these, the treatment for *indralupta* is indeed accomplished. Having observed the symptoms caused by *pitta*, one should wash with milk; cooling applications are prescribed for the *paittika* type. *Dhattūra* leaves, *māgadhī*, *niśā*, *viśālā*, house-soot (*gṛhadhūma*), and *kuṣṭha*, mixed with ghee and ground with water, should be applied as a paste to the head to prevent wounds caused by the disease arising from *pitta* and associated with the *doṣas*.

Having ground either the leaf of *paṭola*, or that of *picumanda* (neem), or likewise the fruit of *malakī*, an application with ghee and sugar removes wounds born on the head; this also destroys headaches and various swellings. Taking the soot of an elephant’s tusk, an application with fresh butter [is curative]. An application with fresh butter of the ash of sesame, *arka*, *bhallātaka*, and burnt *māṣa* beans, as well as the use of the ash of a snake, produces a growth of hair on a bald spot (*khalvāṭaka*).
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Indralupta," in the third section of the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-four. Ātreya said: Earache may arise from residual [doshas], or from water remaining in the ear, or from impurities; it may also result from the obstruction of breath, or from the vitiation of Vāta and the other [doshas] (1). Earache in a person may likewise be produced by combinations of two doshas, by all three doshas together, by worms, or by ulcers; furthermore, because of this, the person hears many sounds (2)—the sound of a flute, the roar of clouds, the noise of teeth grinding, pain with burning, and headache.

O child, know that when one hears everything [distorted] due to *pitta*, O best of physicians; likewise, in the case of *kapha*, it spreads faintness and one hears sounds like the rumbling of clouds. O most excellent one, in the disorder of worms (*krimi*), pus mixed with blood flows out; likewise, intense pain arises from injury (*abhighāta*). From a wound (*kṣata*) pus flows, and another type arises from childhood; that ear-pain also arises from the disorder of *lūti*. Filling the ear with water or using powders is not prescribed for these ear diseases.

One who knows the proper procedure should apply beneficial oil and fomentation to the ear; the application of drops of warm tears is also considered beneficial. (7) One should prepare a fine powder of rock salt (*saindhava*) and sea-foam (*samudraphena*); this filling of the ear with the juice of *sauvīraka* is recommended for disorders caused by Vāta. (8) Oil cooked with the juice of fresh *sauvīraka*, ginger, rock salt, and *guggulu*, along with the juice of black gram (*māṣa*) and fermented gruel (*kulmāṣa*), should be applied while still very hot. (9) It should be retained in the ear using a bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*); this is highly praised for ear diseases. (10) [Likewise, oil prepared with] *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *kuṣṭha*, the leaves of *ariṣṭa*, and *niśā*...

For earaches caused by *karṇa-śūla* associated with *pitta*, ghee processed with *viśālā*, *asumanaḥ*, and *pravāla* is recommended. (11) Likewise, *brāhmī* juice, rock salt (*saindhava*), *viḍaṅga*, and *bhṛṅgarāja* combined with ghee, as well as *sauvīra* juice and *pathyā* strained through a cloth—this [mixture] is beneficial for filling the ear canal; it destroys pus, blood, and worms. (12–13) All the aforementioned diseases of the head have been described, along with their oils and ghees; one should also employ [medicines] such as those beginning with *jātī*.

The foremost among those who know the diseases of the head (14); wholesome foods that alleviate *vāta* and those that are burning and heavy (15). Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Ear," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 44.

Chapter Forty-Five. Ātreya said: The humors (doṣas) arising in the eyes become aggravated by hot, excessively alkaline, or pungent substances, or again by injury, or even by looking through a fine cloth or a small opening. (1) I shall now describe the characteristics of those congenital (sahaja) conditions which are difficult to conquer; listen. Dryness, itching, pricking pain, and a continuous flow of dry, cold blood—(2) one should recognize that as the Vātika type. Now hear about the Paittika [type]. (3) In the Paittika type, the eyes are reddish, accompanied by burning, and there is a warm discharge. In the Sannipāta type, there is swelling and itching; in the Kaphaja type, there is coldness and numbness. (4)

In the case of fever born of dual humors (*dvandvaja*), it is characterized by the combined symptoms of both; in the case of that arising from all three (*sānnipātika*), it possesses all those signs. Having understood these characteristics, now hear from me the treatment [5]. For the fever associated with *pitta*, washing with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *surāhvā*, and *surasā* along with warm *kāñjika* is recommended. For that arising from *śleṣman*, this paste of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) with urine is praised, as is what has been declared by other excellent physicians [6]. Ginger, *saṭhī*, turmeric (*rajanī*), the three myrobalans, neem (*nimba*), and *patra* leaves combined with rock salt (*saindhava*) and fermented rice-water (*tuṣāmlaka*) are said to be beneficial.

In cases of eye diseases involving the *sannipāta* (combined humors), those arising from blood (*raktodbhava*), and those accompanied by pain, the three fruits (*phalatrika*) along with turmeric (*niśā*) are recommended as a collyrium (*dhūma*). In disorders born of *kapha*, or those associated with *vāta*, an ointment made with *vacā*, *varṣābhū*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) is indeed beneficial and highly praised. Alternatively, the root of *apāmārga* or the root of *dhattūra*, rubbed in a copper vessel with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), rock salt, and buttermilk (*takra*), serves as a beneficial collyrium (*añjana*) that removes eye diseases caused by *vāta*. Fresh butter produced from milk and *yaṣṭī* [madhuka] are also recommended.

Nimba and sesame seeds combined with Triphalā and jaggery form a plaster that destroys eye diseases caused by Kapha. (11) Śuṇṭhī, Saindhava salt, Tuttha, and Māgadhikā, rubbed on a copper plate with curd and ghee, act as a collyrium that destroys all eye ailments. (12) The juice of Śigru leaves alone, when applied along with honey, instantly removes the great suffering of the eyes arising from the disorders of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha. (13) And [it cures] the swelling in the eyes caused by improper diet and lifestyle.

The first [type] arises and is easily curable; the second is curable with difficulty. The third is curable by surgery, while the fourth is incurable. (14–15) O best of physicians, *śaṅkhapuṣpa*, *rodhra*, *śaṅkhanābhi*, and *manaḥśilā* should be ground together with *kāñjika* and dried in the shade. (16) This collyrium (*añjana*) is beneficial for the wind-disorder (*vātika*) when mixed with *kāñjika*, for the bile-disorder (*paittika*) when mixed with milk, and for the phlegm-disorder (*śleṣmala*) when combined with urine. It is also beneficial for the flower-like eye-disease (*puṣpāñjanaka*). (17) It is likewise beneficial for pacifying the three humors (*tridoṣa*) when prepared with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, along with *harītakī* and *vacā*. (18)

Kuṣṭha, pippalī, and marica (18); or the marrow of vibhītaka, conch-shell navel, and manaḥśilā—these should be ground in equal parts with goat’s milk (19). This destroys timira, itching, pāṭala, and arbuda; it kills puṣpa along with paṭala and cures night-blindness (rātryandhya) (20). It is desired for the eyes in cases of injury from trauma or grief, burns from fire, as well as kāca and nīlikā (21), arising from childhood, the power of the doṣas, or the indulgence in corrupted food.

Due to old age, there may also be a film (paṭala); I shall describe its characteristics. From wind (vāta), it is accompanied by impurities (kaśmala) and is dry; from bile (pitta), it is blue and yellow; from phlegm (kapha), it is white and thick; they know that from blood (rakta), it is reddish. I shall now describe the treatment according to the symptoms of the combination of humors (sannipāta) and so forth. This is a medicinal wick (varti) for rubbing, prepared with ginger, *vacā*, turmeric, copper sulfate (*tuṭtha*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), *śobhāñjana*, collyrium (*añjana*), the root of *viśālā*, conch shell, *vāstūka* root, honey, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *kaṭphala*, combined with *sauvīraka*.

[This preparation] is praised for drying the eyes of one with *chāyāviśuṣka* (eye-drying) and should bring about the destruction of the multitude of eye diseases including *paṭala*. (26) Harītakī with *añjana*, *kaṭphala*, and *manaḥśilā*, along with jaggery and *kaṭphala*, destroys *netrapracchada* (obscuration of the eye). (27) A wick (*varti*) made from the fruit of *mahāvibhītaka*, *śaṅkhanābhi* rubbed [with a base], combined with *saindhava* salt, milk, sour gruel (*amlaka*), and jaggery, is beneficial as an eye-salve (*añjana*) and prevents *paṭala* arising from *pitta*. (28) [One should avoid] smoke, wind, dryness, heat, and similar factors.

Likewise, those suffering from eye diseases should avoid pungent and sour foods, as well as sexual intercourse. Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Eye Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 45.

The forty-sixth chapter. Ātreya said: 1. When the lips of a person are cracked due to excessive speaking or from a Vāta disorder, the consumption of ghee is prescribed for preventing the splitting of the lips. 2. If there is burning and redness, one should diagnose that as being caused by Pitta (paittika). 3. Anointing the two lips with honey and fresh butter is recommended; likewise, applying curd mixed with sugar is advised for diseases of the lips. 4. Upon seeing a lip disease accompanied by blood, one should perform bloodletting; an application of the paste of Dhava, Arjuna, and Kadamba trees will bring relief.

4. When a row of black teeth appears and the root of the tooth is seen to be loose due to wind (vāta), one should diagnose it as being caused by wind (vātika). 5. From bile (pitta) one should identify the flow of bile and inflammation of the gums; in the phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) type of dental suppuration, there is swelling and extreme whiteness. 6. In that born of blood (rakta-ja), itching arises and a bloody discharge is observed; the gums bleed, and likewise the flesh of the tooth-sockets is ulcerated. 7. The root of the tooth becomes perforated, and there is intense pain; the gum-flesh falls away in the case of that born of worms (krimi-ja).

Toothache arises [from these causes]. (8) A paste made of *yavānī*, *vacā*, *sahā*, *citraka*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *viśvā*, and *sindhuvāra*, along with warm water, should be used as five hundred mouthfuls of gargle for tooth disease and oral ailments; this is praised as beneficial for all diseases of the mouth. (9) Rubbing the roots of the teeth with *vacā*, rock salt, and *śuṇṭhī* is recommended. (10) One should hold *yavānī* and *vacā* at the roots of the teeth at night. For tooth diseases born of *pitta*, fresh butter mixed with sugar should be used, rubbed with the fruit of the *dhātrī*. (11) Rubbed with the fruit of the *dhātrī*.

The prevention of dental diseases: For phlegmatic (kaphaja) dental diseases, rubbing with *harītakī* or with jaggery is recommended; likewise, a decoction of *triphalā* combined [with these] is beneficial. By holding a gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*) of a decoction of the root of *ahimāraka*, as well as a decoction of *khadira*, a decoction of *yavānī*, and a decoction of the root of *nimba*, dental diseases are prevented. In cases of blood-born (*raktaja*) disorders, one should rub with salt and mustard seeds and cause the blood to flow from that [affected area]; this is desired for the lip-fold as well. [Use] *viḍaṅga*.

One should rub asafoetida and *sindhuvāra* with the powder of *vacā*; this is beneficial and highly recommended for diseases of the teeth caused by worms. (16) When there is a swelling on the tongue, one should diagnose it as glossitis (*jihvāpāka*). In the Vātika type, it is painful and black; in the Pittaja type, it is accompanied by a burning sensation. (17) In the Kaphaja type, it is thick and white; in all cases combined, it is due to the Sānnipātika type. (18) For the Vātika disease of the tongue, one should apply a rubbing paste of *vacā*, *bhayā*, *viḍaṅga*, ginger, *sauvarcala* salt, and *kaṇā* (long pepper), mixed with ghee. (19) [This may also be done] with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) or buttermilk (*takra*).

Holding a lukewarm gargle of liquorice (*yaṣṭīka*), sandalwood (*candana*), nut-grass (*mustā*), and *māgadhī* mixed with honey (verse 20) is a plaster that prevents the bursting of the tongue in cases of Pitta-type disorders. Holding a cold milk gargle also destroys [these ailments] (verse 21). This is known to be beneficial for dental diseases as well as inflammation of the tongue; furthermore, a warm decoction of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* provides great relief (verse 22). When mouth-sores arise from Kapha, holding a gargle is beneficial; in disorders born of blood, one should cause the blood to flow out. (Verse 23)

For a tongue that has become blood-red (*raktajihvaka*), one should apply a plaster made of *kaṇṭaka*, *mūrvā*, *mustā*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *māgadhī*, and the two types of *rajanī*, combined with jaggery and honey. When a swelling of the tongue (*jihvāpāka*) arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*), they know that rubbing the area with the powder of black pepper, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *harītakī* is beneficial. Furthermore, by consuming oily substances such as sesame, sweets, and the like, or through excessive drinking of fresh water, a disease of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikāgada*) born of phlegm occurs at the root of the tongue and the junction of the throat, arising from both phlegm and blood.

By that, dryness, numbness, and mild fever arise in him (27). There is headache, loss of appetite, drowsiness, and likewise numbness; by pressing the *raktapanthikā* vessel between the index finger and the throat (28), the blood flows out, and then a depleting treatment (*vimlāpana*) is beneficial. One should apply a powder of *vacā*, black pepper, and long pepper there (29). There should be a massage in the region of the throat; by that, the glandular swelling (*granthi*) dissolves. Equal parts of coriander, ginger, *jīmūta*, and *vacā* (30)—this decoction is for fomenting the *ghaṇṭikā*.

The physician should hold a gargle in the mouth during the day and night, and should place a knot of *vacā* in the mouth. By this, there will be comfort for him, and he is liberated from diseases of the mouth. (31-32) In the throat and the passage of the *ghaṇṭikā*, a growth arising from disorders of blood and phlegm increases in men; it should be known as *galagaṇḍikā*. (33) It obstructs the oral cavity and nasal passages, discharge from the eyes is observed, there is headache, dyspnea, and cough; it suppurates along with fever itself. (34) An extremely wise physician should act quickly.

One should apply a surgical treatment by cutting the *śuṇḍikā* (throat-tumor) with a blade; then, one should perform a beneficial scarification (*vimlāpana*).
