(35) A warm decoction of *māgadhī*, black pepper (*marica*), *pathyā*, *vacā*, coriander (*dhānya*), and *yavānikā* should be applied as a fomentation (*sveda*) for the pacification of *galashuṇḍī*. (36) Holding *yavānī* in the mouth during the day and at night is beneficial; moreover, massaging the region of the throat with it brings about comfort. (37) An application to the throat of *siddhārthaka*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, turmeric (*rajanī*), *pāribhadraka*, soot from a house (*grahadhūma*), and salt is also beneficial.

O high-minded one, those wholesome diets prescribed for fever should not be consumed when there is a disease of the throat; neither sweet nor slimy substances, nor oil, should be used in such a condition. Thus ends the treatment of *galaśuṇḍikā* (uvulitis). This concludes the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Mouth," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-Seven. Ātreya said: Impotence is declared to be of five kinds; hear from me a summary of them. (1) From the suppression or excessive indulgence of sexual intercourse, even in a man exhausted by old age, there occurs a loss of semen and impotence also arises. (2) Three types of impotence arise: that which is mental, that which results from the depletion of semen, and innate [impotence]; furthermore, impotence arises in a man from dry perspiration. (3) That which occurs when, upon seeing the lack of passion in women, there is a sense of possessiveness in the mind and perspiration at the touch—that is curable. (4)

Mental impotence is recognized as that condition where, due to aversion toward women, the mind suffers depletion through sexual intercourse; the "breaking of the banner" occurs swiftly from the exhaustion of semen. Another type, characterized by an equilibrium of the humors (*samaprakṛti*), is also considered most difficult to cure. When there is a decline of the mind, an increase of the mind occurs through union with charming women, accompanied by passionate, playful conversations and discourse; thus the mind is nourished. Now I shall describe the methods for increasing semen when semen is diminished. [The following are the ingredients: *vidārikā*, *gokṣura*, *mūṣaka* (rat), and *dhātrī* fruit.

These [medicinal plants] should be equal in measure to the Saindhava salts and the products of Magadha; one should drink this mixture with milk enriched with sugar. (8) The two types of *bṛhatī*, *magadhā*, *trikaṇṭā*, as well as *ātmaguptā* and *śatāvarī*, when taken with cow’s milk, sugar, and ghee, produce virility in men. (9) One should eat the finest *vaṭaka* (pills), prepared from the dehusked flour of barley, wheat, and *māṣa* beans, processed with milk, sugarcane juice, and ghee, having risen early in the morning. Upon that [pill],...

The drinking of milk mixed with long pepper (pippalī) and sugar; likewise, barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), vidārī, and powdered black gram (māṣa); or parched barley (yava) with black pepper and abundant white sugar; and a cake made of ghee—these one should cook and eat in the morning, followed by the drinking of milk. This bestows virility upon men, and the woman takes great delight in him. Guḍūcī, śatamūlī, svayaṃguptā, and balā; as well as śālmalī and the root of musalī—this powder, when combined with cow’s milk, is an excellent drink for men that produces semen and enhances the sexual organs.

15. Vidārikanda, aṃśumatī, the two types of bṛhatī, kākolikā, bhīru, the two types of punarnavā, śṛṅgāṭaka, māgadhikā, and balā—these should be used as a powder enriched with sugar or mixed with sugar. 16. When [the medicine] has been digested, milk or milk-rice (pāyasa) should be administered; this bestows strength and vigor upon men, and even a eunuch may enjoy a thousand women. This is highly recommended when prepared for two months. 17. One should avoid pungent, sour, sharp, hot, burning, and dry foods, as well as sauvīra, which are said to cause the impairment of the senses.

Onions, barley, bulbs, sesame seeds, and black gram should be taken according to one's strength, as well as rice from the *viśālī* plant, milk, and sugarcane juice (19). *Vāstuka* and *cillaka* greens are wholesome even in cases of seminal depletion; however, having excluded *sūraṇa*, one should not employ *śuṇṭhī* unless it is combined with appropriate adjuncts (20). Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Aphrodisiacs," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-Eight. Ātreya said: A woman may become barren (vandhyā) in six ways: either through childhood [impairment], or from the rupture of the womb-cavity, or likewise from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu). In some cases, the conception of a fetus never occurs; one type is the "crow-barren" (kākavandhyā), and the second is the childless (anapatyā). The third is described by the best of sages as the one who miscarries (garbhasrāvī); the fourth is she whose children die (mṛtavatsā); and the fifth is due to the loss of strength (balakṣaya). I shall now describe the treatment for her, by which she may obtain [offspring].

4. If sexual intercourse is performed with women who have not yet reached puberty, by that very act the womb becomes constricted and the female organ (bhaga) undergoes a state of contraction. 5. Because of that, the woman becomes barren and does not conceive at all; yet, O physician, she may eventually become pregnant with great difficulty. 6. Through medicines and therapeutic treatments, there is success without a doubt; even through the power of the *anapatya* [mantra], O best of physicians, a child is born. 7. She shall not be a "crow-barren" woman (*kākavandhyā*), and even one who is childless is cured; while being cured, she attains success.

O best of physicians, that [disorder] arises from the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). For a disease born of *pitta*, one should administer a drink consisting of sandalwood, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *paṭola*, *dhanavālaka*, *madhuka*, *madhuyaṣṭī*, and red sandalwood; likewise, *sārivā*, cumin, *musta*, *padmaka*, and *punarnavā* mixed with milk and sugar. Having ascertained the purification of the womb (*yoni*), one should then apply the great medicine: sandalwood, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *girikarṇī*, and sugar, stirred with milk; this will bring about the successful attainment of menstruation (*puṣpasiddhi*) in cases of *pitta*.

12. One should examine the menstrual blood (*rajaḥ*) to determine whether it is of the nature of *vāta*, *pitta*, or *kapha*. A wise physician should recognize that the menstrual flow which is painful, blackish, and resembles the color of a ripe *jambu* fruit is afflicted by *vāta*. 13–15. For such a case, the wise physician should administer for seven days a decoction of *nāgara*, *pippalī*, *mustā*, *dhanvayavāsaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *pāṭalā*, mixed with jaggery and curd, until the blood flows out cleanly. Once the blood has been purified, he should then have her drink milk combined with *śvetā* and *girikarṇī*. *Śvetā* and *girikarṇī* are [the herbs used]. *(Note: The final line appears to be a fragmentary reference to the medicinal plants mentioned in verse 14.)*

Guñjā and punarnavā—by their application for one month, she obtains a pregnancy. (16) That which resembles the *japā* flower or the juice of safflower, and is accompanied by burning sensations, emaciation, and dysuria, is afflicted by *pitta*. (17) Candana, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, paṭola, ghana, vālaka, madhuka, yaṣṭimadhuka, and likewise red sandalwood; (18) Padmaka, the two types of punarnavā, śārivā, jīraka, ghana—this drink, combined with milk and sugar, is for diseases caused by *pitta*. (19) Having understood [these signs]...

In that case, one should administer the great medicine for the purification of the womb (*yoniviśuddhi*): the root of white *arka* with milk, as well as white *girikarṇikā*. (20) The root of white *adrikarṇī* taken as a drink combined with cow’s milk produces a pregnancy endowed with all auspicious marks even for barren women. (21) When the menstrual flow (*rajas*) is thick, slimy, cold, obstructs the urine, and is accompanied by lethargy, drowsiness, and sleep, they know it to be afflicted by *kapha*. (22) A drink of *triphalā*, *girikarṇī*, *āragvadha*, and *vatsaka*, taken with milk, [is beneficial] for women. (23)

The best of physicians should administer the *garbhakāraṇa* (conception-inducing) powders—namely those beginning with *bala*, those beginning with *candana*, and those beginning with *drākṣā*—to women to bring about conception. Furthermore, the best of physicians should give the powder beginning with *khaṇḍaka*, or else the powder beginning with *punarnavā*, which grants pregnancy to women. Now, O son, listen as I describe the wholesome regimen for women: one should keep at a distance from women things that cause burning sensations, those that are sharp, as well as *kañcara*, *sūraṇa*, sour substances, and fermented gruel (*kāñjika*).

One should avoid the root of the *vandhyākarkaṭakī*, *lāṅgalī*, bitter *tumbikā* (27), *devadālī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *sūryavallī*, and *bhīrukā*; likewise, one should avoid temple offerings (*nirmālya*), used garlands and clothes, as well as sexual intercourse during the menstrual period (28). Bathing water from another woman and the commencement of treatment for women are beneficial (29). Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment for Infertility," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 48.

The forty-ninth chapter. Ātreya said: In the first month, one should have her drink licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), *paruṣaka*, and *madhupuṣpa* as available, along with fresh butter, milk, and honey; and she should be given sweet [food]. In the second month, one should likewise have her drink *kākolī* and sweet [food]. In the third month, *kṛśarā* (rice and sesame) is best; and in the fourth, rice prepared with meat broth (*kṛtaudana*). In the fifth month, one should give milk-rice (*pāyasa*); in the sixth, sweet curd; in the seventh, with sugar-candy and ghee; in the eighth, a ghee-filled cake (*ghṛtapūraka*); and in the ninth, various kinds of cooked food.

In the tenth month, as well as when the third month has arrived, a woman experiences a pregnancy longing (*dohada*). Whatever she desires, that very thing the best of physicians should provide her. One should avoid foods made of split pulses, those that cause burning sensations, heavy foods, sour items, and warm milk; these must be strictly avoided for pregnant women. Earth should not be eaten, nor should *sūraṇa* tubers; garlic and onions must be abandoned by a pregnant woman. However, sweet and flavorful *sūraṇa* tubers should be given, as they are wholesome and beneficial.

The physician should always advise pregnant women to avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, emaciation, and wandering about; by doing so, the prosperity of happiness for the pregnant women will arise. Furthermore, even when the [gestational] period has arrived as prescribed by one's own custom—whether at five months or eight months—a feast for the clan (*gotra*) should be performed with Brahmin auspicious rites and other ceremonies. When the longings (*dohada*) and other requirements are fulfilled, a handsome, brave, wise, and virtuous son is born. Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Care of the Embryo," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The fiftieth chapter. Ātreya said: If movement of the embryo is observed in the first month, then Madhuka, Mṛdvīkā, Candana, and Raktacandana (1), mixed with milk and drunk, will cause the embryo to become stable. (2) If movement occurs in the second month, [one should take] Mṛṇāla and Nāgakeśara. When movement of the embryo is observed in the third month (3), one should drink the excrement of a mouse with sugar and milk. In the fourth month, there is burning sensation, thirst, and even colic (4), along with fever.

If a woman’s fetus moves, she should be made to drink uśīra, sandalwood, nāgakeśara, dhātakī flowers, sugar, ghee, honey, and curd. If the fetus moves in the fifth month, she should be made to drink pomegranate leaves, sandalwood, curd, and honey. In the sixth month, she should drink red ochre, black earth, cow-dung ash, and water strained and cooled, along with sandalwood and sugar.

In the seventh month, one should have her drink a sweet decoction of *gokṣura*, *samaṅgā*, *padmaka*, *ghanasārī*, and *nāgakeśara*. In the eighth month, for women whose fetus has moved, comfort is attained by those who have drunk *rodhra*, honey, and *māgadhikā* together with milk. Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of a Moved Fetus," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 50.

Fifty-first Chapter. Ātreya said: Emaciation, nausea, vomiting, swelling, fever, as well as loss of appetite, diarrhea, and discoloration—these eight are the complications of pregnancy. I shall now describe its treatment according to the appropriate application: the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree, *magadhā*, *uśīra*, and *ghana* [should be used]. A bolus made of these mixed with sugar and placed in the mouth destroys emaciation. One should administer *vatsaka*, *magadhā*, ginger, and the fruit of *āmalakī*, ground together with tender *bilva* and curd.

A drink mixed with sugar is always beneficial for women during pregnancy. (5) The paste of *bhūnimba* drunk with sugar, or combined with honey, removes vomiting and moisture of the heart. (6) Fresh ginger, *kaṭuka*, and the filaments of *mātuluṅga* used for cleansing the teeth and tongue, as well as gargling with warm water, (7) removes all loss of appetite in pregnant women; likewise, *vatsaka*, pomegranate, *pāṭhā*, *bilva*, and *balā*, (8) as well as the sprouts of *jambu* and mango, [should be used] according to the [prescribed] manner.

O Seventh One, for women suffering from diarrhea, [a preparation] combined with sugar and curd is beneficial (9). Harītakī, ginger, or Triphalā decoction cooled with jaggery, when drunk by women, destroys constipation and abscesses (10). For urinary obstruction, one should drink Trapusa, the seeds of Ervaribija, Māgadhī, and Śilābheda, enriched with sugar and mixed with rice-water;

this certainly and quickly removes the retention of urine in pregnant women (11). [One should also take] a paste of Madhuka, Viṣa, and lotus stalks, along with lotus filaments, thickened with Ativiṣā and Indrāhvā seeds, and Uśīra water.

Then, a paste (kalka) made from equal parts [of the aforementioned ingredients] should be administered quickly as a drink; this is beneficial even for young women during miscarriage, provided it is enriched with sugar. (12) Swelling is a complication of pregnancy; one should apply fomentation with warm water. A wise physician must not administer a severe or great purgative. (13) Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications of Pregnancy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. (51)

The fifty-second chapter. Ātreya said: Due to the consumption of incompatible foods, as well as during complications of pregnancy, the infant suffers from the pain of excessive pressure on the head. Furthermore, if the fetus is displaced sideways or passes through the vaginal canal or another opening, the offspring dies, whereby the mother encounters great suffering. Alternatively, due to the modesty of women, when the birth canal is constricted, one should recognize a "mūḍhagarbha" (malpresentation); I shall describe its symptoms. There is also pain in the bladder.

The birth canal becomes obstructed, the abdomen rumbles, and flatulence arises; there is piercing pain, a breaking sensation in the limbs, and loss of sleep—O best of physicians, such obstruction of the fetus arises from Vāta (4–5). From Pitta, there occurs colic, fever, aggravation of the three doṣas, thirst, vertigo, difficulty in urination, and headache; there is also obstruction of the fetus (6). From Kapha, there arise lassitude, drowsiness, excessive sleep, stupor, flatulence, trembling, cough, and a bad taste in the mouth (7).

One should know that [a fetus] caused by dual combinations [of doshas] arises from those combinations (dvandvaja), while everything arising from all three combined is sānnipātika. 7–8 In the case of a dead fetus (mūḍhagarbhaka), there is delusion, fainting, thirst, flatulence, obstruction of wind, and agitation; one becomes unconscious, vomits, experiences roughness, and falls into a state of dejection. 9 One should recognize this as a dead fetus even in a woman who acts quickly [to deliver]. O expert in great delusion, I shall now describe the remedy. 10 In the vātika type, the best of physicians should prescribe massage, anointing, and mild sudation, and should have her drink gruel and the five-spice compound (pañcakola). 11 In the paittika [type]... [text breaks off]

Cool drinks along with cool foods and side dishes are beneficial; likewise, one should drink *yaṣṭika* with milk. (12) In cases of obstructed labor caused by *śleṣman*, a decoction of *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *kuṣṭha*, *rodhra*, *vatsaka*, and *dhātukī*, taken with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be drunk. (13) A decoction of *mūrvā*, *ciñcā*, *vāstuka*, *karṇī*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *rodhra*, *nīlikā*, the root of *karkandhu*, and *saurāṣṭrī*, taken with jaggery, is also beneficial. (14) This brings about purification of the abdomen in disorders of *raktapitta*. Now I shall describe the medicine for a dead fetus (*mṛtagarbha*).

O best of physicians, having diligently massaged the woman, if the fetus within the womb dies due to lack of nourishment, then listen to me regarding the surgical remedies and medicines: having fashioned a well-curved instrument from a tube inserted into the umbilical opening, one should seat the woman suffering from a retained fetus upon it, extend her knees slightly, brace her back with a support, and draw the fetus down from the abdomen.

If [the fetus] is stuck at the vaginal opening, one should lubricate the hand with sesame oil or water and insert it; then, grasping the neck region of the fetus with the index finger and thumb, one should extract it. Alternatively, using a crescent-shaped surgical instrument, one should sever the pair of arms of the dead fetus and extract the limbs. By applying the root of the *lāṅgalī* plant with warm water as an ointment to the navel of women, the fetus quickly comes forth and she gives birth.

One should grind the roots of *balā*, *sūryakānti*, and *somavallī* with collyrium and apply it as an ointment. (18) Having ground the roots of *bhīru*, *bhūnimba*, and *vārttākī*, along with *pippalī*, *yavānī*, *agaru*, and *vacā*, together with warm water, [one should apply it]. (19) By means of this ointment, a woman will give birth from above or below. Furthermore, the roots of *lāṅgalikī*, *devadālī*, and *tumbikā*—(20) All these, including *kośātakī* and others, are prescribed for application; indeed, these are "birth-inducing ointments" (*sūtilepa*), and by them a woman gives birth easily. (21) [This is] on the northern side of the Himavat.

On the bank dwells a rākṣasī named Surasā; by the sound of her anklets, the pregnant woman Viśalyā shall become free from pain. Aiṃ hrīṃ, O Blessed One, Bhagamālinī! Move, move! Cause [the flower] to revolve! Cause the flower to blossom, cause it to blossom! Svāhā! Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the one whose banner is the makara, the one whose bow is flowers, who has stirred the hearts of all gods and asuras, and who dwells in the wombs of young women! Hrīṃ, cause the womb to move, cause it to move! Svāhā!

One should have her drink milk consecrated with this [mantra]; by that, there is an easy delivery. (23) Aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hroṃ hrauṃ hraḥ. (24) Having written this yantra on the upper side of a birch-bark leaf, one should show it to a woman with a difficult labor and place it beneath her bed; by that, there is an easy delivery. (25) She who dwells alone on the bank of the Gaṅgā and wanders in the Himalayas—one should have her drink water from which its wings have fallen; then, in an instant, (26) the woman gives birth, according to the words of Kākarudra. By this [method]. (27)

The messenger should remain agitated until she has been made to drink [the medicine]; by that means, the woman gives birth at home with ease, like a crow. Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Mūḍhagarbha (Obstructed Labor)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-third chapter. Ātreya said: Immediately after delivery, one should administer the seeds of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *devadāru*, and *bījaka*, along with *karkandhū*, as available, into blood that has been purified. The birth-canal, having been cleansed, should be filled with oil and massaged; then, using a heated *vraṇi* (wound-healing) instrument, one should apply fomentation (*sveda*). Having observed a fast in this manner, on the second day, one should administer jaggery, *nāgara*, and *harītakī*. After two watches (six hours) have passed, one should cause her to drink either warm *kulattha* soup or [the aforementioned mixture].

On the third day, one should administer a gruel of five types of *kola* fruits. One should administer a gruel mixed with the four aromatic spices (*caturjātaka*). On the fifth day, one should feed him boiled rice of *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* varieties. Following this sequence, one should provide nourishment for fifteen days. (1) One should grind long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), ginger (*nāgara*), *ghanavāluka*, coriander (*kustumburu*), and *mañjiṣṭhā* together with milk into a paste. (2) For the purpose of purifying the milk, he consumes the paste immediately after drinking the milk. (3) Black pepper (*marīca*) and long pepper root are added to the milk for the sake of increasing the quantity of milk.

Māgadhī, Nāgarī, Pathyā, jaggery, ghee, and milk produce breast milk in women, even when taken in small doses. Having performed these [procedures] for women on the twelfth day, the best of physicians should perform auspicious recitations and show [the child] to the woman. Furthermore, on the twelfth day after birth, once the naming ceremony has been performed, he should carry out the piercing of the ears, the binding of the cloth, and the marriage [ceremony] for the child. Thus [ends] the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya.
In the third section, the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Attendants of Childbirth" (Sūtikopacārī).

The fifty-fourth chapter. Ātreya said: The wise have described five defects of breast milk in women: thick milk, hot milk, sour milk, and another; [the others being] scanty milk, alkaline milk, and soft milk. Soft milk is conducive to well-being, while the other five are causative of defects. From the consumption of thick milk, there arises heaviness, flatulence, constipation, and the onset of dyspnea, cough, and so forth, as well as distension of the abdomen. [The child becomes] of little vitality, emaciated, and dejected.

Afflicted by dyspnea and diarrhea due to the defect of insufficient milk, the son of Ghatavāk may come into being. (4) Fever, emaciation, and weakness arise in the child from warm milk; likewise, fever and diarrhea occur from warm milk. (5) Through mild milk, the infant certainly attains a good disposition, strength, and health, and he is even born handsome. (6) Eye disease, itching, discharge of phlegm from wounds, and a moistening of the nose and mouth occur when alkaline milk is consumed. (7) Therefore, I shall now describe the remedy.

Listen, Hārīta, to my teaching: 8. When the abdomen is distended and bloated due to flatulence, and the child is afflicted by disorders such as dyspnea, this condition is to be known as *utphullikā*, which causes great suffering to children. 9. In the case of *udare* (abdominal swelling), one should first extract blood using leeches and the like; when the fault of *utphullida* is present, a remedy that neutralizes the fault of milk (*kṣīradoṣa*) should be administered. 10. A strong fomentation (*sveda*) with fire, or even cauterization with a probe (*śalākā*), should be applied; O best of physicians, spots shaped like drops (*binduka*) appear on the belly. 11. A decoction of the root and fruit of *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and the two types of *bṛhatī*, mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*), [is the remedy].

This is beneficial for the fever of children (12). For women, the drinking of these [medicines] shall be the destroyer of fever in children (13). A decoction of *parpaṭaka* combined with sugar and honey is beneficial; likewise, *kairāta* combined with honey is for the destruction of fever in children (14). Alternatively, a powder of *bhārṅgī*, *rāsnā*, and *karkaṭaka* combined with honey, or a linctus [made from them], prevents asthma and cough even in a child (15). A powder of *pathyā*, *vacā*, *nāgaraka*, *ghana*, and *karkaṭa* taken with jaggery (*guḍa*) indeed destroys cough in children (16). [Also] *palāśabheda*...

Having ground triphalā, trapusī, varī, and māgadhī with rice-water, one should administer it enriched with sugar; this conquers urinary obstruction (17). One should give the powder of nāgarī, abhayā, dantī, and guḍa to children; it will undoubtedly destroy abscesses as well (18). A drink of pāṭhā, bilva, śilā and others, vatsaka, and the bark of śālmalī with milk prevents diarrhea in children (19). An application of arjuna, kadamba, kuṣṭha, and gairika is a remedy for skin disorders in a child (20). [Also] rodhra...

Rasāñjana, dhātrī, and gairika, combined with honey as an ointment, prevent eye diseases in children. (21) Vacā, brāhmī, maṇḍūkī, musta, kuṣṭha, and nāgara, given in the morning with ghee, promotes nourishment in children. (22) Guḍūcī, apāmārga, viḍaṅga, śaṅkhapuṣpikā, viṣṇukrāntā, vacā, pathyā, nāgara, and śatāvarī—(23) The powder of these, mixed with ghee, when licked, causes intelligence to arise; in three days, one attains a thousandfold [intellect]. (24)

One should master these twenty-four verses. A powder made of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), coriander (dhanyā), bishop’s weed (yavānī), root of the Sal tree (sālamūlikā), sweet flag (vacā), holy basil (brāhmī), and Indian groundsel (bhārṅgī) is beneficial when taken with honey; it bestows eloquence upon children and produces a voice like that of a lute. O best of physicians, he in whom there is labored breathing, loss of consciousness, excessive drowsiness, trembling, headache, and fever is incurable. He who has saliva flowing from the mouth, loss of consciousness, a satisfied appearance, wandering eyes, and stiffness or deformity of the limbs is said to be suffering from epilepsy (apasmāra).

In the case of epilepsy in a child, one should employ cooling measures; indeed, a nasal drop (*nasya*) of *vacā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and long pepper (*pippalī*), or jaggery with ginger (*nāgara*), is beneficial. (28) The juice of *agasti* leaves combined with black pepper (*marica*) should be administered; by this, relief will be obtained, and at that time, swinging the child is wholesome. (29) One should cauterize the end of the head and the forehead with an iron rod. (30) O best of physicians, [the seizure spirits] transfer even to a child in an empty house, a temple, a cremation ground, the midst of a deity, a crossroads, a confluence of two rivers, or when the child is agitated by fear. (31)

Pūtanā, Lohitā, Revatī, Dhvāṅkṣī, Kumārī, Śākunī, Śivā, and Ūrdhvakeśī—these eight are proclaimed as Senās. Now hear from me the names of others as well: Rohiṇī, Vijayā, Kālī, Kṛttikā, Ḍākinī, Niśā, Bhūtakeśī, and Kṛśāṅgī; these eight are proclaimed. I shall now describe their characteristics and the sequence of worship and offerings; listen. Immediately upon birth, a child is [assailed by] the Pūtanā named Lohitā, who has a foul, cadaverous odor.

And she weeps red blood again and again. (36) I shall describe the offering for her, by which well-being arises: on the second day, the *pūtanā* named Revatī seizes the child. (37) Its symptoms are that it weeps and trembles violently. Having made an image out of black clay and anointed it with perfumes, (38) one should cast it at night toward the southwest, along with *kṛśara*, rice flour, lamps, incense, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), betel leaves, and black threads. (39) When the third day arrives, [the *pūtanā*] named Vāyasī...

As soon as he is seized by Pūtanā, the child weeps and will not suckle at the breast (40). He suffers from fever and diarrhea, and cries out excessively like a crow. For her, one should offer an oblation at midday consisting of curd-rice in a vessel, barley-porridge, and *polikā* cakes (41), along with banners, a bowstring, black fragrant unguents, incense, lamps, and consecrated grains (*akṣata*). On the fourth day, the Pūtanā named Kumārī seizes the child; he is not tormented by fever (42-43), but the child enters a vacant state and gazes fixedly at her face.

He becomes extremely parched and weeps; hear now the sequence for her worship and offerings (44). One should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*), ghee, sugar-candy, and three lamps of ghee (45). Having fashioned an earthen image and offered an oblation (*bali*) with flowers, incense, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) toward the direction of Death at midday, one shall become happy (46). On the fifth day, the *pūtanā* named Śākunī seizes the child; seized by her, the infant does not suckle at the breast (47). He suffers from fever, vomits, cries, coughs, and trembles (48). Of her—

An auspicious worship is performed with sesame-sweets (*tilalaḍḍuka*), white perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and incense; one should worship the earthen image [of the deity]. (49) Taking recourse in the northern direction, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) in the forenoon. When the sixth day arrives, a maiden named Śivā cries out, sighs, vomits, and likewise trembles. (50) The child, afflicted by fever and diarrhea, does not take the breast. To her, an oblation should be given consisting of a sacrificial porridge (*caru*) made of seven types of grain, along with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), curd, and lamps; she is to be worshipped. (51)

One should worship the earthen image with sesame powder (52), perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and incense; then, resorting to the northeast direction, one should offer a bali-oblation in the afternoon (53). On the seventh day, when the child is seized by Pūtanā Urdhvakeśī, the symptoms appear as before; likewise, one should offer a bali-oblation (54). When the eighth day arrives, the Pūtanā named Senā seizes the child, who then breathes heavily and shakes his hands violently (55). To her, one should give curd-rice, sesame powder, and fried cakes.

Incense, lamps, perfumes, flowers, betel, and unbroken grains—one should offer this oblation (bali) toward the south-eastern direction at dusk. In this manner, the ritual of offering should be performed for each month and throughout the year. Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Pediatrics," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-fifth chapter. Ātreya said: In deserted temples, on cremation grounds, on the surfaces of streets and main roads, on carriage-roads, in empty cities with ruined pleasure-gardens, in parks, and at crossroads—when these are desolate—armies arise when the heart of a man is agitated by minor planetary spirits (*kṣudragraha*). These well-known planetary spirits are of ten types; I shall now describe them. Ten were proclaimed by the great teachers, though some say there are twenty-one. I shall explain the medical treatment for the ten planetary spirits; listen, my son. [They are] Aindra and Āgneya...

Yama, another, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Graha, the Maruts, Kubera, Aiśānya, Grahaka, and another, Paiśācika—these ten are the leaders of the grahas. Whosoever [is possessed] in a grove, a monastery, or a temple, one should know him to be afflicted by the graha of Indra; by that he rejoices and sings, both with pride and without pride, and is truly seized by madness. In a cremation ground or at a crossroads, the evil graha of Agni seizes him; by that very [possession] he weeps excessively and sees fear on all sides.

On the battlefield and in the cremation ground, Yama is also said to be roused; by him a man is overwhelmed and distressed, and he behaves like a hungry ghost (preta). (8) At an anthill, a crossroads, or a sacred shrine (caitya), the Nairṛta spirit seizes [the person]; by him he acts with hostility, runs about, and even kills. (9) With eyes closed, face discolored, yet possessing great strength and a wicked mind, the Vāruṇa spirit moves along the banks of rivers and lakes. (10) Because of him, saliva flows from the mouth and the man urinates excessively; swelling of the eyes is observed, and he looks about like one who is mute.

11. And when it seizes one in the midst of a whirlwind, it is the seizure by Māruta; by that, the wretched person becomes emaciated, suffers from abdominal pain, or weeps. 12. Agitated and with exhausted eyes, he sits down afflicted by hunger; and when it seizes one during joy, pride, or arrogance, it is the seizure by the King of Yakṣas. 13. By that, he becomes haughty with pride and likewise very fond of ornaments. 14. In a beautiful temple of a deity, the seizure by Śiva provides deception; he applies ash as body-unguent and wanders about naked. 15. He is constantly devoted to the meditation on Śiva.

He is fond of song and instrumental music. 16. The *grahaka* is named after the planets; afflicted by hunger but not by thirst, he neither speaks nor hears. 17. Whether upon leavings or in a state of purity, the *piśāca-graha* seizes him; by that [possession], he dances, cries out, sings, and likewise prattles. 18. He wanders like one intoxicated, naked, with saliva flowing, and suffering from hunger and other such needs. Thus have I described the characteristics of the ten *grahas*. 19. Henceforth I shall declare the remedy; listen, my son, in brief.

Bathing in water is most excellent, as is the performance of the *bali* offering; through these, he obtains the happiness described in the ritual worship. Elā, nutmeg, the two types of *madhūka*, *rāsnā*, as well as *khādira*, camphor, *āmalakī*, *jaṭā*, *bahusutā*, *ghoṇṭā*, and *amlasāra*—these likewise [are used].

Lead, mercury, and pomegranate seeds, combined with liquors and each mixed equally with curd, milk, and the juice of lāṅgalī, should be ground into a paste (kalka). When processed with that juice and formed into pills, this preparation named Candraprabhā conquers severe diseases such as delusions. Śuṇṭhī, the essence of madhuka, cavī, and kiṃśuka, combined with vacā and hiṅgu and mixed with goat’s urine, should be administered; it destroys the afflictions caused by planetary spirits (graha) and is the supreme destroyer of such spirits.

Cat dung, snake slough, neem, peacock feathers, and *rājikā*—this incense, along with snake slough, *piṇḍītaka*, and *sarja-moca*, smeared with clarified butter, is for the pacification of the afflictions caused by planetary spirits (24). Furthermore, the pill known as *cetanā* and *brāhmī-ghṛta* are prescribed; these should be employed here in cases of epilepsy (25). One should fumigate [the patient] with guggulu, honey, and clarified butter using that incense; and with that mantra, O Hārīta, one should threaten the afflicted spirit (26): "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of Beings, whose claws are like the *kalika* flower, the Fierce One."

To the one with fangs as formidable as a mountain peak; to the one whose three eyes are like a blazing fire on a forehead tawny with wrath; to the one of immeasurable splendor, a fire of intense fury; to the one adorned with the noose, trident, skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), bow, arrow, mallet, the gesture of fearlessness, staff, the mudrā of terror, and a fresh staff; to the one wearing a mass of tawny matted hair and the crescent moon; to the one whose body is stained with the glow of ashes; to the one whose throat is adorned by the swelling of the fierce *kālakūṭa* poison—Victory! Victory! O Lord of Beings, Soul of the Immortals! Show, show Your form! Dance, dance!

Move! Move! Bind with the noose! Bind! Frighten with the *huṃ* sound! Frighten! Strike with the vajra-staff! Strike! Cut with the sharp sword! Cut! Pierce with the tip of the trident! Pierce! Grind to powder with the mallet! Grind to powder! Cause the entry of all seizing spirits (*graha*)! Cause them to enter! *Svāhā!* If an excellent offering (*bali*) is given to one possessed by a seizing spirit, he becomes liberated from it; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Science of Spirits" (*Bhūtavidyā*), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-sixth chapter. Ātreya said: The physician has identified poison as being of two kinds: stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama). [Among the stationary poisons: Śṛṅgika, Vatsanābha, and likewise Śārṅgavera; Dāraka, Kālakūṭa, Śaṅkhaka, Saktuka, and Hālāhala—these are the eight species of poison. Śṛṅgika is black in color, and Vatsanābha is yellow. That which is the same color as ginger (śuṇṭhī) is called Śārṅgavera. Dāraka is the color of a monkey (hari-varṇa), and Kālakūṭa...

Madhuprabha, Śaṅkha, Ativiṣābhāṣa, Pītābha, Satsukanduka, Hālāhala, and Kṛṣṇavarṇa—these are the eight species [of poison]. When yellow poison (*pīta-viṣa*) sees a man, it immediately causes excellent vomiting. One should always cause him to vomit for as long as the *ativiṣā* has been ingested; one should quickly sprinkle his face with water cooled by the purified mantra: Oṃ hara hara nīlakaṇṭha amṛtaṃ plāvaya hūṃ-kāreṇa viṣaṃ grasa grasa klīṃ-kāreṇa hara hara hrauṃ-kāreṇa amṛtam.

"Plāvaya plāvaya! Hara hara! There is no poison! Ucchire ucchire! (7) "Oṃ, obeisance to Hara, Hara, whose form is the mantra manifesting as the crescent moon adorned by the tips of matted hair, born from the contact of the blue-necked one with the white-bodied one; withdraw the poison! Hara hara hara! There is no poison! Viṣa viṣa viṣa! Ucchire ucchire ucchire! (8) With this "whisper-in-the-ear" mantra (*karṇejapa-mantra*), one should repeatedly sprinkle cold water on the palate and the mouth. Having ground the roots of the *tāṇḍulīyaka* plant with warm water, drinking it cures the effects of ingested poison through emesis.

Laghava (9): Kākajaṅghā, the root of Sahacarī, and that of Caiḍagaja, as well as Kadara and Kārmuka—when their bark is drunk with warm water, it destroys even the most terrible poison instantly; of this there is no doubt. (10) Khadira (11): The root of Khadira and likewise the fruits of Nimba, when drunk with warm water, would conquer poison at that very moment. (11) Vatsāhva (12): Having drunk Vatsāhva and Aśvagandhā with warm water, the poison that has been swallowed quickly protects the man; such is the word of the Vedas. (12) Now, the principal [remedies]...

I shall describe the remedy for blood and for that poison which enters through a wound, by which well-being is attained. (13) That [poison] located in a vital organ (*marman*) or having reached a vital point is considered incurable; that which resides in the blood is curable, while that residing in the flesh is difficult to cure. (14) O friend, I shall describe the medicine for that which has reached the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), which is incurable; having recognized a man smeared with poison, one should then perform the counter-treatment. (15) Poison [is neutralized] by an ointment of the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric) and *amlaka* ground with fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*).

It destroys [the poison] when smeared; of this there is no doubt. (16) Whether with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, or with *kāñjika* sour gruel, or with very cold water, it destroys [the poison] when smeared; of this there is no doubt. (17) O best of physicians, that which is called "mobile poison" (*jaṅgamaviṣa*) is said to be eightfold: the *dārvīkara* (hooded), the *maṇḍalina* (circled), and the *rājiman* (striped) snakes, as well as the *guṇḍasa* (biting) snakes; (18) the scorpion (*vṛścika*), the *goraka* spider, and likewise the *khaṇḍabinduka*; and the poisons of the *alarka* (mad dog), the rat (*mūṣa*), and the cat (*mārjāra*) are also said to be of many kinds. (19) The poison of all *dārvīkara* snakes is said to be of the nature of wind (*vātātmaka*), and so too that of the *maṇḍalina* snakes.

The poison of all [serpents] is said to be of the *paittika* (bilious) nature. Those which are described as having stripes are also poisons characterized by *kapha*. That [poison] which causes erratic movement, unbearable pain in the head, and distress in the heart is declared by the wise to be incurable. That in which nasal hemorrhage occurs and clouding of the eyes is observed, and the tongue becomes numb, the wise know that to be incurable. That in which the body hairs fall out and the body takes on a yellowish hue, and whose head is not steady—[that too is incurable].

Seeing that which is incurable by *tamas* (darkness/ignorance) as being devoid of these [remedies], the best of physicians should apply its counter-measure: *Oṃ namo bhagavate sugrīvāya sakalaviṣopadravaśamanāya ugrakālakūṭaviṣakavaline viṣaṃ bandha bandha hara hara bhagavato nīlakaṇṭhasyājñā | Oṃ namo hara hara viṣaṃ saṃhara saṃhara amṛtaṃ plāvaya plāvaya nāsti are re viṣa nīla parvataṃ gaccha gaccha nāsti viṣam oṃ hāhā ūcire ūcire ūcire |* With this mantra, one should terrify the mouth with water.

Oṃ, salutations! O Haṃsa, behold, behold the nectar! 25. A plaster consisting of *jayakūṭa*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *magadhā*, and *niśā* is prescribed for a bite-wound; it destroys even the most dreadful poison. 26. *Surasā*, *rajanī*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *yavānī*, and *pāribhadraka*—this plaster is prescribed for a snake-bite wound for the pacification of poison. 27. *Kuṣṭha*, *mustā*, cumin (*ajājī*), *viḍaṅga*, *madhuyaṣṭikā*, and the root of *guñjā*—a plaster made with these and cold water is beneficial for one bitten by a *maṇḍalī* snake. 28. For those whose poisons consist of stripes, house-soot (*gṛhadhūma*)... [is prescribed].

A plaster consisting of *vacā*, *ghanam*, mustard seeds, *yavānī*, and the three fruits of the *picumanda* tree, combined with *vraṇataila*, is for those afflicted by *rājimat* [venom]. (29) *Aṭarūṣaka*, *kirātatikta*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *vacā*, *viśālā*, *picumandaka*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, and the two types of *rajanī* are likewise recommended as a plaster for wounds caused by bites. (30) O best of physicians, whether it be stationary (*sthāvara*) or mobile (*jaṅgama*) poison that has been consumed, it quickly causes severe pain; thus it has been declared by the most excellent of men. (31) *Oṃ namo bhagavate*.

"O you whose crest is upon the head, whose entire body is washed by streams of nectar, who are surrounded by a jar of nectar—drench, drench [me] with nectar! Svāhā! (32). Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Tantra of Poisons," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 56.

The fifty-seventh chapter. Ātreya said: Cut (chinna), pierced (bhinna), fractured (bhagna), abraded (ghṛṣṭa), and likewise crushed (piṣṭa), as well as impacted (āsphālita) and contused (samprahāra)—these are described by the wise as "saṅghāta" (traumatic injury). (1) Upon seeing a man pierced by a weapon, medical treatment must be administered. (2) If the flesh is situated upon the bone and the bone is severed, or if there is a severance of the primary or secondary branches [of the limbs], that is called "chinna" (cut). (3) That which is completely severed at a non-junction (asandhi) should be designated as incurable.

It is always taught that [the wound] is severed by a sword, a crescent-headed arrow, or an axe. First, the application of *cāraṇā* ointment and rubbing are prescribed; it should be quickly fomented with a cotton pad soaked in sesame oil (5). As long as blood flows, one should massage it with oil; indeed, when the blood undergoes a morbid change (*vikṛti*), massage with oil is considered necessary (6). If swellings and other numerous complications arise in the wound, upon seeing a person whose joint has been severed, one should sprinkle him with warm water (7). Of that which has accumulated...

Picu-tailaka is also recommended for a wound; or when pus is discharging, leaves of nimba and āragvadha [should be used]. (8) Having ground pathyā with jaggery, an ointment is applied to purify the pus; even after it has been purified in three days, applying that same ointment there is beneficial. (9) Having ground the bark of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, vṛkṣa, and udumbara with water, an ointment made from that causes the wound to heal. (10) That which is pierced by spears, javelins, arrows, bhallas, swords, tomara-spears, or by the edges and points of knives is called *bhinnam* (pierced).

The physician declares that a fracture occurring away from the vital points (*marman*) is curable, whereas one situated upon a vital point does not heal. Washing with the juice of *apāmārga* as well as *kūṣmāṇḍaka*, or even with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), is praised by the wise. Anointing with sesame oil is beneficial for a fracture in a healthy person, and the previously mentioned ointments should also be applied, which are conducive to recovery. Indeed, [this applies] if it occurs on the chest, the head, the temples, the armpits, the feet, the sacrum, the abdomen, the tip of the face, the eyes, or the ears.

A foreign body (*śalya*) that is difficult to treat becomes curable by surgical instruments if it is not deeply embedded; however, one who knows the proper procedure should extract with medicines those [foreign bodies] located in the branches or sub-branches of the limbs, as well as those situated in the vital points (*marman*), which cannot be remedied by mechanical instruments or surgery. A wise physician should extract the foreign body using instruments, surgical tools, or counter-measures. One should specify twelve types of instruments, twelve types of surgical tools, and four types of bandages for the removal of foreign bodies. These are: the *godhāmukha* (leather-shield-mouth), the *vajramukha* (thunderbolt-mouth), the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs), the *cakrākṛti* (wheel-shaped), the *kaṅkapāda* (heron-foot), and the *ayānaka*.

The Śṛṅgaka, Kuṇḍala, Śrīvatsa, Sauvatsika, and Pañcavaktra—these twelve instruments have been described by the best of physicians. Now, the surgical instruments (śastra) are declared, each with its distinct name: the Ardhacandra, Vrīhimukha, Kaṅkapatra, Kuṭhārikā, Karavīrakapatra, and the Śalākākārapatraka; the Baḍiśa, Gṛdhrapāda, Śūlī, and Ghanamudgara—these instruments are declared for the extraction of foreign bodies (śalya) individually. And the Atigupta...

One should extract a splinter with forceps; once it has been pierced, the remedy must be applied by one who is wise. (21) Having recognized a deep-seated splinter, one should determine the remedy: it should be incised with a blade of *kuśa* grass and the splinter removed with saffron. (22) The remedy for a pierced [wound] should likewise be applied by one who is wise. (23) Where there is intense swelling, there the splinter may have perished; having diagnosed it as being accompanied by a splinter, dense, and painful, (24) one should apply the appropriate instrument there.

Appropriate surgical instruments and appliances should be employed there by those skilled in reasoning and deliberation (ūhāpoha). (25) The intense pain arising from the insertion of a foreign body (śalya), which spreads throughout the body of a living being, finds relief through ghee mixed with bitter substances, slightly warmed, and combined with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu). (26) Sarus tree, arjuna tree, udumbara tree, markaṭī, rodhra, samaṅgā, and surasā—having ground these together with water for application as a plaster, this brings comfort during the extraction of a foreign body. (27) Furthermore, the remaining treatments previously mentioned are beneficial when [the wound] has been incised or punctured.

In that case, *vālukāsveda* (sand-sudation) and *ghaṭīsveda* (jar-sudation) should be performed. Having observed a man with a fractured bone, I shall describe the remedy for him: fractures of the wrist, the elbow, the knee, and likewise the waist, as well as a completely shattered spinal column—these, O best of men, are curable. However, a fracture in the region of the neck, at the *indrabasti*, at *rohiṇī*, below the elbow, between the shoulder and the elbow, in the middle of the *trika* (the sacral triangle), or in the chest and the breast—such a fracture is incurable.

Seeing a man whose [limb] is dislocated, one should bind it with a section of bamboo; one should rub it with fresh butter and wrap it with castor leaves (32). One should sprinkle it with warm water and bind it gently with a cloth (33). Having ground the bark of the *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* trees with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), an application of this paste is beneficial, and through it, relief is produced (34). One should foment those parts with heat and provide a covering once again; when the procedure is thus completed, one should then release the binding (35), even after an interval of one day.

One should continue that procedure as before until a knot is formed; one should not bathe the man until then. (36) Upon seeing the man rubbed, washing with *kāñjika* (sour gruel), urine, or cold water is considered beneficial. (37) As long as blood continues to flow, one should sprinkle the area with oil; one should also apply various medicinal herbs here in small quantities. (38) When the inflammation has subsided, blood-letting and fomentation (*svedana*) are prescribed; one should also provide treatment for a fracture according to the rules. (39)

When a treatment has been administered, the best of physicians must be consulted; through reasoning and refutation [of the diagnosis], he should act, for by that means well-being is attained. (40) The affliction arising from a blow to the head is proclaimed as "head disease" (*śiroroga*); and from a blow to the chest, a liver-tumor (*yakṛdgulma*) is produced. (41) In this manner, one should apply a remedy: bloodletting should be performed, and fomentation (*svedana*) should be employed by the physician for the successful completion of the treatment. (42) Furthermore, oil should not be consumed, nor food that is excessively hot or pungent; likewise, fish and thick meats should be avoided.

And heavy foods (43); soup made from white *śāli* rice, as well as from *āḍhakī* beans; rabbit, quail, eggplant, *kakkola*, and *taṇḍulīyaka* (44); *śatapuṣpā* and other such items, provided they are not combined with asafoetida; and salt should not be consumed in excess if one desires one’s own well-being (45). One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and sleeping during the day according to the prescribed sequence, so that a person may attain happiness and prosperity (46). Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fractures," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 57.

The fifty-eighth chapter. Ātreya said: Having observed a person burnt by fire, that burning is of four types: slightly burnt (*īṣaddagdha*), moderately burnt (*madhyadagdha*), excessively burnt (*atidagdha*), and properly burnt (*samyagdagdha*). O best of physicians, listen to the characteristics, my son. Excessively burnt (*atidagdha*) extends into the muscle tissue and involves vāta, pitta, and kapha; properly burnt (*samyagdagdha*) is free from these defects, and thus it is known to be of four types. That burning by which the skin is sloughed off is born of pitta and is accompanied by blood.

When accompanied by pitta, it appears due to the provocation of pitta; that pitta, located in the flesh, is black in color and causes intense pain. O best of physicians, I shall describe the remedy for its successful treatment. For a slightly burnt area, an application of *kāñjika* (fermented rice water) is for the sake of comfort. Nimba leaves, *surasā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *dhātrī* fruits—O best of physicians, these should be applied as available to a slightly burnt area. For a moderately burnt area, *payasyā* is the soothing application. [An oil] cooked with *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*, along with ghee, [should be used].

Kuṣṭha, yaṣṭīmadhuka, candana, and eraṇḍapatraka are considered beneficial; when applied as a paste ground with milk, it is useful for burns on the body. (8–9) Ghee, powdered camphor, gairika, and rodhra—this dry powder removes pus from a burn and even promotes healing. (10) A paste of āmalakī, sesame, and kuṣṭha is for application on fire-burns; likewise, rodhra, uśīra, and samaṅgā, applied with cold water, are beneficial. (11) Linseed oil for massage and a paste of madhuyaṣṭī with ghee are both beneficial for massage and topical application.

Dagdhārohaṇa prevents burning. 12. In cases of injury from smoke, emesis, drinking milk, and likewise swimming in water are excellent for the alleviation of the burning sensation caused by smoke. 13. Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, named the Section on Therapeutics, in the Hārīta-uttara spoken by Ātreya. The Third Section is completed. 3. The Third Section.

Now, the first chapter of the third section. Ātreya said: "Next, I shall fully explain the causes of the confusion of diseases. From exhaustion, from the suppression of physical exertion, or even from anxiety, grief, and fear; from anger, from the smell of medicine, and especially from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus), the digestive fire (agni) is provoked from the visceral cavity (koṣṭha). Thus, blood-bile (raktapitta) arises externally, and having combined with that which is localized in the skin, it indeed produces fever. Fever may also arise from the aforementioned causes, or from one fever, another fever may become chronic (mandajvara). From a mild fever, it becomes more mild (mandatama)."

Therefore, from the excessive consumption of sour things, jaundice (kāmalā) arises; when that has fully developed, it becomes chlorosis (halīmaka). From chlorosis, anemia (pāṇḍu) occurs; from that, as it is proclaimed, consumption (yakṣman) arises. From consumption, swelling (śopha) is born, and from swelling, abdominal enlargement (udara). From that, abdominal tumors (gulma) caused by Vāta and other humors arise; from the tumor, dyspnea (śvāsa), colic (śūla), weak digestion (mandāgni), hoarseness of voice (svarabheda), and obstruction (rodhana) occur. Indeed, the origin of all these diseases is through fever (jvara); death should be understood to come through fever, but fever does not necessarily lead to death.

Listen, O knower of medicines and diseases, to the second [type of] combination of diseases: first there is a mild fever in men, followed by diarrhea and then fever; from that, hiccups, emaciation, delusion, vertigo, and loss of appetite arise. Death results from the swelling (*śopha*) of these [symptoms]. Now the third [combination] is described: through the defects of sleeping during the day and so forth, catarrh (*pratiśyāya*) arises; from that, cough is declared, and from cough, nasal catarrh (*pīnasa*). From that, consumption (*kṣaya*); from consumption, swelling; and by means of swelling, one goes to death. Fever, consumption, and phthisis (*yakṣmā*) [are thus linked].

Leucoderma, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and intestinal obstruction; (11) urinary gravel, diabetes, insanity, epilepsy, and fistula-in-ano—these most terrible ailments render a man merely manageable (palliable). (12) All diseases arise from the humors such as wind, bile, and those originating from phlegm; I shall now describe their treatment. (13) O best of physicians, wind matures [the disease] in seven days, bile in three nights, and phlegm matures it in even half a day. (14) That which arises from two humors, namely wind and bile, matures in nine nights.

Kapha and Vata are digested in ten days; Pitta and Kapha in five days. For the pacification of dual combinations (dvi-doṣaja), digestion occurs in four days, and likewise for the formidable tri-dosha, digestion occurs on the twelfth day. Sannipāta also digests in fourteen days. Therefore, having ascertained the strength of the doshas and that they are ripe, the digestive (pācana) therapy should be administered. When accompanied by the signs of the etiology, the pacifying (saṃśamana) treatment should follow; even after seven days, the impurities located in the seven tissues (dhātus) are digested, for they may indeed take a long time to digest.

In a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta-jvara*), the cessation of the fever is said to occur on the eighth day; generally, it does not cease on the seventh day, which is the reason for the fever's persistence. (19) A wise physician should administer medicine after careful consideration; one should not give medicine during indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), for the digestive fire is extremely weak and will not digest the medicine. (20) When all the humors have subsided, digestive (*pācana*) and reducing (*laṅghana*) therapies are prescribed. Reducing therapy is classified as moderate (*madhya-laṅghita*) or excessive (*atilaṅghita*). (21) Now, listen as I describe the symptoms of these [conditions] in human beings. (22)

The disappearance of fatigue, absence of aversion and malaise, and clarity of the sense organs indicate the ripening of the *doṣas* in one who has undergone successful fasting (*laṅghana*). This is the characteristic of a properly fasted person. (23) O best of physicians, slight fatigue, aversion, malaise, discoloration of the sense organs, excessive thirst, little hunger, and exhaustion are the signs of moderate fasting. (24) Slight unctuousness in the body, loss of appetite, constipation, and the state of the *doṣas* being only moderately ripened are the characteristics of moderate fasting. (25) A state of physical impairment, drowsiness, diarrhea, insomnia, trembling, and headache [occur in the case of excessive fasting]. (26)

One should recognize the symptoms of one who has undergone excessive fasting (atilaṅghita) by these signs: emaciation from hunger, colic, a darkened face, watering of the eyes, and being afflicted by fainting, delusion, and exhaustion. (26–27) An excellent physician should never administer fasting for seasonal fever (velājvara), fever caused by spirits (bhūtajvara), nor even for fever arising from bile (pittajvara); likewise, he should not do so for fever born of exertion, anger, fear, or passion. (28–29) Furthermore, one should never cause a child, an elderly person, one who is emaciated, one who is debilitated, one suffering from diarrhea or ulcers, a pregnant woman, or one of delicate constitution to undergo fasting. (30) [This applies] when there is undigested matter (sāma).

In cases of mild fever, severe fever, loss of appetite, and constipation, as well as in indigestion (ajīrṇa), fasting (laṅghana) administered in the proper measure is highly recommended. When there is excessive unctuousness of the limbs, the abdomen gurgles loudly, headache, abdominal distension, a burning sensation, and a rattling sound in the throat; when there is anorexia, yellowish urine, drowsiness, and lethargy—the best of physicians, having recognized the patient as suffering from fever caused by undigested matter (āmaja-jvara), should prescribe fasting. [This is to be achieved] through fasting, emesis, purgation, bloodletting, drinking heated water, and procedures involving sudation (sveda).

Six types of fasting (*laṅghana*) have been described. [One should observe fasting] for one who is emaciated by hunger, exhausted, suffering from the onset of vertigo and fever, experiencing internal burning, or whose urine is bloody—these are the signs of remittent fever (*virāmajvara*). A fever of Vata-type is digested by six fasts, while that of Pitta-type is digested in three days; phlegm (*śleṣman*) is digested in seven. One should administer fasting after observing these. A fever of the three *doṣas* is digested by fasts over ten nights; when the fifteenth day arrives, the Sannipatika fever is digested. It may release the patient, it may kill him, or it may remain.

In childhood, irregular fevers (viṣamajvara) arise from the humors associated with blood; thereafter, they stem from phlegm and bile. When the sixteenth year is reached, diseases originate from the three humors (tridoṣa); when the twenty-fifth year is reached, fever indeed becomes of the combined-humors type (sānnipātika). Fever that arises properly from the accumulation of rasa and rakta through vāta, pitta, and kapha should be treated by administering a decoction once it has fully matured. Decoctions are said to be of seven types: digestive (pācana), pacifying (śamana), appetizing (dīpana), moistening (kledana), drying (śoṣī), nourishing (santarpaṇa), and specifically [the seventh]. And [now] the digestive decoction...

One who understands [the proper timing] should administer a sedative (śamana) to a person during the first watch of the night; a digestive stimulant (dīpana) is prescribed for the afternoon; a nourishing (santarpaṇa) and carminative (bhedana) decoction should be given for drinking at dawn; and a drying (śoṣaṇa) decoction is also recommended for drinking in the morning. The first watch of the night is proclaimed as *bhūtavelā*; they call the second watch of the night *niśītha*, and the period following that is known as *gaṇarātra*. This refers to a time when the sun has not yet reached its full course [through the zodiac]. [These divisions include] the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and midday (*madhyāhna*).

Forty-five *parārddhas* remain at the end of the day; and at the conclusion of the day, the administration of medicinal decoctions (*bheṣaja*) begins. (46) The decoction (*kvātha*) is traditionally said to be of seven types: digestive (*pācana*), appetizing (*dīpanīya*), purifying (*śodhana*), pacifying (*śamana*), nourishing (*tarpaṇa*), moistening (*kledana*), and drying (*śoṣī*). (47) The digestive decoction should be reduced to half [its original volume]; the purifying, to one-twelfth; the moistening, to one-fourth; and the pacifying, to one-eighth remaining. (48) The appetizing decoction is reduced to one-tenth, the nourishing to its equal [original] portion, and the drying to one-sixteenth; thus the varieties of decoctions are proclaimed. (49) [The first is] the digestive (*pācana*).

The digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) pacifies the humors (*doṣas*) and kindles the fire; the purgative (*śodhana*) should cleanse the impurities; the palliative (*śamana*) subdues diseases. (50) The nourishing (*tarpaṇa*) satisfies the tissues (*dhātus*); the moistening (*kledī*) produces moisture in the heart; the drying (*viśoṣī*) brings about desiccation. Therefore, one should examine the decoction (*kvātha*). (51) Having recognized whether it is moistening or drying, one should cause the person to undergo emesis. One should not fast after taking a decoction, nor should one disturb the internal organs. (52) One should not dry it out again; it should be kept [in a vessel] and not displayed in an unclean place. Furthermore, that decoction is not recommended if it has been left standing for too long. (53)

It may be a cause for the complication of diseases. (53) One should not evaporate the decoction further, nor should it be allowed to remain on the ground; these [decoctions] are praised for the pacification of the *doṣas* in the treatment of disease. (54) A person [using such decoctions] suffers from cracking, falling [of tissues], or bursting due to the decoction; these decoctions are undesirable and do not lead to the pacification of the *doṣas*. (55) Having observed a decoction that is devoid of these characteristics, one should examine it: that which is black, blue, thick, red, slimy, or thin; that which is burnt, has the smell of a corpse, or the smell of raw meat. (56)

One should avoid [these cases]; by these signs one should know the patient to be incurable, there is no doubt in this. By describing the qualities of substances, one should indicate the smell of the substance. Likewise, that which is pure, well-colored, astringent, and like nectar [is beneficial]. After administering lightening therapy (*laṅghana*) at the end of a vāta-fever, food should be given, and thereafter a digestive medicine (*pācana*) should be administered at night, having ascertained the strength or weakness of the humors (*doṣa*). It should be given on the third day in a pitta-type fever, and on the first day in a kapha-type fever; however, when the humor is not identified, one should not administer a digestive medicine. Indeed, after seven nights...

A fever is characterized by its very limits; therefore, in a new fever (navajvara), that which is drunk neither produces the morbid humors (doṣas) nor removes them. (61) Therefore, for the first three days, a digestive (pācana) medicine should be administered; thereafter, for five nights, a palliative (śamanīya) medicine should be given. (62) One should administer a purifying (śodhana) and digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) medicine for one night. (63) If exhaustion, fainting, or mental confusion is observed during the drinking of decoctions, then emesis (vamana) is prescribed, whether as a palliative or even as a wholesome regimen (pathya). (64) Wholesome food (pathya) should always be employed, never unwholesome (apathya).

A disease is cured by medicine even without a dietetic regimen, yet it is successfully treated by the best of physicians through diet alone. Without a diet, a fever cannot be conquered even with hundreds of medicines; therefore, one suffering from fever should eat wholesome food even if he has no appetite. By refusing to eat at meal times, a patient wastes away and may even die; being emaciated, he falls into a state of great distress and reaches a condition that is truly incurable. Therefore, one must preserve the strength of men, for life itself is dependent on the subsiding of strength. Once the morbid humors have been lightened, one should practice the drinking of gruel (*yavāgū*).

Indeed, they say that a soup made of *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and *mudga* grains is recommended (69). A gruel prepared with the five spices (*pañcakola*) is always excellent for one who has undergone moderate fasting; nourishing therapy is beneficial for him (70). Goat's milk mixed with jaggery should be drunk for the pacification of fever; by this, exhaustion is destroyed and one quickly attains comfort (71). One should have the patient sit facing either the north or the east, and after performing the recitation of the Vedic hymns (*brāhmaṇavācana*), one should administer the decoction drink (72). Having placed the drinking vessel upside down, he should lie down.

And having drunk only knowledge, even one afflicted by thirst should not drink water for a moment; when one sees that a person’s fatigue has departed, then happiness is attained. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Thorough Knowledge of Medicines," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Second Chapter. Ātreya said: What is the use of studying the scriptures for one who is ignorant of medical practice? It is as useless as straw devoid of seeds. (1) It would be better to drink the poison of a venomous serpent, or molten copper, or iron balls heated by a fierce fire, than to accept food, drink, or wealth from a person afflicted by disease who merely wears the garb of those learned in the scriptures but has not sought refuge [in true knowledge]. (2-3) That alone is a proper medicine which results in health, and that indeed...

He who liberates from diseases is the best among physicians. Therefore, with every effort for the purpose of warding off disease, this compendium—endowed with the characteristics of diagnosis and provided with the necessary means—should be studied in its entirety for the sake of attaining knowledge of the compendium. Having understood the remedy for a disease, one should then apply the therapeutic treatment. One who undertakes medical procedures out of delusion without properly understanding the disease, even if he knows the ritual rules and the scriptures, will not achieve success. Diagnosis, the knowledge of diseases, and the merits and defects of medicinal substances [constitute the core].

Success is not far off for one who acts after having understood [the disease]. (8) A wise physician should first ascertain the knowledge of diseases—whether they are curable, incurable, or merely suppressible—and then apply the remedy for all such ailments. (9) Having thus understood the place, time, age, digestive fire (*agni*), suitability (*sātmya*), constitution (*prakṛti*), and medicine, the good physician should then apply the remedy. (10) There is no disease without the humors (*doṣa*); the humors are known as *vāta* and the others. Diseases are known as fever (*jvara*) and so forth; one should correctly observe them. (11) And by the instruction of authoritative persons (*āpta*).

Through direct observation—by looking at the patient and so forth—and by means of touch and inquiries regarding cold sensations and the like, the knowledge of diseases is considered to be threefold: through sight, touch, and questioning. (12–13) A curable disease is said to be of two types: that which is difficult to treat and that which is easily treated. The incurable should be known as being of two types: the difficult and the most difficult. (14) Some diseases are incurable by their very nature, while some curable ones become incurable through neglect; yet other diseases are curable by their inherent nature.

Neglected curable diseases turn into palliable ones, and palliable ones likewise turn into incurable ones; moreover, curable diseases take away the lives of men who fail to treat them (verse 16). A disease that arises upon an existing disease is called a complication (*upadrava*); those with complications do not survive, while those without complications do survive (verse 17). Therefore, even a minor disease, once diagnosed by a physician, must be carefully considered and never neglected, for such a group of diseases may indeed become incurable.

Even a very small enemy is like poison or fire; having gained strength, he does not reach a state of pacification in due time. An enemy, having obtained the strength of his position, exerts his prowess; likewise, a disease, having reached another element (dhatu), exerts its prowess. O knower of the rules, even if it has been brought to a state of subsidence through various kinds of treatment, the root of a disease, however slight, must certainly not be maintained.

Even if a disease is countered by many wholesome remedies, it will not be properly pacified by strength alone if it is merely in its infancy. Just as a small amount of potent poison, a tiny serpent, or a very slight fire [is dangerous], so too is even a subtle enemy in the form of disease. As long as a malady remains established in a location and produces a disorder, its remedy must consist of removing it from that location, especially when it is powerful. Some diseases are born of past actions (*karmaja*), others arise from the humors (*doṣaja*), and others are said to be innate (*sahaja*).

Diseases are considered to be of three types: those which do not subside despite many treatments are designated as the terrible diseases born of karma; those born of the *doṣas* include wind, bile, and so forth; and those born together [with birth] include hunger, thirst, and the like. Therefore, I shall first describe fever—the incomparable malady—affecting horses, elephants, humans, domestic animals, deer, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, and other such creatures.

This fever, which snatches away the life-force of creepers, medicinal herbs, mountains, serpents, birds, and mice, is indeed declared to be difficult to ward off in this world. (26) This incurable disease of fever is most difficult to overcome for cows, buffaloes, horses, and elephants; for humans it is somewhat more arduous, while for others it is a destroyer of life. (27) Just as a powerful hunter prevails over deer, so too is this powerful fever among diseases; no other being on earth—be they gods or others—is able to withstand it, except for human beings. (28) One acquires [this] through one's own karma.

Since a human being attains divinity in heaven, and having fallen from there, even exists again in the human state; therefore, as a human, he endures the fever arising from that divine condition, while all other classes of beings perish when afflicted by fever. This fever is the king of diseases, just as the lord of beasts is among animals; like fire in its burning nature, this disease of fever is most intense. Born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath, it torments all living beings; it is a plague for serpents and a scorching heat for horses.

The fever known as Gavāmīśvara is considered to afflict human beings; Dāridra affects buffaloes, and Mṛgaroga affects deer. That called Pralāpa afflicts goats and sheep, while Alasa occurs in camels. Alarka is declared to affect dogs, and Indramata is considered to affect fish. Abhighāta affects birds, and the one named Aikṣita affects serpents. Nīlikā generally affects water, and that known as Ūṣara affects the earth. Koṭarākṣa is the fever of trees; indeed, this fever is seen everywhere. He has three feet, ashes for weapons, and three heads.

With a very large belly, clothed in a tiger skin, his body radiant and tawny, with reddish-brown eyes, long arms, and shanks like those of a horse—this powerful man, who is known as Jvara, has appeared for the destruction of the world. Just as fire, having consumed its fuel, or poison, having destroyed the bodily constituents (dhātus), attains peace once its purpose is fulfilled, so too does Jvara attain peace after destroying the body. Therefore, O son, listen as I describe his origin, by which this most terrible being was born fourfold and then became eightfold.

When Maheśvara became enraged at Dakṣa, he, distressed by the loss of his beloved, released a fierce breath; from that, fever arises in eight ways according to its eightfold origin. (40) Due to the presence of wind, bile, phlegm, and blood; through indulgence in food and drink according to one's whim; and due to the reversal of the seasons, the humors (doṣas), having reached the seat of the waste products and moved outside the digestive fire, cause the fall of the fire residing in the blood. (41) Therefore, they indeed receive the name "fever" (jvara).

It is established that fever arises from physical exertion, anger, eating, and so forth, due to the occurrence of cold [in the body]. (42) Specifically, it is produced by incompatible foods, by drinking water from mountain torrents, or by being content with well-water, and by the rays of the hot, fierce-rayed sun. (43) Through the assault of the bodily humors (*doṣas*) and by the influence of curses, a most terrible disease called fever (*jvara*) arises intensely in human beings. (44) Fatigue, dullness, watering of the eyes, horripilation, a rattling sound in the throat, yawning, discoloration, aversion to food, and dryness of the mouth are the manifest characteristics of fever.

45. In the case of *samīraṇa* (Vāta), yawning occurs; from *kapha*, dejection and sinking; from *pitta*, burning of the eyes; indeed, all [these symptoms] occur in the *sānnipātika* (combined) type. Therefore, I shall describe the remedy by which well-being may be attained. 46. One should drink at night a decoction of *vacā*, *yavānī*, *dhanikā*, and *viśvā*, warmed thus. This would be for the happiness of a person suffering from Vāta-type fever, from Vāta diseases, or from fevers that produce [the combined symptoms]. 47. A decoction of *niśā*, *nimba*, *mṛtavallikā*, *dhānya*, and *viśvā*, mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be taken at night along with milk and *kola*.

This drink is for the digestion of fever associated with pitta (48). A decoction of vacā, yavānī, triphalā, and viśvā, taken at night, serves as a digestive for a person suffering from fever caused by kapha, as well as for disorders involving the humors (doṣas), colic, coryza, and catarrh (49). A decoction of śaṭhī, vacā, nāgara, kāphala, vatsādanī, and dhanvayavāsaka is beneficial for fever arising from all [three] humors; it acts as a digestive for a person with the three doṣas (50). For the wise, massaging the limbs with a large quantity of lukewarm water at night is wholesome.

Avoidance of sleep and physical exercise [is advised]. Trembling, irregular paroxysms, emaciation, a bad taste in the throat, palate, and mouth, dryness of the body, distension of the abdomen and bowels, yawning, headache, insomnia, blackness of the nails, delirium, and severe breaking pain in the limbs—by these signs, a fever caused by Vāta is recognized; it makes a man feel loathsome and he sleeps as if terrified even while awake. Nāgara, Surataru, Dhānyaka, Kuṇḍalī, and the two types of Bṛhatī are recommended at night during the seventh day of the fever.

Indeed, when the medicine has reached the eighth part [of its digestion], it becomes possessed of eightfold power (54). If the medicine is superior in potency and not deficient in food, it will undoubtedly and swiftly destroy that disease. However, if it is drunk by children, the elderly, women, or those of delicate constitution, it quickly leads to extreme exhaustion and loss of strength (55). Lightness of the senses, clarity of the eyes and face, belching, and heat in the digestive tract are the signs of digested medicine (56). But for one in whom fatigue, nausea, lassitude, headache, vertigo, and excessive secretions arise—

One should recognize the signs of the medicine’s upward movement (utkrāma): burning sensations, lassitude of the limbs, fainting, headache, exhaustion, dejection, vertigo, and a specific form of intense sexual desire. Therefore, when only a remnant of the medicine remains, there is never a pacification of the *doṣas*; rather, the *doṣas* become provoked in many ways. Hence, no medicine should be administered without a digestive agent (*pācana*). [The medicine] undergoes rapid digestion, does not destroy strength when covered by food, and does not repeatedly emerge from the mouth; this very same great medicine should be given to the elderly, children, the timid, and excellent women.

A decoction (kaṣāya) prepared by boiling one *kumbha* each of *bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śukanāsa*, *kapāṭalī*, and *kumbhārikā* cleanses the teeth, subdues wind (*samīra*), and quickly destroys wind-born fever (*marutajvara*) in men. (61) *Kirāta*, *musta*, *mṛtavallī*, *kraṇāsa*, *vit* (vidanga), *gokaṇṭaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *udīcya*, and *tiktā*—these [are used for the same purpose].

A decoction of *śāliparṇī* and *kalaśī* boiled together completely quickly destroys fever born of wind (*samīraṇa*). (62) A decoction of *guḍūcī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *plakṣī*, *rāsnā*, *punarnavā*, and *trāyamāṇaka*, taken with jaggery, removes fever caused by wind.
