(63) Fainting, burning sensation, vertigo, intoxication, thirst, forceful diarrhea, drowsiness, laziness, prostration, vomiting, and inflammation with heat in the mouth;

Perspiration, labored breathing, a bitter taste, exhaustion, or hunger—by these signs, fever of the Pitta type indeed arises in a person. (64) For digestive treatments, one should use Rodhra, Utpala, Amṛtalatā, and Kamala, combined with sugar and Sārivā.

Decoctions [of these herbs] quickly destroy pitta and bring about the pacification of pitta-fever in men. (65) A decoction of *indravāruṇī* together with *kaṭurohiṇī*, boiled with rice-water and mixed with *yaṣṭīmadhu*, is a destroyer of pitta-fevers. (66) A decoction of *durālabhā*, *vāsaka*, *parpaṭa*, *priyaṅgu*, *nimba*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and *kirātatikta*, prepared as a medicinal extract (*kaṣāya*) and enriched with sugar, is a digestive (*pācana*) agent that quickly destroys pitta-fever accompanied by burning sensations, thirst, and vertigo. (67)

Even a single *parpaṭaka* leaf is indeed excellent and suitable for pacifying bile-fevers (*pittajvara*); therefore, when enriched with ginger and *vālaka*, it is like a lion springing upon its prey. (68–69) A decoction of ginger, *uśīra*, *mustā*, sandalwood, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and coriander destroys bile-fever. (70) A decoction of *amṛtā*, *parpaṭa*, and *dhātrī* removes bile-fever. (71) [One should use] grapes, *parpaṭaka*, *tiktā*, *pathyā*, *āragvadha*, and *mustaka*.

A decoction [of these] cures fever caused by pitta that is accompanied by thirst, giddiness, and burning sensations. (72) An application of a paste made from vidārī, rodhra, kapittha, mātuluṅga, and pomegranates—prepared according to their availability—and applied to the palate, destroys burning sensations, thirst, and fainting. (73) Alternatively, one may alleviate burning sensations by placing a stream of cold water on the navel of a person who is lying flat on his back, either in a bronze vessel or a copper bowl. (74) Furthermore, the embrace of a beautiful woman bent by the weight of her breasts, the drinking of grapes through the company of a beloved, and the use of cooling treatments are said to be beneficial.

A white lotus, cool garments sprinkled with sandalwood water, a pearl necklace, and pure snow are for the commencement of the night of the moonlight (kaumudī). By these, one quickly destroys the bile of human beings, as well as burning heat, emaciation, exhaustion, thirst, vertigo, and fainting.

Through these applications, there is complete pacification of the burning sensation caused by *pitta*, and thus the glorious ones should constantly perform these treatments. (76) If a person suffers from dryness of the tongue, throat, and palate, the filaments of the *mātuluṅga* (citron), combined with honey and rock salt, should be ground and applied as a paste to the palate; this immediately removes *pitta*-fever. (77) Stiffness, sweetness in the mouth, numbness, excessive drowsiness, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, horripilation, coldness, and perspiration [are the symptoms].

It causes obstruction of hearing, paleness of the eyes, and a pale complexion; they know these symptoms—stiffness, suppression of excretions, and vomiting—as occurring in Kaphaja fever (78). A paste of Pippalādi drugs is beneficial as a digestive (pācana) remedy for fever born of Kapha (79). Likewise, Vyāghrī, Siṃhī, Rodhra, Kuṣṭha, and Paṭola constitute an excellent digestive remedy for fever arising from Kapha (80). A decoction of Vāsā, Guḍūcī, Triphalā, Paṭolī, Śaṭhī, Tiktā, and Madhuyaṣṭī properly alleviates fever when there is an abundance of Kapha-related ailments.

It quickly destroys [fevers] born of *kapha*. (81) *Āmalakī*, *abhayā*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *ṣaḍgranthā*—these three groups of three [drugs] are purgative, destroyers of *kapha*, alleviators of fever, and digestive stimulants. (82) A decoction of *pippalī*, *śṛṅgavera*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, and the fruit of *vatsaka*, mixed with a profusion of honey, is a destroyer of *śleṣma*-type fever. (83) One should lick *pippalī* powder with honey; it removes *śleṣma*-type fever, destroys splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, and poison, and subdues cough, dyspnea, and indigestion. (84) [It also cures] thirst, fainting, vomiting, and a bitter taste in the mouth.

If there is roughness, internal burning in the body, redness of the eyes, dryness of the throat, loss of sleep, pain and splitting in the head and chest, breaking pain in the limbs, horripilation, and fainting (tamaka), it would be Vātapitta fever. (85) In a fever caused by combined doṣas, a proper digestive treatment (vipācana) should be administered; in Pitta-fever accompanied by Vāta, one should drink a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) combined with śālmalī, or a decoction of rāsnā and kirātatiktaka. (86) A paste (kalka) consisting of the two pañcamūlis along with ginger (nāgara), guḍūcī, bhūnimba, and ghanasāra is highly recommended.

Sugar-candy mixed with *marutsu* (grapes) is a cause for the destruction of fever caused by *pitta* and *vāta*. (87) A decoction of *kirātatikta*, *āmalakī*, *śaṭhī*, *drākṣā*, *uṣaṇa*, *nāgaraka*, and *amṛtā*, well-cooled and combined with sugar-candy, is a cause for the destruction of fever caused by *pitta* and *vāta*. (88) A decoction of *amṛta*, *mustaka*, *vāsā*, *parpaṭa*, and *viśvā* drunk with water, as well as *bhadramuñja*, destroys fever caused by *pitta* and *marut* (vāta). (89) In this [fever], when accompanied by *vāta*, there is drowsiness, heaviness, pain in the joints and head, distress, and a breaking sensation in the limbs; furthermore, the eyes possess a moderate intensity [of symptoms].

In cases of fever with *śleṣman* (phlegm), there is a burning sensation, labored breathing, loss of appetite, a dry obstruction in the ears and throat, as well as drowsiness, delusion, anorexia, and vertigo. Now, for *pittale* (bilious) fever associated with *śleṣman*, [the following is prescribed]: 90. A decoction of *nāgara*, *bhadramustā*, or *guḍūcī* and *āmalaka*, or of *pāṭhā*, *mṛṇāla*, and *udīcya*, serves in *pitta*-type fever with *kapha*. 91–92. It is digestive, appetizing, and a preventer of blood-drying. A decoction of *drākṣā*, *amṛtā*, *vāsaka*, *ariṣṭaka*, *bhūnimba*, *tikta*, *indrayava*, *paṭola*, *mustā*, and *bhārgī* [is also used].

For the destruction of fever caused by pitta and kapha: one should prepare a decoction of *guḍūcī*, neem leaves (*nimba-patra*), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), nut-grass (*mustā*), coriander (*kustumburu*), and sandalwood (*candana*). This "Guḍūcī-ādi" preparation destroys fevers of kapha, pitta, and vāta. It destroys all types of fever, as well as nausea and other symptoms, anorexia, coryza, thirst, emaciation, and burning sensations. A person suffering from pitta and kapha should drink the decoction prepared from *guḍūcī*, neem, *cakravāka*, *śaṭhī*, *kirātatiktaka*, long pepper (*magadhā*), *aṣṭahalyā*, and *dārvī* along with *paṭola*.

In fever (jvara), *paṭolī*, *candana*, *tiktā*, *mūrvā*, *pāṭhā*, and the group of *amṛtā* [96] ward off fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*, as well as vomiting, burning sensations, and itching. The decoction prepared from the roots of *paṭola*, *vāsā*, and *picumanda*, along with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and *ghanā*, is recommended for fever arising from *kapha* and *pitta* [97]. Likewise, the *paṭola-dhānyāśritaka* [decoction] is an appetizer (*sandīpana*), beneficial for fevers of the *pitta-kapha* type as well as those arising from *pitta* and blood (*asṛj*), and it acts as a purgative for the impurities (*malānām pratibhedanaḥ*) [98-99]. It is cooling.

Trembling, breaking pain in the joints, shivering in the limbs, numbness, dullness of heat, loss of appetite, constipation, roughness of the skin, cough, darkness before the eyes, colic, drowsiness, moaning, self-indulgence, or else a sense of stiffness, yawning, loss of relish for food, perspiration, and obstruction of feces and urine—these are the symptoms of fever caused by *kapha* and *vāta*. (100) *Āragvadha*, *tiktakarohiṇī*, *harītakī*, *pippalīmūla*, and *mustā*: this paste, prepared as a decoction, is beneficial for fever associated with *kapha* and *vāta* when accompanied by colic; it is a digestive stimulant. (101) *Kṣudrā* and *guḍūcī* together... [The text ends here.]

A decoction of nagara, vāsā, parpaṭaka, pathyā, mustā, and duḥsparśā is beneficial when drunk for fever caused by vāta and kapha. (102) A decoction of parpaṭa, nāgāhvaya, vacā, tantuka, kaṭphala, elā, abhayā, viśva, and bhūtikā, combined with hiṅgu and honey, is indeed indicated for kapha-vāta disorders accompanied by hiccups, as well as throat obstruction. (103) A decoction of the two sets of five roots (dvipañcamūla), impregnated with the powder of kaṇā, should be administered for pain arising from vāta and kapha, as well as for fever, dyspnea, and coryza. (104) Drowsiness, lassitude, and sweetness in the mouth [are the symptoms].

Spitting, dryness of the throat, loss of sleep, labored breathing, fainting, and anxiety; stiffness of the tongue, or else pain in the back and head, or an internal burning sensation—if these occur, know it to be the disorder of the three *doṣas*. Having seen this terrible fever born of the three *doṣas*, which is life-threatening, one should therefore first proclaim the drying of this *kapha*. One should not perform the pacification of *pitta* if one desires one's own reputation, for [that treatment] would immediately kill a strong person due to the presence of *kapha* and *vāta*.

For one suffering from pain caused by the three *doṣas*, fasting (*laṅghana*), or self-restraint (*damana*), or spitting (*ṣṭhīvana*) should be practiced for three nights, five nights, or even seven nights (107). Fasting is prescribed after having ascertained the relative strength and weakness of the *doṣas* (108). Once the *kapha* is known to have been dried up, then measures to subdue the *vāta* should be taken. After recognizing the provocation of *pitta*, one should perform treatments to pacify it; however, while the *vāta* and *kapha* are to be dried up, one must not destroy the *pitta* (109–110). Thirst, piercing pain, emaciation, labored breathing, and sleeplessness at night [are the signs].

During the day, there occurs drowsiness, delusion, and dryness of the mouth, nose, tongue, and lips; one spits out what has been cooked [in the mouth], becomes emaciated in body, and circular spots appear on the skin. There is darkening of the eyes, lips, and face, along with intoxication, perspiration, flatulence, and wasting. There may be loss of appetite, vertigo, or likewise a churning sensation in the head, headache, obstruction of the channels, vomiting, or the throat being constricted by a rattling sound and piercing pain. (111)

Driven by these symptoms, this disease known as *sannipāta* arises among men; it is a fever that acts swiftly, causing extreme suffering for horses or elephants. (112) In a *sannipāta* fever, one should first apply treatments that alleviate *vāta* and *kapha*; afterwards, when the *śleṣman* has been diminished and the *āmadoṣa* is gone, one should treat the *pitta* and *māruta*. (113) Having exerted effort in treating a *sannipāta* fever, one must conquer excessive drowsiness (*tandrā*), which is the most difficult complication among all fevers, especially so. (114) He who causes wholesome treatment to be administered to patients whose bodies are filled with *kapha*... [is successful].

This [remedy] would be an enemy to him, neither wholesome nor medicinal. (115) Śaṭhī, the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūlaka), durālabhā, koṭaja, paṭola, pauṣkara, along with bhārgavī and pippalī—this ten-ingredient formulation (daśāṅga) destroys fever caused by the combination of all three doṣas (sānnipātika-jvara) and loss of digestive fire. (116–117) A decoction of bhūnimba, dāru, the ten roots (daśamūla), mahauṣadha, abdatikta, indrabīja, dhanika, bhadrakaṇṭaka, and kaṇā quickly destroys fever accompanied by drowsiness, delirium, vertigo, thirst, anorexia, burning sensations, delusion, dyspnea, and weak digestion. (118)

A paste made from equal parts of *śaṇṭhī*, *ghana*, *agaja*, *kaṇā*, *suradāru*, *dhānyāka*, *tikta*, *kaliṅga*, and *daśamūla* is excellent for destroying fevers born of the three *doṣas*, and it cures dyspnea, vertigo, anorexia, constipation, and heart disease. (119) *Mustā*, *uśīra*, *niśā*, *viśāla*, *madhuka*, *pāṭhā*, *balā*, *rohiṇī*, *nīlī*, *dhanvayavāsa*, *kaṭvarā*, *śaṭhī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *samaṅgā*, and *vivṛt*...

A decoction made from yaṣṭī, pippalīmūla, parpaṭa, phalā, pippalyaka, dāru, śyāmā, hemaguḍūcī, and equal parts of payas is known as *jvarānta*. (120) The two types of *bṛhatī*, *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, *kirāta*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *paṭola*, *pauṣkara*, *bhārṅgī*, *vatsaka*, and *durālabhā* constitute the *bṛhatyādika-pācana*. It destroys complications such as cough and quickly overcomes *jvara-sannipāta*; it is highly recommended for alleviating pain, distress, and drowsiness. (121–122) [Also included are: *śaṭhī*, *kirāta*, *kaṭukā*, and *viśālā*.

Guḍūcī, bhṛṅgī, the two types of bṛhatī, mahauṣadha (ginger), pauṣkara, dhanvayāsa, rāsnā, surāhvā, and gajapippalī—these fourteen, beginning with śaṭhī, are excellent when drunk as a decoction for men; they quickly destroy drowsiness, labored breathing, headache, lethargy, and fever accompanied by pain. Likewise, a decoction made from bhūnimba, suradāru, nāgara, ghana, tiktā, kaliṅga, and hastikaṇā, combined with groups of ten and five [herbs], is beneficial.

When drunk, it causes the destruction of all diseases; it kills *sannipāta* fever, and it quickly destroys asthma, wasting, pain in the chest, and drowsiness. (125) A decoction made from equal parts of *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, *ghan* (*mustā*), *parpaṭaka*, *paṭolī*, *bhūnimba*, *vatsaka*, *śaṭhī*, *nāgara*, *tiktā*, *surāhvā*, *gajapippalī*, *māgadhikā*, *yavāsa*, *vāsā*, *balā*, and *gajabalā*—this decoction destroys diseases arising from *marut* (Vāta), as well as asthma, cough, abdominal pain, and cholera. It is the best for men on this earth. (126)

In diseases characterized by digestive disorders or the combination of humors (sannipāta), or those arising from phlegm and wind (kapha-vāta), a decoction of rāsnā, trikaṇṭaka, śatamūlī, bhārgī, puṣkara, ghana, devadāru, and dhānyaka should be administered; this is beneficial for all fevers born of wind and is especially effective for those arising from sannipāta that are extremely severe. A decoction of trivṛt, viśālā, surāhva, āragvadha, and tiktakarohiṇī acts as a purgative for the impurities and destroys the fear of wind-pain (vāta-śūla). [Also] vacā and yavānī.

They say that a powder made from dried *mahauṣadha* is excellent for anointing the body; it certainly brings about the subsiding of the heat of fever through massage. (130) A powder consisting of *māgadhī*, *suradāru*, *viśvaka*, *tiktā*, and *dīpyaka* is also highly recommended for anointing the body; it wards off perspiration from the body, and one will surely become cool-bodied immediately. (131) The essence of *madhūka* mixed with *mahauṣadha*, *vacā*, *uṣaṇā*, and *saindhava*, ground with either urine or warm water—

To awaken lost consciousness, the juice of the root of *śobhāñjanaka* (black mustard) combined with black pepper should be used as a nasal drop (*nasya*) for patients who have become unresponsive; it brings about rapid awakening. A powder consisting of one part each of *bṛhatī* fruit, long pepper (*pippalī*), and dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) is highly recommended; when blown into the nostrils, this "awakening sneeze" restores consciousness and movement. *Śirīṣa* seeds, black pepper, and *upakulyā*, rubbed together with cow's urine and rock salt (*saindhava*), serve as an eye-salve (*añjana*) for the eyes of men.

Awakening restores consciousness to one who has lost it. (135) A wick made of *trikaṭu*, *karañja* seeds, *triphalā*, *suradāru*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *tulasī*, used as an ointment for the eyes, destroys drowsiness. (136) Having prepared a mixture of *kesara*, *mātuluṅga*, *śṛṅgavera*, and *saindhava* combined with *trikaṭu*, one should wear it in the mouth up to the throat. (137) The wise man should rub the teeth, tongue, mouth, and palate; he should spit out everything according to the prescribed rule, doing so repeatedly. (138)

By this, there shall be purification of the throat, and it draws away phlegm; by making the tongue sharp and creating an appetite, asthma and labored breathing are pacified. (139) A powder of *kaṭuka*, *cavya*, and *kāpathyā* combined with rock salt (*saindhava*) should be used to rub the teeth as well as the tongue and the impurities of the palate. (140) This spitting [of the powder] purifies the throat, creates an appetite, and destroys phlegm; nausea comes to an end, and it produces great sharpness [of the senses]. (141) If, however, the body is cold, then sudation (*sveda*) is prescribed; thirteen types of sudation are to be known.

The means for preventing sweating are: *saṅkara*, *prastuta*, *nāḍīpariṣeka*, *apagāhana*, *ātaṅka*, *asmyana*, *karṣa*, *kūṭī*, *bhūkumbhī*, *kūpa*, and *holāka*; these thirteen methods induce perspiration. (142–144) One should administer *kālasveda*, *ghaṭīsveda*, or *vālukāsveda* to the patient’s hands, feet, and head. If there is still no relief through this, one should cauterize with an iron rod. If there is no cooling sensation when the feet are cauterized, one should cauterize the base of the big toes. (145)

Whether at the wrist, the heart, or likewise the head; or if on the forehead of a man afflicted by cold there is perspiration or a cold clamminess that does not reach his chest but remains stuck in the throat, he will surely go to the house of Death. In seven days, ten days, or again in twelve days, or in thirteen or fifteen days, this fever either subsides or kills. Furthermore, in fifteen days, this most terrible *sannipāta* fever, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālāgni*), either kills or protects the man.

O best of physicians, this is the limit regarding the three *doṣas* for both liberation and destruction, concerning the *sannipāta* disorder of this man. (150) If one were to sprinkle a person suffering from internal burning in a *sannipāta* with cold water, how could that patient possibly survive, and how could that physician be worthy of honor? (151) What indeed has not been accomplished by that physician who rescues a man fallen into the ocean of *sannipāta*?

What physician on the surface of the earth would not receive honor if he were endowed with righteousness, fame, and discipline? (152) Furthermore, fever arising from the three humors—wind, bile, and phlegm—and that which is produced by the combination of these three (*tridoṣaja*), as well as that associated with blood, is called *sānnipātika* (arising from the union of all humors). (153) Know indeed that there is no *sānnipātika* fever without blood; through digestive decoctions, the humors reach pacification in a human being. (154) Therefore, when the humors have been pacified, the blood does not dissolve; by that very [blood], swelling (*śopha*) is produced.

If a severe [inflammation] occurs at the root of the ear (155), one should therefore apply a remedy consisting of bloodletting by means of leeches, a gourd, or *bhṛṅga*. Furthermore, an ointment is beneficial; the roots of *bījapūraka* and likewise *agnimantha*—this ointment destroys the [disease] at the root of the ear (156–157). Having ground together house-soot, *rajanī*, *sumana*, *mahauṣadha*, *siddhārtha*, rock salt (*saindhava*), *vacā*, and milk, this ointment is recommended for destroying the blood [disorder] and pacifying swelling and ulcers in the ear of a person (158). When suppuration occurs...

In that case, a remedy should be applied: an ointment made from the bark of *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* promotes the healing of wounds. (159) An ointment consisting of the roots of *nimba* and *āragvadha* combined with *niśā* (turmeric) acts as a purifier for foul-smelling pus and promotes the healing of ulcers. (160) One should avoid sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, excessive water intake, cold water, staying awake at night, physical exercise, and likewise grief. (161) One should also avoid *māṣa* beans, barley, wheat, sesame, *parṇīka*, lentils (*masūra*), and *tripuṭā*, as well as oil.

One should avoid sexual intercourse for one month from afar, and abstain from overeating for half a month; by avoiding [stimulation] at the base of the ear, one attains well-being (163). Old *ṣaṣṭika* rice, or *bālya*, or *sūpa*, as well as *āḍhakī*, horse-gram, and mung-bean soup are recommended for food (164). One should abandon eggplant, onions, and bulbous vegetables; through this, one attains comfort and is quickly liberated from disease (165). When, at the end, the *pitta* remains externally along with *kapha* and *vāyu*...

Then there will be internal burning and dryness, while externally there is perspiration and coldness. (166) One should quickly have him drink a decoction of *amṛtā* and water mixed with honey and long pepper; he will surely be freed from that *sānnipātika* fever. (167) Alternatively, for the subsiding of internal burning, a decoction of *ativiṣā*, *vālaka*, *nāgara*, *ghana*, and *parpaṭa* mixed with sugar may be given. (168) When *pitta* resides on the outside and *kapha* and *vāyu* are at the end [internally], heat arises in the body and coldness arises at the extremities. (169) For that [condition], one should give a decoction of *śaṭī* and other such drugs.

One should administer a remedy that subdues *kapha*. (170) For one in whose upper body *vāta* and *kapha* are present, while *pitta* moves downward, half of the body becomes cold and half becomes hot. (171) For such a person, one should administer a decoction of the *rāsnā* group and likewise a warm [remedy]. (172) For one in whom *rakta-pitta* is in the upper part and both *vāta* and *kapha* are in the middle, heat arises in the upper part and cold arises below. (173) The best of physicians should administer a decoction of the *nāgara* group for him. (174) Furthermore, for one in whom heat is observed...

When the fever arises with a mild onset, one should recognize it as having an external impulse (*bāhyavega*); this fever is curable for one who understands [its nature]. (175) One should know that when heat, thirst, a burning sensation, and headache arise at the end [of the onset], it has a deep impulse (*gambhīravega*); it is difficult to cure even for men. (176) For such a person, one should provide treatment using the eighteen-fold formulation (*yoga*) for men. (177) When *pitta* remains at the end in the body while both *vāta* and *kapha* are present, there is coldness of the body and heat in the hands and feet. (178) For that condition, a decoction of the *rāsnā* group, combined with *pippalī*, should be administered.

179. When *pitta* resides in the body while both *vāta* and *kapha* remain at its extremities, heat arises within the body and coldness occurs in the hands and feet. 180. For such a case, a decoction of grapes and similar fruits mixed with treacle (*guḍa*) should be administered. 181. Wherever there is coldness, sudation (*sveda*) is prescribed; however, the knower [of medicine] should not perform sudation when the fever is excessively hot. 182. By means of *kapha* and *pitta*, the *vāyu* (wind) always becomes motionless; from that very *vāyu*, diseases such as fever and others arise. 183. Dizziness (*bhrama*).

Coolness, a sense of being overwhelmed, trembling, diarrhea, exhaustion, fatigue, perspiration, and delirious talk occur during the release from fever (jvaramokṣa). Furthermore, perspiration, itching, and the swelling of the vessels, as well as sneezing in the face, lightness, a desire for food, and the fullness of the senses—when a person is free from fatigue and pain, these indicate recovery. However, even in one who is released, heaviness of the head does not truly leave; one should recognize that the fever has not been fully liberated, for it will return to him. This is so if the fever residing in the bodily tissues (dhātu) has indeed entered the body.

One should recognize irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*); it is known to be of four types: the quotidian (*ekāhika*), the tertian (*dvyāhika*), the quartan (*tryāhika*), and the wise physician should also recognize the fourth as the *velājvara*. (187–188) In the first case, cold occurs first and heat arises afterwards; this is declared curable in a human being and is quickly cured by medicines. (189) In the latter case, one experiences burning heat first and the fever becomes severe; that fever, which causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-kṣaya*), is not quickly relieved. (190) [The pain] is in the three corners and the hips.

There may be pain from *vāta* and *pitta*, or *pitta* [pain] in the head, vertigo, and pain in the back caused by thin *kapha*; that is the threefold characteristic of *tṛtīyaka* (tertian) fever. (191) From *kapha* and *pitta*, it seizes the *trika* (the sacral region); from *vāta* and *kapha*, it arises in the back; and from *vāta* and *pitta*, it seizes the head—thus *tṛtīyaka* fever is of three types. (192) The fourth type of fever (*caturtha*) should be known as twofold, consisting of *vāta* and *kapha*. That arising from *kapha* is known to be in the calves, while that originating from *vāta* is in the head. (193) Having understood this, the excellent physician should act accordingly therein.

The remedy for *velājvara* [is as follows]: when it has reached the *rasa* (plasma), it is quotidian (*ekāhika*); likewise, when it reaches the *māṃsa* (flesh), it becomes tertian (*tṛtīyaka*); and when it resorts to the *asthi* (bones), it is quartan (*caturtha*). When it has pervaded all the *dhātus*, it is known as chronic (*jīrṇa*) and causes the depletion of the tissues. (194–195) In the case of fever born of the elements (*bhūtaja*), there should be the science of spirits (*bhūtavidyā*); one should employ pacification and striking. For one whose fever arises from a curse (*abhiśāpa*), the remedy is propitiation (*śānti*). (196) In fever born of desire (*kāmajvara*), one should remove the bile (*pitta*) associated with jaundice (*kāmalā*); breathing exercises (*śvasana*) are beneficial. (197) In fever born of anger (*krodhajvara*) or even that born of bile (*pittajvara*), one should pacify it with wholesome words and medicinal herbs (*auṣadhi*). (198)

One should induce a state of intoxication with fragrant substances; such use is beneficial. (198) One should drink a decoction of *nidigdhikā*, *nāgarika*, and *amṛtā* mixed with *pippalī* in cases of chronic fever, loss of appetite, cough, colic, dyspnea, weak digestion, facial paralysis, and catarrh. (199) In cases of cough, indigestion, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, weak digestion, jaundice, and loss of appetite, *pippalī* is recommended for these; when taken with jaggery, it quickly destroys chronic fever in men. (200) A decoction of the light *pañcamūlī* along with *pippalī* and *chinnodbhavā* [is also beneficial].

This [decoction] destroys chronic fever, dyspnea, and diseases caused by *kapha*, as well as weak digestion, colic, anorexia, and catarrh (201). A decoction of *paṭola*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), *vatsaka*, *nimba*, *mokṣa*, *drākṣā*, *amṛtā*, *candana*, and *nāgara* serves to destroy long-standing fevers (202). One should eat jīraka with jaggery, or *harītakī* with jaggery, or sesame seeds with jaggery, in the case of irregular (*viṣama*) fever (203). Or one should consume ginger with jaggery, or a decoction of *triphalā* with jaggery; this decoction also [cures] irregular fevers.

The destroyer of [fever] 204: A decoction prepared with *vāsā*, *āmalaka* (dhātrī), *dāruharidrā*, *pathyā*, and *nāgara*, combined with honey, wards off quartan fever (*cāturthika*). 205: The fresh juice of *agasti* leaves, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), destroys the violent quartan disease; it also eliminates cough, vertigo, and headache, and this nasal therapy is beneficial for men. 206: He who, afflicted by irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*), daily consumes a paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil, is liberated from those irregular fevers.

And by means of extremely terrible wind-related ailments (207), [one is protected]. A fumigation consisting of one *pala* of neem leaves, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, jaggery, *guggulu*, mustard seeds, and *harītakī* combined with clarified butter, is indeed the destroyer of irregular fevers (208). When the root of *surasā* is tied to the hand on an auspicious day, it destroys fevers occurring at specific times (*velājvara*) and so forth, acting as a warder-off of fever caused by spirits (209). Furthermore, a decoction of *mustā*, *amṛtā*, *āmalakī*, *nāgara*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*, combined with the powder of *kaṇā* and honey, [cures] the quotidian fever (*ekāhika*) or... (210) [and other types].

It dispels fever that has arisen beginning with the *velā* period. Having removed the seeds of *rasona* (garlic), having cut them into pieces and placed them in buttermilk during the nights, and consuming them at dawn combined with ghee, it destroys fevers such as those starting with *velā* that have entered the bodily tissues (*dhātu*). One should drink milk in the manner of the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). [One may also take] great medicine (*mahauṣadha*), ginger (*nāgara*), coriander (*dhānya*), sandalwood powder (*candanavāluka*), and *guḍūcī* with milk; this cures tertian fever (*tṛtīyakajvara*). Alternatively, one may take the root of *apāmārga* or the root of *nīlī*.

By tying a red thread, reaching up to the crown of the head, around the left ear and the waist, one destroys tertian fever (216). The divine face of the Lord of Monkeys, possessing the splendor of the rising sun—at that very moment, even a terrible quotidian fever perishes (217). Having drawn the form of a monkey with chalk, listen further: the best of physicians worship it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and incense (218). *Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, to Sugrīva, who possesses great strength and prowess, the son of the Sun, of immeasurable splendor.*

Daha daha! Paca paca! Avata avata! O King of Monkeys, bind, bind the fevers—those of one day, two days, three days, four days, the great fever, the fever of spirits, the fever of wrath, the fever of time, and so forth! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā! There is no fever.

The fever that is capable of removing other fevers is itself terrified [by this]. Furthermore, I shall here describe the forms and characteristics of the fevers: One who has the luster of molten gold, whose radiance is equal to fire, who wears a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) that seems to fly upward, and who is fierce in the form of a Brāhmaṇa; One who resembles a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), possessed of fierce fangs, holding a sword in hand, and being exceedingly fierce—this is considered the Kṣatriya fever belonging to Mahendra; One who has the appearance of five-fold offspring, adorned with molten gold, holding a staff in hand, and possessing moderate speed—this is the Vaiśya fever.

Jvareśvara is considered [the presiding deity]. (223) He has the appearance of a black cloud or collyrium, with sharp fangs and a blazing face; he is three-eyed, possesses the radiance of fire, and is regarded as the Śūdra Kāla. (224) He is characterized by sharp onset and is possessed by hunger; he is pure, yet hateful, and fond of vows. His urine is the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers; he is habituated to recitation and is excessively talkative. (225) He suffers from much labored breathing and is overcome by thirst; he is afflicted by fierce Brahmins. By performing his ritual bath (*snāna*), recitation (*japa*), and fire-oblation (*homa*), peace is attained. (226) [He suffers from] acute fever, extreme thirst, and bloody urine.

He urinates frequently, speaks of war, and rises up afflicted by physical strength. His eyes are inflamed, he has heavy labored breathing, and likewise he is oppressed by hunger. There is a honey-like fragrance in his mouth, perspiration, and he is tormented by the *māhendraka* [demon] among the Kṣatriyas. For him, at the outset, one who is pure should perform oblations to the planets (*graha-homa*) and the praise of the deities; through such acts as giving gifts and reciting prayers (*japa*), union with success (*siddhi*) is attained. He has moderate force, a yellowish body, is prone to sleep, and likewise suffers from loss of appetite. He is chilled by cold winds, his heart is hot, there is perspiration on his throat, and he is extremely agitated. He passes urine in great quantities.

One who is devoted, silent, with yellowish inner eyes, not afflicted by excessive thirst, and affectionate—he should be known as the lord of fever (Jvareśvara). (231) In that case, for the sake of pacification, one should perform all rites such as the Svastyayana, hospitality, the worship of Brahmins and deities, recitation of mantras, and fire-offerings (homa). (232) One who suffers from heart-ache or diarrhea, whose body smells like fish, who is prone to madness, whose eyes are excessively full, whose senses are impaired during sexual acts, (233) who is fond of the road yet fearful, and who has no desire for food—even with a black vessel of time (Kālabhṛṅgāraka), there is no success with a Śūdra. (234)

One should perform bathing, charity, recitation, the ritual of worshiping the gods, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth; furthermore, by means of special offerings, one should bring about the satisfaction of all beings and manifold contentment. Through the gift of cows, land, gold, food, and drink according to the prescribed rites, peace shall arise for all, and the destruction of all diseases—this is what those of true vows proclaim. Just as poison, having gained momentum, dissolves within its seat and then becomes powerful again, provoking a severe reaction at the proper time, so too does the bodily humor (*doṣa*) act like poison. [The remedy is] the soup of *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice and grains.

Mudga, āḍhakī, and the previously mentioned vegetables are indeed pacifiers of vāta (237). Śatapuṣpā, jīvantī, taṇḍulīyaka, vāstuka, and bhājikā prepared with ghee—these leaf-vegetables as well as the meat of lāva, tittira, and other birds, along with vārttāka, should be administered to the patient; likewise, one should employ the meat of wild animals such as mṛga and chikkarika (238–239). Kośātakī, paṭola, and śuṇṭhīka are beneficial; however, one should avoid pulses, foods that cause burning sensations, heavy foods, and unctuous oils (240).

Likewise, the best of physicians should avoid sour things, as well as curd and whey in large quantities, and small, unwholesome foods (241). One should also avoid excessive water, betel leaf, ghee, or even liquor (242). Having abandoned anger and grief, one indeed always enjoys happiness; one should not keep a vigil at night and should avoid sleeping during the day (243). One should always strictly avoid riding in carts, on horses, elephants, or other vehicles; when the wise man—the repository of auspicious ordinances—is present, the patient suffering from fever quickly attains comfort (244).

One who has been freed from fever should not engage in physical exercise, sexual intercourse, eating, or staying awake at night; by doing so, one attains well-being. (245) Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fever," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 2.

The Third Chapter. Ātreya said: Now, my son, listen to the diagnosis and treatment of diarrhea (*atīsāra*), including the diarrhea born of fever (*jvara*) and its medicinal remedies. (1) Substances are considered to be of three types in the context of the regimen for health (*svasthavṛtti*): some are pacifiers of the humors (*doṣa*), some are corrupters of the tissues (*dhātu*), and some are intended for general maintenance. (2) That [regimen] consists of recourse to the path of the divine (*daiva-patha*), recourse to the path of rational application (*yukti-patha*), and the subjugation of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*). It includes mantras, medicines, gems, auspicious marks on the body, offerings, oblations, burnt sacrifices (*homa*), observances (*niyama*), expiations (*prāyaścitta*), fasts (*upavāsa*), rites for well-being (*svastyayana*), and meditative devotion (*praṇidhāna*).

The path of the gods (*daivapatha*) consists of [meditation on] light. The path of reasoning (*yuktipatha*) consists of the application of food, conduct, and medicinal substances. The conquest of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*) consists of restraining the mind from harmful objects. One should eat food that is unctuous, very cold, heavy, cool, and slimy; one should consume food that is spoiled, excessively irregular, or difficult to digest, even when suffering from indigestion, grief, poisons, or fears, or when afflicted by grief, pain, or corrupted breast milk—[provided these are] in their respective contrary states. Weakness caused by irregular eating is broken by water, which destroys the impurity of undigested matter (*ajīrṇa*).

Indeed, when the digestive fire (*agni*) is extinguished in a person, then diarrhea (*atisāra*) arises; having destroyed the digestive fire of the person, diarrhea then occurs. (5) That [diarrhea] further becomes copious with waste matter (*mala*); it is described by the sages who know the methods as being of five types. Briefly stated, for one whose pain is intense, its destruction occurs first through decoctions and other digestive (*pācanaka*) remedies. (6) When fever (*jvara*) and diarrhea arise simultaneously, that is the terrible "fever-diarrhea" (*jvarātisāra*), which is difficult to cure even for the wise. (7) Even that [diarrhea] does not occur without *pitta*.

Listen, my son: fasting is prescribed for him in cases of fever and diarrhea. (8) Suvarcala, ativiṣā, hiṅgu, pathyā, kaliṅgaka, and śuṇṭhī destroy diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āma), alleviate colic, and are astringent and digestive. (9) For the destruction of diarrhea caused by āma, a person should drink a decoction made from these: pathyā, dāru, vacā, mustā, nāgara, and ativiṣā. (10) One should grind together utpala, dhānyaka, śuṇṭhī, pṛśniparṇī, balā, and young bilva fruits with very hot cow’s buttermilk. (11) With that [mixture], one should prepare a scum (maṇḍa) made from parched grain (lāja).

This cooling decoction, which pacifies fever and diarrhea and bestows strength upon the digestive fire, should now be prepared and administered for the alleviation of fever and diarrhea. A decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *viṣā*, *taladharā*, *amṛtā*, *vatsaka*, *tiktāhvaya*, and *kanakaśītalaka* should always be given when properly prepared for the purpose of subduing fever and diarrhea. A decoction of *pāṭhā*, *indrabhū*, *nimba*, *ghana*, *amṛtā*, and *parpaṭa* is highly recommended here; it quickly conquers diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āma*), as well as severe diarrhea associated with fever or that which is innate. [Also included: *śuṇṭhī*, *bālaka*, and *mustā*.

Bilva, pāṭhā, and viṣā, along with grains, act as a digestive (pācana) remedy for loss of appetite; they destroy vomiting, fever, and diarrhea. (15) Vatsaka, suradāru, rohiṇī, grains, bilva, agnimantha, trikaṇṭaka, nimba seeds, gajapippalī, and vṛkī—this decoction is likewise a medicine for diarrhea. (16) Boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, bilva, guḍūcī, musta, and nāgara, along with pāṭhā, bhūnimba, hrīvera, kuṭaja bark, and its fruit—(17) This [decoction] cures all types of diarrhea, vomiting, asthma, fever, and facial paralysis, as well as complications such as colic.

And it destroys the terrible affliction of the Asuras (18). The five roots that are most common should be used in cases of Pitta; however, the great Pañcamūlī is beneficial for fever caused by Vāta and Kapha (19). Blue lotus, pomegranate bark, Keśara, honey, Padmaka, and Dhātrī, ground with rice-water, form a digestive decoction that cures fever and diarrhea (20). Uśīra, coriander, Musta, Bilva, Bālaka, Balā, and Dhātakī flowers—this decoction is highly praised for pacifying fever and diarrhea accompanied by blood and Pitta (21).

It destroys all types of swelling, provides relish, and acts as a digestive. 22. Aralu, when its resin is extracted by the *puṭapāka* method and taken with honey, pacifies long-standing diarrhea that is accompanied by blood and has become excessively severe. 23–24. One should always prepare a collection of these: Jambū, Vaṭa, Udumbara, Plakṣaka, Nāga, Prapauṇḍarika, Śamī, Gundra, Cūta, Ambuda, and Jīvikā. One should drink two *prasthas* of this until a specific portion of it is produced again in the cauldron. 24. (Note: This refers to the process of distillation or extraction where the liquid is returned to the vessel for further processing.)

It should be cooked until it forms a paste on a wooden ladle and reaches its own natural consistency; then, having certainly removed it from the heat, the best of physicians should administer it mixed with honey to cure diarrhea. (25–26) Likewise, Kākamācī has been highly praised by Hārīta and honored even by Ātreya after he had examined numerous treatises. (27) One should boil the bark of Jambū and the inner bark of Vatsaka in water until one-fourth remains; then, having removed it from the fire, one should strain it through a cloth and cook it again in a cauldron. (28)

The decoction of *samyagdārvī* with its paste, having been removed while still warm, should be mixed with honey and licked; this cures even severe diarrhea (29). In all types of diarrhea, there is constant obstruction in the flanks, the abdomen, the chest, the region of the navel, and the lower part of the body, as well as the suppression of flatus and the breaking up of the stool (30). Those who know the truth declare that in diarrhea caused by Vāta, the stool is frothy, slimy, dry, scanty, and passed with a single effort accompanied by undigested matter, sound, and pain; it is black, and there is twitching of the limbs (31). At the onset of that [diarrhea]...

In cases of mild [diarrhea], fasting is either prescribed alone or not at all; therefore, one should administer decoctions, as well as drinks and foods. (32) A paste of *udīcyadhānya* taken with water is beneficial for drinking; it cures diarrhea, removes thirst, destroys burning sensations, and serves to eliminate colic and hiccups. (33) This very same decoction drink, combined with the two types of *bālaka*, *moca*, *harītakī*, and *parpaṭa*, quickly brings about the destruction of diarrhea and the cessation of stool. (34) [The herbs] *śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*...

Bālāśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva, pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka (35)—this [mixture] is beneficial when combined with food for all those suffering from diarrhea. Having taken the bark of tinduka and wrapped it in the leaves of kāśmarī (36), the physician should coat it with clay and burn it according to the prescribed method over a gentle fire; having extracted the juice and mixed it with honey, this drink destroys all types of diarrhea. Then, having crushed one *tulā* of fresh *girimallikā*, one should add one *karṣa* [of other ingredients]; once that is purified, one should add one *pala* of ground *śālmalī* (38).

Having added pāṭhā, samaṅgā, ativiṣā, mustā, bilva, and the flowers of dhātakī, one should boil them further until a paste of dārvī and its expressed juice [is obtained]. When this is drunk at the appropriate time with water, rice-scum (maṇḍa), or even goat’s milk, it destroys all severe types of diarrhea—whether black, white, red, or yellow—as well as various disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), hemorrhaging (raktapitta), blood-stained hemorrhoids, and even incurable menorrhagia; it certainly overcomes these conditions.

This is the Kuṭajāṣṭaka (41). Through heat, the consumption of warm food, the drinking of hot water, grief, distress, anger, pungency, and alkaline substances, the *pitta* and blood become concentrated (42). Consequently, the stool becomes reddish, yellow, or very dark blue, accompanied by foul odor, emaciation, fever, and jaundice; along with giddiness, pain, fainting, thirst, and burning in the limbs—these are the symptoms of *pitta*-type diarrhea (43). A decoction prepared with śāliparṇī, pṛśniparṇī, balā, and bilva, made sour with pomegranate, is beneficial and should be drunk for the pacification of *pitta*-type diarrhea (44).

Having prepared a decoction of the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and sugarcane with water produced from *śālīna* rice, it is recommended for those suffering from *pitta*-type diarrhea (verse 45). A decoction of the roots of the five grains (*dhānyapañcaka*) is likewise for those with *pitta*-type diarrhea (verse 46). Furthermore, the root-bark of *śālmali* ground with jaggery and milk, when drunk, pacifies excessive *pitta* and removes blood, burning sensations, and emaciation (verse 47). [This occurs] due to bad dreams and the like, exhaustion, innate sluggishness, exposure to cold, consumption of unctuous food in excess, or from heavy substances such as sesame, flour, jaggery, and pieces of sugarcane.

Due to excessive bathing in cold water, greed for food mixed with curd while in water, and similar causes, Kaphaja-atisāra (diarrhea caused by phlegm) arises; it destroys the digestive fire in men and results in indigestion. (48) By that [Kapha], one should know that Kaphottha-sāra is characterized by dryness, breaking pain, loss of appetite, thick and foul-smelling stools, heaviness, horripilation, weak digestion, slow movement of the bowels, and laziness. (49) Having ascertained the strength and weakness of the body, fasting (laṅghana) is prescribed at the outset; furthermore, O best of physicians, a digestive remedy (pācana) such as Tryūṣaṇādi should be administered. (50)

Trikaṭu, abhayā, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, rucaka, and vacā, combined with honey as a linctus, would stop even the flowing river Gaṅgā for men. (51) Kāliṅga, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, balā, uśīra, mustā, marica, and śuṇṭhī—this excellent paste, taken with jaggery and honey, serves to pacify dysentery caused by kapha and blood. (52) Vatsaka, ativiṣā, bilva, mustaka, and vālaka, boiled together in water—not as a simple decoction—is a drink that destroys severe colic, blood, and pus in dysentery accompanied by fever. (53) And he who [suffers from] blood... [text truncated]

If, during purgation, there is excessive drying or burning, it should be recognized by highly intelligent physicians as *raktātisāra* (blood-dysentery). (54) A decoction of *dhānyaka*, *nāgara*, *mustā*, *vālaka*, young *bilva* fruit, *balā*, and *nāgabala* is for those suffering from blood-dysentery. (55) Having ground together pomegranate, *kapittha*, *pathyā*, rose-apple, and mango sprouts, they should be administered with buttermilk to ward off blood-dysentery. (56) For a person with blood-dysentery, *bilva* cooked with jaggery should be given; or else *pathyā* mixed with honey or with curd.

Vatsaka, ativiṣā, nāgara, and abhayā, ground together and combined with buttermilk, form a linctus that is recommended even with honey for a person; it effectively wards off even excessive hemorrhaging. (57–58) The powder of kuṭaja bark, pāṭhā, viśva, bilva, and dhātakī, taken with honey, should be administered as a remedy for bloody diarrhea. (59) When the stool flows appearing like the bristles of a boar, like vāsā grass, like sesame seeds, like the wash-water of meat, or resembling the fruit of a ripe jambū tree, it is a case of sannipāta. (60) One should take one tulā of fresh girimallikā...

Having condensed and cooked it, one should extract the juice; when that is well-strained and measured at one *pala*, one should add [the following] after grinding them together with *śālmali* (61): *pāṭhā*, *samaṅgā*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *bilva*, and the flowers of *dhātakī*. Having added these, one should boil it again until it becomes a paste as thick as *dārvī*. When drunk with water, *maṇḍa*, or honey at the appropriate time, it destroys all severe types of diarrhea—whether black, white, red, or yellow—and the disorder of the *grahaṇī* (62–63).

This *kuṭajāṣṭaka* (the eight-fold preparation of *kuṭaja*) certainly destroys various types of hemorrhage, hemorrhoids accompanied by blood, and even forms of menorrhagia that are otherwise incurable. (64) The decoction of *pathyā* and the five roots (*pañcamūla*), reduced to one-fourth of its original volume, is used as the base. Into this decoction, the following medicinal powders are then added: (65) Fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), lac (*lākṣā*), long pepper (*pippalī*), *kaṭurohiṇī*, the powder of pomegranate rind (*dāḍimaphalatvak*), *dārvī*, *vatsaka*, and *viṣa* (aconite). (66) Having added the powder of *āṭarūṣaka*, one should stir it together with goat’s milk (*āja-dugdha*).

One should add half that amount of ghee and one-eighth part [of the remaining ingredients]. Knowing it has been smeared with *dārvī*, sixteen *palas* of jaggery mixed therein should be given before breakfast. This is a digestive for severe diarrhea arising from the three *doṣas* combined (*sannipāta*), as well as for colic, fainting, vertigo, flatulence, and jaundice. This "Amṛta-vat" (Nectar-like) preparation is beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds, emaciation, and wasting. When the powder of *bilva*, *aguru*, and *rodhra* is combined with honey and other [ingredients], it pacifies hemorrhagic diarrhea in children whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are depleted. When...

One should then expel the secret [discharge] and perform this procedure: the juice of *sahacārī* and the herbs, as well as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), should be taken. An application with cooked clarified butter is recommended for it; alternatively, a decoction of *araṇī* sprouts, or a clod of earth mixed with sandalwood (*candana*) may be used. Or else, having extinguished a substance heated until it resembles fire with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), one should apply it in the same manner. Furthermore, immersion in warm water is highly praised for providing relief; having positioned the anus in the middle, it should be held firmly in place.

One should avoid diarrhea that has the stench of garlic or a corpse, or the smell of pus; that which is thick like liquid flesh, or resembles ripe *jambu* fruit, or appears like ghee, honey, or milk; or that which is as dark as oil or algae, or has the color of thick curd. (75) One who suffers from vertigo, intoxication, emaciation, colic, fainting, burning sensations, labored breathing, extreme discoloration, vomiting, thirst, and distress; one who is excessively afflicted by weakness, swelling, and fever—let such a person be avoided from afar by the wise physician, for he is not seen [to survive]. (76) [Symptoms include] swelling, colic, and fever.

One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea upon observing thirst, labored breathing, cough, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, and hiccups (77). Likewise, one should abandon a patient afflicted by edema, abdominal distension, hiccups, vomiting, anorexia, and jaundice who is also suffering from diarrhea (78). When waste matter, consumed in very small quantities and gradually, remains constantly in the receptacle of the rectum, it suppresses the internal digestive fire and produces a disorder in man known as *grahaṇī* (79). Once the diarrhea has ceased, [this condition] excessively diminishes the digestive heat.

Even when afflicted, having consumed impure food, the disease of *grahaṇī* emerges after accumulating waste for many days without ceasing; repeatedly seizing the innate, crooked, ripening, or thick [humors], this terrible form of chronic illness causes pain to a person, and it should be recognized as such in cases of diarrhea. One should know that the disease of *grahaṇī* is of four types: Vātika, Paittika, Ślaiṣmika, and Sānnipātika. Indeed, the disease of *grahaṇī* does not arise from a single humor alone; by that [disease], one's strength is utterly wasted away.

Internal burning of the body is its maturation (vipāka). [It is characterized by] bitter, astringent, pungent, sour, and burning tastes, and is dry. Through those intent on cold and meager food, as well as through physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and the running of elephants, chariots, or horses carrying heavy loads on the road, the wind (vāyu) becomes enraged; when it strikes the fire (*anala*), it imparts its own force to this [disease]. Therefore, being cut at its tip by the wind and joined with blood, it reaches maturation in the wind; thus it arises in a person, and likewise the third [type] is named *gulma*. And that became fivefold. [The fourth is] the spleen (*plīhā*).

The binding of the liver, the stomach, and the filth of the body; *aṣṭhīlā*; worms arising from diseases of the abdomen as the sixth; these, occurring in the *grahaṇī*, become terrible and cause suffering in the mind of a person. (85) Dryness of the throat, darkness of vision, pain in the flanks, emaciation in the navel, severe choleric colic (*ativiṣūcikā*), ringing in the ears, excessive vomiting, exhaustion, pain, and delusion—know that these are indeed the symptoms of *gulma* accompanied by dyspnea. (86) One who possesses these signs is a patient with *gulma*.

The wise know that which is called *grahaṇī*; I shall now describe the symptoms of its curable form. (87) In this condition, one voids stool that is variegated and accompanied by sound; there is swelling and the wind makes the stool exceedingly dry. Accompanied by dyspnea and pain, with looseness of the body, there is discharge due to the provocation of wind in the *grahaṇī*. (88) When the excrement is discharged mixed with substances that cause a burning sensation, is shattered, painful, and attended by thirst, and is foul-smelling, yellow, reddish, blue, or black, it is known as *grahaṇī* arising from bile. (89) Nausea, vomiting, labored breathing, and swelling [occur].

Cough, dullness, coldness, a bad taste in the mouth, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and retention of the ears and feces—these are declared to be the symptoms when [the three doṣas] are combined. Alternatively, when there is anger, sweetness in the mouth, burning sensation, fainting, labored breathing, and dullness, that is the disease of *sannipāta-grahaṇī*. A decoction of *dāru*, *nāgara*, *niśā*, *vāsaka*, *kuṇḍalī*, *magadhajā*, *śaṭhī*, *ghanam*, *rāsnā*, *bhārṅgī*, *sarala*, and *puṣkara* acts as a digestive (*pācana*) remedy for *vātika-grahaṇī*.

The drinking of a decoction made from the roots of *nalaveṇu*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and sugarcane is beneficial for this patient, acting as a digestive aid in cases of *pittaja* *grahaṇī*. (93) *Vyāghrī*, *granthika*, *cavya*, *surasā*, ginger, pomegranate, turmeric, *ghanā*, and *citraka*—this [formula] destroys hiccup, *madhura-kapha*, and *grahaṇī*. (94) Ginger, *kaṇā*, the two types of turmeric, and *ghanā* should likewise be employed; furthermore, *prativiṣā*, *triphalā*, *viḍaṅga*, rock salt, *vahnitrikaṭu*, and the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*) should be combined into a powder and taken with jaggery.

Having prepared five hundred *harītakī* fruits with a *droṇa* of [water] and mixed them with ghee, one should eat them in portions the size of a cat's paw (*biḍālapada*). This is effective even for dysentery (*grahaṇīgada*), and it destroys hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, loss of appetite, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, colic, stones, worms, and jaundice. This is the best elixir (*rasāyana*); it destroys weakness, acts as an aphrodisiac, bestows strength, cures the defect of extreme emaciation, imparts luster to the complexion and all the sense organs, alleviates diseases, and always removes skin diseases and vertigo. (95–97) The wise man [should take] five hundred *harītakī* fruits with a *droṇa*...

It should be cooked with a hundred measures of cow’s urine over a gentle fire until the urine is completely consumed. Once the urine has been fully digested, the knower of the procedure should, according to the rules, extinguish the heat and dry the powder. When it has cooled, one should split the dried pieces in the shade, [collect] the powder, and add ginger, Pippalī, Viṣā, fragrant Mūrvā, Cavya, and Kṛmighna. Having boiled these, the paste of Kuṭaja should be applied with a ladle until it becomes thick enough to coat it. Then, having stirred in jaggery (guḍa) equal to half that amount, one should add milk equal to half of that, or the milk of a goat.

That [preparation] is extinguished with ghee and established by that previously delighted one. Then, the powder of rock salt, the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), and the three aromatics (tri-sugandhi), combined with jaggery and mixed with ghee—by means of that powder, it is an immediate destroyer for all types of grahaṇī, anemia, consumption, urinary stones, worms, abdominal tumors, and diarrhea; and for men suffering from splenic disorders, liver disease, asthma, cholera, chronic catarrh, and pain in the head; likewise for those exhausted by travel, fever, or loss of strength in the abdomen. 101–102.

This electuary beginning with *abhayā* destroys fevers lasting for a single day and so forth; for men, it is like nectar (103). Thus ends the *Abhayādyo'valeha*. Having cooked grapes with milk until it becomes thick and can be smeared with a ladle, the wise man should then stir in these medicinal herbs (104): *parpaṭa*, *ativiṣā*, *mūrvā*, *paṭola*, *ghanavālaka*, as well as the powder of *abhayā* mixed with an equal amount of sugar (105). Having combined that with the milk and the root of *vidārī*, he should form a bolus with fresh ghee and butter.

Having prepared it, one should then consume it; it removes the afflictions of pitta-type grahaṇī, anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice (kāmalā), and thirst, as well as dizziness, fainting, hiccups, epilepsy, insanity, and urinary calculi. It certainly and swiftly destroys urinary disorders (meha), hemorrhagic diseases (pittāsṛj), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diarrhea," in the third section of the *Hārīta-uttara* as spoken by Ātreya, concerning the "Milk with Grapes and Other Ingredients."

Chapter Four. Ātreya said: Listen, my son, I shall explain the characteristics of the *gulmas* (abdominal tumors/lumps), as well as their remedies and specific medicinal treatments. These *gulmas*, which are situated within the abdomen, arise in five ways: they are known to be located in the heart, the side of the abdomen (*kukṣi*), the navel, the bladder (*vasti*), and the fifth is remembered as being in the middle [of the abdomen]. That which resides in the heart is named *yakṛt*; that in the side of the abdomen is called *aṣṭhīlaka*; that in the middle is designated as *plīhā*; and that in the bladder is *caṇḍavivṛddhaka*. A knot (*granthi*) is observed at the navel.

The names of these [types] are distinct from one another; therefore, I shall describe their provocation (prakopa), by which they cause affliction. (4) In the case of that arising from *pitta* and blood (*raktaja*), it occurs due to the natural constitution (*svabhāva*) or from the consumption of sour, burning, hot, and alkaline substances, or from liquor, or from excessive intake of warm drinks. (5) Likewise, through grief, fatigue, walking long distances, emaciation, or agitation; through loud speaking, singing, and the drawing of a bowstring; (6) or by the striking of the back with a fist, or by beating the chest, or even by lifting heavy loads, the blood becomes depleted in the heart. (7) By that [depletion], it is called a *gulma*.

The disease known as *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic fever) sometimes arises; its origin is seen to be from the three *doṣas*. Driven by *vāta*, condensed by *kapha*, and brought to a state of ripening by *pitta*, it is a combination of the three *doṣas* located in the liver (*yakṛt*). I shall describe its symptoms, by which it is recognized and by which a person wastes away and quickly meets death: vomiting, exhaustion, eructation, nausea, labored breathing, vertigo, burning sensation, loss of appetite, thirst, fainting, burning in the throat, and headache.

11-13. Heartache, catarrh, spitting, pain in the heart as if from a thorn, loss of sleep due to delirium, a sensation of hardness in the heart, and the abdomen rumbling excessively—one should recognize these as the symptoms [of a disorder] within the liver, the stomach, or the chest. If one should consume a fine powder consisting of the three pungents (tri-kaṭu), Kuṣṭha, Pañcamūla, Yavānī as the sixth, mixed with Sindhūttha salt and Rāmaṭha (asafoetida), and drink buttermilk over it; [this will cure the ailment].

One should drink water boiled [with these] or sour *sauvīraka*; this quickly destroys liver disease, abdominal enlargement, colic, and cough, and it overcomes cholera, indigestion, disorders of phlegm, the pain of *pāṇḍu* disease, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). The powder of *śuṇṭhī* and other [ingredients] quickly destroys [these ailments], as does the alkali of *muṣkaka*, *kiṃśuka*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, *apāmārga*, *rambhā*, sesame, *jīvantī*, *kanakāhvaya*, turmeric, the *kūṣmāṇḍa* creeper, and likewise [other substances].

Having ignited a fierce fire of *vāsā* and *sūraṇa* and reduced them to ashes, one should consume them with water and then drink a measured amount of milk; this cures liver disease (yakṛt), as well as diseases born of colic, abdominal tumors, constipation, and phlegm, along with jaundice, abscesses, heart pain, anemia, malabsorption syndrome, edema, hemorrhoids, and chronic rhinitis.

In those with weak digestion, it causes indigestion, worms, lassitude, prolapse of the rectum, and delusion. Furthermore, from that [injury], there arises blood-born (kṣataja) enlargement accompanied by burning and pain, as well as eructation, vomiting, and the discharge of phlegm resembling pus, foul-smelling and extremely putrid. There, matter resembling blood falls repeatedly; one spits it out again and again, and likewise blood is discharged through diarrhea. Fatigue increases and the body wastes away. Blood-born [abscesses] appear on the limbs, and when located in the liver or the chest, they cause dyspnea, thirst, vomiting, delusion, and swelling of the hands and feet.

One should abandon cases involving loss of appetite, diarrhea, and enlargement of the liver (yakṛddura). Hereafter, I shall describe the medicine by which well-being is attained: first, fasting alone, and immediately after that, digestive therapy (pācana). A decoction or paste of ginger (śuṇṭhī), black pepper (upakulyā), *timira*, *śaṭhī*, *yavānikā*, *abhīru*, and *harītakī* is recommended for digestion and for those suffering from flatulence, abdominal tumors (gulma), pain, and cholera-like cramps (viṣūcikā). *Bhadra*, black pepper (*upakulyā*), *abhayā*, and fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*)—with *pathyā* making up three parts and long pepper (*kaṇā*) the fourth part—[cures] wasting due to chest wounds and liver disorders.

Fasting and digestive treatments should not be administered; rather, a powder combined with asafoetida (hiṅgu) is beneficial for that patient. (24) A decoction of nimba, nīpa, dhava, vetasa, niśā, kāśmarī, tulasī, and siṃhikā indeed removes heart disease, quickly alleviates colic, and destroys liver disorders. (25) A decoction of saurāṣṭrī, sīsa, mahauṣadha, durālabhā, jātipravālaka, dārvī, yavānī, kakubha, and samaṅgā, taken with ghee, quickly destroys liver disease. (26) [This applies also to] the decoctions of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, śirīṣa, and badarī.

Having boiled [these], the drink destroys undigested matter (*āma*), checks cholera (*viṣūcī*), and wards off colic. (27) Taking either the alkali of plantain (*kadalī-kṣāra*) or the alkali of conch shell (*śaṅkha-kṣāra*), one should strain it and drink it with *hiṅgu* and *sauvarcala* salt. (28) This removes undigested matter when it has been expelled, quickly subdues colic, pacifies cholera, and even digests indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). (29) One should take the juice of *mātuluṅga* (citron) mixed with double the amount of fermented rice water (*kāñjika*), along with *hiṅgu* and *sauvarcala* salt; this drink destroys cholera. (30) Alkali and water should be given for drinking over a burning sensation.

It should be cooked; it quickly destroys colic and flatulence and stimulates the digestive fire (31). In cases of undigested matter (*āma*), one should administer emetics, and once it has been digested, fasting (*laṅghana*). Specific sudation is indicated for drowsiness, and purgation when the essence of the food remains (32). Day-sleep is beneficial in insanity, diarrhea, those afflicted by vomiting or anger, indigestion, and cholera-like cramps (*viṣūcikā*) (33). However, day-sleep is not beneficial in cases of *kapha*, heart disease, headache, nausea, and catarrh; one should avoid day-sleep in these conditions (34). [The group of] three fruits (*phalatraya*).

A wick made from the seeds of *tryūṣa* and *karañja*, as well as the juice of pomegranate and citron mixed with turmeric (*niśā*), when applied as an ointment, destroys cholera (*viṣūcikā*). (35) *Rāsnā*, *viśālā*, fragrant *kuṣṭha*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), *vacā*, ginger (*nāgaraka*), *śatāhvā*, *āgneyī*, *piṣṭā*, *ahapuṣā*, and *vidārī*—when ground together, these ward off *khallī* and cholera (*viṣūcī*). (36) Fomentation (*sveda*) should be administered to the patient using steam from a single pot covered with cloth while heated; likewise, pouring warm water over the hands [of the patient] will thus conquer cholera and abdominal diseases.

37–38. The patient should quickly consume sulphur, rock salt, and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) rubbed with lime juice; this is a swift remedy for the cessation of cholera (viṣūcī). Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gulma," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Five. Ātreya said: Worms are said to be of two kinds, arising externally and internally. The external ones are well known as lice (*yūkā*), and the internal ones are the *kiñcaka*. (1) The external type shall be of seven varieties, and the internal type of six. I shall describe their origin among humans, both external and internal. (2) Indeed, due to dryness, excessive impurity, perspiration, anxiety, and even grief, sharp lice (*yūkā*) arise from the predominance of the *kapha* constituent. (3) These lice are black, others are [dark], and the third kind is white.

The *carma-bhā* is situated on the skin; it is subtle, extremely formidable, rough, and a louse of the skin (*carma-yūkikā*). The fourth is named *bindukī*, which is globular and originates from urine. The fifth is the *matkuṇa* (bedbug), which causes external afflictions. The louse (*yūkā*) resides on the head and dwells in the hair of the head; the *carma-yūkā* is in the skin of the eyes, while the *yaṣṭikā* is in the fine body hair. [These are caused] by dry food, barley-meal, wheat-flour, or molasses; by the absence of milk, by sleeping during the day, by being slimy, by heat, and by the use of heated water.

By that [process], a swarm of worms is produced within the receptacles of impurity, causing disorders of the digestive tract (koṣṭha). They are declared to be of six kinds; I shall describe their characteristics. The receptacle of phlegm (kapha) is the seat of impurity; they crawl within the digestive tract like serpents. Some have broad heads, some resemble sheaths, some resemble sprouts of grain, and some are minute and atomic. They should be known as "needle-mouthed" (sūcīmukha), for they pierce the intestines. I shall describe their symptoms and their treatment; listen to me. [Symptom: Fever.

Heart disease, piercing pain, vomiting, moisture in the heart, vertigo, loss of appetite, discoloration, and frothy diarrhea occur; 12. as well as rumbling in the abdomen, weak digestion, thirst, and yellowness of the eyes in one afflicted by *kiñcuka* [poison]. 13. The intestines are pricked as if by needles, and blood is discharged in diarrhea; others eat the liver, or vomit blood profusely. 14. Moisture in the mouth, loss of appetite, numbness, weak digestion, trembling, hunger, thirst, and fever are to be recognized [as symptoms].

I shall now describe the characteristics of the *sūcīmukha* worms, the *krimi* (parasites) that cause pain, and those that reside in the sprouts of grain. The worms situated in the receptacle of waste (*malāśaya*) devour the waste excessively. By them, the body is afflicted with emaciation, types of abscesses (*vidradhi*), roughness, and pain in the limbs; thus, heart-moistening is considered the mark of *yavakrimis*. Hārīta, overcome by doubt, grasped [the teacher’s] feet and asked: "How do these arise within the body of a human being in the receptacles of waste, urine, and chyle? And how do they first come into existence?"

How do they increase? Furthermore, how is it that when the essence of food (*annarasa*) has decayed and various foods have been consumed, minute worms (*krimi*) arise, some even moving downwards? And why does the fire (*hutāśana*) not burn the various kinds of raw and undigested food? Why are those worms not burned at the end by the internal fire? Thus questioned, the Great Teacher, the bull among sages, replied. Ātreya said: "Listen, O mighty-armed son, to the cause of the origin of worms. O son, [the blood] by means of incompatible food essences..."

Furthermore, his [body] becomes irritated by phlegm for one day, and by semen it proceeds toward its cause; yet these [elements], though born within the body composed of the five elements, possess consciousness. Just as a worm born in poison does not meet death by that poison, so too that which is produced from fire is not digested by fire. I shall now fully declare the medicine by which they indeed cross over, or else fall and attain pacification; hear from me the medicines.

Vacā, ajamodā, krimijit, palāśa seeds, śaṭhī, rāmaṭha, and the three types of viśyā—having ground these together with warm water, one should drink them; the worms fall away quickly by the hundreds. (27) Śaṭhī, yavānī, picumanda, putrāñjana, viḍaṅga, kṛṣṇā, and the juice of ativiṣā—having ground these with urine and combined them with trivṛt, it is the destroyer of all worm-related diseases. (28) Marica, pippalīmūla, viḍaṅga, śigru, yavānikā, and trivṛt—these should be ground with cow's urine and drunk; this quickly kills the worms. (29)

A paste of mustā, viśālā, triphalā, suparṇī, śigru, and surāhva, taken with water along with the powder of kṛṣṇā and krimiśatru, destroys all types of worms and their afflictions. (30) Surasā, suradāru, māgadhī, viḍaṅga, kampilla, viḍaṅga, dantinī, trivṛt, tāḍaka, and rasonaka, when consumed with water, remove worms and heart disease. (31) One should grind the roots of mātuluṅga, rasona, krimijit, trivṛt, ajamodā, and nimba leaves with cow’s urine; this drink is highly recommended. (32)

One should administer the wholesome diets prescribed for fever to ward off the disorder of worms (krimidoṣa). Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Worms," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Sixth Chapter. Ātreya said: Fire is declared to be of four types: balanced (*sama*), irregular (*viṣama*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), and another called dull (*manda*). Now hear their characteristics. (1) Due to the equilibrium of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, the digestive fire (*anala*) becomes balanced (*sama*). When these same factors reach a state of imbalance, the fire becomes irregular (*viṣama*). (2) The abdominal fire (*jaṭharāgni*) becomes sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) due to the predominance of *pitta*; it is designated as dull (*manda*) due to the predominance of *vāta* and *kapha*. (3) That which digests the mass of food exactly as it was consumed, while remaining in its natural state, [is the balanced fire].

That which is called *sama* (balanced) is free from defects and increases all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). It sometimes digests food and sometimes leaves it undigested; it does not cause irregularity or choleric dyspepsia (*viṣūcikā*) through its action. By nature, it causes excessive sweating and one does not feel fully satiated. There is a burning sensation and yellowness in the eyes; indeed, the sharp fire (*tīkṣṇa*) causes the wasting away of strength. That by which one is unable to eat at all due to the predominance of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and strength is called *mandānala* (weak digestive fire), and it is considered to be primarily characterized by abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and enlargement of the abdomen (*udara*). Through *sama*, there is equilibrium in the body.

A man whose body, elements, strength, and senses are delighted, remains active with his limbs fully restored. (8) When wind and the other humors become irregular, there arise disorders of the *grahaṇī*, diarrhea, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, cholera, and those known as colic and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*). (9) Due to an irregular digestive fire (*viṣamāgni*), constipation and lethargy occur; both wind and phlegm become diminished, while the bile becomes intense. (10) One finds pleasure in eating, and what has been eaten is digested [too quickly]; by this, the digestive fire becomes known as *bhasmaka* (the "ash-eater"). (11) [The patient becomes] pale (*pāṇḍu*).

Bilious diarrhea, consumption (rājayakṣmā), jaundice (halīmaka), vertigo, exhaustion, extreme debility, as well as liver disorders and urinary diseases (prameha); 12. colic, fainting, internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), bilious acidity, and dysuria—by these the body is wasted away and a craving for food arises. 13. Even wood and stones, when eaten by that embodied being, are digested; thus has been declared the etiology of the provocation of the digestive fire (agni) in man. 14. Although it could have been stated in many ways, it has not been said here for fear of excessive length of the book. 15. Therefore, I shall speak of it in brief.

Medicines are of various kinds: digestive (pācana), palliative (śamana), and likewise stimulant (dīpana). 16. Rāsnā, śaṭhī, prativiṣā, surasā, śuṇṭhī, rock salt, asafoetida, pippalī, and suvarcalā—this powder, when consumed with jaggery as a bolus or food, balances the irregular digestive fire caused by Vāta. 17. It destroys colic, indigestion, irregular digestion, cholera, and all types of abdominal tumors (gulma) arising from Vāta and other humors; it is best taken lukewarm after a meal, or even as a decoction. 18. Likewise, it is excellent when taken after a meal. 19. This is the best remedy for those suffering from chronic fever, cough, consumption, and piles. 20. [This formulation] is to be enjoyed for all tastes (18). Grapes, *abhayā*, bitter *rohiṇī*, *vidārī*, sandalwood, *vāsaka*, *mustā*, *paṭola*, *kirātaka*, *kṛṣṇā*, *balā*, *vikacā*, and *viṣāṇā* (19), as well as *palāla*, *vaṅga*, *ālaka*, and *padmaka*, along with *bhṛṅgī* and *dhanikā*—these should be combined in equal parts. This powder, when joined with dates and sugar and taken with ghee in a quantity equal to half the strength [of the patient], (20) a person should consume in the morning with milk; it should be administered as a decoction with ghee, which produces an intensity of digestive fire equal to a fierce flame.

This indeed certainly bestows nourishment upon the emaciated; it destroys fatigue, dizziness, and wasting, and pacifies excessive thirst and greed. Blood-bile disorders, consumption, anemia, chlorosis, and jaundice are quickly eliminated. (21-22) For the wise, take two parts of red *śāli* rice and roast them; then grind sesame seeds and mix them with half that amount. Having roasted an equal portion of green gram (*mudga*), combine all these together and properly prepare the *kṛśarā* dish with ghee. (23)

One should feed [him]. (24) For one who eats with a day’s interval between meals, his intense digestive fire perishes. (25) Harītakī possesses six qualities equal to those of Hari and Hara; when combined with four parts of large Pippalī, along with asafoetida and rock salt, this elixir kindles the digestive fire of King Kuru. (26) One should employ Dīpyaka, Agni, Harītakī, and Viḍaṅga in increasing proportions, ground into powder; likewise, very sour Veta, Kola, Dāḍima, and Tintiḍīka—(27) these being taken in equal amounts, each weighing one Karṣa.

In one *karṣa* of each of the other ingredients—*jājī*, *varāṅga*, *suvarcala*, and one hundred *kaṇā* (long pepper)—along with half that amount of black pepper (*marica*), and four *palas* of sugar, having ground them all together into a fine powder, one should consume it to clear abdominal disorders. This preparation creates an appetite, overcomes constipation, and conquers splenic pain along with cough. It destroys asthma, cures heart disease, purifies ailments of the tongue and throat, and serves as a digestive stimulant for those suffering from *grahaṇī*, hemorrhoids, and weak digestion. (28–30)

The preparation known as *yavānikākhaṇḍavikā* is highly praised for alleviating anorexia (31). A gruel made from the five pungent spices (*pañcakola*), or *kulattha*, *āḍhakī*, and *pūṣaka* with mung-bean soup, is beneficial when served with well-prepared rice (32). A side dish enriched with asafoetida and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) is recommended; indeed, it is excellent even for those suffering from a lack of appetite for food, like the *agastighṛta* (33). *Kāravella*, *paṭola*, onion, *sūraṇa*, *śaṭhī*, salt, coriander, and the three pungent spices (*kaṭutrika*) are best used as a thick syrup (*praleha*) (34). *Śaṭhī*.

Mustard greens, vāstuka, śatapuṣpā, kāñcanamācikā, and the leafy vegetables of the roots of tuṇḍīraka are praised as the best. (35) Wheat cakes fried over charcoal are excellent; the best of physicians should also serve meats from wild animals to one suffering from anorexia. (36) Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Weak Digestive Fire," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Seven. Ātreya said: Through physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, staying awake at night, sexual intercourse, grief, excessive carrying of loads, walking, running, and fatigue; through irregular drinking and sleeping, and by eating cold food, the Vāyu becomes aggravated and increases its strength. (1) Furthermore, by the consumption of indigestible, dry, barley, black gram, horse gram, green gram, flat beans, *kodrava*, *masūra*, wheat, small grains, and foods that increase *kapha* or are parching; and by this drinking, as well as the obstruction of feces and urine, (2) the Vāyu, having ascended the downward path, obstructs the root.

One becomes dominated by *vāta* and possesses an internal fire; therefore, when provoked by its own intensity, it causes pain in the forearm and even when the path of the anus is obstructed. O Great-minded one, for a man afflicted by the suffering of *vāta*, there shall be a constant piercing pain in the limbs, and he will become filthy, extremely wretched, and tormented by the agony of wind. It is provoked by anger, exposure to the sun, and the consumption of fire-like substances; by grief, fear, distress, running, and physical exertion; and by alkaline, sour, alcoholic, pungent, hot, burning, dry, fermented gruel (*sauvīra*), dried meat, scraping agents, and black mustard. Thus, impelled by the *anila* (wind), it becomes greatly agitated.
