That *pitta*, however, causes intense colic in the abdomen of a person; by it, the humors burn within the navel, causing burning of the limbs, loss of appetite, fever, thirst, distress, and fainting, as well as a yellowish tint in the mouth. (6) By lack of exercise, consumption of ununctuous substances, eating out of greed, and by excessive use of sugarcane juice, oil, and milk; or by eating little and sleeping excessively—by these practices, one aggravates *śleṣman*. (7) But when *śleṣman* is excessively consumed through black gram, very cold milk and curd, very cold fish, and the flesh of marshy animals, it quickly and thoroughly pacifies the digestive fire.

It causes a sharp pain (śūla) in the abdomen and produces severe disorders in a person. There is nausea, cough, loss of appetite, heaviness of the head, numbness, coldness of the body, and stiffness in the thighs. One who has excessive salivation after eating, a sweet mouth, and a pleasant, oily-feeling face—this is of the nature of phlegm (kapha). Indeed, when phlegm is present and these symptoms occur, that person suffers from colic (sa-śūla). When the signs appear as if they were caused by bile (pitta), yet occur even during indigestion (ajīrṇa), men call that "colic with indigestion" (sa-śūlam). [Symptoms also occur] in the heart, throat, and sides.

Kapha and Pitta [types] occur in the middle of the heart and navel; there is pain from Kapha and Pitta in the bladder, the navel, and the region of the lower abdomen, which fluctuates due to Vāta and Pitta. (11) Even this single type is easily curable, while the dual-type (Dvandvaja) is cured with difficulty; however, that born of the three Doshas (Tridoṣaja) is incurable and accompanied by many complications. (12) Aggravated by etiological factors (Nidānas), the Vāyu moves within the belly; thus it is known as "Śūla" (colic), and ten varieties of it are proclaimed. (13) Three are to be known as originating from Vāta and the others [Pitta and Kapha], and furthermore, three are born from combinations of two.

These two—Sāma and Nirāma—and eight types of colic (śūla) are thus recorded. Indigestion (ajīrṇa) is declared the ninth, and that arising from digestion (pariṇāmaja) is the tenth; in this way, colic occurs in ten forms in human beings. That which occurs after eating should be known as being of the nature of Kapha; and that which occurs when food is digested should be known as arising from digestion (pariṇāmaja). Distension, upward movement [of wind], constipation, yawning, trembling, shivering, eructation, an oily mouth, and excessive salivation—by these, one suffers from colic caused by Vāta.

17–18. Burning sensation, delusion, thirst, difficulty in urination, a bitter taste in the mouth, excessive perspiration, and a yellowish face—the wise declare this to be of the nature of *pitta*. 19. Vomiting, cough, dyspnea, delusion, laziness, drowsiness, numbness, and extreme coldness—O best of physicians, that colic (*śūla*) arising from these is known as being caused by the dual combination of *kapha* and *vāta*. When all three *doṣas* are involved, it is born of the three *doṣas*; thus, including the one caused by blood, eleven types have been described, beginning with those of the nature of *pitta*.

The symptoms that manifest are: vomiting of blood, emaciation, thirst, burning sensations, as well as cough, dyspnea, and excessive pain arising from blood. (20-21) There is no colic without Vāta, no vertigo without Pitta, no vomiting without Kapha, and no darkness (fainting) without blood. (22) This is the thorough diagnosis of colic; hereafter I shall describe the remedy by which the alleviation of the pain of colic is achieved and the sufferer attains comfort. (23) Having observed the colic, one should administer fasting, digestive remedies, and purgation.

For the alleviation of colic, one should administer emetics, sudation, alkaline powder, or medicinal flour; these are beneficial when used for drinking, massage, or as an enema in a person suffering from cough and flatulence (24). A decoction of hiṅgu, ginger, śaṭhī, suvarcalā, devadāru, puṣkaramūla, musta, and punarnavā is beneficial for those with colic; it is a digestive that is also suitable for those suffering from abdominal enlargement and gulma (25). Likewise, a decoction of hiṅgu, puṣkaramūla, śaṭhī, and suvarcalā is beneficial for those with colic; it is praised for pacifying vāta-type colic and is declared to be a digestive (26). [One should also use] rock salt, hiṅgu, and rucaka salt...

A powder made from equal parts of *śaṭhī*, *yavānī*, *pathyā*, and *yavakṣāra*, when administered with lukewarm water, destroys colic of a Vāta nature, or even Vāta-type pain, without delay. (27) *Hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, *punarnavā*, *balā*, *eraṇḍa*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *tuvara*, and *tryūṣaṇa*—this [mixture] combined with *kṣāra* and *sauvarcala*, whether as a decoction or as a powder, instantly destroys Vāta-type colic and instantly cures *viṣūcikā*. (28–29) Alternatively, one may take *tumburu*, *pauṣkara*, *hiṅgu*, *yavānī*, and *tryūṣaṇa* in three times the quantity of *trivṛt*.

This powder of the eight salts (lavaṇāṣṭaka) is appropriate, as it is capable of warding off colic. A decoction [of these] destroys the multitude of colics arising from Vāta. Hingu combined with eraṇḍa, nāgara, suvarcalā, and rāmaṭha, along with pathyā, vacā, indrayava, and water of nāgara, indeed destroys colic; and hingu combined with suvarcalā also destroys colic. Hingu, nāgara, ṣaḍgranthā, yavānī, both types of ubhayā, trivṛt, viḍaṅga, dāru, cavya, tumburu, kuṣṭha, mustaka, hapuṣā, kalaśī, rāsnā, vatsaka, durālabhā, and sitāravī—[these constitute the formulation].

One should mix together two parts each of *bṛhatī*, *lāṅgalī*, the five types of *jīraka*, *puṣkara*, *tintiḍīka*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlavetasa*, along with the two alkalis (*kṣāra*) and the five salts (*pañcalavaṇa*). Having subjected this mixture to a single saturation with urine and dried it in the shade, one should then saturate it for three days with the juice of *bījapūraka*. One should administer a dose the size of a cat's paw-print for the pacification of colic (*śūla*); when combined with warm water and white sugar, it is also used for disorders of Vāta. A decoction of *triphalā* taken with wine is recommended for diseases of Kapha.

It destroys colic, abdominal distension, constipation, weak digestion, abdominal tumors (gulma), abscesses, splenic enlargement, and especially jaundice and fever—just as a gale disperses a mass of clouds by shattering the body's accumulation of humors. One should prepare a powder of *dhātrī* fruit, iron filings, *pathyā*, and *tryūṣaṇa* in equal parts, processed with the juice of either pomegranate or citron; this, combined with abundant sugar, is used for colic accompanied by bile. Alternatively, one should administer a powder of *biḍālaka*, *dāḍimapūtanā*, and *dhātrī*, along with the juice of citron.

One should consume the prepared *jīvantyādi-ghṛta* for the pacification of bile-related colic (40). Alternatively, milk mixed with sugar should be drunk; purgation must be performed regularly to ward off bile-induced colic (41). For the root cause of the bile disorder, one should follow this procedure: immersion in cool, refreshing water; applying sandalwood paste within a clean, folded cloth; sleeping at night on a bed made of gold, silver, bronze, or lotus leaves; and using ice fashioned from gold or silver (42). Parched rice flour derived from white *śāli* rice, along with milk mixed with sugar and honey, [removes] the burning sensation...

It immediately destroys fever caused by *pitta*, vomiting, and colic. (43) Wild meats are recommended for food; likewise, ghee and milk mixed with sweet substances are praised for those suffering from *pitta*-type colic. (44) For those suffering from *kapha*-type colic, fasting, emesis, and digestive stimulants (*pācana*) are indicated; however, thick or excessively sweet foods and lying down in bed should be avoided. (45) A decoction made from equal parts of *bilva*, *agnimantha*, *vṛṣa*, *citraka*, *nāgara*, *eraṇḍa*, *hiṅgu*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) quickly destroys colic arising from *kapha*.

It immediately destroys [the disease] and increases the digestive fire (jaṭharānala). 46 The juice of *mātuluṅga* (citron) mixed with the juice of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) and *saindhava* salt; and the juice of the root of *śobhāñjanaka* (black mustard) combined with black pepper (marica); 47 When combined with alkali (*kṣāra*) and honey, this [mixture] wards off cough caused by phlegm (*śleṣma*) and pain, and it undoubtedly destroys the cough arising from consumption (*kṣaya*). 48 A powder consisting of *tuvara*, *granthika*, *airaṇḍa*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *pathyā* (myrobalan), and *ajamoda*, combined with alkali and salt, is used for pain caused by phlegm (*kapha*). 49 [Also used are: *eraṇḍa*, *bilva*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *mātuluṅga*.

A decoction prepared from *pāṣāṇabhedin*, *kaṭu*, and *mūlaka*, mixed with oil combined with alkali (*kṣāra*), vermilion (*hiṅgula*), and salt, should be applied to the hips, thighs, penis, heart region, breasts, and abdomen. (50) The leaves of *paṭola* and *ariṣṭa* combined with *triphalā*, taken as a drink with honey and decoction, is for [fevers] caused by bile (*pitta*) and wind (*samīraṇa*). It wards off bile-fever, thirst, burning sensations, and internal hemorrhaging (*raktapitta*). (51–52) This paste (*kalka*) consisting of *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *viśvā*, *paṭola*, *nimba*, *ambuda*, and *tintiḍīka*, should be administered together with sugar.

For the pacification of colic arising from pitta and vāta: powder of *sauvarcala* salt together with *śaṭhī* and *nāgara*, drunk with boiled water mixed with ginger, destroys colic associated with vāta and kapha; it is highly recommended for severe pain in the flanks, abdominal disorders, impaired digestion, and heart disease. (53–54) A decoction of *dāru*, *nāgaraka*, *vāsā*, *hiṅgu*, and *sauvarcala* [is effective] in colic caused by vāta and kapha, in cases of undigested matter (*āma*), indigestion, and constipation. (55) Furthermore, *palāśa*, *kadalī*, *vāsā*, *pāmārga*, and *kokilākṣa*, boiled with cow’s urine and combined with *hiṅgu* and *nāgara*, [should be used]. (56)

56. It is beneficial in colic born of the three doṣas, in jaundice and constipation; it pacifies abdominal tumors and enlargements of the abdomen, and it regulates weak digestive fires. 57. Kubera-akṣa alone removes all types of colic; how much more so when combined with the three—pathyā, rucikara, and amaṭha? 58. Conch-ash (śaṅkhakṣāra), salt, asafoetida (hiṅgu), and the triad of pungents (vyoṣa), when drunk with warm water, destroy colic born of the three doṣas. 59. Fasting, emesis, purgation, unctuous enema (anuvāsana), and non-unctuous enema (nirūha)—these enema therapies are indicated in cases of digestive disorders (pariṇāma).

In cases arising from the three doṣas (60), the wise man should prepare boluses (*modaka*) with equal parts of powdered *citraka*, *trivṛt*, *dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, and the "three pungents" (*kaṭukatraya*), mixed with jaggery (61). One should eat them upon rising in the morning and afterwards drink warm water; this destroys the colic of a person arising from the transformation of food (*pariṇāma-śūla*) as well as [other] colic (62). *Yavānī*, *hiṅgu*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), alkali (*kṣāra*), *sauvarcala* salt, and *abhayā* should be drunk with wine from a jar that previously held liquor, in cases of colic from the three doṣas during the stage of digestion (63). *Hiṅgu*, the "three acrids" (*vyoṣa*), *vacā*, *ajamoda*, *hapuṣā*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, and *śaṭhī*...

Take cumin, long pepper root, pomegranate, *vṛkī*, *cavya*, ginger, and *tintiḍī*; from that, add sour *suvarcalā* and also alkali of barley (*yavakṣāra*), as well as *sarjikā*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and powdered *viḍa* salt. These should be made in equal parts and placed in the juice of *bījapūra*. One should make pills from this powder in the measure of a *kṣa* (bean) or a *phala* (fruit), or administer it as a paste; this bestows the fruit of health upon those suffering from wind disorders, colic, hemorrhoids, and splenic enlargement.

This formulation known as Hiṅgvādika quickly destroys cough, abdominal distension, urinary disorders, and pain in the heart; it is the destroyer of all types of colic and pain, the subduer of all vāta disorders, and the preventer of all wasting diseases (kṣaya). Diarrhea, thirst, fainting, constipation, heaviness, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and hiccups—these ten are the complications of colic. A physician desiring success, as proclaimed by Śrī, should avoid treating colic when accompanied by complications, but may treat it when free from complications. One suffering from colic should likewise avoid foods containing split pulses (dvidala).

One should avoid thick, cold, and slimy curd, as well as sleeping during the day (69). O best of physicians, *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), fermented grain-water (*sauvīraka*), liquor (*surā*), jaggery, and dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) are excellent for drinking (70). *Śatapuṣpā* and *vāstuka* are declared to be beneficial and are highly praised (71). O best of physicians, the meats of the black antelope (*eṇa*), partridge (*tittiri*), quail (*lāva*), crane (*krauñca*), rabbit (*śaśaka*), and *sārasa* crane are recommended (72). Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Colic," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The Eighth Chapter. Ātreya said: "Listen, my son, I shall explain the great disease of *pāṇḍuroga*. There are exactly five types of *pāṇḍuroga* that arise here among human beings: the *vātika*, the *paittika*, the *ślaiṣmika*, the *sānnipātika*, and the fifth is called the *rūkṣaṇa*; I shall now describe their origin. A man who is afflicted by long journeys, or by fever, or by blood-loss, or by wounds, or who indulges in anxiety, exhaustion, and suppression [of natural urges], becomes *pāṇḍu*. [Likewise, one who consumes] alkali..."

Through sour foods, the consumption of *kalya* and *maireya* wines, lack of physical exercise, excessive sexual indulgence, exhaustion, lack of sleep, excessive sleep, daytime sleep, these practices, as well as the eating of clay; or when the body is weakened on a journey or afflicted by disease, through the consumption of salt, pungent, and astringent substances, sourness, and clays; or through the excessive and constant consumption of very delicious things—these lead to the drying up of the blood, and thereby indeed to jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*). Because of that, swelling occurs in the eye-sockets, yellowness comes to the body, the urine becomes yellow, one spits, and the skin breaks open.

In such a person, premonitory symptoms arise: pricking pain, roughness, heaviness of the head, and yellowness of the skin, urine, eyes, and nails. Know that this wind-natured (vātika) jaundice in a human being is characterized by these signs. (6-7) Indeed, in this world, the jaundice born of bile (pittaja) produces a raw, yellowish complexion, causes emaciation, and results in a bitter taste in the mouth; it is accompanied by mild fever, thirst, delusion, and swelling, and the skin appears yellow. (8) Furthermore, in that [kaphaja type], drowsiness, swelling, cough associated with phlegm, as well as laziness, excessive perspiration, and heaviness arise. (9)

This disorder of paleness in a person is of the nature of *kapha*. It is characterized by drowsiness, laziness, swelling, vomiting, cough, nausea, emaciation, diarrhea, lassitude, roughness of the eyes, fever, and distress from hunger.

One should quickly observe the exhaustion caused by delusion and thirst in a person; such a case of *pāṇḍu* arising from *sannipāta* must be abandoned by physicians of sharp intellect. (10) Now hear, O son, regarding the great disease resulting from eating clay: even the most severe *pāṇḍuroga* becomes a destroyer of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (11) By eating clay, the impurities are dispersed and the channels are satisfied by the earth; however, they do not transform the blood, nor do they nourish the body with essence. (12) [This occurs] from drinking alkaline, astringent, or sweet substances... sa-... (text fragment)

Mud quickly aggravates a person's *mṛtsā* (mucous/impurity), and due to the provocation of *śleṣman*, it becomes sweet; thus, mud that has not been consumed does not prove beneficial. Indeed, the three humors (*doṣas*)—Vāta and the others—are powerful only when in a state of derangement; these humors quickly destroy one's luster, strength, and life-force.

In this way, the body becomes emaciated in *pāṇḍuroga* (anemia), and through the eating of clay, the digestive fire (*jaṭharavahni*) is destroyed. (14) A wise person should place iron in cow’s urine for seven nights; from that, a powder should be administered with honey to remove the disease of *pāṇḍu*. (15) Take equal parts of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *mustā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *citraka*. (16) Add one part of iron powder and macerate it with sugarcane juice for seven days; having been ground in a mortar, it will once again become excellent. (17) It should be consumed with honey as well.

This [preparation] with ghee is declared by wise and learned men to be a remover of anemia (pāṇḍuroga) and heart disease, and a destroyer of jaundice (kāmalā), hemorrhoids (arśas), and chlorosis (halīmaka). (18) One should combine these ingredients—tryūṣaṇa, triphalā, citraka, meghanāda, cavya, suradāru, mākṣika, granthika, śikhin, and bhṛṅgarāja—in portions of one pala each. (19) To this powder, one should add twice its weight of iron filings (lohacūrṇa) which has the luster of collyrium (kajjala). This should be cooked with urine equal to one-eighth of the total weight; when prepared, it bestows strength. (20) One should employ this as a therapeutic regimen for the restoration of strength.

Likewise, this excellent compound, when combined there [with honey], destroys *kapha*, jaundice, worms, anemia, skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and *halīmaka*. (21) One should mix equal parts of *punarnavā*, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *trivṛt*, *surāhvaya* (rāsnā), *niśāhvaya* (dāruharidrā), *cavya*, the three fruits (*phalatraya*), *ghana* (musta), barley, and *tiktavarohiṇī*; then add two parts of iron powder. (22) Having added twice as much cow’s milk and mixed it with *dārvī*, the wise physician should apply a plaster, dry it in the shade, and form pills to be taken with honey or cow’s urine.

One should consume [this] after considering the strength of the person and the severity of the disease (verse 23). It is for the sake of treating anemia (*pāṇḍvāmaya*), jaundice, all types of urinary disorders (*sarvamēha*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abdominal enlargement (*udarā*), indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), choleraic dysentery (*viṣūcikā*), edema (*śōpha*), diarrhea (*atisāra*), malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), constipation (*vibandha*), colic (*śūla*), worms (*krimi*), and the afflictions of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) (verse 24). One part each of *pañcakōlaka*, the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), *ghanā* (musta), *dēvadāru*, *kṛmiśatru* (viḍaṅga), and *kolaka* (black pepper)—these being combined in equal portions—are to be mixed with iron powder (*āyasa-rajas*) (verse 25). This should be cooked in eight times its quantity of urine until it becomes a paste (*lēpikā*), which one should then administer in a dose the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*).

Furthermore, one should perform the grinding with *chāyā* (shade-dried) [substances] and the drying; and with the churning of *surabhi*, one should prepare a beverage (*pānaka*) that pacifies jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), diarrhea, loss of appetite, consumption (*śoṣa*), urinary disorders (*meha*), anal fistula, and even worms. One should take one *prastha* of the juice of *dhātrī* fruits, one *prastha* of sugarcane juice, one *prastha* of the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd, and one *prastha* of the juice of *arka*; having mixed these together, they should be cooked over a mild fire until all defects have vanished.

One should mix this collection of medicinal ingredients and subsequently boil them in a quantity of exactly one *pala*. [The ingredients are: *bhṛṅgī*, *surāhva* (devadāru), *śatapuṣpā*, *dhānyaka*, fragrant *śuṇṭhī*, *madhuka*, *viśālā*, along with *pippalī* and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), as well as *viḍaṅga*, *mustā*, *hapuṣā*, and *dalāni*. 30–31. A powder of these—namely, *haridrā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *durālabhā*, *pauṣkara*, *vatsaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *ajamodā*, and *surasā dalāni*—should be employed. Into the middle [of the mixture], one should add double the amount of old jaggery (*guḍa*) and cow’s ghee (*goghṛta*), and then form it into pills (*vaṭikā*).

It prevents jaundice, hemorrhoids, anemia, and most severe fevers from arising through consumption; it destroys swelling, emaciation, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), wind-disorders, diarrhea, wasting, cough, and abdominal tumors. Wheat, *śāli* rice, barley, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, black gram, and *āḍhakī*—combined with ghee, milk, and buttermilk, along with *gāṇḍīra*, *vāstuka*, and *śatapuṣpā*—are declared to be wholesome and beneficial for a person suffering from anemia. Furthermore, the meat of wild animals is recommended for food, as are bitter, dry, and pungent substances.

In cases of *pāṇḍu* disease, strong burning substances, fermented gruel (*kāñjika*), sour spirits (*surāmla*), *sauvīraka*, *bījapūra*, and oils should be avoided. (36) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Pāṇḍu* Disease," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Ninth Chapter. Ātreya said: Listen, O best of physicians, to how a terrible disease arises among men who engage in improper activities and are dominated by wind (vāta). This disease, which causes a long-term accumulation [of humors] and brings about humiliation here through the ripening of one's natural past actions, is the destruction of a human being. It effects the ruin of the gods, or the torment of an embryo, the killing of cows, the earth, mountains, Brahmins, and children, and the devastation of gardens.

That man who effects the destruction of dwellings and the killing of women incurs, through these grave deeds, a great wasting disease that robs him of his body and wealth. He who burns the property of the gods, he who causes a miscarriage, he who administers poison, and he who destroys a grove—these take away his divinity.

By that very rule, there indeed arises for men a sharp pain that causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), which is terrible, soul-destroying, and fatal to human beings. (3) This wasting disease (*kṣaya*) should be understood as being of ten types by the best of physicians. (4) It may arise from exhaustion, or from carrying heavy loads, or from sleeping on uneven ground, or from long journeys, or from eating when the previous meal is undigested, or from excessive indulgence in sexual pleasure.

In those overcome by fever and lying on uneven beds, the phlegm, wind, and bile perish within their bodies due to excessive coldness; or, for one afflicted by disease, lying on uneven beds, or suffering from mild fever, the phlegm, bile, and wind may lead to the wasting away of the body.

Chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these seven, along with the aforementioned three, should be known as the ten types of depletion (*kṣaya*) that occur in the bodies of men. (6) Furthermore, their symptoms will be described; listen to them. (7) Through excessive sweating, extreme heat, anxiety, emaciation, fear, and so forth, as well as by the aggravation of Vāta and the other humors, the depletion of Vāta arises. (8) Due to that depletion of Vāta, there occurs drowsiness, burning in the limbs, thirst, loss of appetite, trembling, darkness of vision, exhaustion, and vertigo. (9) Therefore, products from marshy regions (*anūpa*) should be consumed.

One should consume juices, meat pastes, and the paste of garlic (*rasona*) and other such substances to destroy Vāta. (10) When Pitta is diminished, there arises sluggishness of the digestive fire (*agnimāndya*), as well as loss of appetite, lethargy, cough, nausea, swelling, and dullness of activity. (11) In cases of the depletion caused by Pitta, one should employ sudation, massage, and appetizing food and drink; one should consume the meat-juices of wild animals (*jāṅgala*). (12) Through physical exercise, sexual indulgence, the consumption of dry foods, and through heat and anger, the production of Kapha occurs. (13) By that [Kapha], a burning sensation or pallor (*pāṇḍu*) arises.

Swelling, labored breathing, dizziness, insomnia, hunger, and thirst occur; yet he finds pleasure even in sexual union. (14) For him, the consumption of cold food and drinks, along with the juices of tubers and vegetables, or the use of marshy products, curd, and milk, is recommended. (15) When the three *doṣas* have reached a state of depletion, death is indeed certain; therefore, O high-minded one, a balanced treatment should be applied for him. (16) Now, O Hārīta, listen as I describe the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*): rasa, rakta, māṃsa, and medas—each one individually.

The symptoms of depletion (kṣayalakṣaṇa): 17. In the depletion of rasa (plasma), there occurs excessive emaciation, sluggish digestion, trembling, headache, lethargy, and fatigue and vertigo. 18. In the depletion of rakta (blood), a person becomes pale, weak, and inactive; dyspnea, spitting, dryness, and sluggish digestion arise. 19. In the depletion of māṃsa (muscle), there is extreme thinness, difficulty in movement, a sense of breaking in the limbs, loss of sleep or excessive sleep, unconsciousness, and diminished vigor. 20. In the depletion of medas (fat), one has diminished strength, unconsciousness, a sensation of breaking in the limbs, and impaired gait.

Roughness, labored breathing, excessive coughing, loss of appetite, and weak digestion occur; by that [wind], dryness arises, and from it the emaciation of the body is produced. (21) In the depletion of bone, there is extreme sluggishness of movement and diminished vigor. In the depletion of fat, there is loss of consciousness, leanness, trembling, breaking pain in the limbs, vomiting, roughness, (22) wasting away of the humors, exhaustion, swelling, convulsions, and emaciation and irritability arise, O best of physicians; you should know these as the symptoms. In the depletion of marrow, there is trembling alone, or (23) dizziness, fatigue, extreme sluggishness of movement, and swelling.

Staying awake at night, drowsiness, mild fever, emaciation, and similar symptoms occur in a person when there is a depletion of semen; these are the movements and signs of the body during such a loss. Dryness, vertigo, trembling, wasting, anger, aversion toward women, deformity, physical impairment, and emaciation occurring in the joints [are also present]. Now I shall explain the medicines in their proper order: oleation, drying, and likewise depleting therapy are beneficial. One should consume the meat of wild animals as food, along with *guḍūcī*, ginger, and water boiled with *yavānī*.

Milk boiled with twenty-seven *marica* peppers is recommended for drinking at night; by this, there is an increase in the bodily fluids (*rasas*), and one is quickly liberated [from deficiency]. (28) The best of physicians have declared that the juices of wheat, barley, and *śāli* rice, and especially those of wild animals (*jāṅgala*), cause an increase in the bodily fluids. (29) Ghee, milk, sugar, honey, black pepper, and long pepper—this drink is highly praised for humans as a supreme means of increasing the blood. (30) One should prepare light foods and nourishing meals using grains from marshy lands (*anūpa*). (31ab)

One should consume ghee, milk, and other such items, as well as sweet substances (31). O best of physicians, the juices of wild animals should also be used for consumption (32). A powder made from sugar candy and other ingredients, goat’s milk with jujube fruits, and drinking [these] at dawn before breakfast are beneficial in cases of wasting disease (kṣaya) (33). O best of physicians, various cooked milks praised for their ghee content, sandalwood, and powders of grapes and other fruits should be used (34). O son, all types of meat from wild animals should be consumed, and one should employ all kinds of sweet foods (35).

In cases of seminal depletion (*śukrakṣaya*), one should especially consume soups that are well-cooked, as well as fresh butter, milk, and sweet substances (verse 36). Drinking the root of *karkaṭī* with milk, or the tuber of *vidārī* along with *śālmalī* and abundant sugar, is beneficial; sweet substances are likewise recommended (verse 37). Now, powders (*cūrṇa*) that cause the increase of semen will be described (verse 38). Equal parts of *balā*, *vidārī*, the minor five roots (*laghupañcamūlī*), the barks of the five milky trees (*pañcakṣīradruma*), *punarnavā*, *megha*, and *tugākṣīrī*, combined with the *sañjīvanīya* group and *madhuka*, should be employed (verse 39).

All these [ingredients] should be ground to the same measure as the *akṣa* fruit and mixed together; one should add hundreds of *kaṇā* seeds there, and having ground barley, wheat, and barley-meal in equal parts with *tugākṣīrī*, this should be combined with white rice and well-blended with *subhṛṅgāraka*. It should be prepared up to half the ear-length, and sugar should be used in all its parts. One should process it three times with the juice of *āmalakī* and then with cow’s milk; thereafter, it should be processed again with all [the ingredients] along with sugar and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

One should prepare that [medicine] and consume half a *pala* mixed with honey. When it has been digested, one should eat food avoiding pungent and sour tastes; [one may take] milk, ghee, white sugar, or foods made of barley, wheat, and *śāli* rice. Knowing the digestive fire within a person's stomach, those who know the procedure should administer this for the pacification of the disease of consumption (*kṣaya*), as well as for those exhausted by the depletion of wholesome food, those afflicted by long-standing heat, and those suffering from headache (43–44). It is also for those afflicted by bile (*pitta*), those with loss of blood, those oppressed by fatigue from travel, those with jaundice (*kāmalā*), and those afflicted by asthma (*śvāsa*).

This [powder] is recommended for those suffering from diabetes (madhumeha) and those with impaired senses, as it bestows strength. Furthermore, for a woman who has conceived, this powder made of *balā* and other herbs is highly commended. Thus ends the *Balādi-cūrṇa*. *Bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śoṇāka*, *kāśmarī*, *pāṭalī*, *śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *bhṛṅgī*, *śītā*, *āmalakī*, *jayantī*, *puṣkara*, *drākṣā*, *abhayā*, *amṛtā*, *medā*, *candana*, *aguru*, *padmaka*, and the two types of *balā*—these are the ingredients. (47–48) [The two types of *balā* are: *karṇe dve*. (49)

The physician, the best among healers, should add one *pala* each of both Jīvaka and Ṛṣabha, Kākolī, Kṣīrakākolī, and the fleshy root of Vidārī (49). He should take five hundred well-ripened Dhātrī fruits and boil them with one *droṇa* of water until reduced to one-fourth (50). Having thus boiled it and strained the decoction, the wise man should extract the medicinal pastes (*kalka*). He should then cook that decoction with the paste until it reaches the consistency of a *darvīpralepaka* (51), and subsequently boil the Āmalaka fruits with oil and clarified butter. (52)

The best of physicians should cook all these ingredients until they are powdered, then mix them with an equal amount of sugar and four *pala* of *tugākṣīrī*. He, the most excellent one, should add one thousand *pippalī* fruits, as well as two *pala* each of cinnamon bark (*tvac*), cardamom (*elā*), and cinnamon leaves (*patraka*). Having ground all these together, he should incorporate them into the previously described linctus. This elixir (*rasāyana*) for men should be licked with care in equal portions; it dries up asthma, cough, consumption, anemia, and jaundice, and is beneficial for those emaciated by disease, for children, and for the elderly.

It protects the body (56); it removes hoarseness of voice, thirst, heart disease, bile-blood disorders, defects of semen, severe headache, and chronic catarrh (57). It destroys chronic fever, weak digestion, skin diseases, fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, painful micturition, and stones; likewise, it acts as a digestive stimulant (58). It undoubtedly eliminates heart disease, colic, and abdominal distension. For barren women, it brings about the birth of sons; for the elderly and those with diminished virility, it restores potency (59). Even a eunuch becomes a supreme man capable of constant sexual union. It bestows intelligence and memory.

In this way, it certainly and swiftly increases one's vital energy (*tejas*); it bestows happiness and good fortune, and even an old man becomes like a youth. This great remedy for the destruction of consumption (*kṣaya*) was proclaimed by Atri; it is known as *Cyavanaprāśana*, spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya. Thus ends the electuary named *Cyavanaprāśana*. [The next formulation: Bhāṅgī, Puṣkaramūla, Citraka, Kaṇāmūla, Gajāhvā, Śaṭhī, Śaṅkhāhvā, Daśamūla, Citraka, Balā, Yāsā, and Ātmaguptā; likewise—

O best of physicians, having boiled one hundred *pathyā* fruits in five *āḍhakas* of water with two *palas* each of these [drugs] over a low fire continuously for a long time, one should then extinguish the heat, extract the strained liquid, and remove the hundred *pathyā* fruits. Once the decoction has cooled completely, this excellent decoction from a good vessel is highly recommended.

Having added one *tulā* of aged treacle (*guḍa*) and one *kuḍava* of honey, along with half that amount of ghee as the oily medium, one should then add five hundred and ten grains (*akṣaka*) of *magadhā* (long pepper). One should place the powder therein and stir it vigorously once more. Taken with two pieces of parched grain (*pathyā*) and honey, this is highly beneficial and destroys all diseases.

It destroys yellowish discoloration, *kāsaha*, *līmakā*, and anal diseases, as well as heart disease, hiccup, vertigo, chronic rhinitis, urinary disorders, hemorrhagic conditions, leprosy, and disorders of the *grahaṇī*. It expands the [menstrual] flow and alleviates swelling, wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, pain, consumption, urinary disorders, flatulence, and obstructive diseases; it is beneficial for those whose senses have declined.

The *abhayā* (harītakī) prepared by Agasti, which is equal to the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*), pacifies weak digestion, cures loss of appetite, or brings about its destruction while bestowing physical well-being. (66) A decoction of *balā*, *gokṣuraka*, and the two types of *bṛhatī*, combined with *kaṇā* (pippalī), milk, honey, and plenty of sugar, is beneficial when drunk; it destroys jaundice or consumption (*kṣaya*).

It destroys the thirst and the underlying cause of urinary disorders (meha) and bestows strength upon those with impaired senses. (67) One should prepare *pippalī* in increasing doses with milk and ghee, starting with five, then seven, then nine in sequence; (68) then eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen, nineteen, and twenty-one, each separately according to the order. (69) In this manner, the increase should proceed until reaching a dose of one hundred; thereafter, it should again be decreased gradually until the remainder is five.

One should feed [the patient] sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭikānna) combined with mung beans and ghee; in this way, both the young and the old man shall possess the strength of an elephant. The increasing dose of long pepper (pippalī-vardhamāna) is recommended when fever has subsided, as well as for weak digestion (mandāgni), jaundice (pīta), or hemorrhoids (gudaja). Thus ends the Pippalī-vardhamāna. Two palas each of bhṛṅgarāja (mārkava), realgar (dhātu), honey (mākṣika), punarnavā, tugākṣīrī, pṛkkā, śāliparṇī, vāsaka, and durālabhā should be taken. This should be combined with an amount of powder equal to half of the total, along with the three aromatics (trigandha) and black pepper (marica).

Take forty parts of *magadhā* (iron sulfate) and half that amount of *śilodbhava* (bitumen); add half that amount of *śilābheda* (red ochre), and mix all these together with an equal quantity of sesame powder and an amount of sugar equal to the whole. One should consume this with milk or with ghee; it is highly recommended. By this, consumption (*kṣaya*), pulmonary tuberculosis (*rājayakṣmā*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*) are destroyed. It quickly conquers epilepsy (*apasmāra*), and one becomes superior in strength and virility. Great diseases are pacified, and the man becomes rich in semen. Thus ends the section on the powder of *śilājatu*.

Take *jīvantikā*, *vatsaka*, *yaṣṭikā*, *pauṣkara*, *gokṣuraka*, the two types of *bala*, blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *āmalakī*, *yavāsa*, *trāyamāṇā*, *magadhā*, and *kuṣṭha*. (78) One *prastha* of the juice of grapes and *āmalakī*, two *prasthas* of goat’s milk, and one *prastha* of curd—boil these with ghee in a fire. This is highly recommended for consumption in cases of *vahni-vāta* (fire-wind), as well as for use as a nasal drop (*nasya*) and enema (*basti*). By its application, *rājayakṣmā*, *halīmaka*, jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), and fainting (*mūrchā*) are quickly destroyed. (79)

Dizziness, trembling, headache, and colic (80), as well as large stones, hemorrhoids, and leprosy—any disease located in the head—is destroyed by its administration; likewise, jaundice and consumption (rājayakṣmā) (81) go to their destruction and pacification by drinking it; anemia or diseases arising from the rectum are destroyed in men by administering it as an enema (basti); and erysipelas and boils are cured by sprinkling it (82). One should cook equal parts of long pepper (kaṇā), palāśa, five times the amount of milk, and ghee—the first [ingredient]—together, for use either in drinking or with food.

This excellent remedy should be given for the purpose of destroying the king’s consumption (rājakṣaya). 83. One part each of the five spices (pañcakola), the tips of barley, milk, curd, and ghee, along with equal portions of bhārṅgī, kuṣṭha, and pauṣkara; 84. one hundred harītakī fruits should be added to four times as much water, and this decoction should be combined with the other three ingredients and boiled over a gentle fire. 85. This ghee, prepared by gentle cooking, is used for drinking, nasal administration, and enemas; it brings about superior benefits for men suffering from jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), chlorosis (halīmaka), 86. and pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) due to wasting (kṣaya).

And this is indeed praised and declared by the best of physicians (87). One should take equal parts of liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), *balā*, *guḍūcī*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*), and prepare a decoction from them. To this, one should add an equal amount of *dhātrī* juice, as well as sugarcane juice (88), and the juice of *vidārī*. Then, one should add an equal portion of ghee, milk equal to the quantity of curd, and fresh butter equal to that (89). One should incorporate grapes and *tālīsa* as they are available. This prepared ghee should be administered for drinking, as nasal drops (*nasya*), or via enema (*basti*) (90). It conquers consumption (*rājayakṣmā*) and anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).

It is a most potent remedy for *halīmaka*, hemorrhoids, and blood-bile disorders; when used as a paste, it removes malignant erysipelas, bile-induced burns, and wounds. (91–92) One should take *balā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *parṇī*, *gokṣuraka*, *sthirā*, the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba*, *musta*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *durālabhā*. Having prepared a decoction from these and reduced it to its remaining essence, one should add this powder once it has been strained: *drākṣā*, *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *dhātrī*, and *tamālakī*. This decoction should be taken with an equal amount of milk. (93–94)

Fresh butter (navanītaka) mixed with ghee should be administered; that ghee should be applied at half the [usual] dose. This prepared ghee is indicated for drinking, as well as for enemas (basti), nasal drops (nasya), massage, and food. (95) It is recommended for chronic cough, consumption (kṣaya), jaundice (kāmalā), and for those whose strength and senses have wasted away due to royal consumption (rājakṣaya). It is also praised in cases of swelling and wounds, and it destroys headaches, pain in the flanks, and diseases of the anus. (96) [The ingredients are: sandalwood (candana), pine resin (sarala), deodar (dāru), liquorice (yaṣṭī), cardamom (elā), vālaka, śaṭhī, nala, śaileyaka, pṛkkā, padmaka, and vanakesara. (97)

Kaṅkolaka, murā, māṃsī, śairīya, two types of harītakī, reṇukā, tvak, kuṅkuma, the two types of sārivā, tiktā, aguru, nalikā, bale, and drākṣā—having thoroughly strained this decoction, one should cook oil with an equal portion of whey (mastu) and parched grain flour (lājā-rasa) over a gentle fire. Once prepared, the excellent physician should employ this oil for drinking, enemas, nasal administration, and massage. It destroys anemia, consumption, and cough; it is a destroyer of evil spirits, promotes strength and complexion, and cures chronic fever, epilepsy, and skin diseases.

Furthermore, [this medicine] removes scabies (101); it produces strength, nourishment, vigor, intelligence, wisdom, and increases longevity; it is said to bestow beauty and good fortune, and to bring glory to all beings (102). From approaching one's master’s wife, from longing for the wife of a guru, or from stealing gold belonging to a king, the disease of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā) arises (103). Or else, it is born of a malignant disease; listen, O son! Now hear how pulmonary consumption is produced by four causes (104): through physical exertion, travel, sexual intercourse, or by bodily affliction due to improper movement.

This great disease arises in a person from a body emaciated by the pain of wounds, or from excessive anger, grief, fasting, fear, and the observance of vows; it also arises from old age, or from excessively drawing a bow with a heavy string, or from lifting an excessive weight, or from slaughter, calamity, and captivity resulting from war; furthermore, its manifestation occurs due to over-distension of the abdomen, the consumption of bad food, anxiety, and excessive sexual indulgence—this is known as *rājayakṣmā*, the "kingly consumption" that seizes human strength and the heart. It may also arise from chest wounds, wasting, exhaustion, or even from a sudden affliction, or from excessive addiction to sexual intercourse.

Likewise, from the excessive consumption of dry [substances] (107), the body is emaciated by that, fever becomes mild, and at the end of the fever, swelling arises, along with excessive stool and urine (108). Diarrhea occurs, and through overeating, one coughs excessively, spits, and suffers greatly from wasting (109). Furthermore, there is an extreme longing for women and aversion to food; this disease is known as *rājayakṣmā* (consumption), and it is incurable (110). Both feet become numb, yet one considers a morsel of food to be much.

And for one who has clarity of voice but whose consumption (rājayakṣmā) does not subside, whatever food, whatever diet, and whatever kind he requests, that should be given to him—sweet and substantial. Whatever food the man suffering from consumption desires, or even a person [to visit], by obtaining each of those, his bodily tissues (dhātavaḥ) are restored. When swellings accompanied by blood occur and reach a state of suppuration in the patient, then a decoction of *punarnavā* with salt is prescribed. He shall live for four [years].

One who possesses superior strength may live for six months or a year with excellent treatments; however, beyond a thousand days, there is no life remaining for one afflicted by *rājayakṣman*. Deprived of breath, vitality, and vigor, wasted away, and with impaired senses, there can be no further recovery; such a patient, though maintained as chronic, eventually succumbs. When that disease becomes full of distress and coughing recurs again, the most terrible *rājayakṣman* shall become a snatcher of his life within three months, six months, or even three years.

Furthermore, having separately boiled one *prastha* of the juice of *śatamūlī*, one *prastha* of *guḍūcī* paste, one hundred *harītakī* fruits, and one *tulā* of *kuṭaja* bark, one should mix them together with *pūtanā*. Having applied a coating of *dārvī* (daruharidrā) to five hundred balls of jaggery (*guḍa*), one should add sugar, *āmalakī* powder, cinnamon, cardamom, *citraka*, *śaṭhī*, grapes, *kuṣṭha*, *śilājatu*, *śilābheda*, and *tālaka*, each in the measure of one *akṣa*. One should consume this with purified ghee (*śuddhasarpis*) on top of it.

One should drink milk and take food thereafter. (122) The one suffering from *rājayakṣman* (consumption) shall obtain happiness; he shall conquer *pāṇḍu* and *kāmalā*; his diarrhea will perish, and in strength he will become as powerful as an elephant. (123) Tālaka, śilābheda, and likewise śilājatu; the two types of kṣīraka, samaṅgā, kuṣṭha, nāgabalā, and balā; (124) elā, patrakatālīsa, tamāla, haricandana, mustā, drākṣā, rāsnā, muṇḍī, śaileyaka, and pura; (125) and surasā—these should be combined with black sesame seeds.

One should administer a fine powder consisting of two parts [of the aforementioned ingredients], combined with jaggery and honey (126). Thereafter, one should drink cow’s milk and take meals with milk. This should be vigorously employed for those emaciated by consumption (rājayakṣmā) and other diseases, those afflicted by malabsorption (grahaṇī), and those whose bodily tissues (dhātu) and strength are depleted (127). Even an old man becomes young again and delights in women; even a barren woman obtains a son, and even a eunuch attains virility. This is the formula named Tālakāmrātaka, as expounded by Kṛṣṇātreya (128–129). And there is also guḍūcī.

Two *bala* roots, *dhātrī*, and black pepper—this powder combined with jaggery (*guḍa*) removes *rājayakṣmā* (consumption) from men. (130) *Rice*, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat, *vāstuka* greens, and meat from wild animals; likewise, mung beans, cow’s milk, and the flesh of rabbits, *eṇa* deer, and *kuraṅga* deer; (131) The flesh of partridges, cranes, quails, eggplants, peacocks, and goat—these are declared to be beneficial as meat-based applications (*pralepa*) in this world. (132) One should feed the patient suffering from *kṣaya* or *rājayakṣmā* milk and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), avoiding alkaline, sour, pungent, or sharp substances and oil.

Sauvīraka, *surā*, and those [fermented drinks] excluding *rāji* should be used in cases of wasting (*kṣaya*) or pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*). 133. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wasting Disease," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 9.

The Tenth Chapter Due to excessive heat, or from the consumption of pungent, hot, and acrid substances; or from the use of alkaline and sour foods, or from the consumption of wine and similar drinks; (1) or from excessive sexual indulgence, cold exposure, or the consumption of dried vegetables and the like—by these causes, the *pitta* becomes aggravated and merges with the blood. (2) Then the son, fallen into doubt, questioned his father again. (3) Hārīta said: "How does *pitta* become aggravated? By what is it stirred up? Likewise, by what cause does the blood become aggravated? They are seen to manifest simultaneously. (4)

"By what means or in what manner does it thus proceed? Being asked this, the great teacher, the bull among sages, replied. Ātreya said: "Listen, O wise one of great luster, you who have reached the further shore of the medical scriptures: by whatever [factor] the *pitta* becomes aggravated, by that very same factor the blood (*rakta*) becomes aggravated. When the *pitta* is thus provoked within the digestive tract (*koṣṭha*), the *vāyu* violently tears [the channels]; the *prāṇa* leads it upward, while the *apāna* drives it downward. In the middle [of the body], the *samāna* causes the provocation of the *raktapitta*. In this way, the *pitta* and the blood become provoked simultaneously."

Anger is observed to be of four kinds, and its course is considered to be twofold. When it is mixed with *śleṣman* (phlegm) and moves upward, blood flows from the nose, mouth, and the openings of the ears; this condition is curable by one who desires victory. When it has moved downward and is mixed [with phlegm], it also flows through the anus; this is known as *raktapitta*, and it achieves success only with great difficulty. When it moves both downward and upward, being associated with *vāta* and *śleṣman*, one should know that it is incurable, even if it should be cured with great effort. This is due to the strength of the single path.

Or, if the *raktapitta* has arisen due to the force of the *nābhi* (abdominal region), it may be curable even with ease provided it is free from complications. (13) That which follows a single *doṣa* is curable; that which involves two *doṣas* is said to be palliable (*yāpya*); however, when *raktapitta* proceeds with all three *doṣas*, it is incurable. (14) In cases of upward-moving *raktapitta*, the wise physician should administer purgation (*vireka*); when the blood flows through the lower channels, emesis (*vamana*) is beneficial for him. (15) [In a patient] emaciated by disease, whose complexion is unimpaired, whose body lacks weakness, yet who has weak digestion, or suffers from sneezing, pallor, burning sensations, or wasting;

Thirst, vomiting, labored breathing, restlessness, aversion to food, delusion, cardiac pain, and vertigo may occur due to the complications of *rakta-pitta*. (16) These eighteen are declared to be the complications of *rakta-pitta*. Without complications it is curable; likewise, with complications it is incurable. (17) One who is afflicted by spitting blood, has red eyes, suffers from vertigo, and passes blood in the urine—such a person who vomits blood does not survive. (18) Thus the meaning of the diagnosis has been stated; next, I shall describe the treatment endowed with its proper characteristics.

Blood-bile (raktapitta) that is easily managed is as follows: when it is reddish, accompanied by wind and froth, or excessively black, or has the luster of yellow safflower due to bile, the wise call that "blood-bile caused by bile" (pittaja-pitta). When it is thick, pale, very dense, and associated with phlegm, it is called "blood-bile caused by phlegm" (kaphaja-pitta). One should not administer strong purgation to one who is depleted of flesh, emaciated, elderly, a child, afflicted by fever, or suffering from wasting, fainting, and vertigo. One should extract the juice of *vāsā* by pressing it and drink it with honey and sugar; [it is also used] for the nose, mouth, and ears.

The blood flowing from the eyes quickly returns to a state of normalcy. 22 Having drunk a decoction of *vāsā*, *utpala*, clay, *priyaṅgu*, *rodhra*, collyrium (*añjana*), and the filaments of the lotus mixed with honey and sugar, one should apply it; thus, even aggravated [blood] residing in the bile is quickly pacified. 23 If this remedy is applied using a cotton swab (*picuvāsaka*), how could a man suffer from hemorrhage (*raktapitta*), wasting (*kṣaya*), cough, dyspnea, or consumption (*yakṣma*)? Why do physicians not take care of their patient [with this]? 24 Or if, in the past, the mother of physicians performed such a rite, then the current treatment depends upon that prior action. 24 (continued)

It bestows success in cases of *raktapitta* (hemoptysis), wasting (*kṣaya*), and cough. (25) While *vāsā* exists, and while there is hope for life, why should one suffering from *raktapitta*, wasting, or cough despair? (26) Powdered *tālīsa* mixed with the juice of *vṛṣa* leaves should be drunk; beginning with this, it destroys phlegm-pitta cough, dizziness, and the distress arising from the combination of asthma and cough, and quickly provides relief for broken voice. (27) A decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*, combined with sugar and abundant honey—

It wards off asthma, cough, and hemorrhagic disorders (raktapitta). Goat’s milk or cow’s milk, boiled with four parts water and mixed with a paste [of the aforementioned drugs] along with sugar, is an excellent drink that quickly destroys raktapitta. Milk prepared with *balā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *āmalakī* fruits, *drākṣā*, *madhūka*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā* is beneficial as a drink for the pacification of a person suffering from raktapitta. Furthermore, the powder of the flowers of *khadira*, *priyaṅgu*, *kovidāra*, and *śālmali* [is also used].

One should lick [this] with honey; may you have good health. (31) Pippalī and Abhayā, processed seven times with the juice of Āṭarūṣaka and dried again, when combined with honey, conquer even most difficult-to-overcome *raktapitta*. (32) Equal parts of *elā* fruits, *padmaka*, *nāgakeśara*, *drākṣā*, *ghanā*, *madhuka*, and *pippalikā*, mixed with an equal amount of white sugar and used as a linctus (*leha*), completely destroys *raktapitta*. (33) It also overcomes burning sensations, the pain of fever, labored breathing, delusion, thirst, and fainting.

Likewise, if blood should flow from the nose, then one should grind *āmalakī* fruits with clarified butter and water and apply it as a paste to the head; that quickly stops the *raktapitta*. Alternatively, in cases of *raktapitta*, one should take grape juice enriched with clarified butter and sugar, or water enriched with white sugar; likewise, barley-food (*yavānna*) with sugarcane juice and white sugar destroys consumption (*kṣaya*), cough, and hemorrhage from injury. One should administer nasal drops (*nasya*) using the juice of *haritālīkā* or even the juice of lac (*lākṣā*).

A nasal drop (*nasya*) made from the juice produced by the blossoms of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*) may be used even when there is bleeding from the blood. (37) A nasal drop rich with sugar derived from mango stones and *jambu* fruits, or enriched with white sugar, is beneficial for fevers; it stops blood flowing from the nose and subdues hiccup, vomiting, and labored breathing. (38) A nasal drop consisting of the exudation from onion leaves, combined with licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*) and honey, subsequently conquers the flow of blood from the tip of the nose. (39) Having prepared the juice of *vāsā* leaves, the wise physician should further employ these: *rodhra*,... [and so forth].

This digestive powder, consisting of blue lotus (*utpala*), clay (*mṛttikā*), licorice (*madhuka*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and *priyaṅgu*, mixed with flower-nectar, is beneficial for disorders located in the *pitta* humor; it alleviates cough, jaundice, anemia, hemorrhagic diseases, dyspnea, and chest pain. (40) The juice of pomegranate flowers, or likewise the juice of lotus filaments (*kiñjalka*) and blue lotus, or lac-resin taken as a nasal drop (*nasya*) with milk, stops blood flowing from the nose. (41) If blood flows from the mouth, the prescribed remedy for that shall be performed; it will be described [below].

In humans, [this condition] is not easily curable; among humans, it follows that it occurs in the female womb, and bleeding from the vagina is incurable. (42) Honey, *madhuka*, *uśīra*, the filaments of the lotus, and the juice of *dūrvā* grass, when drunk here, along with pomegranate, sandalwood, white *kuṣṭha*, *padmaka*, and tender leaves; honey, *madhuka*, tender leaves, and the two types of *kodrava* grain—these should all be combined together. (43) Alternatively, milk scented with fragrant substances, or rice-water, should be prepared and mixed with a fourth part of these ingredients.

Even if it has flowed only slightly into the fire, it becomes effective; when the redness has spread to the circumference of the mouth, drinking this [blood] is prescribed. 44. If it has reached the path of the ears or the nose, then filling the ears and nose is ordained; blood stops the flow from the wound, as well as dyspnea, vomiting of blood, urinary disorders, insanity, and disease. 45. When it flows from the nose, nasal medication (nasya) should be used; when from the mouth, drinking is to be administered; when from the ears or eyes, filling is required; and when from the anal passage, a non-unctuous enema (nirūhaṇa) is indicated. 46.

One should lick the powder of pomegranate rind mixed with sugar, or again, one should lick the powder of lotus filaments mixed with sugar. This certainly and quickly stops bleeding from the mouth, as well as vomiting, exhaustion, dyspnea, emaciation, giddiness, and thirst. (47–48) The tender leaves of the Jambu and Āmra trees combined with Harītakī, and mixed with honey and sugar, serve to ward off blood from the mouth. Or likewise, [the tender shoots] of the Vaṭa, Arjuna, Vṛkṣaka, Kadamba, Jambu, Āmra, or Khadira, as they may be available— (49)

A linctus made with honey instantly stops bleeding from the mouth. (50) Śatāvarī, madhuka, balā, sugar, kākolī, pomegranate, fat, kṣīravidārī, phalinī, tamarind, and balā—this preparation, cooked with cow’s milk and ghee, is beneficial when used as a drink or in enemas; it cures bleeding from the vagina, penis, and anus, as well as cough and wasting. (51) Mṛdvīkā, madhuka, vidārī, vasudhā, nīlī, samaṅgā, the fruits [of madana], the two types of kākolī, the pair of bṛhatīs, vṛṣa, mahāmedā, and black sandalwood.

Jātī-pallava, paṭola, śyāmā, amṛtā, sañjīvaka, along with abhayā, the two types of medā, kucandana, and madhurasā—these śyāmā drugs in equal parts (52) should be boiled with cow’s milk according to the purified method until one-fourth remains; then, adding sugar and madhuka, this prepared decoction is recommended as a drink for men when seeking health.

It also destroys the blood that is beneficial for women; when it occurs in the rectum, the penis, or the path of the hair follicles, it destroys the flow of blood. This ghee known as Drākṣā-ghṛta is also prescribed for hemorrhagic fever (raktapitta), fever, gout (vātāsra), vaginal pain, vertigo, intoxication, insanity, and urinary disorders involving blood.

This [preparation] has been declared by Ātreya to be beneficial for men when drunk, used as an enema (basti), or applied as a nasal drop (nasya) in cases of bile disorders, acidity, severe skin diseases (kuṣṭha), consumption (kṣaya), chest wounds, hemorrhage, pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), and anemia (pāṇḍu). (54) Having extracted the inner bark, one should prepare slices of pumpkin (kūṣmāṇḍa); these should be quickly washed with sour gruel (kāñjika) and then again with water. (55) Afterwards, one should grind them in a prastha measure of milk and meat-broth, and then cook this again with ghee according to the proper method. (56) When they have become honey-like in appearance, one should then set them aside together with sugar.

In this regard, one should prepare these medicinal ingredients: 57 two *pala*s each of long pepper (*pippalī*) and ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), along with black pepper (*marica*), the two types of cumin (*jīraka*), as well as emblic myrobalan (*dhātrī*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), and cinnamon leaves (*patraka*). 58 One should add a powder of half a *pala* to that [mixture] and stir it with *dārvī* wood until it becomes a linctus (*leha*). 59 Then, having assessed the patient’s strength and weakness, one should lick it with honey and ghee. It cures hemoptysis (*raktapitta*), consumption (*kṣaya*), cough, jaundice, edema, and vertigo. 60

It cures vomiting, thirst, fever, dyspnea, anemia, chest wounds, consumption, epilepsy, headache, and severe pain in the female reproductive organs (yoniśūla). It stops chronic bleeding from the womb, alleviates mild fevers, and enables even an old man to become youthful and sexually potent; it makes a barren woman fertile. A man who lacks virility gains potency and becomes beloved by women. This *kūṣmāṇḍaka* linctus is a remedy for all diseases. One should take fifty palas of well-softened pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd and an equal amount of white sugar, adding water.

Having made this resolve, the wise one should prepare a *prastha* of [milk] thoroughly cooked with ghee (64). Knowing it is cooked, he should again mix it there with a decoction of *vāsā*; thereafter he should cook it until it reaches the consistency of a ladle-smeared paste (*darvīlepa*). Then, having understood this, he should add these ingredients once more (65): *dhātrī*, *ghanā*, *bhārṅgī*, and the three aromatics (*sugandhatraya*)—all of these should be added in a measure of one *karṣa*. Furthermore, *punarnavā*, ginger (*nāgara*), and coriander (*dhānyaka*) are said to be measured at one *pala* each (66). This is eight *pala*s of *śyāmā*.

One should prepare a powder and then thoroughly rub it all together with a ladle; when combined equally with honey, it destroys all diseases, quickly subdues cough, fever, and hemorrhaging from chest wounds, as well as hiccup (67). It overcomes heart disease, blood-bile, consumption, chronic catarrh, bilious acidity, asthma, and fainting; it is beneficial for women and excellent for children and the elderly, providing the destruction of all ailments (68). [The ingredients are] *śatāvarī*, *muṇḍitikā*, *amṛtā*, and the bark of *phala*.

Take five *pala*s each of *puṣkaramūla*, *bhārgī*, *vṛṣa*, *bṛhatī*, *khadira*, and *māṃsī*. Having quickly boiled them in water until it is reduced, once it has been strained, the wise man should add twelve *pala*s of honey and an equal amount of powdered iron mixed with sugar and ghee—sixteen *pala*s in total—and cook it in an iron vessel according to the prescribed method. (69–71) [With jaggery.]

Take equal parts of tugākṣīrī, viḍaṅga, magadhā (pippalī), śuṇṭhī, the two types of jīraka, kaṇṭaka, the three myrobalans (triphalā), bhṛṅgarāja, dhānyaka, marica, and kesara. One should prepare a dose of one pala for each ingredient; this well-ground powder should be placed in a ghee-smeared cauldron and used in a measure of one karṣa. At dawn, one should drink water from a lake and avoid heavy, sour, or wind-increasing foods; this "Red-Sour" preparation destroys fistula-in-ano and other swellings.

It is prescribed as a drying agent for consumption (yakṣman), leprosy (kuṣṭha), and abdominal tumors (gulma); it bestows strength and is highly aphrodisiac. It suddenly destroys internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), disorders of the female reproductive tract (yoniprabhāva), and painful menstrual bleeding accompanied by blood (sarakta-śūla). When applied to the penis and bladder of men, it cures bloody diarrhea (raktātisāra) and urinary disorders with blood (rudhira-prameha). It is declared to grant good fortune, produce luster, and extend brilliance, vitality, nourishment, and strength. Furthermore, the three fruits (phalatrika) should always be employed in cases of bloody diarrhea, painful discharge of blood, and burning sensations.

The powder of *samaṅgā*, *parpaṭa*, pomegranate, and *dhātakī* (77), combined with honey and sugar—or likewise with curd, ghee, and linctus—quickly wards off bloody diarrhea, continuous discharge of blood, and [disorders] of women; it is beneficial for men and suitable for alleviating diarrhea in children. (78–79) In cases of vaginal discharge (*yonipravāha*), this paste consisting of *madhuka*, *samaṅgā*, *elā* leaves, *nimba* leaves, *pathyā*, *mustā*, *viśālā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*, mixed with sugar, is beneficial. (80) It [stops] the vaginal discharge.

One should ward off vaginal pain, painful discharge, and thirst with equal parts of *elā*, *samaṅgā*, *śālmalī*, *harītakī*, and *māgadhikā*; a decoction prepared from these, taken with sugar and honey, will also stop the flow from the vagina. At the end of the summer heat, for the benefit of a person suffering from *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), one should strictly avoid foods that cause burning, sour things, *sauvīraka* (sour gruel), pungent, astringent, or alkaline substances, as well as *surā* liquor. Vegetables such as *vāstūka*, *cillī*, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *jīvantikā*, or *śatapuṣpikā* are beneficial.

In cases of *rakta-pitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), red rice, as well as mung beans and red-sesame rice, are beneficial. Barley, wheat, chickpeas, *kośātakī*, and *paṭola*—along with mung and black gram—are likewise helpful for warding off *rakta-pitta*. The meat of the antelope, rabbit, *kalāva*, partridge, *kuliṅga*, *kakerā*, peacock, crane, and pigeon, when prepared as minced meat (*palala*), increases wind and bile; yet it is beneficial if it provides strength, undiminished vitality, mental vigor, and luster. Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Rakta-pitta," in the third section of the *Hārīta-uttara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Eleventh Chapter. Ātreya said: Now, therefore, O son, the treatment of hemorrhoids (arśas) shall be explained; hear also the characteristics of those which are said to be of six types. (1) Those born from the three humors—wind, bile, and phlegm—and the fourth occurring in their combination (sannipāta); the fifth arises from blood; (2) the sixth is to be known as congenital (sahaja). Thus, the painful growths of the anus (gudaja) arise in these six ways. (3) Through fasting and the consumption of light and dry food...

Through the consumption of pungent, salty, and burning foods, or from the obstruction of *vāta*, there occurs constant straining; indeed, when deprived of a proper seat, the manifestation of hemorrhoids (*arśas*) arises from the force of the provoked wind. (4) In one who sits fasting, by the retention of feces and urine, and even by exposure to cold, the anal disease becomes aggravated. (5) By the consumption of salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter substances, by eating food that is excessive or too light, and by the extreme obstruction caused by cold, the provoked impurity is discharged through the anal passages; thus, blood and wind are emitted through the channels of the anus. (6)

Through the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, hot, burning, and heavy foods along with wind (vāyu) and water, or due to fatigue, the affliction of physical exercise, or the defects of travel and sexual intercourse, hemorrhoids arise from Pitta. (7) From a lack of exercise, habitual coldness, constant exposure to cold, or from another cause, as well as through greed for excessively sour food and being smeared with oil and fat, hemorrhoids arise from a disorder of Kapha. (8) Coldness, pricking pain, roughness, insomnia, abdominal tumors (gulma), enlargement of the abdomen (udara), prostate enlargement (aṣṭhīlā), cholera-like cramps (viṣūcikā), swelling in both [hands and feet], black nails, and [clouded] eyes are the symptoms.

9. Burning sensations, vertigo, fever, thirst, emaciation of the body, fainting, loss of appetite, and a yellowish discoloration of the eyes, teeth, and face, as well as diarrhea—these are the symptoms of hemorrhoids (gudaja) born from Pitta. 10. Excessive sleep, lethargy, lack of strength, mild pain, swellings, colic, abdominal tumors (gulma), and fissures in the anus—O knower of medicine, these are indeed the symptoms of hemorrhoids arising from Kapha, along with constipation, piercing pain, loss of appetite, and sluggishness of movement. 11. Colic, flatulence, loss of appetite, and cough [are also present].

Nausea, loss of appetite, and stiffness in the shoulders—all these indeed occur in cases of hemorrhoids (arśas). I shall now describe the symptoms of hemorrhoids: those caused by Vāta are characterized by itching, discharge of blood, roughness, irregularity, and length. Those caused by Pitta are accompanied by burning, are variegated, yellowish, or bluish in appearance, and discharge warm blood. Those caused by Kapha are accompanied by burning, are hard, subject to suppuration, associated with constipation, cold, itchy, and thick. They are also accompanied by burning and pain.

Darkness, itching, and dryness arise, and blood flows continuously; these are your hemorrhoids born of itching and blood (kaṇḍvāsṛgbhavārśas). (16) Worms resembling grains and sprouts also appear, and hemorrhoids with symptoms similar to those of wind and feces indeed arise. (17) Some are curved, sharp, and cracked at the tip, resembling long bimba fruits; some resemble mustard seeds, and others have the appearance of black dates.

Some [hemorrhoids] have the appearance of jujube fruits, some resemble *kalambaka* flowers, and others are like lotus seeds; O Manuja, this is the origin of hemorrhoids caused by the wind (*vāyu*). (18) In the anus, the nostrils, the ear-cavities, the mouth, or likewise in the eyelids, the corners of the eyes, and the middle of the vagina—these diseases that arise in men are not easily curable; treatment must be applied with great effort. (19) One should know that there are indeed three locations for hemorrhoids: within the three folds of the anus, externally, and internally. (20) Those located externally are easily cured.

O best of physicians, one arising internally from a weak seed may be cured with difficulty in the middle stage, but is incurable [in the final stage]. External hemorrhoids are best treated with medicinal pastes, suppositories, and fomentations; those in the middle stage with surgical instruments, and those arising internally with internal medicines. Therefore, my son, a knowledgeable physician should exert effort in treatment so that the patient may be protected and the disease may be averted. Indeed, if men suffer from swelling, emaciation, and fever in the hands, feet, face, navel, penis, or anus...

Dyspnea, vomiting, fainting, pain in the heart and flanks, emaciation, anorexia, constipation, and diarrhea—these are the twelve complications that arise from hemorrhoids (24). Indeed, hemorrhoids without complications are curable, but those with many complications are incurable (25). One afflicted by colic, anorexia, thirst, excessive discharge of blood, and suffering from pain, swelling, and diarrhea—a patient with hemorrhoids certainly does not survive (26). Therefore, O best of physicians, I shall now describe the treatment for hemorrhoids, by which pills, alkalis, and surgical instruments may be successfully employed for one's well-being.

27. The treatments for hemorrhoids have been declared; they destroy hemorrhoids, increase strength, pacify pitta and blood, and do not aggravate vāta. 28. At the outset, purgation is best; thereafter, one should administer medicine. A decoction of *pathyā*, *amṛtā*, and *dhanikā* taken with jaggery as a drink [is effective]. 29. A thick paste of *dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, *magadhā*, coriander, *bhallātaka*, jaggery, sesame, and *kuṣṭha*, when sprinkled with milk and drunk, destroys diseases of the anus. 30. *Nāgara*, *pippalī*, *bilva*, *viḍaṅga*, and *dantī*...

This paste of *śaṭī*, *bhayā*, and *trivṛt*, taken with treacle as a drink, brings about the destruction of hemorrhoids in men. (31) A decoction of *patra*, *kesara*, *śuṇṭhī*, *samarica*, *elā*, *tumburu*, *dhānya*, *viḍaṅga*, and sesame seeds, when drunk with *harītakī*, clarified butter, and treacle, destroys diseases of the rectum. (32) If a man eats this—*pippalī* and *abhayā* combined with treacle—in the morning, it quickly destroys his piles (*gudakīlaka*), along with the group of diseases such as jaundice and anemia. (33) The water of well-boiled eggplant fruit, [taken] with curd...

One should administer white sugar with water as a drink for hemorrhoids; it destroys worms and diseases born of worms. (34) Bhallātaka, black sesame, and myrobalan—this powder should be consumed by a man with jaggery. When drunk, it destroys hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, colic, piles, and cough; it utterly eradicates them. (35) A *sūraṇa* tuber wrapped in *arka* leaves and smeared with mud should indeed be heated until it reaches the color of fire. That [tuber], mixed with milk, rock salt, and oil, [should be eaten]. (36) He eats it.

Or, for the purpose of destroying hemorrhoids, even for a person who is free from disorders of Vāta, one should employ sesame seeds in equal parts with Citraka, Puṣkaramūla, and Śaṭī; to these one should add an equal amount of pieces of Sūraṇa tubers and Agnikaphala (Myrobalan) fruits. Having added four times as much rock salt (Saindhava) to all of this and having impregnated it with the juice of Arka leaves, one should place it in a jar of ghee and cook it over a fire of wild cow-dung. This milk, cooked with salt and ghee, when taken along with buttermilk as a post-drink, destroys [hemorrhoids] even more so.

It destroys hemorrhoids, piles, cholera, and fistula-in-ano; it is the destroyer of jaundice, anemia, abdominal distension, tumors, and loss of appetite, and is known as *Bhadraka-saindhava*, which eradicates urinary disorders, throat diseases, itching, and worms. (40–41) One should take equal parts of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), long pepper root (*magadhāmūla*), leadwort (*citraka*), and the three aromatics (*trigandha*); to these, an amount equal to all of them combined of marking-nut (*bhallātaka*) should be added. Having thoroughly ground these together, one should add jaggery (*guḍa*) weighing twice the total amount. (42) Having crushed everything together, [it should be placed] in an oiled vessel.

Having prepared this, it should be consumed daily by the wise in a dose of one *akṣa*; it destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal diseases, colic, tumors, and worms, while it extinguishes the "mare's fire" (excessive digestive heat) and cures anemia or consumption. (43) One should employ three *pala*s each of ginger and *triphalā*, four *pala*s of black pepper, and two *pala*s of long pepper. (44) One *pala* of *cavya* should be added there by the best of physicians; half a *pala* of *tālīśa* and half a *pala* of *padmaka* should be given, along with one *pala* of cumin. (45) [End of verse 45] [Verse 46 begins: ...of cumin...

Equal portions of treacle (guḍa) and Śyāmā (black jīvantī), weighed together, along with three hundred well-ripened and thick Pippalīs, should be ground in a mortar and kept in an oiled vessel. A pill the size of an Akṣa fruit should be administered to men every morning; it destroys all diseases and cures hemorrhoids, anemia (pāṇḍuroga), chlorosis (halīmaka), jaundice (kāmalaka), vertigo, abdominal tumors (gulma), diarrhea with blood, consumption (kṣaya), chest wounds (kṣata), and even incurable tuberculosis (yakṣmā), as well as chronic fever, loss of appetite, and catarrh (pīnasa). It is beneficial for these conditions.

This *Prāṇada-modaka* would be [efficacious]. (49) Having taken two *palas* each of *jājī*, *pippalīmūla*, *kola*, *magadhā*, *pathyā*, *agnika*, and *nāgara*, along with one *pala* of *sūkṣmailā* and one *pala* of *saindhava* salt; then, taking five hundred fruits of *bhallātaka*, one should add to that entire amount double the quantity of old *sūraṇa* root. Then, an equal amount of treacle (*guḍa*) should be added to all of this. (50) Having ground it, [one should take] a dose the size of a *vaṭaka* pill; the specific quality arising therefrom is that it wards off hemorrhoids, cures consumption, and likewise bestows nourishment and a healthy complexion.

It stimulates the weak digestive fire like a submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*), removes dizziness, and cures heart disease, anemia, colic, constipation, fistula-in-ano, and fear; it is a banisher of malignant pain. (51) Even though this formulation was prepared by the wise sage Kāṅkāyana, who was endowed with yogic discipline, one who desires happiness should employ it even when there is a disorder of the humors. (52) If you wish to rub away the afflictions of the anus, drink for seven days the best salt (*lavaṇottama*) combined with *vahni*, *kaliṅga*, *vacā*, *cirabilva*, and great *picumanda*, all well-churned together. (53) [Take] *viśva*, *upakulyā*, black pepper, and *kesara*...

A powder made from *patra*, *lavaṅga*, *elā*, and *vṛddhi* (pippalī), when combined with sugar, is beneficial for hemorrhoids (*gudāmaya*) and for the alleviation of abdominal pain. (54) A bolus (*modaka*) made of fresh jaggery (*guḍa*), *nāgara*, *puṣkara*, and *vṛddhadāruka*, along with *ambudāruka*, acts as a destroyer of the disease known as *durnāmaka* (hemorrhoids); it instantly makes even a grown man appear like a child. (55) A person who, at dawn, eats a single bolus (*vaṭaka*) made of equal parts of the powder of *trikaṭuka*, *abhayā*, *puṣkara*, *citraka*, and *kṛmiripu* (viḍaṅga), combined with jaggery, [attains health].

One who has suppressed hemorrhoids (guda-roga) gains an increase in digestive fire (agni-vṛddhi). 56 Having crushed black pepper (marica), ginger (nāgara), and *citraka* with one additional part of *sūraṇa*, and mixing it all in equal measure with jaggery (guḍa), one should consume a bolus (modaka) the size of a bilva fruit. This destroys the various disorders of bile (pitta-vikāra) in men and produces nourishment for the body. 57 The wise man should take sixteen dried parts of *sūraṇa* root that has attained a red color, having cut it into six pieces. 58 To that, an amount of *citraka* and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) equal to half of that [total weight] should be added.

One part of *marica* bound with jaggery forms a bolus (*modaka*) which, when consumed by people, possesses excellent qualities; it quickly destroys all diseases of the rectum, is said to stimulate the digestive fire, and cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and stomach pains. Take equal parts of the three fruits (*triphalā*), roots of *magadhajā*, *tālīsapatra*, *krimiripu* (mustard), *magadhā* (long pepper), and *puṣkaramūla*; add one part of *marica* and *dahana* (cinnamon), and an amount equal to the total of these, one part of *śuṇṭhī*, and one part of *sūraṇa* (yam). This [mixture], combined with *madana* and *capala* (mercury), [is effective].

One who consumes a bolus (vaṭaka) prepared here from powdered *vṛddhadāru*, *elā*, and *bhṛṅga*, with double the amount of jaggery (*śīrṇakhaṇḍa*), quickly and thoroughly overcomes abdominal disease. This renowned "King of Formulas" (*yogarāja*) cures hemorrhoids, bleeding, and bile disorders; cough, weak digestion, and colic; consumption, fever, and jaundice; as well as jaundice and worms. It bestows strength and nourishment, quickly restores the channels, and kindles the digestive fire. One should employ this King of Formulas, even by merely remembering it, as was done by Agastya.

By the application of this yoga, even Bhīma became a great consumer of food. (64) Having ground together cavya, pāṭhā, the three pungents (trikaṭu), magadhā, radish, tumburu, bilva, cumin, turmeric, surasā, pathyā, and rock salt, one should cook this well-prepared mixture with equal parts of ghee; when used for drinking or as an external massage, it removes hemorrhoids, wind diseases, and urinary stones. (65) Śyāmā, kuṣṭha, madhuka, madana, puṣpaka, citraka, bilva, dāru, prativiṣā, śatāhvā, kaliṅga, and aśaṭhī—[these are the ingredients]. (66)
