Oil ground with these and cooked with double the amount of milk is beneficial for both enemas and massage for the purpose of destroying anal diseases. (66) This oil is excellent for treating wind-diseases, ear-discharges, bleeding, earache, urinary stones, and for the piercing pain of wind in the calves, back, waist, head, and veins; it is also superior for constipation, suppression of flatus, diarrhea, obstructed labor, and for managing all types of accumulated disorders. (67) Take one *pala* each of Musta, Viśva, Viḍaṅga, Cavya, Kaśaṭhī, Pathyā, Tejovatī, Dantī, Indrayava, and Trivṛt, with an equal portion of each.

Therefore, one should add eight palas of *puruṣakara* and six palas of *vṛddhadāru*, and boil the entire decoction until it is reduced to one-sixteenth in a *droṇa* of water known as *sūraṇa*. Once it has become solid, one should cook it again with three times its weight of jaggery (*guḍa*). Having removed it, one should then add *citraka*, *trivṛt*, *tejovatī*, and *sūraṇa*. This makes one a speaker of eloquent words.

One should take equal parts of cardamom, cinnamon leaf, nagakesara, and clove, powder them, and add a sixteenth part of each; having placed all of this together in a smooth jar, one should consume it at dawn in a dose the size of a *vata* fruit. When that has been digested, a person of great intelligence should likewise drink abundant milk during meals.

It destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, jaundice, colic, constipation, cough, wasting diseases born of injury, and consumption (rājayakṣmā). One should boil two thousand bhallātaka fruits in one droṇa of water until one-quarter remains; into that decoction, one should again cook one tulā of jaggery. To that same mixture, one should add five hundred bhallātaka fruits—or three palas of them—along with trikaṭu, cumin, musta, rock salt, cardamom, cloves, cinnamon leaves, and nāgakeśara.

One *karṣa* each [of the ingredients] should be weighed and applied; having crushed them, they should be placed in oil or in a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). In the morning, one should eat jaggery (*guḍa*) in the size of a ball (*vaṭaka*). This indeed destroys diseases such as fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), worms, consumption (*yakṣman*), and anemia (*pāṇḍu*). It also cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*), urinary stones (*aśmarī*), urinary disorders (*meha*), chlorosis (*halīmaka*), and blood-bile (*raktapitta*), and it destroys chronic diarrhea (*grahaṇī*). It produces nourishment, bestows strength, brings about excellence of complexion, and grants happiness. [The decoction should be prepared with] *daśamūla*, *guḍūcī*, *śaṭī*, *ikṣuraka*, along with *citraka*, *bhārgī*, and *phala*.

One should take five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits and boil them in one *droṇa* of water (75). Once boiled, it should be removed from the heat and cooled completely; then one should add one hundred *guḍa* (molasses) that has been well-digested, along with equal parts of *elā*, *kesara*, *bhṛṅga*, and *lavaṅga*. Having made this into a powder, one should mix it all together (76). After saturating it with ghee for one day, one should place it in a vessel of ghee for seven days, or a person should store it in a greasy jar; when administered, this [remedy] destroys the entire multitude of diseases caused by hemorrhoids (77). One should consume a single *modaka* every morning; it utterly destroys [the disease].

It destroys hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, and pain; it is beneficial for cough, halīmaka, and jaundice, and indeed promotes the brilliance of the digestive fire. (78) That which, when thrown into cold water, dissolves by that very water, and turns red as it boils—this is the "single-boil" (*ekapāka*) variety of jaggery. (79) One should take four *pālikas* each of granthika, *citraka*, *musta*, *cavika*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *amṛtā*, *sahadevī*, *gajakarṇā*, *apāmārga*, and *kuṭheraka*. A wise person should grind these along with two thousand seeds of *bhallātaka* fruit in one *droṇa* of water. (80)

When the paste has been reduced to one-eighth part, one should add half a *tula* of iron powder and two *kuḍavas* of clarified butter; all of this should be stirred together in a single vessel. (82) Then, equal parts of the three fruits (*phalatrika*), the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *citraka*, the eight salts, and *viḍaṅga*—all totaling one *pala* each—should be added. (83) Four *palas* of *vṛddhadāru* and four *palas* of the plant called *mūrvā* should be included, along with eight *palas* of the powdered, dried *sūraṇa* tuber. (84) Having mixed these, one should taste the powder once it has been removed from the heat and cooled completely; it should then be stored in honey.

Having combined [these] in a quantity of two *kuḍavas*, this paste should first be administered in the morning before breakfast for hemorrhoids (*gudāmaya*). It quickly destroys piles, disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), jaundice, pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*), abdominal tumors, worms, urinary stones, weak digestion, urinary disorders, and blood diseases; it swiftly overcomes consumption and bestows physical vigor upon the person. By means of this elixir (*rasāyana*) formulation, it rapidly produces growth and destroys wrinkles and graying hair; through its application, a man becomes as strong as an elephant. O son, listen as I describe the treatment for bleeding piles (*raktārśas*): one should consume sesame seeds in the morning.

One should eat fresh butter mixed [with other ingredients], or fresh butter combined with sugar and ginger, or *keśara* (Mesua ferrea) and *mātuluṅga* (citron) along with sugar and *viḍaṅga*. One should consume the electuary of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* with fresh butter and sugar; by this, the wise pacify hemorrhoids characterized by blood. Having ground *samaṅgā*, the flowers of *śālmalī*, sandalwood, the bark of *kakubha*, blue lotus, and goat’s milk, one should drink it as a remedy for blood diseases. One drinks milk boiled with the root and filaments of *kuṭaja*, blue lotus, and the roots of *khadira* and *dhātukī*.

The application of *mrakṣaṇa* (an ointment) produced from blood, which causes the disorder that devours those born in the rectum; 93. And the excrement of a cock and likewise of a pigeon, house-soot, white mustard, *dhattūra*, and plantain leaves—having ground these with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should apply a wick (*varti*) to the rectum. 94. A wick made from the *sūraṇa* tuber should be applied after being smeared with jasmine juice and clarified butter; it quickly destroys the *gudakīlaka* (rectal protuberance) in the diseased rectum, as well as hemorrhoids and worms. 95. Turmeric, *mārkava*, costus, and house-soot...

Suvarcala and the juice of siddhārthaka are ground with kāñjika; when this forms a suppository (varti) mixed with honey and is inserted into the rectum, it quickly destroys hemorrhoids (arśas) in men. One pala of devadālī, along with huta-bhuj-yoṣā, the six groups of juices (rasānāṃ gaṇāḥ), ṣaḍgranthā, picumanda, water, kaṇā, bhārṅgī, śilā, and oil [are to be prepared].

Having ground [the ingredients] into a fine paste and combined them with *kañjika* (sour gruel), applying this as a plaster upon the stone [of the rectum] destroys hemorrhoids (*durnāma*), as well as anal fistulas (*gudaja*) and all diseases of dysentery (*atisāra*). (98) The application of instruments, surgical tools, and cauterization has been described; however, that is intended for *śalyaka* (foreign bodies). By means of an instrument, they are excised, and there, cauterization (*dāha*) should be performed. (99) Likewise, having cut away the *carmakīla* (skin tag or wart), it should be cauterized with alkali (*kṣāra*) by the wise physician. When cauterized with alkali, a color resembling a ripe *jambu* fruit is considered excellent. (100) Alternatively, one may cauterize with the alkali of *sūraṇa* (yam), along with the juice of *kadalī* (plantain) and *mudga* (mung bean).

The alkali of *palāśa* and *kokilākṣa*, combined with *apāmārga* and ghee, is recommended for the burning sensation caused by alkaline application; or alternatively, *kuṣṭha*, *pathyā*, nimba leaves, and realgar (101–102) should be mixed with honey and ghee and placed upon smokeless charcoal to fumigate the hemorrhoids until comfort is attained. Realgar, *nāgara*, guggulu, mustard seeds, *devadāru*, *pauṣkara*, *viśalyā*, and the juice of *sarjikā* should be used with ghee to fumigate the hemorrhoids and anal diseases. (103–104)

This destroys fistula-in-ano, malignant chronic rhinitis, and foul-smelling ulcers filled with pus. (105) A fumigation consisting of *nirguṇḍī* leaves, *patra*, *haritāla*, mustard powder, and *devāhva*, combined with ghee, sugar, and honey, [is used] for hemorrhoids and similar ailments.

This fumigation destroys Durnāma, Saruja, Vraṇa, Viṣama, Duṣṭa, Visarpa, Pāmā, Pīnasa, and Kāsa, and it eradicates the influence of the planets (Grahas). (106) Thus the procedure for the treatment has been declared; now hear from me the wholesome diet (pathya): Śāli rice, Ṣaṣṭika rice, Mudga beans, Kulattha, Āḍhakī, and Vāstuka; (107) Cillī, Śatapuṣpā, Kūṣmāṇḍaka, Paṭola, Kāravella, Tuṇḍīra, Sūraṇa, Rājikā, and Arjaka; (108) as well as jaggery, buttermilk, and ghee—these are always recommended for those suffering from hemorrhoids (Arśas), along with the meat of the boar and the Śallakī. (109)

The iguana, the mouse, or the reptile (109); and the flesh of the quail, the partridge, and the eggplant have been declared [as beneficial] (110). Dried meat, fish, curd, slimy oil, and a meal of bilva and eggplant must be strictly avoided (111), as well as unnatural postures, sleeping at night or during the day, and cold things or those that end in coldness; these should be carefully shunned. Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 111.11.

Chapter Twelve. Ātreya said: Now I shall declare the etiology and treatment of coughs; listen, O high-minded son, to the eight types of coughs as well. (1) Cough arises in men in every dwelling from laughter, excessive laughing, dust, suppression of wind, food moving through the wrong channels, and likewise from the suppression of the urge to sneeze. (2) It is produced by the consumption of sweet and slimy foods, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, and eating curd, sour substances, and cold items.

Madana oil, or even a small tuber, when processed with wine, brings about the birth of phlegm (kapha). Due to the reversal of the upward movement of the *udāna* breath, the phlegm follows the *prāṇa* breath and, becoming elongated, exits through the heart and causes coughing in the throat; by this means, it receives the name "cough" (*kāsa*). Eight types of cough have been described, and another, born of injury (*kṣataja*), is proclaimed. These are the vātika, paittika, ślaiṣmika, and sānnipātika [types]. Furthermore, there is that arising from vāta and pitta, that arising from śleṣma and pitta, the seventh here is that caused by blood (*lohita*), and the eighth is the [injury-born] one.

Consumption (kṣaya) arises from wasting; there is no dyspnea (śvāsa) without vāta, no cough (kāsa) without phlegm (śleṣman), and no wasting without blood (rakta), nor is there consumption devoid of pitta. Thus the origin of dyspnea has been described; now I shall state the characteristics by which the eightfold supreme cough is recognized in men. A person whose senses are diminished, who suffers pain in the flanks, who has excessive force [of breath], who is enveloped by piercing pain, whose throat is constricted, who appears drowsy, and whose voice is broken—such a person manifests the cough caused by vāta. There is a burning sensation in the throat.

In cough caused by *pitta*, there is fever, emaciation, fainting, thirst, giddiness, a pungent taste in the mouth, headache, and one spits out yellow phlegm; the nails and eyes turn yellow. (10) In cough born of *kapha*, there is stiffness, vomiting, a pale complexion, and one spits out thick phlegm; there is also loss of appetite and a heavy voice due to the body being filled with *kapha*. (11) In cough arising from all three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaja*), the patient is afflicted by itching, burning sensations, dyspnea, vomiting, emaciation, and anorexia; there is headache, swelling, and nausea. (12) Cough and itching... [The text ends here].

Thirst, pain in the abdomen, insomnia, dry cough, thirst, and phlegm arising from wind and bile; a smell of smoke, yellow discoloration, inflammation of the eyes, blood-stained [discharge], red eyes, and thirst—these are the symptoms of phlegm associated with bile and phlegm (pitta-śleṣmānvita). Due to excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse, suppression of natural urges, injury, or the exertion of lifting heavy loads, "blood-born" (kṣataja) phlegm arises. By this, there is pain in the heart, one coughs up dry matter mixed with blood, and there is labored breathing, emaciation of the body, and dejection.

Afflicted by mild fever (16), trembling, suffering from pain in the joints, and oppressed by delusion and vertigo—thus is described the blood-born *kapha* (raktaja-kapha) which robs men of their lives (17). From slight exertion, injury, emaciation, trauma, or eating at improper times, and through the application of falls and blows, the blood-born *kapha* arises (18). Accompanied by a cadaverous odor in the mouth, distressing pain in the heart, impaired senses (19), spitting of blood, dyspnea, or intoxication, the body constantly wastes away, and delusion and thirst arise—one who possesses these symptoms [is afflicted]. (20)

One should designate [this] as blood-cough (raktakāsa). 20. Now, the symptoms of cough are observed by inference from [the presence of] wasting (kṣaya), as well as in cases of jaundice (pāṇḍuroga), consumption (yakṣma), abdominal tumors (gulma), or chest-wound wasting (kṣatakṣaya). 21. Cough necessarily arises in cases of edema (śopha), hemorrhoids (arśas), and catarrh (pratiśyāya); one should carefully recognize the cough by inferring from these conditions. 22. Blood-cough occurs in the elderly, and it is declared to be palliable (yāpya). Cough arises in children due to the impairment of the wet-nurse (dhātrī). 23. These coughs have been fully described by the ten best of physicians; of them—

The remedy for the disorder consists of therapeutic measures as well as wholesome diet and medicine. (24) A decoction of *śatamūlī* boiled with the powder of *kaṇā*, drunk while lukewarm, destroys cough caused by Vāta accompanied by pain and acts as a digestive stimulant for men. (25) An electuary (*avaleha*) made from *bhārṅgī*, *śaṭhī*, *gostanī*, *śṛṅgavera*, *śṛṅgī*, and the powder of *kaṇā*, mixed with jaggery and oil, is beneficial for men and destroys the affliction of Vāta-born cough. (26) [The drugs are: *viśvā*, *duḥsparśa*, *śṛṅgī*, *śaṭhī*, *puṣkara*, *dāru*, *bhārṅgī*, *kaṇā*, and *musta*.

A powder combined with *rāsnā* and sugar, taken daily, indeed destroys cough arising from asthma and wind. (27) One should grind together *kaṭphala*, *kaṭutṛṇa*, *bhārṅgī*, *mustā*, *vacā*, *dhānyaka*, *parpaṭa*, *devadāru*, as well as *dārvī*, *viśvā*, and *karkaṭa*. This paste, when consumed by a person along with honey, serves as a remedy for coughs—whether they arise from phlegm, wasting (*kṣaya*), nasal catarrh (*pīnasa*), constriction of the throat, or dryness caused by wind—and it quickly destroys phlegm, hiccup, and fever. (28–29)

30. A linctus made from one *kola* (approx. 48g) each of grapes (*drākṣā*), emblic myrobalan (*āmalakī*), long pepper fruits (*phalapippalī*), and dates (*kharjūra*)—combined with phlegm (*śleṣman*)—destroys hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*), cough, and consumption (*kṣaya*), as well as jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and chlorosis (*halīmaka*). 31. A paste consisting of *vālā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, licorice (*madhuka*), *vṛṣa*, as well as costus (*kuṣṭha*) and neem (*picumandaka*), combined with *gavāstanī*, is beneficial when drunk for disorders arising from both bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*kapha*). 32. [A decoction] endowed with *mustā*, *āṭarūṣaka*, the three myrobalans (*phalatrika*), *dāru*, *bhārṅgī*, *vyāghrī*, along with its flowers, fruits, roots, and leaves, as well as *rāsnā* and *viṣā*.

A powder made from *madhurasā* (licorice) taken with boiled water destroys cough. Alternatively, a pill (*guṭikā*) formed by combining honey, jaggery, rock salt, and *magadhā-samahauṣadha* (long pepper and ginger), held in the mouth at night, possesses vast medicinal virtues; it destroys asthma, consumption, and cough caused by chest injury. Sugar, dates, grapes, parched rice, long pepper, honey, and ghee combined form a beneficial electuary (*lehya*) for warding off cough due to *pitta*. [The leaves of] *āṭarūṣaka* and the leaves of *picumanda* (neem)... [are used].

One should lick the fresh juice of *tulasī* along with *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, black pepper, and powdered ginger mixed with jaggery in cases of cough caused by *kapha*. One should drink a comfortably warm decoction of *bhārṅgī* and *nāgapippalī*. A wise person, having taken the juice of fresh ginger, should drink it with honey in cases of cough, asthma, coryza, and fever arising from *śleṣman*. Furthermore, *kaṭphala*, *bhūtṛṇa*, *bhārṅgī*, ginger, *parpaṭaka*, *vacā*, and *surāhva* boiled in water have likewise been declared by the learned to be used with honey.

This formulation, combined with honey, is used in cases of cough caused by vāta and kapha, dyspnea, hiccups, fever, consumption, and severe chronic cough (40). One should take tālīsa leaf, black pepper, and ginger, along with śyāmā, increasing each subsequent ingredient in double the quantity; likewise, add cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and small cardamom, and eight times the amount of long pepper and sugar (41). One should lick this in the morning for asthma and cough, as well as for splenic enlargement, anorexia, rhinitis, vomiting, hiccups, edema, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome, anemia, wasting, and pulmonary tuberculosis (42). [The formula begins with] tālīsa...

Triphalā, priyaṅgu, pippalīmūla, mustā, śaṭhī, dāruharidrā, elā, patra, nāgakeśara, lavaṅga, and likewise ginger; pippalī, kola, bālaka, along with cavikā, mūrvā, viṣā, karkaṭa, drākṣā, kuṣṭha, niśā, agni, vatsaka, vṛṣa, gokaṇṭa, and tiktā (43); as well as vṛkṣāmla, together with the sour juice of pomegranate and ripe jujube fruits—of these, a powder made in equal parts should be prepared, to which an equal amount of sugar is to be added.

Half a *pala* [of this] should be administered; it destroys hemorrhagic cough as well as asthma, and is always recommended for those suffering from anemia (*pāṇḍu*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), consumption of fat (*medaḥ-śoṣa*), anal diseases, and consumption (*yakṣman*). In wasting-cough (*kṣaya-kāsa*) caused by the three *doṣas*, there is pain from undigested matter (*āma-ja*), affliction from colic (*śūla-roga*), splitting of the joints, vertigo, exhaustion, emaciation, headache, and moisture in the eyes; it desires the deep-seated [condition]. Whether it be *khallī* or loss of consciousness, vomiting arises from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*); that vomiting is also of two kinds: oily (*snigdha*) and dry (*rūkṣa*). [One with] deep-set eyes... *(Note: The final line "gambhīranetro" appears to be a fragmentary conclusion or descriptor of a patient's condition.)*

When there is vomiting accompanied by constipation, flatulence, diarrhea, aching pain throughout the limbs, swelling, and extreme fainting (47), when the patient has deformed limbs, suffers from vertigo, perceives the world as spinning, experiences headache, trembles excessively, and his hands and feet feel cold as ice (48)—one should avoid from afar such vomiting characterized by these symptoms. It is incurable despite all medicinal combinations; likewise, that which arises from indigestion (ajīrṇa) should be avoided by the wise (49). [The remedy is: a decoction boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), along with rock salt and a paste of āmalaka, [to be taken with] the decoction...

One should drink [milk] mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*), which wards off vomiting caused by wind (*vāta*). (50) One should give milk with sugar to a man; it very quickly destroys vomiting born of bile (*pitta*). Alternatively, a linctus made from the powder of grapes (*drākṣā*) or *kṣīradārvī* drunk with honey destroys [vomiting]. (51) One should lick a powder of the three fruits (*phalatrika*), lotus stalk (*puṣkaraka*), *vacā*, as well as *abhayā* and rock salt (*saindhava*), along with jaggery (*guḍa*); drinking this combined with cow's urine destroys a person's vomiting caused by phlegm (*kapha*). (52) [The ingredients are: *śaṭhī*, *dārvī*, *abhayā*, ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), and long pepper (*māgadhī*).

Powder combined with ghee or mixed with buttermilk (takra) destroys vomiting caused by the three doṣas. (53) Parched rice flour (lāja) derived from red śāli rice, combined with honey and sugar, quickly destroys the affliction of fever in a young woman; this is my firm opinion. (54) Sandalwood rubbed with the juice of āmalakī, combined with honey, taken as a bolus weighing one pala or as a linctus, certainly destroys vomiting. (55) The fresh juice of pomegranate, cumin, and sugar, or else oil and honey—these four constitute the gargles (kavalagraha). (56)

It destroys the four types of *arocaka* (anorexia), as well as those caused by wind (*vāta*) and others, and those arising from the combination of two humors. (57) This powder—consisting of *trikaṭu*, the two types of *rajanī*, *phalatrika*, honey, and *yāvaśūka*—prepared in equal parts and mixed with honey, wards off vomiting. (58) Pomegranate with jaggery, or *drākṣā* and *pathyā* combined with ginger and jaggery, or *trivṛt* and ginger combined with jaggery, bring about the cessation of vomiting. (59) One should cause men to drink a cold decoction of *parpaṭa* with jaggery; it destroys even the most terrible vomiting accompanied by *pitta*.

A decoction of *kākolī* and *kākamācī* combined with sugar, or parched rice (*lāja*) mixed with sugar, destroys bilious vomiting in men. (60–61) The juice of *mātuluṅga* together with *pathyā* and sugar quickly cures and subdues bilious vomiting characterized by a coppery tint. (62) Upon seeing a severe bilious vomiting that causes burning sensations and vertigo, one should administer the leaves of *āragvadha* combined with honey and sugar. (63) Alternatively, drinking milk mixed with *mustā* and sugar is recommended. (64)

Jambu, mango sprouts, pomegranate, and emblic myrobalan, drunk with buttermilk after fasting, destroy vomiting caused by *kapha* in men. (65) One should administer the powder of *sarja*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, *kadamba*, and *kalola*, combined with ginger, coriander, and jaggery; this quickly destroys vomiting arising from *kapha* in men. A linctus made of *śaṭhī*, *kaṇā*, honey, and *viḍaṅga* likewise destroys it. (66) Having licked the powders of cardamom, cloves, *gajakesara*, *kola*, *sarja*, parched rice, *priyaṅgu*, sandalwood, and long pepper, mixed with *mārkava* and sugar, one overcomes vomiting.

It destroys [the disorders] born of phlegm, wind, and bile. (67) Having licked a powder made from equal parts of cardamom, cinnamon leaves, nakha, the bark of *gajakesara*, cardamom, *lāmajjaka*, *tagara*, *musta*, *priyaṅgu*, sandalwood, and *magadhajā* (long pepper), one overcomes vomiting caused by the three *doṣas* along with sugar. (68) When the *doṣa* has moved to the upper part [of the body], purgation is recommended; once that has occurred, emesis directed toward the lower part certainly brings relief. (69) Alternatively, when it has moved to both parts, then *bhayā* (harītakī), honey, and *krimija* (vacha) should be administered, knowing it to be an emetic for worms. (70)

The pacifying treatment (śamanakriyā): It should not be hot, nor excessively sour, nor pungent, nor likewise light; nor should there be *taṇḍulīyaka* greens, nor wine, nor fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*). This has been declared as beneficial in cases of vomiting (*vamidoṣa*); now hear from me what is wholesome here: meat from marshy regions (*anūpa*), boiled *śāli* rice, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vāstuka*; *āḍhakī*, lentil soup (*mudgayūṣa*), and curd combined with jaggery and ghee; and also *aṅgāramaṇḍaka*—this is praised as wholesome in vomiting. [One should administer] according to strength, according to time, according to the disease, and according to the digestive fire. Thus...

Having observed [these signs], they should administer wholesome therapeutic measures (74). One should employ daytime sleep in cases of vomiting, dyspnea, diarrhea, hiccups, emaciation, indigestion, or nausea, or again in cases of excessive salivation (75). Neither the drinking of hot water, nor overeating, nor physical exercise should be performed; one afflicted by vomiting should avoid these (76). Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named "The Treatment of Vomiting," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 12.

Chapter Thirteen. Ātreya said: From fear, fatigue, loss of strength, the consumption of split pulses and dry foods, exposure to the sun, or when fever has become chronic, and likewise from wasting (kṣaya) and injury (kṣataja), the three humors—Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha—become aggravated. The fourth type is declared to be that born of injury, while the fifth is remembered as that born of wasting. The sixth is proclaimed to be from indigestion (ajīrṇa), and the seventh from the consumption of dry foods. The eighth arises from [pre-existing] fever; hear my description of their symptoms. Emaciation, a darkish complexion of the face, a bad taste in the mouth, and trembling likewise [occur].

That thirst should be recognized by the best of physicians as being caused by Vāta. A desire for cold water, along with vertigo, burning sensations, delirium, fainting, and reddened eyes, is considered thirst born of Pitta. Drowsiness, a darkish complexion of the face, lassitude, an excess of phlegm (balāsa), a desire for warmth, and a thick, darkish coldness of the limbs arise from thirst born of Śleṣman. Pain in the eyes, vomiting, a burning sensation, vertigo, headache, trembling, and a coldness of the limbs constitute thirst originating from the three doṣas (tridoṣaja). Dryness of the mouth and yawning [occur].

Headache, heaviness in the abdomen, indigestion, and thirst are observed as the symptoms of disease in a person [suffering from] *ajīrṇa* (8). When thirst occurs due to the depletion of plasma (*rasakṣaya*), the patient suffers from weakness, hunger, exhaustion, emaciation, vertigo, dyspnea, and dejection; these manifest quickly (9). The thirst that arises in cases of chest injury and wasting is not relieved by food; another type of thirst described in one afflicted by fever is born from the force of the fever itself (10). Furthermore, thirst should be recognized by excellent physicians in cases of diarrhea or colic (11), as well as that which arises from diarrhea, vomiting, burning sensations, fainting, vertigo, and emaciation.

Know that thirst is incurable when it cannot be satisfied even by water. (12) Having observed that thirst arising from wind (*vāta*), curd with jaggery is recommended; likewise, drinking a decoction of *amṛtā* with jaggery removes thirst born of wind. (13) One should drink a paste of ginger, cumin, and fresh ginger mixed with water and *sauvarcala* salt, or a very cold decoction; this quickly destroys thirst arising from wind. (14) A decoction of *kāśmarya*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, grapes, *madhuka*, sandalwood, and *vālaka*, combined with sugar— [Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence.]

It removes thirst caused by *pitta*. (15) The bark of the *vaṭa* tree, *rodhra*, sugar, and sandalwood, together with pomegranate, ground with rice-wash or even with cold water and drunk, removes thirst arising from *pitta*. (16) A pill made from powdered *kuṣṭha*, blue lotus (*utpala*), parched grain (*lāja*), and the sprouts of the *nyagrodha* tree, mixed with sugar, wards off thirst. (17) Grape, blue lotus, and *yaṣṭīmadhu* are recommended for consumption with sugarcane juice; when drunk, they destroy thirst born of *pitta* and the burning sensation (*dāha*) produced by *pitta*. (18) [Up to the throat...]

A person should likewise drink milk mixed with sugar and induce emesis; this destroys thirst associated with pitta (sapaittikī). [19] For the destruction of thirst, one should drink water that has been heated by a red-hot clod of earth and then cooled, or water infused with sandalwood. [20] The fresh sprouts of *jambu* and mango, parched grain (*lāja*), sandalwood, and *dhātakī* flowers—these, ground together and combined with the juice of *vāsā*, form a linctus that removes phlegmatic thirst (*śleṣmatṛṣṇā*) and cures burning sensations, fainting, and vertigo. One should also drink a soup of *āḍhakī* mixed with parched grain and sugar. [21]

22. For the destruction of thirst caused by *śleṣman*, one should drink milk with black pepper, or water mixed with black pepper, or *kola* fruit boiled in milk. 23. A well-cooled decoction of *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *priyaṅgu*, the *lodhra* tree, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and *kuṣṭha*, combined with honey and sugar, destroys thirst arising from all three *doṣas*. 24. *Kāla*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *sārivā* taken with equal parts of sugar; or *pathyā* with pomegranate powder mixed with the juice of *mātuluṅga*. 25. Water that has been properly boiled in a wooden vessel and then cooled.

Likewise, one should have that water, which has been churned many times, drunk; and the best of physicians should also administer ghee in cases of parched palate. This [remedy] removes thirst, burning sensations, vertigo, vomiting, emaciation, and fainting. It certainly and swiftly wards off thirst born of injury or exhaustion. Pomegranate, *kola*, *cukrikā*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlavetasa*, along with the juice of *pathyā*, used as a plaster on the palate, quickly wards off emaciation and destroys thirst accompanied by fever. [So too does] *kesara*.

A paste of *mātuluṅga* ground with rice-water and applied to the palate while warm with honey removes dryness of the mouth. A paste of *mātuluṅga* with honey and sugar prevents dryness. A cold application of *padmaka* root boiled in cool water quickly destroys dryness of the palate. So too do the tender leaves of the *jambu* and *āmra* trees. A person afflicted by thirst should not first eat neem, *mātuluṅga*, fermented gruel (*sauvīra*), or ginger; for upon seeing them or tasting them from the mouth, saliva flows profusely.

By this, it removes wasting and also subdues thirst. (34) Red *śāli* rice is recommended, served with curd and sugar; such food is praised, whereas alkaline or pungent foods are not. (35) In cases of wasting (*śoṣa*), vomiting, thirst, exhaustion, alcoholism (*pānātyaya*), diarrhea, and wasting, sleeping during the day brings comfort. (36) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Thirst and Dryness of the Palate," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 13.

Chapter Fourteen. Ātreya said: Due to the suppression of natural urges, excessive obstruction, emaciation from injury, or thirst, as well as by the consumption of incompatible foods, the vitiated *doṣas* produce fainting (*mūrchā*). (1) The twelve channels (*nāḍikās*) associated with each of the five sense organs, when combined, number sixty; these block the openings of the channels, whereby the mind becomes faint. Due to the destruction of consciousness, the person quickly becomes unconscious and remains so for a long time. (2–3) He falls.

Fainting characterized by a state like that of wood is called *mūrchā*; it is declared to be of six types, arising from *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, as well as from blood, injury, wine, or poison. These [factors] provoke *pitta* and the combined wind and blood. Due to that, there is loss of consciousness and weakness; thus fainting (*mūrchā*) is described as delusion (*moha*). I shall now briefly describe their individual symptoms. One sees blue or black objects and enters darkness in an instant; trembling and softness of the limbs occur in these [states] in a moment.

One regains consciousness; fainting occurs, emaciation, distortion of the face, watering of the eyes, and a burning sensation arise, along with flatulence for a moment. (8) One sees yellow, blue, or green, and enters deeply into darkness; there is fever and thirst, and the eyes become red or yellow. (9) Furthermore, the body is perspiring, there is exhaustion, and the stools are broken up; from Pitta, a state of fainting arises, and headache is produced. (10) One perceives the quarters of the sky as filled with smoke, and sees darkness before one's eyes.

Turbidity of the eyes, weak digestion, darkness in the limbs, and coldness; one awakens only after a long time, and the throat makes an excessively gurgling sound. There is nausea and fainting born of *kapha*, along with various other symptoms. O best of physicians, epilepsy (*apasmāra*) is seen arising from the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*); it destroys living beings if accompanied by blood. One faints from the smell of blood; because of that fainting, there is headache, trembling, loss of motor function, muttering, and vomiting again and again. The mind becomes utterly bewildered.

One with red eyes, who is habitually inclined toward sleep and is under the influence of liquor (15), may experience another type [of fainting] due to chest wounds and wasting, or from the consumption of *kodrava* grain; because of that, he sleeps with a troubled mind, afflicted by delusion and fainting. Indeed, for a person, fainting arises from an excess of *pitta*, while dizziness in men arises from *pitta* and *vāyu*. A person’s lethargy (*tandrā*) results from *vāta* and *kapha*, and sleep (*nidrā*) occurs when *kapha*, *vāyu*, and darkness (*tamas*) prevail in a man (17). [This is prescribed] for the purpose of alleviating perspiration, affliction, massage, and wind.

For the pacification of pitta caused by cold food, drinks, or the breeze of a fan, the drinking of decoctions is always truly recommended; likewise, it is prescribed for fainting and delusions arising from kapha. (18) One should cause [the patient] to drink a cooled decoction of triphalā mixed with sugar, and one should also cause them to drink a decoction of durālabhā mixed with sugar. (19) Having ground long pepper (*kaṇā*), the marrow of *kola*, saffron, *uśīra*, and sandalwood with cold water, this "unbroken" drink (*akhaṇḍapāna*) destroys fainting. (20) Upon seeing fainting born of blood (*raktajā*), this should be administered.

In cases of wasting (kṣayaja), a cooling regimen is prescribed; for one who is weak and emaciated, it serves as a means to nourish the fainting state. When a man has reached a state of lost motor function, one should restore consciousness by squeezing his thumbs and pressing on his nostrils. Alternatively, one should gently press his body with the teeth or forceps, or apply cauterization (dāhana) to the forehead, the back, or the occipital region (mālaka). If he is not restored even thus, then swinging (āndolana) is beneficial. One should sprinkle the patient suffering from fainting with all kinds of cold water and fan him.

Indeed, swinging on a swing made from the seeds of *śikhipiccha* removes a person's fainting, delusion, dizziness, or alcoholism. (25) Where one grinds the seed of *karañja* with rock salt (*saindhava*), the juice of *rasona* leaves, *mārka*, and *vacā* with water to make a collyrium (*añjana*), it destroys the lethargy of the day. (26) A collyrium for the eyes made of horse saliva, black pepper, and salt is recommended; it utterly destroys a person’s lethargy or sleep for a hundred days. (27)

One who consumes fragrant, well-decocted *triphalā* with jaggery and fresh ginger in the morning, followed by sweet water for seven days, destroys intoxication, fainting, and insanity. (28) They desire the extraction of blood for the pacification of delusion and fainting; therefore, one should carefully perform bloodletting (*raktāvasecana*) in those conditions. (29) In all types of fainting, one should apply cold sprinklings, immersions, sandalwood paste, the breeze of fans, and cool food and drink. (30) [One should treat] wind-type fainting with syrups (*prapānaka*) made from sugar, sugarcane juice, and grapes.

A person may conquer fainting due to *pitta* with *kāśmarya* and *madhuka* alone. (31) One should drink a decoction of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, or ghee boiled [with it], or a decoction of *āmalaka* juice; one may also drink warm or cold juice mixed with sugar and parched grain (*lāja*). (32) It destroys fainting when taken with honey, and one should restore consciousness by means of medicinal plasters (*ālepa*). (33) Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fainting," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (34)

Chapter Fifteen. Ātreya said: When one dispels drowsiness and daytime sleep by means of songs, dances, and laughter of leaders [of the group], yet finds no sleep at night, then one should perform this procedure: (1) The best of physicians, having tied the root and the crest of the *kākamācī* plant, and having tied the crest with its tip pointing downward, produces sleep during the night. (2) For those seeking sleep, one should massage the soles of the feet with curd-whey (*mastu*); for him who has no sleep during the day, there shall be sleep during the nights. (3) [That sleep which arises] through fear, anxiety, or greed...

If one abandons that anxiety, sleep will not fail to come at night; indeed, sleep arises in an instant. (4) A decoction of the roots of *siṃhī*, *vyāghrī*, *siṃhamukhī*, *kākamācī*, *punarnavā*, and *vārttākī* induces sleep in men. (5) A decoction of *kākajaṅghā*, *apāmārga*, *kokilākṣa*, and *suparṇikā* quickly induces sleep, or one may tie their root as a crest-lock (*śikhā-bandha*). (6) Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Sleep," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. (15)

Chapter Sixteen. Ātreya said: O Lord of Sages, it has been taught that for those who have abandoned their worthy disciples and younger brothers, there arises a thirst equal to the *hālāhala* poison; from this separation, vomiting, labored breathing, delusion, burning sensations, and thirst are produced, along with the extreme loss of refuge and the impairment of the senses. (1) Those men who constantly indulge excessively in liquor become utterly corrupted; wine is like unwholesome food, acting as a cause of delusion. Just as poison is life-destroying when taken alone, yet is called nectar when combined with [proper] application (*yoga*), so too wine is beneficial when joined with [proper] application. (2)

If one indulges excessively due to improper application, it becomes extremely painful: wine causes distress for one afflicted by hunger or overcome by thirst, as does food for one who has not drunk wine; likewise, for those whose digestive powers are diminished, there is no benefit without food, nor without excessive drinking. (3–4) Even when there is overeating or indigestion, wine consumed causes pain. (5) In *vāta-madātyaya* (wind-type alcoholism), there is delirium and speech disorders. In *pitta-madātyaya* (bile-type alcoholism), there is burning sensation, fainting, diarrhea, and fever. (6) In *kaphaja-madātyaya* (phlegm-type alcoholism), there is vomiting, loss of appetite, lassitude, drowsiness, a sense of heaviness, numbness, coldness, and catarrh. (7)

O best of physicians, that intoxication which arises from the three *doṣas* and is treated with symptoms consistent with all three is called *madātyaya*. Emesis is recommended, as is the indulgence in sleep; bathing is beneficial, as is the drinking of milk. For food, curd mixed with jaggery is advised. A linctus consisting of whey (*mastu*), sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), dates (*kharjūra*), raisins (*mṛdvīkā*), *sārivā*, *amlīkā*, *āmalaka*, and *parūṣaka* destroys *madātyaya*. Alternatively, one may prepare a paste with the juice of grapes (*drākṣā*), *āmalaka*, dates, and *parūṣaka*, or with milk; this drink is effective for every type of *madātyaya*.

11. For intoxication from liquor (*madātyaya*), the drinking of milk combined with a decoction of *pathyā* (harītakī) is recommended. 12. In intoxication from betel nut (*pūgīphala*), trembling, delusion, fainting, exhaustion, darkness before the eyes, perspiration, agitation, and salivation occur. 13. One overwhelmed by dizziness and fatigue should be recognized as being in a state of betel-nut intoxication; a person should be known as "betel-intoxicated" by these symptoms. 14. For such a person, cold water drunk or an enema (*vasti*) would be beneficial; or sugar should be given for consumption, or *mustā* mixed with sugar. 15. [This applies to] intoxication from *kodrava* grains.

If fainting occurs, very cold milk should be given; in the case of intoxication by *dhattūra*, curd mixed with sugar should be administered. (16) One should quickly induce vomiting using *halinī*, *karavīra*, *mohinī*, *madayantī*, or other tubers. One should cause [the patient] to drink milk mixed with sugar, or curd, or sugar. (18) Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Alcoholism," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (16)

Chapter Seventeen. Ātreya said: When the *samāna* [vāyu] is provoked, it causes even the beautiful *pitta* located in the skin of a person's limb to become excessively burning, and indeed most terrible.

When there is rubbing of the teeth, a burning sensation arises in humans, as well as suffering from cold, dyspnea, emaciation, and restlessness; these symptoms are identical to those of Pitta-fever. O best of physicians, one should begin treatment for the pacification of the Doshas as in the case of Pitta-fever. A decoction of Kuśa grass, Ikṣumūla, Uśīra, Tagara, and Vālaka, combined with sugar, subdues cold and burning sensations. Parpaṭa, along with Tagara and Uśīra, boiled and mixed with sugar, when drunk cold, quickly destroys the burning sensation of Pitta-fever.

For men, an ointment made of *lāmajja*, sandalwood, and *uśīra* should be applied to alleviate the burning sensation; one should fan with palm-leaf fans over a bed of plantain leaves and lotuses. (5) An ointment mixed with *kālīyaka* resin is recommended for burning sensations; cool water is praised for warding off both feverish heat and thirst. (6) While the patient lies supine, one should place a bell-metal vessel above the navel; by pouring streams of cold water into it, he attains relief. (7) One should diligently fill the vessel with water until it overflows, whereby the patient attains comfort; likewise, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) washed a hundred times may be applied over that burning area.

One should hold *dhātrī* fruit in the mouth, or apply a cooling plaster for one suffering from burning sensations and dehydration; or else, a linctus may be taken to bring relief. (9) Having ground the tender leaves of *jambu* and mango, along with *nimba* and the juice of *bījapūra*, one should apply this as a plaster for burning sensations if one desires swift comfort. (10) Furthermore, a fountain-house, the cool moonlight of the moon, cooling drinks, a breeze, sandalwood paste, lotuses, and the bond of affection—these [bring relief].

Embracing and massaging Rāma, applying moist white garments to the pair of breasts, and [using] milk, sugar, iron, copper, and silver are beneficial for the pacification of burning sensations. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Burning Sensations," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Eighteen. Ātreya said: When pitta, vāyu, and kapha severely aggravate the udāna-vāyu, and the prāṇa-vāyu becomes intensely disturbed in the head, it causes a loss of motor function (naṣṭaceṣṭatā). It leads to unconsciousness, blocks the channels and the sense organs, and causes the person to fall like a log of wood while drooling from the mouth. The throat makes a gurgling sound, or foam is vomited; the hands and feet tremble, and the eyes become bloodshot and rolling. O best of physicians, these are the signs that arise in apasmāra (epilepsy).

The eyes become withdrawn and emaciated; there is darkness, burning sensations, and headache. One whose luster, senses, and consciousness are destroyed becomes an epileptic and perishes. For such a person suffering from epilepsy, a wise physician should administer medicinal drinks, collyrium, ointments, massages, and internal potions, as well as ghee and oil. Leaves of the *agasti* plant and black pepper, ground with urine, are recommended for use as a nasal drop (*nasya*); this quickly destroys epilepsy in a man. Alternatively, the root of the *bandhyākarkoṭikā* plant mixed with ghee and sugar may also be used as a nasal drop.

This should be employed for the pacification of epilepsy (8). Slices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd) with their cooked juices, along with *tryūṣaṇa*, *elā* leaves, *nāgakeśara*, *kumedhikā*, *granthika*, and *dhānyaka* in equal parts, mixed with white sugar and clarified butter (9), should be consumed at dawn; it is recommended that an unlimited amount of milk be taken over this. It quickly destroys the disorder of epilepsy and swiftly eliminates blood disorders (10). [Likewise,] a powder made from *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *brāhmī*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *punarnavā*, and *surasā* [is effective].

Combined with sugar and honey (11), it is beneficial for consumption to destroy epilepsy (*apasmāra*), and it is likewise helpful for insanity (*unmāda*) and disorders of bile and blood (*pittarakta*); furthermore, it bestows pregnancy upon a barren woman (*vandhyā*). (12) One should take two *palas* each of the roots of *rāsnā*, *māgadhikā*, *daśamūla*, and *śatāvarī*, as well as *caṇa*, *trivṛt*, and *eraṇḍa*. (13) Excellent physicians should add *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *śatāvarī*, *rāsnā*, *samaṅgā*, *śṛtaka*, the three aromatics (*trisugandha*), and *bhīru*. (14) As well as *kuṣṭha* and *vaitadīpaka*; clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be employed [in this preparation].

It destroys epilepsy, insanity, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and diseases of the rectum. (15) One should cook old ghee with the juices of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*; this indeed subdues epilepsy. (16) The oil known as *mahābalādya-taila* is recommended for use as an enema (*basti*) or as nasal drops (*nasya*); likewise, the *śatāvaryādi* group and the *sa-daiva* group are beneficial. (17) Furthermore, the *candanādya-ghṛta* should be employed here by the best physicians; it is beneficial in cases of epilepsy, insanity, or wind-diseases (*vāta-roga*). (18) [The formulation of] the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*)...

Asafoetida, rock salt, *kaṭukā*, *vacā*, seeds of *naktamāla*, and likewise white mustard seeds (19)—these, ground with goat’s urine and formed into pills dried in the shade, constitute a collyrium that destroys epilepsy and even terrible insanity (20). It is the destroyer of defects such as loss of memory and vertigo, and of the afflictions caused by malevolent spirits; it removes fever occurring on the first, second, or fourth day (21). It destroys the veil of cataracts, night-blindness, and headache; it restores consciousness to a person who has lost their senses due to a *sannipāta* disorder (22). [The next ingredient is] sandalwood.

Tagara, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭī, the three aromatics (trisugandha), vāsaka, mañjiṣṭhā, abhīru, mṛdvīkā, pāṭhā, śyāmā, and priyaṅgu; 23. svayaṃguptā, pīluparṇī, viṣā, rāsnā, gavādanī, the two types of kākoli, jīraka, medā, puṣkara, ghana, and vāluka; 24. vidārī, vāsumantī, vṛddhadantī, viḍaṅga, padmaka, aindravṛkṣa, as well as āragvadha and citraka; 25. dhānyaka with the five types of jīra, as well as tālīsapattraka, khadira, niryāsa, tagara, and kālīyaka.

One should grind *kaikaṭa* (26), *nāgakesara*, *parūṣaka*, and *kharjūra* together; this should then be processed (*bhāvita*) repeatedly with honey and ghee (27). This linctus is always recommended for severe epilepsy, insanity, jaundice, anemia, and chlorosis (28); for pulmonary consumption, internal hemorrhaging, those afflicted by bile-induced diarrhea, blood-dysentery, emaciation, diseases of the head, and chronic fever (29); for asthma, vertigo, vomiting, burning sensations, and cholera-like collapse; and for urinary calculi, urinary disorders, cough, and dyspnea.

In cases of chronic catarrh (pīnasa), this [preparation] should be employed; it wards off all diseases and should be administered to those who are barren, especially to the elderly (31). It is also beneficial for children; hear now the prescribed dosage. When used in this manner for a disease, it is considered by the wise to be a "Great Paste" (mahākalka) (32). It becomes powerful, efficacious, and fruitful in this world; it is called a linctus (leha) and is praised by the physician Kṛṣṇātreya (33). [The ingredients are: grapes, devadāru, as well as niśā, madhuka, kṛṣṇā, kaliṅga, trivṛt, and yaṣṭīkā.

Triphalā, viḍaṅga, kaṭukā, saffron, sandalwood, pomegranate, the four spices (cāturjātaka), nimba, turagī, tālīśapatra, musta, the two types of medā, devadāru, kuṣṭha, kamala, rodhra, samaṅgā, varī, bhārṅgī, kola, pomegranate, sour [substances], kāśmarya, śṛṅgāṭaka, kāmbojī, śaṇaghaṇṭikā, laghutarā, kṣudrā, and rāsnā—[these should be combined].

One should lick one *karṣa* of this powder mixed with equal parts of sugar, honey, ghee, and dates; it bestows all strength and quickly destroys epilepsy (35). It also conquers most dreadful insanity, consumption, phthisis, anemia, asthma, cough, urinary disorders, and hemorrhoids; it is recommended as beneficial for women (36). If no relief is obtained by these means, one should cauterize the forehead between the eyebrows with an iron rod, or cauterize the person on the crown of the head (37). One should avoid pungent and sour foods.

For those suffering from disorders of *rakta-pitta*, the decoction of liquor and betel nut (*surā-pūga-kaṣāya*) should be especially avoided (38). Indeed, things that cause delusion or fainting should not be consumed during an episode of epilepsy (39). Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Epilepsy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 18.

Chapter Nineteen. Ātreya said: This mental disease is known as *unmāda* (insanity). The aggravated *doṣas*, having become deranged, ascend upwards by way of the wrong channels. This condition called *unmāda* is difficult to cure even for the best of physicians; it is proclaimed to be of various types: one arising from a single *doṣa*, another from a combination of two (*dvi-doṣaja*), another from the combination of all three (*sannipāta*), and yet another arising from poison (*viṣa*). Furthermore, [it occurs] in an impure place, a deserted house, in the middle of a forest, or in a terrifying thicket, a street, or a temple. And then...

In some way, with a mind distressed by fear and apprehension, one should abandon the path of the agitated mind and instead follow the right path. 3. The birth of madness in men has been described by the most eminent authorities as arising from anxiety, pain, fear, joy, hesitation, greed, divine influence, the honoring of guests, twice-born ones, kings, and gurus, or from excessive love and separation from a beloved woman. 4. Because of that, a person may become agitated, cry out, recite distorted words, or when agitated, vomit; likewise, they may tremble, laugh, 5. run about, and even strike their own tongue.

If the patient's complexion fades away and he sees excessive light, the afflicted one should perceive wealth; then the best of physicians must perform the treatment for epilepsy (apasmāra). I shall explain this specifically within the section on the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā) hereafter. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Insanity," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty. Ātreya said: There are eighty-four well-known types of wind (vāta) that cause affliction in human beings; I shall describe their etiology briefly, one by one. Due to contradictory thoughts, improper diet, staying awake at night, excessive physical exercise, exposure to intense darkness, bloodletting, purgation, sitting in an uneven posture, and the suppression of the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and udāna breaths—when the strength and senses are diminished by travel and fatigue, the vāyu, though situated in the nearby tissues (dhātus), becomes provoked. Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these [functions] become vitiated by the fault of vāta, resulting in these disorders of vāta.

Headache, earache, pain in the temples, blood disorders, and afflictions of the half-head arise from the increase of the [doshas] day by day. (4) Furthermore, nasal complications, stiffness of the neck (manyā-stambha), lockjaw (hanu-graha), stiffness of the tongue, palate pain, as well as asthma (tamaka), vertigo (bhrama), (5) drowsiness (tandrā), dyspnea, throat disorders, and so forth—these sixteen diseases located in the head proceed from the provocation of the vital breath (prāṇa) when impelled by pitta. (6) Hiccups, dyspnea, labored breathing, cough, wasting with pain, hoarseness of voice (ghaṇṭikā), nausea, and pain in the heart.

Vomiting caused by bile, wind, and other humors (7); sneezing, yawning, as well as hoarseness of voice, nasal catarrh, loss of appetite, and rhinitis—these are said to arise from the *udāna* [vital air] (8). When the *udāna* is joined with phlegm (*śleṣman*), it becomes aggravated in the heart due to a disorder (9). We shall now describe the provocation of the wind known as *vyāna*; this wind pervades all limbs and causes a severe derangement of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) (10). It should be understood as residing within those constituents, and is described separately for each: in the case of skin-wind (*tvag-vāta*), there is horripilation, stiffness of the neck (*manyā*), and the shoulders (*aṃsa*) (11).

When Vāta resides in the muscle (māṃsa), there is swelling and piercing pain; when it resides in the fat (medas), there is trembling and breaking pain; when it reaches the bone (asthi), there is falling down; and when it reaches the marrow (majjan), falling occurs. (12) When it reaches the semen (śukra), there is swelling of the joints. Therefore, one should suppress the Vātas located in these tissues according to their skin-related symptoms, determining which are curable and which are incurable. (13) Vāyu residing in the muscle and fat, once abandoned [by other humors], is cured by medicines; others are cured with difficulty, or perhaps they are not cured at all. (14) There is horripilation, piercing pain, loss of sleep, loss of appetite, darkness, and the body feels as if pierced by needles.

Ants appear as if being pierced as they crawl about. Roughness occurs in the skin and the eyes, and emaciation arises again. There is a loss of the embryo, the menses, and the semen, as well as trembling. A weak digestive fire develops, and he sees various dreams; there is loss of sleep and agitation—this is the general symptom of Vāta. He repeatedly convulses his limbs, and there is piercing pain, pricking, and much fever; this condition, born from the provocation of Vyāna, is called Ākṣepaka (convulsive seizure). The body bends like a bow and convulses.

With eyes repeatedly moistened and fixed, he coos like a pigeon; the best of physicians call this by the name *apatantraka*. (19) According to another school of thought, others say it is considered *prahvapratānaka*; because the wind has seized half [the body], it is also known as *ardhāvabhedaka* or *apratānaka*. (20) That wind, resting upon the *kapha*, torments like a staff and quickly stiffens the limbs; that too is called *daṇḍāpratānaka*. (21) It rests upon the heart, the breasts, the hands, the fingers, the ankles, and the joints, seizing the sinews (*snāyu*).

He who causes the extension [of the body] is also called *snāyupratānaka* (22). Furthermore, the wind (*māruta*) that extends the external channels (*nāḍī*), or that which resides in the waist, makes one feel as if pierced by a thorn (23). The wise declare that this wind, *pratānaka*, is incurable; another, the fourth, is *ākṣepa*, arising from trauma (24). That *pratānaka* which is born from trauma is not curable. That which stretches upward and dries up the limbs (25), causing delusion and darkness, is known as *asthisaṃdhi-saṃśuṣkaka*.

From that, there occurs a half-karṣa of difficulty, and the back becomes contracted and withered; he who indeed possesses this half-extension is considered to have a single-limbed affliction (ekāṅgika). If one suffers from hemiplegia (ekāṅga-pakṣaghāta), the wind (vāyu) is cured only with great difficulty by all wind-destroying medicines. There is piercing pain, fainting, trembling, and a loss of sensation to touch due to contraction; when the limbs perish, that wind is designated as *tūnī*. Furthermore, he who experiences trembling, piercing pain, contraction, and yet retains the sense of touch— [is afflicted by another form].

It causes the limbs to tremble and is described as "pratitūnī. Heart-stiffness, back-stiffness, and thigh-stiffness, as well as *gṛdhrasī*, have been explained separately; listen further, O wise one. These sixteen types are proclaimed to arise from the provocation of the *vyāna* wind: colic (*śūla*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), flatulence (*ādhmāna*), and upward movement of wind with flatulence; indigestion due to transformation (*pariṇāma*), irregular digestion (*viṣamāgni*), indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and *vātiguḷmaka*; excessive moisture (*parikledin*), residual chyle (*rasaśeṣa*), chyle with impurities (*malavālaka*), obstructive (*bandhin*), breaking (*bhedī*), and *vilāsī*. These are the sixteen.

From the perspective of the *samāna* [vāyu], there are primarily sixteen disorders that should be recognized by the wise: fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara), pain in the bladder (bastiśūla), urinary disorders (meha), hemorrhoids (arśas), severe skin eruptions (koṭhaka), defects of the male organ (liṅgadoṣa), prolapse of the rectum (gudabhraṃśa), as well as other rectal pains (gudaśūlaka), retention of urine (mūtrarodha), and retention of feces (viḍrodha). These disorders have been described in detail and proclaimed at length. Furthermore, burning sensation (dāha), heat (santāpa), emaciation (śoṣa), and fainting (mūrchā) are caused by *marut* associated with *pitta*. Coldness (śaitya), swelling (śopha), loss of appetite (aruci), and numbness (jāḍya) are caused by *vāta* associated with *śleṣman*. These are the disorders arising from the combination of two humors (*dvandvaja*).

The wise know that [Vata] to be curable (Sādhya) when it is located in the Maruta [region]. (38) Even if it is solitary or located in the Samīra [region], it is considered most curable (Sādhyatama). (39) When one side of the face becomes distorted, the neck is bent, there is a deformity of the eyes, and the patient suffers from pain and stiffness; and for whom there is excessive pain in the neck, the cheeks, and the sides of the teeth—(40) those who are experts in the diseases of Vata call that condition Ardita (facial paralysis). (41) Furthermore, when there is salivation, dryness, lockjaw, loss of taste, and toothache, it is indeed Ardita caused by Vata.

In the Pittaja type, the limbs become yellow, fever and thirst arise, and there is delusion; furthermore, swelling and stiffness occur in this condition, or it may manifest as Ardita (facial paralysis). The prognostic signs for one who is about to recover from Ardita are: trembling, turbid eyes, emaciation, unblinking eyes, and speaking in a continuous yet indistinct manner. Even a severe and irregular case of Ardita may be cured in such a person. A terrible throat constriction occurs when yawning with the mouth wide open for the purpose of swallowing; likewise, lockjaw (Hanustambha) arises. These conditions are indeed difficult to cure, especially in cases of irregular [wind].

In cases of daytime sleep (divāsvapna) and inverted gazing (vivartitanirīkṣaṇa), the bodily wind (vāsanānila) obstructs the speech-carrying vessel (vāgvādinī śirā) and causes stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), whereby one looks toward the side with great difficulty. 46–47 Furthermore, when the wind (pavana) residing in the blood takes refuge in the vessels of the head and causes headache, that condition known as "seizure of the head" (śirograha) is also incurable. 48 Therefore, I shall describe the countermeasures by which the wind may be successfully treated: oleation (snehana), drying (rūkṣaṇa), digestive processing (pācana), and pacification (śamana) therapies should be employed. 49 Sudation (svedana), massage (mardana), and anointing (abhyaṅga) [are also required].

When [the disease] has reached the tendons, joints, and bones, the wise physician should administer oil enemas (basti-sneha) and non-unctuous enemas (nirūhaṇa), and perform surgical excision (bhedana). Then, using the Māṇimantha instrument, he should clear away the wind; in cases of vitiated semen (śukra-ga) involving the Vāyu humor, one should treat it like a case of infertility (bīja-vat). Muṇḍī, Guḍūcī, the two types of Bṛhatī, Rāsnā, and Samaṅgā—this decoction (kaṣāya) should be prepared from these combined ingredients. This may be mixed with milk, curd, or fresh butter (navanītaka). The wise physician should cook this over a gentle fire; once prepared, this ghee (ghṛta) serves as an unctuous agent (snehana) for men.

A dose of one *karṣa* is prescribed for drinking, as well as for massage and food; likewise, oleation (unctuous therapy) is beneficial for men suffering from disorders of Vāta for a period of seven days. (53–54) This very drink—consisting of *rāsnā*, *viḍaṅga*, *rajanī*, *nāgara*, *sauvīraka*, *surasā*, and *saindhava* salt, taken warm in a dose of one *karṣa* for five days—acts as a drying agent (*virūkṣaṇa*) for men. (55) Thereafter, for seven days, it serves as a proper digestive (*pācana*) agent; and once the morbid humors (*doṣa*) have been fully digested, [the treatment may proceed]. (56)

Therefore, one should administer a pacifying treatment. (56) I shall describe for you [the treatment] when [Vāta] has reached the *puṣṭi* stage and resorted to the *dhamanī* vessels: through abundant food and sudation, one destroys the wind (*samīra*); and sprinkling with warm water for seven days [is also effective]. (57) A decoction of *rāsnā*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *eraṇḍa*, *śataparvā*, and *punarnavā* quickly destroys Vāta diseases located in all parts of the body. (58) A decoction combined with *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, *dāru*, *nāgara*, and *eraṇḍa* is beneficial even for Vāta in all limbs that has entered the constituent elements (*dhātu*). (59) *Rāsnā*, *aśvagandhā*, *kāśīśa*, and *vacā*...

A decoction of *kapikacchu* drunk with castor oil destroys Vāta (60). A decoction of *rāsnā*, coriander, ginger, *yavānī*, and *daśamūla* is declared to be digestive (*pācana*) for men suffering from Vāta disorders (61). These *rāsnā*-based preparations are said to be purifying and beneficial (62). One should consume half a *pala* of garlic daily for one month, combined with asafoetida, rock salt, cumin, black salt (*sauvarcala*), as well as the three pungent spices (*kaṭutrika*) (63), along with clarified butter; this cures Vāta diseases.

It overcomes ardita (facial paralysis), pratānaka (tetanus), diseases affecting a single limb as well as those affecting all limbs, ūrustambha (rigidity of the thighs), disorders caused by worms, and also gṛdhrasī (sciatica). Half a pala and one pala of well-minced garlic, along with asafoetida, cumin, rock salt, sauvarcala salt, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya)—all these being finely powdered and mixed with an equal amount of oil—one should consume according to one's digestive fire in the morning, followed by a decoction of ruvuka as an after-drink. By using this for one month, one conquers all diseases of vāta.

It cures paralysis of a single limb (*ekāṅga*), paralysis of all limbs (*sarvāṅga*), stiffness of the thighs (*ūrustambha*), sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*), facial paralysis (*ardita*) located in the waist, back, bones, and joints, as well as *apatantraka*, chronic fever that has entered the bodily tissues (*dhātugata*), and the disease known as *saikarāhvaya*. A person should drink the fine powder of *nāgara*, *haridrā*, *kaṇā*, *jājī*, *ajamodā*, *vacā*, *saindhava*, *rāsnā*, and *madhuka* in equal parts daily with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*). Within twenty-one days, he destroys these diseases without a doubt; he shall become a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*).

The glorious [preparation], which has the resonance of a cloud or a drum, destroys all wind-diseases (*vātāmaya*) through its application as a linctus (*leha*), and it brings about well-being. (72) Śatāvarī, vacā, śuṇṭhī, rāsnā, kadara, śallakī, daśamūlī, balā, kiṇva, tumburu, and guḍūcī—(73) this paste (*kalka*), when combined with ghees (*ghṛta*), destroys the wind that has entered the body. (74) A decoction of the bark of *śallakī* and *cikkaṇī*, mixed with oil, shall restore a man afflicted by wind-disease (*vātārdita*) to health within twenty-one days. (75) Therefore, massage (*abhyaṅga*) should also be performed using both oils and ghees.

One should prepare guggulu and garlic according to the prescribed ritual (76). Take eight parts of *balā* root and four parts of *daśamūla*; boil these in four times the amount of water, or according to the measure of one *droṇa* (77). To that, one should add one *āḍhaka* of milk and mix in one *āḍhaka* of curd; one should also quickly add one *āḍhaka* of the soup of *kulattha* beans that has been left to stand overnight (78). One *droṇa* of sesame oil should be cooked slowly in a cauldron with *jīvantī*, the *jīvanīya* group, the two *kākali*s, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabha* (79), the two types of *medā*, *sarala*, and *devadāru*.

One should mix together the following: śallaka, kucandana, kālīyaka, sarjarasa, mañjiṣṭhā, the three aromatics (trisugandhika), 80; māṃsī, śaileyaka, kuṣṭha, vacā, kālānusārivā, śārivā, śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, punarnavā, 81; fermenting agent (kiṇvaka), wine (surā), mustā, as well as tālīśapatra, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), and the two types of sandalwood (vālukau). Having performed the auspicious recitation (maṅgalavācana), one should prepare this excellent, perfected substance endowed with all virtues, [placing it] in a golden or silver vessel, or otherwise in one made of clay or iron. 82–83.

Having heated it, one should administer it for drinking, massage, or as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha-basti) according to the strength of the person. It should be administered in cases of affliction by Vata, fractures, or even ruptures; likewise for women who are barren or men with scant semen. It should also be used for those who are emaciated, weak, or suffering from chronic fever, as well as for those afflicted by Ama-vata, after adding Kañcaṭa. It should be applied in the morning for dryness of the jaw, earache, and eye pain.

In cases of stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha) and pain in the flanks (pārśvaga), oil is as beneficial as nectar for all disorders of Vāta; it destroys dyspnea, cough, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, and diseases of the digestive tract (grahaṇī). It also swiftly subdues the eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha), as well as the influence of planets, spirits (bhūta), and demons (piśāca), as well as ḍākinīs and śākinīs. These beings flee to distant lands at the mere sight of Bala-oil, and it likewise drives away defects such as epilepsy (apasmāra) from afar. Through this oil, the elderly become young again, and even barren women obtain sons. This is the oil.

This is known as Mahābalādyam, and it is remembered as a remedy that removes severe wind disorders (mahāvāta). (91) One should add one āḍhaka of curd to one āḍhaka of a decoction of balā, as well as one āḍhaka of kulattha pulse broth and one āḍhaka of sauvīra (sour gruel). (92) Having combined these together, one should cook them and then incorporate the medicinal herbs: śatapuṣpā, devadāru, pippalī, gajapippalī, (93) the three aromatics (trisugandhi), surāmāṃsī, kuṣṭha, and daśamūla. One should cast the powder into this mixture and remove it from the heat once it is cooked. (94) It is to be employed for drinking, as well as for massage and non-unctuous enemas (nirūha).

In the administration of nasal therapy (nasya), this oil—consisting of excellent qualities—is the best for destroying eighty types of wind disorders (vātāmayas). Just as Mahābala oil is [renowned], so too is this [oil] an increaser of virtues. One should take the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, the juice of bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*), the juice of fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), and a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*). One should also include the broth of fermented black gram (*māṣakulmāṣa*) and horse-gram (*vāja*), along with curd; all these should be taken in equal parts, and oil should be used in half that quantity. It should be cooked over a gentle fire and removed once prepared for use as an external massage (*abhyaṅga*).

It should not be administered as a drink nor in enema therapy (99). It is used for filling the ears in ear diseases, for severe headache, for disorders of the half-head (hemiplegia), and for pain in the eyebrows, temples, and eyes (100). Through its application, a person quickly attains happiness; it destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha) and scabies (pāmā) when used as an ointment for skin diseases (101). It leads to rapid destruction [of disease], overcomes violent epilepsy (apasmāra), and prevents pain in the bladder, fatigue, and exhaustion caused by Vāta (102). This is to be known as Āmapākī; one should not perform [the treatment] upon it.

One should not administer digestive (pācana) or purgative (virecana) treatments; rather, one should employ a stabilizing (stambhana) therapy for it. (103) There is pricking pain in the waist, back, and chest region, as well as pain in the bladder. Furthermore, at the end [of the disease], the abdomen thunders like a *gulma* and there is swelling (*śopha*). (104) Heaviness of the head occurs and [the patient] falls violently to the left side. That [condition] which spreads to all limbs should also be recognized by the wise physician. (105) For that [condition], one should perform digestive treatment, and thereafter a purgative. Another type is proclaimed as being obstructive (*viṣṭambhin*), causing suppuration of the *gulma*, and spreading to all limbs. (106)

Among those [types of epilepsy], that which is to be cured is to be recognized; the other two are difficult to cure. Having suppressed the seizure, the patient should be treated with oleation and the left side [of the body] is said [to require specific care]. (107) Śyonāka, Pāṭalā, Bilva, Tarkārī, Pāribhadraka, Aśvagandhā, Kaṇṭakārī, Prasāriṇī, Punarnavā, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Atibalā, and Balā—these should be taken in equal parts. One should boil them until one-fourth remains in a *droṇa* of water and then strain it. (108–109) The medicinal herbs mentioned [in the following verses] should be employed by the best of physicians. (110) [These are: Śatapuṣpā, Vacā, and Māṃsī.

Dāru, śaileyaka, varā, pataṅga, candana, kuṣṭha, and likewise another, red sandalwood (raktacandana) [111]; karañja seeds, aṃśumatī, the three aromatics (trisugandhi), punarnavā, rāsnā, turaṅgagandhā, rock salt (saindhava), and durālabhā [112]; and miṣṭāsurasa—each of these two palas in weight—one should make them into a powder and add it there, along with one āḍhaka of lac juice [113], the juice of śatāvarī, four times as much goat’s milk, one āḍhaka of cow’s curd, and sesame oil.

One should employ this; once it is proven effective there, then the recitation of auspicious verses (*maṅgalavācana*) should follow. Having welcomed and installed him, this is known as the *Nārāyaṇa* [oil]. It destroys disorders of wind (*vāta*), as well as epilepsy and seizures (*apasmāra-graha*), diseases of the head, diseases of the ears, and even the eighteen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). A barren woman obtains a son, and even a eunuch attains virility. The emaciated become robust, and the fool becomes intent upon the pursuit of knowledge. This *Nārāyaṇa* oil was spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya. [There are] others...

One should employ those [medicines] with ghee and oil; by this, well-being arises and wind-disease (vātaroga) is subdued. 119. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wind-Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 20.

Chapter Twenty-One. Ātreya said: Listen, my son, I shall describe the symptoms to you in brief. In one who has been nourished by heavy food and drink, possesses weak digestion, and indulges in sexual intercourse, 1. when the body is satiated with bulbs and leafy vegetables, the undigested matter (*āma*), impelled by the wind (*vāyu*), undergoes putrefaction in the seat of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and gives rise to great pain. 2. This manifests as *āmātisāra* (diarrhea caused by undigested matter), swelling arises in the joints, there is a sense of aging in the limbs, and a falling away of phlegm occurs from the mouth. 3. When the back and neck are afflicted and pained, the body sinks down in exhaustion. The limb [is thus affected].

O best of physicians, in the case of Āmavāta, there occurs a state of deficiency; for that patient, oleation therapy (snehana) should not be administered, but rather digestive treatment (pācana) is prescribed. The wise physician should eliminate the Āma by means of the four types of signs of its digestion. There are six types of Āma: Viṣṭambhī, Gulmakṛt, Mehī, Pakvāma, Sarvāṅgaga, and another; I shall now describe their symptoms as well. In the case of Viṣṭambhī, heaviness, flatulence, and pain in the bladder arise; for that too, digestive treatment should be performed and oleation therapy should be applied. [The symptoms of the others follow: In whom the abdomen gurgles...

The waist region is afflicted as if by a *gulma* (abdominal tumor), and there is numbness; this is suspected to be an *āmagulma* (undigested morbid mass). At the outset, fasting (*laṅghana*) should be administered after assessing the strength and weakness of the body. One must never perform digestive processing (*pācana*), for if the *gulma* undergoes suppuration, it becomes delirious and death is certain. Furthermore, if the *gulma* is processed while still in a state of undigested morbidity (*āmāma*), death occurs swiftly and inevitably. In a patient whose limbs are oily, who has numbness, weak digestion, yet possesses strength, and whose *sneha-āma* (oily undigested matter) is not liquefied—such a condition is proclaimed as "vāma" (obstructed/retained *sneha*). For such a person, oleation therapy (*snehana*) should not be performed; instead, one should prescribe fasting.

Digestive (pācana) therapy must indeed be administered, yet one should also manage the diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āma). For a patient who has swelling of the face, stiffness, a distended abdomen, anorexia, and diarrhea, the disease is considered incurable by the wise. When life itself is in jeopardy, treatment should be abandoned; however, once digestion is known to have occurred, one should administer medicinal powders. When the undigested matter (āma) is digested, it falls downward with the stool, becoming clear and dark; there is no pain in the bladder, nor does fatigue or exhaustion persist in the case of āmavāta. This state should be recognized as "the digestion of āma."

One should administer digestive therapy (pācana) for that [type of Gulma]; purgation (virecana) should not be performed, but rather one should apply a styptic treatment (stambhana). (16) There is pricking pain in the waist, back, and chest; one suffering from bladder pain (basti-śūla), as well as abdominal rumbling (garjana) due to Gulma, and likewise swelling (śopha). (17) Heaviness of the head occurs and undigested matter (āma) falls off excessively; that too should be recognized by the wise as being localized in all limbs (sarvāṅga-ga). (18) For that, one should perform digestive therapy, followed immediately by purgation. Another type is considered to be obstructive (viṣṭambhī), characterized by the ripening of Gulma (gulma-pākī), and affecting all limbs. (19)

In this context, those [types of *āmavāta*] that are curable should be understood; two others are difficult to cure (*kaṣṭasādhya*), namely the oiled (*snehī*) and the undigested (*āma*). This pair is considered difficult to treat (*kṛcchrasādhya*). On the other hand, the ripened-undigested (*pakvāma*) is easily curable (*sukhasādhya*); having identified [the type], one should perform the treatment. Rāsnā, *trikaṇṭa*, eraṇḍa, *śatapuṣpā*, and *punarnavā*—this drink is recommended as a digestive (*pācanaka*) for undigested wind (*vāma-vāta*), O best of physicians. A man should drink a well-boiled, lukewarm decoction of rāsnā, *śyonāka*, *kāśmīra*, *cikkaṇīka*, and *puṣkara*. This is the digestive (*pācanaka*).

Know that this has been declared for *āmavāta*. In *āmavāta*, one should drink water boiled with *daśamūlī* mixed with *kaṇā* (pippalī). This powder of *guḍūcī*, *nāgara* (ginger), and *pathyā* (harītakī) combined with jaggery [is also beneficial]. 24 *dhānya*, *nāgara*, *rājāmla*, *devadāru*, *vacā*, and *abhayā* constitute a digestive (*pācana*) formulation for *āmavāta*; it is excellent and brings comfort. 25 Alternatively, one should drink the powder of *kola* (jujube) with warm water; it destroys *āmavāta*, weak digestion, colic, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). 26 Having added one *āḍhaka* of *balā* decoction, one should add one *āḍhaka* of curd and buttermilk.

One should cook together one āḍhaka of horse-gram (*kulattha*) soup and one āḍhaka of fermented barley gruel (*sauvīra*), and add these medicinal herbs: *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, long pepper (*pippalī*), elephant pepper (*gajapippalī*), the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), *murā*, *māṃsī*, costus (*kuṣṭha*), and the two sets of five roots (*pañcamūla*). One should cast the powder into that while it is boiling, and once prepared, one should remove it from the heat. It should be administered internally as a drink and used in the *nirūha* enema procedure; it destroys all wind-related diseases (*vātāmaya*) and is excellent for bestowing a multitude of virtues. One should drink oil extracted from castor seeds (*eraṇḍa*).

This is indeed the best purgative for *āmavāta* affecting all parts of the body when combined with jaggery and milk. (31) One part of ginger (*nāgara*), two parts of *krimija* (black pepper), and three parts of *trivṛt* should be added; having mixed this powder with an equal amount of jaggery, one should eat it like a bolus (*vaṭa*). Then, one should drink warm water and subsequently warm milk. By this means, a comfortable purgation occurs in cases of *āmavāta*. (32–33) The best of physicians should prepare a decoction of *viḍaṅga*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rāsnā*, *pathyā*, and *trikaṭu*, reducing it until one-eighth remains. (34)
