One should add milk, half as much decoction, and likewise castor oil (eraṇḍaja) in the measure of one karṣa; this purgative should be well-drunk as a follow-up drink (anupāna). (35) One should eat guḍūcī, triphalā, and harītakī (pathyā) together with jaggery (guḍa); for in cases of āmavāta, this purgative is excellent and brings comfort. (36) Abhayā ground with whey (mastu) and combined with honey and sugar will arrest diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra); likewise, jaggery and āmalaka [are effective]. (37) Vatsaka and the two types of jīraka, ground with curd (dadhi), should be administered; it pacifies āmātisāra and pain in the bladder (basti-śūla).

One should administer guggulu, garlic, and asafoetida combined with ginger; this decoction is for the destruction of Vāma and is a pacifier of Māruta. Ajamodā, ugragandhā, kuṣṭha, the three pungents (trikaṭuka), śaṭhī, the three fruits (phalatrika), bhārṅgī, puṣkara, the eight salts, the two types of jīraka, viḍaṅga, the two types of tumburu, and likewise dāru; as well as bilva, śilābhedaka, rodhra, vatsaka, vāsaka, the flower of dhātakī, the bark of śālmalī, and dāḍima—these [are the ingredients].

One should have these made into fine powders in equal proportions. (42) Combined with ghee, it certainly destroys Vāta quickly; taken with asafoetida and alkaline water, it destroys the pain of colic. (43) Likewise, it subdues Vāma-vāta even with warm water, as well as sciatica (gṛdhrasī) and hip pain with a decoction of the ten roots (daśamūla). (44) With intestinal obstructions, it is used with castor oil; in severe swelling, with cow’s urine; and for abdominal tumors (gulma), combined with jaggery, it conquers anemia (pāṇḍuroga). (45) Combined with honey, it [treats] urinary disorders (prameha); combined with sugar, it destroys consumption (yakṣman). It kills [the disease].

When properly administered, it wards off all terrible diseases (verse 46). One should avoid split pulses, sweet substances, oil, and slimy foods. O best of physicians, one should not bathe with cold water in cases of *āmavāta* (verse 47). Once the *āma* disorder has been cooked [digested], one should not indulge in *āmavāta*-provoking factors; nor should one consume hot, liquid, or especially liquefying foods (verse 48). Those wholesome diets prescribed for fever should also be employed here (verse 49). Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Āmavāta*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 21.

Chapter Twenty-two. Ātreya said: O high-minded one, hear now of the disorders arising from blood and wind (*raktavāta*). Intense pain arises in the region between the hips, thighs, and knees; one should recognize this as *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica), though its specific symptoms have not been mentioned here. A swelling may occur in the middle of the knee accompanied by acute pain; this, arising from blood and wind, is to be known as *koṣṭhaśīrṣikā*. That which causes the wasting away of the tendons (*kaṇḍarā*) in the arms, back, and between the fingers and toes should be recognized by the wise as such. [Also] *pādaharṣa* (cramp of the feet).

In this condition, there may be horripilation in the feet; at the conclusion of the provocation of *kapha* and *vāta*, perspiration occurs in the hands and feet (5). When combined with *pitta* and *vāta*, heat appears in the hands and feet at the end; one should then induce the flow of blood from these [limbs] and apply sudation (6). For massage, oil that subdues *vāta* should be used; for drinking, the "fivefold" (*pañcaka*) preparation of *rāsnā*, *śatāvarī*, the two types of *bala*, *pippalī*, and *puṣkaramūla* (7)—this powder, taken with castor oil, removes *gṛdhrasī*. The powder beginning with *ajamoda* is prescribed for *āmavāta*; that [should be applied] here as well (8).

The application [of these treatments] serves to ward off *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica), yet through these no relief is produced; one should cauterize with an iron rod. (9) In all diseases of the feet, one should perform a transverse cauterization two *aṅgulas* above the two ankles; having observed the vein in the foot, one should cauterize it. (10) One should also employ the wholesome diets prescribed for diseases of the wind (*vāta*). (11) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, named "The Treatment of *Gṛdhrasī*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (22)

Chapter Twenty-three. Ātreya said: Blood becomes aggravated in the body by pungent, alkaline, sour, and salty substances, or through suppression [of natural urges], restraint, or the indulgence in sleeping during the day and similar habits. (1) When the provocation of Vāyu is seen simultaneously in every limb of men, it is called Vātarakta, which manifests in the bodies of men. (2) O best of physicians, it arises in those who are delicate, as well as in women; furthermore, Vāta-śoṇita is especially aggravated in those who are corpulent. (3) Lassitude, itching, and the appearance of circular patches [occur].

One should recognize *vātarakta* by discoloration, throbbing, swelling, emaciation, burning sensation, and softness; likewise, by the darkening of the teeth and blood. Having observed these symptoms, which are distinct from others, one must apply the remedy. (5) One should administer purgation, bloodletting, and drinks, ointments, and electuaries; furthermore, one should give milk mixed with coriander (*dhānya*) and ginger (*nāgara*). (6) Having boiled the leaves of *paṭolī* and *nimba*, they should be taken with honey as a digestive for those suffering from *vātarakta*, as well as other pacifying treatments. (7) [The paste should be] ground with fermented rice-water (*kāñjika*).

The leaves of *picumanda* (neem) are recommended as an ointment for the pacification of *vātarakta* (gout/rheumatism). (8) *Dūrvā*, *mūrvā*, *śaṭhī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *dhānyaka*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā*—this is a medicinal paste to be applied with cold water as an ointment for *vātarakta*. (9) One *karṣa* of *dhānyaka* and two types of *jīraka* (cumin and black cumin), cooked with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be administered for consumption to alleviate the humors of those suffering from *vātarakta*. (10) If no relief is obtained by these means, then bloodletting (*raktāvasecana*) should be performed; furthermore, one should administer the wholesome diets prescribed for fever (*jvara*) in this case as well. (11)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktavāta," in the third section of the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-four. Ātreya said: Due to the consumption of jaggery and sour foods, as well as those indicated by incompatible diets (viruddhāhāra), the acid pitta (amla-pitta) becomes aggravated; by this, the throat is scorched. Either a burning sensation arises in his heart or a headache occurs; he emits sour eructations, and even sour hiccup assails his throat. Listen now to its remedy: one should quickly induce emesis. When the acid pitta has moved downward, a purgative (vireka) is administered. [The remedy consists of] a decoction of the leaves of the Pāribhadra tree and the fruits of the Āmalakī.

It should be administered; it removes *amlapitta*. A decoction of *paṭola* and *pāṭalā*, combined with *dhānya* and *nāgara*, is declared to be beneficial when taken with water for the alleviation of *amlapitta*. A decoction of *paṭola*, *viśva*, *amṛtavallī*, *tiktā*, *patra*, *nimba*, and *vatsaka* destroys *amlapitta* caused by *visarpa*, as well as circular skin eruptions (*maṇḍalaka*) and *dadru*. At night, a digestive stimulant (*sampācana*) mixed with the paste of *dhānya* and *nāgara* should be given. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Amlapitta*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-five. Ātreya said: Swelling (śopha) occurs when the strength of the body and the sense organs and hair-follicles are diminished by the consumption of sour, pungent, and hot substances; likewise, from the use of cold, clear, and slimy things; or from dryness, injury, falling, or from the retention [of urine or feces]. In a person whose wind (vāta), having reached the stomach (āmāśaya), subsequently rushes toward the extremities, this disorder of the humors (doṣa) arises. This movement of the swelling-disorder manifests separately in the hands and feet, or it occurs through the combination of two humors (dvandva). Thus it happens for a man.

Swellings originating internally that are localized on the face are curable; however, those that spread throughout the entire body, or occur on the feet in women or on the face in men, are incurable. This same type of swelling may also arise from the depletion of *vāta* in the region of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), in pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), or in abdominal enlargements (*udara*). A swelling born of blood (*rakta*) may likewise appear on the limbs, manifesting as a variety of swellings and disorders. Furthermore, other upward-moving swellings arising from *kapha* and *pitta* should be known as difficult to cure and accompanied by many complications. When *kapha* has reached the head...

When [the humor] is located in the *pakvāśaya* (large intestine), swelling arises in the middle [of the body], and even when the waste matter has moved downward, swelling occurs above. When the *rasa* (plasma) is affected, swellings pervade all [parts of the body], as do the *rasas* which follow the entire body; thus, there are swellings of the whole body or swellings of the middle part. Swellings of the whole body should be rejected [as incurable], as well as those occurring in the elderly or children, those born of trauma (*kṣataja*), those arising from wasting (*kṣayottha*), and those accompanied by vomiting, diarrhea, and dyspnea. Furthermore, a swelling that arises in a person who is dizzy, feverish, or emaciated, or one that results from [another] swelling, is incurable; it is not treatable by a physician if it is caused by no other disorder.

O best of physicians, [the disease] is to be treated as follows: from Vāta arise piercing pain, dryness, and dyspnea; from Pitta, fatigue, swelling, and a burning sensation; in the Kapha type, there is coldness, thick secretions, distressing itching, and it arises from the combination of two humors according to their dual characteristics. Therefore, I shall describe its treatment: fomentation, digestive (pācana) or purifying (śodhana) measures, purgation, and bloodletting; this is the prescribed procedure for swellings caused by decoctions (kaṣāya). Neither oleation nor drying (virūkṣaṇa) should be performed here. [The herbs] Punarnavā and Magadhajā...

A decoction of the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), nimba, abhayā, kaṭukā, paṭola, and dārvī, boiled until pleasantly warm, quickly causes swelling and abdominal enlargement to subside in a person through its digestive action. (13) Punarnavā, guḍūcī, and guggulu, taken as an equal paste, destroy the humors causing swelling, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and this type of *udara* caused by phlegm (*kapha*). (14) The urine of an elephant, a buffalo, or a bull, as well as parched grain (*lāja*) with black salt (*kaṇa*), should be employed; by drinking it, swelling quickly disappears, or likewise, milk mixed with castor oil (*eraṇḍa-taila*). (15)

In that case, the procedure of fomentation (saṃsvedana) should be performed again and again, either with castor leaves or with tamarind leaves. Having boiled hairy bitter gourd (kaṭutumbī) with either sour gruel (kāñjika) or water, fomentation should likewise be performed with that warm decoction. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Swelling" (śophacikitsā), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-Six. Ātreya said: By those same treatments that give rise to swelling (śvayathu), the Vāyu becomes aggravated; through impaired and irregular digestion, a Gulma arises in the abdomen. One should diagnose a Vāta-gulma when the abdomen gurgles, irregular digestion is observed, and there is pricking pain (todo) and colic (śūla) in the body. Emaciation, restlessness, a yellowish tint, affliction by mild fever, darkness of vision, vertigo, thirst, and pain—such a Gulma is born of Pitta. Emaciation, numbness, nausea, drowsiness, lethargy, and a sensation of cold [are its signs].

Weak digestion, constipation, and abdominal tumors (gulma) arising from phlegm (kapha); delusion, confusion, dullness, restlessness, hunger, thirst, laziness, and excessive sleep—these characterize the kapha-pitta type of gulma. Sleep, laziness, burning sensations, swelling, pain accompanied by fever, discoloration, restlessness, dullness, constipation, and deformity of the limbs; likewise, diarrhea, fainting, thirst, nausea, trembling, dyspnea, loss of appetite, and indigestion—this is the sānnipātika (tridiscordant) gulma, which is curable.

A dual disorder (*dvandva*) arising from a single *doṣa* is cured with difficulty; that which arises from *sannipāta* is incurable. We shall now describe its treatment. (8) The very same treatment prescribed for the liver (*yakṛt*) and the *grahaṇī* is declared [for this], as well as fasting (*upavāraṇa*); likewise, the spleen (*plīhā*) has been fully described, and need not be stated again here. (9) Now listen as the treatment for abdominal enlargement (*udara*) and abdominal tumors (*gulma*) is being explained: oleation (*snehana*), drying (*rūkṣaṇa*), digestive processing (*pācana*), purifications (*śodhana*), (10) pacification (*saṃśamana*), purgation (*vireka*), enemas (*basti*), oil-massages (*sneha*), dry massages (*nirūkṣaṇa*), the drinking of alkali (*kṣārapāna*), and medicinal powders (*cūrṇa*).

The therapeutic procedure for the treatment of *gulma* (abdominal tumors): 11–12. One should prepare a decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *dāru*, *surasā*, *mūrvā*, and the five minor roots (*laghu-pañcamūla*), reduced to one-eighth its original volume. To this, an equal amount of milk and an equal amount of curd should be added, along with an equal amount of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). This should be cooked over a moderate fire until the ghee appears distinct; it is then declared "prepared. 13–14. This should be administered as a drink, for massage (*abhyaṅga*), or applied to the vessel [of the disease]. Since there are seven types of oleation (*sneha*), dry therapy (*rūkṣaṇa*) is beneficial following that. This should be performed for three days; I shall now explain it here.

One who is skilled [in treatment] should prescribe *śuṇṭhī*, *sauvarcala* salt, the two types of *jīra*, and *hiṅgu*, along with *kāñjika* as a drink; this drying therapy brings relief to *gulma*. For the treatment of *gulma*, the cooking of alkali (*kṣārapāka*) is employed here. One should mix the alkali of *palāśa*, *arjuna*, and *sūraṇa*, as well as the alkali of *yavaśūka*, *sauvarcala*, rock salt (*sindhu*), *udbhida*, or sea salt (*sāmudra*). Having strained the water according to the prescribed method, these should be combined with the medicinal herbs.

A powder consisting of *pathyā*, *agni*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rajanī*, *surāhva*, *kuṣṭha*, *viśālā*, *javānikā*, *ajamodā*, the two types of *jīraka*, *ṣaḍgranthikā*, and *hiṅgu*, when mixed with alkaline water and drunk, destroys all diseases arising in the abdominal cavity (18–19). It destroys all types of *gulma*, cholera (*viṣūcikā*), sluggish digestion, colic, fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, and constipation; it eradicates these three classes of diseases in men (20). [Also beneficial are] *pathyā*, *samaṅgā*, *kalasī*, *vṛṣa*, and *mahauṣadha*.

Vātaviṣā and surāhva should be boiled in water; this drink indeed promotes digestion in cases of abdominal tumors (gulma). (21) A decoction of vacā, yavānī, trikaṭu, and daśamūlī is prescribed; or alternatively, a warm decoction of dhānya and nāgara is beneficial for drinking. (22) In all types of vāta-gulma and in irregular fevers (viṣama-jvara), the five-fold group beginning with rāsnā (rāsnādi-pañcaka) is a digestive agent for vāta-gulma. (23) Śaṭhī, sauvarcala salt, and śuṇṭhī are also digestive remedies for one suffering from gulma. (24) Furthermore, vidulā, drākṣā, kaṭukā, and nimba leaves [are used].

A digestive medicine with jaggery (guḍa) should be given to a patient suffering from a bile-dominant (paittika) abdominal tumor (gulma). (25) A paste of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) mixed with sugar is a digestive remedy for a bile-dominant abdominal tumor. Similarly, *yavānī*, *ugragandhā*, and the three pungents (*kaṭukatraya*) should be drunk warm at night as a digestive medicine for a phlegm-dominant (ślaiṣmika) abdominal tumor. (26) A powder consisting of *nāgara* (ginger), *krimijit* (viḍaṅga), and *pathyā* (myrobalan), combined with three times the amount of *trivṛtā* (turpeth) and mixed with jaggery, should be administered as a purgative for a wind-dominant (vātika) abdominal tumor. (27) One part of *dantī*, two parts of *harītakī*, and three parts of *trivṛtā* [should be used].

One should take exactly four parts of dry ginger (28), mix them all together with an equal amount of jaggery, and eat a bolus (vaṭaka) in the morning; one should drink water over it (29). This boiled preparation leads to purgation for the pacification of vāta-gulma (abdominal tumors due to wind). (30) One should drink castor oil combined with sugar and milk for the purgation of pitta-gulma (tumors due to bile); this is excellent and brings comfort. (31) Similarly, the tender shoots and leaves of *āragvadha* should be processed with castor oil and wrapped in castor leaves. (32)

Then, having smeared it with mud and placed it over glowing coals, one should eat that well-steamed *bharjikā* mixed with sugar. (33) Purgation is beneficial for a *gulma* caused by *pitta*; pure purgatives are likewise recommended. (34) Having prepared a powder of *triphalā*, *surasa*, and *śuṇṭhī*, one should saturate it once with the milky sap (*kṣīra*) of *snuhī* and mix it with jaggery. (35) This purgative destroys all types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*) and is effective for a *gulma* caused by *śleṣman*. (36) [The powder consists of] *śuṇṭhī*, *sauvarcala* salt, *pathyā*, *viḍaṅga*, *punarnavā*, and the seeds of *apāmārga*.

One should eat [the powder] processed with the milky sap of *snuhī* (37) combined with jaggery, and afterwards drink warm water; this purgative is praised as beneficial for all types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*). [The following ingredients are used: sour gruel, alkali, turmeric, *viśāla*, plantain, *sūraṇa*, *kokilākṣa*, *pālāśa*, *dahanārjuna*, *śaṭhī*, *jayā*, *apāmārga*, and *kūṣmāṇḍaka*.

Hingu (Asafoetida) that has been burnt, processed with alkali, washed, and combined with the three pungents (trikaṭu) removes abdominal tumors, distension, constipation, and colic, and is beneficial for all types of abdominal enlargements (udara). Ajamodā, śaṭhī, dantī, viḍaṅga, kuṣṭha, tumburu, the three myrobalans (triphalā), citraka, śuṇṭhī, and karkaṭaśṛṅgikā; trivṛtā, surāhvā, puṣkaramūla, vṛddhadāruka, as well as amlavetasa, tintiḍīka, and ciñcinī— all these should be taken in equal parts and processed together with an equal amount of mātuluṅga (citron juice).

Powdered [with these ingredients] and combined with one-third *hiṅgu* and ghee, it is beneficial; it destroys *vātagulma* as well as abdominal pain accompanied by colic. (42) *Hiṅgu*, the three fruits (*trika*), the two types of *jīraka*, *citraka*, *bhārṅgī*, *kuṣṭha*, *viḍaṅga*, *tumburu*, *puṣkara*, *viśva*, *surāhva*, along with alkali and the five salts—this [mixture], when taken for the purpose of destroying *vātika-gulma*, destroys the pain of colic in men. (43–44) *Hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala* salt, *ajājī*, *viśvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *viḍaṅga*, when drunk with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), destroy *gulma*.

A linctus made from *savātika* (45 parts), two parts each of *jīraka*, *trikaṭu*, *śaṭhī*, *tumburu*, and *citraka*, taken with honey, is beneficial for a *gulma* of pitta-nature and serves to alleviate swelling. (46) A powder of *yaṣṭimadhu*, nimba leaves, as well as *dhātrī* fruit and sugar, licked with honey, is a remedy that wards off *pittagulma*. (47) A powder combined with *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *citraka*, and the fruit of the *vaṭaka* tree, when drunk with wine or with a decoction of the aforementioned fruits, is beneficial. (48) This is wholesome for the destruction of *śleṣmagulma* and brings comfort. (49) [And] *rodhra*...

A powder consisting of *kamala*, *viśvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *citraka*, combined with *nāgara* and *hiṅgu* and mixed with urine, destroys phlegmatic abdominal tumors (*śleṣmagulma*), as well as colic and abdominal diseases. (50) One should drink *ugragandhā*, *marica*, and alkaline powder (*kṣāracūrṇa*) combined with urine; this destroys phlegmatic abdominal tumors. (51–52) A powder consisting of *śuṇṭhī*, *sauvarcala*, *bhārṅgī*, *vatsaka*, *yāvaśūka*, the two types of *jīra*, *āṭarūṣa*, *yavānī*, *hiṅgu*, *saindhava*, and *āragvadha*—[this powder... (53)

Indeed, when a gulma arises from vāta and śleṣman, it quickly and easily finds relief through [the administration of] ghee alone. (54) Ugragandhā, triphalā, devadāru, punarnavā, trivṛt, and sauvarcala salt, combined with alkaline water (kṣārodaka), when drunk, is considered an excellent remedy that brings comfort in cases of gulma caused by vāta and kapha. (55) If the treatment for grahaṇī and gulma should be applicable here, it may be employed; furthermore, purgation (virecana) should be administered in all cases of swelling and abdominal enlargement (śophodara). (56) When accompanied by swelling and diarrhea, gulma and udara kill the person; for such a case, the drinking of alkaline water (kṣārodaka) is prescribed.

The powder of *bṛhat*, *hiṅgu*, and so forth (57), or that beginning with *ajamoda*, is for the pacification of swelling and diarrhea. Although vomiting and diarrhea may also occur in cases of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), one should recognize them as curable; however, treatment is beneficial even when the prognosis is doubtful. One should drink *guḍa*, *dāḍima*, and *pathyā* combined with honey (59). This should be administered repeatedly for both vomiting and diarrhea. A tumor possessing all these symptoms is of the *sānnipātika* (tri-discordant) type (60), characterized by piercing pain, restlessness, discoloration, fainting, diarrhea, vomiting, and excessive moisture.

Lassitude as well; that [disease] born of the three *doṣas* is incurable. (61) Listen now, O son of great wisdom, with a one-pointed mind, as I, the knower, shall describe the procedure for the removal of swelling (*śopha*) in men. (62) Likewise, *trivṛt* combined with sugar and molasses, when subsequently drunk with lukewarm water, destroys abdominal enlargement (*udaraka*) along with swelling; or it causes the *pitta*-type [swelling] to leave men. (63) *Harītakī*, *trivṛt*, and *śuṇṭhī* combined with molasses likewise destroy swelling; or [a decoction of] the ten roots (*daśamūla*) boiled [with them]. (64) *Trivṛt* combined with *śuṇṭhī* and honey likewise destroys swelling; or *trivṛt* combined with *śuṇṭhī* and *guḍa*. (65) *Trivṛt* combined with *śuṇṭhī* and *guḍa* likewise destroys swelling; or *trivṛt* combined with *śuṇṭhī* and *guḍa*. (66) *Trivṛt* combined with *śuṇṭhī* and *guḍa* likewise destroys swelling; or *trivṛt* combined with *śuṇṭhī* and *guḍa*. Warm castor oil applied as a poultice removes swelling (64). Varuṇa oil mixed with cow’s urine is beneficial when drunk and destroys swelling (65). One suffering from the disease of swelling should avoid meat from domestic or marshy animals, salt, dried vegetables, fresh grain, molasses-based foods, flour preparations, curd, rice-and-pulse porridge, waterless wine, food, grains, dried meat, heavy or unwholesome items, burning foods, sleeping at night, and sexual intercourse (66). An application of *aruṣkara* (marking nut) destroys swelling.

In cases of dryness caused by poison, the pacifying treatment prescribed for poison should be employed; this includes fasting, digestive stimulants, unctuous substances, warm treatments, and the soothing of Vāta. However, for those suffering from all types of Gulma, the food should be nourishing (Bṛṃhaṇa). One suffering from Gulma should not eat dried meat, radish, fish, dried vegetables, or pulses. Furthermore, one with Gulma should not eat *vāluka* or sweet and salty foods. In the case of blood-type Gulma (*saraktagulma*), however, digestive stimulants (*pācana*) are not to be used.

Drinking asafoetida, moving the waist, fomentation, and massage are beneficial; likewise, walking and jumping are not [recommended], yet they are beneficial. (71) A decoction of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, *khadira*, *māgadhikā*, and *samaṅgā*, combined with *amlavetasa*, honey, and ghee, quickly destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) even when accompanied by blood, dries up moisture in the heart, and subdues provoked blood. (72) Milk mixed with ghee and *sauvarcala* salt should be administered for the destruction of blood-born tumors (*raktagulma*), or even in cases arising from liver injury. (73) And not...

For gulma born from blood or from injury, asafoetida (hiṅgu) is wholesome when combined [with other drugs], provided it is neither hot nor burning; likewise, the meat of wild animals is beneficial. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, named "The Treatment of Gulma," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-Seven. Ātreya said: From sitting in an uneven posture, or from drinking water [at improper times], or when one has emerged from exhaustion, travel, or labored breathing, or even after excessive physical exertion—water that is thus drunk results in *jalodara* (ascites). When the abdomen contains water, it produces a gurgling sound; when greatly increased, there is swelling of the feet and edema—these are the symptoms of *jalodara*. One should administer purgation and emesis, and cause digestive (*pācana*) treatments to be performed; furthermore, an application of alkali (*kṣāra*) and pills (*vaṭaka*) prepared with it will pacify that condition. Therefore, [one should apply it] starting from the navel to the region of the folds of skin.

Leaving aside a space of one finger-breadth and taking account of the water-channel, one should wrap it with a blade of *kuśa* grass. (4) A wise man should insert a castor-oil stalk (*eraṇḍa-nāḍī*) there; once the internal water has been drained, he should then quickly apply a bandage. (5) When that [bandage] does not hold, then cauterization (*dāha*) is recommended; having strained the paste of *kaṇa*, four times as much clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be added. (6) Having cooked it with an equal amount of ginger and *viṣā*, drinking it or applying it as an ointment is beneficial. The best of physicians should perform the surgical procedure (*śastra-karma*) only when [the condition] is properly diagnosed. (7) It is difficult to perform.

One should not perform surgical intervention in every case; for where there is non-action, death is certain, whereas where action is taken, there is doubt [as to the outcome]. Therefore, the procedure must certainly be performed by the physician, with the Lord as his witness. Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Jaṭhara (Ascites)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The twenty-eighth chapter. Ātreya said: Thus, there are twenty types of *prameha* (urinary disorders) in men; here are their characteristics. (1) From physical exertion, sexual indulgence, as well as from the consumption of food that is contrary to the heat of summer, or that is sharp and hot, or from wine, or from the habitual use of milk and pungent substances—the origin of *meha* has been described by the lords of sages. (2) *Jalaprameha*, *rudhiraprameha*, *pūyaprameha*, *lavaṇaprameha*, *takraprameha*, *khaṭikāprameha*, and *śukraprameha* have been described previously. (3) There may also be *śarkarāmeha* and *avasāprameha*.

One should recognize that there are those with *rasaprameha*, *anyaghṛtaprameha*, *pittaprameha*, *kaphaprameha*, and *madhuprameha*. O best of physicians, just as these names are, so too do their symptoms and the loss of strength quickly manifest in the body; therefore, one should apply therapeutic measures for their pacification according to the cause. For *jalaprameha*, a decoction of *dhava*, *arjuna*, *candana*, *śāla*, and *vallī* is beneficial; for *raktaprameha*, cold milk mixed with grapes, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *candana* should be used.

In *pūyameha*, sexual indulgence is minimal; a decoction of *dhava* and *arjuna* is beneficial. For *lavaṇameha*, a decoction of *dūrvā*, *kaseruka*, *kadalī*, *nalinī*, and *lavaṇa* is prescribed. (7) The decoctions of *kadamba*, *śāla*, *arjuna*, *dīpyaka*, *viḍaṅga*, *dārvī*, *dhava*, and *śallakī*—all these should likewise be consumed with honey in cases of *kapha-prameha*. (8) *Rodhra*, *arjuna*, milk, and the leaves of *ariṣṭa* are used therein; likewise, *dhātrī*, *phala*, and *candana* are for *takraprameha*. For *khaṭikāprameha*, a beneficial decoction of *guḍa* and *avaṭa* should be administered.

9. Durvā, mūrvā, the roots of kuśa and kāśa, dantī, samaṅgā, and śālmalī—this [decoction] boiled with water is beneficial as a drink for seminal prameha (śukraprameha), or it is beneficial for blood prameha (rudhiraprameha). 10. Or, a decoction boiled with triphalā, the root of āragvadha, mūrvā, the leaves of śobhāñjana and ariṣṭa, along with mocā and drākṣā, serves to ward off ghee-prameha (sarpiḥprameha). 11. Likewise, kuṣṭha, parpaṭaka, and tiktā, with sugar added, boiled into a thick decoction, combined with mūrvā, arka, and pāṭalikā—[this is used for the same purpose].

A decoction of *durālabhā*, *kiṃśuka*, and *ṭuṇṭuka* is always beneficial for those suffering from *rasaprameha*. (12) The wise declare that for the pacification of *pittaprameha*, one should boil blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *arjuna*, *kaliṅga*, *dhava*, *amlīkā*, *dhātrī* fruits, and *picumanda* leaves in water; this, when taken with sugar, is said to cure it. (13) A decoction of *viḍaṅga*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *kapittha*, *kadamba*, *rodhra*, *aśana*, and *vṛkṣaka* taken with water is beneficial for men and destroys their *kaphaprameha*. (14) [Also beneficial are] *mustā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), and *niśā*...

A decoction made from *suradāru*, *mūrvā*, and *indrā* with *rodhra* water is beneficial when drunk for diseases arising from all types of *meha*; it should be administered to relieve all forms of urinary retention (*mūtragraha*). (15) Furthermore, a powder of *abhayā*, iron filings, and *nikumbha*, combined with sugar, is beneficial; they say that a linctus of the three fruits (*phalatrika*) with honey is beneficial in all cases of *prameha*. (16) In *madhumeha*, a wise person should employ the drinking of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or milk mixed with sugar, or a decoction, or medicinal pills (*guṭikā*). (17)

Nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, āragvadha, tuṇṭuka, piyāla, kukubha, jambū, kapittha, and āmrātaka; (18) madhuka, yaṣṭimadhuka, rodhra, pāribhadraka, paṭola, cāriṇī, dantī, and meṣaviṣāṇikā; (19) citraka, karañja, śakrāhva, and triphalā combined with an equal amount of bhallātaka, the three aromatics, and the three pungents—(20) these should be given as a fine powder, this Nyagrodhādi group being highly efficacious when mixed with honey.

It destroys madhumeha (diabetes). 21. Whether as a decoction, an oil preparation, or even a ghee preparation, it is recommended for drinking and massage; it truly destroys diseases born of the urine. 22. This powder, beginning with Nyagrodha (the *Nyagrodhādi* group), should be drunk mixed with milk; when combined according to availability, there is nothing else that is better for madhumeha. 23–24. Mākṣika, dhātumākṣika, śilodbheda, śilājatu, candana, raktadhātu, likewise kapūraka, kaṇā, and vaṃśarocanaka—these should be taken with milk.

One should drink this together; it cures Madhu-prameha, and one is liberated from urinary diseases. (25) Now we shall describe the treatment for the pustules of Prameha. A decoction for washing the urinary tract should be made from Dhava, Arjuna, Kadamba, Badarī, Khadira, Śiṃśapā, and Pāribhadraka. (26) The inner bark of Arjuna, Kadamba, and Ṭiṇṭukī is recommended for washing the urinary tract during the stage of suppuration, for the purpose of purifying the pus. (27) One should take the juice of Bhṛṅgarāja as well as the leaves of Surasa, Niṣpāva, and Paṭola.

Having ground these with sour gruel (kāñjika), it is an ointment for wind-blisters (vātapiṭikā) and for the penis (mehana). Likewise, licorice (yaṣṭīmadhu), costus (kuṣṭha), sandalwood (candana), red sandalwood (raktacandana), ushira, kattṛṇa, red mineral (raktadhātu), and lotus stalk (mṛṇālaka)—O best of physicians, when combined with the cream of milk (kṣīramaṇḍaka) according to availability, this ointment pacifies the burning sensation of the penis caused by bile and blood (pittarakta). Washing with cold milk and rubbing with fresh butter (navanīta), as well as the use of the husks (kaṇa) of kadamba, arjuna, and oil-cake (piṇyāka), and the leaves of pomegranate (dāḍima) and khadira—[are also recommended].

Likewise, having ground the leaves of *dalā* and *āmalakī* with warm water, one should perform a wash (*dhāvana*) in cases of urinary disorders (*meha*) and inflammation (*pāka*). Alternatively, a powder of *triphalā* prevents dried suppuration; the wash may be performed with *kāñjika*, *takra*, or water from boiled rice-husks. In cases of inflammation due to excessive cold, the wash should be done with very cold water. For food, red *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *āḍhakī* (pigeon pea), or *kulattha* (horse gram) are prescribed, along with a small amount of sweet ghee. Furthermore, alkaline, sour, or pungent substances, as well as sleeping during the day, should be especially avoided.

Beholding women, sexual intercourse, as well as overeating, walking, running, and likewise the suppression of the urge to urinate—37—the best of physicians should avoid these, as well as the wind from clothing and red garments; singing, women, and children within the house in a secluded place—38—and ornaments, betel, and anger or emaciation; one who desires happiness and prosperity should keep these far away and renounce them. 39. A decoction of the two types of turmeric, ginger, viḍaṅga, and harītakī is prescribed for urinary disorders caused by *kapha*.

One suffering from *pīta-prameha* (urinary disorders characterized by yellow urine) should drink a decoction of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *uśīra*, *pathyā*, *āmalaka*, and *mustaka*, mixed with honey. (40–41) Likewise, for *pitta-prameha*, this decoction of *kamala*, *rodhra*, *uśīra*, and *arjuna*, taken with honey, is prescribed. (42) The fresh juice of *āmalaka* mixed with honey, or the powder of *harītakī*, prevents all types of urinary disorders. (43) One should drink the powder of *khadira*, sugar, *dāru-haridrā*, and *musta*. (44)

For the pacification of all urinary disorders (prameha): 44. Kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, devadāru, pāṭhā, guḍūcī, triphalā, and musta—the powder of these, when mixed with honey, removes urinary disorders caused by urine (mūtraprameha) as well as pain. 45. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Prameha," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 28.

Chapter Twenty-nine. Ātreya said: A powder of *elā*, *śilājatu*, *māgadhikā*, and *pāṣāṇabheda*, when drunk with rice-water, certainly cures the disease of *prameha*. (1) The roots of *eraṇḍa*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, and *gokṣuraka*, as well as *elā*, *āṭarūṣa*, and *pippalī*, combined with *yaṣṭīmadhu*—(2) a person should drink a decoction of these mixed with *śilāditya*. For urinary stones (*aśmarī*) and gravel (*śarkarā*), two *palas* of sugar [should be added]; (3) it should be very cold water measuring one *karṣa*, which removes dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*).

Iron powder mixed with curd and water provides relief. (4) For dysuria caused by all three doṣas, one should drink a powder of yava-kṣāra combined with hiṅgu, or take kūṣmāṇḍa fruit together with sugar. (5) Indeed, this is a remedy for dysuria arising from the three doṣas; one should drink the root of śatāvarī ground into a powder and mixed with cold water. (6) Therefore, for one suffering from the disease of gravel (śarkarā), one should administer sugar. [The following is the decoction: āragvadha fruit and root, durālabhā, dhānyaka, śatāvarī, (7) pāṣāṇabheda, and pathyā—this is the decoction.

In cases of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), *pāṣāṇabheda*, *trivṛt*, *pathyā*, *durālabhā*, *gokṣura*, and *puṣkara*—or a decoction of *elā*, *kuruṇṭaka*, and the seeds of *karkaṭī*—should be used for severely obstructed urine. (9) A decoction of *paṭolī* root mixed with *kulattha* and combined with *puṣkaramūla*, when administered repeatedly, destroys urinary disorders (*prameha*) and stone diseases (*pāṣāṇaroga*). (10) He who drinks the root of *mātuluṅgikā* with water that has stood overnight, the suffering caused by internal gravel (*śarkarā*) is instantly dissolved. (11) [The powder] ground with cow’s buttermilk...

One whose humors are corrupted by sugar should drink the medicine called Kṣipranāmaka for a short time and buttermilk for a long time. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Dysuria," in the third section of the Hārīta-uttara as spoken by Ātreya. 29.

Chapter Thirty. Ātreya said: One should drink the seeds of *karkaṭikā* mixed with *triphalā* and rock salt (*saindhava*), powdered and taken with warm water; when drunk, it brings relief from the obstruction of urine (1). The man who drinks the alkali of *tila* stalks mixed with curd and honey destroys the obstruction of urine and immediately attains comfort (2). One should drink *jātī* root ground with goat’s milk, since it pacifies burning sensations, heat in the urine, and pain (3). [One should take] *padminīkanda* cooked in oil and mixed with boiled cow’s urine.

One should drink [this] in cases of urinary obstruction accompanied by intense pain. Furthermore, due to substances that aggravate Pitta—such as those that are pungent, sour, or hot—as well as by indulging in women who are pale-complexioned, blood may also flow out. By drinking hot wine and being afflicted by fatigue or physical exercise, one quickly aggravates Pitta, which causes dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). Because of that, one urinates with difficulty, a stream of heat issues forth, it obstructs the urinary channels, and blood also flows out. I shall now describe the medicine for this, by which—

It brings about happiness. (7) Yaṣṭīmadhuka, mṛdvīkā, and candana, along with raktacandana, taken with water from red rice, remove the pain of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*). (8) This linctus, consisting of sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree combined with grapes and sugar, destroys dysuria; it is declared by the best of physicians to be a pacifier of the body when provoked by immersion in cold water. In cases of dysuria, a sweet diet is said to be beneficial. (10) When there is an obstruction of urine due to the breaking of intercourse while lying on one's back, or due to burning sensations born of physical exertion, *vacā* [is the remedy]. (11)

One should provide various obstructive measures there. In a person who lacks physical exercise, eats wholesome food, and bathes in cold water, the aggravated *vāyu*, joined with *śleṣman*, obstructs the urinary passage; this most wicked disease is said to be extremely difficult to cure. Listen now to its remedy: a decoction enema (*anuvāsana*) or a non-unctuous enema (*nirūha*), as well as the procedure for urinary obstruction using decoctions, is beneficial. Furthermore, general sudation and remaining in a place that is like a narrow path are recommended, as is riding horses or carts and running.

A decoction of the three myrobalans (*phalatrika*) with an equal amount of jaggery, taken with milk or meat broth, cures obstructions of urine; or, when caused by *pitta*, it may be taken with salt and sour substances. A decoction of *pāṭalā*, *ṭuṇṭukā*, nimba, and *gokṣuraka*, as well as cardamom (*elā*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), and cinnamon leaves (*patra*), combined with the three myrobalans and drunk with jaggery, destroys urinary obstruction. Furthermore, [the decoction] combined with pomegranate and sour substances is beneficial for men suffering from urinary pain. A decoction of the three myrobalans, sugarcane, and sugar, along with jaggery and rock salt (*saindhava*), prevents the retention of urine.

Alternatively, Pathyā combined with jaggery, or the application of a pricking sensation [to the area], as well as sexual intercourse with a woman, should be practiced; by this, comfort will quickly arise. Furthermore, for women, the massaging of the vulva [is recommended]. Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Obstruction," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 30.

Chapter Thirty-One Ātreya said: The disease of urinary calculi (*aśmarī*) arises due to defects in the father or mother, from the obstruction of urine, or from the practice of unwholesome habits. (1) If the parents engage in sexual intercourse while their urine is suppressed, the embryo develops in conjunction with that urine and is expelled along with it. (2) In one whose body is thus formed, five [components] arise therein; the urine causes a binding obstruction within the three [channels] at the site of the urine. (3) This urinary disease is incurable, and it occurs in humans during youth due to minor [causes]. (4)

Furthermore, urinary gravel (mūtraśarkarā) arises as something curable [only] through contrary measures; when a woman or a man lies on their back, his semen flows forth, and the woman extracts that semen. Again, due to Vāta, blood enters the penis and clothing; these two substances, having been introduced, reach the urinary opening and obstruct it. Because of that, obstruction of urine occurs along with intense pain; the gravel, situated at the joint of the testicles, moves about and must be treated with surgical instruments (śastra-sādhya). Therefore, O son, listen as I describe the medicinal treatment.

O Mahāmati, a decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *gokṣuraka*, and the bark of *varuṇa*, combined with jaggery (*guḍa*) and alkali from barley (*yavakṣāra*), destroys urinary calculi (*aśmarī*). Likewise, a decoction of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *nala*, bamboo (*veṇu*), *agnimantha*, *akṣanṛttaka*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *moraṭā*, and *pāṣāṇabhedaka*, mixed with jaggery, when drunk, destroys stone in the bladder and removes pain in the bladder. Also, *elā*, *kaṇā*, *vṛṣa*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *reṇukā*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, *madhuka*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*) [are similarly used].

A decoction consisting of castor oil, *kaśilājatu*, sugar, and other ingredients likewise destroys urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), as does its warm administration (12). A powder made from the seeds of *gokṣuraka* combined with metallic gold (*mākṣika*) and drunk with buffalo milk brings about the falling away of the stone (13). The surgical procedure is described in the *Uttara-tantra* and is also recorded in the chapter on clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the *Sūtra-sthāna* (14). Ancient *ṣaṣṭika* rice, red rice, *śyāmāka*, *kodrava*, *dāla*, *markaṭī*, and grass-grains (*tṛṇadhānyaka*) [are recommended] (15).

Barley, wheat, horse-gram (*kulattha*), and likewise *āḍhakī*—these should be employed by the physician in the diet of those suffering from wind disorders (*vāta*) to alleviate the wind. (16) The meats of the *krauñca* crane and others are wholesome for the destruction of urinary calculi (*aśmarī*). (17) Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Calculi," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (31)

Chapter Thirty-two. Ātreya said: Henceforth, O best of physicians, the enlargement of the scrotum (aṇḍavṛddhi) is described. In childhood, it arises following the testicles due to the defects of the mother or the father. Furthermore, through corrupted sexual intercourse, the Vāyu (vital air), having reached the bladder and then the site of the scrotum, indeed causes its enlargement. There are four types: those caused by each individual Dosha, the Sannipātika (caused by all three combined), that from Pitta, and likewise that from Sannipāta; these are considered incurable. I shall now describe the Doshas and their remedies; listen to them, O best of physicians.

Fomentation, oleation, decoctions, and drinking [of medicated liquids] are prescribed. O best of physicians, I shall describe the symptoms of those [diseases], including head-draughts: trembling occurs from mild wind (vāta), and burning fever from bile (pitta). From phlegm (kapha), there is thickening and dryness, and the testicles become hard. For the purpose of consuming decoctions in cases of scrotal enlargement associated with wind, one should use a decoction of *rasāla*, *śallakī*, *tarkārī*, and *kaṭutumbikā*. Furthermore, immersion in cold water or the application of cold substances is likewise [prescribed] for a scrotum affected by bile.

It is recommended [to use] *vacā*, salt water, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and mustard seeds, along with the application of decoctions, for the removal of harmful phlegm in the scrotum. O best of the wise, a decoction of *aruṇa*, *varuṎa*, *kola*, *śāliparṇī*, and *śatāvarī* is prescribed for hydrocele caused by *pitta* and *sannipāta*. Furthermore, drinking a decoction of *varuṇa*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *daśamūlī*, and *śatāvarī* is beneficial for hydrocele caused by *vāta*. Through this, comfort is attained; then, one should perform the procedure in the middle of the ear-cavity.

One should let blood from the left [side] for enlargement of the left scrotum, but one should let blood from the right side for enlargement of the right; for both types, two veins are to be pierced, or by that means it may become comfortable. Thus has the procedure for *caṇḍakriyā* been declared, and it is for the patient whose condition has been diagnosed. Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Scrotal Enlargement (*vṛṣaṇavṛddhi*)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Thirty-three. Ātreya said: O best of physicians, when blood and bile (raktapitta) become aggravated by salty, sour, alkaline, and pungent foods, as well as by heat, sweating, and excessive morbidity, it becomes *visarpa* (erysipelas). It should be understood to be of seven types: those arising from the individual doṣas, those born from combinations of two doṣas (*dvandvaja*), another which is purely blood-born (*raktaja*), and the seventh, which arises from the combination of all three doṣas (*sannipāta*). Furthermore, others will declare its names individually: it is to be known as *ājñeya*, the terrible *granthika*, and another called *kardama*. Among these, *ājñeya* is caused by vāta and pitta, while *granthika* is caused by vāta and kapha.

The *kardama* type arises from *pitta* and *kapha*, while the *sānnipātika* type, arising from *vāta* and *kapha*, is terrible. Blood, lymph, skin, and flesh are the corrupted tissues (*dūṣya*), and the three *doṣas* are the impurities; these seven constituents should be known as the origin of the spreading fevers (*visarpa*). A decoction of *nyagrodha*, *bilva*, and *khadira* is beneficial for washing; it may be used with sour *kāñjika*, or with *picchilā*, or with the juice of *sauvīraka*. Washing with the juice of *mātuluṅga* is also recommended for *vāta*-type spreading fevers. For *pitta*-type spreading fever, washing should be done with milk or cold water. Or else, for *kapha*-type spreading fever, [the same applies].

A wash with *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* is recommended for a spreading (*visarpa*) erysipelas caused by *sarpis*; or alternatively, with wine (*surā*) or *sauvīraka*. A wash is also beneficial for one suffering from a spreading erysipelas arising from a combination of humors (*sannipāta*), prepared with *yava*, *agnimantha*, *śaṭhī*, *nyagrodha*, and mustard seeds; this decoction is beneficial as a wash for spreading erysipelas born of a combined humor. One should grind *pañcajīraka* and *kapittha* with *kāñjika* or with the juice of *mātuluṅga* for an application on a wind-type (*vāta*) spreading erysipelas. An ointment consisting of *dhava*, *rodhra*, sesame, *elā*, *vidārī*, and *kaṇṭaka* is likewise [recommended].

In cases of Pitta-type erysipelas (pittavisarpa), an ointment made from Guñjā leaves should be applied. Ghee cooked with rock salt (saindhava), Ariṣṭa, Tumbīkā, and Paṭola leaves is recommended for application as a means to ward off all types of erysipelas. In erysipelas born of blood (raktaja-visarpa), one should perform bloodletting. Subsequently, the smoke of Dhava and Kadamba trees, along with household smoke (gṛhadhūma), should always be used. It is declared that washing with fermented rice-water (kāñjika) is beneficial for the application. Furthermore, Kuṭheraka, Surasa, Cakramarda, the two types of Niśā (turmeric and yellow turmeric), and mustard seeds should be ground with kāñjika and used as an ointment.
"Beneficial. Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Visarpa," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 33.

Chapter Thirty-four. Ātreya said: The disorder arising from *vātarakta* (leprosy) is of four types; due to the corruption of the odor (*gandhadoṣa*), their names are distinct from one another. 1. When small eruptions appear, it is called *kṣudraka*; when terrible ones appear, it is *antaka*; or else, when eruptions resembling *masūrikā* or mustard seeds are seen, it is *vasanta*. 2. That which is characterized by very small eruptions due to the corruption of *pitta* and blood is called *kṣudratara*. 3. That in which eruptions are seen that burn like fire is called *agnidagdha*. 4. That which spreads excessively and causes constant suffering is known as *visarpa*.

When one's eruptions are dense and the phlegm ripens simultaneously, burning, restlessness, and discoloration arise immediately for him. (5) When round eruptions resembling lentils (*masūraka*) are seen on one's body and they subside quickly through ripening, that should be known as *masūrikā*. O Great-minded One, I shall describe its treatment according to the rules. (6) One should keep it hidden and well-guarded by means of protective rituals; there should be no contact with women nor any association with low people. (7) [One should stay] in a very cool and refreshing place.

One should apply this with great care; furthermore, one should have an ointment applied here for the minor affliction (kṣudropasarga). A plaster made of kuṣṭha, uśīra, nyagrodha, and the bark of udumbara is recommended as a protection against the minor affliction. Milk mixed with honey and sugar is a pleasant drink. One should cause [the patient] to drink the juice of jambu and mango sprouts combined with curd and honey; this destroys the diarrhea and the digestive fire of this minor affliction. Gokṣura, ativiṣā, karkaṭādyā, and parpaṭaka [should also be used].

This paste should be administered mixed with honey and sugar; likewise, the fresh juice of *harītakī* and *mātuluṅga* combined with sugar [is beneficial]. This is a remedy for the minor affliction (*kṣudraka*) that wards off vomiting and emaciation; it should also be applied as an ointment for the *agnika* affliction. Red sandalwood, *mañjiṣṭhā*, neem leaves, and *arjuna*—these, when mixed with milk and fresh butter, constitute a beneficial ointment. Having observed a severe complication, [the physicians] do not apply fomentation, nor massage, nor an ointment.

Wise physicians should, as appropriate, apply a cleansing wash using forest cow-dung, alkali, and oil (15). Anointing with oil is not beneficial; rather, one should perform treatment only with medicinal pastes. A paste composed of *candana*, *madhuka*, *rodhra*, *nyagrodha*, *utpala*, and *sārivā*, combined with honey, removes complications when taken as a drink (16–17). When there is a complication, a severe fever arises along with bloody urine; I shall describe its treatment by which one attains well-being (18). [The decoction of] *paṭola*, *parpaṭa*, *śuṇṭhī*, *mustā*, and *khadira* in equal parts [is used].

The paste [of these], combined with honey, taken as a drink, is beneficial and destroys fever. (19) Sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, puṣkaramūla, and dantadhāvana—this decoction, taken with honey, removes fevers caused by complications. (20) In cases of vomiting and diarrhea, pomegranate and *kuṭaja* taken with honey and curd are a drink that wards off diarrhea. (21) The remaining minor diseases have been described; here, the appropriate treatment should be applied. A single specific procedure must be performed for *masūrikā* (smallpox) according to the prescribed rules. (22) All [substances] that increase *vāta* as well as those that are dry [should be avoided].

A wise man should avoid association with women and harsh grief from afar. (23) One should administer those wholesome remedies prescribed for fever here as well; in this way, within three weeks, the person attains comfort. (24) Then, after performing the recitation of auspicious verses, an ablution should be performed; having dressed [the patient] in new, fine, and white garments, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) and the serving of desired food should be carried out. (25-26) Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Afflictions," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (34)

Chapter Thirty-Five. Ātreya said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the treatment of ulcers (*vraṇa*). Ulcers are said to be of many kinds, arising from various constituent elements (*dhātu*) of the body. A malignant ulcer (*duṣṭavraṇa*), which is terrible, arises from drinking or eating contaminated water and food, or from indulgence in anger, excessive burden, or addiction; it may also arise from another corruption of the blood. It is produced by Vāta, Pitta, or Kapha—either individually, in pairs, or by the combination of all three humors (*doṣa*)—which, having agitated the flesh and scattered the blood, bring about its formation.

Even a malignant ulcer (duṣṭavraṇa) is terrible; the aggravated doṣas, having vitiated the skin, blood, and fat, and taking refuge in the bone, gradually produce a severe and formidable swelling. An ulcer arising from vāta should be recognized as being accompanied by blood, pain, throbbing, and tremors, and it is rough and painful. A wound produced by pitta is characterized by a burning sensation and a hissing sound, yet it tolerates touch; it is cold, provides relief, and suppurates quickly. A wound that is hard, circular in shape, and terrible [is known to arise from kapha].

A Kaphaja ulcer is yellowish, associated with mild pain, tolerant of heat, very unctuous, and slow to heal (7). One should recognize a Sannipātika ulcer by the presence of all these symptoms; in a Dvandvaja ulcer, however, the characteristics of two doshas are observed (8). Those arising from trauma (Abhighāta) should be known as fourfold; others are sinus ulcers (Nāḍīvraṇa), which are accompanied by wind and pain (9). But others occur within the channels (Srotas); hear now their treatment: first is drainage with sour gruel (Maṇḍavisrāva), and second is fomentation (Svedana) is prescribed (10). Third...

It is declared that for a ripened [wound], ripening (pācana) is prescribed; likewise, incision (pāṭana), purification (śodhana), and healing (rohaṇa) should be applied. Subsequently, the same sequence of treatment should be followed, which is beneficial for ulcers. Rāsnā, vacā, and śuṇṭhī, along with the juice of mātuluṅga and sour gruel (kāñjika), used together as a wash, are for wind-type (vātika) ulcers. Yaṣṭīmadhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, paṭola, and nimba leaves boiled in milk and cooled constitute a wash for bile-type (paittika) ulcers. Triphalā, kadamba, and jambu [are also used].

A decoction of *kapittha* is excellent for washing a wound arising from *kapha* when it is accompanied by heat (15). A paste of *mātuluṅga*, *agnimantha*, and their roots with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), as well as *suradāru* and *śuṇṭhī*, is beneficial as an application for a wind-born (*vāta*) wound (16). *Nala*, *mūrvā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, and *raktacandana*, ground with rice-water, destroy wounds caused by *pitta* (17). Having ground *aṅkolaka*, *rodhra*, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, *vetasa*, and the leaves of *pāribhadra*, one should apply them as a plaster to the wound (18) once the inflammation has subsided.

In a wound that is deep, painful, or has a sinus tract, purification (śodhana) and washing (dhāvana) should be performed by the best of physicians. (19) Washing for deep wounds should be done with a decoction of *karañja*, *dhava*, *nimba*, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and *vetasa*, boiled down to one-quarter of its original volume. (20) *Mañjiṣṭhā*, lac-resin (*lākṣā-rasa*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and the two types of turmeric (*niśā-yuga*) should be ground together, strained through cloth, and mixed with honey; this is a purifier of wounds and is beneficial. Crushed *nimba* leaves mixed with honey also serve as a purifier of wounds. (21)

22. Nimba leaves, sesame, honey, along with dārvī and madhuka, as well as a paste of sesame seeds, are used for the purification of wounds. 23. A paste of sesame, nimba, the leaves of sītā, and jasmine (sumanā), as well as a decoction, is beneficial for the purification of wounds. 24. Having recognized that the wound is purified, one should then smear the wound with fresh butter; this is excellent, for by it the wound does not burn. 25. Jātī, karañja, picumanda, paṭola, yaṣṭīmadhu, rajanī, and kaṭurohiṇī [are also used].

Equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, utpala, muśīra, karañja seeds, sārivā, trivṛt, and māgadhikā should be used; this ghee, when cooked, is indeed beneficial for wounds, highly recommended for those that have become sinus-like, painful, or bloody, and it destroys spider-bites and erysipelas (visarpa). It heals even deep wounds, those accompanied by burning sensations, and those that are hard, and it causes them to heal completely. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wounds," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya, concerning the *Jātyādi-ghṛta*.

Chapter Thirty-Six. Ātreya said: Elephantiasis (ślīpada) arises through the same treatments mentioned for ulcers. That caused by Vāta appears cracked, dry, and dark-colored. That caused by Pitta is seen with burning and suppuration, as well as fever. That caused by Kapha is unctuous, dense, and accompanied by swelling. All these types arise from the combination of the three humors (sannipāta), O best of physicians. When it is located in the fat (medas), it is called vālmīka and appears like an anthill. One should recognize its symptoms as being similar to those arising from Vāta.

One should perform for that condition the treatments prescribed for wounds according to the rules (4). Ghee prepared with *jāti* and other ingredients is recommended, as are various ointments. Furthermore, an application should be made using *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadambaka* (5). Having ground the root of *girikarṇikā* and also *vṛkṣādanī*, an application should be made for elephantiasis (*vālmīka-ślīpada*) (6). Having ground the tuber of *sūraṇa* with honey and ghee, this application is beneficial and removes elephantiasis caused by *vālmīka* (7). Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Elephantiasis," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Thirty-Seven. Ātreya said: Furthermore, due to injury from wind, exposure to drafts, or even from a wound, blood-carrying channels (raktanaḍīs) sprout and likewise become obstructed. By that, the passage of the blood is blocked, and because of that obstruction, a very large tumor (arbuda) arises. The wise should recognize it as being soft and rough from Vāta, dense and cold from Kapha, and characterized by burning and suppuration from Pitta. From the combination of all three (Sannipāta), it becomes hard, dense, and like a stone.

O best of physicians, a *gaḍuka* that is increasing in size is incurable; at the outset, one should perform incision while avoiding the vital points (*marmasthāna*), and one should apply an ointment of rock salt (*saindhava*) and ghee. O best of physicians, burning the *sūraṇa* tuber and applying it with ghee and jaggery (*guḍa*) as an ointment destroys tumors (*arbuda*). The remaining treatments for wounds (*vraṇakriyā*) are prescribed for the pacification of tumors, as well as Vata-alleviating, wholesome, and sweet foods. Thus ends the section spoken by Ātreya in the *Hārītottara*.

The thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Treatment of Arbuda," in the third section. Chapter Thirty-Eight. Ātreya said: Thus, O best of physicians, the treatment of wounds has been described in brief; one should apply the remedies correctly after understanding the appropriate course of action. From drinking contaminated water and from consuming unwholesome food, a cluster of swellings (*gaṇḍamālā*) arises due to the presence of parasites. When there is a disorder born of Vāta, Kapha, and Pitta, the host of defects produced by parasites spreads from the swelling. Due to Vāta, the symptoms resemble those of Vāta; due to Pitta, there is burning, pain, ulceration, emaciation, and heat; and due to Kapha, there is adhesion.

From the combination of these [fevers], there arises that caused by *sannipāta*, characterized by all the symptoms together. O son, listen as I shall describe its remedy: *rohiṇī*, *viśadā*, *vijayā*, *vibhedinī*, *kāntārī*, *vajrapuṣpā*, and likewise *indrāyudhā*—these are the seven kinds of *lūtā*; listen further to each one individually. *Rohiṇī* is red and appears on a red spot; *viśadā* is white in color and appears on a fleshy part; and *dīrghikā* is likewise. And *vijayā*...

In the middle of the head is the yellow-colored *yavaprabhā* (7); at the site of the fat (*medas*) is the *bhedinī*, which is white with a blue line (8). In the middle of the bladder is the *kāntārī*; the *śvetāṅgā* has a red crest; and in the middle of the bones is the *vajrapuṣpā*. The *śirā* is considered to be white and black (9). At the end of the head is the *indrāyudhā*, and the *śirā* is considered to be smoky-black (10). The *rohiṇī* is the size of a finger-joint, clear and even; the *vijayā* is shaped like a barley grain, and the *vijayā* is likewise circular (11). Others among men should be known as resembling the thorns of the *taṇḍulīka* plant.

The *rohiṇī*, *vijayā*, and *viṃśā* are located in the region of the flesh; the *bhedinī* is seen at the ankle or in the joints of the bones in a man. Know, O son, that the *kāntārī* is in the belly, between the ears, and at the outer corner of the eye. The *vajrapuṣpā* is in the head, and the *indrāyudhā* is considered to be at the end of the head. Therefore, I shall speak of the medical treatment; listen, my son, with diligence. They know a wound to be deep when it exudes thick pus and has a foul odor; another type is painful and has the appearance of a ripe *jambu* fruit. [This applies] to the wounds caused by *lūtā* [spiders].

One should avoid these [sites] as long as they appear unripe, excluding spiders located at joints or vital points (*marmasthāna*); once that wound is ready, cauterization with heated oil should be performed immediately. (16) *Ankola*, liquors, leaves of the *pāribhadra*, soot from a house (*gṛhadhūma*), and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīra*) ground together with cow’s urine—this application is highly recommended as the supreme means for destroying spiders (*lūtā*). (17) One should apply a paste made by grinding *piṇḍītaka*, *viḍaṅga*, the root of *iṅguda*, and the roots of *bījapūraka* to treat *gaṇḍamālā*.

Likewise, it quickly destroys the terrible *prakaṇṭakas*. One should apply the milky sap of *snuhī* and the milky sap of *arka* into the opening of the spider; by that means, the insect dies within it—of this there is no doubt. Having ground *girikarṇī*, sandalwood, and [other ingredients] in equal parts, one should apply a paste to the mouth [of the wound]; it destroys even the most dreadful spider-bite. One should cook *karavīra*, the milky sap of *arka*, *kaṭutumbikā*, the two types of *niśā*, and *jāṅgalikā* in sesame oil; by anointing with this, it destroys the spider-bite.

One should also apply ghee known as Jātyādika-ghee for severe gaṇḍamālā, as well as other treatments prescribed according to the rules for wounds. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Lūtā and Gaṇḍamālā," in the third section of the Hārīta-uttara spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Thirty-nine. Ātreya said: Consuming incompatible drinks, heavy foods, sour substances, and water while fasting, as well as sleeping during the day and staying awake at night, causes the Pitta located in the blood to become aggravated. When that morbid humor reaches the skin, it spreads; the wise call this disease by the name Kuṣṭha (leprosy). O knower of the rules, these diseases arise from past sins and manifest intensely in the bodies of men who greatly provoke the humors. They say there are eighteen types of Kuṣṭha; I shall describe their characteristics individually.

These [diseases] are incurable, curable, born of karma, arising from the humors (*doṣa*), or innate; they consist of compassion, roughness, itching, horripilation, exhilaration, numbness, piercing pain, and aching in the body—these are the signs when [the disease] resides in the skin. Furthermore, there are *kapālaka*, *udumbara*, *dadru*, *maṇḍala*, *visarpaka*, *hastibala*, *kiṇa*, *gojihvaka*, red *maṇḍalas*, *vaipādika*, *carmadala*, and others.

Now, eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*), multiple ulcers (*bahuvraṇa*), itching (*kaṇḍū*), and *vicarcī* are described; likewise, other diseases established as occurring in the skin arise from the differentiation of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (6) That which resembles a skull and is white in color is called *kapālya* by those who know the rules. That which is oily, spreads over the entire body, and is itchy, the wise call *udumbara*. (7) That which resembles *dadrū* is *dadrū*; they call that circular patch *maṇḍalaka*. That which creeps along is *visarpa*, and another type of *visarpa* is like an elephant's hide (*gajacarma*). (8)

That which is rough, harsh, and stinging, appearing like a cow’s tongue, is indeed fit for excision (*gojihvaka*). Those that are yellowish-red, circular, accompanied by itching, and associated with ulcers, should be known as *lohita-maṇḍala*; they arise from blood and are dependent on the blood. That which is painful, spreading, and occurs in one afflicted by pain is called *vipādikā*. It is produced by blood and aggravated wind (*vāta*), resembling a small boil (*visphoṭaka*); it is also known by another name, *bahuvraṇa*, and is characterized by minute eruptions. Thus it is well understood.

In a person, itching and eczema (vicarcikā) are well-known in this world; when a man has white, fine, and pale-red eruptions spreading [over the body], and his blood [is affected], no youth can ever be cured. 12. Shirīṣa flowers, shirīṣa fruits, loss of sensation, and a subtle [itching]—pricking pain as well as trembling are the signs of wind (vāta); by bile (pitta) there is emaciation, vertigo, burning sensation, and thirst. 13. When arising from phlegm (śleṣman), it is hard, cold, and pale; [there is discoloration] in the eyes and nails, and a lack of desire for the body; in the case of a combination [of humors], it is mixed.

That which arises from the combination of all three [doshas] possesses the symptoms of each; it is characterized by many signs. (14) One should know that when located in the skin (*tvak-stha*), it is dry, itchy, soft, and cold, with a discharge that is burning and blood-colored. When located in the blood (*rakta-ga*), it is known by these traits. (15) One should designate that which is located in the flesh (*māṃsa-ga*) as being very unctuous, characterized by pricking pain (*toda*), and deep-seated. When located in the fat (*medas-stha*), there is a sensation of constriction (*veṣṭa*), it is very unctuous, and the eyes become bloodshot. When located in the bone (*asthi-saṃstha*), the visarpa is deep-seated and affects the nose and mouth. (16) And when located in the marrow (*majja-saṃstha*), the patient becomes incapacitated.

A discharge of marrow occurs and the entire body becomes shattered; this is likewise known as the stage involving the semen (śukra). 17. Therefore, O best of physicians, I shall describe the remedial treatments in brief. 18. When [the disease] resides in the skin, fomentation and ointments are used; when it resides in the blood, bloodletting is prescribed. When it resides in the flesh, purgation is declared; when it resides in the fat, decoctions and digestive remedies are used. 19. Now, these three [stages] and those residing in the bone and marrow are treated thus: in the Vātika type, fomentation is beneficial; in the Pittaja type, cooling measures are employed. 20. This [Vātika] is said to be difficult to cure, while the Sānnipātika type is incurable.

Having considered the cause of the disease, one should then begin the treatment. For leprosy (kuṣṭha), one should perform purification (śodhana) and digestive processing (pācana) every fortnight, and induce purgation (recana) every month; for thorough purification, bloodletting (asṛgmokṣaṇa) should be performed every sixth month. One should quickly drink a decoction of vāsā, paṭola, phalinī, lavaṇa, vacā, and nimba bark; this, combined with madana, induces emesis in cases of leprosy. In emetic treatments involving madana, a decoction of pathyā (harītakī) is used. Triphalā, trivṛt, and dantī are the purgatives.

O best of physicians, the decoction should be drunk with warm water; O supreme physician, this is the remedy for its consumption. (24) If the veins in the head are to be pierced for the sake of regulating inhalation and exhalation, then a meal consisting of decoction and unctuous substances should be administered. (25) A decoction prepared with ginger, long pepper, khadira, pāṭalī, paṭolī, mañjiṣṭhā, kṣura, viṣa, bilva, yavānikā, vāsā, and triphalā, when taken with water, destroys the disorder of leprosy in a person. (26)

A decoction of vāsā, viḍaṅga, picumanda, paṭola, pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, surendrataru, the roots of the five trees (pañcataru), and pathyā destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) caused by Vāyu; this great medicine should be administered for twenty-one days. (27) The powder of chinnodbhavā, taken daily with its own decoction, and when digested, followed by milk mixed with ghee and ṣāṣṭika rice, destroys all types of kuṣṭha, even those that have reached the seven bodily constituents (dhātus). (28–29) [Also effective are] kāśmarya, darada, ghana, kuṣṭha, and the two types of niśā.

This *kāñjikakuṣṭha* is recommended for external application; it destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), as well as *vicarcikā* and the affliction of *visarpa*. (30) In that case, these [drugs] ground with *madhuka*, *kāñjika*, and urine, when applied as a paste, destroy even severe *kuṣṭha* and *vicarcikā*. (31) For the affliction of *visarpa*, one should perform washes (*dhāvana*) as prescribed; the wash may be done with the juice of fermented gruel (*sauvīraka-rasa*) or with water decocted with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (32) For *kuṣṭha* caused by Vāta, this is declared by the wise to be highly effective: a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* mixed with a decoction of *nimba* leaves and milk. (33)

Even with a cold decoction of *vidārī*, one destroys most terrible leprosy (*kuṣṭha*); however, [using it as] a wash is not recommended. (34) A decoction of *agnimantha*, *paṭola*, the leaves of *mātuluṅga*, *śaṭhī*, and *parpaṭaka* is a wash for those suffering from diseases of phlegm (*śleṣman*). (35) O best of the wise, having washed *vipādikā* with fresh butter (*navanīta*) and having applied heat with the milks of the *arka* plant, an ointment of honey and oil should be applied. (36) Likewise, *khadira*, *nimba*, *kadambaka*, *kakubha*, *pāṭalī*, *śirīṣa*, *kuṭaja*, *kiṃśuka*, *vāsa*, and *samoraṭa*—[these are used for the treatment].

Vaṭa, kuṭaja, naṭa, pippali, pīlu (37), dhava, mudgara, amra, and vetasa—these, boiled together and drunk with ghee according to the prescribed method, bring about the destruction of all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and the man’s body becomes equal in luster to the moon. (38) Āragvadha, dhātakī, karṇikāra, dhava, arjuna, *sajjaka*, and *kiṃśuka*; likewise, *kadamba*, nimba, *kuṭaja*, *āṭarūṣa*, and *khadira*, as well as *mūrvā* (39)—having properly collected the roots of these, a decoction is prepared until one-eighth remains; this is mixed with an equal amount of ghee.

It destroys all skin diseases born of the body caused by pride (40). It quickly cures all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), ringworm (*dadru*), and scabies (*vicarcikā*) in a man (41). The roots of *khadira*, *kadara*, *mūrvā*, and *vālaka*, along with *karṇikāra*, *kuṭaja*, *saptaparṇa*, *bhadra*, and *āragvadha*—these, when ground and boiled down to one-tenth their original quantity, taken as a decoction with ghee, destroy all forms of leprosy, erysipelas, and prideful ailments (42). [The powder of] *bhallātaka*, *tryūṣaṇa*, *akṣa*, *kuṣṭha*, *guñjā*, the five salts, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*)...

Oil cooked with these, when used as an ointment, destroys ringworm and leprosy (43). A mixture of the roots of *aśvaghna*, soot, *samaṅgā*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric), mustard, *citraka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *kuhatumbikā*, *kuṣṭha*, *viḍaṅga*, and *magadhā* (long pepper) [44]—this powder, when cooked in sesame oil with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, once fully prepared, certainly destroys ringworm and itching when applied as an ointment for a man (45). [Also included are: *haridrā*, *samaṅgā*, *surāhva* (guggulu), *citraka*, and *viḍaṅga*.

Kṛṣṇā, viśālā, ambu, kuṣṭha, as well as lāṅgalī, cakramarda, guñjā, viśālā, and the leaves of ariṣṭa—this powder, once prepared and processed with jaggery, should be cooked over a gentle heat; it is beneficial for application and very quickly destroys kuṣṭha, pāmā, and vicarcī in a person. Nimba, paṭola, kirātaka, jātī, viśālā, punarnavā, payoda, the juice of lākṣā, vāsā, trāyantikā, bilva, kuṣṭha, and yaṣṭi—these should be finely powdered.

Ghee cooked with milk and curd is beneficial for sprinkling; it destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha), wounds, ringworm (dadru), blood disorders, scabies (pāmā), and eczema (vicarcī), as well as itching (kaṇḍū). Bile itself, when provoked by wind (vāta) and accompanied by blood, becomes aggravated and produces a pale complexion. Its symptoms include a stiff mind and deformity; the best of physicians should determine whether such leprosy is incurable or curable. That which arises from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta) is slightly reddish and pale.

That which arises with discoloration over the entire body and is oily is incurable; however, that which has become yellowish, pale, and rough is known to be most treatable. Purgation, cleansing, emesis, and bloodletting are recommended. (52–53) A paste made from vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, karañja, paṭola, nimba, arjuna, vetasa, along with kṛṣṇā and samaṅgā, is beneficial when drunk for the treatment of *citraka-maṇḍala*. (54) [One should also use] khadira, vāsaka, nimba, paṭola, dhava, yavāsa, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*).

It conquers all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), circular patches (*maṇḍala*), and the pallor of a person. 55 *Pāṭhā*, *viḍaṅga*, *magadhā*, *suradāru*, *citraka*, the two types of *dadrughna*, and *rātri*, as well as *samaṅgā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, and *madhuka*—ground together with *saindhava* salt and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), or else with urine, blood, or meat-broth—56 when applied as a plaster, this proven remedy destroys variegated leprosy (*citra-kuṣṭha*), as well as itching leprosy (*kaṇḍu-kuṣṭha*). It also eliminates scabies (*vicarcikā*), itching, boils (*visphoṭa*), and spreading eruptions (*pratisarpana*). 57 *Bhṛṅgarāja*... [text continues]

Turmeric, dūrvā grass, jasmine, viḍaṅga, black sesame, citraka, and likewise yellow sandalwood (58)—these, ground with urine and applied as a plaster, destroy all types of ringworm and leprosy in one afflicted by variegated skin diseases, including scabies and eczema (59). Furthermore, one should employ those foods prescribed as wholesome for fever which are not burning, not sour, and not aggravating to wind; these are beneficial for those undergoing treatment for ulcers and patches of leprosy (60). Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Leprosy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 39.

Chapter Forty. Ātreya said: Due to excessive burden or over-exertion, from the state of extreme sharpness and heat, or from coldness due to lack of oil massage—especially through pitta; or due to the disorder of worms, a disease of the head arises in men. It may be caused by vāta, rakta, kapha, or pitta, and especially by pitta alone. Others are to be known as arising from sannipāta (the combination of all three humors) or from worms. There is also the disorder known as *ardhaśīrṣa* (hemicephalus), which increases day by day. Pain occurs at night due to vāta, and the patient's head then suffers agony.

She obtains relief through fomentation and massage, or from pain in the anus and testicles caused by Vāta. (4) He whose limbs become hot in the head during the heat of the day or at night, finds relief from smoking or pungent substances when there is Kapha; or he attains comfort and health from cold at night. (5) Or he finds comfort from cold, yet first experiences thirst and intense pain arising from Pitta; or it occurs at sunrise or at the end of the day, with dizziness and very intense thirst. (6) And his head becomes cold, accompanied by numbness.

If a pair of eyes joined by sweat certainly appear similar, or if there is a desired disorder of the head due to *kapha*; (7) if a web-like film issues from the nostrils due to blood, with thirst in the rest of the mouth, bloodshot eyes, and [discharge] in the abdomen—that one is called a head disease born of blood; (8) if it spreads after corrupting the middle [of the head], with yellow discharge from the nose, accompanied by feces and water, along with numbness, delusion, and labored breathing, and if the headache arises from the obstruction of the three *doṣas*—(9) for whom it is excessive...

Even when the head is being split open by a goad, there is a discharge from the tip of the nose consisting of blood and pus, accompanied by the emergence of worms and headache. Another type arises from anger or grief, as does that caused by excessive physical exertion and over-fatigue; such is the headache in men arising from Vāta along with pain. Furthermore, from excessive scraping or reading, from looking at minute objects, or even from seeing from a great distance, pain born of Vāta and blood (Vātarakta) occurs. There is pain in one half of the nose, and pain in the pair of eyebrows, which becomes blue and black.
