One should observe that the pain is located at the head (13). Bile does not exist without blood, and blood is moved by bile; there is no headache without bile, for bile is moved by wind (vāta) (14). Therefore, I shall describe the treatment; listen to the characteristics of the medicine: fomentation, plastering, nasal drops, drinking, massage, and rubbing (15). Fomentation is indicated in cases born of wind and phlegm, as well as in injury; however, one should not perform fomentation in those two [types] when they are born of bile or blood (16). In the case of blood-born [headache], a vein should be pierced; in the case of bile-born, [treatment should be applied].

Alternatively, in some cases, one should apply a decoction made from the plant called *kokilā*, *tarkārī*, *kaṭukā*, neem leaves, and the seeds of *śobhāñjanaka*; by means of this, one should foment the area, and through the application of these as a paste, relief will arise for him. In the case of a Pitta-born [fever], there should be cold sprinklings and cold applications using licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhuka*), sandalwood, *kesara*, and *mātuluṅga*. O best of physicians, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and *sindhuvāra* are also used for application; or alternatively, ginger with jaggery, or *pathyā* with jaggery may be used.

Through the application of snuff (nasya) using jaggery and the juice of *śobhāñjana* separately, or with goat's urine as a snuff, headache is pacified. O best of physicians, for a severe headache arising from phlegm (*kapha*), a snuff consisting of black pepper, *pathyā*, and *kaṭphala*, taken with either urine or warm water, is prescribed. For a headache caused by the derangement of the three humors (*sannipāta*), the use of a snuff made from *vacā*, the essence of *madhuka*, or the root of *girikarṇikā* is ordained. Furthermore, for a headache born of worms (*krimija*), one should administer a measured dose of the root of *vandhyākarkaṭakī*, ground with warm water, as a snuff.

For diseases located in the head (śirogada), one should add the following to it: one part of *mṛṅgarāja-rasa* and two parts of *kāñjika*, along with three parts of *śobhāñjana*. Then, add five parts of *sauvīraka-rasa* and six parts of *tumbikā-rasa*, as well as *śuṇṭhī*, *saindhava*, *amlīkā*, *paṭola*, *vāsaka*, *śivā*, *abhayā*, and *surasā*, together with four parts of oil. Once cooked, this should be administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) in a dose of six drops. Likewise, it is beneficial for anointing the head and is also beneficial when used as ear-drops (*karṇapūraka*).

In diseases born of wind (vāta) and the like, in headaches, and likewise in those caused by worms (krimija), O wise one, one should extract oil from the seeds of *karañja* and *vibhītaka* using a closed vessel (*puṭapāka*), and apply three drops of it as nasal medication (*nasya*); this destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and disorders born of worms. Having taken *kuṣṭha*, *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, and the juices of *paṭola*, *jātī*, and *surasa*, and having cooked them with fresh butter (*navanītaka*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), this is certainly effective for *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders). This [butter] mixed with sugar should be administered during the day when the humors (*doṣa*) have increased in intensity.

Lac juice, sandalwood, liquorice, patola, emblic myrobalan, sugar, curd, milk, and fresh butter—when cooked together, this is employed in the procedure for nasal administration (nasya). It is used for defects of the eyebrows, pain in the temples, loss of blood, or when the humors (doṣas) increase day by day. Saffron, liquorice, and costus, mixed with an equal amount of sugar and cooked with fresh butter and ghee, should be administered as a nasal medicine. By administering it in increasing doses day by day, diseases born of pitta and disorders of the half-head (hemiplegia) are destroyed.
It quickly attains pacification. Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Head," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 40.

Chapter Forty-one. Ātreya said: In one who is habitually prone to excessive reading, or due to the observation of minute objects, or by looking into the distance, or by heat, the disorder known as *bhrū-doṣa* arises. (1) The morbid humor (*doṣa*), localized in the blood and wind (*vāta*) and intensified by bile (*pitta*), produces pain in the eyebrows and in the vessels originating from the bridge of the nose. (2) It aches during times of heat and especially when cooled; furthermore, one perceives blue and yellow circles in the center of the eye. (3) For that condition, one should first perform the treatment: the veins must be diligently venesected.

The previously mentioned sudation (svedana) should be performed, followed by nasal therapy (nasya) consisting of six drops and so forth. (4) Devadāru, rajanī, ghana, śaṭī, puṣkara, seeds of kuṭaja, māgadhī, kuṣṭha, rodhra, cavikā, and yavāsaka should be boiled and then strained again. (5) Into that [decoction], one should further add guggulu, along with powdered śuṇṭhī, saindhava salt, and the three fruits (triphalā), which are beneficial. This should be mixed with curd and milk, cooked, and turned into fresh butter (navanītaka). (6) Once prepared, this should be administered cold; mixed with sugar, it is a beneficial nasal medicine (nasya).

Nasal therapy (*nasyakarma*) applied to the region of the eyebrows, forehead, shoulders, and the roots of the temples removes pain from the head (7). Even for diseases of the entire head or hemiplegia (*ardhaśīrṣaka*), when administered as a simple application (*todana*), it wards off disease; likewise, oil is supreme for curing diseases of the head (8). The juice of betel leaf (*tāmbūlapatra*), combined with *biḍaṅga*, rock salt (*sindhūdbhava*), and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), ground with jaggery (*guḍa*) and water, when prepared as a nasal treatment, destroys defects of the eyebrows and temples as well as worms (9). Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Eyebrow Defects," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 41.

Chapter Forty-two. Ātreya said: O wise one, O best of physicians, nasal disease may be caused by worms, by the [humoral] defects, or by blood; hear from me its symptoms. (1) In the case of wind (vāta), there is headache and swelling; in that involving both wind and bile (vātapaittika), it is accompanied by the [defects]; in the phlegm-born (kaphaja) type, it is thick and cold; in the worm-born (krimija) type, there is discharge of blood. (2) For nasal suppuration (nāsāpāka), in the wind-type, a nasal drop (nasya) of jaggery and ginger is prescribed; in the bile-type, a nasal drop of sugar, ghee, and liquorice is prescribed. (3) In the phlegm-type, it is prepared with the juice of *surasā* and *vāsā*.

In cases of worm-infestation, *viḍaṅga*, *hiṅgu*, and *māgadhā* are considered beneficial. In diseases born of blood (*raktaja*), bloodletting is the primary treatment for head ailments. Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Nose," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-three. Ātreya said: Now listen, Hārīta, to the treatment for hair-destroying diseases (keśaghna). Due to Vāta, it is dry and pale; due to Pitta, it is red and accompanied by a burning sensation; when associated with Kapha, it becomes oily; and from blood, it undergoes suppuration. That which arises from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) manifests with symptoms resembling all of these. For hair-destroying disease born of Vāta, washing the head with jaggery, Surasā, ginger, and the juice of Mātuluṅga is recommended. Furthermore, Triphalā, Vacā, and Rōhitaka ground together with jaggery [is also beneficial].

Washing (the head) is recommended in cases of *aindralupta* arising from *kapha*. In the *paittika* type, milk combined with fresh butter (*navanīta*) is beneficial; likewise, sugar, *āmalaka* fruit, and *yaṣṭīmadhu* are considered suitable for washing in the *paittika* type. One should take the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* as well as the juice of *śṛṅgavera*; having ground sesame seeds with the juice of *sauvīraka*, an ointment should be applied, after which the man should bathe with warm water. A decoction of *dhava*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *śirīṣa*, and *rohitaka* [is used] for the head and for *dadrū*.

One should pacify *indraluptaka* (alopecia) with the flower of the *kurabaka* and the blossom of the *japā*. By rubbing [the area] with these, the treatment for *indralupta* is indeed accomplished. Having observed the symptoms caused by *pitta*, one should wash with milk; cooling applications are prescribed for the *paittika* type. *Dhattūra* leaves, *māgadhī*, *niśā*, *viśālā*, house-soot (*gṛhadhūma*), and *kuṣṭha*, mixed with ghee and ground with water, when applied as a paste to the head, will prevent wounds in diseases associated with *pitta* and the provoked *doṣas*.

Having ground either the leaf of *paṭola*, or that of *picumanda* (neem), or likewise the fruit of *malakī*, an application with ghee and sugar-candy prevents wounds born on the head; this also destroys headaches and various swellings. Taking the soot of an elephant’s tusk, an application with fresh butter (*navanītaka*) [is used]. An application with fresh butter of the ash of sesame, *arka*, *bhallātaka*, and burnt beans, as well as the application of the ash of a snake, produces a growth of hair on a bald spot (*khalvāṭaka*).
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Indralupta," in the third section of the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-four. Ātreya said: Earache may arise from residual [doshas], or from water trapped [in the ear], or from impurities; it may also occur due to the obstruction of breath, or from the vitiation of Vāta and the other [doshas]. Earache in a person may likewise be produced by combinations of two doshas, by all three doshas, or even by worms and ulcers. Because of this, the person hears many sounds: the sound of a flute, the roar of clouds, the noise of teeth grinding, a piercing pain accompanied by burning, and headache.

O child, know that when one hears everything [distorted] due to *pitta*, O best of physicians; likewise, in the case of *kapha*, it spreads faintness and one hears sounds like the roar of clouds. In the disorder caused by worms (*krimi-doṣa*), O most excellent one, pus mixed with blood flows out; likewise, intense pain arises from injury (*abhighāta*). From a wound (*kṣata*) pus flows out, and another type arises from childhood; furthermore, that ear-pain is produced by the defect of *lūti*. In ear diseases, neither filling with water nor this powder [is indicated]; thus it has been declared.

One who knows the procedure should apply beneficial oil and fomentation to the ear; it is also considered beneficial to apply drops of warm tears. (7) One should prepare a fine powder of rock salt (*saindhava*) and sea-foam (*samudraphena*); this filling of the ear with the juice of *sauvīraka* is indicated for disorders caused by Vāta. (8) The juice of fresh *sauvīraka*, along with ginger, rock salt, and *guggulu*, should be cooked with oil and the juice of fermented black gram (*kulmāṣa*); when extremely hot, it should be held in the ear, as it is highly praised for ear diseases. (9–10) [Likewise,] liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), leaves of *ariṣṭa*, and turmeric (*niśā*)...

In cases of earache arising from *karṇa* (the ear) associated with *pitta*, ghee processed with *viśālā*, *asumanaḥ*, and *pravāla* is recommended. (11) Similarly, the juice of *brāhmī*, *saindhava* salt, *viḍaṅga*, and *bhṛṅgarāja* combined with ghee, as well as the juice of *sauvīra* and *pathyā* strained through a cloth until fully saturated—this is beneficial for filling the auditory canal; it destroys pus, blood, and worms. (12–13) All the aforementioned diseases of the head have been described, along with the oils and ghees; one should also employ formulations containing *jātī* and other such ingredients. (14)

The foremost among those who know the diseases of the head (14). Wholesome foods that remove wind, as well as those that cause burning and are heavy (15). Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Ear Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 44.

Chapter Forty-Five. Ātreya said: The humors (*doṣas*) residing in the eyes become aggravated by hot, excessively alkaline, or pungent substances, or again by injury, or even by looking through a fine cloth or a small opening. (1) I shall now describe the characteristics of those congenital (*sahaja*) conditions that are difficult to conquer; listen. Dryness, itching, pricking pain, and a continuous flow of dry, cold tears—(2) one should recognize that as the *vātika* type. Now hear about the *paittika* type: (3) in the *paittika* [type], the eyes are reddish, accompanied by burning, and there is a warm discharge. In the *sannipāta* [type], there is swelling and itching; in the *kaphātman* [type], there is coldness and stiffness. (4)

In cases arising from dual combinations (*dvandvaja*), [the treatment] is with those having mixed characteristics; in the case of the combined (*sānnipātika*) type, it is with all of them. Having understood these symptoms, now hear from me the therapeutic procedure (5). For the Pitta-type, washing with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *surāhvā*, and *surasā* along with warm sour gruel (*kāñjika*) is prescribed. For that arising from Kapha (*śleṣmodbhava*), this paste of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) with urine is commended, as well as other formulations described by the best of physicians (6). Ginger, *saṭhī*, turmeric (*rajanī*), the three myrobalans, neem (*nimba*), and cinnamon leaves (*patrāṇi*), combined with rock salt (*saindhava*) and fermented rice-water (*tuṣāmlaka*), they declare to be excellent.

In cases of eye diseases involving the *sannipāta* (combined humors), those arising from blood, and those accompanied by pain, the three fruits (*triphalā*) along with turmeric (*niśā*) are recommended as a collyrium (*dhūma*). In disorders born of *kapha*, or those associated with *vāta*, an ointment made of *vacā*, *varṣābhū*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) is likewise beneficial and highly praised. Alternatively, the root of *apāmārga* or the root of *dhattūra*, rubbed in a copper vessel with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), rock salt, and buttermilk (*takra*), serves as a beneficial collyrium that removes diseases of the eyes caused by *vāta*. Fresh butter produced from milk and liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*) [are also beneficial].

Nimba and sesame seeds combined with Triphalā and jaggery form a plaster that destroys eye diseases caused by Kapha. (11) A collyrium made of Śuṇṭhī, Saindhava salt, Tuttha, and Māgadhikā, rubbed on a copper vessel with curd and clarified butter, cures all eye ailments. (12) The juice of Śigru leaves alone, when applied along with honey, instantly removes the great suffering of the eyes arising from the humors of Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha. (13) And due to improper diet and lifestyle, [a growth called] Puṣpa appears in the eyes.

The first [type] arises and is easily curable; the second is difficult to cure (14). The third is treatable by surgery, while the fourth is incurable (15). O best of physicians, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *rodhra*, conch-shell navel, and realgar, ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and dried in the shade, [are beneficial]. (16) For the wind-type (*vātika*), it is beneficial with sour gruel; for the bile-type (*paittika*), with milk; for the phlegm-type (*śleṣmala*), combined with urine; and for the application of the flower, it is beneficial. (17) It is also beneficial for pacifying the three humors (*tridoṣa*) when taken with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, along with *harītakī* and *vacā*.

Kuṣṭha, pippalī, and marica (18), or the marrow of vibhītaka, conch-shell navel, and realgar—these, taken in equal parts, should be ground with goat’s milk (19). This destroys timira, itching, pāṭala, and arbuda; it kills puṣpa along with paṭala and cures night-blindness (rātryāndhya). It is desired for the eyes in cases of injury from trauma, grief, or burns by fire, as well as for kāca and nīlikā (20–21). [These arise] from childhood, the power of the humors (doṣas), or the consumption of corrupted food and drink.

Due to old age, there may also be a film (paṭala); I shall describe its characteristics. From *vāta*, it is accompanied by *kaśmala* (dimness) and is dry; from *pitta*, it is blue and yellow; from *kapha*, it is white and thick; and from blood, they know it to be reddish. Because of the symptoms of *sannipāta* (combined humors) and so forth, I shall hereafter describe the remedy. This is a medicinal wick (*varti*) for rubbing, prepared with *śuṇṭhī*, *vacā*, turmeric, *tuttha*, realgar, *śobhāñjana*, collyrium, *viśālā*, the root of *jaṭā*, conch-shell, *vāstūka* root, honey, rock salt, and *kaṭphala*, combined with *sauvīraka*.

In cases of eye-ointment made from *chāyā* and dried substances, this is recommended; it brings about the destruction of the entire host of diseases such as *paṭala* and other ocular ailments. (26) Harītakī with *añjana* and *kaṭphala*, along with realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and *kaṭphala* mixed with jaggery, destroys *netrapracchada*. (27) A wick (*varti*) made from the fruit of the great *vibhītaka*, rubbed with conch-shell (*śaṅkhanābhi*), combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), milk, sour gruel, and jaggery, is beneficial for eye-ointment and serves to ward off *paṭala* arising from bile (*pitta*). (28) [One should avoid] smoke, wind, dryness, heat, and similar [conditions].

Likewise, those suffering from eye diseases should avoid pungent and sour foods, as well as sexual intercourse. Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Eye Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 45.

Chapter Forty-Six. Ātreya said: If one's lips are cracked due to excessive speaking or from a Vāta disorder, the consumption of ghee is recommended for preventing the splitting of the lips (1). If there is burning and heat, one should diagnose that as Pittaja (2). Anointing the lips with honey and fresh butter is prescribed; likewise, applying curd mixed with sugar is beneficial for lip diseases (3). Upon seeing a lip disease accompanied by blood, one should perform bloodletting; an application of the paste of Dhava, Arjuna, and Kadamba will bring relief.

4. When a row of black teeth appears and the root of the tooth is seen to be loose due to wind (vāta), one should diagnose it as being caused by vāta. 5. From pitta, one should diagnose a flow of bile and inflammation of the gums; in the case of a phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) dental abscess, there is swelling and extreme whiteness. 6. In that born of blood (raktaja), itching arises and a bloody discharge is observed; the gum tissue oozes, and likewise the blood-filled socket of the tooth is affected. 7. When the root of the tooth is perforated and painful, and the gum tissue falls away, it is caused by worms (krimija).

Toothache arises [from these causes]. (8) A paste made of *yavānī*, *vacā*, *sahā*, *citraka*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and *viśvā*, along with *sindhuvāra* and warm water, should be used as five hundred mouthfuls of gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*) for tooth disease and oral ailments; this is praised as beneficial for all diseases of the mouth. (9) Rubbing with *vacā*, rock salt, and *śuṇṭhī* at the roots of the teeth is recommended. (10) One should apply *yavānī* and *vacā* to the roots of the teeth at night. For toothaches caused by *pitta*, fresh butter (*navanīta*) mixed with sugar should be used, rubbed with the fruit of the *dhātrī*. (11) [Rubbed] with the *dhātrī* fruit...

The prevention of dental diseases: For phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) dental diseases, rubbing with *harītakī* or jaggery is recommended; likewise, a decoction of *triphalā* combined [with these] is beneficial. A decoction of the root of *ahimāraka*, when held as a gargle (*gaṇḍūṣa*), [is effective]. Similarly, a decoction of *khadira*, a decoction of *yavānī*, and a decoction of the root of *nimba* prevent dental diseases. In cases of blood-born disorders (*raktaja*), one should rub [the teeth] with salt and mustard seeds and cause the blood to flow from the lip-cavity as desired. *Viḍaṅga*... [is used].

One should rub asafoetida and *sindhuvāra* with the powder of *vacā*; this is beneficial and highly recommended for dental diseases caused by worms. (16) When there is a swelling on the tongue, one should diagnose it as glossitis (*jihvāpāka*). In the Vata-type, it is painful and black; in the Pitta-type, it is accompanied by a burning sensation. (17) In the Kapha-type, it is thick and white; indeed, in the Sannipatika-type, all these features are present. (18) For the Vata-type disease of the tongue, one should apply a rubbing paste of *vacā*, *bhayā*, *viḍaṅga*, ginger, *sauvarcala* salt, and *kaṇā* (long pepper), combined with ghee. (19) [This may be prepared] with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) or buttermilk (*takra*).

Holding a lukewarm gargle of liquorice, sandalwood, nut-grass, and long pepper mixed with honey (20) is an application that prevents the bursting of the tongue in cases of Pitta-type disorders; likewise, holding a cold milk gargle destroys [such ailments]. (21) In diseases of the teeth as well as inflammation of the tongue, they know this to be beneficial; moreover, a warm decoction of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* is easily administered. (22) In mouth ulcers arising from Kapha, holding a gargle is beneficial; in disorders born of blood, one should cause the blood to flow out. (23)

For a tongue that has become red, one should apply a plaster made by rubbing even a thorn on the tongue, combined with *mūrvā*, *mustā*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *māgadhī*, and the two types of *rajanī*, mixed with jaggery and honey. When a swelling caused by phlegm (*śleṣman*) arises in the tongue, they know that rubbing it with the powder of black pepper, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *harītakī* is beneficial. Furthermore, from the consumption of sesame, slimy substances, sweets, and the like, as well as from excessive fluids and new water, a disease of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*) born of phlegm arises at the root of the tongue and the junction of the throat, originating from both phlegm and blood.

From that, dryness of the mouth, numbness, and mild fever arise (27). Headache, loss of appetite, drowsiness, and numbness of the face occur; by pressing the *raktapanthikā* vessel between the index finger and the throat, blood flows out, and then decongestion (*vimlāpana*) is beneficial. One should apply a powder of *vacā*, black pepper, and long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*) there (28–29). There should be massage in the region of the throat; by this, the glandular swelling (*granthi*) dissolves. Equal parts of coriander (*dhānya*), ginger (*nāgara*), *jīmūta*, and *vacā* (30)—this decoction is for fomentation (*sveda*) of the *ghaṇṭikā*.

The physician should hold a gargle in the mouth during the day and night, and should place a knot of *vacā* root in the mouth; by this, there will be comfort for him, and he is liberated from diseases of the mouth. (31-32) When a growth caused by disorders of blood and phlegm develops in the throat and the passage of the epiglottis in men, it should be known as *galagaṇḍikā*. (33) It obstructs the oral cavity and the nasal passages, and discharge from the eyes is observed; accompanied by headache, dyspnea, cough, and fever, it suppurates quickly. (34) An intelligent physician, acting with haste, [should treat it] immediately.

One should apply a surgical treatment by cutting the *śuṇḍikā* (the uvula); then, one should perform a beneficial scarification (*vimlāpana*). (35) A warm decoction of *māgadhī*, black pepper, *pathyā*, *vacā*, coriander, and *yavānikā* should be used as a fomentation (*sveda*) for the pacification of the *galashuṇḍī*. (36) Holding *yavānī* in the mouth during the day and at night is beneficial; by rubbing it on the region of the throat, comfort is attained. (37) An application to the throat of *siddhārthaka*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, turmeric, *pāribhadraka*, soot from a house (*grahadhūma*), and salt is also beneficial.

38. O Great-minded one, those wholesome diets prescribed for fever should not be consumed; likewise, sweet, slimy substances and oil must never be used in diseases of the throat. 39. Thus ends the treatment of *galaśuṇḍikā* (uvulitis). This concludes the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Mouth," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-Seven. Ātreya said: Listen to me as I describe briefly the five types of impotence that have been proclaimed. (1) From the suppression [of sexual desire] or from excessive sexual indulgence, even in a man exhausted by old age, there occurs a loss of semen and impotence also arises. (2) Impotence is born in three ways: mental, from the depletion of semen, and innate; in a man, impotence is also produced by dry perspiration. (3) That which occurs when, upon seeing the lack of passion in women, there is a sense of possessiveness in the mind and sweating at the touch—that is curable. (5)

Mental impotence is recognized as that condition where, due to aversion toward women, the mind suffers depletion through sexual intercourse; the "breaking of the banner" (loss of erection) occurs quickly due to the exhaustion of semen. Another type, characterized by a balanced constitution, is considered most difficult to cure. When there is a depletion of the mind, an increase of the mind occurs through union with charming women, along with passionate amorous gestures and conversations; thus the mind is nourished. Now I shall describe the increase of semen when semen is diminished. [The following are the ingredients: *vidārī*, *gokṣura*, *mūṣaka*, and *dhātrī* fruit.

These [preparations] may be the same for those from Sindh and those from Magadha; one should drink them mixed with milk and enriched with sugar (8). Bṛhatī, the two types of bṛhatī, magadhā, trikaṇṭā, as well as ātmaguptā and śatāvarī—this drink, taken with cow’s milk, ghee, and sugar, produces virility in men (9). One should eat the excellent *vaṭaka* (ball) prepared from the dehusked flour of barley, wheat, and black gram, processed with milk or sugarcane juice and cooked in ghee, having risen in the morning (10). Upon that...

The drinking of milk mixed with long pepper (pippalī) and sugar; likewise, barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), vidārī, and powdered black gram (māṣa); or barley with black pepper enriched with sugar; or a cake (prapolikā) made of ghee—one should cook these and eat them in the morning, followed by the drinking of milk. This increases the virility of men, and the woman takes great delight in him. Guḍūcī, śatamūlī, svayaṃguptā, and balā; likewise, the powder of śālmalī and the root of musalī, when taken with cow’s milk as a drink, is excellent for men and acts as a stimulant for the seed and the senses.

15. Vidārikanda, aṃśumatī, the two types of bṛhatī, kākolikā, bhīru, the two types of punarnavā, śṛṅgāṭaka, māgadhikā, and balā—this powder, enriched with sugar, should be administered with sugar. 16. Once it is digested, milk or milk-porridge (pāyasa) should be used; this bestows strength and vigor upon men. Even an impotent man may enjoy a thousand women; this is highly recommended when prepared for two months. 17. One should avoid pungent, sour, sharp, hot, burning, and dry foods, as well as sauvīra (sour gruel), which have been declared to cause the impairment of the senses.

Onions, barley, bulbs, sesame seeds, and mung beans in appropriate quantities, as well as rice from the *viśālī* variety, milk, and sugarcane juice; likewise, *vāstuka* and *cillaka* greens are wholesome even in cases of seminal depletion (*śukrakṣaya*). However, one should avoid *sūraṇa* and ginger, and should not employ them except when combined with specific medicinal formulations. Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Vājīkaraṇa" (Aphrodisiacs), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-Eight. Ātreya said: A woman may become barren (vandhyā) in six ways: either due to childhood [disease], or from the rupture of the uterine cavity, or likewise from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu). Sometimes the conception of a fetus does not occur at all; one type is the "crow-barren" (kākavandhyā), and the second is the childless (anapatyā). The third is described by the best of sages as the one who miscarries (garbhasrāvī); the fourth is she whose children die (mṛtavatsā), and the fifth is due to the loss of strength (balakṣaya). I shall describe the treatment for her, by which she may obtain [offspring].

4. If sexual intercourse is performed with women who have not yet reached puberty (*ajātarajas*), it causes the contraction of the womb (*garbhasaṅkoca*) and results in the condition known as *bhagatva*. 5. Because of that, a woman becomes barren (*vandhyā*) and does not conceive at all; yet, O physician, she may eventually become pregnant with great difficulty. 6. Through medicines and therapeutic procedures, success is achieved without a doubt; even for those who are childless by nature, offspring are born, O best of physicians. 7. She shall not be a "crow-barren" woman (*kākavandhyā*); even one who is childless is cured, and being thus cured, she succeeds.

O best of physicians, that [condition] arises from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus). For a disease born of Pitta, one should administer a drink consisting of sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, paṭola, dhanavālaka, madhuka, madhuyaṣṭī, and likewise red sandalwood; along with sārivā, cumin, musta, padmaka, and punarnavā, mixed with milk and sugar. Having ascertained the purification of the womb, one should there apply the great medicine: sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, girikarṇī, and sugar, stirred with milk; this will bring about the successful attainment of menstruation in cases of Pitta.

One should examine the menstrual blood (*rajaḥ*) to determine whether it is characterized by *vāta*, *pitta*, or *kapha*. The wise physician should recognize that the menstrual flow which is painful, blackish, or resembles a ripe *jambu* fruit is afflicted by *vāta*. For this condition, the wise one should administer for seven days a decoction of *nāgara*, *pippalī*, *mustā*, *dhanvayavāsaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *pāṭalā*, mixed with jaggery and curd, as long as the blood continues to flow. Once the blood has been purified, he should then have her drink milk combined with *śvetā* and *girikarṇī*.

Guñjā and Punarnavā—by their application for one month, she conceives a fetus. (16) That which resembles the Japā flower or the juice of Kusumbha, and is accompanied by burning sensations, emaciation, and dysuria, is afflicted by Pitta. (17) Candana, Uśīra, Mañjiṣṭhā, Paṭola, Ghana, Vālaka, Madhuka, Yaṣṭimadhuka, and likewise Lohitacandana; (18) Padmaka, the two types of Punarnavā, Śārivā, Jīraka, and Ghana—this drink, combined with milk and sugar, is for diseases caused by Pitta. (19) Having understood [these]:

In that case, one should administer the great medicine for the purification of the womb (*yoniviśuddhi*): the root of white *arka*, white *girikarṇikā*, and the root of white *adrikarṇī*, drunk together with cow’s milk. This brings about conception for barren women, resulting in offspring endowed with auspicious marks. They know that when the *rajas* (menstrual blood) is thick, slimy, cold, obstructing the urine, and accompanied by lassitude, drowsiness, and sleep, it is corrupted by *kapha*. For women, a drink of *triphalā*, *girikarṇī*, *āragvadha*, and *vatsaka*, taken with milk, [is likewise beneficial].

The best of physicians should administer the *garbhakāraṇa* (conception-inducing) powder consisting of *balā* and others, as well as the powders beginning with *candana* and *drākṣā*, to women in order to produce conception. 23–24. Furthermore, the best of physicians should give the *khaṇḍakādya* powder to women, or else the *punarnavādya* powder, which grants pregnancy to women. 25. Now, O son, listen as I describe the wholesome regimen for women: one should keep at a distance from women things that cause burning, those that are sharp, as well as *kañcara*, *sūraṇa*, sour substances, and *kāñjika*. 26. [One should avoid] anything that causes internal heat (*vidāhika*) and anything that is pungent. 27. One should keep far away from women [such things]. 28. [One should avoid] those who are angry, those who are distressed, and those who are excessively passionate. 29. One should avoid those who are very talkative, those who are very restless, and those who are very fickle. 30. One should avoid those who are very greedy, those who are very wrathful, and those who are very deceitful. 31. One should avoid those who are very envious, those who are very malicious, and those who are very cruel. 32. One should avoid those who are very jealous, those who are very spiteful, and those who are very wicked. 33. One should avoid those who are very proud, those who are very vain, and those who are very boastful. 35. One should avoid those who are very stubborn, those who are very obstinate, and those who are very headstrong. 36. One should avoid those who are very stubborn-willed, those who are very rigid, and those who are very unyielding. 37. One should avoid the root of the *vandhyākarkaṭakī*, *lāṅgalī*, bitter *tumbikā* (27), *devadālī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *sūryavallī*, and *bhīrukā*. Likewise, one should avoid temple offerings (*nirmālya*), garlands, and clothing, as well as sexual intercourse during the menstrual period (28). Bathing water from another woman and [the use of] women [as practitioners] are the beneficial treatments (29). Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment for Barrenness," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 48.

The forty-ninth chapter. Ātreya said: In the first month, one should cause [the pregnant woman] to drink yaṣṭīmadhu, paruṣaka, and honey-flowers as available, along with fresh butter, milk, and honey; and she should consume sweet food. In the second month, one should likewise cause her to drink kākolī and sweet food. In the third month, kṛśarā (rice and peas) is best; in the fourth, rice prepared with meat-broth (kṛtaudana). In the fifth month, one should give milk-rice (pāyasa); in the sixth, sweet curd; in the seventh, [food] with ghee and sugar-candy (khaṇḍa); in the eighth, ghee-filled cakes (ghṛtapūraka). In the ninth month, various kinds of cooked foods.

In the tenth month, as well as when the third month has arrived, a woman experiences a pregnancy longing (*dohada*). Whatever she desires, that very thing the best of physicians should provide her. One should avoid foods made from split pulses, those that cause burning sensations, heavy foods, sour things, and warm milk; these must be strictly avoided for pregnant women. Earth should not be eaten, nor should *sūraṇa* tubers; garlic and onions must be abandoned by a pregnant woman. However, *sūraṇa* tubers that are sweet and flavorful should be given, as they are wholesome and beneficial.

A physician should always cause pregnant women to avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, emaciation, and wandering about; by doing so, the prosperity of their well-being is produced. Now, even though it is prescribed according to one's own custom, a meal for the clan (*gotra-bhojana*) should be performed at the fifth or eighth month with auspicious rites for Brahmins and other ceremonies. When the longings (*dohada*) and other requirements are fulfilled, a handsome, brave, wise, and virtuous son is born. Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Care of the Fetus," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Fifty-first Chapter. Ātreya said: If movement is perceived in the embryo during the first month, then Madhuka, Mṛdvīkā, Candana, and Raktacandana (1), mixed with milk and drunk, will cause the embryo to become stable. (2) If movement occurs in the second month, [one should take] Mṛṇāla and Nāgakeśara. When movement of the embryo is perceived in the third month (3), then one should drink the excrement of a mouse with sugar and milk. In the fourth month, there is burning sensation, thirst, and indeed colic (4), along with fever.

If a woman’s fetus moves, she should be made to drink uśīra, sandalwood, nāgakeśara, dhātakī flowers, sugar, ghee, honey, and curd. If the fetus moves in the fifth month, one should have her drink pomegranate leaves, sandalwood, curd, and honey. In the sixth month, she should drink red ochre, black earth, cow-dung ashes, water strained through a cloth, cooled, along with sandalwood and sugar.

In the seventh month, one should have her drink a sweet decoction of *gokṣura*, *samaṅgā*, *padmaka*, *ghanasārī*, and *nāgakeśara*. In the eighth month, for women whose fetus has moved, comfort is attained by those who have drunk *rodhra*, honey, and *māgadhikā* together with milk. Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of a Moved Fetus," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 50.

The fifty-first chapter. Ātreya said: Emaciation (śoṣa), nausea, vomiting, swelling, fever, as well as loss of appetite, diarrhea, and discoloration—these eight are the complications of pregnancy. I shall now describe its treatment according to the appropriate application: the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree, *magadhā*, *uśīra*, and *ghana* [should be used]. A bolus made of these mixed with sugar, placed in the mouth, removes emaciation. One should administer *vatsaka*, *magadhā*, ginger, and the fruit of *āmalakī*, ground together with tender *bilva* and curd.

A drink mixed with sugar is always beneficial for women during pregnancy. (5) The paste of *bhūnimba* drunk after being saturated with sugar, or combined with honey, removes vomiting and moisture in the heart. (6) Fresh ginger, *kaṭuka*, and the filaments (*keśara*) of *mātuluṅga*, used for cleansing the teeth and tongue, as well as gargling with warm water, (7) alleviates the loss of appetite in all pregnant women. Likewise, *vatsaka*, pomegranate, *pāṭhā*, *bilva*, and *balā* (8) as well as the tender leaves of *jambu* and mango, [are used] according to the method. (9)

O Seventh One, for women suffering from diarrhea, [a preparation] combined with sugar and curd is beneficial. (9) Harītakī, ginger, or Triphalā decoction taken cold with jaggery destroys constipation and abscesses in women when drunk. (10) For urinary obstruction, one should drink the seeds of Trapusa, Ervaru, and Māgadhi, along with Śilābheda, mixed with plenty of sugar and rice-water;

this certainly and quickly removes the blockage of urine in pregnant women. (11) A paste of Madhuka, Viṣa, and lotus stalks, the filaments of the lotus, Ghanā, Ativiṣā, and Indrā-bīja, mixed with Uśīra water—[this is used for cooling].

Then, a paste (kalka) made from equal parts [of the ingredients] should be administered quickly as a drink; this is beneficial even for young women during the movement of the fetus, provided it is enriched with sugar. 12 Swelling is a complication of the fetus; one should apply fomentation with warm water. A wise physician must not administer a severe or great purgative. 13 Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications of Pregnancy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 51

The fifty-second chapter. Ātreya said: Due to the consumption of incompatible foods, as well as during the distresses of pregnancy, the infant suffers pain from excessive pressure upon the head. Or, the fetus may die by exiting transversely through the vaginal opening or another passage; thus, the offspring meets with hardship. Alternatively, due to the modesty of women, when the vagina is constricted, one should recognize a "confused fetus" (mūḍhagarbha); I shall now describe its symptoms. There is also pain in the bladder.

The birth canal becomes obstructed, the abdomen roars, and distension occurs; there is piercing pain, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of sleep—O best of physicians, from wind (vāta) arises the obstruction of the fetus. There is colic, fever, the three doṣas, thirst, impairment of the senses, vertigo, difficulty in urination, and headache; from bile (pitta) arises the obstruction of the embryo. From phlegm (śleṣman) arise lethargy, drowsiness, sleep, stupor, distension, trembling, cough, and a bad taste in the mouth.

In the case of a dead fetus (mūḍhagarbhaka), one should recognize that which arises from dual combinations (dvandvaja) through their respective pairs [of symptoms], while everything arising from the combination of all three doshas (sānnipātika) possesses all [symptoms]. One should know a dead fetus by the presence of dizziness, fainting, thirst, flatulence, obstruction of wind, agitation, fainting, vomiting, roughness, and a state of dejection; this applies even to a woman who acts with haste. O expert in great delusion, I shall now describe the remedy for this. In the case of a vātika [fetus], the best of physicians should prescribe massage, anointing, mild sudation, and should have her drink gruel (yavāgū) and the five-spice compound (pañcakola). In the case of a paittika [fetus]...

Cool drinks along with cold side dishes and condiments should be given; likewise, one should drink *yaṣṭika* with milk. (12) Trikaṭu, triphalā, kuṣṭha, rodhra, vatsaka, and dhātukī, boiled together with jaggery, should be drunk for the removal of a dead fetus caused by kapha. (13) A decoction of mūrvā, ciñcā, vāstuka, karṇī, mañjiṣṭhā, rodhra, nīlikā, the root of karkandhu, and saurāṣṭrī, taken with jaggery, is beneficial. (14) In disorders of *raktapitta*, purification of the abdomen occurs; now I shall describe the medicine for a dead fetus.

O best of physicians, having first carefully massaged the woman's human [womb], if the fetus within the woman dies due to lack of nourishment, then listen to me regarding the surgical remedies and medicines: having fashioned a well-curved instrument (sukuṇḍalikā) to fit into the opening of the navel, one should seat the woman with the obstructed fetus upon it, extend her knees slightly, and, supporting her back with a common prop, draw the fetus down from the abdomen.

If [the fetus] is stuck at the vaginal opening, one should lubricate the hand with sesame oil or water and insert it; then, grasping the neck region of the fetus with the index finger and thumb, one should extract it. Alternatively, using a crescent-shaped surgical instrument, one should cut through the pair of arms of the dead fetus and extract the limbs. By applying the root of the *lāṅgalī* plant to the navel of women with warm water as an ointment, the fetus quickly comes forth and she gives birth.

One should grind the roots of *balā*, *sūryakānti*, and *somavallī* with collyrium and apply it as an ointment. (18) Having ground the roots of *bhīru*, *bhūnimba*, and *vārttākī*, along with *pippalī*, *yavānī*, and *aggravacā*, together with warm water, one should apply it as an ointment below the navel; by this application, she shall give birth. (19) The root of *lāṅgalikī*, *devadālī*, *tumbikā*, *kośātakī*, and all other such [plants] are prescribed for application as an ointment; indeed, these are "birth-inducing ointments" (*sūtilepa*) for women, and by them she gives birth easily. (20–21) [This is found] on the northern side of the Himavat.

On the bank [of the river] is a rākṣasī named Surasā; by the sound of her anklets, the pregnant woman Viśalyā shall become free from pain. Aiṃ hrīṃ, O Blessed One, O Bhagamālinī, move, move! Cause it to revolve! Open the flower, open it! Svāhā! Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the one whose banner is the makara, the one whose bow is flowers, who has stirred the hearts of all gods and asuras, who dwells in the wombs of young women: hrīṃ, cause the womb to move, cause it to move! Svāhā!

One should have her drink milk consecrated with this [mantra]; by that, there is an easy delivery. (23) Aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hroṃ hrauṃ hraḥ. (24) Having written this yantra on the upper side of a birch-bark leaf, one should show it to a woman with a difficult labor and place it beneath her bed; by that, there is an easy delivery. (25) She who dwells alone on the banks of the Gaṅgā and wanders in the Himalayas—one should have her drink water from which its wings have fallen; then, in an instant, (26) the woman gives birth, according to the words of Kākarudra. By this [means]. (27)

The messenger should remain agitated until she has been made to drink [the medicine]; by that means, the woman gives birth at home with the ease of a crow. Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Treatment for Mūḍhagarbha (Obstructed Labor)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-third chapter. Ātreya said: Immediately after delivery, one should administer the seeds of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *devadāru*, and *bījakāhva*, along with *karkandhū* as available, into the cleansed blood. The birth-canal, having been purified, should be filled with oil and massaged; then, using a heating substance (*vahnin*), one should apply fomentation (*sveda*). Having observed a fast in this manner, on the second day, one should administer jaggery, ginger, and *harītakī*. After two watches of the night have passed, one should cause her to drink either warm *kulattha* soup or [the aforementioned mixture].

On the third day, one should administer a gruel made of five *kola* fruits. One should administer a gruel mixed with the four aromatic spices (*caturjātaka*). On the fifth day, one should feed him boiled rice of *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* varieties. Following this sequence, one should provide nourishment for fifteen days. 1. One should grind together long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), ginger (*nāgara*), *ghanavāluka*, coriander (*kustumburūṇi*), and *mañjiṣṭhā* with milk to form a paste. 2. For the purpose of purifying the milk, one consumes the paste immediately after drinking the milk. 3. Black pepper (*marīca*) and long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*) [are added] to the milk for the sake of increasing the quantity of milk.

Māgadhī, Nāgarī, Pathyā, jaggery with ghee, and milk—this drink produces breast milk for women, even when taken in a dose of one-fourth part milk. (4) Having performed this for women on the twelfth day, the best of physicians, after conducting an auspicious recitation (*vācana*), should perform the rite for the woman. (5) Furthermore, on the twelfth day following the birth of a son, once the naming ceremony (*nāmakarma*) has been completed, he should perform the piercing of the ears. (6) He should also cause the tying of the cloth (*vastrabandha*) and the marriage ceremony (*vivāha*) to be performed for the child. (7) Thus [ends] the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
In the third section, the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Attendants of Childbirth" (Sūtikopacārī), ends.

**The Fifty-fourth Chapter** Ātreya said: The wise have described five defects of breast milk in women: thick milk, hot milk, sour milk, and another; [furthermore], there is scanty milk, alkaline milk, and soft milk. Of these, soft milk leads to well-being, while the other five cause defects. From the consumption of thick milk, there occurs abdominal distension, constipation, and the onset of dyspnea, cough, and so forth, as well as a bloated abdomen. [The child becomes] one of little vitality, emaciated, and dejected.

Afflicted by dyspnea and diarrhea due to the defect of insufficient milk, the son of Ghatavāk may come to be [thus]. (4) Fever, emaciation, and thinness arise in a child from warm milk; likewise, fever and diarrhea occur from warm milk. (5) Through mild milk, the infant certainly attains a good disposition, strength, and health, and he also becomes handsome. (6) Eye disease, itching, discharge of blood and phlegm, and a moistening of the nose and mouth occur when alkaline milk is consumed. (7) Therefore, I shall now describe the remedy.

Listen, Hārīta, to my teaching: 8. When the abdomen is distended and swollen due to flatulence, and afflicted by disorders such as dyspnea, this condition is to be known as *utphullikā*, which causes great suffering for children. 9. In the case of *udare* (abdominal swelling), one should first extract blood using leeches and the like; when the *utphullidoṣa* is present, a remedy that neutralizes the defect of milk (*kṣīradoṣa*) should be administered. 10. A strong fomentation (*sveda*) with fire, or even cauterization with a probe (*śalākā*), should be applied; O best of physicians, spots shaped like drops then appear upon the belly. 11. A decoction of *bilva* root and fruit, *pāṭhā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and the two types of *bṛhatī*, mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*), [is the remedy].

This is beneficial for children suffering from fever (12). For women, the drinking of these [decoctions] will destroy the fever of children (13). A decoction of *parpaṭaka* combined with sugar and honey is beneficial; likewise, *kairāta* combined with honey destroys the fever of children (14). Alternatively, a powder of *bhārgī*, *rāsnā*, and *karkaṭaka* combined with honey, or a linctus [made from them], prevents asthma and cough even in a child (15). A powder of *pathyā*, *vacā*, *nāgaraka*, *ghana*, and *karkaṭa* mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*) indeed destroys the cough of children (16). [Also] *palāśabheda*...

Having ground triphalā, trapusī, varī, and māgadhī with rice-water, one should administer it enriched with sugar; this conquers urinary obstruction (17). One should give the powder of nāgarī, abhayā, dantī, and guḍa to children; it will undoubtedly destroy abscesses as well (18). A drink of pāṭhā, bilva, śilā and others, vatsaka, and the bark of śālmalī with milk prevents diarrhea in children (19). An ointment of arjuna, kadamba, kuṣṭha, and gairika wards off skin disorders in a child (20). [Also] rodhra...

Rasāñjana, dhātrī, and gairika, combined with honey as a collyrium, prevent eye diseases in children. (21) Vacā, brāhmī, maṇḍūkī, ghanasāra, kuṣṭha, and nāgara, given in the morning with ghee, promotes nourishment in children. (22) Guḍūcī, apāmārga, viḍaṅga, śaṅkhapuṣpikā, viṣṇukrāntā, vacā, pathyā, nāgara, and śatāvarī—(23) The powder of these, mixed with ghee, when licked, brings forth intelligence; in three days, one gains a thousand [verses]. (24)

One should master these twenty-four verses. A powder made of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), coriander (dhanyā), caraway (yavānī), *sālamūlikā*, *vacā*, *brāhmī*, and *bhārṅgī* is beneficial when taken with honey; it bestows eloquence upon children and produces a voice as melodious as a lute. O best of physicians, he in whom there is labored breathing, loss of consciousness, excessive drowsiness, trembling, headache, and fever is incurable. He who has saliva flowing from the mouth, loss of consciousness, a satisfied expression, wandering eyes, and stiffness or deformity of the limbs is called one afflicted by epilepsy (*apasmāra*).

In the case of epilepsy in a child, one should employ cooling treatments; indeed, *vacā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and long pepper (*pippalī*) as a nasal drop (*nasya*), or jaggery with ginger, or the juice of *agastya* leaves combined with black pepper, should be used. By this, there will be relief from the affliction, and at that time, swinging [the child] is beneficial. One should cauterize the area at the back of the head and on the forehead with an iron rod. O best of physicians, these seizures transfer to a child even when they occur in an empty house, a temple, a cremation ground, amidst deities, at a crossroads, at the confluence of two rivers, or when the child is agitated by fear.

Pūtanā, Lohitā, Revatī, Dhvāṅkṣī, Kumārī, Śākunī, Śivā, and Ūrdhvakeśī—these eight are proclaimed as Senās. Now hear from me the names of others as well: Rohiṇī, Vijayā, Kālī, Kṛttikā, Ḍākinī, Niśā, Bhūtakeśī, and Kṛśāṅgī; these eight are also proclaimed. I shall now describe their characteristics and the sequence of worship and offerings; listen. Immediately after birth, the Pūtanā named Lohitā possesses a cadaverous stench.

And she weeps blood again and again. (36) I shall describe the offering for her, by which well-being arises: on the second day, the *pūtanā* named Revatī seizes the child. (37) Its symptoms are that it weeps and trembles violently. Having made an image out of black clay and anointed it with fragrant unguents, (38) one should cast [the offering] at night in the southwest direction—consisting of *kṛśara*, rice-flour, lamps, incense, likewise unbroken grains (*akṣata*), betel leaves, and black threads—(39) when the third day has arrived, to the one named Vāyasī.

As soon as she is seized by Pūtanā, the child weeps and will not suckle at the breast. He suffers from fever and diarrhea, and cries out excessively like a crow. For her, one should offer at midday an oblation (*bali*) consisting of curd-rice, barley-mash, and *polikā* cakes in a vessel, along with banners, a bowstring, black perfumes, ointments, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). On the fourth day, the Pūtanā named Kumārī seizes the child; he is then tormented by fever and wanders into empty places, staring vacantly at her face.

He becomes extremely parched and weeps; hear now the sequence of worship and offerings for her: (44) milk-rice, ghee, sugar-candy, and three lamps of ghee; (45) having fashioned an earthen image and offered an oblation with flowers, incense, and unbroken rice grains toward the direction of Yama at midday, one shall become happy. (46) On the fifth day, the Pūtanā named Śākunī seizes the child; seized by her, the infant does not suckle at the breast. (47) Afflicted with fever, he vomits, cries, coughs, and trembles. (48) Of her—

An auspicious worship is performed with sesame sweets (*tilalaḍḍuka*), white perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and incense; one should worship the earthen image [of the deity]. (49) Taking recourse in the northern direction, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) in the forenoon. When the sixth day arrives, a maiden named Śivā cries out, sighs, vomits, and likewise trembles. (50) The child, afflicted by fever and diarrhea, does not take the breast. To her, a sacrificial offering should be given—a *caru* made of seven types of grain—along with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), curds, and lamps; she is to be worshipped. (51)

One should worship the earthen image with sesame flour, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and incense; having taken recourse to the northeast direction, one should offer the oblation in the afternoon. On the seventh day, when the child is seized by Pūtanā Urdhvakeśī, the symptoms appear as before, and one should likewise offer the oblation. When the eighth day arrives, the Pūtanā named Senā seizes the child; he breathes heavily and shakes his hands violently. To her, one should give curd-rice, sesame flour, and fried cakes.

Incense, lamps, perfumes, flowers, betel-leaf, and unbroken grains (akṣata)—one should offer this oblation (bali) in the south-eastern direction at dusk. In this manner, the ritual of offering should be performed for each month and for the year in succession. Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Pediatrics," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-fifth chapter. Ātreya said: In deserted temples, on cremation grounds, at the base of streets and main roads, on carriage-roads, in pleasure-gardens, in empty cities, in parks, and at crossroads—when these are disturbed, the forces of the minor *grahas* arise within the heart of a man. These well-known *grahas* are of ten types; I shall now describe them. Ten have been declared by the great teachers, though some say there are twenty-one. I shall explain the treatment for the ten *grahas*; listen, my son. [The first two are] Aindra and Āgneya.

Yama, another, Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Graha, the Maruts, Kubera, Aiśānya, Grahaka, and another, Paiśācika—these ten are the leaders of the grahas. Whosoever is found in a grove, a monastery, or a temple, one should know him to be possessed by the graha of Indra; through him he rejoices and sings, both with pride and without pride, and is truly seized by madness. In a cremation ground or at a crossroads, the evil graha of Agni seizes him; through that very [possession], he weeps excessively and perceives fear on all sides.

On the battlefield and in the cremation ground, Yama is also said to be roused; by him a man is overwhelmed and distressed, and he behaves like a hungry ghost (preta). (8) At an anthill, a crossroads, or a sacred shrine (caitya), the Nairṛta spirit seizes [the person]; by him he acts with hostility, runs about, and even kills. (9) With eyes closed, face discolored, yet physically strong but wicked-minded, the Vāruṇa spirit moves along the banks of rivers and lakes. (10) By him saliva flows from the mouth, and the man urinates excessively; swelling of the eyes is observed, and he looks about as if mute.

11. And when it seizes one in the midst of a whirlwind, it is the seizure by Māruta; by that, the wretched person is withered, becomes emaciated, or weeps. 12. Agitated and with exhausted eyes, he sits down, afflicted by hunger; and when it seizes one in states of joy, pride, or arrogance, it is the seizure by the King of Yakṣas. 13. By that, he becomes haughty with pride and likewise very fond of ornaments. 14. In a beautiful temple of the gods, the seizure by Śiva provides deception; he applies ash as body-unguent and wanders about naked. 15. He is constantly devoted to the meditation on Śiva.

He is fond of song and instrumental music. 16. The *grahaka* is named after the planets; afflicted by hunger but not by thirst, he neither speaks nor hears. 17. Whether on what is leftover or pure, the *piśāca-graha* seizes him; by that [possession], he dances, cries out, sings, and likewise prattles. 18. He wanders about naked like one intoxicated, with saliva flowing, suffering from hunger and other such needs. Thus, the characteristics of the ten *grahas* have been described by me. 19. Hereafter I shall describe the remedy; listen, my son, in brief.

Bathing in water is highly meritorious, as is the offering of bali; through these, one attains the happiness described in the ritual worship. Elā, jātiphala, the two types of madhūka, rāsnā, khādira, karpūra, āmalakī, jaṭā, bahusutā, ghoṇṭā, amlasāra, and likewise—

Lead, mercury, and pomegranate seeds, combined with wines and each mixed equally with curd, milk, and the juice of *laṅgalā*, should be ground into a paste. 21. This should be impregnated with the [mercury] juice, and pills prepared from it—known as *Candraprabhā*—conquer severe diseases such as fainting and the like. 22. Dry ginger, the essence of *madhuka*, *cavī*, and *kiṃśuka*, together with *vacā* and asafoetida, combined with goat’s urine, should be administered; it destroys the afflictions caused by planetary spirits (*graha*) and is the supreme destroyer of those spirits. 23.

Cat excrement, snake slough, neem, peacock feathers, and mustard seeds; a fumigation of snake slough, piṇḍītaka, sarja, and mocaka resin, smeared with ghee, is for the pacification of the afflictions of the *grahas*. (24) The pill named *cetanā*, as well as *brāhmī-ghṛta*, are prescribed; these should be employed here in cases of epilepsy (*apasmāra*). (25) One should fumigate with guggulu, honey, and ghee. With that incense, O Hārīta, one should threaten the afflicted *graha* with this mantra: (26) "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Lord of Beings, whose nails are like the *kalika* flower, the Fierce One..."

To the one with fangs terrifyingly formidable; to the one whose three eyes on the forehead are tawny and flickering like fire; to the one of immeasurable splendor from the fire of intense wrath; to the one adorned with the noose, trident, skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), bow, arrow, mallet, the gesture of fearlessness, staff, the gesture of terror, the ocean, the inexhaustible, the ten-fold battle, and the fresh staff; to the one wearing a mass of tawny matted hair and the crescent moon; to the one whose body is stained with the glow of ashes; to the one whose throat is adorned by the swelling of the fierce *phaṇi* and *kālakūṭa* poisons; Victory! Victory! O Lord of Beings, Soul of the Immortals! Show, show Your form! Dance, dance!

Move! Move! Bind with the noose! Bind! With the syllable *huṃ*, terrify! Terrify! Strike with the vajra-staff! Strike! Cut! Cut with the sharpened sword! Pierce! Pierce with the tip of the trident! Pound! Pound with the mallet! Cause the entry of all seizing spirits (*graha*)! Cause them to enter! *Svāhā!* If the supreme offering (*bali*) is given to one possessed by a seizing spirit, he becomes liberated from it; of this there is no doubt. Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Science of Spirits" (*Bhūtavidyā*), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-sixth chapter. Ātreya said: The physician has declared poison to be of two kinds: stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama). Śṛṅgika, vatsanābha, and likewise śārṅgavera; dāraka, kālakūṭa, śaṅkhaka, saktuka, and hālāhala—these are the eight species of stationary poison. Śṛṅgika is black in color, vatsanābha is yellow, and that which is the same color as ginger is called śārṅgavera. Dāraka is the color of a monkey, and kālakūṭa... [is] the color of a crow.

Madhuprabha, Śaṅkha, Ativiṣābhāṣa, Pītābha, Satsukanduka, Hālāhala, and Kṛṣṇavarṇa—these are the eight species [of poison]. When yellow poison is seen by a man, it causes immediate and excellent vomiting. One should always cause him to vomit as long as the *ativiṣā* poison has been ingested; one should quickly sprinkle his face with water consecrated by the mantra. Oṃ hara hara nīlakaṇṭha amṛtaṃ plāvaya hūṃ! By the syllable *hūṃ*, swallow the poison, swallow! By the syllable *klīṃ*, remove, remove! By the syllable *hrauṃ*, [swallow] the nectar!

"Plāvaya plāvaya! Hara hara! There is no poison! Ucchire ucchire! (7) "Oṃ, salutations! O Hara, Hara! To the one whose mantra-form flashes forth as the crescent moon adorned by the tips of matted hair, born from the contact of the blue-necked [Śiva] with the white-bodied [Pārvatī]; remove the poison! Hara hara hara! There is no poison! Viṣa viṣa viṣa! Ucchire ucchire ucchire! With this mantra whispered into the ear, one should repeatedly sprinkle cold water on the palate and the mouth. (8) Having ground the roots of the *tāṇḍulīyaka* plant with warm water, drinking it destroys the effects of ingested poison when used for emesis.

Laghava (lightness) occurs. 9. Kākajaṅghā, the root of Sahacarī, and that of Eḍagaja, as well as Kadara and the bark of Kārmuka—when drunk with warm water, this undoubtedly destroys even the most terrible poison instantly. 10. The root of Khadira and likewise the fruits of Nimba, when drunk with warm water, would conquer poison at that very moment. 11. Having drunk Vatsāhvā and Aśvagandhā with warm water, the poison swallowed is quickly protected against; this is the word of the Vedas. 12. Now, the principal [remedy]...

I shall describe the remedy for blood and for poison when they enter a wound, by which well-being is attained. (13) That [poison] which has reached a vital spot (*marman*) is considered incurable; that which resides in the skin and blood is curable, while that residing in the flesh is difficult to cure. (14) O friend, I shall describe the medicine for that which has reached the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), which is incurable; having recognized a man smeared with poison, one should then apply the counter-measure. (15) Poison [is neutralized] by an ointment made from the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric) and *amlaka* ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

It destroys [the poison] when smeared; there is no doubt about this. (16) Whether with the juice of *mātuluṅga* or with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), or even with very cold water, it destroys the poison when smeared; there is no doubt about this. (17) O best of physicians, the poison of mobile beings is said to be of eight kinds: the *darvīkara*, the *maṇḍalin*, the *rājimat*, and the *guṇḍasa*; (18) the scorpion (*vṛścika*), the *goraka*, and likewise the *khaṇḍabinduka*; and the poison of the *alarka* (mad dog), the rat (*mūṣa*), and the cat (*mārjāra*) is said to be of many kinds. (19) The poison of all *darvīkara* snakes is said to be of the nature of wind (*vātātmaka*), and that of the *maṇḍalina*s is likewise.

The poison of all [serpents] is said to be of the *paittika* (bilious) nature. Those which are described as having stripes (*rājimat*) are also poisons of the *kapha* (phlegmatic) nature. That [poison] which causes erratic movement, excessive and unbearable pain in the head, and distress in the heart is declared by the wise to be incurable. That in which there is bleeding from the nose and swelling of the eyes is seen; the tongue becomes numb—that too the wise know to be incurable. That in which the body hairs wither and the body takes on a yellowish appearance, and whose head is not steady, is likewise incurable.

Seeing that which is incurable by *tamas* (ignorance/darkness) as being devoid of these [remedies], the best of physicians should apply its counter-measure. *Oṃ namo bhagavate sugrīvāya sakalaviṣopadravaśamanāya ugrakālakūṭaviṣakavaline viṣaṃ bandha bandha hara hara bhagavato nīlakaṇṭhasyājñā | Oṃ namo hara hara viṣaṃ saṃhara saṃhara amṛtaṃ plāvaya plāvaya nāsti are re viṣa nīla parvataṃ gaccha gaccha nāsti viṣam oṃ hāhā ūcire ūcire ūcire.* With this mantra, one should terrify the mouth with water.

Oṃ, salutations! O Haṃsa, behold, behold the nectar! (25) A plaster consisting of jayakūṭa, vacā, kuṣṭha, saindhava, magadhā, and niśā is prescribed for a wound from a bite; it destroys even the most dreadful poison. (26) Surasā, rajanī, vyoṣa, yavānī, and pāribhadraka are prescribed as a plaster for a wound from a snakebite to pacify the poison. (27) A plaster of kuṣṭha, mustā, ajājī, viḍaṅga, madhuyaṣṭikā, and the root of guñjā, applied with cold water, is beneficial for one bitten by a maṇḍalī snake. (28) For those whose poisons consist of stripes, house-soot [is recommended].

A plaster consisting of *vacā*, *ghanasārā*, mustard seeds, *yavānī*, and the three fruits of the *picumanda* tree, combined with *vraṇataila*, is for those afflicted by *rājimat* [venoms]. (29) *Sṛṣṭi*, *kirātatikta*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *vacā*, *viśālā*, *picumandaka*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, and the two types of *rajanī* are likewise recommended as a plaster for wounds caused by bites. (30) O best of physicians, whether it be stationary (*sthāvara*) or mobile (*jaṅgama*) poison that has been ingested, it quickly causes severe pain, as declared by the most excellent of men. (31) *Oṃ namo bhagavate*.

"To the one with a crest upon his head, whose entire body is washed by streams of nectar, who is surrounded by a jar of nectar—drench, drench [me] with nectar, svāhā! (32). Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Tantra of Poisons," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-seventh chapter. Ātreya said: Severed, split, likewise fractured, abraded, and crushed—as well as *āsphālita*, *saṃprahāra*, and *saṅghāta*—these are described by the wise. (1) Upon seeing a man pierced by a weapon, medical treatment must be administered. (2) If the flesh remains attached to the bone, yet the bone itself is severed, or if it is severed at the primary or secondary branches [of the limbs], that is called *chinna* (severed). (3) That which is completely severed at a non-junction (*asandhi*) should be designated as incurable.

It is always taught that [the wound] is severed by a sword, a crescent-headed arrow (ardhacandra), or an axe. At the beginning of that process, the application of a paste and rubbing are prescribed; it should be quickly fomented with a cotton pad soaked in sesame oil. One should continue to anoint it with oil as long as blood flows; indeed, when the blood undergoes abnormality, anointing with oil is recommended. If swellings and other complications arise in abundance at the site of the wound or joint, upon seeing a person whose limb has been severed, one should sprinkle them with warm water. [This applies to] that which has accumulated.

Picu-tailaka is also recommended for a wound; when pus is discharging, leaves of nimba and āragvadha [should be applied]. (8) Having ground pathyā with jaggery, this ointment cleanses the pus; once it has been purified after three days, applying that same ointment there is beneficial. (9) Having ground the bark of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, vṛkṣa, and udumbara with water, an ointment made from that causes the wound to heal. (10) That which is pierced by spears, arrows, bhalla-shafts, swords, tomara-javelins, or the sharp edges of razor-blades is called *bhinnam*.

The physician declares that a fracture occurring away from the vital points (marmas) is curable, whereas one situated at a vital point does not heal. Washing with the juice of *apāmārga* or *kūṣmāṇḍaka*, as well as with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), is praised by the wise. Anointing with sesame oil is beneficial for a fracture in a healthy person, and the previously mentioned ointments should also be applied for the patient's welfare. Indeed, if [the fracture] occurs in the chest, head, temples, armpits, feet, the sacrum, the abdomen, the tip of the face, the eyes, or the ears— [This concludes the section on fractures.]

A foreign body (*śalya*) that is difficult to treat becomes manageable with surgical instruments if it is not deeply embedded; however, one who knows the proper procedure should extract a foreign body from the branches or sub-branches of the limbs or from a vital spot (*marman*) using medicinal remedies rather than mechanical instruments or surgery. (14–15) One should specify twelve types of instruments (*yantra*), twelve types of surgical tools (*śastra*), and four types of bandages for the extraction of foreign bodies. (16) These are: the *godhāmukha* (alligator-mouth), the *vajramukha* (thunderbolt-mouth), the *saṃdaṃśa* (tongs), the *cakrākṛti* (wheel-shaped), the *kaṅkapāda* (heron-foot), and the *ayānaka*.

The Śṛṅgaka, Kuṇḍala, Śrīvatsa, Sauvatsika, and Pañcavaktra—these twelve instruments have been described by the best of physicians. Now, the surgical instruments (śastra) are declared, each with its distinct name: the Ardhacandra, Vrīhimukha, Kaṅkapatra, Kuṭhārikā, Karavīrakapatra, Śalākākārapatraka, Baḍiśa, Gṛdhrapāda, Śūlī, and Ghanamudgara. These instruments are specified individually for the extraction of foreign bodies (śalya). And [the instrument] called Atigupta.

One should extract a splinter with forceps; once it has been pierced, the remedy should be applied by a wise person. (21) Having recognized a deep-seated splinter, one should determine the remedy: it should be incised with a blade of *kuśa* grass and the splinter removed with *kuṅkuma*. (22) Just as in the case of a perforation, the remedy should be applied by a wise person. (23) Where there is intense swelling, the splinter has perished; having diagnosed it as being accompanied by a splinter, dense, and painful, (24) one should apply the appropriate instrument there.

Appropriate mechanical instruments and surgical tools should be employed there by those skilled in reasoning and analysis (ūhāpoha). (25) The intense pain arising from the striking of a foreign body (śalya) that spreads through the body of a living being attains pacification through ghee mixed with bitter substances, slightly warmed, and combined with *yaṣṭīmadhu*. (26) *Sarja*, *arjuna*, *udumbara*, *markaṭī*, *rodhra*, *samaṅgā*, and *surasa*—having ground these together with water for application as a plaster, this brings comfort upon the extraction of the foreign body. (27) Furthermore, the remaining treatments previously mentioned are beneficial when [the wound] has been incised or punctured.

In that case, both *vālukāsveda* (sand-sudation) and *ghaṭīsveda* (jar-sudation) should be performed. Having observed a man with fractured bones, I shall now describe the remedy for him: fractures of the wrist, the elbow, the knee, as well as the hip, and a completely broken spinal column—these, O best of men, are curable. However, a fracture at the region of the neck, at the *indrabasti*, at *rohiṇī*, below the elbow, between the shoulder and the elbow, in the middle of the *trika* (the sacral region), and likewise on the chest or the breast—such a fracture is incurable.

Having seen a man whose [limb] is shattered, one should bind it with a section of bamboo; one should rub it with fresh butter and wrap it with *eraṇḍa* leaves. One should sprinkle it with warm water and bind it gently with a cloth. Having ground the bark of *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* trees with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), an application of that paste is beneficial, and through it, comfort arises. One should foment those parts with heat and provide a covering once again. When this procedure is completed, one should then release the bandage after an interval of one day.

One should maintain that treatment as before until a knot forms; as long as the knot has not formed, one should not bathe the person. (36) Upon seeing the person rubbing [the wound], bathing with *kāñjika* (sour gruel), urine, or cold water is considered beneficial. (37) As long as blood continues to flow, one should sprinkle it with oil; furthermore, various medicinal herbs should be applied here in small quantities. (38) In the stage of suppuration, bleeding and fomentation (*svedana*) are prescribed; one should also provide treatment for a fracture according to the rules. (39)

When a remedy has been administered, the best of physicians must be consulted; through reasoning and refutation [of the diagnosis], one attains well-being by his means. (40) A disorder arising from a blow to the head is proclaimed as "head disease" (*śiroroga*); furthermore, from a blow to the chest, a liver-tumor (*yakṛdgulma*) arises. (41) Thus, one should apply a remedy: bloodletting should be performed, and fomentation (*svedana*) should be employed by the physician for the success of the treatment. (42) One should not consume oil, nor food that is excessively hot or pungent; likewise, no fish or thick meats [should be eaten].

And heavy [foods] (43); soup made from white *śāli* rice, and likewise from *āḍhakī* beans; rabbit, partridge, eggplant, *kakkola*, and *taṇḍulīyaka* (44); *śatapuṣpā* and other such items, as well as anything combined with asafoetida; salt should not be consumed in excess if one desires one's own well-being (45). One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and sleeping during the day in due order; thus a man attains happiness and prosperity (46). Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fractures," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 57.

The fifty-eighth chapter. Ātreya said: Having observed a person burnt by fire, that burning is fourfold: slightly burnt (*īṣaddagdha*), moderately burnt (*madhyadagdha*), excessively burnt (*atidagdha*), and properly burnt (*samyagdagdha*). O best of physicians, listen to the characteristics of these, my son. Excessively burnt burns the flesh and involves *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*; properly burnt is known to be free from defects, and it is likewise fourfold. That burning by which the skin is sloughed off is born of *pitta* and is accompanied by blood.

When it is associated with pitta, it appears due to the provocation of pitta; that pitta, located in the flesh, is blackish in color and causes intense pain. O best of physicians, I shall now describe the treatment for its successful cure. For a slightly burnt area, an application of sour gruel (kāñjika) is for the sake of comfort. Nimba leaves, surasā, kuṣṭha, and āmalaka fruits—O best of physicians, these should be applied as available to a slightly burnt area. For a moderately burnt area, the application of payasyā is a provider of relief. [An ointment of] madhuka, kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, and ghee, cooked together, [should be used].

Kuṣṭha, yaṣṭīmadhuka, candana, and eraṇḍapatraka are considered beneficial; when applied as a paste ground with milk, it is beneficial for burns on the trunk. (8–9) A powder of ghee, camphor, gairika, and rodhra—applied as a dry powder—removes pus and even promotes the healing of a burnt wound. (10) For burns caused by fire, a plaster of āmalakī, sesame, and kuṣṭha is recommended; likewise, a plaster of rodhra, uśīra, and samaṅgā mixed with cold water is beneficial. (11) Anointing with linseed oil and a plaster of madhuyaṣṭī with ghee are both beneficial for application and massage.

Dagdhārohaṇa prevents burning. 12. In the event of injury from smoke, emesis, drinking milk, and likewise swimming in water are excellent for the alleviation of the burning sensation caused by smoke. 13. Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "Therapeutics," in the Hārīta-Uttara spoken by Ātreya. The third section is completed. 3.

Ātreya said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the causes of the confusion of diseases. From exhaustion, from the suppression of physical exertion, or even from anxiety, grief, and fear; from anger, from the odor of medicinal herbs, and especially from the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātu), the digestive fire (agni) is provoked from the visceral cavity (koṣṭha). Thus, blood-bile (raktapitta) likewise arises externally, and having combined with that which is located in the skin, it indeed produces fever (jvara). Fever may also arise from the aforementioned causes, or from one fever another fever may develop. It should be known as mild, or even more mild than mild, arising from the excessive consumption of sour substances.

From that [fever], *kāmalā* arises; from fully developed *kāmalā*, *halīmaka*; from *halīmaka*, *pāṇḍu* occurs; and from these, as they have been proclaimed, *yakṣman* (consumption) is born. From *yakṣman* comes swelling (*śopha*), and from swelling, abdominal enlargement (*udara*). From that, *gulma* (abdominal tumors) caused by wind and other humors arises; from *gulma*, asthma and colic; from that, weak digestion (*mandāgni*); and from that, hoarseness and obstruction of speech. Indeed, the origin of all these diseases is through fever; death is to be known as occurring through fever, for there can be no death without fever. Listen further, O knower of medicines and diseases, to the second [section].

A mixture of diseases occurs in men, beginning with mild fever, followed by diarrhea and then fever again (8). From that, hiccup, emaciation, delusion, vertigo, and loss of appetite arise; death results from swelling (*śopha*) among these, which is now described as the third [stage] (9). Or, due to the faults of daytime sleep and other causes, catarrh (*pratiśyāya*) arises; from that, cough is declared, and from cough, nasal catarrh (*pīnasa*) follows (10). From that comes consumption (*kṣaya*), from consumption swelling, and through swelling one meets death. Fever, consumption, pulmonary consumption (*yakṣmā*), leprosy, abdominal tumors, hemorrhoids, and urinary gravel (*śarkarā*) [are the diseases resulting from this progression] (11).
