Dropsy, insanity, epilepsy, and fistula-in-ano—these most terrible ailments render a man merely manageable (palliable). (12) All diseases arise from the humors (doṣas), such as wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and those originating from phlegm (śleṣman); I shall describe their treatment. (13) O best of physicians, wind (vāta) digests [the morbid matter] in seven days, bile (pitta) in three nights, and phlegm (śleṣman) in even half a day. (14) That which arises from two humors, namely wind and bile (vātapitta), is digested in nine nights; that of phlegm and wind (śleṣmavāta) in ten days.

Pitta-Ślaiṣmika fever is pacified in five days; for dual-type (dvi-doṣaja) fevers, digestive treatment (pācana) is likewise given on the fourth day; and for severe Tridoṣaja fever, digestive treatment is given on the twelfth day. Sannipāta fever may take even fourteen days to digest. Therefore, having ascertained the strength of the Doshas and that they are ripe, digestive medicine should be administered. When accompanied by the signs of the etiology, the pacifying (saṃśamana) procedure should follow; for impurities located in the seven tissues (dhātus) are digested within seven days. Indeed, in Sannipāta fever, the impurities are digested even after a long time.

Therefore, remission is also declared [to occur] on this day; generally, fever does not persist on the eighth day. On the seventh day, the wise physician, having considered the cause of the remitting fever, should administer medicine; for if there is indigestion, the medicine will not digest it, as the digestive fire is exceedingly weak. When all the humors have subsided, digestion (pācana) and fasting (laṅghana) are prescribed. Fasting is of three types: moderate, excessive, and very excessive. Listen now as I describe the characteristics of these for human beings.

The disappearance of fatigue, absence of aversion or malaise, and clarity of the sense organs indicate the ripening of the *doṣas* in one who has undergone fasting; this is the characteristic of successful fasting (*śuddha-laṅghita*). (23) O best of physicians, slight fatigue, aversion, malaise, discoloration of the sense organs, excessive thirst, slight emaciation, and exhaustion are the signs of moderate fasting. (24) A slight unctuousness in the body, loss of appetite, constipation, and the ripening of the *doṣas* at a moderate level are the characteristics of moderate fasting (*madhya-laṅghita*). (25) Deformity, drowsiness, diarrhea, insomnia, trembling, and headache [occur in cases of excessive fasting]. (26)

One should recognize the following symptoms in one who has undergone excessive fasting (atilaṅghita): emaciation from hunger, colic, a darkened face, watering of the eyes, and being afflicted by fainting, delusion, and exhaustion. (26–27) An excellent physician should never administer fasting (laṅghana) in cases of fever occurring at specific times (velājvara), fever caused by spirits (bhūtajvara), nor in bile-fever (pittajvara). This also applies to fevers born of physical exertion, anger, fear, or passion. (28–29) Furthermore, one should never cause a child, an elderly person, one who is emaciated, one who is depleted, one suffering from diarrhea or ulcers, a pregnant woman, or one of delicate constitution to undergo fasting. (30) [In the case of] undigested matter (sāma)...

In cases of mild fever, severe fever, loss of appetite, and constipation, as well as in indigestion (ajīrṇa), fasting (laṅghana) administered in the proper measure is highly recommended. (31) Excessive unctuousness of the limbs, a rumbling sound in the abdomen, headache, abdominal distension, a burning sensation, and a rattling sound in the throat; (32) loss of appetite, yellowish urine, drowsiness, and lethargy—in a person afflicted by these, the best of physicians, having recognized the fever to be of the "āma" type, should prescribe fasting. (33) [This condition is treated] through fasting, emesis, purgation, bloodletting, drinking heated water, and procedures involving sudation (sveda).

Six types of fasting (laṅghana) have been described. [One should observe fasting] for one who is emaciated by hunger, exhausted, suffering from the onset of vertigo and fever, experiencing internal burning, or passing blood in the urine—these are the signs of remittent fever (virāmajvara). A fever of Vāta origin is digested by six fasts; a Pitta-originated fever, however, in three days; Kapha is digested in seven days. One should administer fasting after observing these signs. A fever of all three doṣas (tridoṣaja) is digested by fasts over ten nights; when the fifteenth day arrives, the Sānnipātika fever is digested. It may either release the patient, kill him, or leave him as it was.

In childhood, irregular fevers arise from disorders consisting of blood; thereafter, they stem from phlegm and bile (38). When the sixteenth year is reached, diseases originate from the three humors (tridoṣa); when the twenty-fifth year is reached, fever indeed becomes of the combined type (sānnipātika) (39). The fever that arises properly from the collection of rasa and rakta through vāta, pitta, and kapha should be treated with a decoction once it has matured (40). Decoction is said to be of seven kinds: digestive (pācana), pacifying (śamana), appetizing (dīpana), moistening (kledana), drying (śoṣī), nourishing (santarpaṇa), and specifically [the seventh]. (41) And the digestive [decoction]...

One who understands [the proper time] should administer a sedative (śamana) to a person during the early part of the night, while a stimulant (dīpana) is prescribed for the afternoon. A nourishing (santarpaṇa) and a purgative (bhedana) decoction should be given for drinking in the morning; likewise, a drying (śoṣaṇa) decoction is recommended for drinking at dawn. The first watch of the night is proclaimed as *bhūtavelā* (the hour of spirits); they call the second watch of the night *niśītha* (midnight), and what follows that is known as *gaṇarātra* (the period of many nights). This refers to the time when the sun has not yet reached its full course. [The divisions of the day are] the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and midday (*madhyāhna*).

Forty-five *parārddhas* remain until the end of the day; at the conclusion of the day, the administration of medicinal decoctions (*bheṣaja*) begins. (46) The decoction (*kvātha*) is traditionally said to be of seven types: digestive (*pācana*), appetizing (*dīpanīya*), purifying (*śodhana*), pacifying (*śamana*), nourishing (*tarpaṇa*), moistening (*kledana*), and drying (*śoṣī*). (47) The digestive decoction should be reduced to half [its original volume]; the purifying, to one-twelfth; the moistening, to one-fourth; and the pacifying, to one-eighth remaining. (48) The appetizing decoction is reduced to one-tenth, the nourishing to its equal [original] portion, and the drying to one-sixteenth; thus the varieties of decoctions are proclaimed. (49) [The first is] the digestive (*pācana*).

The digestive stimulant (*dīpana*) pacifies the humors (*doṣas*) and kindles the fire; the purgative (*śodhana*) should cleanse the impurities; the palliative (*śamana*) subdues diseases. (50) The nourishing (*tarpaṇa*) satisfies the tissues (*dhātus*); the moistening (*kledī*) produces moisture in the heart; the drying (*viśoṣī*) brings about desiccation. Therefore, one should carefully examine the decoction (*kvātha*). (51) Having recognized whether it is moistening or drying, one should cause the person to undergo emesis (*vāmana*). One should not fast after taking a decoction, nor should one disturb the internal [organs] in between. (52) One should not dry it out again, but keep it stable; it should not be kept in an impure place. If it is left exposed, that decoction is not recommended. (53)

It may be a cause for the complication of diseases. (53) One should not dry the decoction again, nor should it be allowed to touch the ground again; these [qualities] are praised for the pacification of the *doṣas* in the treatment of disease. (54) If a person [using the decoction] suffers from cracking, falling [of tissues], or bursting due to the decoction, these decoctions are undesirable and do not serve to pacify the *doṣas*. (55) Having observed a decoction that is devoid of these characteristics, one should examine it: that which is black, blue, dense, red, slimy, or thin; that which is burnt, smells like a corpse, or has a cadaverous odor. (56)

One should avoid [these]; by these signs one should know the patient to be incurable, there is no doubt in this. By describing the qualities of substances, one should indicate the scent of the substance. Likewise, that which is pure, well-colored, astringent, and like nectar should be given after fasting in a fever caused by Vāta; thereafter, food should be provided at night, having ascertained the strength or weakness of the *doṣas*. In a Pitta-type fever, it should be given after three nights; in a Kapha-type fever, on the first day. And when the *doṣa* is unknown, one should not administer a digestive (*pācana*) medicine. Indeed, after seven nights...

A fever is characterized by its very limits; therefore, in a new fever (navajvara), what is drunk neither produces the humors (doṣas) nor removes them. (61) Therefore, for the first three days, a digestive (pācana) medicine should be administered; thereafter, for five nights, a palliative (śamanīya) medicine should be given. (62) One should administer a purifying (śodhana) and digestive-stimulating (dīpanīya) medicine for one night. (63) If exhaustion, fainting, or mental distress are observed during the drinking of decoctions, or when emesis is prescribed, or even when a palliative diet is indicated—(64) In such cases, wholesome food (pathya) must always be employed, never unwholesome (apathya). (65)

A disease may be cured by medicine even without a dietetic regimen, yet it is cured by the best of physicians through diet alone (65). Without a diet, a fever cannot be mastered even with hundreds of medicines; therefore, one suffering from fever should eat what is beneficial, even if a lack of appetite occurs (66). By not eating at the proper times for meals, one wastes away or even dies; being emaciated, one falls into misery and reaches a state of incurability (67). Therefore, one should protect the strength of men, for life itself is dependent on the pacification of strength; once the humors have been lightened, one should practice the drinking of gruel (68).

Indeed, they say that a soup made of *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, and *mudga* grains is recommended (69). For one who has undergone moderate fasting (*madhyalaṅghita*), gruel prepared with the five spices (*pañcakolaka*) is always excellent; for such a person, nourishing therapy (*santarpaṇa*) is beneficial (70). Goat's milk mixed with jaggery should be drunk for the pacification of fever; by this, exhaustion is destroyed and one quickly attains comfort (71). One should have the patient sit facing either the north or the east, and after performing the recitation of the Vedic hymns (*brāhmaṇavācana*), one should administer the decoction drink (72). Having placed the drinking vessel beneath [the patient], he should lie down.

Even one afflicted by thirst, having drunk only knowledge, would not drink water for even a moment; seeing a person whose fatigue has departed, one then attains happiness. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Method for the Thorough Knowledge of Medicines," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The Second Chapter. Ātreya said: What is the use of studying the scriptures for one who is ignorant of medical practice? It is as useless as straw devoid of seeds. (1) It would be better to drink the venom of a poisonous serpent or molten copper, or to swallow iron balls heated in a fierce fire, than to accept food, drink, or wealth from a person afflicted by disease who merely wears the garb of those learned in the scriptures but has not sought refuge [in true knowledge]. (2-3) That alone is a proper medicine which results in health, and that indeed...

He who liberates from diseases is the best among physicians. Therefore, with every effort for the purpose of warding off disease, this compendium—equipped with the characteristics of the causes [of disease] and endowed with the means [of treatment]—should be studied in its entirety for the sake of attaining knowledge of the compendium. Having understood the remedy for a disease, one should then apply the counter-measure. One who undertakes medical treatments out of delusion without properly understanding the disease, even if he knows the procedures and the scriptures, will not achieve success. Diagnosis, the knowledge of diseases, and the qualities and defects of medicines [constitute the core].

For one who acts after having understood [the disease], success is not far off. (8) A wise physician should first ascertain the knowledge of diseases—whether they are curable, incurable, or merely suppressible—and then apply the remedy for all ailments. (9) Having thus understood the place, time, age, digestive fire (*agni*), suitability (*sātmya*), constitution (*prakṛti*), and medicine, the good physician should then apply the remedy. (10) There is no disease without the humors (*doṣa*); the humors are known as *vāta* and the others. Diseases such as fever and so forth are recorded [in scripture]; one should correctly observe them. (11) And by means of the instruction of authoritative persons (*āpta*).

Through direct observation, by looking at the patient and others, and by means of touch and inquiries regarding cold sensations and so forth—(12) it is held that the knowledge of diseases is threefold: through sight, touch, and questioning; specifically, by observing the face and eyes, by touch, and by inquiries regarding cold sensations and so forth. (13) A curable disease is said to be of two types: that which is difficult to treat and that which is easily treated; the incurable is known to be of two types: the difficult and the most difficult. (14) Some diseases are incurable by their very nature, some are maintained [in a stable state] despite being curable, and some diseases are curable by their inherent nature.

15–16. Curable diseases become manageable when neglected, and likewise, manageable diseases turn incurable; moreover, curable diseases take away the lives of men who fail to treat them. 17. A disease that arises upon an existing disease is called a complication (*upadrava*); those with complications do not survive, whereas those without complications do survive. Even a minor disease, once recognized, must be carefully considered by a physician and never neglected, for such a group of diseases may indeed become incurable.

Even a very slight enemy is like poison or fire; having gained strength, he does not reach a state of pacification in due time. An enemy, having attained the strength of his position, exerts his prowess; likewise, a disease, having reached another element (dhātu), exerts its prowess. O knower of the rules, even if it has been brought to a state of subsidence through many kinds of treatment, a root of disease that is diminished must certainly not be maintained.

Even if turned away by many wholesome remedies, a powerful disease does not truly subside merely because it is young (20). Just as a small amount of potent poison, a tiny serpent, or a very slight fire [is dangerous], so too is even a subtle enemy in the form of disease (21). As long as a malady remains established in its location and produces disorder, its remedy consists in removing it from that place, for the stronger [remedy] overcomes it (22). Some diseases are born of past actions (*karma*), others arise from the humors (*doṣa*), and others are said to be innate (*sahaja*).

Diseases are considered to be of three types: (23) those which do not subside despite numerous treatments are designated as the terrible diseases born of karma; furthermore, there are those born of the humors (*doṣaja*), such as wind (*vāta*) and bile (*pitta*), and those born together with birth (*sahaja*), such as hunger and thirst. (25) Therefore, I shall first describe fever—the incomparable malady—affecting horses, elephants, humans, domestic animals, deer, buffaloes, donkeys, camels, and even trees.

This fever, which snatches away the life-force of creepers, medicinal herbs, mountains, serpents, birds, and mice, is indeed declared to be difficult to ward off in this world. (26) This incurable disease of fever is most difficult to overcome for cows, buffaloes, horses, and elephants; it is somewhat more grievous for humans, while for others it is a destroyer of life. (27) Just as a powerful hunter prevails over deer, so too is this formidable fever among diseases; no other being on earth—be they gods or others—is able to withstand it, with the sole exception of a human. (28) One acquires [this] through one's own karma.

Because a human being attains divinity in heaven, and having fallen from there, he likewise returns to the human state; therefore, as a human, he endures the fever resulting from that divine condition, whereas all other classes of beings perish when afflicted by fever. This fever is the king of diseases, just as the lord of beasts is among animals, and just as fire is the essence of burning, so too is fever the most intense of maladies. Born from the fire of Rudra’s wrath, it torments all living creatures; it is a plague for serpents and a scorching heat for horses.

The fever known as Gavāmīśvara is considered to afflict human beings; Dāridra affects buffaloes, and Mṛgaroga affects deer. That called Pralāpa afflicts goats and sheep, while Alasa occurs in young camels. Alarka is declared to affect dogs, and Indramata is held to affect fish. Abhighāta affects birds, and the one named Aikṣita affects serpents. Nīlikā generally affects water, and that known as Ūṣara affects the soil. Koṭarākṣa is the fever of trees; thus the fever is seen everywhere. It has three legs, ashes for its weapon, and three heads.

He has a very large belly, is clothed in a tiger skin, and his body is radiant with a tawny hue. With tawny eyes, long arms, and shanks like those of a horse, this powerful man—known as Jvara—is destined for the destruction of the world. Just as fire, having consumed its fuel, or poison, having destroyed the bodily constituents (dhātus), attains peace once its purpose is fulfilled, so too does Jvara attain peace after destroying the body. Therefore, O son, listen as I describe his origin, by which this most terrible being was born fourfold and subsequently became eightfold.

When Maheśvara became enraged at Dakṣa, he, distressed by the loss of his beloved, released a fierce breath; from that, fever arises in eight ways according to its eightfold origin. (40) Due to the presence of wind, bile, phlegm, and blood, through indulgence in food and drink according to one's whim, and through the reversal of the seasons, the humors (doṣas), having moved from the receptacle of waste (malāśaya) outside the digestive fire, impel the descent of the fire residing in the blood. (41) Therefore, they indeed receive the name "fever" (jvara).

It is established that fever arises from physical exertion, anger, eating, and so forth, due to the occurrence of cold [in the body] (42). Especially from incompatible food, by drinking water from mountain torrents or well-water, and through the rays of the hot, fierce-rayed sun (43), and by the wind carrying odors, or from the striking and the cursing of the *doṣas*, a most terrible disease called fever (*jvara*) arises intensely in human beings (44). Fatigue, dullness, watering of the eyes, horripilation, a rattling sound in the throat, yawning, discoloration, aversion to food, and dryness of the mouth are the manifest symptoms of fever.

45. In the case of *samīraṇa* (Vāta), yawning occurs; from *kapha*, dejection and sinking; from *pitta*, burning of the eyes; indeed, all [these] occur in the *sānnipātika* (combined) type. Therefore, I shall describe the remedy by which well-being is attained. 46. One should drink at night this warm decoction of *vacā*, *yavānī*, *dhanikā*, and *viśvā*. This will lead to the happiness of a person suffering from Vāta-type fever, from Vāta diseases, or from the production of fevers. 47. A decoction of *niśā*, *nimba*, *mṛtavallikā*, *dhānya*, and *viśvā*, mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be taken at night along with milk and *kola*.

This drink is for the digestion of fever associated with pitta (48). A decoction of vacā, yavānī, triphalā, and viśvā, taken at night, serves as a digestive agent for a person suffering from fever caused by kapha, as well as for disorders involving the *doṣas*, colic, coryza, and catarrh (49). A decoction of śaṭhī, vacā, nāgara, kāphala, vatsādanī, and dhanvayavāsaka is beneficial for fever arising from all [three] *doṣas*; it acts as a digestive agent for a person with the three *doṣas* (50). For the wise, massaging the limbs with an abundance of lukewarm water at night is wholesome.

Avoidance of sleep and physical exercise; trembling, irregular onset, and emaciation; a bad taste in the throat, palate, and mouth; dryness of the body; distension of the abdomen and waist; yawning, headache, and insomnia; blackness of the nails, delirium, and severe breaking pain in the limbs; and sleeping in a state of fear as if waking from a nightmare—by these signs, a fever caused by Vāta is characterized in a man. (vv. 51–53) Nāgara, Surataru, Dhānyaka, Kuṇḍalī, and the pair of Bṛhatīs are recommended at night on the seventh day of the fever. (v. 54)

Indeed, when the medicine has reached the eighth part [of digestion], it becomes possessed of eightfold power (54). A medicine that is superior in potency and not deficient in its substance will undoubtedly and quickly destroy that disease; however, if drunk by children, the elderly, women, or those of delicate constitution, it quickly leads to extreme exhaustion and loss of strength (55). Lightness of the sense organs, clarity of the eyes and face, belching, and heat in the digestive tract are the signs of a digested medicine (56). But for one in whom fatigue, nausea, lassitude, headache, dizziness, and excessive secretions arise, [the medicine is undigested].

One should recognize the signs of the medicine’s upward movement (utkrāma): burning, prostration of the limbs, fainting, headache, exhaustion, dejection, giddiness, and a specific form of intense sexual desire. Therefore, when only a residue of the medicine remains, there is never a pacification of the *doṣas*; rather, the *doṣas* become provoked in many ways. A digestive (*pācana*) medicine must not be administered without [the previous medicine being digested]. [The medicine] undergoes digestion quickly; it does not destroy strength when covered by food, nor does it repeatedly exit through the mouth. This very same great medicine should be administered to the elderly, children, the timid, and excellent women.

A decoction (kaṣāya) prepared by boiling one *kumbha* each of *bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śukanāsa*, *kapāṭalī*, and *kumbhārikā* cleanses the teeth, subdues wind (*samīra*), and quickly destroys wind-born fever (*marutajvara*) in men. *Kirāta*, *musta*, *mṛtavallī*, *kraṇāsa*, *vit* (vid), *gokaṇṭaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *udīcya*, and *tiktā*—these [are used for tooth-cleansing].

A decoction of *śāliparṇī* and *kalaśī* boiled together quickly destroys fever born of Vāta (62). A decoction of *guḍūcī*, *śatapuṣpā*, *plakṣī*, *rāsnā*, *punarnavā*, and *trāyamāṇaka*, taken with jaggery, removes Vāta-fever (63). Fainting, burning sensation, vertigo, intoxication, thirst, forceful diarrhea, drowsiness, laziness, prostration, vomiting, and inflammation with heat in the mouth [occur].

Perspiration, labored breathing, a bitter taste in the mouth, exhaustion, or hunger—by these signs, fever caused by Pitta indeed arises in a person. (64) For digestive treatments, one should use Rodhra, Utpala, Amṛtalatā, and Kamala, combined with sugar and Sarivā.

Boiled quickly, it destroys Pitta and brings about the pacification of Pitta-fever in men. (65) Śakrāhvā (Indrayava), Kaṭurohiṇī, and Yaṣṭīmadhu, boiled with rice-water, constitute a decoction that destroys Pitta-fevers. (66) A decoction of Durālabhā, Vāsaka, Parpaṭa, Priyaṅgu, Nimba, Kaṭurohiṇī, and Kirātatikta, prepared as a thickened extract (kaṣāya) and enriched with sugar, is a digestive (pācana) agent that quickly destroys Pitta-fever accompanied by burning sensations, thirst, and vertigo. (67)

Even a single *parpaṭaka* leaf is indeed excellent and suitable for pacifying bile-fevers (*pittajvara*), especially when enriched with ginger and *vālaka*, like a lion set upon a herd of elephants. (68–69) A decoction of ginger, *uśīra*, *mustā*, sandalwood, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and coriander destroys bile-fever. (70) A decoction of *amṛtā*, *parpaṭa*, and *dhātrī* removes bile-fever. (71) [One may also use] grapes, *parpaṭaka*, *tiktā*, *pathyā*, *āragvadha*, and *mustaka*.

A decoction [of these] removes fever caused by pitta accompanied by thirst, vertigo, and burning sensations. (72) An application of a paste made from vidārī, rodhra, kapittha, mātuluṅga, and pomegranates—prepared according to their availability—along with *tālu* (tamarind), destroys burning sensations, thirst, and fainting. (73) Alternatively, for one who is lying flat on their back, placing a stream of cold water upon the navel in a bronze or copper vessel will ward off the burning sensation. (74) Furthermore, the embrace of a beautiful woman bent by the weight of her breasts, the company of beloved ones, the drinking of grape juice, and the use of cooling substances are said to be beneficial.

A white lotus, cool garments sprinkled with sandalwood water, a pearl necklace, and bright snow—these, for the commencement of the moonlit night, swiftly dispel the bile, burning, emaciation, fatigue, thirst, giddiness, and fainting of human beings. (75)

Through these methods, there is complete pacification of the burning sensation caused by *pitta*, and such treatment becomes constantly appropriate for those who possess the means. (76) If a person suffers from dryness of the tongue, throat, and palate, the filaments of the *mātuluṅga* (citron), ground together with honey and rock salt, should be applied as a paste to the palate; this immediately removes *pitta*-fever. (77) Dullness, sweetness of the mouth, numbness, excessive drowsiness, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, forgetfulness, horripilation, coldness, and perspiration [are the symptoms].

It causes obstruction of hearing, paleness of the eyes, and a pale complexion; they know these to be the symptoms of *śleṣmajvara* (phlegm-fever), characterized by constipation and the vomiting of *malavṛttika-āsava*. (78) In fever born of *kapha*, a paste (*kalka*) of *pippalādi* is beneficial as a digestive (*pācana*). (79) Similarly, *vyāghrī*, *siṃhī*, *rodhra*, *kuṣṭha*, and *paṭola*—this is an excellent digestive remedy for fever arising from *kapha*. (80) A decoction (*kaṣāya*) of *vāsā*, *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, *paṭolī*, *śaṭhī*, *tiktā*, and *madhuyaṣṭī* properly [subdues] fever in diseases where phlegm is predominant.

It quickly destroys disorders born of *kapha*. (81) *Āmalakī*, *abhayā*, *kṛṣṇā*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, and *trivṛt*—this group of three [medicines] is a purgative that ends *kapha*, destroys fever, and stimulates the digestive fire. (82) A decoction of *pippalī*, *śṛṅgavera*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, and the fruit of *vatsaka*, mixed with a profusion of honey, is a destroyer of *śleṣma*-fever. (83) One should lick the powder of *pippalī* with honey; it removes *śleṣma*-fever, destroys splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, and poison, and subdues cough, dyspnea, and indigestion. (84) [It also treats] thirst, fainting, vomiting, and a bitter taste in the mouth.

If there is roughness, internal burning in the body, redness of the eyes, dryness of the throat, loss of sleep, pain and splitting in the head and chest, breaking pain in the limbs, horripilation, and tamaka (labored breathing), it would be vātapitta fever (85). When the doshas are combined, a proper digestive treatment should be administered; in vātapitta fever, one should drink a decoction of the three fruits (triphalā) combined with śālmalī, or a decoction of rāsnā and kirātatiktaka (86). A paste made from the two groups of five roots (daśamūlī), along with ginger, guḍūcī, bhūnimba, and musta, is highly recommended.

Sugar-candy mixed with *marutsu* (grapes) is a cause for the destruction of fever caused by *pitta* and *vāta*. (87) A decoction of *kirātatikta*, *āmalakī*, *śaṭhī*, *drākṣā*, *uṣaṇa*, *nāgaraka*, and *amṛtā*, well-cooled and combined with sugar-candy, shall be a cause for the destruction of fever caused by *pitta* and *vāta*. (88) A decoction of *amṛta*, *mustaka*, *vāsā*, *parpaṭa*, and *viśvā* drunk with water, as well as *bhadramuñja*, will destroy fever caused by *pitta* and *marut* (vāta). (89) In this [fever], there is drowsiness, heaviness, pain in the joints and head, affliction, and a breaking sensation in the limbs; the eyes possess a moderate intensity of *vāta*.

In cases of fever with *śleṣman* (phlegm), there is burning heat, labored breathing, loss of appetite, dryness in the ears and throat, as well as drowsiness, delusion, anorexia, and vertigo; this is the Pitta-type of *śleṣmajvara*. (90) A decoction of *nāgara*, *bhadramustā*, or *guḍūcī* and *āmalaka*, or of *pāṭhā*, *mṛṇāla*, and *udīcya*, is for *pittajvara* caused by *kapha*. (91) It is digestive (*pācana*), appetizing (*dīpanīya*), and a remedy for the wasting of blood. (92) A decoction prepared from *drākṣā*, *amṛtā*, *vāsaka*, *ariṣṭaka*, *bhūnimba*, *tikta*, *indrayava*, *paṭola*, *mustā*, and *bhārgī* [is likewise effective].

For the destruction of fever caused by pitta and kapha: one should prepare a decoction of *guḍūcī*, neem leaves (*nimba-patra*), ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), nut-grass (*mustā*), coriander (*kustumburu*), and sandalwood (*candana*). This "Guḍūcī-ādi" preparation destroys fevers of kapha, pitta, and vāta. It destroys all types of fever, as well as nausea, anorexia, catarrh, thirst, wasting, and burning sensations. A person suffering from pitta and kapha should drink the decoction prepared from *guḍūcī*, neem, *cakrāvāsaka*, *śaṭhī*, *kirātatikta*, long pepper (*magadhā*), *aṣṭahalyā*, and *dārvī* with *paṭola*.

In fever (jvara), *paṭolī*, *candana*, *tiktā*, *mūrvā*, *pāṭhā*, and the group beginning with *amṛtā* (96) ward off fever caused by *pitta* and *kapha*, as well as vomiting, burning sensations, and itching. (97) This decoction prepared from the roots of *paṭola*, *vāsā*, and *picumanda*, along with *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and *ghanā*, is recommended for fever arising from *kapha* and *pitta*. (98) It is an appetizer (*sandīpana*) for fevers of the *pitta-kapha* type and likewise for those arising from *pitta-asṛj* (blood); it breaks up the impurities (*malas*) and is highly praised. (99) [It is] cooling.

Trembling, breaking pain in the joints, shivering in the limbs, numbness, dullness of heat, loss of appetite, constipation, roughness of the skin, cough, darkness before the eyes, colic, drowsiness, moaning, restlessness, or else a sense of stiffness, yawning, loss of relish, perspiration, and obstruction of feces and urine—these are the symptoms of fever caused by *kapha* and *vāta*. (100) *Āragvadha*, *tiktakarohiṇī*, *harītakī*, the root of *pippalī*, and *mustā* should be boiled; this paste, when administered as a decoction, is beneficial for fever associated with *kapha* and *vāta* and accompanied by colic, as it promotes digestion. (101) *Kṣudrā* and *guḍūcī* together... [The text continues].

A decoction of nagara, vāsā, parpaṭaka, pathyā, mustā, and duḥsparśā is beneficial when drunk for fever caused by vāta and kapha. (102) A decoction of parpaṭa, nāgāhvaya, vacā, tantuka, kaṭphala, elā, abhayā, viśva, and bhūtikā, combined with hiṅgu and honey, is indeed used for kapha-vāta disorders accompanied by hiccups, as well as for throat obstruction. (103) A decoction of the two groups of five roots (dvipañcamūla), saturated with the powder of kaṇā, should be administered for pain arising from vāta and kapha, as well as for fever, dyspnea, and coryza. (104) Drowsiness, lassitude, and sweetness in the mouth [are the symptoms].

Spitting, dryness of the throat, loss of sleep, labored breathing, fainting, and anxiety; numbness of the tongue, or else pain in the back and head, or an internal burning sensation—if these occur, know that the disorder is caused by all three *doṣas*. (105) Having observed this terrible fever born of the three *doṣas*, which is life-threatening, one should therefore first proclaim the drying up of this *kapha*. (106) One who desires their own reputation should not employ pacification of *pitta*; [for if done so], it would immediately kill a strong person afflicted by *kapha* and *vāta*.

For a patient afflicted by pain arising from the three *doṣas*, fasting (*laṅghana*) or self-restraint (*damana*), as well as spitting (*ṣṭhīvana*), should be practiced for three nights, five nights, or even seven nights (107). Fasting is prescribed after having assessed the strength and weakness of the *doṣas*; once the *kapha* is known to be dried up, then measures to subdue the *vāta* are taken (108). Once the provocation of *pitta* is recognized, measures to pacify the *pitta* should be performed; however, while the *vāta* and *kapha* are to be dried up, one must not destroy the *pitta* (109). Thirst, colic, emaciation, labored breathing, and sleeplessness at night [are the signs].

During the day, there occurs drowsiness, delusion, and dryness of the mouth, nose, tongue, and lips; one spits out what has been cooked [in the mouth], becomes emaciated in body, and circular spots appear on the skin. There is darkening of the eyes, lips, and face, perspiration, flatulence, and wasting. Either there is loss of appetite or vertigo, as well as a churning sensation in the head, headache, obstruction of the channels, vomiting, or the throat being constricted by a rattling sound, pain, and piercing aches. (111)

Driven by these symptoms, this disease known as *sannipāta* arises among men; it is a fever that acts swiftly, causing extreme suffering for horses or elephants. (112) In a *sannipāta* fever, one should first apply treatments that remove wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*); subsequently, when the phlegm has been depleted and the morbid matter (*āma*) is gone, one should treat the bile (*pitta*) and wind. (113) Having exerted effort in treating a *sannipāta* fever, one should overcome excessive drowsiness (*tandrā*), which is the most difficult complication of all fevers, especially so. (114) He who administers wholesome food to patients whose bodies are filled with phlegm...

This [fever] becomes his enemy; it is neither wholesome nor medicine. (115) Śaṭhī, the two groups of five roots (*dvipañcamūlaka*), *durālabhā*, *koṭaja*, *paṭola*, *pauṣkara*, along with *bhārgavī* and *pippalī*—this ten-ingredient formulation (*daśāṅga*) destroys *sānnipātika* fever and impaired digestion (*agnimāndya*). (116–117) A decoction (*kaṣāya*) of *bhūnimba*, *dāru*, the ten roots (*daśamūla*), *mahauṣadha*, *abdatikta*, *indrabīja*, *dhanika*, *bhadrakaṇṭaka*, and *kaṇā* quickly destroys fever accompanied by drowsiness, delirium, vertigo, thirst, loss of appetite, burning sensations, delusion, dyspnea, and impaired digestion. (118)

A paste made from equal parts of *śaṇṭhī*, *ghanā*, *agaja*, *kaṇā*, *suradāru*, *dhānyā*, *tikta*, *kaliṅga*, and *daśamūla* is excellent for destroying fevers born of the three *doṣas*, and it cures dyspnea, giddiness, anorexia, constipation, and diseases of the heart. (119) *Mustā*, *uśīra*, *niśā*, *viśāla*, *madhuka*, *pāṭhā*, *balā*, *rohiṇī*, *nīlī*, *dhanvayavāsa*, *kaṭvarā*, *śaṭhī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *samaṅgā*, and *vivṛt*—[these are combined].

A decoction made from yaṣṭī, pippalīmūla, parpaṭa, phalā, pippalyaka, dāru, śyāmā, hemaguḍūcī, and equal parts of payas is known as *jvarānta*. (120) The two types of bṛhatī, śaṭhī, śṛṅgī, kirāta, kaṭurohiṇī, paṭola, pauṣkara, bhārṅgī, vatsaka, and durālabhā—this is the *bṛhatyādika* digestive decoction (*pācana*). It destroys complications such as cough and quickly overcomes *jvara-sannipāta*; it is highly recommended for alleviating colic pain and drowsiness. (121–122) [Also included are: śaṭhī, kirāta, kaṭukā, and viśālā.

Guḍūcī, bhṛṅgī, the two types of bṛhatī, mahauṣadha (ginger), pauṣkara, dhanvayāsa, rāsnā, surāhvā, and gajapippalī—these fourteen ingredients beginning with śaṭhī, when boiled and drunk, are beneficial for men; they destroy drowsiness, labored breathing, heaviness of the head, and colicky fever, curing them swiftly. Similarly, a decoction prepared from bhūnimba, suradāru, nāgara, ghana, tiktā, kaliṅga, and hastikaṇā, combined with the five groups of two [ingredients each], is beneficial.

Yellow [turmeric] brings about the destruction of all diseases; it destroys *sannipāta* fever, and quickly eliminates asthma, dryness of the chest, pain in the breast, and drowsiness. (125) A decoction made from equal parts of *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, *ghan* (*mustā*), *parpaṭaka*, *paṭolī*, *bhūnimba*, *vatsaka*, *śaṭhī*, *nāgara*, *tiktā*, *surāhvā*, *gajapippalī*, *māgadhikā*, *yavāsa*, *vāsā*, *balā*, and *gajabalā*—this decoction destroys diseases arising from *vāta*, as well as asthma, cough, abdominal pain, and cholera; it is the best for men on this earth. (126)

In diseases involving digestive disorders (pācana-sannipāta), or those caused by phlegm (kapha) and wind (samīraṇa), a decoction of rāsnā, trikaṇṭaka, śatamūlī, bhārṅgī, puṣkara, ghana, suradāru, and dhānyaka should be administered; it is beneficial for all types of fevers born of vāta, even those arising from sannipāta that are extremely severe. A decoction of trivṛt, viśālā, surāhva, āragvadha, and tiktakarohiṇī acts as a purgative for the impurities (malas) and, in cases of vāta-śūla, it destroys the fear of death. [Also] vacā and yavānī.

They say that a powder made from dried *mahauṣadha* is excellent for anointing the body; it certainly brings about the subsiding of the fever's heat through massage. (130) A powder consisting of *māgadhī*, *suradāru*, *viśvaka*, *tiktā*, and combined with *dīpyaka* is also praised for anointing the body; it wards off perspiration from the body, and one will surely become cool-bodied immediately. (131) The essence of *madhūka* mixed with *mahauṣadha*, *vacā*, *uṣaṇā*, and *saindhava*, ground with either urine or warm water—

To awaken lost consciousness, the juice of the root of *śobhāñjanaka* combined with black pepper should be administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) for patients who have become unresponsive; it brings about swift awakening. A single fruit of *bṛhatī*, along with long pepper (*pippalī*) and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), is an excellent powder to blow into the nostrils; the resulting sneeze restores consciousness and movement. *Śirīṣa* seeds, black pepper, and *upakulyā*, ground together with cow’s urine and rock salt (*saindhava*), serve as an eye-salve (*añjana*) for the eyes of men.

Awakening restores consciousness to one who has lost it. (135) A wick made of *trikaṭu*, *karañja* seeds, *triphalā*, *suradāru*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *tulasī*, used as an eye-salve (*añjana*), destroys drowsiness of the eyes. (136) Having prepared a mixture of *kesara*, *mātuluṅga* [seeds], *śṛṅgavera*, and *saindhava* combined with *trikaṭu*, one should wear it in the mouth up to the throat. (137) The wise person should perform friction on the teeth, tongue, mouth, and palate; he should spit out everything according to the prescribed method, doing so repeatedly. (138)

By this, purification of the throat occurs and phlegm is expelled; it produces clarity of the tongue and relish, and both cough and asthma are pacified. (139) A powder made of *kaṭuka*, *cavya*, and *kāpathyā*, combined with *saindhava* salt—one should rub the teeth and the tongue with it to remove the impurities of the palate. (140) Spitting [the powder] out purifies the throat, creates relish, and destroys phlegm; nausea comes to an end, and it produces great clarity [of the senses]. (141) Alternatively, if the body is cold, then sudation (*sveda*) is prescribed; thirteen types of sudation are to be known.

The means for preventing sweating are: *saṅkara*, *prastuta*, *nāḍīpariṣeka*, *apagāhana*, *ātaṅka*, *asmaryana*, *karṣa*, *kūṭī*, *bhūkumbhī*, *kūpa*, and *holāka*; these thirteen [methods] induce perspiration. (142–144) One should administer *kālasveda*, *ghaṭīsveda*, or *vālukāsveda* to the patient’s hands, feet, and likewise the head. If there is still no relief in this way, one should cauterize with an iron rod. If coolness is not achieved when the feet are cauterized, one should cauterize the base of the big toes. (145)

Whether at the wrist, the heart, or the head, if a person afflicted by cold has perspiration on the forehead or a cold clamminess on the neck that does not reach the chest, he will surely go to the house of Death. Whether in seven days, ten days, or twelve days, or again on the thirteenth or fifteenth day, this most terrible *sannipāta* fever, resembling the fire of time (*kālāgni*), either brings about his end or spares the man.

O best of physicians, this is the limit regarding the three humors for both liberation and destruction for this man afflicted by the disorder of *sannipāta*. (150) If one were to sprinkle a person suffering from internal burning in a *sannipāta* with cold water, how could that patient possibly survive, and how could that physician be worthy of honor? (151) What indeed has not been accomplished by that physician who rescues a man fallen into the ocean of *sannipāta*?

By virtue of his righteousness, fame, and discipline, what honor would a physician not receive upon the surface of the earth? (152) Fever arising from the three humors—wind, bile, and phlegm—and further combined with blood, becomes a fever born of the combination of all three (sānnipātika). (153) Know that there is no sānnipātika fever without blood; yet the humors in a human being are pacified by digestive decoctions. (154) Therefore, when the humors have been pacified, the blood does not dissolve; instead, swelling is produced by that very [blood].

But when it is severe at the root of the ear (155), one should therefore apply a remedy consisting of bloodletting by means of leeches, a gourd, or a *bhṛṅga* horn; thereafter, an ointment is beneficial (156). The roots of the *bījapūraka* and likewise the *agnimantha*—this ointment destroys the [inflammation] at the root of the ear (157). Having ground together house-soot, *rajanī*, *mahauṣadha*, *siddhārtha*, rock salt, *vacā*, and milk, this ointment is recommended to destroy the blood, pacifying the swelling and ulcer in a person's ear (158). When suppuration occurs...

In that case, a remedy should be applied: an ointment made from the bark of *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* promotes the healing of wounds. (159) An ointment consisting of the roots of *nimba* and *āragvadha* combined with *niśā* (turmeric) serves to drain pus from foul-smelling wounds and promotes their healing. (160) One should avoid sleeping during the day, sexual intercourse, excessive water intake, cold water, staying awake at night, physical exercise, and likewise grief. (161) As well as black gram (*māṣa*), barley, wheat, sesame, *parṇīka*, lentils (*masūra*), and *tripuṭā*, and [one should avoid] oil.

One should avoid sexual intercourse for one month from afar, and abstain from overeating for half a month; by avoiding [sexual contact] at the base of the ear, one attains comfort (163). Old *ṣaṣṭika* rice, or *bālya*, or *sūpa*, as well as *āḍhakī*, horse-gram, and mung-bean soup are recommended for food (164). One should abandon eggplant, onions, and bulbous vegetables; through this, one attains comfort and is quickly freed from disease (165). When, at the end, the bile (*pitta*) remains externally along with phlegm (*śleṣman*) and wind (*samīraṇa*), [the patient recovers].

Then there will be internal burning and dryness, while externally there is perspiration and coldness. (166) One should quickly have him drink a decoction of *amṛtā* with water, combined with honey and long pepper; he will surely be freed from that *sānnipātika* fever. (167) Alternatively, for the subsiding of internal burning, a decoction of *ativiṣā*, *vālaka*, *nāgara*, *ghanasāraka*, and *parpaṭa*, mixed with sugar, may be given. (168) When *pitta* resides externally and *kapha* and *vāyu* reside internally, heat arises in the body and coldness arises at its extremities. (169) For that [condition], one should give a decoction of *śaṭhī* and other such [herbs].

One should administer a remedy that pacifies *kapha*. (170) For one whose *vāta* and *kapha* are located in the upper body while the *pitta* moves downward, half of the body becomes cold and half becomes hot. (171) For such a person, one should administer a decoction of the *rāsnā* group and likewise a warm [remedy]. (172) For one who has *rakta-pitta* in the upper part and both *vāta* and *kapha* in the middle, heat arises in the upper part and cold arises in the lower part. (173) The best of physicians should administer a decoction of the *nāgara* group for him. (174) Furthermore, for one in whom heat is observed...

When the onset is slow, one should recognize it as having an external impulse (*bāhyavega*); such a fever is curable by one who understands [the treatment]. (175) One should know that when heat, thirst, burning sensations, and headache arise at the end [of the onset], it has a deep-seated impulse (*gambhīravega*); it is difficult to cure even for men. (176) For that, one should provide a remedy: the eighteen-fold formulation (*yoga*) for men. (177) When bile (*pitta*) remains in the body at the end, while both wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*kapha*) [are present], there is coldness in the body and heat in the hands and feet. (178) For that, a decoction of the *rāsnā* group, combined with long pepper (*pippalī*), should be administered.

179. When *pitta* resides in the body while both *vāta* and *kapha* remain at its extremities, heat arises within the body and coldness occurs in the hands and feet. 180. For such a case, a decoction of grapes and similar fruits mixed with jaggery should be administered. 181. Wherever there is coldness, sudation (*sveda*) is prescribed; however, the wise practitioner should not apply sudation when the fever is excessively hot. 182. Due to *kapha* and *pitta*, the *vāyu* (wind) always becomes inactive; from that very *vāyu*, diseases such as fever and others arise. 183. Dizziness (*bhrama*).

Coolness, exhaustion, trembling, diarrhea, fatigue, weariness, perspiration, and delirious talk occur during the release from fever (jvaramokṣa). 184 Perspiration, itching, and the swelling of the veins, as well as sneezing in the face, lightness of body, desire for food, and clarity of the senses—when a person is free from fatigue and free from pain; 185 yet even when released, heaviness of the head does not leave him; one should know that the fever has not been truly released, for it will return to him. 186 If the fever has indeed entered the bodily tissues (dhātu) and persists within the body...

One should recognize irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*); it is known to be of four types: the quotidian (*ekāhika*), the tertian (*dvyāhika*), the quartan (*tryāhika*), and the wise physician should also recognize the fourth as the "time-bound" (*velājvara*). (187–188) If cold occurs first and heat arises afterwards, that fever is declared curable in a human being; it is quickly cured by medicines. (189) If one subsequently experiences a burning sensation, the fever becomes severe; that fever, which causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-kṣaya*), does not quickly subside. (190) [It is felt] in the three corners and the hips...

There may be pain from Vāta and Pitta, or Pitta in the head with vertigo, and in the back it causes thinness and pain from Kapha; this is the threefold characteristic of Tṛtīyaka fever (191). From Kapha and Pitta it seizes the sacrum (trika), while that consisting of Vāta and Kapha seizes the back; seizing the head through Vāta and Pitta, Tṛtīyaka is thus of three types (192). The fourth type of fever should be known as twofold, the fever consisting of Vāta and Śleṣma (Kapha); the Kapha-type is known to arise from the calves, while the one originating from Anila (Vāta) arises from the head (193). Having understood this, the good physician should act accordingly therein.

The remedy for *velājvara* is [to be applied when it occurs] in the blood; likewise, that which is daily (*ekāhika*) resides in the blood, while that which is every third day (*tṛtīyaka*) resides in the flesh, and the fourth resides in the bones. That which has pervaded all the tissues (*dhātu*) should be known as chronic (*jīrṇa*), causing the depletion of the tissues. (194–195) For fever born of the elements (*bhūtaja*), the science of spirits (*bhūtavidyā*) is the remedy; one should employ pacification and beating. For one whose fever arises from a curse (*abhiśāpa*), the remedy is peace. (196) In fever born of desire (*kāmajvara*), one should remove the bile (*pitta*) by means of jaundice-inducing treatments and beneficial breath-control (*śvasana*). (197) In fever born of anger (*krodhajvara*) or even that born of bile, one should pacify it with virtuous words and medicinal herbs. (198)

One should induce a state of intoxication with fragrant substances; such use is beneficial. (198) One should drink a decoction of *nidigdhikā*, *nāgarika*, and *amṛtā* mixed with *pippalī* in cases of chronic fever, loss of appetite, cough, colic, dyspnea, weak digestion, facial paralysis, and coryza. (199) In cases of cough, indigestion, dyspnea, heart disease, anemia, weak digestive fire, jaundice, and loss of appetite, *pippalī* is recommended for these; when taken with jaggery, it quickly destroys chronic fever in men. (200) A decoction of the *laghupañcamūlī* along with *pippalī* and *chinnodbhavā* [is also beneficial].

This [decoction] destroys chronic fever, dyspnea, and diseases caused by *kapha*, as well as weak digestion, colic, loss of appetite, and rhinitis (201). A decoction of *paṭola*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, the three fruits (*triphalā*), *vatsaka*, *nimba*, *mokṣā*, *drākṣā*, *amṛtā*, *candana*, and *nāgara* serves to destroy long-standing fever (202). One should eat jīraka with jaggery, or *harītakī* with jaggery, or sesame seeds with jaggery, during a fever accompanied by irregularity (viṣamajvara) (203). Or one should consume jaggery and fresh ginger, or a decoction of *triphalā* with jaggery; for this decoction also [removes] irregular fevers.

The one who causes destruction [of fever] (204): A decoction prepared with *vāsā*, *āmalakī* fruit, *devadāru*, *harītakī*, and *śuṇṭhī*, combined with honey, wards off quartan fever (205). The fresh juice of *agasti* leaves, used as a nasal drop (*nasya*), destroys the violent quartan disease; it also destroys cough, vertigo, and headache, and this nasal treatment is beneficial for men (206). He who, suffering from irregular fever, daily consumes a paste of garlic mixed with sesame oil, is liberated from those irregular fevers.

And also by wind-diseases of extremely terrible form. (207) A paste of *nimba* leaves, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, jaggery, *guggulu*, mustard seeds, and *harītakī*, combined with clarified butter, is indeed an incense that destroys irregular fevers (*viṣamajvara*). (208) The root of *surasā*, tied to the hand on an auspicious day, wards off fevers caused by spirits (*bhūta*) and destroys fevers occurring at specific times (*velājvara*). (209) A decoction of *mustā*, *amṛtā*, *āmalakī*, *nāgara*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*, mixed with the powder of *kaṇā* and honey, [cures] the quotidian fever (*ekāhika*). (210) Or...

It dispels fever that has arisen starting from the evening (velā). Having removed the seeds of garlic (*rasona*) and cut them into pieces, one should place them in buttermilk during the nights; when consumed at dawn combined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), it destroys fevers such as those beginning in the evening, even those that have reached the bodily tissues (*dhātu*). One should drink milk in the manner of the *pippalī-vardhamāna* regimen as a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). [One may also take] great medicine (*mahauṣadha*), ginger (*nāgara*), coriander (*dhānya*), sandalwood (*candana*), and *vāluka*. One should drink *guḍūcī* with milk to remove tertian fever (*tṛtīyaka-jvara*). Likewise, the root of *apāmārga* or the root of *nīlī* [may be used].

By tying a red thread from the navel up to the crown of the head around the left ear and the waist, one destroys tertian fever (216). The divine face of the Lord of Monkeys, possessing the splendor of the rising sun, causes even a terrible quotidian fever to perish at that very moment (217). Having drawn the form of the Monkey with chalk, listen further: the best of physicians worship it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and incense (218). *Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ klīṃ, to Sugrīva, who possesses great strength and prowess, the son of the Sun, of immeasurable splendor.*

Daha daha! Paca paca! Avata avata, O King of Monkeys! Bind bind the fevers—those of one day, two days, three days, four days, great fevers, fevers caused by spirits, fevers born of anger, fevers of the critical hour, and so forth! Hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ phaṭ svāhā! There is no fever.

The fever that is capable of removing other fevers is itself terrified [by this mantra]. (219) Furthermore, I shall here describe the forms and characteristics of the fevers: One who has the luster of molten gold, whose radiance is equal to fire, who wears a sacred thread that seems to fly upward, and who is fierce—such is the Brāhmaṇa-form [fever]. (220–221) One who resembles a hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), who possesses fierce fangs, who holds a sword in his hand, and who is most terrible—this is considered the Kṣatriya-form [fever], belonging to Mahendra. (222) One who has the appearance of the five products [of the cow], who is adorned with molten gold, who holds a staff in his hand, and who possesses moderate speed—this is the Vaiśya-form [fever]. (223)

Jvareśvara is considered [the presiding deity]. (223) He has the appearance of a black cloud or collyrium, possesses sharp fangs and a blazing face, is three-eyed, and has the radiance of fire; he is Time (Kāla) and is likewise considered a Śūdra. (224) He is of fierce speed, possessed by hunger, pure, hateful, and fond of vows; his urine is the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers; he is habituated to recitation and is excessively talkative. (225) He suffers from much labored breathing, is overcome by thirst, and is afflicted by fierce Brāhmaṇas. By performing bathing, recitation, and fire-offerings for him, peace is attained. (226) [The patient] has a sharp fever, extreme thirst, and bloody urine.

He urinates frequently, engages in talk of war, and rises up afflicted by physical strength; his eyes are inflamed, he has heavy labored breathing, and is likewise oppressed by hunger (227). There is a honey-like scent in his mouth, perspiration, and he is afflicted by the *māhendraka* [demon] among the Kṣatriyas (228). For him, at the outset, one who is pure should perform oblations for the seizing spirits (*graha-homa*) and the praise of deities; through such acts as giving gifts and reciting prayers, union with success is attained (229). With moderate force, his body is yellowish, he is prone to sleep, and likewise suffers from loss of appetite; he is chilled by cold winds, his heart feels hot, there is perspiration on the throat, and he is extremely distressed (230). He passes much urine.

One who is devoted, silent, with yellowish inner eyes, not afflicted by excessive thirst, and affectionate—such a person is to be known as the Lord of Fever (Jvareśvara). (231) In that case, for the sake of pacification, one should perform all rites such as auspicious prayers (*svastyayana*), hospitality, worship of the twice-born and the deities, recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth. (232) One who suffers from heart-pain or diarrhea, whose body smells like fish, who is insane, whose eyes are excessively full, whose senses are impaired during sexual acts, (233) who is fond of the road yet fearful of it, and who has no desire for food—even with a black vessel of time (*kālabhṛṅgāraka*), there is no success with a Śūdra. (234)

Bathing, charity, recitation of mantras, the ritual worship of the gods, burnt offerings (*homa*), and so forth, as well as the propitiation of spirits, should be performed in various ways to bring about specific satisfaction. Through the gift of cows, land, gold, food, and drink, peace shall prevail for all; those who observe the vow of truth proclaim that this brings about the destruction of all diseases. Just as poison, having gained momentum, dissolves within the body and then becomes exceedingly powerful and agitated again at the proper time, so too does the humoral disorder (*doṣa*) act like poison. [One should consume] the soup of *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice.

Mudga, āḍhakī, and the previously mentioned leafy vegetables (śāka) are indeed pacifiers of vāta. 237. Śatapuṣpā, jīvantī, taṇḍulīyaka, vāstuka, and bhājikā prepared with ghee—these are the leaf-vegetables [recommended]. 238. For a patient, one should employ the meat of lāva, tittiri, and other birds, as well as vārtāka; likewise, one should use the meat of wild animals such as mṛga and chikkarika. 239. Kośātakī, paṭola, and śuṇṭhīka are beneficial; however, one should avoid pulses (vidalānna), foods that cause burning (vidāhin), and heavy foods. 240. One should not use slimy oils.

Likewise, the best of physicians should avoid sour things, as well as large quantities of curd and whey, and minor foods (241). He should also avoid betel with excessive water, ghee, or even liquor (242). Having abandoned anger and grief, one always enjoys happiness; one should not keep a vigil at night and should avoid sleeping during the day (243). One should always strictly avoid riding in carts, on horses, elephants, or other vehicles; the wise man, who is a repository of auspicious rites, should quickly eat for his comfort when suffering from fever (244).

One who has been freed from fever should not engage in physical exercise, sexual intercourse, eating, or staying awake at night; by doing so, he attains well-being. (245) Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fever," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 2.

The Third Chapter. Ātreya said: Now, my dear son, listen to the diagnosis and treatment of diarrhea (*atīsāra*). The diarrhea born of fever and its treatment are now being taught. (1) Some substances are considered to pacify the *doṣas*, some to vitiate the *dhātus*, and some for the maintenance of health; thus, substance is said to be threefold. (2) That [treatment] consists of recourse to the path of the divine (*daivapatha*), recourse to the path of logic (*yuktipatha*), and the subjugation of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*). It includes mantras, medicinal herbs, gems, amulets, offerings, oblations, burnt sacrifices (*homa*), observances (*niyama*), expiations (*prāyaścitta*), fasting (*upavāsa*), auspicious rites (*svastyayana*), and prayers (*praṇidhāna*).

The path of the gods (*daivapatha*) consists of [the practice of] *dīti*. The path of reasoning (*yuktipatha*) consists of the application of food, worldly transactions, and medicinal substances. The conquest of the mind (*sattvāvajaya*) consists of the restraint of the mind from harmful objects. One should eat food that is unctuous, very cold, heavy, cool, and slimy; likewise, one may consume spoiled food, excessive or irregular food and drink, and what is unfit for eating. Furthermore, one may eat during indigestion, or when afflicted by grief, poisons, or fears, or due to the distress of sorrow, or when the milk is spoiled—[these are the exceptions to the rules]. Weakness results from irregular eating. Indigestion is destroyed when it is broken up in water by means of [proper] cleansing.

Indeed, when the digestive fire (*agni*) of a person is destroyed, then diarrhea (*atisāra*) arises; that diarrhea arises because the digestive fire of the person has been extinguished. (5) Furthermore, it occurs with excessive *mala* (waste matter); thus it is described as fivefold by sages who know the methods. Briefly, for one whose pain is intense, its destruction occurs first through decoctions and other digestive (*pācanaka*) remedies. (6) When fever and diarrhea arise simultaneously, that terrible fever-diarrhea (*jvarātisāra*) is difficult to cure even for the wise. (7) Moreover, that [diarrhea] does not occur without *pitta*.

Listen, my son: fasting is prescribed for him in cases of fever and diarrhea. (8) Suvarcala, ativiṣā, hiṅgu, pathyā, kaliṅgaka, and śuṇṭhī destroy undigested matter (āma), diarrhea, and colic; they are constipating and digestive. (9) For the destruction of āmātisāra, a person should drink a decoction made from pathyā, dāru, vacā, mustā, nāgara, and ativiṣā. (10) One should grind utpala, dhānyaka, śuṇṭhī, pṛśniparṇī, balā, and young bilva with very hot cow’s buttermilk. (11) With that [mixture], one should prepare a *maṇḍa* (gruel-scum) using parched grain (*lāja*).

Having brought this cooling decoction, which pacifies fever and diarrhea and bestows strength upon the digestive fire, [one should proceed]. 12. A decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *viṣā*, *taladharā*, *amṛtā*, *vatsaka*, *tiktāhvaya*, and *kanakaśītalaka*, properly prepared, should now be administered for the drinking; it should always be given to pacify fever and diarrhea. 13. A decoction of *pāṭhā*, *indrābhū*, *nimba*, *ghana*, *amṛtā*, and *parpaṭa* is highly recommended here; it quickly conquers diarrhea caused by undigested matter (*āma*), as well as that associated with fever, even when severe and chronic. 14. [The ingredients are] *śuṇṭhī*, *bālaka*, and *mustā*.

Bilva, pāṭhā, and viṣā, along with grains, act as a digestive (pācana) for loss of appetite; they destroy vomiting, fever, and diarrhea. (15) A decoction of vatsaka, suradāru, rohiṇī, grains, bilva, agnimantha, trikaṇṭaka, nimba seeds, gajapippalī, and vṛkī is likewise a medicine for diarrhea. (16) Boiled with the five roots (pañcamūlī), balā, bilva, guḍūcī, musta, and nāgara, as well as pāṭhā, bhūnimba, hrībera, kuṭaja bark, and its fruit—this [decoction] overcomes all types of diarrhea, vomiting, dyspnea, fever, and facial paralysis, along with their complications such as colic. (17)

It destroys the terrible affliction of the asuras. (18) The five roots (*pañcamūla*) are generally used in cases of *pitta*, while the smaller one is used for *kapha*; however, the larger *pañcamūla* is beneficial in fevers caused by *vāta* and *śleṣman*. (19) Blue lotus (*utpala*), pomegranate bark, filaments (*kesara*), honey, *padmaka*, and *dhātrī*—when ground with rice-water, this is a digestive remedy that cures fever and diarrhea. (20) A decoction of *uśīra*, coriander (*dhānyaka*), *musta*, *bilva*, *bālaka*, *balā*, and *dhātakī* flowers is highly recommended; it pacifies fever and diarrhea accompanied by blood and *pitta*. (21)

It destroys all types of swelling, stimulates the appetite, and acts as a digestive. 22. Aralu, processed by *puṭapāka* and taken with honey, pacifies long-standing diarrhea that has become excessive, whether accompanied by blood or not. 23–24. One should always prepare a collection of these: Jambu, Vaṭa, Udumbara, Plakṣa, Nāga, Prapauṇḍarika, Śamī, Gundra, Cūta, and Ambudajīvikā. One should drink two *prasthas* of this until a specific portion is produced again in the cauldron. 24. (Note: The text implies a specific consistency or yield is reached.)

One should cook it until it forms a paste on a wooden ladle and its own juice is extracted; then, having removed it, the best of physicians should certainly administer it mixed with honey to cure diarrhea. (25-26) Likewise, Kākamācī has been highly praised by Hārīta; after examining many treatises, it was also honored by Ātreya. (27) Having boiled the bark of Jambū and the inner bark of Vatsaka in water until one-fourth remains, one should remove it from the fire and strain it through a cloth. Then, one should boil it again in a cauldron. (28)

The decoction of *samyagdārvī* (properly prepared bark) should be strained while still hot; once cooled, it should be mixed with honey and licked. This relieves even severe diarrhea. (29) In all types of diarrhea, there is constant obstruction in the flanks, the abdomen, the chest, the region of the navel, and the lower part of the body, as well as the suppression of flatus and the breaking up of feces. (30) Experts declare that in diarrhea caused by Vāta, the stool is frothy, slimy, dry, scanty, and passed with a single effort accompanied by the sound of undigested matter (*āma*) and pain; it is black, and there is twitching of the limbs. (31) At the beginning of that [condition]...

In cases of mild [diarrhea], fasting is either prescribed alone or not at all; therefore, one should administer decoctions, as well as drinks and food. A paste of *udīcyadhānya* (coriander) taken with water is beneficial for drinking; it cures diarrhea, removes thirst, destroys burning sensations, and serves to eliminate colic and hiccups. This very same decoction, prepared with water along with the two types of *bālaka*, *moca*, *harītakī*, and *parpaṭa*, quickly brings about the destruction of diarrhea and the cessation of stool. *Śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *bṛhatī*, and *kaṇṭakārikā*...

Bālā, aśvadaṃṣṭrā, bilva, pāṭhā, nāgara, and dhānyaka (35)—this is beneficial when combined with food for all those suffering from diarrhea. Having taken the bark of tinduka and wrapped it in the leaves of kāśmarī (36), the physician should coat it with clay and burn it with a gentle fire according to the prescribed method; having extracted the juice and mixed it with honey, this drink cures all types of diarrhea. Then, having crushed one *tulā* of fresh *girimallikā*, one should add one *karṣa* [of other ingredients]; once that is purified, one *pala* [of the resulting powder] should be given after grinding it together with *śālmali*. (37–38)

Having added pāṭhā, samaṅgā, ativiṣā, mustā, bilva, and the flowers of dhātakī, one should boil them again until a paste of dārvī and its expressed juice is obtained. When this is drunk at the appropriate time with water, rice-scum, or goat’s milk, it destroys all severe types of diarrhea—whether black, white, red, or yellow—as well as various disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī), hemorrhagic fever (rakta-pitta), blood-stained hemorrhoids, and even incurable menorrhagia; it certainly overcomes these conditions.

This is the Kuṭajāṣṭaka (41). Due to heat, the consumption of warm food, the drinking of hot water, grief, fever, anger, pungency, and alkaline substances, there arises an aggravation of bile and blood (42). By that, [the stool becomes] reddish, yellow, or very dark blue, accompanied by foul odor, emaciation, fever, and jaundice; along with giddiness, pain, fainting, thirst, and burning in the limbs—these are the symptoms of Pitta-type diarrhea (43). A drink prepared with Śāliparṇī, Pṛśniparṇī, Balā, and Bilva, soured with pomegranate, is beneficial for the pacification of Pitta-type diarrhea (44).

Having prepared a decoction of the roots of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and sugarcane with water produced from *śālīna* rice, it is recommended for those suffering from bile-induced diarrhea (pittātisāra). (45) A decoction of the five medicinal roots (*pañcamūla*) is likewise beneficial for those with bile-induced diarrhea. (46) The root-bark of the *śālmali* tree ground with jaggery and milk, when drunk, pacifies excessive bile and removes blood, burning sensations, and emaciation. (47) [This condition arises] from bad dreams and the like, from fatigue, from innate dullness, from exposure to cold, from unctuous food, from overeating, and from heavy substances such as sesame, meat, jaggery, and pieces of sugarcane.

Due to excessive bathing in cold water, greed for food mixed with curd while in water, and similar causes, Kaphaja-atisāra arises; it is a state of undigested food that destroys the digestive fire in men. (48) By that [Kapha], one should know that Kaphottha-sāra is characterized by dryness, piercing pain, loss of appetite, thick and foul-smelling stools, heaviness, horripilation, weak digestion, slow movement of the bowels, and lassitude. (49) Having ascertained the strength or weakness of the body, fasting (laṅghana) is prescribed for this at the outset; furthermore, O best of physicians, a digestive treatment (pācana) using Tri-ūṣaṇa and other such drugs should be administered. (50)

A linctus composed of the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa), abhayā, hiṅgu, ativiṣā, rucaka, and vacā, combined with honey, can even stop the flow of the river Gaṅgā. (51) A paste made of kāliṅga, pāṭhā, ativiṣā, balā, uśīra, mustā, marica, and śuṇṭhī, taken with jaggery and honey, is excellent for alleviating dysentery caused by phlegm (kaphaja-raktātisāra). (52) Vatsaka, ativiṣā, bilva, mustaka, and vālaka, when boiled together with water and drunk as a decoction, destroy severe colic, blood, and pus in cases of dysentery accompanied by fever. (53) As for that which is blood... [text ends]

If, during purgation, there is excessive drying or burning, it should be recognized by highly intelligent physicians as *raktātisāra* (blood-dysentery). (54) A decoction of coriander (*dhānyaka*), ginger (*nāgara*), musta, vetiver (*vālaka*), young *bilva* fruit, *balā*, and *nāgabala* is for those suffering from blood-dysentery. (55) Having ground pomegranate, wood-apple (*kapittha*), yellow myrobalan (*pathyā*), rose-apple (*jambu*), and mango sprouts, they should be administered with buttermilk to ward off blood-dysentery. (56) *Billva* cooked with jaggery should be given to one suffering from blood-dysentery; or else, *pathyā* mixed with honey or curd should be given to the person. (57)

Vatsaka, ativiṣā, nāgara, and abhayā, ground together and combined with whey (mastu), form a linctus that is recommended even with honey for a person; it effectively checks even severe hemorrhaging. (57–58) The powder of kuṭaja bark, pāṭhā, viśva, bilva, and dhātakī, taken with honey, should be administered as a cure for bloody diarrhea. (59) Sannipāta fever flows out [in its characteristic colors]: like the bristles of a boar, like the color of vāsā grass, like sesame oil, like the wash-water of meat, or resembling the fruit of a ripe jambū tree. (60) One should take one tulā of fresh girimallikā...

Having crushed and cooked it, one should extract the juice; when that is well-strained and measured at one *pala*, one should add [the following] after grinding them together with *śālmali*: *pāṭhā*, *samaṅgā*, *ativiṣā*, *mustā*, *bilva*, and the flowers of *dhātakī*. Having added these, one should boil it again until it becomes suitable for application as a paste with *dārvī*. When drunk then at the proper time with water, gruel (*maṇḍa*), or even with honey, it destroys all severe types of diarrhea—whether black, white, red, or yellow—and the disorder of the *grahaṇī*.

This *kuṭajāṣṭaka* (the eight-fold preparation of *kuṭaja*) certainly destroys various types of hemorrhage, hemorrhoids accompanied by blood, and even incurable forms of menorrhagia. (64) The decoction of *pathyā* and the five roots (*pañcamūla*) should be reduced to one-fourth its original volume. Into that decoction, these medicinal powders should be added: (65) Fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), lac (*lākṣā*), long pepper (*pippalī*), *kaṭurohiṇī*, the powder of pomegranate rind (*dāḍimaphalatvak*), *dārvī*, *vatsaka*, and poison (*viṣa*). (66) Having added the powders of *āṭarūṣaka*, one should stir them together here with goat’s milk (*ājaṃ dugdha*).

One should add half of that amount of ghee and one-eighth part [of the other ingredients] (verse 67). Knowing it has been smeared with *dārvī*, sixteen *palas* of jaggery mixed therein should be given before breakfast (verse 68). This is a digestive for severe diarrhea arising from the three doṣas combined (*sannipāta*), as well as for colic, fainting, vertigo, abdominal distension, and jaundice (verse 69). This "Amṛta-vat" (Nectar-pot) is beneficial for those suffering from chest wounds, emaciation, and consumption (verse 70). Powdered *bilva*, *aguru*, and *rodhra*, combined with honey and other substances, pacifies bloody diarrhea and is for children whose bodily tissues (*dhātu*) are depleted (verse 71). When...

One should then expel the secret [discharge] and perform this procedure: the juice of *sahacara* and *balā*, as well as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), should be taken. An application with cooked *ghṛta* is recommended for it; alternatively, a decoction of *araṇī* sprouts, or a clod of earth mixed with sandalwood (*candana*) may be used. Or else, having quenched a heated object resembling fire with *kāñjika* vinegar, one should apply it in the same manner. Furthermore, sitting comfortably, inserting the anus into the middle [of the vessel], and securing it with a firm bandage is highly praised for providing relief.

One should avoid diarrhea that has the smell of garlic or a corpse, the stench of pus, or is thick like liquid flesh; that which resembles ripe *jambu* fruit, or has the appearance of ghee, honey, or milk; or that which is as dark as oil or moss, or the color of thick curd. (75) One who suffers from vertigo, intoxication, consumption, colic, fainting, burning sensations, labored breathing, extreme discoloration, vomiting, or is afflicted by fainting and thirst; one who is excessively debilitated and tormented by swelling, fever, and pain—such a person should be avoided from afar by a wise physician, for he is not seen to survive. (76) [Symptoms include] swelling, colic, and fever.

One should abandon a patient suffering from diarrhea upon observing thirst, labored breathing, cough, anorexia, vomiting, fainting, and hiccups (77). Likewise, one should abandon a patient afflicted by edema, flatulence, hiccups, vomiting, anorexia, and jaundice who also suffers from diarrhea (78). When waste matter, consumed in very small quantities and gradually, remains constantly lodged in the receptacle of the rectum, it suppresses the internal digestive fire and produces a disorder in man known as *grahaṇī* (79). Once the diarrhea has ceased, this condition further diminishes the digestive heat.

Even when afflicted, having consumed impure food, it excretes the undigested portion after accumulating it for many days without ceasing. Seizing its natural functions again and again, whether immature or fully ripened, this chronic disease of terrible form causes pain to a person; such is *grahaṇī*. One should recognize that in cases of diarrhea (*atisāra*), the disorder of *grahaṇī* is to be understood as being of four types: Vātika, Paittika, Ślaiṣmika, and Sānnipātika. Indeed, the disease of *grahaṇī* does not arise from a single *doṣa* alone; by [the combination of these], it is brought about and thereby the body is wasted away.

Internal burning of the body is its maturation (82). It is bitter, astringent, pungent, sour, burning, and dry. Through those devoted to cold and meager food, as well as through physical exertion, sexual intercourse, and running while carrying loads on foot, elephant, or chariot, the wind becomes provoked; when it strikes the fire, it gains momentum (83). Therefore, being cut by the foremost wind and joined with blood, it undergoes maturation in the wind; thus it arises in a person, and that third [type] is named *gulma*, which became fivefold (84): the *plīhā* (spleen).

The binding of the liver, the stomach, and the filth of the intestines; the *aṣṭhīlā* (hard tumor), worms, and the sixth, which arises from diseases of the stomach—these, occurring in the course of *grahaṇī*, become terrible and cause suffering in the mind of a person. (85) Dryness of the throat, darkness of vision, pain in the sides, extreme emaciation in the navel, severe colic (*atisūcikā*), ringing in the ears, excessive vomiting, exhaustion, pain, and delusion—know these to be the symptoms of *gulma* accompanied by dyspnea. (86) One who possesses these signs is a patient suffering from *gulma*.

The wise know that which is called *grahaṇī*; I shall now describe the symptoms of its curable form. (87) In this condition, one voids stool that is varied in color and accompanied by sound; there is swelling and the wind makes the stool exceedingly dry. Accompanied by labored breathing and pain, with a sense of physical looseness, there is a discharge from the *grahaṇī* due to the provocation of Vāyu. (88) When the stool is discharged mixed with other secretions—burning, decomposed, painful, causing thirst, foul-smelling, yellow, reddish, blue, or black—that is known as *grahaṇī* arising from Pitta. (89) Nausea, vomiting, dyspnea, and swelling [occur].

Cough, dullness, coldness, a bad taste in the mouth, heaviness of the limbs, loss of appetite, and retention of the ears and feces—these are declared to be the symptoms when [the three doṣas] are combined. Alternatively, when there is anger, sweetness in the mouth, burning sensation, fainting, labored breathing, and dullness, that is the disease of *sannipāta-grahaṇī*. Dāru, nāgara, niśā, vāsaka, kuṇḍalī, magadhajā, śaṭhī, ghana, rāsnā, bhārṅgī, sarala, and puṣkara constitute a digestive formulation (*pācana*) for *vātika-grahaṇī*.

The root of *nalaveṇu*, *kuśa*, *kāśa*, and sugarcane, taken as a decoction, is beneficial for this patient; it acts as a digestive aid in cases of *pittaja* *grahaṇī*. (93) *Vyāghrī*, *granthika*, *cavya*, *surasā*, *śuṇṭhī*, pomegranate, *rajanī*, *ghan*, and *citraka* likewise destroy hiccups and *kaphaja* *grahaṇī*. (94) Furthermore, one should employ *śuṇṭhī*, *kaṇā*, the two types of *rajanī*, and *ghana*; then again, *prativiṣā*, *triphalā*, *viḍaṅga*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *vahnitrikaṭu*, and the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*)—this powder, combined with jaggery, [is effective].

Having mixed it with ghee and prepared fifty *modaka* pills the size of a cat's paw, one should consume them; this is excellent for *grahaṇī* disease, hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, loss of appetite, abdominal tumors, urinary disorders, colic, stones, worms, and jaundice. This is a preeminent elixir (*rasāyana*) that destroys debility, acts as an aphrodisiac, bestows strength, cures the defect of extreme emaciation, imparts luster to the complexion and all the sense organs, alleviates diseases, and always removes skin diseases and vertigo. [The wise man should take] five hundred *harītakī* fruits with a *droṇa* of...

It should be cooked with a hundred measures of cow’s urine over a gentle fire until the urine is entirely consumed. Once the urine has been digested, the knower of the procedure should extinguish the fire according to the rules and allow it to dry completely. When cool, one should split open the shells and dry them in the shade.
