Then, having prepared a decoction of the powder of *śuṇṭhī*, *magadhā* (pippalī), *viṣā*, fragrant *mūrvā*, *cavikā*, and *krāntā*, along with a paste of *kuṭaja* that is thick enough to coat a ladle, one should churn it with half as much jaggery and half as much milk—either cow’s or goat’s. 98–100.

That [preparation] should be cooked in ghee and prepared by that delighted one; then, a powder made of rock salt, the three pungents (trikaṭu), and the three aromatics (trisugandhi), combined with jaggery and mixed with ghee—by means of that powder, it is an immediate destroyer of all types of grahaṇī disorders, anemia, consumption, urinary stones, worms, abdominal tumors, diarrhea, splenic enlargement, liver disease, asthma, cholera, chronic catarrh, and all pains of the head in men, as well as of fevers and the exhaustion of those whose strength is depleted by the fatigue of travel. 101–102.

This electuary beginning with *abhayā* destroys fevers lasting for a single day and other types; it is like nectar for men. (103) Thus ends the *Abhayādyo-avaleha*. Having cooked grapes with milk until it becomes thick and can be smeared by a ladle, the wise man should then stir in these medicinal herbs: (104) *parpaṭa*, *ativiṣā*, *mūrvā*, *paṭola*, *ghanavālaka*, as well as the powder of *abhayā* mixed with an equal amount of sugar. (105) Having combined that with the milk and the tuber of *vidārī*, he should form a bolus with fresh butter and clarified butter.

Having prepared it, one should then consume it. It removes the afflictions of pitta-type grahaṇī, anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice (kāmalā), and thirst; it certainly and quickly destroys vertigo, fainting, hiccups, epilepsy, insanity, urinary calculi, urinary disorders (meha), hemorrhaging (pittāsṛj), and skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diarrhea," in the third section of the *Hārīta-uttara* as spoken by Ātreya, concerning the "Milk with Grapes and Other Ingredients."

The Fourth Chapter. Ātreya said: Listen, my son, I shall explain the characteristics of the *gulmas* (abdominal tumors/lumps), as well as their remedies and specific medicinal treatments. (1) These *gulmas*, which are associated with the abdomen, arise in five ways: located in the heart, in the side of the abdomen, at the navel, in the bladder, and the fifth is known to be in the middle [of the torso]. (2) That situated in the heart is called *yakṛt*; that in the side of the abdomen is called *aṣṭhīlā*; that in the middle is designated as *plīhā*; and that in the bladder is *caṇḍavivṛddhaka*. (3) A knot (*granthi*) is observed at the navel.

The names of these [diseases] are distinct from one another; therefore, I shall describe their provocation by which they cause affliction. (4) In the case of [gulma] arising from *pitta* and blood (*rakta*), it is provoked by nature through the consumption of sour, burning, hot, or alkaline substances, or alcohol, or by the excessive intake of warm drinks. (5) Likewise, grief, fatigue, walking long distances, emaciation, or agitation, as well as loud speaking, singing, and the drawing of a bowstring, (6) or striking the back with the fist, or beating the chest, or even lifting heavy loads—these cause the blood to dry up in the heart. (7) Because of that, it is called *gulma*.

Indeed, that which is called *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) sometimes arises; its occurrence is seen when all three *doṣas* are involved. Driven by *vāta*, solidified by *kapha*, and brought to a state of ripening by *pitta*, it becomes a combination of the three *doṣas* within the liver (*yakṛt*). I shall describe its symptoms by which it is recognized, and how a person is wasted away and quickly meets death. Vomiting, exhaustion, eructation, nausea, labored breathing, vertigo, burning sensation, loss of appetite, thirst, fainting, a burning sensation in the throat, and headache [are its signs].

Heartache, catarrh, spitting, pain in the heart as if pierced by a thorn, loss of sleep, and delirium; one should recognize these symptoms [as occurring] when there is a sense of hardness in the heart and the abdomen gurgles intensely—[indicating the disease] in the liver, the pelvic cavity, or the chest. If one should take Trikaṭu, Kuṣṭha, Pañcamūla, Yavānī, and Sindhu salt (rock salt) as the sixth ingredient, mixed with Hingu, into a fine powder and consume it, followed by a drink of buttermilk, [the ailment will be cured].

One should drink water boiled [with these] or sour *sauvīraka* gruel; this quickly destroys liver disease, abdominal enlargement, colic, and cough, and it overcomes cholera, indigestion, diseases of *kapha*, the pain of *pāṇḍu*, and *grahaṇī* with *gulma*. The powder of *śuṇṭhī* and other [aromatics] quickly destroys [these ailments], as does the alkali of *muṣkaka*, *kiṃśuka*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, *apāmārga*, *rambhā*, sesame, *jīvantī*, *kanakāhvaya*, turmeric, and the *kūṣmāṇḍa* creeper.

Having ignited and reduced to ashes *vāsā* and *sūraṇa*, which possess intense burning power, one should consume them with water and then drink a measured amount of milk; this cures liver disease (yakṛt), as well as diseases born of colic, abdominal tumors, constipation, and phlegm, including jaundice, abscesses, heart pain, anemia, malabsorption syndrome, edema, hemorrhoids, and chronic rhinitis.

In those with weak digestion, it causes indigestion, worms, lassitude, prolapse of the rectum, and delusion; likewise, from that [injury], there arises blood-born enlargement (kṣataja-vṛddhi) accompanied by burning, pain, belching, vomiting, and the discharge of pus-like phlegm with a foul and extremely putrid odor. There, phlegm resembling blood falls repeatedly, as if expectorated; one suffers from bloody diarrhea, exhaustion, and emaciation of the body. Blood-born [tumors] spread through the limbs, and when located in the liver or chest, they cause dyspnea, thirst, vomiting, delusion, and swelling of the hands and feet.

One should abandon cases of loss of appetite, diarrhea, and enlargement of the liver (yakṛddura). Hereafter, I shall describe the medicine by which well-being is attained: first, fasting alone, and immediately after that, digestive therapy (pācana). A decoction or paste of dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), black pepper (upakulyā), *timira*, *śaṭhī*, *yavānikā*, *abhīru*, and *harītakī* is recommended for digestion and for those suffering from flatulence, abdominal tumors (gulma), pain, and cholera-like cramps (viṣūcikā). *Bhadra*, black pepper (*upakulyā*), *abhayā*, and fresh ginger (*śṛṅgavera*)—with *pathyā* being three parts and long pepper (*kaṇā*) the fourth part—[cures] wasting due to chest wounds and disorders of the liver.

One should not prescribe fasting or digestive (pācana) treatments; rather, a powder combined with asafoetida (hiṅgu) is beneficial for that patient. (24) A decoction of nimba, nīpa, dhava, vetasa, niśā, kāśmarī, tulasī, and siṃhikā quickly removes heart disease, alleviates colic, and destroys liver disorders. (25) A decoction of saurāṣṭrī, sīsa, mahauṣadha, durālabhā, jāti, pravālaka, dārvī, yavānī, kakubha, and samaṅgā, taken with ghee, quickly destroys liver disease. (26) [The same applies to] a decoction of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, śirīṣa, and badarī.

Having boiled [these], this drink destroys undigested matter (*āma*), checks cholera (*viṣūcī*), and wards off colic. (27) Taking either the alkali of plantain (*kadalī*) or the alkali of conch shell (*śaṅkha*), one should strain it and drink it with *hiṅgu* and *sauvarcala* salt. (28) This removes undigested matter when it has been expelled, quickly subdues colic, pacifies cholera, and even digests indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). (29) One should take the juice of citron (*mātuluṅga*) mixed with twice as much fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), along with *hiṅgu* and *sauvarcala*; this drink destroys cholera. (30) Alkali and water should be given for drinking over a burning sensation.

It cures colic and flatulence, quickly destroys them, and stimulates the digestive fire (31). In cases of undigested matter (*āma*), one should administer emetics; once it has been digested, fasting (*laṅghana*) is prescribed. Specific sudation is for sleeplessness, and purgation is for residual chyle (32). In insanity, diarrhea, those afflicted by vomiting or anger, indigestion, and cholera-like illness (*viṣūcikā*), sleeping during the day is beneficial (33). However, it is not beneficial in cases of *kapha*, heart disease, headache, nausea, and coryza; one should avoid sleeping during the day in these conditions (34). [The group of] three fruits (*phalatraya*).

A wick made from the seeds of *tryūṣa* and *karañja*, the juice of pomegranate and citron, and turmeric (*niśā*), ground together and applied as an ointment, destroys *viṣūcikā*. (35) *Rāsnā*, *viśālā*, fragrant *kuṣṭha*, *śigru*, *vacā*, ginger (*nāgaraka*), *śatāhvā*, *āgneyī*, *ahapuṣā*, and *vidārī*, when ground together, ward off *khallī* and *viṣūcī*. (36) Fomentation (*sveda*) should be administered to the patient using the steam from a single pot covered with cloth and heated; likewise, pouring warm water over the hands [of the patient] will thus conquer *viṣūcī* and abdominal diseases.

The patient should quickly consume sulphur, rock salt, and the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper) rubbed with lime juice; this is a swift remedy for the prevention of choleraic dysentery (*viṣūcī*). Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gulma," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Five. Ātreya said: Worms are said to be of two kinds, arising externally and internally; the external ones are well known as lice (*yūkā*), and the internal ones are the *kiñcaka*s. (1) The external type is of seven varieties, while that arising internally is of six varieties. I shall describe their origin among humans, both external and internal. (2) Indeed, due to dryness, excessive impurity, perspiration, anxiety, and even grief, sharp lice (*yūkā*) arise from the predominance of the *kapha* constituent. (3) These lice are black, others are [reddish], and the third kind is white.

The *carma-bhā* is situated on the skin; it is subtle, extremely formidable, rough, and a louse of the skin (*carma-yūkikā*). The fourth is named *bindukī*, which is round and originates from urine. The fifth is the *matkuṇa* (bedbug), which causes external afflictions. The louse (*yūkā*) resides in the region of the head and dwells upon the head; the *carma-yūkā* is on the skin of the eyes, while the *yaṣṭikā* is on the fine hair. [These are caused] by dry food, barley-meal, wheat-flour, or molasses; by the absence of milk, by sleeping during the day, by being slimy, by heat, and by the use of heated water.

By that [process], a swarm of worms is generated within the receptacles of impurity, causing disorders in the digestive tract (koṣṭha). They are declared to be of six types; I shall describe their characteristics. The receptacle of phlegm (kapha) is the reservoir of impurities; they crawl within the digestive tract like snakes. Some have broad heads, some resemble sheaths, some resemble grain-sprouts, and others are minute and atomic. They should be known as "needle-mouthed" (sūcīmukha), for they cause the intestines to waste away. I shall describe their symptoms and their treatment; listen to me. [Symptom: Fever...

Heart disease, piercing pain, vomiting, moisture in the heart region, vertigo, loss of appetite, discoloration, and frothy diarrhea occur; 12. as well as rumbling in the abdomen, weak digestion, thirst, and yellowness of the eyes in one afflicted by *kiñcuka* [poison]. 13. The intestines are pricked as if by needles, and blood is discharged in diarrhea; others vomit excessively, as if eating liver or blood. 14. Moisture in the mouth, lack of appetite, numbness, weak digestion, trembling, hunger, thirst, and fever are to be recognized [as symptoms].

I shall now describe the symptoms of the *sūcīmukha* worms and those that reside in the sprouts of grain. The worms situated in the receptacle of waste (*malāśaya*) devour the waste excessively; by them, the body is afflicted with emaciation, various types of abscesses, roughness, pain in the limbs, and moisture in the heart—these are known as the *yavakrimis*. Hārīta, overcome with doubt, clasped his feet and asked: "How do these arise within the body of a human being, in the receptacles of waste, urine, and chyle? And how do they first come into existence?"

How do they increase? Furthermore, how is it that when the essence of food is decayed or when various foods are consumed, minute worms arise—even those that move downwards? And how is it that the fire does not burn the various uncooked foods and meals? Why is it that those worms are not burned at the end by the internal fire? Thus questioned, the Great Teacher, the bull among sages, spoke. Ātreya said: Listen, O mighty-armed son, to the cause of the origin of worms; O son, [it arises] from blood [corrupted] by incompatible food essences.

Furthermore, it becomes aggravated by phlegm for one day, and by semen it proceeds to its cause; though born within this body composed of the five elements, they remain endowed with consciousness. (22–23) Just as a worm born in poison does not meet death by that poison, so too that which is produced from fire is not digested by fire. (24–25) I shall now declare the medicine by which even those [afflictions] are indeed overcome; listen to me regarding the medicines by which they fall away or attain pacification. (26)

Vacā, ajamodā, krimijit, palāśa seeds, śaṭhī, rāmaṭha, and trivṛt should be ground together with warm water and drunk; then the worms fall away quickly by the hundreds. (27) Śaṭhī, yavānī, picumanda, putrajīvaka, viḍaṅga, kṛṣṇā, and ativiṣā—these juices should be ground with urine and administered with trivṛt; this is the destroyer of all worm-related diseases. (28) Marica, pippalīmūla, viḍaṅga, śigru, yavānikā, and trivṛt should be ground with cow's urine and drunk; this quickly kills the worms. (29)

A paste of mustā, viśālā, triphalā, suparṇī, śigru, and surāhva, taken with water along with the powder of kṛṣṇā and krimiśatru, destroys all types of worms and their diseases. (30) Surasā, suradāru, māgadhī, viḍaṅga, kampilla, viḍaṅga, dantinī, trivṛt, tāḍaka, and rasonaka, when consumed with water, remove worms and heart disease. (31) One should grind the roots of mātuluṅga, rasona, krimijit, trivṛt, ajamodā, and nimba leaves with cow’s urine; this drink is highly recommended. (32)

One should administer the wholesome remedies prescribed for fever to ward off the disorder of worms (krimidoṣa). Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Worms," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Sixth Chapter. Ātreya said: Fire is declared to be of four types: balanced (*sama*), irregular (*viṣama*), sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), and another which is called dull (*manda*). Now listen to their characteristics. Due to the equilibrium of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha*, the digestive fire (*anala*) becomes balanced (*sama*). When these same factors reach a state of imbalance, the fire becomes irregular (*viṣama*). The gastric fire (*jaṭharāgni*) becomes sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) due to the predominance of *pitta*. It becomes known as dull (*manda*) due to the predominance of *vāta* and *kapha*. That which digests the mass of food while it remains in its natural state [is the balanced fire].

The *sama* (balanced) fire is indeed faultless and increases all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). It sometimes digests food and sometimes leaves it undigested; it does not cause irregularity, nor does it produce cholera (*viṣūcikā*). By its very nature, it bathes [the body] excessively, yet one does not obtain satisfaction from it. There is always a burning sensation and yellowness in the eyes; such is the sharp (*tīkṣṇa*) fire, which causes depletion of strength. That which is unable to digest even what is eaten due to the predominance of phlegm (*śleṣman*) is called the dull fire (*mandānala*), and it is considered to be primarily responsible for abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and enlargement of the abdomen (*udara*). Through the *sama* fire, equilibrium is maintained in the body.

A man whose body, elements, strength, and senses are delighted, and whose limbs are fully developed, remains active. (8) Due to irregular [digestion], wind and the other humors become disturbed, as do *grahaṇī*, diarrhea, splenic enlargement, abdominal tumors, cholera, and that which is known as colic and upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*). (9) Obstipation and sluggishness of movement arise from irregular digestive fire; both wind and phlegm are diminished, while the bile becomes intense. (10) He finds pleasure in food, and even after eating, it is digested; by this, the gastric fire comes to be known as *bhasmaka* (the "ash-maker"). (11) [The patient becomes] pale.

Bile-induced diarrhea, consumption (rājayakṣmā), jaundice (halīmaka), vertigo, exhaustion, extreme debility, as well as liver disease and urinary disorders; 12. colic, fainting, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), bilious acidity, and dysuria—by these the body is wasted away and a craving for food arises. 13. Even wood and stones, when consumed, are digested by that person's body. Thus has been stated the etiology of the provocation of the digestive fire (agni) in a man. 14. Although it could be described in many ways, it is not spoken of here for fear of excessive length. 15. Therefore, I shall speak of it in brief.

Medicines are of various kinds: digestive (pācana), pacifying (śamana), and likewise stimulant (dīpana). Rāsnā, śaṭhī, prativiṣā, surasā, śuṇṭhī, rock salt (sindhūttha), asafoetida (hiṅgu), long pepper (magadhā), and suvarcala—this powder, when consumed with jaggery as a sweetmeat (modaka) or as a food item, balances the irregular digestive fire caused by vāta. It serves to destroy colic, indigestion, irregular digestion, cholera-like disorders (viṣūcikā), and all types of abdominal tumors (gulma) arising from vāta and other humors. It is best to drink this well-warmed decoction after a meal. Furthermore, it is excellent for use thereafter.

To be enjoyed for all tastes: grapes, *abhayā*, bitter *rohiṇī*, *vidārikā*, sandalwood, *vāsaka*, *mustā*, *paṭola*, and *kirātatiktaka*; *kṛṣṇā*, *balā*, *vikacā*, and *viṣāṇā* (19); *palāla*, *vaṅgā*, *lasa*, and *padmaka*; and *bhṛṅgī* and *dhanikā* should be combined in equal parts. This powder, mixed with dates and sugar, along with an amount of ghee equal to half its weight (20), should be consumed by a person in the morning with milk; or, having decocted it, a drink with ghee should be administered. It produces a digestive fire equal to a fierce flame.

This indeed surely bestows nourishment upon the emaciated; it destroys fatigue, dizziness, and wasting, and pacifies excessive thirst and greed. Blood-bile disorders, consumption, anemia, chlorosis, and jaundice are quickly destroyed. For the wise, two parts of red *śāli* rice, having roasted sesame seeds and crushed them, one should mix them with half that amount [of rice]. Having roasted an equal portion of mung beans and combined them all together, one should properly cook this *kṛśarā* with ghee.

One should feed [the patient]. For one who eats with a day’s interval between meals, even if he possesses a sharp digestive fire, that fire may perish. Harītakī is sixfold the measure of Hari and Hara (i.e., mercury and sulfur), and twenty-four large pippalīs are fourfold [that]. Combined with asafoetida and rock salt, this elixir kindles the digestive fire of King Kuru. Having increased the portions progressively, one should employ a powder of dīpyaka, agni, harītakī, and viḍaṅga. Likewise, add very sour vetra, kola, pomegranate, and tamarind. These ingredients should be equal in measure, each weighing one karṣa.

In one *karṣa* of the other ingredients, there should be *jājī*, *varāṅga*, and *suvarcala*; one hundred *kaṇās* (long pepper), half that amount of black pepper (*marica*), and four *palas* of sugar. Having ground these together into a fine powder, one should consume it to clear abdominal diseases. This preparation creates an appetite and overcomes constipation, as well as splenic pain and cough. It destroys asthma, cures heart disease, purifies disorders of the tongue and throat, and serves as a digestive stimulant for those with chronic diarrhea, hemorrhoids, and weak digestion.

The preparation known as *yavānikākhaṇḍavikā* is highly praised for alleviating anorexia (31). A gruel made from the five spices (*pañcakola*), or *kulattha*, *āḍhakī*, and *pūṣaka*, or a meal with well-prepared rice accompanied by mung-bean soup, is beneficial (32). A side dish enriched with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*) is recommended; indeed, like *agastighṛta*, it is excellent even for those suffering from a loss of appetite for food (33). *Kāravella*, *paṭola*, onion, *sūraṇa*, *śaṭhī*, salt, coriander, and a thickened electuary (*praleha*) of the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*) are also excellent (34). *Śaṭhī*.

Mustard greens, *vāstuka*, *śatapuṣpā*, *kāñcanamācikā*, and the leafy vegetables of the roots of *tuṇḍīraka* are praised as the best. (35) Wheat cakes fried over glowing coals are excellent for loss of appetite; the best of physicians should also serve the meat of wild animals. (36) Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Weak Digestive Fire," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Seven. Ātreya said: Through physical exertion, suppression of natural urges, staying awake at night, sexual intercourse, grief, excessive carrying of loads, walking, running, and fatigue; through irregular drinking and sleeping, and by eating cold food, the Vāyu becomes aggravated and increases its strength. (1) Furthermore, by the consumption of indigestible, dry, barley, black gram, horse gram, green gram, flat beans, *kodrava*, *masūra*, wheat, and small, dry, phlegm-increasing foods; and by this drinking that obstructs the channels of waste and the retention of urine, (2) the Vāyu, having ascended the downward path, invades the root [of the rectum].

One becomes dominated by *vāta* (wind) and possesses an internal fire; therefore, when provoked by its own intensity, it causes pain in the forearm and even when the passage of the rectum is obstructed. O high-minded one, for a person afflicted by the suffering of *vāta*, there shall be a constant tingling in the limbs, accompanied by a state of extreme filth and wretchedness. Through the causes of anger, exposure to heat, and the consumption of fire-like substances, as well as grief, fear, distress, running, and physical exertion; and by means of alkaline, sour, alcoholic, pungent, hot, burning, and dry foods, along with *sauvīra* vinegar, dried meat, scratching, and black mustard—thus incited, the *vāyu* (wind) becomes greatly agitated.

That *pitta* causes intense colic (*śūla*) in the abdomen of the person; by it, the humors burn within the navel, causing burning of the limbs, loss of appetite, heat, thirst, affliction, and fainting, and the mouth becomes yellowish. (6) By lack of exercise, by consuming ununctuous things, by eating greedily, by [excessive] intake of sugarcane juice, oil, and milk, by eating little food, and by sleeping—by the practice of these factors, one aggravates *śleṣman*. (7) But *śleṣman*, when excessively consumed with black gram (*māṣa*), very cold milk and curd, very cold fish, and the flesh of marshy animals, quickly and thoroughly pacifies the digestive fire (*anala*).

It causes a sharp pain (śūla) in the abdomen and produces a severe disorder in the person. There is nausea, cough, loss of appetite, heaviness of the head, a sense of numbness or coldness, and a feeling of coldness in the body; there is a constriction in the waist, excessive salivation after eating, a sweet taste in the mouth, and the face becomes pleasant-looking and oily—this is the type caused by phlegm (kapha). When phlegm indeed exists and these symptoms are present, that person suffers from colic (sa-śūla); when the signs are like those of bile (pitta), men call that "colic even in indigestion" (ajīrṇe'pi sa-śūla). [This occurs] in the heart, throat, and flanks.

Kapha and Pitta [combined] cause pain in the region between the heart and the navel; when located in the bladder, the navel, and the region of the rectum, it moves restlessly due to Vāta and Pitta. (11) Even this single [type] is easily curable, while the dual-type (dvandvaja) is cured with difficulty; however, that born from all three doṣas (tridoṣaja) is incurable and accompanied by many complications. (12) Aggravated by etiological factors (nidāna), the Vāyu moves within the abdomen; because of this, it is known as "colic" (śūla), and ten types of it are proclaimed. (13) Three are to be known as originating from Vāta and the others [individually], while there are another three born from combinations of two.

These two, sāma and nirāma, along with the eight types of *śūla*, are thus remembered; indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) is declared the ninth, and that which arises from transformation (*pariṇāmaja*) is the tenth. In this way, *śūla* occurs in ten forms in human beings. That which occurs after eating should be known as being of the nature of *kapha*; and that which occurs when food is digested should be known as *pariṇāmaja*. Distension, upward movement of wind, constipation, yawning, trembling, shivering, eructation, an oily mouth, and excessive salivation—by these, one suffers *śūla* caused by *vāta*.

One who knows the procedure [states]: burning sensation, delusion, thirst, difficulty in urination, a bitter taste in the mouth, excessive perspiration, and a yellow face—the wise declare this to be of the nature of *pitta*. Vomiting, cough, dyspnea, delusion, laziness, drowsiness, stupor, and extreme coldness—O best of physicians, that colic (*śūla*) arising from these is known as being born of the dual combination (*dvandvaja*), while that which arises from all three *doṣas* is called *tridoṣaja*; thus, eleven types including those of the *pitta* nature have been described.

The symptoms that manifest include vomiting of blood (20), as well as emaciation, thirst, burning sensations, cough, dyspnea, and severe pain arising from blood (21). There is no colic without Vāta, no vertigo without Pitta, no vomiting without Kapha, and no darkness [of vision] without blood (22). This concludes the diagnosis of colic; hereafter I shall describe the remedy by which the patient afflicted by colic attains ease through the pacification of the pain (23). Upon observing the colic, one should administer fasting, digestive remedies, and purgation.

For the alleviation of colic, one should administer emetics, sudation, alkali, or powders; these are beneficial for drinking, massage, and enemas in a person suffering from cough and flatulence. (24) A decoction of hiṅgu, nāgara, śaṭhī, suvarcala, dāru, pauṣkara, ghana, and apunarnavā is beneficial for those with colic, acting as a digestive aid for those suffering from abdominal enlargement and gulma. (25) Likewise, a decoction of hiṅgu, pauṣkara, śaṭhī, and suvarcala is beneficial for those with colic; it is praised for pacifying vāta-type colic and is declared to be a digestive stimulant. (26) [Also beneficial are] rock salt, hiṅgu, and rucaka.

A powder made from equal parts of *śaṭhī*, *yavānī*, *pathyā*, and *yavakṣāra*, when administered with lukewarm water, destroys colic of a vāta nature, or even general pain, in no time at all. (27) *Hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, *punarnavā*, *balā*, *eraṇḍa*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *tuvara*, and *tryūṣaṇa*—this decoction, or likewise this powder combined with *kṣāra* and *sauvarcala*, instantly destroys colic of a vāta nature and instantly [cures] *viṣūcikā*. (28–29) Or, [one may take] *tumburu*, *pauṣkara*, *hiṅgu*, *yavānī*, and *tryūṣaṇa* in three times the quantity of *trivṛt*.

This powder of the eight salts (lavaṇāṣṭaka-cūrṇa) is properly effective for warding off colic. A decoction [of these] destroys the multitude of colics arising from Vāta. 30 Hiṅgu combined with eraṇḍa, nāgara, suvarcalā, and rāmaṭha, along with pathyā, vacā, indrayava, and water of nāgara, as well as hiṅgu joined with suvarcalā, indeed destroys colic. 31 Hiṅgu, nāgara, ṣaḍgranthā, yavānī, both types of ubhayā, trivṛt, viḍaṅga, dāru, cavya, tumburu, kuṣṭha, mustaka, 32 hapuṣā, kalaśī, rāsnā, vatsaka, durālabhā, and sitāravī—[these constitute the formulation].

One should mix together two parts each of *bṛhatī*, *lāṅgalī*, the five types of *jīraka*, *puṣkara*, *tintiḍīka*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlavetasa*, along with the two alkalis (*kṣāra*) and the five salts (*pañcalavaṇa*). Having given it one saturation (*bhāvanā*) with urine and dried it in the shade, one should then saturate it for three days with the juice of *bījapūraka*. One should administer a dose the size of a cat’s paw (*biḍālapadikā*) for the alleviation of colic (*śūla*); when combined with hot water and white sugar, it is used for disorders of Vāta. A decoction of *triphalā* taken with wine is recommended for diseases of Kapha.

It destroys colic, abdominal distension, constipation, weak digestion, abdominal tumors (gulma), abscesses (vidradhi), splenic enlargement, and especially jaundice and fever; it scatters the mass of the body just as the wind disperses a multitude of clouds. (37-38) Amalaki fruit, iron powder, harītakī, and the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa)—having impregnated these in equal parts with the juice of pomegranate or citron—one should administer this powder enriched with sugar for bile-type colic. (39) One should prepare a powder consisting of biḍālaka, pomegranate, pūtanā, and amalaki, along with the juice of citron.

One should consume this prepared [mixture] to pacify bile-related colic (40). One should drink *jīvantī* and other [herbs] with ghee, or milk mixed with sugar; purgation should be administered daily to ward off bile colic (41). For the cause of bile-rooted [fever], one should follow this method: bathing in cool water, applying sandalwood paste to the center of a clean cloth, sleeping at night on a bed made of gold, silver, bell-metal, lotus leaves, or gold, and using ice (42). [One should also take] parched rice from white *śāli* paddy, along with sugar, honey, and milk, to alleviate the burning sensation.

It instantly destroys fever caused by *pitta*, vomiting, and colic. (43) Wild meats are recommended for food; likewise, ghee and milk mixed with sweet substances are praised for those suffering from *pitta*-type colic. (44) For those suffering from *kapha*-type colic, fasting, emesis, and digestive remedies are prescribed; however, thick or excessively sweet foods and sleeping [during the day] should be avoided. (45) A decoction made from equal parts of *bilva*, *agnimantha*, *vṛṣa*, *citraka*, *nāgara*, *eraṇḍa*, *hiṅgu*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) instantly destroys colic arising from *kapha*.

It instantly destroys [the pain] and increases the digestive fire (46). The juice of *mātuluṅga*, the juice of *dhātrī* combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), and the juice of the root of *śobhāñjanaka* mixed with black pepper (47), when combined with alkali and honey, wards off phlegmatic colic (*śleṣma-śūla*) and undoubtedly destroys cough arising from consumption (*kṣaya*). (48) A powder consisting of *tuvara*, *granthika*, *airaṇḍa*, the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), *pathyā*, and *ajamoda*, combined with alkali and salt, is used for colic caused by phlegm (*kaphātmake śūle*). (49) [Also used are] *eraṇḍa*, *bilva*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *mātuluṅga*.

A decoction made from *pāṣāṇabheda*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, and *mūlaka*, mixed with oil combined with alkali (*kṣāra*), vermilion (*hiṅgula*), and salt, should be applied to the hips, thighs, penis, heart, breasts, and abdomen. (50) The leaves of *paṭola* and *ariṣṭa* combined with *triphalā*, taken as a drink with honey and decoction, [is effective] against pain caused by *pitta* and *vāta*. (51) It wards off *pitta*-fever, thirst, burning sensations, and *raktapitta*. (52) This paste (*kalka*) consisting of *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *viśvā*, *paṭola*, *nimba*, *ambuda*, and *tintiḍīka*, should be administered with sugar.

For the pacification of colic arising from *pitta* and *vāta*: powder of *sauvarcala* salt together with *śaṭhī* and *nāgara* (ginger), drunk with water boiled with *śuṇṭhī*, destroys colic associated with *marut* (vāta) and *śleṣman* (kapha); it is highly recommended for severe pain in the flanks, abdominal ailments, impaired digestion, and heart disease. A decoction of *dāru* (devadāru), *nāgaraka* (ginger), *vāsā*, *hiṅgu*, and *sauvarcala* [salt] is effective against colic caused by *vāta* and *kapha*, as well as in cases of undigested matter (*āma*), indigestion (*jīrṇa*), and constipation (*vibandha*). Furthermore, *palāśa*, *kadalī*, *vāsā*, *apāmārga*, and *kokilāhvaya* (guñjā), boiled with cow's urine and combined with *hiṅgu* and *nāgara*, [is likewise beneficial].

56. It is beneficial for colic born of the three doṣas, for jaundice and constipation; it pacifies abdominal tumors and enlargements, and it restores the digestive fire in those with weak digestion. 57. Kubera-akṣa (Pippalī) alone removes all types of colic; how much more so when combined with Pathyā (Harītakī), Āruṣkara, and Amatha (Hingu)? 58. Conch-ash, salt, Hingu, and Vyōṣa (the three pungents), when drunk together with warm water, destroy colic born of the three doṣas. 59. Fasting, emesis, purgation, unctuous enema, and non-unctuous enema—these basti-procedures are indicated in cases of *pariṇāma* (digestive disorders).

In the case of a disorder arising from the three *doṣas* (60), the wise man should prepare boluses (*modaka*) with equal parts of powdered *citraka*, *trivṛtā*, *dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, and the "three pungents" (*kaṭukatraya*), mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*). One should eat them upon rising in the morning and afterwards drink hot water; this destroys the colic produced by the transformation of food (*pariṇāma-śūla*) and the colic of a person [caused by other factors] (61–62). *Yavānī*, *hiṅgu*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), alkali (*kṣāra*), *sauvarcala* salt, and *abhayā* should be drunk with wine from a liquor jar in cases of colic from the three *doṣas* during the transformation of food (63). [Also beneficial are: *hiṅgu*, the "three pungents" (*vyoṣa*), *vacā*, *ajamoda*, *hapuṣā*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, and *śaṭhī*.

Take *jājī*, *pippalīmūla*, pomegranate, *vṛkī*, *cavya*, *agni* (citraka), and *tintiḍī*; from that, add sour *suvarcalā*, as well as *yavakṣāra*, *sarjikā*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), and powdered *viḍa* salt in equal proportions. This should be prepared with the juice of *bījapūra*. One should make pills (*guṭī*) from this powder, each measuring one *māṣa*—the size of a *kṣava-phala*—or it may be used as a paste (*kalka*). When administered, it cures disorders of Vāta, colic (*śūla*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and splenic enlargement (*plīha*).

It quickly destroys cough, abdominal distension, urinary disorders, and pain in the heart. This formulation, known as Hiṅgvādika, is the destroyer of all types of colic and pain, the subduer of all vāta disorders, and the preventer of all wasting diseases (kṣaya). Diarrhea, thirst, fainting, constipation, heaviness, loss of appetite, dyspnea, cough, vomiting, and hiccups—these ten are the complications of colic. A physician desiring success should avoid treating colic when it is accompanied by complications and thirst; however, when free from complications, it is said that physicians may proceed with treatment for the sake of prosperity. One suffering from colic should likewise avoid pulses (dvidala).

One should avoid thick, cold, and slimy curd, as well as sleeping during the day. (69) O best of physicians, *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), fermented grain water (*sauvīraka*), liquor (*surā*), jaggery (*guḍa*), or ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) are excellent for drinking. (70) *Śatapuṣpā* and *vāstuka* greens are declared beneficial and are highly praised. (71) O best of physicians, the meats of the black buck (*eṇa*), partridge (*tittiri*), quail (*lāva*), crane (*krauñca*), hare (*śaśaka*), and *sārasa* crane are recommended. (72) Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Colic," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 7.

The Eighth Chapter. Ātreya said: Listen, my son, I shall explain the great disease of *pāṇḍuroga* (anemia/jaundice). There are five types of *pāṇḍuroga* that arise here among human beings: the *vātika*, the *paittika*, the *ślaiṣmika*, the *sānnipātika*, and the fifth is called *rūkṣaṇa*. I shall now describe their origin. A man who travels long distances, or is afflicted by fever, or is distressed by the loss of blood through wounds, or who indulges in anxiety, exhaustion, and suppression [of natural urges], becomes *pāṇḍu* (pale/anemic). [He who consumes] alkaline substances... [text continues].

Sour food, the consumption of *kalya* and *maireya* liquors, lack of physical exercise, excessive sexual indulgence, exhaustion, insufficient sleep, excessive sleep, daytime sleep, these practices, as well as the eating of clay, [lead to this condition]. (4) On the road, when the body is weakened or afflicted by disease, the consumption of salt, pungent, and astringent foods, sourness, clay, and the constant, excessive intake of very fragrant substances leads to the drying up of the blood; by that indeed comes jaundice (*pāṇḍuroga*). (5) By that, swelling occurs in the eye-sockets, yellowness spreads over the body, the urine becomes yellow, one spits, and the skin cracks.

For that person, premonitory symptoms arise: pricking pain, roughness, heaviness of the head, and yellowness of the skin, urine, eyes, and nails. Know that this wind-natured (vātika) jaundice in a human being is characterized by these signs. (6–7) Indeed, the jaundice born of bile (pittaja-pāṇḍu) produces a raw state and yellowness in the world; it brings about emaciation and a bitter taste in the mouth, as well as mild fever, thirst, delusion, and swelling, with a yellowish complexion. (8) In the case of kapha-born jaundice, one is drowsy and afflicted with swelling, phlegm, and cough; likewise, lassitude, perspiration, and heaviness arise for him. (9)

This disorder arising from paleness (pāṇḍu) in a person is of the nature of kapha; it is characterized by drowsiness, laziness, swelling, vomiting, cough, nausea, emaciation, loose stools, lassitude, rough eyes, fever, and a lack of appetite despite hunger.

When a person quickly exhibits delusion, thirst, and exhaustion, physicians of keen intellect should recognize that this is *pāṇḍu* arising from *sannipāta* and must be abandoned at a great distance. (10) Now hear, O son, regarding the great disease caused by eating clay: even though it is a most severe form of *pāṇḍu*, it brings about the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (11) By eating clay, the channels are obstructed with waste; thus, they are satisfied by the clay itself, yet they do not circulate the blood nor nourish the body with essence. (12) [This occurs] from drinking alkaline, astringent, or sweet substances... [he]... sa-... (text fragment)

The earth quickly provokes the wind (vāta) in a person; due to the provocation of phlegm (kapha), the earth becomes sweet. Earth that has not been consumed does not prove beneficial. Indeed, the three humors—wind and the others—are powerful when in a state of disorder; these defects quickly destroy luster, strength, and the hope for life.

In this way, the body becomes emaciated in *pāṇḍuroga* (anemia), and through the consumption of earth, it destroys the digestive fire (*jaṭharavahni*). (14) The wise man should place iron in cow’s urine for seven nights; from that, a powder should be administered with honey to remove the disease of *pāṇḍu*. (15) Take equal parts of the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *mustā*, *viḍaṅga*, and *citraka*. (16) Add one part of iron powder and macerate it with sugarcane juice for seven days; having been ground in a mortar, it shall again become excellent. (17) When consumed with honey, it [is effective].

This [preparation] with ghee is said by wise and learned men to remove anemia and heart disease, and to cure jaundice, hemorrhoids, and chlorosis. (18) One should combine these ingredients—tryūṣaṇa, triphalā, citraka, musta, cavya, suradāru, mākṣika, granthika, śikhī, and bhṛṅgarāja—in portions of one *pala* each. (19) One should add iron powder, which has the luster of collyrium, twice the amount of the powdered herbs; this should be cooked with eight parts of cow's urine and is indeed a bestower of strength. (20) One should employ this as a therapeutic procedure to restore strength.

Likewise, this excellent compound prepared there is present here; it destroys Kaphaja-Kāmala, worms, anemia (pāṇḍu), skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhoids (gudāja), and Halīmaka. (21) One should mix equal parts of Punarnavā, Vyōṣa, Trivṛt, Surāhvaya, Niśāhvaya, Cavya, the three fruits (Triphalā), Ghanā, Yava, and Tikta-Varōhiṇī, along with two parts of iron filings. Having added either double the quantity of cow's milk or water, the wise physician should apply a paste of Dārvī and allow it to dry in the shade; then, pills should be made with honey and cow's urine. (22)

One should administer this after ascertaining the strength of the patient and the severity of the disease—specifically for cases of *pāṇḍu* (anemia), jaundice, all types of urinary disorders (*meha*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), abdominal enlargement (*udara*), indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), cholera-like dysentery (*viṣūcikā*), edema, diarrhea, chronic diarrhea (*grahaṇī*), constipation, colic, worms, and the afflictions of hemorrhoids. Take one part each of the five spices (*pañcakola*), the three pungents (*kaṭutrika*), *ghanā*, *devadāru*, *kṛmiśatru* (viḍaṅga), and *kola* (jujube). Having separated these into equal portions, one should subsequently mix them with iron powder (*ayas-rajas*). Then, one should cook this in eight times the amount of urine until it becomes a paste; from this, one should prepare pills the size of a jujube fruit (*badara*).

Furthermore, one should cause the flesh to be cooked with *chāyā* (Citrullus colocynthis) and dried; then, with the churned juice of *surabhi*, one should prepare a drink that pacifies jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), diarrhea, loss of appetite, consumption (*śoṣa*), urinary disorders (*meha*), anal fistula (*gudaja*), and even worms. One should take one *prastha* of the juice of *dhātrī* (Emblica officinalis) fruits, one *prastha* of sugarcane juice, one *prastha* of the juice of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (Lagenaria siceraria), and one *prastha* of the juice of *arka* (Calatropis procera). Having combined these, they should be cooked over a mild fire until all defects have vanished.

One should mix this collection of medicinal herbs and subsequently boil it with a measure of one *pala*. Then, one should employ the powder of these [following ingredients]: *bhṛṅgī*, *surāhva* (tagara), *śatapuṣpa*, *dhānya*, fragrant *śuṇṭhī*, *madhuka*, *viśālā*, along with *pippalī* and the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), as well as *viḍaṅga*, *mustā*, *hapuṣā*, and *dalāni*; furthermore, a large quantity of *haridrā*, *kaṭurohiṇī*, *durālabhā*, *pauṣkara*, *vatsaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *ajamodā*, and *surasā-dalāni*. Into the middle of this, one should add double the amount of old jaggery and cow's ghee to form pills.

It obstructs [the channels] from eating [unwholesome food], and it conquers jaundice, hemorrhoids, anemia, and most dreadful fevers; it destroys swelling, wasting, and malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), as well as wind-disorders, diarrhea, consumption, cough, and abdominal tumors. Wheat, *śāli* rice, barley, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mung beans, black gram (*śyāmā*), and pigeon pea (*āḍhakī*), combined with ghee and milk, along with whey (*satakra*), *gāṇḍīva*, *vāstuka*, and *śatapuṣpā*—this regimen is declared beneficial and wholesome for a person suffering from anemia (*pāṇḍu*). Meats from wild animals (*jāṅgala*) are also recommended for the diet. Bitter, dry, and pungent substances [are likewise advised].

Strong alkaline preparations (*kāñjika*), fermented liquors, sour gruel (*surāmla*), *sauvīraka*, *bījapūra*, and oils should be avoided in cases of *pāṇḍu* disease. (36) Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Pāṇḍu* Disease," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Ninth Chapter. Ātreya said: Listen, O best of physicians, to this terrible disease that afflicts men who engage in improper activities and are of a windy (vātalā) temperament. This wasting away (kṣaya) of a human being, caused by the ripening of natural past actions, brings about long-term accumulation [of humors] and leads to humiliation in this world. It causes the ruin of the gods, or the destruction of the embryo, the torment of the earth, mountains, brahmins, and children, and the devastation of gardens.

That man who destroys the dwellings of others and commits the murder of women incurs, through these grave deeds, a great wasting disease that robs him of his body and wealth. Furthermore, one who burns the property of the gods, one who causes a miscarriage, one who steals the divinity [of the image], one who administers poison, and one who destroys a grove—all these suffer the same fate.

By that very rule, there arises for men indeed a sharp pain that causes the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), which is terrible, fatal to the person, and life-taking. (3) This depletion (*kṣaya*) should be understood by the best of physicians as being of ten kinds: [arising] from fatigue, or from heavy loads, or from sleeping on uneven ground, or from long journeys, or from eating when indigestion persists, or from devotion to excessive sexual indulgence. (4)

In those overcome by fever due to irregular postures, the phlegm (śleṣmā), wind (pavana), and bile (pitta) within the bodies go to destruction through excessive cooling treatments. Or, for one afflicted by disease due to irregular postures, or from that mild fever, the phlegm, bile, and wind, or the body itself, undergoes decay.

Chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—these seven, along with the [five] elements, are to be known as the ten types of depletion that occur in the bodies of men. (6) Furthermore, their symptoms will be described; listen to them from me. (7) Depletion of wind (*māruta-kṣaya*) arises from excessive sweating, extreme heat, anxiety, emaciation, fear, and the like, as well as by the aggravation of *vāta* and other humors. (8) Due to that depletion of wind, there occurs drowsiness, burning in the limbs, thirst, loss of appetite, trembling, darkness of vision, exhaustion, and vertigo. (9) Therefore, marshy regions (*anūpa*) should be resorted to.

One should consume juices, meat pastes, and the paste of garlic (*rasona*) and similar substances to destroy Vata. (10) When Pitta is diminished, there arises a dullness of the digestive fire (*agnimāndya*), as well as loss of appetite, heaviness, cough, nausea, swelling, and lethargy. (11) In such cases of Pitta depletion, one should employ sudation, massage, and appetizing foods and drinks; one should consume the meat-juices of wild animals (*jāṅgala*) and other Pitta-generating foods. (12) Through physical exercise, sexual indulgence, the consumption of dry foods, and likewise through heat and anger, the production of Kapha occurs. (13) By that [Kapha], there arises either a burning sensation or pallor.

Swelling, labored breathing, dizziness, insomnia, hunger, and thirst occur; yet he finds pleasure even in sexual union with women. (14) For him, the consumption of cold food and drinks, along with the juices of tubers and leafy vegetables, or the use of marshy meat, curd, and milk, is desired. (15) When the three *doṣas* have reached a state of depletion, death is indeed certain; therefore, O high-minded one, a general treatment should be applied for him. (16) Now, O Hārīta, listen as I describe the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*): chyle, blood, flesh, and fat—each one [in turn].

The symptoms of depletion (kṣayalakṣaṇa): 17. In the depletion of rasa (plasma), excessive emaciation, weak digestion, trembling, headache, sluggishness of movement, and fatigue and dizziness arise. 18. In the depletion of rakta (blood), a person becomes pale, weak in movement, suffers from dyspnea, spitting, dryness, and weak digestion. 19. In the depletion of māṃsa (muscle), there is extreme leanness, difficulty in moving, a sense of breaking in the limbs, loss of sleep or excessive sleep, unconsciousness, and lightness of gait. 20. In the depletion of medas (fat), one has diminished strength, unconsciousness, a sense of breaking in the limbs, and difficulty in walking.

Roughness, labored breathing, excessive coughing, loss of appetite, and weak digestion occur; by that [depletion] desiccation arises, and from that the body becomes emaciated. (21) In the depletion of bone, there is extreme sluggishness of movement and diminished vitality. In the depletion of fat, there is loss of consciousness, leanness, trembling, breaking pain in the limbs, vomiting, roughness, wasting of the humors, exhaustion, swelling, tremors, and emaciation and irritability arise, O best of physicians; you should know these as the signs. In the depletion of marrow, there is trembling alone, or perhaps vertigo, fatigue, extreme sluggishness of movement, and swelling. (22–23)

Staying awake at night, drowsiness, mild fever, and emaciation are the bodily symptoms in a person suffering from the loss of semen (śukrakṣaya). 24. Dryness, vertigo, trembling, wasting, anger, aversion toward women, deformity, physical impairment, and emaciation of the joints [are also present]. 25. Now I shall describe the medicines in their proper order; oleation, drying, and likewise depleting therapy are beneficial. 26. One should consume the meat of wild animals as food, as well as water boiled with *guḍūcī*, ginger, and *yavānī*.

Milk boiled with twenty-seven *marica* peppers is recommended for drinking at night; by this, there is an increase in the bodily fluids (*rasas*), and one is quickly liberated [from the disease]. (28) The best of physicians prescribe preparations of wheat, barley, and *śāli* rice, and especially the meat of wild animals, to increase the bodily fluids. (29) Ghee, milk, sugar, honey, black pepper, and long pepper—this drink is highly commended for humans as a supreme means of increasing the blood. (30) One should prepare light foods consisting of marshy grains and other such items that are easily digestible. (31ab)

One should consume ghee, milk, and other such items, as well as sweet substances (31). O best of physicians, the juices of wild animals should also be used for consumption (32). A powder made from white sugar and other ingredients, goat’s milk with jujube fruits, and drinking [these] at dawn before breakfast are beneficial in cases of wasting (kṣaya) (33). O best of physicians, various cooked milks praised for their ghee content, sandalwood, and powders of grapes and other fruits should be used (34). O son, all types of meat from wild animals should be consumed, and one should employ all kinds of sweet foods (35).

In cases of seminal depletion (*śukrakṣaya*), one should especially consume soups that are easily digestible, as well as fresh butter, milk, and sweet substances (verse 36). Drinking the root of *karkaṭī* with milk, along with *vidārī* tuber, *śālmalī*, and sugar, is beneficial; sweet substances are likewise recommended (verse 37). Now, powders (*cūrṇa*) that cause the increase of semen will be described (verse 38). Equal parts of *balā*, *vidārī*, the minor five roots (*laghupañcamūlī*), the barks of the five milky trees (*pañcakṣīradruma*), *punarnavā*, *megha*, and *tugā*, combined with the *sañjīvanīya* group and *madhuka*, should be employed (verse 39).

All these [substances] should be ground to the same measure as the seeds (*akṣa*) and mixed together; one hundred grains of *kaṇā* (long pepper) should be added there. Having ground barley, wheat, and barley-meal, they should be combined with an equal portion of *tugākṣīrī* and white rice. This should be mixed with *subhṛṅgāraka* and prepared until it reaches the consistency of thick gruel (*prākarṇaka*); sugar should be used in an amount equal to all the other ingredients. It should be processed three times with the juice of *āmalakī*, then processed with cow’s milk; thereafter, it should again be processed with all the aforementioned ingredients along with sugar and clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

One should consume half a *pala* of that [preparation] mixed with honey; once it has been digested, one should eat food avoiding pungent and sour tastes. Milk, ghee, white sugar, or foods made of barley, wheat, and *śāli* rice should be taken. 43 Knowing the digestive fire within the person's stomach, those who know the procedure should administer this for the pacification of consumption (*kṣaya*), as well as for those exhausted by the loss of wholesome food, those long afflicted by heat, those suffering from headaches, 44 those afflicted by bile (*pitta*), those with loss of blood, those oppressed by fatigue from travel, those with jaundice, and those suffering from asthma.

This is beneficial for those suffering from diabetes (madhumeha) and for those with impaired senses, as it bestows strength. Furthermore, for a woman who has conceived, this powder of *balā* and other herbs is highly recommended. Thus ends the *Balādi-cūrṇa*. *Bilva*, *agnimantha*, *śoṇāka*, *kāśmarī*, *pāṭalī*, *śāliparṇī*, *pṛśniparṇī*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *bhṛṅgī*, *śītā*, *āmalakī*, *jayantī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *drākṣā*, *abhayā*, *amṛtā*, *medā*, *candana*, *aguru*, *padmaka*, and the two types of *balā*—these are the ingredients. (45–48)

The physician, the best among healers, should employ one *pala* each of both Jīvaka and Ṛṣabha, Kākolī, Kṣīrakākolī, and the fleshy root-tuber of Vidārī (verse 49). He should take five hundred well-ripened Dhātrī fruits along with their juice (verse 50) and boil them in one *droṇa* of water until reduced to a quarter part; having thus decocted them, the wise man should extract the medicinal pastes (*kalka*) (verse 51). He should then thicken that decoction by adding the paste until it reaches the consistency of a coating on the ladle (*darvīpralepaka*); finally, having cooked the Āmalakī fruits again with oil and clarified butter (verse 52), [he should prepare the medicine].

The best of physicians should cook all these [medicinal substances] until they are powdered, then mix them with an equal amount of sugar and four *pala* of *tugākṣīrī*. (53) The most excellent practitioner should add one thousand *pippalī* fruits, as well as two *pala* each of cinnamon (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), and cinnamon leaves (*patraka*). (54) He should incorporate all these powders into the previously described linctus; this elixir (*rasāyana*) for men should be licked with care in equal portions. (55) It dries up asthma, cough, consumption (*kṣaya*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*), and is beneficial for those emaciated by disease, the wounded, children, and the elderly.

It protects the body (56); it removes hoarseness of voice, thirst, heart disease, bile-blood disorders, defects of semen, severe headaches, and chronic catarrh (57). It destroys chronic fever, weak digestion, skin diseases, malignant fistula-in-ano, urinary disorders, painful micturition, and stones; likewise, it acts as a digestive stimulant and an aphrodisiac (58). It undoubtedly eliminates heart disease, colic, and abdominal distension; it brings about the birth of sons for barren women, and restores vigor to the aged and those with diminished semen (59). Even a eunuch becomes a supreme, ever-fertile man, possessing intelligence and memory.

In this way, it certainly and swiftly increases one's vitality (*tejas*); it bestows happiness and good fortune, and even an old man becomes like a youth. This great remedy, named *Cyavanaprāśana*, spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya for the destruction of the disease of consumption (*kṣaya*), has been described by Atri. Thus ends the electuary (*avaleha*) named *Cyavanaprāśana*. Bhārgī, Puṣkaramūla, Citraka, Kaṇāmūla, Gajāhvā, Śaṭhī, Śaṅkhāhvā, Daśamūla, Citraka, Balā, Yāsā, and likewise Ātmaguptā;

The best of physicians has prescribed two palas of these [drugs] for five āḍhakas of *pathyā* (harītakī); having boiled one hundred *pathyās* thoroughly with a mild fire, [the decoction] should be cooled down. Then, having extracted the purified liquid and removed the hundred *pathyās*, once it has become very cold, this excellent decoction of the noble house is recommended.

Having added one *tulā* of aged jaggery (*guḍa*) and one *kuḍava* of honey, along with half that amount of ghee as oil, one should add five hundred and ten *akṣas* of *magadhā* (long pepper). One should place the powder therein and stir it vigorously once more. Taken with two pieces of parched grain (*pathyā*) and honey, this is highly beneficial and a destroyer of all diseases.

It destroys yellowish discoloration, *kāsaha*, *līmakā*, anal diseases, heart disease, hiccup, vertigo, catarrh, urinary disorders, hemorrhagic conditions, leprosy, and malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*). It expands the [menstrual] flow and alleviates swelling, wind-disorders, abdominal tumors, pain, consumption, urinary disorders, flatulence, and obstructive diseases; it is beneficial for those with impaired senses.

The *Abhayā* (Harītakī) prepared by Agasti, which is equal to the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*), pacifies weak digestion, cures loss of appetite, or brings about its destruction while bestowing bodily comfort. (66) A decoction of *Balā*, *Gokṣuraka*, and the two types of *Bṛhatī*, combined with *Kaṇā* (Pippalī), milk, honey, and plenty of sugar, is beneficial when drunk; it destroys jaundice or consumption (*kṣaya*).

It destroys the underlying cause of thirst in cases of urinary disorders (meha) and bestows strength upon those with impaired senses. (67) One should prepare *pippalī* in increasing doses with milk and ghee, starting with five, then seven, and then nine in succession. (68) Eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen, nineteen, and twenty-one are prescribed individually according to the sequence. (69) In this manner, the increase should proceed until the dose reaches one hundred; thereafter, it should be decreased gradually back down to the original five.

One should feed [the patient] sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭikānna) combined with mung beans and clarified butter; thus, both the young and the old man shall possess the strength of an elephant. The increasing dose of long pepper (pippalī-vardhamāna) is recommended when fever has subsided, as well as for weak digestion (mandāgni), jaundice (pāṇḍu), and hemorrhoids (gudaja). Thus ends the Pippalī-vardhamāna. Two palas each of bhṛṅgarāja (mārkava), dhātuprasādana (dhātu), honey (mākṣika), punarnavā, tugākṣīrī, pṛkkā, śāliparṇī, vāsaka, and yavāsa (durālabhā) should be taken. These should be combined with an amount of powder equal to half of that total, along with the three aromatics (trigandha) and black peppers (marica).

Take forty parts of *magadhā* (iron sulfate) and half that amount of *śilodbhava* (bitumen); add half that amount of *śilābheda* (mica), and mix all these together in equal proportions with sesame powder and sugar. One should consume this with milk or, preferably, with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). By this, consumption (*kṣaya*), pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), and jaundice (*kāmalā*) are destroyed. It quickly overcomes epilepsy (*apasmāra*), increases strength and virility, pacifies great diseases, and causes a man to become rich in semen. Thus ends the section on the powder of *śilājatu*.

Take *jīvantikā*, *vatsaka*, *yaṣṭikā*, *pauṣkara*, *gokṣuraka*, the two types of *bala*, blue water-lily (*nīlotpala*), *āmalakī*, *yavāsa*, *trāyamāṇā*, *magadhā*, and *kuṣṭha*. (78) One *prastha* of the juice of *drākṣā* and *āmalakī*, two *prasthas* of goat’s milk, and one *prastha* of curd—cook ghee with these over a fire. This is highly recommended for consumption in cases of *vahni-vāta* (fire-wind), as well as for use as nasal drops (*nasya*) and enemas (*basti*). By its application, *rājayakṣmā*, *halīmaka*, jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), and fainting (*mūrchā*) are quickly destroyed. (79)

Dizziness, trembling, headache, and colic (80), as well as large stones, hemorrhoids, and leprosy—any disease located in the head—is destroyed by its administration; likewise, jaundice and consumption (rājayakṣmā) (81) reach destruction and pacification through its drinking; anemia or diseases arising from the rectum are eliminated in men by its application as an enema (basti); and erysipelas and boils are cured by sprinkling it (82). One should cook equal parts of long pepper (kaṇā), palāśa, five times the amount of milk, and ghee as the first ingredient, to be used either for drinking or with food.

This excellent medicine should be given for the purpose of destroying the king's consumption (83). One part each of *pañcakola*, the tip of barley, milk, curd, and ghee, along with equal portions of *bhārṅgī*, *kuṣṭha*, and *pauṣkara* (84), and one hundred *harītakī* fruits, should be combined with four times as much water. One should prepare a decoction by boiling these three together over a gentle fire (85). This ghee, prepared by gentle cooking, is effective when used for drinking, as nasal drops (*nasya*), or in enemas (*basti*); it brings about great benefit for men suffering from anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), jaundice (*halīmaka*), (86) pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*), and wasting (*kṣaya*).

And this is indeed praised and declared by the best of physicians (87). Equal parts of liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), *balā*, *guḍūcī*, and the five roots (*pañcamūla*) are boiled; the juice of *dhātrī* and sugarcane juice should be equal to the decoction (88). The juice of *vidārī* and ghee should each be an equal portion, along with milk equal to the [other] liquids, and fresh butter (*navanīta*) equal to that (89). One should add grapes (*drākṣā*) and *tālīsa* as available. This prepared ghee should be administered for drinking, as nasal drops (*nasya*), or via enema (*basti*) (90). It conquers consumption (*rājayakṣmāṇa*) and anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).

It is a most potent remedy for *halīmaka*, hemorrhoids, and the suppression of *raktapitta* (91). When used as an external paste, it removes malignant erysipelas (*duṣṭavaisarpa*), Pitta-related disorders, and burns on wounds (92). Take *balā*, *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, the two types of *parṇī*, *gokṣuraka*, *sthirā*, the leaves of *paṭola* and *nimba*, *musta*, *trāyamāṇā*, and *durālabhā* (93). Having prepared a decoction from these and reduced it to its remaining essence, one should add this powder once it has been strained: *drākṣā*, *śaṭhī*, *puṣkaramūla*, *dhātrī*, and *tamālakī*. This decoction should be taken with an equal amount of milk (94).

Fresh butter (navanītaka) mixed with ghee should be administered; that ghee should be used at half the [usual] dose. This prepared ghee is for drinking, as well as for enemas, nasal drops, massage, and food. (95) It is recommended for chronic cough, consumption, jaundice, and for those whose strength and senses have wasted away due to royal malady (rājayakṣman). It is also praised in cases of swelling and ulcers, and it destroys headaches, pain in the flanks, and diseases of the anus. (96) [The ingredients are: sandalwood, pine resin, deodar, liquorice, cardamom, vālaka, śaṭhī, reed-grass, śaileyaka, pṛkkā, padmaka, and vanakesara. (97)

Kaṅkolaka, murā, māṃsī, śairīya, two types of harītakī, reṇukā, tvak, kuṅkuma, the two types of sārivā, tiktā, aguru, nalikā, bale, and likewise grapes—having well-strained this decoction, one should cook it with oil, curd-whey (mastu), and parched grain flour (lājā) in equal parts over a gentle fire. Once prepared, the excellent physician should employ this oil for drinking, enemas, nasal administration, and massage. It destroys anemia, consumption, and cough; it is a destroyer of [evil] planetary influences, promotes strength and complexion, and cures chronic fever, epilepsy, and leprosy.

Furthermore, it removes skin diseases (101); it produces strength, nourishment, vigor, intellect, wisdom, and longevity; it is said to bestow beauty and good fortune, and to bring glory to all beings (102). From approaching the wife of one's master, from longing for the wife of a guru, or from stealing gold belonging to a king, the disease of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣmā) arises (103). Or else, it is born from a malignant disease; listen, O son! Listen now to how consumption is produced by four causes (104): through physical exertion, travel, sexual intercourse, or by a bodily ailment resulting from improper movement.

This great disease arises in a person from a body emaciated by the affliction of wounds, or from excessive anger, grief, fasting, fear, and religious observances; it occurs through old age, or by the extreme drawing of a bow with a heavy string, or from excessive carrying of loads, or from killing, calamities, and captivity resulting from war; it is produced by over-distension of the abdomen, the consumption of bad food, anxiety, and excessive sexual indulgence—this is known as *rājayakṣman*, the wasting away of human strength and the heart. It may also arise from chest-wounds, exhaustion, or even from sudden misfortune, or through excessive addiction to sexual intercourse.

Likewise, from the excessive consumption of dry (rūkṣa) substances [107], the body is emaciated by that, fever becomes mild, and at the end of the fever, swelling arises, as does excessive urination of feces and waste [108]. Diarrhea occurs, and through over-eating, one excessively coughs and spits, and suffers greatly from wasting (śoṣa) [109]. Furthermore, there is an extreme longing for women and aversion to food; this disease is known as Rājayakṣmā (Phthisis), and it is incurable [110]. Both feet become numb, yet one considers a morsel of food to be much.

And for one who has clarity of voice but whose consumption (rājayakṣmā) does not subside, whatever food, whatever diet, and whatever kind of meal he requests, that should be given to him—sweet and substantial. Whatever food the man suffering from consumption desires, or whatever [other] person he seeks, by obtaining each of those, his bodily constituents (dhātavaḥ) are restored. When his swellings become reddish and reach a state of suppuration in the person, then a decoction of *punarnavā* with salt is prescribed. He shall live for four [years].

One who possesses greater strength may live for six months or half a year with excellent treatments, but at most he lives for a thousand days (eleven and one-third months). Beyond a thousand days, there is no life remaining for one afflicted by *rājayakṣman*. His breath, vitality, and vigor have departed; he is emaciated and his sense organs are impaired. There can be no further recovery, and even a palliative disease abandons him. For one who is thus overcome by exhaustion, if coughing should occur again, that most terrible *rājayakṣman* will become a snatcher of his life, occurring within three months, six months, or even three years.

Again, having separately decocted one *prastha* of the juice of *śatamūlī*, one *prastha* of *guḍūcī* paste, one hundred *harītakī* fruits, and one *tulā* of *kuṭaja* bark, one should mix them together with *pūtanā*. Having applied a coating of *dārvī* to five hundred balls of jaggery (*guḍa*), one should add sugar, *āmalakī* powder, cinnamon, cardamom, *citraka*, *śaṭhī*, grapes, *kuṣṭha*, *śilājatu*, *śilābheda*, and *tālaka*, each in the measure of one *akṣa*. One should consume this with purified ghee on top of it.

One should drink milk and thereafter take food; then the patient suffering from *rājayakṣman* (tuberculosis) shall obtain happiness, conquer *pāṇḍu* and *kāmalā*, diarrhea will be destroyed, and his strength will become equal to that of an elephant. *Tālaka*, *śilābheda*, and likewise *śilājatu*; the two types of *kṣīraka*, *samaṅgā*, *kuṣṭha*, *nāgabalā*, and *balā*; *elā*, *patraka*, *tālīsa*, *tamāla*, yellow *candana*, *mustā*, *drākṣā*, *rāsnā*, *muṇḍī*, *śaileyaka*, *pura*, and *surasā*—these should be combined with black sesame seeds.

One should administer two parts of fine powder mixed with jaggery and honey (126). Thereafter, there should be the drinking of cow’s milk and eating food with milk. This should be vigorously prescribed for those emaciated by consumption (rājayakṣmā) and other diseases, those afflicted by malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), and those whose bodily constituents (dhātu) and strength are depleted (127). Even an old man becomes young again and delights women; even a barren woman obtains a son, and even a eunuch attains virility. This is called Tālakāmrātaka, as expounded by Kṛṣṇātreya (128–129). And [there is] guḍūcī.

Two *bala* (two *palas*), *dhātrī*, and *marica*—this powder combined with jaggery (*guḍa*) removes *rājayakṣmā* in men. (130) *Rice* (*śāli*), *ṣaṣṭika* rice, wheat (*godhūma*), *vāstuka* greens, and the meat of wild animals; likewise, mung beans (*mudga*), cow’s milk, and the meat of hares, *eṇa* deer, and *kuraṅgin* deer; (131) The flesh of partridges (*tittiri*), cranes (*krauñca*), quails (*lāva*), eggplants (*vārttāka*), peacocks (*piccha*), and goat—these are declared to be beneficial as meat-based applications (*pralepa*) in this world. (132) One should feed the patient suffering from *rājayakṣmā* with milk and clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) during the wasting phase (*kṣaya*); however, one should avoid alkaline, sour, pungent, and sharp substances, as well as oil.

Sauvīraka, surā, and those [fermented drinks] excluding rāji-kā are [recommended] in cases of wasting or consumption (rājayakṣman). 133. Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wasting Disease," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 9.

The Tenth Chapter Due to excessive heat, or from the consumption of pungent, hot, and acrid substances; or from the consumption of alkaline and sour substances, or from the consumption of wine and similar drinks; (1) or from excessive sexual indulgence, cold exposure, or the consumption of dried vegetables and the like—by these causes, the *pitta* becomes aggravated and merges with the blood. (2) Then the son, fallen into doubt, questioned his father once again. (3) Hārīta said: How does the *pitta* become aggravated? By what is it set in motion? Likewise, for what reason does the blood become aggravated? (4) They are seen simultaneously.

"By what means or in what manner does this occur? Thus questioned, the great teacher, the bull among sages, replied. Ātreya said: "Listen, O wise one of great luster, you who have reached the further shore of the medical scriptures. By that very same cause by which *pitta* becomes provoked, blood (*rakta*) is also provoked. When the *koṣṭha* (visceral cavity) is thus greatly agitated, the *vāyu* tears it apart violently; the *prāṇa* leads [the blood] upward, while the *apāna* draws the *apāna* downward. In the middle, the *samāna* brings about the provocation of *raktapitta*. In this way, *pitta* and blood are provoked simultaneously."

Anger is seen to be fourfold, and its course is considered to be twofold. When it is mixed with phlegm (śleṣman) moving upwards, blood flows from the nose, mouth, and the openings of the ears; this is curable by one who desires victory. When mixed with [phlegm] moving downwards, it flows through the anus as well; that is known as *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease), which seeks success only with great difficulty. When it moves both downwards and upwards, being associated with wind (vāta) and phlegm, one should know that to be incurable, even if it succeeds only with great hardship. By the strength of a single path...

Or, if the *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disease) has arisen due to the force of [suppressed] eructation (*nābhi-vega*), it may be cured easily even with mild treatment, provided it is free from complications. (13) That which follows a single *doṣa* is curable; that which involves two *doṣas* is said to be palliable (*yāpya*); however, when *raktapitta* manifests through all three *doṣas*, it is incurable. (14) In cases of upward-moving *raktapitta*, the wise physician should administer purgation (*vireka*); when the blood flows through the lower tract, emesis (*vamana*) is beneficial for the patient. (15) When a person is emaciated by disease, yet their complexion remains unimpaired, though their body is deficient in strength, or when there is weak digestion, sneezing, or pallor, along with burning sensations and wasting—

Thirst, vomiting, labored breathing, restlessness, aversion to food, delusion, cardiac pain, and vertigo may occur as complications of *rakta-pitta*. (16) These eighteen are declared to be the complications of *rakta-pitta*. Without complications it is curable; likewise, with complications it is incurable. (17) One who suffers from spitting blood, has red eyes, is afflicted by vertigo, and passes blood in the urine—such a person who vomits blood and has bloody urine does not survive. (18) Thus the meaning of the diagnosis has been stated; thereafter, I shall describe the treatment endowed with its excellent characteristics.

Blood-bile (raktapitta) that is easily managed is as follows: when it is reddish, accompanied by wind and froth, or excessively black, or has the luster of yellow safflower, the wise declare that to be "blood-bile caused by bile" (pittaja-pitta). When it is thick, pale, very dense, and associated with phlegm, it is "blood-bile caused by phlegm" (kaphaja-pitta). One should not administer strong purgation to one whose flesh is wasted, who is emaciated, elderly, a child, or afflicted by fever; nor to one suffering from consumption, fainting, or vertigo. One should extract the juice of *vāsā* by squeezing it, and take it for drinking mixed with honey and sugar, [or apply it] to the nose, mouth, and ears.

The blood flowing from the eyes quickly returns to its normal state. (22) Having drunk a decoction of vāsā, utpala, earth, priyaṅgu, rodhra, añjana, and the filaments of the lotus mixed with honey and sugar, one should apply it; thus, aggravated blood residing in the bile is quickly pacified. (23) When the blood-pitta is present, how can a man suffer from nasal catarrh, consumption, cough, or asthma? Why do physicians not show concern for a patient suffering from phthisis? (24) If the ancient medical practice were dependent upon the actions of physicians, then the mother of physicians would herself be a physician. (25)

It bestows success in cases of *raktapitta* (hemoptysis), consumption (*kṣaya*), and cough. (25) While the *vāsā* plant exists, and while there is hope for life, why should one suffering from *raktapitta*, consumption, or cough despair? (26) Powdered *tālīśa* mixed with the juice of *vṛṣa* leaves should be drunk; beginning this treatment, it destroys coughs caused by phlegm and bile, as well as dizziness and the combined affliction of asthma and cough, and quickly provides comfort to one whose voice is broken. (27) A decoction of *āṭarūṣaka*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *pathyā*, combined with sugar and abundant honey—

It wards off asthma, cough, and internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta). Goat’s milk or cow’s milk, boiled with four parts water and mixed with a paste [of the aforementioned drugs] and sugar, is an excellent drink; it quickly destroys raktapitta. Milk processed with *balā*, *aśvadaṃṣṭrā*, *āmalakī* fruits, *drākṣā*, *madhūka*, and *madhuyaṣṭikā* is beneficial for a person to pacify raktapitta. Furthermore, the powder of the flowers of *khadira*, *priyaṅgu*, *kovidāra*, and *śālmali* [is also used].

One should lick [this] with honey for health; may you be free from disease. (31) Pippalī and Abhayā, processed seven times with the juice of Āṭarūṣaka and dried again, when combined with honey, conquer even most difficult-to-overcome *raktapitta*. (32) Equal parts of cardamom fruits, *padmaka*, *nāgakeśara*, grapes, *ghanā*, *madhuka*, and pippalī, mixed with an equal amount of white sugar and used as a linctus—this *kharjūrikā* completely destroys *raktapitta*. (33) It destroys burning sensations, the distress of fever, labored breathing, delusion, thirst, and fainting.

Likewise, if blood should flow from the nose, then one should grind *āmalakī* fruits with ghee and water and apply it as a paste to the head; that quickly stops *raktapitta*. Alternatively, grape juice enriched with ghee and sugar, or water enriched with sugar, [is beneficial] in cases of *raktapitta*. Barley-food (*yavānna*) and sugarcane juice enriched with sugar destroy consumption (*kṣaya*), cough, and hemorrhage from injury. One should administer nasal medication (*nasya*) using the juice of *haritālīkā* or even the juice of lac (*lākṣā*).

An errhine (nasya) made from the juice produced by the blossoms of the pomegranate (*dāḍima*) may be used even when there is bleeding from the blood. An errhine rich with sugar derived from mango stones and *jambu* fruit, or enriched with white sugar, is beneficial for fevers; it destroys blood flowing from the nose, as well as hiccups, vomiting, and labored breathing. An errhine consisting of the exudation from onion leaves, followed by *yaṣṭīmadhu* and honey, subsequently conquers the flow of blood from the nose. A wise person, having prepared the juice of *vāsā* leaves, should also employ these [other] ingredients: *rodhra*, and so forth.

This digestive powder, composed of blue lotus (*utpala*), clay (*mṛttikā*), licorice (*madhuka*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), and *priyaṅgu*, when mixed with flower-nectar, is beneficial for disorders located in the *pitta* humor; it alleviates cough, jaundice, anemia, hemorrhaging, and asthma. (40) The juice of the pomegranate flower, or likewise the juice of the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of the blue lotus, or lac-resin taken with milk as a nasal drop (*nasya*), stops blood flowing from the nose. (41) If blood flows from the mouth, the prescribed remedy for that should be applied; it will now be described.

For a human being, it is not easily curable; among humans, that which follows from the female womb is incurable when there is a flow of blood. (42) Honey, *madhuka*, *uśīra*, the filaments of the lotus, and the juice of *dūrvā* grass, drunk here together with the fruit of the pomegranate; sandalwood, white *kuṣṭha*, *padmaka*, and tender *bālaka*—honey, *madhuka*, the two types of *bālaka*, and the two types of *kodrava*—all these should be used together. (43) Alternatively, milk scented with fragrant substances, or a decoction of rice, should be prepared and combined with a fourth part [of the aforementioned ingredients].

Even if it has flowed only slightly into the fire, it becomes effective when drunk while the red [blood] is flowing from the mouth (44).
