If it has reached even the path of the ears or has begun to flow through the nose, then even that which was prescribed [elsewhere] would serve as a filling for the ears and nose; it stops the bleeding, quickly heals the wound, or cures dyspnea, vomiting of blood, urinary disorders, insanity, and disease (45). When [blood] flows from the nose, nasal drops should be administered; when from the mouth, drinking is to be prescribed; when from the ears or eyes, filling is required; and when from the anal passage, a non-unctuous enema (nirūha) is indicated (46).

One should lick the powder of pomegranate rind mixed with sugar, or again, one should lick the powder of lotus filaments (padmakiñjalka) with sugar. This certainly and quickly stops bleeding from the mouth, as well as vomiting, exhaustion, dyspnea, emaciation, giddiness, and thirst. (47–48) The tender leaves of Jambu and Āmra, combined with Harītakī and mixed with honey and sugar, serve to ward off blood from the mouth. Or likewise, [the leaves] of Vaṭa, Prabhāla, Arjuna, Vṛkṣaka, Kadamba, Jambu, Āmra, or Khadira, as they may be available. (49)

A linctus made with honey instantly stops bleeding from the mouth. (50) Śatāvarī, madhuka, balā, sugar, kākolī, pomegranate, marrow, kṣīravidārī, phalinī, tamarind, and balā—this preparation, cooked with cow’s milk and clarified butter, is beneficial when used for drinking as well as for enemas. It cures bleeding from the vagina, penis, and anus, along with cough and consumption. (51) Mṛdvīkā, madhuka, vidārī, vasudhā, nīlī, samaṅgā, the fruits [of madana], the two types of kākolī, the pair of bṛhatīs, vṛṣa, mahāmedā, and black sandalwood.

Jātī leaves, paṭola, śyāmā, amṛtā, sañjīvaka, abhayā, the two types of medā, kucandana, and madhurasā—these śyāmā plants taken in equal parts (52), boiled with cow’s milk according to the purified procedure until one-fourth remains, and combined with sugar candy and madhuka, constitute a proven and excellent drink for men when prepared for consumption.

It also destroys the blood that is beneficial for women; or it may arise from pitta in the anus, the penis, or even the path of the hair follicles, and when applied as a circular ointment, it destroys hemorrhaging. This ghee known as Drākṣā-ghṛta is also prescribed for internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), fever, gout (vātāsra), vaginal pain, vertigo, intoxication, insanity, and urinary disorders involving blood.

In cases of bile disorders, acidity, severe skin diseases, consumption, chest wounds, blood disorders, pulmonary tuberculosis, and anemia, this [preparation] is beneficial when administered as a drink, an enema, or an errhine; thus it was spoken by Ātreya for the benefit of men. (54) Having extracted the rind, one should prepare pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd), quickly washed with *kāñjika* (sour gruel) and then again with water. (55) Afterwards, one should grind them in a *prastha* measure of milk and meat-broth, and then cook this again with clarified butter according to the prescribed method. (56) When they have become honey-like in appearance, then one should set them aside together with sugar.

And in this regard, one should prepare these medicinal ingredients: (57) two *pala*s each of long pepper (*pippalī*) and ginger (*śṛṅgavera*), along with black pepper (*marica*), the two types of cumin (*jīraka*), as well as *dhātrī*, cinnamon bark (*tvak*), cardamom (*elā*), and cinnamon leaves (*patraka*). One should add a powder of half a *pala* to that [mixture] and stir it with *dārvī* wood until it becomes a solid mass (*leha*). (58–59) Then, having assessed the patient's strength and weakness, one should lick it with honey and ghee. It cures hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*), consumption (*kṣaya*), cough, jaundice, edema, and vertigo. (60)

It cures vomiting, thirst, fever, dyspnea, anemia, chest wounds, consumption, epilepsy, headache, and severe pain in the female reproductive tract (61). It stops chronic bleeding from the womb and alleviates mild fevers; even an old man becomes youthful and lustful, while a barren woman becomes the mother of sons (62). A man lacking virility regains his potency and becomes beloved by women; this *kūṣmāṇḍaka* electuary is a remedy for all diseases (63). One should take fifty palas of well-softened pieces of *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd and mix them with sugar and water.

The wise one, having made a formal resolve, should prepare a *prastha* measure of ghee until it is thoroughly cooked (64). Knowing it is cooked, he should again mix into it a decoction of *vāsā* and subsequently cook it until it reaches the consistency of a ladle-smeared preparation (*darvīlepa*). Then, having understood this, he should add these ingredients once more (65): *dhātrī*, *ghanā*, *bhārṅgī*, and the three aromatics (*sugandhatraya*); all of these should be added in a quantity of one *karṣa*. Furthermore, *punarnavā*, ginger (*nāgara*), and coriander (*dhānyaka*)—the measured dose for these is declared to be one *pala* (66). This [mixture] consists of eight *pala*s of *śyāmā*.

One should prepare a powder and then thoroughly rub it all together with a ladle; mixed with an equal amount of honey, it destroys all diseases. It quickly subdues cough, fever, and wasting from chest wounds, as well as hiccup (67). It overcomes heart disease, blood-bile, consumption, chronic catarrh, acid dyspepsia due to bile, asthma, and fainting. It is beneficial for women and excellent for children and the elderly, providing the destruction of all ailments (68). [The ingredients are] *śatāvarī*, *muṇḍitikā*, *amṛtā*, and the bark of the fruit.

Take five *palas* each of *puṣkaramūla*, *bhārgī*, *vṛṣa*, *bṛhatī*, *khadira*, and *māṃsī*. Having quickly boiled these in water until reduced, once it has been strained, the wise man should add twelve *palas* of honey and an equal amount of powdered iron, along with an equal amount of sugar and ghee. Knowing the procedure, he should cook this in an iron vessel for sixteen *palas* [of total liquid]. It may also be prepared with jaggery (*guḍa*).

One should take equal parts of tugākṣīrī, viḍaṅga, magadhā, śuṇṭhī, the two types of jīraka, kaṇṭaka, the three myrobalans (triphalā), bhṛṅgarāja, dhānyamarica, and kesara. One should prepare this finely ground powder in a measure of one pala for each ingredient. Having placed it in a ghee-smeared cauldron, one should administer a dose of one karṣa; this powder should be taken at dawn with lake water, and it destroys hemorrhoids, swellings, and other ailments caused by heavy, sour, or wind-increasing foods. Or, it may be taken with blood and sour gruel.

It is prescribed for those suffering from consumption (yakṣman), as it dries up [the humors], cures leprosy and various diseases, provides strength, and is the most potent aphrodisiac. It suddenly destroys internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), vaginal disorders, and painful menstrual bleeding accompanied by blood. When applied to the penis and bladder of men, it cures bloody diarrhea and urinary disorders involving blood; it is declared to bestow good fortune, produce luster, and extend vitality, vigor, nourishment, and strength. Furthermore, the three fruits (triphalā) should always be employed in cases of bloody diarrhea, painful discharge of blood, and burning sensations.

The powder of *saviṣā*, *samaṅgā*, *parpaṭa*, pomegranate, and *dhātakī* (77), combined with honey and sugar—or likewise with curd, ghee, and linctus—quickly stops bloody diarrhea, continuous discharge of blood, and [disorders] of women; it is beneficial for men and suitable for the alleviation of diarrhea in children (78–79). For vaginal discharge, a paste of *madhuka*, *samaṅgā*, *elā* leaves, *nimba* leaves, *pathyā*, *mustā*, *viśālā*, and *kaṭurohiṇī*, mixed with sugar, is beneficial for this vaginal discharge (80).

One should ward off vaginal pain, painful discharge, and thirst by means of equal parts of *elā*, *samaṅgā*, *śālmalī*, *harītakī*, and *māgadhikā*. A decoction prepared from these with an equal amount of sugar and honey will also stop the flow from the womb. At the end of the heat of summer, for the benefit of a person suffering from *raktapitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), one should strictly avoid foods that cause a burning sensation, sour things, *sauvīraka* (sour gruel), pungent, astringent, or alkaline substances, as well as *surā* liquor. Vegetables such as *vāstūka*, *cillī*, *suniṣaṇṇaka*, *jīvantikā*, or *śatapuṣpikā* are beneficial.

In cases of *rakta-pitta* (hemorrhagic disorders), red rice, as well as mung beans (*mudga*) and red-sesame rice (*lohitataṇḍula*), are beneficial. Barley, wheat, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), *kośātaki*, and *paṭola*—along with mung beans and black gram (*māṣa*)—are likewise helpful for the alleviation of *rakta-pitta*. The meat of the antelope (*hariṇa*), rabbit (*śaśaka*), *kalāba*, partridge (*tittira*), *kuliṅga*, *kakerā*, peacock (*mayūra*), curlew (*krauñca*), and pigeon (*pārāvata*)—the flesh of these—is indeed a promoter of wind (*vāyu*) and bile (*pitta*). However, when properly prepared, it is beneficial for providing strength, undiminished vitality (*sattva*), splendor (*tejas*), and luster (*kānti*). Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Rakta-pitta," in the third section of the *Hārīta-uttara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The Eleventh Chapter. Ātreya said: Now, therefore, O son, the treatment of hemorrhoids shall be explained; listen to the characteristics of those which are said to be of six types. (1) Those born from the three *doṣas*—namely Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha—and the fourth occurring in *sannipāta* (the combination of all three); the fifth is that which arises from blood (*rakta*). (2) The sixth is to be known as congenital (*sahaja*); such is the sixfold origin of hemorrhoids. Thus, these painful ailments of the rectum arise in six ways. (3) [They are caused] by fasting, and by the consumption of light and dry food.

Through the consumption of pungent, salty, and burning foods, or from the obstruction of *vāta*, there arises constant straining and a lack of physical strength; thus, due to the force of the provoked wind, the manifestation of hemorrhoids occurs. (4) In one who remains seated without eating, the anal disease becomes aggravated by the suppression of feces and urine, as well as by the exposure to cold. (5) By the consumption of salty, pungent, astringent, and bitter substances, by eating food that is insufficient or too light, and by excessive suppression of natural urges through coldness, the provoked impurities are discharged into the anal passages; thus, blood and wind are produced within the channels of the anus. (6)

Through the consumption of pungent, sour, salty, hot, burning, and heavy foods with wind (vāyu) or water, or due to fatigue, the affliction of physical exercise, or the defects of travel and sexual intercourse, hemorrhoids arise from Pitta. (7) From the habit of not exercising, constant exposure to cold or other [unwholesome] things, or through the excessive consumption of sour substances and oily, slimy food, hemorrhoids arise from the disease of Kapha. (8) Coldness, pricking pain, roughness, insomnia, abdominal tumors, enlargement of the abdomen, prostate-like growths, choleraic symptoms, swelling in both [hands and feet], and black nails and eyes are the signs [of this condition].

For hemorrhoids arising from *vāta*, there is burning, vertigo, fever, thirst, exhaustion, fainting, anorexia, and yellowness of the eyes, teeth, and face; and for hemorrhoids born of *pitta*, the symptoms include diarrhea and a yellowish complexion. For hemorrhoids produced by *śleṣman* (kapha), O knower of medicine, there is excessive sleep, heaviness, dullness, mild pain, swelling, colic, abdominal tumors (*gulma*), curvature of the rectum, constipation, piercing pain, anorexia, and sluggishness of movement. There is also cough accompanied by colic, flatulence, and anorexia.

Nausea, loss of appetite, and stiffness of the shoulders—all these indeed arise from hemorrhoids (arśas). I shall now describe the symptoms of anal fistula (gudaja): with Vāta, the fistulas are characterized by itching, discharge of blood, roughness, irregularity, and length. With Pitta, they are accompanied by burning, are variegated, yellowish, or bluish in appearance, and discharge warm blood. Those which are accompanied by burning, are hard, characterized by suppuration and constipation, and are cold, itchy, and thick, are considered to be caused by Kapha. They are also accompanied by burning and pain.

Darkness, itching, and dryness arise, and blood flows continuously; these are hemorrhoidal growths born of itching and blood (kaṇḍvāsṛgbhavārśas). (16) Worms resembling grains and sprouts also appear; indeed, hemorrhoids with symptoms similar to those of wind and feces (vātavarca) come into being. (17) Some are curved, sharp, and cracked at the tip, resembling long bimba fruits; some resemble mustard seeds in size, while others have the appearance of black dates.

Some [piles] have the appearance of jujube fruits, some resemble *kalambaka* flowers, and others are like lotus seeds; O Manuja, this is the origin of hemorrhoids caused by the wind (*vāyu*). (18) In the anus, the nostrils, the ear-cavities, the mouth, or likewise in the eyelids, the corners of the eyes, and the middle of the vagina—these diseases that arise in men are incurable; treatment may be attempted with effort and ease only if they are not [in these locations]. (19) One should know that there are indeed three locations for hemorrhoids: within the three folds of the anus, externally, and internally. Of these, those located externally are easily curable. (20)

O best of physicians, one arising internally from a seed (antarbalījāta) may be cured with difficulty in the middle stage, but it is incurable [in the final stage]. External hemorrhoids are best treated with medicinal pastes, suppositories, and fomentations; those in the middle stage with surgical instruments, and those arising internally with internal medicines. Therefore, my son, an intelligent person should exert effort in treatment so that the patient may be protected and the disease may be removed. Indeed, if men suffer from swelling, emaciation, and fever in the hands, feet, face, navel, penis, or anus...

Dyspnea, vomiting, fainting, pain in the heart and flanks, emaciation, anorexia, constipation, and diarrhea are the complications that arise from hemorrhoids; thus, there are twelve such complications. Hemorrhoids without complications are curable, but those with many complications are incurable. One afflicted by colic, anorexia, thirst, excessive discharge of blood, and suffering from pain, swelling, and diarrhea—such a patient suffering from hemorrhoids will certainly not survive. Therefore, O best of physicians, I shall describe the treatment for hemorrhoids, by means of which pills, alkalis, and surgical instruments may be successfully employed for one's well-being.

27. The treatments for hemorrhoids have been declared; they destroy hemorrhoids, increase strength, pacify pitta and blood, and do not aggravate vāta. 28. At the outset, digestive treatment (pacana) is best, and thereafter one should administer medicine: a decoction of *pathyā*, *amṛtā*, and *dhanikā* taken with jaggery as a drink. 29. A thick paste (*atikalka*) of *dantī*, *viḍaṅga*, *magadhā*, coriander, *bhallātaka*, jaggery, sesame, and *kuṣṭha*, when sprinkled over with milk and drunk, destroys diseases of the rectum. 30. *Nāgara*, *pippalī*, *bilva*, *viḍaṅga*, and *dantī*...

This paste of *śaṭī*, *bhayā*, and *trivṛt*, taken with jaggery as a drink, brings about the destruction of hemorrhoids in men. (31) A decoction of *patra*, *kesara*, *śuṇṭhī*, *sama*, *elā*, *tumburu*, *dhānya*, *viḍaṅga*, and sesame seeds, when drunk with *harītakī*, ghee, and jaggery, destroys diseases of the rectum. (32) If a man eats *pippalī* and *abhayā* combined with jaggery in the morning, it quickly destroys his piles (*gudakīlaka*), along with the group of diseases such as jaundice (*kāmalā*) and anemia (*pāṇḍu*). (33) The water of well-steamed eggplant fruit, [taken] with curd...

One should administer *sitāhvā* (guduchi) with the nectar of water for drinking in cases of hemorrhoids; it destroys worms and diseases born of worms. (34) A powder of *bhallātaka*, black sesame, and *pathyā* (harītakī) should be consumed by a person along with jaggery (*guḍa*). When drunk, it destroys hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, colic, piles, and cough; it utterly eradicates these for him. (35) Indeed, a *sūraṇa* tuber wrapped in *arka* leaves and smeared with mud should be heated until it reaches the color of fire; that [tuber], mixed with milk, rock salt (*saindhava*), and oil, [is used]. (36) He eats it.

Or, for the purpose of destroying hemorrhoids, even for a man who is free from disorders of Vāta, sesame seeds should be added in equal parts to Citraka, Puṣkaramūla, and Śaṭī; to these, one should add an equal amount of Sūraṇa tubers and Agnikaphala (Myrobalan) pieces. To that whole mixture, four times as much rock salt (Saindhava) should be added, and it should all be infused with Arka leaves. Having placed this in a jar of ghee and cooked it over a fire of wild cow-dung, this milk—cooked with salt and ghee and combined with buttermilk—will, when drunk, destroy [the disease] even more so.

It destroys hemorrhoids, piles, and even *viṣūcī* and fistula-in-ano (bhagaṇḍara). It is the destroyer of jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), abdominal distension, intestinal obstruction, tumors (*gulma*), and loss of appetite; it is known as Bhadraka-saindhava, the destroyer of urinary disorders, throat ailments, itching, and worms. (40–41) One should take equal parts of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), Pippalī root, Citraka, and the three aromatics (*trigandha*). To these, an equal amount of *bhallātaka* should be added. Having thoroughly powdered all these together, one should add jaggery (*guḍa*) weighing twice the total amount. (42) Having crushed everything together, [it should be placed] in a vessel smeared with oil.

Having prepared this, it should be consumed daily by the wise in a dose of one *akṣa*; it destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal diseases, colic, tumors, and worms, while quenching the "mare's fire" (excessive digestion), and curing anemia or consumption. (43) One should employ three *pala*s each of ginger and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), four *pala*s of black pepper, and two *pala*s of long pepper. (44) One *pala* of *cavya* should be added there by the best of physicians; half a *pala* of *tālīśa* and half a *pala* of *padmaka* should be given, along with one *pala* of cumin. (45) [Jīraka]...

Equal parts of treacle (guḍa) and the same amount of well-ripened, thick black jaggery (śyāmā), along with three hundred long peppers (pippalī), should be ground together in a mortar and stored in a greased vessel. A pill the size of an akṣa fruit should be administered to men every morning; it destroys all diseases, and it overcomes hemorrhoids (arśāṃsi), anemia (pāṇḍuroga), chlorosis (halīmaka), jaundice (kāmalaka), vertigo (bhrama), abdominal tumors (gulma), diarrhea (atisāra), internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), consumption (kṣaya), chest wounds (kṣata), and even incurable tuberculosis (yakṣmā). It is beneficial for chronic fever, loss of appetite (arocaka), and chronic rhinitis (pīnasa).

This *Prāṇada-modaka* would be [efficacious]. (49) Having taken two *palas* each of *jājī*, long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), *kola*, *magadhā*, *pathyā*, ginger (*agnika*), and small cardamom (*nāgara-sūkṣmailā*), and one *pala* of rock salt (*saindhava*); then, with that entire quantity, five hundred fruits of marking-nut (*bhallātaka*)—and even when the jaggery (*guḍa*) is double the total weight—thereafter, old *sūraṇa* equal to the whole mass of jaggery; (50) having ground these into pills the size of a *vaṭaka*, a specific quality arises: it wards off hemorrhoids, cures consumption (*kṣaya*), and likewise bestows nourishment and a healthy complexion.

It stimulates the weak digestive fire like a submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), removes dizziness, and cures heart disease, anemia, colic, constipation, fistula-in-ano, and fear; it is the expeller of malignant pain. (51) Even though this formulation was prepared by the wise sage Kāṅkāyana, who was endowed with yogic power, for a specific purpose, one who desires happiness should nevertheless employ it. (52) If you wish to rub and soothe the afflictions of the anus, drink for seven days the best salt (saindhava) combined with citraka, liṅga, vacā, cirabilva, and great picumanda (neem), all well-churned together. (53) [Take] viśva, upakulyā, marica, and kesara...

A powder made from *patra*, *lavaṅga*, *elā*, and *vṛddhi* (cinnamon), when combined with sugar, is beneficial for hemorrhoids (*gudāmayas*) and for the alleviation of abdominal pain. (54) A bolus (*modaka*) consisting of *nāgara*, *puṣkara*, *vṛddhadāruka*, and fresh jaggery (*guḍa*), along with *dāruka*, acts as a destroyer of the disease known as *durnāmaka* (hemorrhoids); it instantly makes even a grown man appear like a child. (55) One who, at dawn, eats a single bolus (*vaṭaka*) made of *trikaṭuka*, *abhayā*, *puṣkara*, *citraka*, and a *tila*-measure of powdered *kṛmiripu* (vit) mixed with jaggery— [The remainder of the verse is omitted as per instructions.]

One who has suppressed a disease of the rectum increases the digestive fire (agni). 56. Having crushed black pepper, ginger, and *citraka* with one part of *sūraṇa* added, and mixing it all with an equal amount of jaggery (*guḍa*), one should consume a bolus (*modaka*) the size of a *bilva* fruit; this destroys the various disorders of bile (*pitta*) in men and produces nourishment for the body. 57. A wise person should take sixteen dried parts of *sūraṇa* root that is of a red color and has been divided into six pieces. 58. To that, half as much *citraka* and ginger (*śuṇṭhī*) should be added and weighed.

One part of *marica* bound with jaggery (*guḍa*) forms a bolus (*modaka*) which, when consumed by people, possesses excellent qualities; it quickly destroys all diseases of the rectum, stimulates the digestive fire, and cures abdominal tumors (*gulma*) and pains of the stomach. Take equal parts of the three fruits (*triphalā*), roots of *magadhā*, *tālīśapatra*, *krimiripu* (mustard), and *magadhā* flowers, as well as *puṣkaramūla*. Add one part of *marica* and *dahana* (cinnamon), and an amount of *śuṇṭhī* equal to the total weight of the above. Then add one part of *sūraṇa* (yam) combined with *madana* and *capala* (mercury). [This formulation is known as] *Madanacapalayukta*. (Note: The text provided ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)

Vṛddhadāru, labhṛṅga, and śīrṇakhaṇḍa (in a ratio of one part each to two parts) are ground into a fine powder and made into boluses (*vaṭaka*). The person who consumes this quickly removes abdominal disease in its most severe form. This renowned "King of Formulas" (*yogarāja*) cures hemorrhoids, bleeding, bile disorders, cough, weak digestion, colic, consumption, fever, anemia, jaundice, and worms; it bestows strength and nourishment, purifies the channels, and swiftly kindles the digestive fire. One should employ this *yogarāja*, even by merely remembering the sage Agastya.

By the application of this yoga, even Bhīma became a great consumer of food. (64) Having ground together chavya, pāṭhā, the three pungents (trikaṭu), magadhā, mūlaka, tumburu, bilva, ajājī, rajanī, surasā, pathyā, and rock salt (saindhava), one should cook this well-prepared mixture with equal parts of clarified butter (ghṛta). When used for drinking or as an external massage, it removes hemorrhoids, wind-diseases, and urinary stones. (65) Śyāmā, kuṣṭha, madhuka, madana, puṣpaka, citraka, bilva, dāru, prativiṣā, śatāhvā, kaliṅga, and aśaṭhī—[these should be prepared]. (66)

Oil ground with these and cooked with double the amount of milk is beneficial for both enemas (*anuvāsa*) and massages (*abhyaṅga*), for the purpose of destroying diseases of the rectum (66). This oil is excellent for treating wind-diseases, ear-discharge, blood-issues, earache, urinary stones, and for the piercing pain of wind in the calves, back, waist, head, and temples; it is also superior for constipation, abdominal seizures, diarrhea, and obstructed labor, as it sustains the body against the accumulation of all diseases (67). [The ingredients are: *mustā*, *viśva*, *viḍaṅga*, *cavya*, *kaśaṭhī*, *pathyā*, *tejovatī*, *dantī*, *indrā* (indrayava), and *trivṛtā*, each one *karṣa* in measure.

Therefore, one should add eight *pala*s of *puruṣakara* and six *pala*s of *vṛddhadāru*; having boiled all this in one *droṇa* of water from the *sūraṇa* plant until it is completely reduced to a paste, one should boil it again with three times as much jaggery (*guḍa*). Once prepared, one should take out [the mixture] and then add *citraka*, *trivṛt*, *tejovatī*, and *sūraṇa*. One who uses this becomes a master of speech.

Take equal parts of cardamom, cinnamon leaf, nagakesara, and clove; having ground these together, prepare a portion consisting of sixteen parts of all of them and place it in a smooth jar. At dawn, one who possesses great self-control should consume a dose the size of a *vata* fruit. Once that has been digested, he may drink abundant milk, both as a beverage and with his food.

It destroys hemorrhoids, abdominal tumors, fistula-in-ano, malabsorption syndrome (grahaṇī), anemia, jaundice, colic, constipation, cough, wounds, and consumption (rājayakṣmā). One should boil two thousand *bhallātaka* fruits in one *droṇa* of water until one-quarter remains. Into that decoction, one should again cook one *tulā* of jaggery (*guḍa*). Then, having added five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits—or three *palas*—of the following to that very mixture: the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), cumin (*javanī*), ginger (*ghana*), rock salt (*saindhava*), cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), cinnamon leaves (*dalana*), and *nāgakeśara*.

One *karṣa* each [of these] should be weighed out and applied; having crushed them, they should be placed in oil or a vessel of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). In the morning, one should eat jaggery (*guḍa*) in the size of a *vaṭaka* (ball). This indeed destroys diseases such as fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), worms, consumption (*yakṣman*), and anemia (*pāṇḍu*). It also destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*), urinary stones (*aśmarī*), urinary disorders (*meha*), chlorosis (*halīmaka*), blood-bile (*raktapitta*), and malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*). It produces nourishment, bestows strength, brings about excellence of complexion, and grants happiness. [This preparation should be made with] *daśamūla*, *guḍūcī*, *śaṭī*, *ikṣuraka*, along with *citraka*, *bhārṅgī*, and *phala*.

One should take five hundred *bhallātaka* fruits and boil them in one *droṇa* of water (verse 75). Once boiled, it should be removed from the heat and cooled completely; then one should add one hundred *guḍa* (molasses) that has been well-digested, along with equal parts of *elā*, *kesara*, *bhṛṅga*, and *lavaṅga*. Having made these into a powder, this entire mixture should be kept for one day saturated in ghee within a vessel of ghee (verse 76). A person should place this in a smooth jar and administer it for seven days in cases of the entire multitude of diseases caused by hemorrhoids (*gudaja*). By consuming a single *modaka* every morning, it destroys [the disease] (verse 77).

It destroys hemorrhoids, urinary disorders, and pain; it is beneficial for cough, halīmaka, and jaundice, and indeed kindles the digestive fire. (78) That which, when thrown into cold water, dissolves by the water itself, and turns red as it boils, is known as the "single-boil" (*ekapāka*) of jaggery. (79) The wise man should take four *pālikas* each of granthika, *citraka*, *musta*, *cavika*, the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), *amṛtā*, *sahadevī*, *gajakarṇā*, *apāmārga*, and *kuṭheraka*. Having ground these along with two thousand seeds of *bhallātaka* fruit in one *droṇa* of water, he should cook them until the water is reduced to half. (80–81)

When the paste has been reduced to one-eighth part, one should add half a *tula* of iron powder and two *kuḍavas* of clarified butter; all of this should be stirred together in a single vessel. (82) Then, one should add the three fruits (*phalatrika*), the three acrids (*vyoṣa*), *citraka*, the eight salts, and *viḍaṅga*—all in equal parts measuring one *pala* each. (83) Four *palas* of *vṛddhadāru* and four *palas* of the plant called *mūrvā* should be added, along with eight *palas* of the powder of dried *sūraṇa* tubers. (84) Having mixed these, one should taste the powder once it has been removed from the heat and cooled completely; it is then stored in honey.

Having combined [the ingredients] in a quantity of two *kuḍavas*, this paste should first be administered in the morning before breakfast for hemorrhoids (*gudāmaya*). It quickly destroys hemorrhoids, disorders of the digestive tract (*grahaṇī*), jaundice, pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*), abdominal tumors, worms, urinary stones, weak digestion, urinary disorders, and blood diseases; it swiftly cures consumption and bestows physical vigor upon the body. Through the application of this elixir (*rasāyana*), it rapidly promotes growth, destroys wrinkles and graying hair, and a man shall attain the strength of an elephant. O son, listen as I describe the treatment for bleeding hemorrhoids: one should consume sesame seeds in the morning.

One should eat fresh butter mixed with sugar and ginger; or fresh butter with sugar and *keśara* (Mesua ferrea) and *mātuluṅga* (citron); or *viḍaṅga* combined with sugar; or the electuary of *kūṣmāṇḍaka* (Cucurbita pepo) with fresh butter and sugar. By these means, the wise subdue hemorrhoids characterized by blood. Having ground *samaṅgā*, the flowers of *śālmalī*, sandalwood, the bark of *kakubha*, blue lotus, and goat’s milk, one should drink it as a remedy for blood diseases. One drinks milk boiled with the root and filaments of *kuṭaja*, blue lotus, and the roots of *khadira* and *dhātukī*.

One should prepare a medicinal paste (*mrakṣaṇa-yoga*) consisting of blood-born substances that cause the growth of anal polyps; likewise, one should grind together the excrement of a cock and a pigeon, house-soot, white mustard, *dhattūra*, and plantain leaves with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), and apply this as a suppository (*varti*) into the anus. (93–94) A suppository made from the *sūraṇa* tuber should be prepared and smeared with jasmine juice and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). When applied to the diseased anus, it quickly destroys anal warts (*gudakīlaka*), hemorrhoids (*gudaja*), and worms. (95) [Also used are] turmeric, *mārkava*, costus, and house-soot.

Suvarcala and the juice of siddhārthaka are ground with sour gruel (kāñjika). When this is made into a suppository (varti) with honey and inserted into the anus, it quickly destroys hemorrhoids (arśas) in men. One pala each of devadālī, citraka, and yavānikā, along with the six groups of juices (rasa-gaṇa), ṣaḍgranthā, nimba, water, kaṇā, bhārṅgī, śilājatu, and oil—

Having ground [the ingredients] into a fine paste and combined them with *kāñjika*, applying this as a plaster on the stone [instrument] destroys hemorrhoids (*durnāmāni*), as well as anal fistulas (*gudaja*) and all types of dysentery (*atisāra*). (98) The application of instruments, surgical tools, and cauterization has been described; that [procedure] is performed according to the method for *śalyaka* (foreign bodies). By means of an instrument, [the growth] is excised, and there the application of cauterization (*dāha*) should be performed. (99) Likewise, having cut off a skin-wart (*carmakīla*), it should be cauterized with alkali (*kṣāra*) by the wise physician. When cauterized with alkali, a color resembling a ripe *jambu* fruit is considered excellent. (100) Alternatively, one may cauterize with the alkali of *sūraṇa* (yam), along with *kadalī* (plantain), *jīva* (a type of plant), and *mudga* (mung beans).

The alkali of *palāśa* and *kokilākṣa*, combined with *apāmārga* and ghee, is recommended for the burning sensation caused by alkali; or alternatively, *kuṣṭha*, *pathyā*, nimba leaves, and realgar (101–102) should be placed in smokeless charcoal mixed with honey and ghee. One should fumigate the hemorrhoids (*gudaja*) with this until comfort is achieved. Realgar, *nāgara*, guggulu, mustard seeds, *devadāru*, *pauṣkara*, *viśalyā*, and the juice of *sarjikā* (103–104)—one should fumigate the hemorrhoids and anal diseases with these using ghee.

It destroys fistula-in-ano, malignant chronic catarrh, and foul-smelling ulcers. 105 A fumigation consisting of *nirguṇḍī* leaves, *haritāla*, mustard powder, and *devāhva*, combined with ghee, sugar, and honey, is used for hemorrhoids and similar ailments.

This fumigation destroys bad names, diseases, ulcers, irregularities, and malignant conditions; it cures erysipelas, scabies, chronic catarrh, and cough, and it eradicates the influence of malevolent planets. (106) Thus the procedure for the treatment has been declared; now hear from me the wholesome diet: Śāli rice, Ṣaṣṭika rice, mung beans, horse-gram, Āḍhakī, and Vāstuka. (107) Cillī, Śatapuṣpā, Kūṣmāṇḍaka, Paṭola, Kāravella, Tuṇḍīra, Sūraṇa, Rājikā, and Arjaka. (108) Molasses, buttermilk, and ghee—these are always recommended for those suffering from hemorrhoids, as well as the meat of the boar and the porcupine.

The iguana, the mouse, or reptiles (109), as well as the meat of the common quail (*lāva*), the francolin (*tittiri*), and the eggplant (*vārttāka*)—these have been declared [as forbidden]. Dried meat (*vallūra*), fish, curd, slimy oil, and a meal consisting of *bilva* and eggplant must be strictly avoided (110). Likewise, unnatural postures, sleeping at night or during the day, and coldness—both extreme cold and that which ends in cold—should be diligently shunned (111). Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Hemorrhoids," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 111.11.

Chapter Twelve. Ātreya said: Now I shall explain the etiology and treatment of coughs; listen, O high-minded son, to the eight types of coughs. (1) From excessive laughter, suppressed passion, wind, and the obstruction of food moving into the wrong channels, as well as from the suppression of the urge to sneeze, cough arises in men in every part of the body. (2) It is produced by the consumption of sweet and slimy foods, staying awake at night, sleeping during the day, and eating curd, sour substances, and cold items.

Madanataila, or the small tuber [madana-kaṇḍu], should be processed with wine; this is the origin of kaphaja cough. Due to the reversal of the upward movement of udāna-vāyu, the kapha follows the prāṇa-vāyu and, having entered the heart, produces a long-lasting cough in the throat characterized by phlegm; for this reason, it is designated as "kapha-cough. Eight types of cough have been described, and another, born of injury (kṣataja), is proclaimed. These are: vātika, paittika, ślaiṣmika, and sānnipātika. Furthermore, there is that arising from vāta and pitta, that arising from śleṣma and pitta, the seventh here is that caused by blood (lohita), and the eighth is the [injury-born] one.

Consumption (kṣaya) does not arise without vāta; there is no dyspnea (śvāsa) without vāta, no cough (kāsa) without phlegm (śleṣman), and no wasting (pīkṣa) without blood (rakta); nor is consumption possible without pitta. Thus, the origin of dyspnea has been described; now I shall state the characteristics by which the eightfold supreme cough (kāsa) is recognized in men. A person whose senses are diminished, who suffers from pain in the flanks, who is characterized by excessive force, who is enveloped by piercing pain, who is constricted in the throat, who appears as if asleep, and whose voice is broken—such a person manifests the cough caused by vāta. There is a burning sensation in the throat.

In cough arising from *pitta*, there is fever, emaciation, fainting, thirst, giddiness, a pungent taste in the mouth, headache, and one spits out yellow phlegm; the nails and eyes turn yellow. In cough arising from *kapha*, there is stiffness, vomiting, a pale complexion, and one spits out thick phlegm; there is also loss of appetite and a heavy voice when the body is filled with *kapha*. In cough arising from all three *doṣas* (*tridoṣaja*), the patient is afflicted by itching, burning sensations, dyspnea, vomiting, emaciation, and anorexia; there is headache, swelling, nausea, and itching. Cough and itching [are also present].

Thirst, pain in the abdomen, insomnia, dry cough, thirst, and phlegm arising from vāta and pitta; a smell of smoke, yellow discoloration, inflammation of the eyes, blood-stained [expectoration], red eyes, and thirst—these are the symptoms of kapha associated with pitta and śleṣman (phlegm). Due to excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse, suppression of natural urges, injury, or the lifting of heavy loads, kapha arises from the chest (kṣataja-kapha). By this, there is pain in the heart, one coughs up dry matter mixed with blood, and there is labored breathing, emaciation of the limbs, and a state of dejection.

Afflicted by a mild fever (16), trembling, suffering from pain in the joints, and oppressed by delusion and vertigo—thus is described the blood-born [fever] which takes away the lives of men (17). From slight exertion, from injury, from emaciation, from a sudden blow, or from eating at irregular intervals, the Kapha associated with blood arises through the application of falls and blows (18). Accompanied by a fishy odor in the mouth, chest pain, and dejection, with impaired senses (19), characterized by spitting of blood, or even breathlessness and intoxication; the body constantly wastes away, and delusion and thirst arise—one who possesses these symptoms [is afflicted]. (20)

One should diagnose it as *raktakāsa* (blood-cough). Now, the symptoms of cough are observed by inference through [the presence of] consumption (*kṣaya*), as well as in cases of anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), tuberculosis (*yakṣma*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), or chest injury (*kṣatakṣaya*). Cough necessarily arises in cases of edema (*śopha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and catarrh (*pratiśyāya*); one should thoroughly recognize cough by inferring these conditions. Hemorrhagic cough in the elderly is declared to be palliable (*yāpya*). Cough occurs in children due to the deficiency of the wet-nurse (*dhātrī*). These coughs have been fully described by the ten best of physicians; of these—

The remedy for the disease consists of wholesome diet and medicine. (24) A decoction of *śatamūlī* boiled with powdered *kaṇā* (long pepper), when drunk lukewarm, destroys cough caused by Vāta along with its pain and acts as a digestive. (25) An electuary (*avaleha*) made from *bhārṅgī*, *śaṭhī*, *gostanī*, ginger, *śṛṅgī*, and powdered *kaṇā*, combined with jaggery and oil, is beneficial for men and destroys the disorder of Vāta-born cough. (26) [The ingredients are: *viśvā*, *duḥsparśa*, *śṛṅgī*, *śaṭhī*, *puṣkara*, *dāru*, *bhārṅgī*, *kaṇā*, and *musta*.

A powder containing *rāsnā* and sugar, taken daily, indeed destroys cough arising from asthma and wind (27). One should grind together *kaṭphala*, *kaṭutṛṇa*, *bhārgī*, *mustā*, *vacā*, *dhānyaka*, *parpaṭa*, *devadāru*, *dārvī*, and *viśvā* along with *karkaṭa* (28); this paste, when drunk by a person combined with honey, serves as a remedy for coughers against coughs born of phlegm (29), as well as consumption, chronic rhinitis, throat obstruction, wasting due to wind, phlegm, hiccups, and fever; it quickly destroys them all.

30. A linctus made from one *kola* (approx. 48g) each of the fruits of *drākṣā*, *āmalakī*, and *pippalī*, combined with *kharjūra*, destroys *raktapitta*, cough, and consumption, as well as jaundice (*kāmalā*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and *halīmaka*. 31. A paste consisting of *vālā*, *bṛhatī*, *madhuka*, *vṛṣa*, *kuṣṭha*, *picumandaka*, and *gavāstanī*, when drunk, is beneficial for diseases arising from *pitta* and *kapha*. 32. [A decoction] composed of *mustā*, *āṭarūṣaka*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *dāru*, *bhārṅgī*, *vyāghrī*, along with its flowers, fruits, roots, and leaves, together with *rāsnā* and *viṣā*.

The powder of *madhurasā* taken with boiled water destroys cough (33). Alternatively, a pill (*guṭikā*) made from *magadhā*, *mahauṣadha*, *sindhūdbhava* salt, and honey, when held in the mouth at night, possesses vast virtues; it destroys asthma, consumption, and cough caused by chest injury (34). A linctus (*lehya*) consisting of sugar, *kharjūra*, grapes, parched rice (*lāja*), *kaṇā*, honey, and ghee is beneficial for warding off cough due to *pitta* (35). [Likewise,] the leaves of *āṭarūṣaka* and the leaves of *picumanda*...

One should lick the fresh juice of *tulasī* along with *śaṭhī*, *śṛṅgī*, black pepper (36), and powdered *śuṇṭhī* mixed with jaggery, in cases of cough caused by *kapha*. One should drink a comfortably warm decoction of *bhārṅgī* and *nāgapippalī* (37). Having taken the juice of fresh ginger, the wise person should drink it with honey in cases of cough, asthma, coryza, and fever arising from *śleṣman* (38). Likewise, *kaṭphala*, *bhūtṛṇa*, *bhārṅgī*, *śuṇṭhī*, *parpaṭaka*, *vacā*, and *surāhva* boiled in water have been declared by the learned to be used with honey (39).

This formulation, when combined with honey, should be used in cases of cough caused by *vāta* and *kapha*, dyspnea, hiccups, fever, wasting, and severe chronic cough. (40) One should lick a preparation consisting of *tālīsa* leaf, black pepper, ginger, and *śyāmā*, each increasing in quantity by one part respectively; along with cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and *elā*; and eight times the amount of long pepper (*pippalī*) and sugar. (41) Taken in the morning, it destroys dyspnea, cough, splenic enlargement, anorexia, catarrh, vomiting, hiccups, edema, diarrhea, malabsorption syndrome (*grahaṇī*), anemia, consumption, and pulmonary tuberculosis. (42) [The formula begins with] *tālīsa*.

Triphalā, priyaṅgu, pippalīmūla, mustā, śaṭhī, dārvī, lādalā, nāgakeśara, lavaṅga, and likewise nāgara; kṛṣṇā, kola, bālaka, along with cavikā, mūrvā, viṣā, karkaṭa, drākṣā, kuṣṭha, niśā, agni, vatsaka, vṛṣa, and likewise gokaṇṭa and tiktā (43); vṛkṣāmla, together with the sour juice of pomegranate and ripe jujube fruits—of these, equal parts of powder are prepared, to which an equal amount of sugar should be added.

Half a *pala* [of this] should be administered; it destroys hemorrhagic cough (*kṣataja-kāsa*) as well as asthma (*śvāsaka*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), consumption of fat (*meda-śoṣa*), and hemorrhoids (*guda-ja*). It is always recommended for those suffering from consumption (*yakṣmin*). In wasting-cough (*kṣaya-kāsa*), [it is used]; in cases born of the three *doṣas*, with liquorice (*madhuyaṣṭikā*). In that born of undigested matter (*āmaja*), there is pain from colic (*śūla-roga*), splitting of the joints, vertigo (*bhrama*), exhaustion (*klama*), emaciation (*śoṣa*), headache, and discharge in the eyes. Deep-seated [disease] desires [this]. Whether it be facial paralysis (*khallī*) or loss of consciousness (*cetana*), vomiting arises from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). That vomiting also arises in two forms: oily (*snigdha*) and dry (*rūkṣa*). [Deep-seated disease] causes deep-sunken eyes.

When there is vomiting accompanied by constipation, flatulence, diarrhea, aching in the limbs, swelling, excessive fainting (47), deformity of the limbs, affliction with vertigo, seeing the world spinning, headache, extreme trembling, and hands and feet feeling cold as if frozen (48)—one should avoid from afar vomiting characterized by these symptoms. It is incurable despite all treatments; furthermore, it is incurable for the wise even when caused by indigestion (49). [The remedy is: a decoction boiled with the five roots (*pañcamūlī*), along with rock salt (*saindhava*) and a paste of *āmalaka*. [One should take] the decoction...

One should drink milk mixed with long pepper (*pippalī*), which wards off vomiting caused by *vāta*. Milk with sugar, when given to a man, very quickly destroys vomiting arising from *pitta*. Alternatively, a linctus made from the powder of grapes (*drākṣā*) or of *kṣīradārvī* drunk with honey destroys it. One should lick a powder of the three fruits (*phalatrika*), *puṣkaraka*, *vacā*, as well as *abhayā* and rock salt (*saindhava*), combined with jaggery (*guḍa*); drinking this with cow’s urine destroys a man’s vomiting caused by *kapha*. [Also mentioned are: *śaṭhī*, *dārvī*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, and *māgadhī*.

Powder mixed with ghee or combined with *takra* (buttermilk) destroys vomiting caused by the three *doṣas*. (53) Parched rice (*lāja*) derived from red *śāli* rice, when combined with honey and sugar, quickly destroys the affliction of fever in a young woman; this is my firm opinion. (54) Alternatively, sandalwood ground with the juice of *āmalakī*, mixed with honey, and taken as a bolus weighing one *pala* as a linctus, certainly destroys vomiting. (55) The exudation of fresh pomegranate, cumin, and sugar, or else oil and honey—these four [substances] used as gargles (*kavalagraha*) [are effective]. (56)

It destroys the four types of *arocaka* (anorexia), as well as those caused by wind (*vāta*) and others, and those arising from the combination of two humors. (57) This powder—consisting of the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), the two types of turmeric (*rajanī*), the three fruits (*phalatrika*), honey, and barley-germ (*yāvaśūka*)—prepared in equal parts and mixed with honey, wards off vomiting. (58) Pomegranate with jaggery (*guḍa*), or grapes, or *pathyā* combined with ginger and jaggery, or *trivṛt* with ginger, or ginger combined with jaggery—these alleviate vomiting. (59) One should cause the person to drink a cooled decoction of *parpaṭa* with jaggery; it destroys even the most terrible vomiting accompanied by bile (*pitta*).

A decoction of *kākolī* and *kākamācī* combined with sugar, or parched grain (*lāja*) mixed with sugar, destroys vomiting due to *pitta* in men. (60–61) The juice of *mātuluṅga* along with *pathyā* and sugar quickly cures and subdues *kāṃsya-pitta* (bronze-colored bile) and vomiting. (62) Upon seeing a severe *pitta*-vomiting that causes burning sensations and vertigo, one should administer the leaves of *āragvadha* combined with honey and sugar. (63) Alternatively, drinking milk mixed with *mustā* and sugar is recommended. (64)

The sprouts of the *jambu* and mango trees, as well as pomegranate and *āmalaka*, drunk with buttermilk after fasting, destroy vomiting caused by *śleṣman* (phlegm) in men. One should administer a powder of *sarja*, *arjuna*, *dhava*, *kadamba*, and *kalola*, combined with ginger, coriander, and jaggery; this quickly destroys vomiting arising from *śleṣman* in men. A linctus composed of *śaṭhī*, *kaṇā*, honey, and *viḍaṅga* is likewise effective. Having licked a powder of *elā*, *lavaṅga*, *gajakesara*, *kola*, *sarja*, parched rice (*lāja*), *priyaṅgu*, *ghana*, sandalwood, and *pippalī*, mixed with *mārkava* and sugar, one overcomes vomiting.

It destroys [diseases] born of phlegm, wind, and bile. (67) Having licked a powder made from equal parts of cardamom, cinnamon leaves, elephant-crest (nāgakeśara), cinnamon bark, cardamom, lāmajjaka, ginger, musta, and priyaṅgu, along with sandalwood and black pepper, one overcomes vomiting caused by the three doṣas when mixed with sugar. (68) When the doṣa has moved to the upper part [of the body], purgation is recommended; once that has occurred, emesis directed toward the lower part certainly brings relief. (69) Alternatively, if it has moved to both parts, then *bhayā* (trivṛt) and honey should be administered; knowing it to be an emetic for worms, one should treat the worms.

Regarding the treatment for *śamana* (pacification): it should not be hot, nor excessively sour, nor pungent, nor too light; nor should there be *taṇḍulīyaka* greens, nor wine, nor *kāñjika*. This has been declared as beneficial in cases of vomiting (*vamidoṣa*); now hear from me what is wholesome here: meat from marshy lands (*anūpa*), boiled *śāli* rice, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vāstuka*; *āḍhakī*, mung bean soup, curd, along with jaggery and ghee, and *aṅgāramaṇḍaka*—these are praised as wholesome in vomiting, according to one's strength, according to the time, according to the disease, and according to the digestive fire. Thus [it should be administered].

Having observed [the symptoms], they undertake beneficial treatments. (74) One should employ daytime sleep in cases of vomiting, dyspnea, diarrhea, hiccups, emaciation, indigestion, or again, in cases of nausea and salivation. (75) Neither the drinking of hot water, nor excessive eating, nor physical exercise should be performed; one afflicted by vomiting should avoid these. (76) Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Vomiting," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 12.

Chapter Thirteen. Ātreya said: From fear, fatigue, loss of strength, the consumption of split pulses and dry foods, exposure to the sun, or when a fever has become chronic, and likewise from wasting (kṣaya) and injury (kṣataja), the three humors—Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha—become aggravated. The fourth type is declared to be born of injury (kṣataja), and the fifth is remembered as born of wasting (kṣayaja). The sixth is proclaimed to arise from indigestion (ajīrṇa), and the seventh from the consumption of dry substances. The eighth occurs upon the onset of fever; hear now its symptoms from me. Emaciation, a dark-brown complexion of the face, a bad taste in the mouth, and trembling [are the signs].

That thirst should be recognized by the best of physicians as being caused by Vāta (4). A desire for cold water, along with vertigo, burning sensations, delirium, fainting, and redness of the eyes, is considered thirst born of Pitta (5). Drowsiness, a darkish complexion of the face, lassitude, an aversion to heat due to Kapha, and a thick, darkish coldness of the limbs arise from thirst born of Śleṣman (Kapha) (6). Eye pain, vomiting, a burning sensation, vertigo, headache, shivering, and coldness of the limbs constitute thirst originating from the three Doṣas (7). Dryness of the mouth and yawning [occur in this state].

Headache, heaviness in the abdomen, indigestion, and thirst are observed as the symptoms of this disease in a person. (8) When thirst occurs due to the depletion of *rasa* (plasma), the patient suffers from weakness, hunger, exhaustion, emaciation, vertigo, dyspnea, and dejection; these manifest quickly. (9) The thirst that arises in cases of chest wounds and wasting is characterized by a lack of desire for food. Another type of thirst mentioned in one afflicted by fever is born from the force of the fever itself. (10) In cases of diarrhea or colic, thirst should be recognized by the best of physicians as distinct. (11) [This thirst] arises from diarrhea, vomiting, burning sensations, fainting, vertigo, and emaciation.

Know that thirst is incurable when it cannot be satisfied even by water. (12) Having observed that thirst arising from wind (*vāta*), curd with jaggery is recommended; likewise, drinking a decoction of *amṛtā* with jaggery removes thirst born of wind. (13) One should drink a paste of *śuṇṭhī*, *ajājī*, and *śṛṅgavera* mixed with water and *sauvarcala* salt, or a very cold decoction; this quickly destroys thirst arising from wind. (14) A decoction of *kāśmarya*, *padmaka*, *uśīra*, *drākṣā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, and *vālaka*, combined with sugar— [The text continues: ...should be drunk. This removes thirst arising from wind and bile (*pitta*). (15) *Kharjūra*, *mṛdvīkā*, *parūṣaka*, *āmalaka*, *kharjūra*, *mṛdvīkā*, *parūṣaka*, *āmalaka*, *drākṣā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, *uśīra*, *vālaka*, *śarkarā*, *kharjūra*, *mṛdvīkā*, *parūṣaka*, *āmalaka*, *drākṣā*, *madhuka*, *candana*,

This [remedy] removes thirst caused by pitta. (15) The banyan tree (*vaṭadruma*), *rodhra*, sugar, and sandalwood, together with pomegranate, ground with rice-wash or even with cold water and drunk, removes thirst arising from pitta. (16) *Kuṣṭha*, blue lotus (*utpala*), parched grain (*lāja*), and the sprouts of the banyan tree—these, powdered and mixed with sugar, form a pill that wards off thirst. (17) Grape (*drākṣā*), blue lotus, and licorice (*yaṣṭīka*) are recommended; when consumed with sugarcane juice, they drunk remove thirst born of pitta and the burning sensation (*dāha*) arising from pitta. (18) [Up to the throat...]

A person should likewise drink milk mixed with sugar and induce emesis; this destroys thirst associated with pitta (sapaittikī). (19) For the destruction of thirst, one should drink water that has been heated by a red-hot clod of earth and then cooled, or water infused with sandalwood. (20) The leaves of the rose-apple (*jambu*) and mango (*āmra*), parched grain (*lāja*), sandalwood, and *dhātakī* flowers, when ground together and combined with the juice of *vāsā*, form a linctus that removes phlegmatic thirst (*śleṣmatṛṣṇā*), as well as burning sensations, fainting, and giddiness. One should also drink a soup of *āḍhakī* pulse mixed with parched grain and sugar. (21)

22. For the destruction of thirst caused by *śleṣman*, one should drink milk with black pepper, or water mixed with black pepper, or milk with *kola* fruit. 23. A well-cooled decoction of *durālabhā*, *parpaṭaka*, *priyaṅgu*, the *lodhra* tree, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), and *kuṣṭha*, combined with honey and sugar, destroys thirst arising from all three *doṣas*. 24. *Kāla*, pomegranate, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *sārivā* taken with equal amounts of sugar; or *pathyā* and pomegranate powder mixed with the juice of *mātuluṅga*. 25. Water boiled properly in a wooden vessel and cooled [is also beneficial].

Likewise, one should have that water, which has been churned many times, drunk; and the best of physicians should also administer ghee in cases of parched palate (tāluśoṣa). This [ghee] removes thirst, burning sensations, vertigo, vomiting, emaciation, and fainting (mūrchā). It certainly and quickly wards off thirst born of injury or exhaustion (kṣaya). Pomegranate, *kola*, *cukrīkā*, *vṛkṣāmla*, and *amlavetasa*—the juice of these combined with *pathyā* (harītakī) as an application for the palate—quickly wards off emaciation and destroys thirst accompanied by fever. [Likewise,] *kesara* (flower-stamens)...

A paste of *mātuluṅga* ground with rice-water and applied to the palate while warm with honey removes dryness of the mouth. An application of honey and sugar to the palate prevents dryness. A cold application of lotus-root boiled in cool water quickly destroys dryness of the palate; likewise, the tender leaves of the *jambu* and *āmra* trees [are effective]. A wise person should not give one afflicted by thirst the fruits of the *nimba*, *mātuluṅga*, fermented gruel (*sauvīra*), or ginger to eat first; for upon seeing them or having them in his mouth, excessive saliva flows forth.

By this, it removes wasting (śoṣa) and also subdues thirst. (34) Red rice (*raktaśāli*) boiled with curd and sugar is recommended as food; furthermore, alkaline or pungent foods are not advised. (35) In cases of wasting, vomiting, thirst, exhaustion, alcoholism (*pānātyaya*), diarrhea, and wasting, sleeping during the day brings comfort. (36) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Thirst and Dryness of the Palate," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 13.

Chapter Fourteen. Ātreya said: Due to the suppression of natural urges, excessive obstruction, emaciation from injury, or even by thirst, or by the consumption of incompatible foods, the vitiated *doṣas* bring about fainting (*mūrchā*). (1) The twelve channels (*nāḍīs*) associated with each of the five sense organs, when combined, number sixty; these block the openings of the channels, whereby the mind becomes utterly bewildered. Due to the destruction of consciousness, the person quickly becomes unconscious and remains so for a long time. (2–3) He falls [unconscious].

Fainting (mūrchā) is described as a state of swoon like a piece of wood; it is declared to be of six types, arising from vāta, pitta, and kapha, as well as from blood, trauma, wine, or poison. These [factors] aggravate the pitta, which, when combined with wind and blood, causes loss of consciousness and weakness; thus fainting is called delusion (moha). I shall now describe their individual symptoms in brief. One sees blue or black visions, enters into darkness in an instant, and experiences trembling and flaccidity; these occur momentarily.

One regains consciousness; fainting occurs due to wind (vāta), as do emaciation, distortion of the face, watering of the eyes, salivation, and momentary flatulence. The patient sees yellow, blue, or green, and enters deeply into darkness; there is fever and thirst, and the eyes become red or yellow. The body is perspiring, there is exhaustion, and the stools are broken up; from pitta arises this state of fainting, and headache is produced. One perceives the quarters of the sky as filled with smoke and sees darkness before him.

Turbidity of the eyes, weak digestion, and coldness in the limbs; one awakens only after a long time and the throat makes an excessive gurgling sound; nausea and fainting occur due to phlegm arising from various symptoms. O best of physicians, epilepsy is seen to arise from *sannipāta* (the simultaneous derangement of all three humors); if it is accompanied by blood, it kills living beings. By the smell of that [blood], people faint; thus, fainting occurs, along with headache, trembling, loss of motor function, muttering, and vomiting again and again, as the mind becomes utterly bewildered.

One with red eyes, who is habitually prone to sleep and is under the influence of liquor (15), may experience another type [of fainting] due to wasting from chest wounds or from the consumption of *kodrava* grain; because of that, he sleeps with a troubled mind. Indeed, the fainting of a person arises from an excess of *pitta*, while dizziness in men arises from *pitta* and *vāyu*. A person's lethargy (*tandrā*) arises from *vāta* and *kapha*, and sleep arises for a man when *kapha*, *vāyu*, and darkness (*tamas*) predominate (17). For the purpose of alleviating perspiration, affliction, massage, and wind, [one should apply]...

For the pacification of *pitta* caused by cold food, drink, or the breeze of a fan, the drinking of decoctions (*kaṣāya*) is always truly recommended; likewise, it is effective for fainting and delusions arising from *śleṣman*. (18) One should cause [the patient] to drink a cooled decoction of *triphalā* mixed with sugar, and one should also cause them to drink a decoction of *durālabhā* mixed with sugar. (19) Having ground long pepper (*kaṇā*), the marrow of *kola*, saffron, *uśīra*, and sandalwood with cold water, this "unbroken" drink (*akhaṇḍapāna*) destroys even deep fainting. (20) Upon seeing fainting born of blood (*raktajā mūrcchanā*), this [remedy] should be administered.

In cases of wasting (*kṣayaja*) and in those who are weak or emaciated, cooling therapy is the cause for nourishing the fainting patient. When a man has reached a state of lost motor function, one should restore consciousness by pressing the new thumb and the nose together, or by gently squeezing the body with the teeth or tongs. Alternatively, one should apply cauterization (*dāhana*) on the forehead, the back, or the occipital region (*mālaka*). If even this does not succeed, then swinging (*āndolana*) is beneficial. One should sprinkle the patient suffering from fainting with all cold water and fan him.

Indeed, swinging on a swing made from the seeds of the *śikhipiccha* plant removes a person's fainting, delusion, dizziness, or alcoholism (25). Where one grinds the seed of *karañja* with rock salt (*saindhava*), the juice of *rasona* leaves, *mārka*, *pathyā*, and *vacā* with water into a collyrium (*añjana*), it destroys the day-long lethargy (26). A collyrium for the eyes consisting of horse saliva, black pepper, and salt is recommended; it utterly destroys a person's lethargy or sleep lasting for a hundred days (27).

A fragrant decoction of the three myrobalans (triphalā) mixed with sugar and fresh ginger, taken in the morning with sweet water for seven days, destroys intoxication, fainting, and insanity caused by [excessive] drinking. (28) They desire the extraction of blood for the pacification of delusion and fainting; therefore, one should carefully perform bloodletting in those conditions. (29) One should employ cold sprinklings, baths, sandalwood paste, the breeze of fans, and cool food and drink in all cases of fainting. (30) [One should treat it] with sugar, sugarcane juice, grapes, and refreshing drinks (prapānaka) for wind-induced fainting.

A person should conquer fainting caused by *pitta* with *kāśmarya* and *madhuka* alone. One should drink a decoction of *yaṣṭīmadhu*, or boiled ghee, or boiled *āmalakī* juice; one may also drink warm or cold juice mixed with sugar and parched grain (*lāja*). Honey cures fainting, and one should restore consciousness with medicinal plasters. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fainting," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Fifteenth Chapter. Ātreya said: When one dispels drowsiness and daytime sleep by means of songs, dances, and laughter of leading performers, yet finds no sleep at night, then one should perform this procedure: (1) By tying the root and the crest of the *kākamācī* plant, the best of physicians—having tied the crest with its tip pointing downward—induces sleep at night. (2) For those seeking sleep, one should massage the soles of the feet with curd-whey (*mastu*); for one who has no sleep during the day, there shall be sleep during the nights. (3) [That sleep which arises] through fear, anxiety, or greed...

If one abandons that anxiety, sleep will not fail to come at night; indeed, sleep arises in an instant. (4) A decoction made from the roots of *siṃhī*, *vyāghrī*, *siṃhamukhī*, *kākamācī*, *punarnavā*, and *vārttākī* induces sleep in men. (5) A decoction of *kākajaṅghā*, *apāmārga*, *kokilākṣa*, and *suparṇikā* quickly produces sleep, or one may bind their root upon the crown of the head. (6) Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Sleep," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 15.

Chapter Sixteen. Ātreya said: O Lord of Sages, it has been stated that through the loss of those worthy of service—disciples and younger kinsmen—one encounters a poison equal to *hālāhala*. From this arises thirst, vomiting, labored breathing, delusion, burning sensations, and extreme thirst, as well as the total loss of the senses. (1) Those men who constantly and excessively indulge in liquor become utterly corrupted; wine is like unwholesome food, acting as a cause of delusion. Just as poison is life-destroying when separated [from medicinal ingredients], yet they call it nectar when combined with them, so too wine is beneficial when joined with the proper application (*yoga*). (2)

If one begins [drinking] improperly, it causes extreme suffering: for one afflicted by hunger or overcome by thirst, wine taken without food, or by those who are emaciated without food, or without sufficient nourishment and drink, leads to ruin. (3–4) Even when there is overeating or indigestion, wine consumed causes pain. (5) In *vāta-madātyaya* (wind-type alcoholism), there is delirium and speech disorders; in *pitta-madātyaya* (bile-type alcoholism), there is burning sensation, fainting, diarrhea, and fever. (6) In *kaphaja-madātyaya* (phlegm-type alcoholism), there is vomiting, anorexia, nausea, drowsiness, a sense of heaviness, coldness, and catarrh. (7)

O best of physicians, that intoxication which arises from the three *doṣas* and for which treatment is prescribed by means of signs common to all three is called *madātyaya*. Emesis is recommended, as is the indulgence in sleep; bathing is beneficial, as is the drinking of milk. For food, curd with jaggery is advised. A linctus (*leha*) consisting of whey (*mastu*), sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), dates (*kharjūra*), raisins (*mṛdvīkā*), *sārivā*, *amlīkā*, *āmalaka*, and *parūṣaka* destroys *madātyaya*. Alternatively, one may prepare a paste with the juice of grapes (*drākṣā*), *āmalaka*, dates, and *parūṣaka*; this drink, taken with milk, cures all forms of *madātyaya*.

11. In cases of alcoholism (*madātyaya*), drinking milk combined with a decoction of *pathyā* (harītakī) is beneficial. 12. When one is intoxicated by betel nut (*pūgīphala*), trembling, delusion, fainting, exhaustion, darkness of vision, perspiration, agitation, and salivation occur. 13. One overwhelmed by dizziness and fatigue should be recognized as such; a person exhibiting these symptoms is to be known as one who has fainted from betel nut. 14. For him, drinking cold water or an enema (*vasti*) would be beneficial; or sugar should be given to eat, or *mustā* mixed with sugar. 15. [This applies to] those intoxicated by *kodrava* grains.

If fainting occurs, very cold milk should be given; in the case of intoxication from *dhattūra*, curd mixed with sugar should be administered. (16) One should quickly induce vomiting using *halinī*, *karavīra*, *mohinī*, *madayantīkā*, or other tubers. One should cause [the patient] to drink milk mixed with sugar, or curd, or sugar. (18) Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Alcoholism," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 16.
Chapter Seventeen. Ātreya said: When the *samāna* [vāyu] is provoked, it causes even the beautiful *pitta* located in the skin of a person's limb to become intensely burning and even terrible.

When there is gnashing of teeth in humans at the onset of burning sensations, or when there is pain from coldness, labored breathing, emaciation, and restlessness—these symptoms are identical to those of Pitta-fever (pittajvara). O best of physicians, one should begin treatment for the pacification of the humors (doṣas) as in the case of Pitta-fever. A decoction of Kuśa grass, Ikṣumūla, Uśīra, Tagara, and Vālaka, combined with sugar, subdues coldness and burning sensations. A cold drink consisting of Parpaṭa, Tagara, and Uśīra boiled and mixed with sugar quickly destroys the burning sensation of Pitta-fever.

For men, an ointment made of *lāmajja*, sandalwood, and *uśīra* should be applied to alleviate burning sensations; one should fan them with palm-leaf fans while they rest upon a bed of plantain leaves and lotuses. (5) An ointment mixed with the juice of *kālīyaka* is recommended for burning sensations; cool water is praised for quenching both feverish heat and thirst. (6) One should place a bell-metal vessel above the navel of a person lying on their back and asleep, so that they may find relief through the streams of cold water [falling from it]. (7) One should carefully fill the vessel with fragrant water (*surata*), by which the patient attains comfort; furthermore, clarified butter washed a hundred times (*śatadhauta-ghṛta*) should also be applied over that burning area. (8)

One should apply *dhātrī* fruit (myrobalan) as a cooling plaster for one afflicted by burning sensations and dryness; alternatively, it may be licked as a soothing remedy. (9) For one desiring swift relief from burning sensations, one should grind the tender leaves of the *jambu* and mango trees along with *nimba* and the juice of *bījapūra*, and apply it as a plaster. (10) Likewise, a fountain-house, the cool moonlight of the moon, cooling drinks, a cool breeze, sandalwood, lotuses, and the bond of affection [bring comfort].

Embracing and massaging Rāma (the *rāma* plant), applying moist white garments to the pair of breasts, and [using] milk, sugar, iron, copper, and silver are beneficial for the pacification of burning sensations. 11. Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Burning Sensations," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 17.

Chapter Eighteen. Ātreya said: When pitta, vāyu, and kapha severely aggravate the udāna-vāyu, and the prāṇa-vāyu becomes intensely disturbed in the head, it causes a loss of motor function. It leads to unconsciousness, blocks the channels and the sense organs, and the person falls like a log of wood while discharging saliva from the mouth. The throat makes a gurgling sound, or foam is vomited; the hands and feet tremble, and the eyes become bloodshot and rolling. O best of physicians, these are the signs that arise in apasmāra (epilepsy).

The eyes turn away, become emaciated, and there is darkness, burning sensations, and headache; one whose luster, senses, and consciousness are destroyed becomes an epileptic and perishes. For such a person suffering from epilepsy, the wise physician should administer drinking, collyrium, ointment, massage, and medicinal drinks, as well as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and oil. The leaf of *agasti* and black pepper ground with urine is recommended for nasal administration (*nasya*); it quickly destroys epilepsy in a man. Alternatively, the root of *bandhyākarkoṭikā* mixed with clarified butter and sugar may be used for nasal administration.

This should be employed for the pacification of epilepsy (8). Slices of *kūṣmāṇḍa* (pumpkin gourd) with their cooked juices, along with *tryūṣaṇa*, *elā* leaves, *nāgakeśara*, *kumedhikā*, *granthika*, and *dhānyaka* in equal parts, mixed with white sugar, *priyaṅgu*, and clarified butter (9), should be consumed at dawn; it is recommended that an unlimited amount of milk be taken over this. It quickly destroys the disorder of epilepsy and swiftly eliminates blood disorders (10). A powder made from *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *brāhmī*, *ṣaḍgranthā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *punarnavā*, and *surasā* [is also effective].

Combined with sugar and honey (verse 11), it is beneficial for consumption to destroy epilepsy (*apasmāra*); it is also effective for insanity (*unmāda*), deranged bile and blood (*pittarakta*), and it bestows pregnancy upon the barren woman (*vandhyā*). (Verse 12) One should take two *palas* each of the roots of *rāsnā*, *māgadhikā*, *daśamūla*, and *śatāvarī*, as well as *caṇa*, *trivṛt*, and *eraṇḍa*. (Verse 13) The physician should employ *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, *mṛdvīkā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *śatāvarī*, *rāsnā*, *samaṅgā*, the decoction of the three aromatics (*trisugandha*), *bhīru*, (Verse 14) *kuṣṭha*, and *dīpaka*, along with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (Verse 15)

It cures epilepsy, insanity, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and diseases of the anus. (15) One should cook old ghee with the juice of *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *śaṅkhapuṣpī*; this subdues epilepsy. (16) The oil known as *Mahābalādya-taila* is recommended for use as an enema (*basti*) or as nasal drops (*nasya*); likewise, the *Śatāvaryādika* [oil] and *Sādaiva* [oil] are beneficial. (17) Furthermore, the *Candanādya-ghṛta* should be employed by the best physicians in cases of epilepsy, insanity, or wind-diseases (*vātaroga*). (18) [The formulation of] *tryūṣaṇa* and *triphalā*...

Asafoetida, rock salt, *kaṭukā*, *vacā*, seeds of *naktamāla*, and likewise white mustard seeds (19)—these, ground with goat’s urine and formed into pills dried in the shade, as an ointment destroy epilepsy and even terrible insanity (20). It is the destroyer of defects causing loss of memory and vertigo, and of afflictions caused by spirits; it removes fever occurring on the first day, second day, or every fourth day (21). It destroys the film of cataracts, night-blindness, and headache; it quickly restores consciousness to a person suffering from the confusion of *sannipāta* (22). [Also] sandalwood...

Tagara, kuṣṭha, yaṣṭī, the three aromatics (trisugandha), vāsaka, mañjiṣṭhā, abhīru, mṛdvīkā, pāṭhā, śyāmā, and priyaṅgu; 23. svayaṃguptā, pīluparṇī, viṣā, rāsnā, gavādanī, the two types of kākoli, jīraka, medā, puṣkara, ghana, and vāluka; 24. vidārī, vāsumantī, vṛddhadantī, viḍaṅga, padmaka, aindravṛkṣa, as well as āragvadha and citraka; 25. dhānyaka with the five types of jīra, as well as tālīsapattraka, khadira, niryāsa, tagara, and kālīyaka.

One should grind *kaikatam*, *nāgakesara*, *parūṣaka*, and *kharjūra* together, and then saturate them repeatedly with honey and ghee. This linctus is always recommended for severe epilepsy, insanity, jaundice, anemia, and chlorosis; for consumption, hemorrhagic disorders, those afflicted by bile-induced diarrhea, blood-dysentery, wasting, diseases of the head, and chronic fever; as well as for asthma, vertigo, vomiting, burning sensations, alcoholism, urinary calculi, urinary disorders, cough, and dyspnea.

In cases of chronic rhinitis (pīnasa), these thirty [ingredients] should be employed as a remedy that wards off all diseases; it should be administered to those who are barren and especially to the elderly. It is beneficial for children as well; hear now the standard measurements for this. When applied in such a manner to a disease, this great medicinal paste (mahākalka) is esteemed by the wise. Powerful and endowed with excellent qualities, it yields its fruit in this world; it is called a linctus (leha) and is praised by the physician Kṛṣṇātreya. [The ingredients are: grapes, *dāru*, as well as *niśā*, *madhuka*, *kṛṣṇā*, *kaliṅga*, *trivṛt*, and *yaṣṭīkā*.

Triphalā, viḍaṅga, kaṭukā, saffron, candana, pomegranate, the four aromatics (cāturjātaka), nimba, turagī, tālīsapatra, ghanā, the two types of medā, devadāru, kuṣṭha, kamala, rodhra, samaṅgā, varī, bhārṅgī, kola, pomegranate, sour [ingredients], kāśmarya, śṛṅgāṭaka, kāmbojā, śaṇaghaṇṭikā, laghutarā, kṣudrā, and rāsnā. 34.

One should lick one *karṣa* of this powder, mixed with an equal amount of sugar, honey, ghee, and dates; it bestows all strength and quickly destroys epilepsy (35). It also cures most severe insanity, consumption, phthisis, anemia, asthma, cough, urinary disorders, and hemorrhoids; it is recommended as beneficial for women (36). If no relief is obtained by these means, one should cauterize the forehead between the eyebrows with an iron rod, or cauterize the person on the crown of the head (37). One should avoid pungent and sour foods.

For those suffering from disorders of *rakta-pitta*, the decoction of wine and betel nut (*surā-pūga-kaṣāya*) should be especially avoided (38). Indeed, substances that cause delusion or fainting should not be used in cases of epilepsy (39). Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Epilepsy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 18.

The Nineteenth Chapter. Ātreya said: This mental disease is known as *unmāda* (insanity). The aggravated *doṣas*, having become deranged, ascend upward by way of the wrong channels. This condition called *unmāda* is difficult to cure even for the best of physicians; it is proclaimed to be of various types: one arising from a single *doṣa*, another from a combination of two (*dvandvaja*), another from the conjunction of all three (*sannipāta*), and yet another arising from poison (*viṣa*). Furthermore, [it occurs] in an impure place, a deserted house, in the middle of a forest, or in a terrifying, dense street, or a temple. And then...

In some way, with a mind distressed by fear and apprehension, one should abandon the path of the agitated mind and instead follow the right path. 3. The birth of insanity in men has been described by the most eminent authorities as arising from anxiety, pain, fear, joy, deliberation, greed, divine influence, the honor shown to guests, twice-born brahmins, kings, and teachers, or from excessive love, the loss of wealth, or separation from a young woman. 4. Because of that, a person may become agitated, cry out, recite distorted words, or when excited, vomit, tremble, and laugh; likewise, they run about, strike themselves, and even [move] their tongue. 5. [And] likewise the tongue.

If the patient's vision perishes, or if he sees excessive light, or if the afflicted person sees wealth, then the foremost of physicians should perform the treatment for epilepsy (apasmāra). I shall explain this specifically among the sciences of spirits (bhūtavidyā) hereafter. Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Diagnosis of Insanity," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty. Ātreya said: There are eighty-four well-known types of wind (vāta) that cause pain in human beings; I shall describe their etiology briefly and individually. Due to contradictory thoughts, improper diet, staying awake at night, excessive physical exercise, excessive exposure to darkness, bloodletting, purgation, sitting in an uneven posture, and the suppression of the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and udāna breaths—when the strength and senses of those who travel on a journey or undergo exhaustion are diminished, the vāyu, whether located near the surface or deep within the tissues (dhātu), becomes provoked. Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these [five] vāta disorders arise from the vitiation of these [breaths].

Headache, earache, pain in the temples, blood disorders, and afflictions of the half-head arise from the increase of the [doshas] over the course of days. (4) Furthermore, nasal complications, stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha), lockjaw (hanugraha), stiffness of the tongue, palate pain, as well as asthma (tamaka), vertigo (bhrama), (5) drowsiness, dyspnea, throat disorders, and so forth—these sixteen located in the head proceed from the provocation of the vital breath (prāṇa), impelled by bile (pitta). (6) Hiccups, dyspnea, labored breathing, cough, wasting with pain, hoarseness of voice, nausea, and heart pain.

Vomiting caused by bile, wind, and other humors; sneezing, yawning, as well as hoarseness of voice, nasal catarrh, loss of appetite, and chronic rhinitis—these are said to arise from the *udāna* [vital air]. (7–8) When the *udāna* is joined with phlegm (*śleṣman*), it becomes aggravated in the heart due to the bodily humors (*doṣa*). (9) We shall now describe the provocation of the wind named *vyāna*; this wind, pervading all limbs, produces severe disorders of the bodily tissues (*dhātu*). (10) That [wind] should be known as having entered the tissues, and is described individually as follows: in *tvag-vāta* (skin-wind), there is horripilation, stiffness of the neck (*manyā*), and the shoulders (*aṃsa*). (11)

When Vāta resides in the muscle (māṃsa), there is swelling and piercing pain; when it resides in the fat (medas), there is trembling and breaking pain; when it reaches the bone (asthi), falling [of the limb] occurs; and when it resides in the marrow (majjan), falling occurs. When it resides in the semen (śukra), there is swelling of the joints. Therefore, one should suppress the Vātas located in these tissues according to their symptoms—distinguishing those that are curable from those that are incurable. Vāyu residing in the muscle and fat can be cured by medicines; others are cured with difficulty, or perhaps they are not cured at all. There may be horripilation, piercing pain, loss of sleep, anorexia, darkness [of vision], and the body feeling as if pierced by needles.
