Ants appear as if being pierced [by needles]; dryness occurs in the corners of the eyes, and emaciation arises again; there is loss of the seminal essence (*śukra*) and of the menstrual blood (*garbharajas*), as well as trembling (*vepathu*). 16. There is sluggishness of the digestive fire (*mandāgni*), and he sees various dreams; insomnia agitates him—these are the general symptoms of Vāta. 17. He repeatedly convulses his limbs, and there is piercing pain, pricking, and much fever; this condition, born from the provocation of the Vyāna Vāyu, is known as Ākṣepaka (convulsive seizure). 18. The body bends like a bow and convulses.

With eyes repeatedly moistened and fixed, he coos like a pigeon; the best of physicians call this by the name *apatantraka*. (19) According to another school of thought, others say it is considered *prahvapratānaka*; when the wind (*vāyu*) seizes half [the body], it is known as *apratānaka*. (20) That wind, resting upon the phlegm (*kapha*), torments like a staff and quickly stiffens the limbs; that too is *daṇḍāpratānaka*. (21) It rests upon the heart, the breasts, the fingers, the ankles, and the joints, seizing the sinew (*snāyu*).

He who causes the extension [of the limbs] is also known as *snāyupratānaka* (22). Furthermore, when the wind (*māruta*) extends the external channels (*nāḍī*), it may reside in the waist and cause a sensation as if there were a thorn lodged there (23). The wise declare that this *pratānaka* wind is incurable; another fourth type is *ākṣepa*, which arises from injury (24). That *pratānaka* which is born from injury is not curable; however, that which stretches the body upward and dries up the limbs (25), causing delusion and darkness, and parching the joints of the bones, is incurable.

From that, half a *karṣa* of *kṛcchra* occurs, and it causes dryness and contraction (26). That which indeed involves half a spreading [contraction] of the back is considered *ekāṅgika* (27). And if there is paralysis of one limb (*ekāṅga-pakṣaghāta*), or whichever [limb], the *vāyu* is cured only with great difficulty by all *vāta*-subduing medicines (28). There may be piercing pain, fainting, trembling, convulsions, and insensitivity to touch; that *vāyu* which causes the limbs to perish is called *tūnī* (29). Furthermore, he who experiences trembling, piercing pain, convulsions, and yet retains the sense of touch—

It causes the limbs to tremble; this condition is called *pratitūnī*. 30. Heart-stiffness (*hṛdistambha*), back-stiffness (*pṛṣṭhastambha*), thigh-stiffness (*urustambha*), and *gṛdhrasī* have been described separately; listen further, O wise one. 31. These sixteen [disorders] are proclaimed to arise from the provocation of the *vyāna* wind. 32–33. *Śūla*, *gulma*, *udāvarta*, flatulence (*ādhmāna*), and *udāvarta* itself, *pariṇāma*, irregular digestion (*viṣamāgni*), indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and *vātiguḷmaka*; 33. *parikledī*, *rasaśeṣa*, *rasa*, *malavālaka*, *bandhī*, *bhedī*, and *vilāsī*—these are the sixteen.

34–36. Fistula-in-ano, pain in the bladder, urinary disorders, hemorrhoids, severe skin eruptions (koṭhaka), defects of the penis, prolapse of the rectum, other types of rectal pain, retention of urine, and retention of feces—these sixteen [diseases] should be primarily understood by the wise as arising from the provocation of the *apāna* wind. These disorders have been described; they have also been proclaimed in detail. Burning, feverish heat, emaciation, and fainting are caused by *marut* (vāyu) associated with *pitta*. Coldness, swelling, loss of appetite, and numbness are caused by *vāyu* associated with *śleṣman* (kapha). That which is dependent on a combination of two [humors] is known as *dvandvaja* (dual-origin).

The wise know that [Vata] to be curable (sādhya). Even when it is alone, that wind is considered most curable. When one half of the face becomes distorted, the neck also turns, there is a deformity of the eyes, and the patient suffers from pain and loss of function; when there is extreme pain in the neck, the cheeks, and the sides of the teeth, those who are experts in the diseases of Vata call that "Ardita" (facial paralysis). Furthermore, when there is salivation, dryness, lockjaw, loss of taste, and toothache, it is indeed Ardita caused by Vata.

42. In the Pittaja type, the limbs are yellow, accompanied by fever and thirst, as well as delusion; furthermore, swelling and stiffness occur in this condition, or it may manifest as Ardita (facial paralysis) arising from Kapha. 43-44. For one who exhibits the following prognostic signs—trembling, turbid eyes, emaciation, unblinking gaze, and speaking in a continuous yet indistinct manner—even severe and irregular facial paralysis (Ardita) may be cured. 45. A terrible throat [obstruction] occurs for the purpose of swallowing, along with yawning when the mouth is opened wide; jaw-stiffness (Hanustambha) also arises, and these conditions are indeed difficult to treat, especially when occurring in an irregular [manner].

In cases of sleeping during the day or distorted vision, the bodily wind (vāyu), obstructing the speech-carrying vessels, produces stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha) and causes one to look toward the side with great difficulty; this is known as *vasanānila*. Furthermore, when the wind residing in the blood takes refuge in the channels of the head and causes headache, that condition is called *śirograha*, which is incurable. Therefore, I shall describe the remedies by which the wind may be pacified: oleation (*snehana*), drying (*rūkṣaṇa*), digestive processing (*pācana*), and palliative measures (*śamana*). These include sudation (*svedana*), massage (*mardana*), and anointing (*abhyaṅga*).

When [the Vāyu] has reached the tendons, joints, and bones, the wise physician should administer an oil enema (basti-sneha) followed by a decoction enema (nirūhaṇa), and then perform surgical incision (bhedana). Then, using the Māṇimantha instrument, he should cleanse the area and subsequently pacify the undigested Vāyu. In cases of semen-related disorders involving the Vyāna Vāyu, one should treat it like a seed-disorder. Muṇḍī, Guḍūcī, the two types of Bṛhatī, Rāsnā, and Samaṅgā—these should be boiled into a decoction (kaṣāya). This may be mixed with milk, curd, or fresh butter. The wise physician should cook this over a gentle fire; once prepared, this ghee serves as a nourishing unctuous agent for men.

A dose of one *karṣa* is prescribed for drinking, as well as for massage and food; likewise, oleation is beneficial for men suffering from Vāta disorders when administered rectally for seven days. (53–54) This very same drink—consisting of *rāsnā*, *viḍaṅga*, *rajanī*, *nāgara*, *sauvīraka*, *surasā*, and *saindhava* salt, taken warm in a dose of one *karṣa* for five days—acts as a drying agent (*virūkṣaṇa*) for men. (55) Thereafter, it serves as a proper digestive (*pācana*) for seven days; and once the morbid humors (*doṣa*) have been properly digested...

Therefore, one should administer a pacifying treatment. (56) I shall now describe [the remedy] when [Vāta] has reached the *puṣṭigata* stage and taken refuge in the vessels (*dhamanī*): through abundant food and sudation, one destroys the wind (*samīra*); and for seven days, there should be sprinkling with warm water. (57) A decoction of *rāsnā*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *eraṇḍa*, *śataparvā*, and *punarnavā* quickly destroys Vāta diseases pervading the entire body. (58) A decoction combined with *rāsnā*, *guḍūcī*, *dāru*, *nāgara*, and *eraṇḍa* is beneficial even for Vāta in all limbs that has entered the constituent elements (*samadhātugata*). (59) *Rāsnā*, *aśvagandhā*, *kāśīśa*, and *vacā*... [and so forth].

A decoction of *kapikacchu* drunk with castor oil destroys the wind (*samīraṇa*). (60) A decoction of *rāsnā*, coriander, ginger, *yavānī*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*) is declared to be a digestive (*pācanaka*) for men suffering from wind disorders. (61) The *rāsnā*-based preparations mentioned above are said to be beneficial as purifiers (*pāvana*). (62) One should eat half a *pala* of garlic daily for one month, combined with asafoetida, rock salt, cumin, black salt (*sauvarcala*), and likewise the three pungent spices (*kaṭutrika*). (63) Taken together with ghee, this daily regimen destroys wind diseases.

It cures ardita (facial paralysis), pratānaka (epilepsy), diseases affecting a single limb as well as those affecting all limbs, ūrustambha (stiffness of the thighs), disorders caused by worms, and also gṛdhrasī (sciatica). One should finely grind half a pala and one pala of garlic, along with asafoetida, cumin, rock salt, sauvarcala salt, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya). All these powdered ingredients should be mixed with an equal amount of oil and consumed according to one's digestive fire in the morning, followed by a decoction of ruvuka as an after-drink. By using this for one month, one conquers all diseases of vāta.

It cures paralysis of a single limb as well as that of all limbs, thigh-stiffness (*ūrustambha*), sciatica (*gṛdhrasī*), pain located in the waist, back, bones, and joints, facial paralysis (*ardita*), convulsions (*apatantraka*), chronic fever affecting the bodily tissues (*dhātugata*), and the constant fever known as *saikarāhvaya*. A person should drink the fine powder of *nāgara*, *haridrā*, *kaṇā*, *jājī*, *ajamodā*, *vacā*, *saindhava*, *rāsnā*, and *madhuka* in equal parts daily with clarified butter. Within twenty-one days, it undoubtedly destroys these diseases, and the person becomes a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*).

The glorious [medicated] linctus, which has the resonance of clouds and thunder, destroys all wind-diseases (*vātāmaya*) and brings comfort. (72) Śatāvarī, vacā, śuṇṭhī, rāsnā, kadara, śallakī, daśamūlī, balā, fermenting agent (*kiṇva*), tumburu, and guḍūcī—(73) this paste, when combined with ghee, destroys the wind that has entered the body. (74) A decoction of the bark of śallakī and cikkaṇī, mixed with oil, shall restore a man afflicted by *vātārdita* to health within twenty-one days. (75) Therefore, massage should also be performed using both oils and ghees.

One should prepare guggulu and garlic according to the prescribed ritual (verse 76). Take eight parts of *balā* root and four parts of *daśamūla*; boil these in four times the amount of water, or in a quantity measured by one *droṇa*. To that, one should add one *āḍhaka* of milk and mix in one *āḍhaka* of curd; then quickly add one *āḍhaka* of the soup of *kulattha* beans that has been left to stand overnight (verse 78). One should slowly cook one *droṇa* of sesame oil in a cauldron, adding *jīvantī*, the *jīvanīya* group of herbs, the two *kākālī*s, *jīvaka*, and *ṛṣabha* (verse 79), as well as the two types of *medā*, *sarala*, and *devadāru*.

One should mix together the following: śallaka, kucandana, kālīyaka, sarjarasa, mañjiṣṭhā, the three aromatics (trisugandhika), 80; māṃsī, śaileyaka, kuṣṭha, vacā, kālā, aṣṭaśārivā, śatāvarī, aśvagandhā, śatapuṣpā, punarnavā, 81; fermenting agent (kiṇvaka), surā, mustā, as well as tālīsapatra, the three pungents (kaṭutraya), and vāluka—all these should be blended therein. Having prepared this excellent preparation endowed with all virtues, one should perform the auspicious recitation (maṅgalavācana) and place it in a vessel made of gold, silver, clay, or iron. 82–83.

Having heated it, it should be administered according to the patient's strength as a drink, an external massage, or as a non-unctuous enema (nirūha-basti). It should be given to one afflicted by Vāta, or to one with a fracture, or even to one with a wound. It should also be given to a woman who is barren, or to men with scanty semen. Likewise, for those who are emaciated, weak, or suffering from chronic fever, and for those afflicted by Āmavāta, it should be administered after adding Kañcaṭa. It should be used in the morning for dryness of the jaw, as well as for earache and eye pain.

In cases of stiffness of the neck (manyāstambha) and pain in the sides (pārśvaga), oil is as beneficial as nectar for all disorders of Vāta; it destroys dyspnea, cough, abdominal tumors (gulma), hemorrhoids, and diseases of the digestive tract (grahaṇī). It also swiftly subdues the eighteen types of skin diseases (kuṣṭha). Furthermore, upon the mere sight of this Bala-oil, malevolent spirits (graha), ghosts (bhūta), demons (piśāca), ḍākinīs, and śākinīs flee to distant lands. It also keeps disorders such as epilepsy (apasmāra) at a distance. Through this oil, the elderly become young again, and even barren women obtain sons. [The oil]... [is] oil.

This is known as Mahābalādyam, and it is remembered as a remedy that removes severe wind disorders (mahāvāta). (91) One should add one āḍhaka of curd to one āḍhaka of a decoction of *balā*, as well as one āḍhaka of the soup of *kulattha* beans and one āḍhaka of *sauvīra* (sour gruel). (92) Having combined these together, one should cook them and then incorporate the following medicinal ingredients: *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, *pippalī*, and *gajapippalī*; (93) the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), *surāmāṃsī*, *kuṣṭha*, and the ten roots (*daśamūla*). One should cast the powder into this and, once prepared, remove it from the heat. (94) It is to be employed for drinking, as well as for massage and non-unctuous enemas (*nirūha*).

In the administration of nasal therapy (*nasyakarma*), this excellent preparation, composed of various medicinal qualities, destroys eighty types of wind disorders (*vātāmaya*). Just as *mahābala* oil is [potent], so too does this increase one’s virtues. One should take the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, the juice of bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*), the juice of fermented gruel (*sauvīraka*), and a decoction of the ten roots (*daśamūla*). One should also incorporate the broth of fermented black gram (*kulmāṣa*) and curd; all these ingredients should be used in equal parts, with half that amount of oil. It should be cooked over a gentle fire and removed once prepared for use as an external massage (*abhyaṅga*).

It should not be administered as a drink nor in enema therapy (99). It is used for filling the ears in ear diseases, in severe headache, in disorders of the half-head (hemicrania), and in pain of the eyebrows, temples, and eyes (100). By its application, a person quickly attains well-being; moreover, by means of massage, it destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha), scabies (pāmā), and skin diseases (101). It quickly leads to destruction [of disease], overcomes violent epilepsy (apasmāra), and prevents pain in the bladder, exhaustion, and fatigue caused by Vāta on the left side (102). This is known as Āmapākī; one should not apply it [to that condition].

One should not administer digestive (pācana) or purgative (virecana) treatments; rather, one should employ a constipating (stambhana) therapy for that [condition]. (103) There is pricking pain in the waist, back, and chest region, as well as colic in the bladder; the abdomen roars like a tumor (gulma), and finally, swelling (śopha) occurs. (104) Heaviness of the head arises and there is frequent falling to the left side; this too should be recognized by the wise physician as a condition affecting all parts of the body (sarvāṅgaga). (105) For that [condition], one should perform digestion (pācana) and thereafter purgation (virecana); another type is proclaimed as being obstructive (viṣṭambhī), causing suppuration of the tumor (gulmapākī), and affecting all parts of the body. (106)

Among those, the one who is to be treated [successfully] should be identified; the other two are difficult to cure. Having suppressed the seizure (apasmāra), the physician should administer oleation and emesis. 107 Śyonāka, Pāṭalā, Bilva, Tarkārī, Pāribhadraka, Aśvagandhā, Kaṇṭakārī, Prasāriṇī, Punarnavā, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Atibalā, and Balā—these should be taken in equal parts. Having boiled them until one-fourth remains in a *droṇa* of water, one should strain the decoction. 108–109 The following medicinal substances should be added by the best of physicians as they are being recited: Śatapuṣpā, Vacā, and Māṃsī. 110

Dāru, śaileyaka, varā, pataṅga, candana, kuṣṭha, and likewise another, raktacandana; 111 Karañja seeds, aṃśumatī, the three aromatics (trisugandhi), punarnavā, rāsnā, turaṅgagandhā, rock salt (saindhava), and durālabhā; 112 And miṣṭāsurasa—each of these being two palas. Having made them into a powder, one should add it there, and then add an āḍhaka of lac juice; 113 Likewise, the juice of śatāvarī, goat’s milk four times that amount, an āḍhaka of cow’s curd, and sesame oil.

One should employ it; when it has been perfected, the recitation of auspicious verses (*maṅgalavācana*) should be performed there. Having welcomed and installed this [oil], it is known as "Nārāyaṇa. It destroys disorders of wind (*vāta*), as well as epilepsy and seizures (*apasmāra-graha*), diseases of the head, diseases of the ears, and even the eighteen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*). A barren woman obtains a son, and even a eunuch becomes virile. The emaciated become youthful, and the fool becomes intent upon the pursuit of knowledge. This Nārāyaṇa oil was spoken by Kṛṣṇātreya. [There are] others...

One should employ those [medicines] along with ghee and oil here; by this, well-being arises and one subdues wind-disease (vātaroga). 119. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wind-Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 20.

Chapter Twenty-One. Ātreya said: Listen, my son, I shall describe the symptoms to you in brief. In one who is nourished by heavy food and drink, has weak digestion, and indulges in sexual intercourse, 1. when the body is satiated with bulbs and leafy vegetables, the undigested matter (āma), impelled by the wind (vāyu), undergoes putrefaction in the seat of phlegm (śleṣman) and gives rise to great pain. 2. This condition manifests as diarrhea caused by undigested matter (āmātisāra), swelling occurs in the joints, there is a sense of aging in the limbs, and a discharge of phlegm (balāsa) from the mouth. 3. When the back and neck become afflicted with pain, the person suffers from exhaustion; [and] the limb— (Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)

O best of physicians, in the case of Āmavāta, there occurs a state of deficiency; for that, oleation is not to be performed, but digestive treatment (pācana) is prescribed. O wise one, the undigested matter (āma) is diminished through the four types of symptoms of its differentiation. The *viṣṭambhī* type causes abdominal tumors (gulma), urinary disorders (meha), and is characterized by undigested matter (āma) as well as digested and undigested matter (pakvāma); another type affects all the limbs. I shall now describe its symptoms as well. In the *viṣṭambhī* type, heaviness, flatulence, and pain in the bladder arise; for that too, digestive treatment should be performed and oleation should indeed be administered. [This applies] to him whose abdomen gurgles.

The waist region is afflicted as if by a *gulma* (abdominal tumor), and there is numbness; this is suspected to be an *āmagulma* (undigested matter tumor). At the outset, fasting (*laṅghana*) should be administered after assessing the strength and weakness of the body. One must never perform digestive processing (*pācana*), for if the *gulma* undergoes putrefaction (*pāka*), it leads to certain death. Furthermore, if the *gulma* is putrefied, death occurs swiftly and inevitably. In a patient whose limbs are oily, who has numbness, weak digestion, and is strong, and whose unctuous matter is undigested and immobile, that is proclaimed as "unctuous *āma*" (*snehāma*). For such a person, oleation (*snehana*) should not be performed; instead, one should prescribe fasting (*upavāsa*).

One should administer digestive (pācana) therapy, yet one must also manage the undigested matter (āma) that causes diarrhea. For a patient who has swelling of the face, numbness, as well as a distended abdomen (ghano-dara), anorexia, and diarrhea, the condition is incurable according to the wise. When life itself is in jeopardy, treatment should be abandoned; however, once digestion is known to have occurred, one should then administer medicinal powders. When the āma-vāta is digested, the stool becomes watery, dark-colored, and falls downward; there is no pain in the bladder, nor is there fatigue or exhaustion. This state should be recognized as "the digestion of the āma."

One should administer digestive therapy (pācana) for that [type of Gulma]; purgation (virecana) should not be performed, but rather one should apply a styptic (stambhana) treatment. (16) There is pricking pain in the waist, back, and chest; the abdomen roars due to Gulma accompanied by bladder pain, as well as swelling (śopha). (17) Heaviness of the head occurs and undigested matter (āma) falls off profusely; this too should be recognized by the wise as being located in all the limbs (sarvāṅgaga). (18) For that [condition], one should perform digestive therapy, followed by purgation. Another type is considered to be obstructive (viṣṭambhī), characterized by the ripening of Gulma (gulmapākī), and located in all the limbs. (19)

In this context, those [types of *āmavāta*] which are curable should be understood; the other two, characterized by *sneha* (unctuousness) and *āma*, are considered difficult to cure (*kaṣṭasādhya*). The pair consisting of *pakvāma* (ripened *āma*) is easy to cure (*sukhasādhya*); having thus identified [the condition], one should perform the treatment. O best of physicians, for *āmavāta* associated with *āma*, the drinking of a decoction of *rāsnā*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *eraṇḍa*, *śatapuṣpā*, and *punarnavā* is recommended as a digestive (*pācanaka*) agent. A man should drink a comfortably warm decoction boiled from *rāsnā*, *śyonāka*, *kāśmīra*, *cikkaṇīka*, and *puṣkara*; this is known as the *pācanaka*.

Know that this has been declared for *āmavāta*. In *āmavāta*, one should drink water boiled with *daśamūlī* mixed with *kaṇā* (Piper longum). This powder of *guḍūcī*, *nāgara* (Zingiber officinale), and *pathyā* (Terminalia chebula), combined with jaggery, [should be taken]. *Dhānyaka*, *nāgara*, *rājāmla*, *devadāru*, *vacā*, and *abhayā* constitute a digestive (*pācana*) formulation for *āmavāta*; it is excellent and brings comfort. Likewise, one should drink the powder of *kola* (Zizyphus jujuba) with warm water; it destroys *āmavāta*, weak digestion, colic, and abdominal tumors (*gulma*). Having added one *āḍhaka* of *balā* decoction, one should add one *āḍhaka* of curd-fermented milk (*dadhitakra*).

One should cook a *droṇa* of horse-gram (*kulattha*) soup together with one *āḍhaka* of fermented barley water (*sauvīra*), and once prepared, add these medicinal herbs: *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, long pepper (*pippalī*), elephant pepper (*gajapippalī*), the three aromatics (*trisugandhi*), *murā*, *māṃsī*, costus (*kuṣṭha*), and the two sets of five roots (*pañcamūla*). One should cast the powder into it and remove it from the heat once cooked. This should be administered internally as a drink and used in the *nirūha* enema procedure; it destroys all wind-related diseases and is excellent for bestowing a multitude of virtues. One should drink castor oil (*eraṇḍaja-taila*).

Indeed, this purgative combined with jaggery and milk is excellent for *āmavāta* affecting the entire body. (31) Having added one part of ginger (*nāgara*), two parts of *krimija*, and three parts of *trivṛt*, one should form a bolus (*vaṭa*) equal in weight to the jaggery. (32) One should eat it with warm water and then drink warm milk; by this, a comfortable purgation occurs in cases of *vāta*. (33) The best of physicians should prepare a decoction of *viḍaṅga*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rāsnā*, *pathyā*, and *trikaṭu*, reducing it until one-eighth remains. (34)

One should add half a *kvātha* (decoction) of milk, oil, and likewise castor oil, each measuring one *karṣa*; this purgative is to be well-drunk as a follow-up drink (anupāna). (35) One should consume *guḍūcī*, *triphalā*, and *pathyā* together with jaggery (*guḍa*). This is indeed the best purgative for *āmavāta* and brings about comfort. (36) *Abhayā* ground with buttermilk and combined with honey and sugar will arrest *āmātisāra* (diarrhea caused by undigested matter); so too will *guḍa* and *āmalaka*. (37) One should administer *vatsaka*, the two types of *jīraka* (cumin), and *dadhi* (curd) ground together; it pacifies *āmātisāra* and pain in the bladder (*bastiśūla*).

One should administer guggulu, garlic, and asafoetida combined with ginger; this decoction is for the destruction of Vāma and is a pacifier of Māruta (38–39). Ajamoda, ugragandhā, kuṣṭha, the three pungents (trikaṭu), śaṭhī, the three fruits (phalatrika), bhārṅgī, puṣkara, the eight salts, the two types of jīraka, viḍaṅga, the two types of tumburu, and likewise dāru (40–41); dhātakī flowers, śālmalī bark, and pomegranate—these [are the ingredients].

One should have these made into fine powders in equal proportions (42). Combined with ghee, it certainly destroys Vāta quickly; taken with *hiṅgu* and alkaline water (*cāranāla*), it destroys the pain of colic (43). Likewise, it subdues *vāmavāta* even with warm water; and with the decoction of *daśamūla*, it treats *gṛdhrasī* and pain in the hips (44). With *eraṇḍa* oil, it treats constipation; and in cases of even very severe swelling, it is used with cow’s urine. Combined with jaggery and cow’s urine, it conquers *pāṇḍuroga* (45). Combined with honey, it [treats] *prameha*; combined with sugar, it destroys *yakṣman*.

One should avoid all terrible diseases by applying the appropriate treatment (verse 46). One should avoid foods that split easily (dvidala), those that are sweet, oil, and slimy substances. O best of physicians, one should not bathe with cold water in cases of *āmavāta* (verse 47). When the *āma-doṣa* has been cooked [digested], one should not indulge in *āmavāta*; nor should one consume hot things, liquids, or especially those that cause liquefaction (verse 48). Whatever wholesome regimens have been prescribed for fever (*jvara*), those should be employed here as well (verse 49). Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Āmavāta*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 21.

Chapter Twenty-two. Ātreya said: Listen, O high-minded one, to the disorders arising from *rakta-vāta* (blood-wind). Great pain arises in the region between the hips, thighs, and knees; one should recognize this as *gṛdhrasī*, though its specific characteristics have not been mentioned here. A swelling may occur in the middle of the knee accompanied by intense pain; this, arising from *vāta-rakta*, should be known as *koṣṭhaśīrṣikā*. That which causes the wasting away of the tendons (*kaṇḍarā*) in the arms, the back, and within the fingers, should be recognized by the wise as [the disease] that destroys the hands and feet. [This is] *pādaharṣa*.

In this condition, there may be horripilation in the feet; at the conclusion of the aggravation of *kapha* and *vāta*, perspiration occurs in the hands and feet. When combined with *pitta* and *vāta*, there is heat in the hands and feet at the end; one should then cause the bleeding of these [limbs] and apply sudation. For massage, oil that subdues *vāta* should be used, and for drinking, the five-fold preparation (*pañcaka*) of *rāsnā*, *śatāvarī*, the two types of *bala*, *pippalī*, and *puṣkaramūla*. This powder, taken with castor oil (*eraṇḍataila*), removes *gṛdhrasī*; furthermore, the powder beginning with *ajamoda* is prescribed for *āmavāta*. That [is the case] here.

The application [of these remedies] serves to ward off *gṛdhrasī* (sciatica); however, if comfort is not produced by these, one should cauterize with an iron rod. (9) In all diseases of the feet, one should perform a transverse cauterization two *aṅgulas* from the two ankles; having observed the vein on the foot, one should cauterize it. (10) One should also employ the wholesome regimens prescribed for wind-diseases (*vātaroga*) here. (11) Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Gṛdhrasī*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. (22)

Chapter Twenty-three. Ātreya said: Blood becomes aggravated in the body by pungent, alkaline, sour, and salty substances, or through suppression [of natural urges], restraint, or the indulgence in sleeping during the day and similar habits. (1) When a simultaneous provocation of Vāyu is observed in every limb of men, it is called Vātarakta, which manifests in the bodies of men. (2) O best of physicians, it arises in those who are delicate, as well as in women; moreover, Vāta-śoṇita is especially aggravated in those who are corpulent. (3) There is also lassitude, itching, and the appearance of circular patches (maṇḍalas).

One should recognize vātarakta by discoloration, throbbing, swelling, emaciation, burning sensation, and softness; likewise, by the darkening of the teeth and blood. Having observed these distinct symptoms, a remedy must be administered. (5) One should prescribe purgation, bloodletting, and drinks, ointments, and electuaries; one should also give milk mixed with coriander (*dhānya*) and ginger (*nāgara*). (6) Having boiled the leaves of *paṭolī* and *nimba*, they should be taken with honey as a digestive for those suffering from vātarakta, as well as other pacifying treatments. (7) [This should be done] after grinding [the herbs] with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

The leaves of *picumanda* are recommended as an ointment for the alleviation of *vātarakta* (gout/rheumatism). (8) *Dūrvā*, *mūrvā*, *śaṭhī*, dry ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), coriander (*dhānyaka*), and liquorice (*madhuyaṣṭikā*)—these, when ground with cold water, form a paste to be applied as a plaster for *vātarakta*. (9) One *karṣa* of coriander and the two types of cumin (*jīra*), cooked with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be administered for consumption to pacify the humors in cases of *vātarakta*. (10) If no relief is obtained by these means, then bloodletting (*raktāvasecana*) should be performed; furthermore, one should provide the wholesome diets prescribed for fever in this condition as well. (11)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Raktavāta," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-four. Ātreya said: Due to the consumption of jaggery and sour foods, as well as those indicated by incompatible diets (viruddhāhāra), the acid bile (*amlapitta*) becomes provoked; by this, the throat is scorched. A burning sensation arises in his heart, as does pain in the head; he emits sour eructations, and even sour *hikkā* (hiccup) rushes up to the throat. Listen now to the remedy for that: one should quickly induce emesis. When the acid bile has moved downward, a purgative (*vireka*) is administered. One should drink a decoction of *pāribhadra* leaves and *āmalaka* fruits.

It should be administered; it removes *amlapitta*. A decoction of *paṭola* and *pāṭalā*, combined with *dhānya* and *nāgara*, is declared to be beneficial when taken with water for the alleviation of *amlapitta*. A decoction of *paṭola*, *viśva*, *amṛtavallī*, *tiktā*, *patrā*, *nimba*, and *vatsaka* destroys *amlapitta* caused by *visarpa*, as well as circular skin eruptions (*maṇḍala*) and *idārū*. At night, a digestive stimulant (*sampācana*) mixed with the paste of *dhānya* and *nāgara* should be given. Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of *Amlapitta*," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-five. Ātreya said: Swelling (śopha) occurs when the strength is diminished and the channels of the sense organs and body hair are obstructed by the consumption of sour, pungent, and hot substances; likewise, from the use of cold, clear, and slimy things; or from dryness, injury, falling, or from the retention [of urine or feces]. In a person whose wind (vāta) has entered the stomach (āmāśaya) but subsequently rushes to the extremities, this disorder of the humors (doṣa) arises; it manifests as a swelling affecting the hands and feet either individually or produced by two humors combined. Such is the movement of the swelling-disorder in a man.

Swellings arising internally may be curable when they are localized on the face; however, those that spread throughout the entire body, or occur on the feet in women or on the face in men, are incurable. This same swelling produced by blood occurs in cases of wasting (kṣaya), vāta, abdominal tumors (gulma), consumption (rājayakṣman), and abdominal enlargements (udara); it is a formidable disorder characterized by various types of swelling. Other swellings that ascend upward and arise from phlegm (śleṣman) and bile (pitta) should be known as difficult to cure and accompanied by many complications, especially when the phlegm has reached the head.

When [the humor] is located in the *pakvāśaya* (large intestine), swelling arises in the middle [of the body]; even when the waste has moved downward, [swelling occurs]. When it is in the *rasa* (plasma), swellings follow all [parts], as the *rasas* follow the entire body. Thus, there are swellings of the whole body and swellings of the middle [body]. Swellings of the whole body should be avoided, as well as those occurring in the elderly or children, those born of injury, those arising from wasting (*kṣaya*), and those accompanied by vomiting, diarrhea, and dyspnea. That swelling which arises in a person suffering from giddiness, fever, or emaciation, and that which occurs in one who has already developed [another] swelling, is incurable; furthermore, that which is caused by no other [single] humor is likewise not curable for the physician.

O best of physicians, [this condition] is to be treated as follows: from Vāta arise piercing pain, dryness, and labored breathing; from Pitta, fatigue, swelling, and a burning sensation; and in the Kapha type, there is coldness, heaviness, distress, and itching. That which arises from two [humors] possesses the characteristics of both. Therefore, I shall describe its treatment: fomentation, digestion-promoting therapy, purification, purgation, and bloodletting; this is the prescribed regimen for swellings caused by decoctions. Neither oleation nor drying therapy should be performed in this case. [The herbs] Punarnavā and Magadhajā...

A decoction of the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), nimba, *abhayā*, *kaṭukā*, *paṭola*, and *dārvī*, boiled until pleasantly warm, quickly causes the swelling and abdominal enlargement of a person to subside through its digestive action. (13) Punarnavā, *guḍūcī*, and *guggulu* taken as an equal paste destroy swellings caused by the humors (*doṣas*), abdominal tumors (*gulma*), and this type of *udara* caused by phlegm (*kapha*). (14) The urine of an elephant, a buffalo, or a bull, as well as parched grain (*lāja*) with *kaṇā*, should be used for drinking; or milk mixed with castor oil will cause the swelling to depart quickly. (15)

In that case, the procedure of fomentation (saṃsvedana) should be performed repeatedly, either with castor leaves or with tamarind leaves. Alternatively, having boiled hairy bitter gourd (kaṭutumbī) with either sour gruel (kāñjika) or water, one should apply fomentation with that same warm liquid. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Swelling" (śophacikitsā), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-Six. Ātreya said: By those treatments that provoke swelling (śvayathu), the Vāyu becomes aggravated; due to impaired and irregular digestion, a Gulma arises in the abdomen. One should diagnose Vāta-gulma by the rumbling of the abdomen, the observation of irregular digestion, pricking pain (todo) in the body, and colic (śūla). Emaciation, restlessness, a yellowish tint, affliction with mild fever, darkness of vision, vertigo, thirst, and pain—such a Gulma is born from Pitta. Emaciation, numbness, nausea, drowsiness, laziness, and a sensation of cold [are the signs].

Slow digestion, constipation, and abdominal tumors (gulma) arising from phlegm (kapha); delusion, confusion, dullness, restlessness, hunger, thirst, laziness, excessive sleep, and fainting—these characterize a gulma caused by phlegm and bile (kapha-paittika). Excessive sleep, laziness, burning sensations, swelling, pain, fever, discoloration, restlessness, dullness, constipation, deformity of the limbs, diarrhea, fainting, thirst, nausea, trembling, dyspnea, loss of appetite, and indigestion—these characterize a gulma caused by the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika). This [first type] is curable.

A dual disorder (*dvandva*) arising from a single *doṣa* is cured with difficulty; that which arises from *sannipāta* (the combination of all three) is incurable. We shall now describe its treatment. (8) The very same treatment prescribed for liver disease (*yakṛt*) and *grahaṇī* is declared [for this], along with fasting (*upavāraṇa*); likewise, splenic enlargement (*plīhā*) is described, and nothing further needs to be said here. (9) Now listen as the treatment for abdominal enlargement (*udara*) and abdominal tumors (*gulma*) is explained: oleation (*snehana*), drying (*rūkṣaṇa*), digestive processing (*pācana*), and purifications (*śodhana*); (10) pacification (*saṃśamana*), purgation (*vireka*), enemas (*basti*), oleation and drying [enemas], the drinking of alkali (*kṣāra*), and medicinal powders (*cūrṇa*).

The procedure for the treatment of *gulma* (abdominal tumors): 11. A decoction should be prepared from ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), *dāru*, *surasā*, *mūrvā*, and the "small five-roots" (*laghu-pañcamūla*), reduced to one-eighth. To this, an equal amount of milk should be added, 12. as well as an equal amount of curd and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). One should cook it over a moderate fire until the clarified butter is clearly visible; then it is declared ready. 13. This should be administered as a drink, for massage, or applied to the vessel [of the abdomen]. Since there are seven types of unctuous substances (*sneha*), drying therapy (*rūkṣaṇa*) is beneficial following that. 14. This should be performed for three days; I shall now explain it here.

One who is skilled [in treatment] should prescribe *śuṇṭhī*, *sauvarcala* salt, the two types of *jīra* (cumin and black cumin), combined with *hiṅgu*, along with *kāñjika* as a drink; this drying therapy brings relief to *gulma*. For the treatment of *gulma*, the process of alkali-burning (*kṣārapāka*) is applied here. One should mix the alkali of *palāśa*, *arjuna*, and *sūraṇa*, as well as the alkali of *sahā* and *yavaśūka*, with *sauvarcala*, rock salt (*sindhuja*), *udbhida*, or sea salt (*sāmudra*). Having strained the liquid according to the prescribed method, these should be combined with the medicinal herbs.

A powder consisting of *pathyā*, *agni*, *śuṇṭhī*, *rajanī*, *surāhva*, *kuṣṭha*, *viśālā*, *javānikā*, *ajamodā*, the two types of *jīraka*, and *ṣaḍgranthikā*, combined with *hiṅgu* and drunk mixed with alkaline water, destroys all diseases arising in the abdominal cavity (18–19). It destroys all types of *gulma*, cholera (*viṣūcikā*), indigestion, colic, fistula-in-ano (*bhagaṃdara*), splenic enlargement, abdominal distension, and constipation; it eradicates these three groups of diseases in men (20). [Also, a powder of] *pathyā*, *samaṅgā*, *kalasī*, *vṛṣa*, and *mahauṣadha*...

Vātaviṣā and surāhvā should indeed be boiled in water; this drink is a digestive stimulant for diseases of the abdominal lumps (gulma). (21) A decoction of vacā, yavānī, trikaṭu, and daśamūlī is prescribed; or alternatively, a warm decoction of dhānyaka and nāgara is beneficial as a drink. (22) In all types of vāta-gulma and in irregular fevers (viṣama-jvara), the five-fold compound beginning with rāsnā is a digestive stimulant for vāta-gulma. (23) Śaṭhī, sauvarcala salt, and śuṇṭhī are also digestive stimulants for one suffering from gulma. (24) Likewise, vidulā, drākṣā, kaṭukā, and nimba leaves [are used].

A digestive medicine with jaggery (guḍa) should be given to a patient suffering from a Pitta-type abdominal tumor (gulma). A paste of *dhātrī* (myrobalan) mixed with sugar is a digestive remedy for a Pitta-type gulma. Yavānī, ugragandhā, and the three pungents (*kaṭukatraya*) should be drunk warm at night as a digestive medicine for a Kapha-type gulma. A powder consisting of ginger (*nāgara*), *krimijit* (viḍaṅga), and *pathyā* (harītakī), combined with three times the amount of *trivṛt*, mixed with jaggery, should be administered as a purgative for Vata-type gulma. One part of *dantī*, two parts of *harītakī*, and three parts of *trivṛt* [should be used].

One should take exactly four parts of dry ginger (28), mix them all together with an equal amount of jaggery, and eat a bolus (vaṭaka) in the morning; one should drink water over it, boiled for the purpose of purgation, to pacify vāta-gulma (29). One should drink castor oil combined with sugar and milk for the purgation of pitta-gulma; this is excellent and brings comfort (30-31). Likewise, the tender sprouts of *āragvadha* and the bark of *āragvadha* should be processed with castor oil and wrapped in castor leaves (32).

Having smeared it with mud and placed it upon glowing coals, one should cook the *bharjikā* until well-steamed; this should then be eaten mixed with sugar. (33) Purgation is beneficial for a *gulma* caused by *pitta*; pure purgatives are likewise recommended. (34) Having prepared a powder of *triphalā*, *surasā*, and *śuṇṭhī*, one should saturate it once with the milky sap of *snuhī*. When mixed with jaggery, this acts as a purgative for a *gulma* caused by *śleṣman* and destroys all types of abdominal enlargements (*udara*). (35–36) [The powder consists of] *śuṇṭhī*, *sauvarcala* salt, *pathyā*, *viḍaṅga*, *punarnavā*, and the seeds of *apāmārga*. (37)

One should eat [the powder] processed with the milky sap of *snuhī* (37) combined with jaggery, and afterwards drink warm water; this purgative is praised as beneficial for all types of abdominal tumors (*gulma*). [The following ingredients should be used: *śuktikṣāra*, *niśā*, *viśāla*, *kadala*, *sūraṇa*, *kokilākṣa*, *pālāśa*, *dahanārjuna*, *śaṭhī*, *jayā*, *apāmārga*, and *kūṣmāṇḍaka*.

Hingu (Asafoetida) that has been burnt, processed with alkali, and well-squeezed, combined with the three pungents (trikaṭu), removes abdominal tumors, distension, constipation, and colic, and is beneficial for all types of abdominal enlargements (udararoga). Ajamodā, śaṭhī, dantī, viḍaṅga, kuṣṭha, tumburu, the three myrobalans (triphalā), citraka, śuṇṭhī, and karkaṭaśṛṅgikā; trivṛtā, surāhvā, puṣkaramūla, vṛddhadāru, as well as amlavetasa, tintiḍīka, and ciñcinī—these should be taken in equal parts and mixed together with citron (mātuluṅga).

Powdered [with these ingredients] and combined with one-third *hiṅgu* and ghee, it is beneficial; it destroys *vāta-gulma*, as well as abdominal pain accompanied by colic. (42) *Hiṅgu*, the three myrobalans (*phalatrika*), the two types of *jīraka*, *citraka*, *bhārṅgī*, *kuṣṭha*, *viḍaṅga*, *tumburu*, *puṣkara*, *viśva*, *surāhva*, along with alkali and the five salts—this [mixture], when taken with fermented rice-gruel (*āranāla*), destroys *vātika-gulma* and the pain of colic for men. (43–44) *Hiṅgu*, *sauvarcala* salt, *ajājī*, *viśvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *viḍaṅga*, when drunk with *āranāla*, destroy *gulma*.

A linctus consisting of *sāvarikā* (45 parts), two parts of *jīraka*, *trikaṭu*, *śaṭhī*, *tumburu*, and *citraka*, taken with honey, is beneficial for a *gulma* of pitta-nature and serves to alleviate swelling. (46) A powder of *yaṣṭimadhu*, nimba leaves, as well as *dhātrī* fruit, and sugar, licked with honey, is a remedy for pitta-type *gulma*. (47) A powder combined with *trikaṭu*, *triphalā*, *citraka*, and the fruit of the *vaṭaka* tree, when drunk with wine or with a decoction of the *vaṭaka* fruit, is beneficial. (48) This is wholesome and brings comfort for the destruction of kapha-type *gulma*. (49) [Also] *rodhra*...

A powder of *kamala*, *viśvā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *citraka*, combined with *nāgara* and *hiṅgu* and mixed with urine, destroys *śleṣma-gulma* (phlegmatic abdominal tumors) and relieves colic and abdominal diseases. (50) One should drink *ugragandhā*, *marica*, and alkaline powder (*kṣāra-cūrṇa*) combined with urine; this destroys *śleṣma-gulma*. (51–52) A powder consisting of *śuṇṭhī*, *sauvarcala*, *bhārṅgī*, *vatsaka*, *yāvaśūka*, the two types of *jīra*, *āṭarūṣa*, *yavānī*, *hiṅgu*, *saindhava*, and *āragvadha* [is likewise effective]. (53)

In cases where a gulma arises from vāta and śleṣman, [the aforementioned treatment] combined with ghee brings about relief quickly and easily. (54) Ugragandhā, triphalā, devadāru, punarnavā, trivṛt, and sauvarcala salt, combined with alkaline water (kṣārodaka), when drunk, is considered an excellent remedy that brings comfort in gulma caused by vāta and kapha. (55) If the therapeutic measures for grahaṇī and gulma are applicable here, they should be employed; furthermore, purgation (virecana) should be administered in all cases of swelling and abdominal enlargement (śophodara). (56) A person afflicted with both swelling and diarrhea who suffers from gulma and udara is destroyed; for such a person, the drinking of alkaline water is the remedy.

The powder of *bṛhat*, *hiṅgu*, and other ingredients (57), or likewise that of *ajamodā* and others, is for the pacification of swelling (*śopha*) and diarrhea (*atisāra*). Although vomiting (*vamī*) and diarrhea also occur in cases of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), one should recognize them as curable by this [remedy]; however, if the treatment is beneficial, it may be declared incurable. One should drink *guḍa*, *dāḍima*, and *pathyā* combined with honey (59). One should administer this repeatedly for both vomiting and diarrhea. A tumor (*gulma*) accompanied by all symptoms is of the *sānnipātika* type (60), characterized by piercing pain (*todo*), restlessness (*arati*), discoloration (*vivarṇatva*), fainting (*mūrchā*), diarrhea, vomiting, and excessive moisture (*kleda*).

Lassitude as well; that which is born from the three *doṣas* is incurable. 61. Listen now with an attentive mind, O son of great wisdom, for the procedure for the removal of swelling in men shall be explained by me, the knower. 62. Likewise, *trivṛt* combined with jaggery and subsequently drunk with lukewarm water destroys abdominal disease along with swelling; or it causes the *pitta*-derived [swelling] to leave men. 63. *Harītakī*, *trivṛt*, and *śuṇṭhī* combined with jaggery likewise destroy swelling; and the two sets of five roots (*pañcamūla*) boiled [and taken]...

Warm castor oil relieves swelling (64). Varuṇa oil mixed with cow’s urine is beneficial when drunk and destroys swelling (65). One suffering from the disease of swelling should avoid: meat of domestic or marshy animals, salt, dried vegetables, fresh grain, products of molasses, flour-based foods, curd, rice-and-pulse porridge, waterless wine, food, grains, dried meat, heavy and unwholesome items, burning foods, sleeping at night, and sexual intercourse (66). An ointment of *aruṣkara* destroys swelling.

In cases of dryness caused by poison, the pacifying treatments prescribed for poison should be employed; these include fasting, digestive stimulants, unctuous substances, warm applications, and the soothing of Vāta. However, nourishing food is beneficial for those suffering from all types of Gulma (abdominal tumors). One suffering from Gulma should not eat dried meat, radish, fish, dried vegetables, or pulses. Furthermore, one with Gulma should not consume *vāluka* (a type of grain), nor sweet or *samāna* (neutral) foods. In the case of blood-associated Gulma (*saraktagulma*), however, digestive stimulants (*pācana*) are not to be used.

Drinking asafoetida, moving the hips, fomentation, and massage are beneficial; likewise, walking and jumping are not [recommended], though they may be wholesome in certain cases. (71) A decoction of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, *khadira*, *māgadhikā*, and *samaṅgā*, combined with sour vetasa, honey, and ghee, quickly destroys abdominal tumors (*gulma*) even when accompanied by blood, dries up moisture in the heart, and subdues provoked blood. (72) Milk mixed with ghee and black salt (*sauvarcala*) should be administered for the destruction of blood-born tumors (*raktagulma*), or even in cases arising from injuries to the liver. (73) And not...

For gulma born of blood or from injury, food combined with asafoetida is wholesome, provided it is neither hot nor burning; meat from wild animals is also beneficial. Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Gulma," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Twenty-Seven. Ātreya said: From sitting in an uneven posture, or from drinking water [at improper times], or when one has emerged from exhaustion, travel, or labored breathing, or even when one has over-exerted oneself—if water is drunk under such conditions, it leads to *jalodara* (water-belly). When the abdomen contains water, it produces a gurgling sound; the swelling greatly increases, and there is edema in the feet—these are the symptoms of *jalodara*. One should administer purgation and emesis, and cause digestive treatments (*pācana*) to be performed; furthermore, a pill (*vaṭaka*) prepared with an alkali formulation (*kṣārayoga*) pacifies that condition. Therefore, [it should be treated] at the fold of skin below the navel.

Leaving aside a space of one finger-breadth and taking account of the water-channel, one should wrap it with a blade of *kuśa* grass. (4) A wise man should insert a castor-oil stalk (*eraṇḍa-nāḍī*) there; once the internal water has been drained, he should then quickly apply a bandage. (5) When that [stalk] no longer remains [in place], then cauterization (*dāha*) is recommended; having strained the paste of *kaṇā*, four times as much clarified butter (*ghṛta*) should be added. (6) Having cooked it with an equal amount of *śuṇṭhī* and *viṣā*, drinking it or applying it as an ointment is beneficial. The best of physicians should perform surgical intervention (*śastra-karma*) only when [the condition] is properly diagnosed. (7) It is difficult to accomplish.

One should not perform surgical intervention in every case; for where there is no action, death is certain, whereas where there is action, there is doubt [as to the outcome]. Therefore, the physician must certainly act, having the Lord as his witness. Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Jalodara (Ascites)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The twenty-eighth chapter. Ātreya said: Thus, there are twenty types of *prameha* (urinary disorders) in men; here are their characteristics. From physical exhaustion, sexual indulgence, as well as from the consumption of food that is contrary to the heat of summer, or that is sharp and hot, or from wine, or the habitual use of milk and pungent substances, the onset of *meha* is described by the lords of sages. *Jalaprameha*, *rudhiraprameha*, *pūyaprameha*, *lavaṇaprameha*, *takraprameha*, *khaṭikāprameha*, and *śukraprameha* have been described previously. There would also be *śarkarāmeha* and *avasāprameha*.

One should recognize *rasaprameha*, *anyaghṛtaprameha*, *pittaprameha*, *kaphaprameha*, and *madhuprameha*. O best of physicians, these [disorders] quickly produce symptoms corresponding to their names as well as a loss of strength within the body; therefore, one should apply therapeutic measures for their pacification according to their causes. For *jalaprameha*, a decoction of *dhava*, *arjuna*, *candana*, *śāla*, and *vallī* is beneficial; for *raktaprameha*, cold milk mixed with grapes, *yaṣṭimadhu*, and *candana* is recommended.

In *pūyameha*, sexual indulgence is minimal, and a decoction of *dhava* and *arjuna* is beneficial; for *lavaṇameha*, a decoction of *dūrvā*, *kaseruka*, *kadalī*, *nalinī*, and salt is prescribed. (7) Decoctions of *kadamba*, *śāla*, *arjuna*, *dīpyaka*, *viḍaṅga*, *dārvī*, *dhava*, and *śallakī*—all these should likewise be consumed with honey in cases of *kapha-prameha*. (8) For *rodhra-arjuna-meha*, milk from the leaves of *ariṣṭa* is used; for that same [condition], *dhātrī*, *phala*, and *candana* are also indicated. In *takrameha*, chalk (*khaṭikā*) is beneficial, and a decoction with jaggery (*guḍa*) and *avaṭa* should be administered for *khaṭikā-prameha*.

9. Dūrvā, mūrvā, the roots of kuśa and kāśa, dantī, samaṅgā, and śālmalī—this decoction boiled with water is beneficial as a drink for *śukra-prameha* (semenuria), or it is beneficial for *rudhira-prameha* (hematuria). 10. A decoction of the three fruits (*phalatrika*), the root of *āragvadha*, *mūrvā*, the leaves of *śobhāñjana* and *ariṣṭa*, along with *mocā* and grapes, is used for the prevention of *sarpir-prameha* (ghee-like urine). 11. A decoction of *kuṣṭha*, *parpaṭaka*, *tiktā*, and sugar, boiled with a large quantity of water, combined with *mūrvā*, *ariṣṭā*, and *pāṭalikā* [is also used].

A decoction of *durālabhā*, *kiṃśuka*, and *ṭuṇṭuka* is always beneficial for *rasaprameha*. 12. The wise declare that for the alleviation of *pittaprameha*, one should boil *nīlotpala*, *arjuna*, *kaliṅga*, *dhava*, *amlīkā*, *dhātrī* fruits, and *picumanda* leaves in water; this, when taken with sugar, is said to cure it. 13. A decoction of *viḍaṅga*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *kaṅkola*, *kadamba*, *rodhra*, *aśana*, and *vṛkṣaka* taken with water is beneficial for men and destroys their *kaphaprameha*. 14. [Likewise, a decoction of] *mustā*, the three fruits (*phalatrika*), and *niśā*...

A decoction prepared with *suradāru*, *mūrvā*, and *indrayava* with the water of *rodhra* is beneficial when drunk for all diseases arising from urinary disorders (*meha*), and it should be administered to relieve all types of urinary retention (*mūtragraha*). (15) Furthermore, a powder of *abhayā*, iron filings, and *nikumbha*, combined with sugar, is beneficial; they say that a linctus made from the three fruits (*phalatrika*) with honey is beneficial in all forms of *prameha*. (16) In cases of *madhumeha*, the wise physician should prescribe the drinking of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), or milk mixed with sugar, or a decoction, or medicinal pills. (17)

Nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, āragvadha, tuṇṭuka, piyāla, kukubha, jambū, kapittha, and āmrātaka; (18) madhuka, yaṣṭimadhuka, rodhra, pāribhadraka, paṭola, cāriṇī, dantī, and meṣaviṣāṇikā; (19) citraka, karañja, śakrāhva, along with triphalā, bhallātaka, the three aromatics (trigandha), and the three pungents (kaṭukatraya)—(20) these should be given as a fine powder, this "Nyagrodhādi" group being highly efficacious when combined with honey.

It destroys diabetes mellitus (madhumeha). 21. Whether as a decoction, an oil preparation, or even a ghee preparation, it is recommended for drinking and massage; it truly destroys diseases arising from the urine. 22. This powder, beginning with *nyagrodha* (the *nyagrodhādi* group), should be drunk mixed with milk; when combined according to availability, there is nothing else that is better for diabetes mellitus. 23–24. Honey, mineral honey (*dhātumākṣīka*), *śilodbheda*, bitumen (*śilājatu*), sandalwood, red mineral (*raktadhātu*), camphor, long pepper (*kaṇā*), bamboo manna (*vaṃśarocanaka*), and [other ingredients] should be taken with milk.

One should drink this together; it removes honey-like urinary disorders (madhu-prameha), and one is liberated from diseases of the urine. (25) Now we shall describe the treatment for the pustules of prameha. A decoction of *dhava*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *badarī*, *khadira*, *śiṃśapā*, and *pāribhadraka* is excellent for cleansing the urinary tract. (26) The inner bark of *arjuna*, *kadamba*, and *ṭiṇṭukī* is recommended for cleansing the urinary tract during the healing stage, for the purpose of purifying pus. (27) One should take the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, as well as the leaves of *surasā*, *niṣpāva*, and *paṭola*.

Having ground these with *kāñjika* (sour gruel), it is an ointment for *vātapiṭikās* (wind-blisters) and for the penis. Likewise, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, *kuṣṭha*, *candana*, *raktacandana*, *uśīra*, *kattṛṇa*, red mineral (*raktadhātu*), and lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*)—O best of physicians, when combined with the cream of milk according to availability, this ointment pacifies the burning sensation of the penis caused by *pitta* and blood. Bathing with cold milk and rubbing with fresh butter [is beneficial]. Also, *kaṇa*, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, oil-cake, the leaves of pomegranate (*dāḍima*), and [the bark] of *khadira* [are used].

Likewise, having ground the leaves of *dalā* and *āmalakī* with warm water, one should use them for washing during the ripening of *meha*. Alternatively, the powder of *triphalā* prevents the drying of pus; it should be used for washing with *kāñjika*, or with buttermilk, or with water from boiled rice-husks (33–34). Washing during the ripening of *meha* should also be done with very cold water. For food, red *śāli* rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, *āḍhakī* (pigeon pea), or *kulattha* (horse gram) are prescribed, along with some sweet ghee. Furthermore, alkaline, sour, or pungent substances, as well as sleeping during the day, must especially be avoided (35–36).

Beholding women, sexual intercourse, as well as overeating, walking, running, and likewise the suppression of the urge to urinate; the wind from clothing and red garments—the best of physicians should avoid these. Singing, women, children, and amorous play within a secluded house or the interior of the home; ornaments, betel, and the wasting away caused by anger—one should keep these far away if one desires happiness and prosperity. A decoction of the two types of turmeric, ginger, viḍaṅga, and harītakī is prescribed for *kapha*-type urinary disorders (*prameha*).

One suffering from *pītaprameha* (urinary disorders characterized by yellow urine) should drink a decoction of blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), *uśīra*, *pathyā*, *āmalaka*, and *mustaka*, mixed with honey. (40–41) Likewise, for *pittaprameha* (urinary disorders caused by *pitta*), this decoction of *kamala*, *rodhra*, *uśīra*, and *arjuna*, taken with honey, is prescribed. (42) The fresh juice of *āmalaka* mixed with honey, or the powder of *harītakī*, wards off all types of urinary disorders. (43) One should drink the powdered mixture of *khadira*, sugar, *dāruharidrā*, and *musta*.

For the pacification of all urinary disorders (prameha): 44. Kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, devadāru, pāṭhā, guḍūcī, triphalā, and musta—indeed, the powder of these mixed with honey removes urinary disorders (mūtraprameha) and pain. 45. Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Prameha," in the third section of the Hārīta-uttara as spoken by Ātreya. 28.

Chapter Twenty-nine. Ātreya said: A powder of *elā*, *śilājatu*, *māgadhikā*, and *pāṣāṇabheda*, when drunk with rice-water, certainly cures the disease of *prameha*. (1) The roots of *eraṇḍa*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, *gokṣuraka*, as well as *elā*, *āṭarūṣa*, and *pippalī*, combined with *yaṣṭīmadhu*—(2) a person should drink the decoction of these mixed with *śilāditya*. [In cases of] urinary stones (*aśmarī*) and gravel (*śarkarā*), two *palas* of sugar [should be added]; (3) very cold water in the measure of one *karṣa* removes dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*).

Iron powder mixed with curd and water provides relief. (4) For dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), one should drink a powder of *yavakṣāra* combined with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*). One should also take *kūṣmāṇḍa* along with sugar and drink it; this indeed wards off dysuria arising from the three *doṣas*. (5–6) One should drink the root of *śatāvarī* ground into a powder and mixed with cold water. Therefore, for one suffering from the disease of gravel (*śarkarā*), one should employ sugar [as a remedy]. A decoction of *āragvadha* fruit and root, *durālabhā*, coriander (*dhānyaka*), *śatāvarī*, (7) *pāṣāṇabheda*, and *pathyā*—this is the [prescribed] decoction.

In cases of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), *pāṣāṇabheda*, *trivṛtā*, *pathyā*, *durālabhā*, *gokṣura*, and *puṣkara* [should be used]; or a decoction of *elā*, *kuruṇṭaka*, and the seeds of *karkaṭī* for severely obstructed urine. A decoction of *paṭolī* root combined with *kulattha* beans and mixed with *puṣkara* root, when administered repeatedly, destroys urinary disorders (*prameha*) and stone diseases. He who drinks the root of *mātuluṅgikā* with water that has stood overnight, his suffering arising from internal gravel (*śarkarā*) is instantly dissolved. [The root] ground with cow’s buttermilk...

One who is afflicted by the disorder caused by sugar should drink the medicine known as Kṣipranāmaka quickly, and buttermilk after a long interval. Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Dysuria," in the third section of the Hārīta-uttara as spoken by Ātreya. 29.

Chapter Thirty. Ātreya said: One should drink the seeds of *karkaṭikā* mixed with *triphalā* and rock salt (*saindhava*), powdered and taken with warm water; when drunk, it brings relief from the obstruction of urine (1). The man who drinks the alkali of *tila* stalks mixed with curd and honey destroys the obstruction of urine and immediately attains comfort (2). One should drink *jātī* root ground with goat’s milk, because it pacifies burning sensations, heat in the urine, and pain (3). [One should take] *padminīkanda* cooked with oil and mixed with matured cow’s urine.

One should drink [this] in cases of urinary obstruction accompanied by intense pain. Due to substances that aggravate pitta, such as those with pungent or sour tastes and colors, or even from consorting with fair-skinned women, blood may also flow out. Furthermore, through the drinking of hot liquor or by those afflicted by fatigue and physical exertion, pitta is quickly provoked and causes dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra). Because of this, one urinates with difficulty, a stream of warm [blood] flows forth, it obstructs the urinary channels, and blood also flows out. I shall now describe the medicine for that, by which—

Happiness is attained. (7) Yaṣṭīmadhuka, Mṛdvīkā, and Candana, along with Raktacandana, taken with the water of red rice, removes the pain of dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*). (8) This linctus, consisting of sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree combined with grapes and sugar, destroys dysuria; it is the best among physicians. (9) It is declared to be a pacifier of the body when [the condition] is provoked by immersion in cold water; furthermore, in cases of dysuria, a sweet diet is said to be beneficial. (10) When there is an obstruction of urine due to the breaking of intercourse while lying on one's back, or from burning sensations born of physical exertion, *vacā* [is the remedy]. (11)

One should provide various obstructive measures there. In a person who does not exercise, eats wholesome food, and bathes in cold water, the provoked Vāyu, accompanied by Kapha, blocks the urinary passage; this most wicked disease is said to be extremely difficult to cure. Listen now to its remedy: a decoction enema (anuvāsana) or a non-unctuous enema (nirūha), as well as the procedure for urinary obstruction, all types of sudation, and staying in a place that is like a narrow path. Riding horses, carts, and running are also considered beneficial.

A decoction of the three myrobalans (*phalatrika*) with an equal amount of jaggery, taken with milk or meat broth, cures urinary obstructions; or, in cases arising from *pitta*, one may take it with salt and sour substances. A decoction of *pāṭalā*, *ṭuṇṭukā*, nimba, and *gokṣuraka*, along with cardamom (*elā*), cinnamon bark (*tvak*), and cinnamon leaves (*patra*), combined with the three myrobalans and jaggery, when drunk, destroys urinary obstruction. Furthermore, [the above] combined with pomegranate and sour substances is beneficial for men suffering from urinary pain. A decoction of the three myrobalans, sugarcane, and sugar, together with jaggery and rock salt (*saindhava*), wards off the retention of urine.

Either *pathyā* (haritaki) combined with jaggery, or the administration of *todana*, and sexual intercourse with a woman [should be practiced]. By this, comfort will quickly arise, as well as the massaging of the women's vulva. Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Obstruction," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 30.

Chapter Thirty-One. Ātreya said: The disease of *aśmarī* (urinary calculi) arises due to defects in the father or mother, from the obstruction of urine, or from the practice of unwholesome habits. (1) If the parents engage in sexual intercourse while their urine is suppressed, the embryo, joined and permeated by that urine, is expelled. (2) In one whose body [is thus affected], five [types of calculi] may arise; it produces an obstruction of the urine in three locations. (3) That urinary disease is incurable when it occurs in a human being during youth, even if it is slight. (4)

Furthermore, urinary gravel (mūtraśarkarā) arises as a curable condition [when the following occurs]: when the woman or the man lies on their back in a contrary position, his semen flows forth and the woman extracts that semen. Again, due to Vāta, blood enters the penis; these two substances, having been introduced, reach the opening of the urethra and obstruct it. Because of that, obstruction of urine and intense pain arise. The gravel, situated at the joint of the testicles, moves and becomes treatable by surgical means (śastrasādhyakā). Therefore, O son, listen as I describe the medicinal treatment.

Mahāmati, a decoction of *śuṇṭhī*, *gokṣuraka*, and the bark of *varuṇa*, combined with jaggery and alkali from barley, destroys urinary calculi (*aśmarī*). [Likewise,] a decoction of *kuśa*, *kāśa*, *nala*, bamboo, *agnimantha*, *akṣa*, and *nṛttaka*; or *śvadaṃṣṭrā*, *moraṭā*, and *pāṣāṇabheda*; or a decoction of *palāśa* and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) mixed with jaggery—when drunk, these destroy stone in the bladder and alleviate pain in the bladder. [Also,] *elā*, *kaṇā*, *vṛṣa*, *trikaṇṭaka*, *reṇukā*, *pāṣāṇabheda*, *madhuka*, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*).

A decoction consisting of castor oil, *kaśilājatu*, sugar, and other ingredients likewise destroys urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), as does its warm administration. (12) The powder of *gokṣuraka* seeds combined with metallic gold (*dhātumākṣika*), when drunk with buffalo milk, causes the falling out of stones. (13) The surgical procedure is described in the *Uttaratantra* and is also recorded in the chapter on clarified butter (*ghṛta*) in the *Sūtrasthāna*. (14) Old *ṣaṣṭika* rice, red rice, *śyāmāka*, *kodrava*, *dāla*, *markaṭī*, and grass-grains (*tṛṇadhānyaka*) [are recommended]. (15)

The physician should prescribe barley, wheat, horse-gram (*kulattha*), and likewise *āḍhakī*, which remove wind (*vāta*), in the diet of those suffering from wind disorders. (16) Furthermore, the meats of the *krauñca* crane and others are wholesome for the destruction of urinary calculi (*aśmarī*). (17) Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Urinary Calculi," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 31.

Chapter Thirty-two. Ātreya said: Henceforth, O best of physicians, the enlargement of the scrotum (vṛddhi) is described. In childhood, it arises following the testicles due to the defects of the mother or the father. Furthermore, through corrupted sexual intercourse, the vāta situated in the bladder reaches the site of the scrotum and indeed causes its enlargement. There are types caused by each of the [three] doṣas individually, and the fourth is that caused by the combination of all three (sannipātika). Those arising from pitta and those from the combination of all doṣas (sannipāta) are considered incurable. O best of physicians, I shall now describe the doṣas and their remedies; listen to them.

Fomentation, oleation, decoctions, and potions are prescribed; O best of physicians, I shall now describe the symptoms of those [afflictions], as well as head-draughts. Trembling occurs from Vāta, while burning fever arises from Pitta (5). From Kapha, there is thickening and dryness, and the testicles become hard. For the purpose of consuming decoctions, a decoction of Rasāla, Shallakī, Tarkārī, and Kaṭutumbikā is used in cases of scrotal enlargement caused by Vāta. Furthermore, immersion in cold water or the application of cold substances is likewise [prescribed]; for a scrotum affected by Pitta, one should apply very cold plasters (6).

It is praised [to treat this] with water mixed with *vacā* salt, along with *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and mustard seeds, and by the use of astringent decoctions; this is said to remove the harmful [condition] of *kapha* in the scrotum. O best of the wise, a decoction of *aruṇa*, *varuṇa*, *kola*, *śāliparṇī*, and *śatāvarī* is prescribed for *pitta*-dominant or *sannipāta*-type enlargement of the scrotum. Furthermore, drinking a decoction of *varuṇa*, *vṛkṣādanī*, *daśamūlī*, and *śatāvarī* is beneficial for the wind-type (*vātika*) enlargement of the scrotum. Through this, comfort is attained; then one should have the surgical procedure performed in the middle of the ear-cavity.

One should extract blood from a vein on the left side for an enlargement of the left scrotum, and from a vein on the right side for an enlargement of the right; or both veins may be pierced, by which means relief will be obtained. Thus has the procedure for *caṇḍakriyā* been described, and it is intended for the patient whose condition has been diagnosed. Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Scrotal Enlargement (*vṛṣaṇavṛddhi*)," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Thirty-three. Ātreya said: O best of physicians, raktapitta (hemorrhagic disease) becomes aggravated by salty, sour, alkaline, and pungent foods, as well as by heat, sweating, and excessive morbidity. It manifests as visarpa (erysipelas). It should be understood to be of seven types: those arising from the individual doṣas, those born from combinations of two doṣas, another which is purely blood-born, and the seventh from the combination of all three doṣas (sannipāta). Furthermore, others will describe their names individually: Ājñeya, the terrible Granthika, and Kardama. Ājñeya is caused by vāta and pitta; Granthika...

The *kardama* type arises from *pitta* and *śleṣman*; the *sānnipātika* type, arising from *vāta* and *śleṣman*, is terrible. Blood, lymph, skin, and flesh are the corrupted tissues (*dūṣya*), while the three *doṣas* are the impurities; these seven constituents should be known as the origin of the spreading fevers (*visarpa*). A decoction of *nyagrodha*, *bilva*, and *khadira* is beneficial for washing; it may be used with sour *kāñjika*, *picchilā*, or the juice of *sauvīraka*. Washing with the juice of *mātuluṅga* is also recommended for *vāta*-dominant spreading fevers. Washing with milk or cold water is for the *pitta*-dominant spreading fever, and likewise for the *śleṣman*-dominant spreading fever.

A wash (dhāvana) made from *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* is recommended for one suffering from spreading erysipelas (*visarpa*) caused by *sarpis*; or it may be prepared with wine (*surā*) or *sauvīraka* vinegar. (8) Furthermore, a wash is beneficial for that spreading erysipelas arising from the combination of all three humors (*sannipāta-visarpa*), using *yava*, *agnimantha*, *śaṭhī*, *nyagrodha*, and mustard seeds. A decoction of these is beneficial as a wash for spreading erysipelas born of the combined humors. (9) One should grind the five types of cumin (*pañca-jīraka*) and *kapittha* with sour gruel (*kāñjika*). Alternatively, for spreading erysipelas caused by *vāta*, an ointment should be applied using the juice of *mātuluṅga*. (10) Likewise, an ointment consisting of *dhava*, *rodhra*, sesame, *caila*, *vidārī*, and *kaṇṭaka* [should be used].

In cases of Pittaja Visarpa (bilious erysipelas), an ointment made from Guñjā leaves should be applied. Ghee cooked with Saindhava salt, Ariṣṭa, Tumbī, and Paṭola leaves is recommended for application as it wards off all types of Visarpa. In cases of Visarpa born of blood (Raktaja), one should perform bloodletting; thereafter, the smoke of Dhava and Kadamba wood, along with household soot, should always be used. This is declared beneficial when applied as an ointment. Furthermore, washing with fermented rice-gruel (Kāñjika) is advised. Kuṭheraka, Surasa, Cakramarda, the two types of Niśā (turmeric and yellow myrobalan), and mustard seeds should be ground with Kāñjika and used as an ointment.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Visarpa," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 15. *Hitam*.

Chapter Thirty-four. Ātreya said: The disorder arising from *vātarakta* (leprosy) may be of four types; due to the corruption of the odor (*gandhadoṣa*), their names are distinct for each. 1. When small eruptions appear, it is called *kṣudraka*; when terrible ones appear, it is *antaka*; or else there is *anyamasūrikā*. When eruptions resembling mustard seeds are seen on one's body, that is called *vasanta*. 2. That which is even smaller than the *kṣudraka* is declared to arise from the corruption of *pitta* and blood. 3. When eruptions are seen that burn like fire, that is called *agnidagdha*. 4. That [type] spreads excessively and causes constant suffering.

When one’s eruptions are dense and the phlegm ripens uniformly, burning, restlessness, and discoloration arise immediately in him. (5) When eruptions resembling round lentils (*masūraka*) are seen, and they subside quickly through suppuration, that should be known as *masūrikā*. O Great-minded One, I shall describe its treatment according to the rules. (6) One should keep it hidden and well-guarded by means of protective rites; there should be no contact with women, nor with the low-born, nor any social indulgence. (7) A very cool and refreshing place [is required].

One should apply this with great care; furthermore, one should have an ointment applied here for minor afflictions (kṣudropasarga). A plaster made of kuṣṭha, uśīra, nyagrodha, and the bark of udumbara is recommended as a protection against minor afflictions. Milk mixed with honey and sugar is a pleasant drink. One should cause the patient suffering from this minor affliction to drink the juice of jambu and mango sprouts combined with feces, curd, and honey; this destroys diarrhea and the digestive fire. Gokṣura, ativiṣā, karkaṭādyā, and parpaṭaka [should also be used].

This paste should be administered mixed with honey and sugar; likewise, the fresh juice of *harītakī* and *mātuluṅga* combined with sugar [is beneficial]. This is a remedy for the minor affliction (*kṣudraka*) that wards off vomiting and emaciation; it should also be applied as an ointment for the *agnika* affliction. Red sandalwood, *mañjiṣṭhā*, nimba leaves, and *arjuna*—these, when used with milk and fresh butter, constitute a beneficial ointment. Having observed a severe complication, [the physicians] do not employ fomentation, nor massage, nor do they apply an ointment.

Wise physicians should, as appropriate, apply a cleansing wash using forest cow-dung, alkali, and oil; however, one should not perform an oil massage, but rather apply it only as an external ointment. (15–16) A paste composed of *candana*, *madhuka*, *rodhra*, *nyagrodha*, *utpala*, and *sārivā*, combined with honey, removes complications when taken internally. (17) When a complication arises, a severe fever occurs along with blood in the urine; I shall describe its treatment by which one may attain well-being. (18) [The decoction of] *paṭola*, *parpaṭa*, *śuṇṭhī*, *mustā*, and *khadira* in equal parts [is used].

A paste mixed with honey, when drunk, is beneficial and destroys fever. (19) Sandalwood, uśīra, mañjiṣṭhā, puṣkara, and dantadhāvana—this decoction, when drunk with honey, removes fevers caused by complications. (20) In cases of vomiting and diarrhea, drinking pomegranate and *kuṭaja* combined with honey and curd is a remedy that wards off diarrhea. (21) The remaining minor diseases have been described; here, the appropriate treatment should be applied. A single specific treatment for *masūrikā* (smallpox) should be performed according to the prescribed rules. (22) All [substances] that increase *vāta* as well as those that are parched [should be avoided].

The wise man should avoid association with women and harsh grief from afar. (23) One should administer those wholesome remedies prescribed for fever here as well; in this way, within three weeks, the person attains well-being. (24) Then, after performing the recitation of auspicious verses, an ablution should be performed, having dressed [the patient] in new, fine, and white garments. (25) Having clothed him thus, the performance of the fire-oblation (homa) and the serving of desired food should be carried out. (26) Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Afflictions," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. (34)

Chapter Thirty-Five. Ātreya said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the medical treatment of ulcers (*vraṇa*). Ulcers are said to be of many kinds, arising from various morbidities of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). A malignant ulcer (*duṣṭavraṇa*), which is terrible, arises from drinking or eating contaminated water and food, or from indulgence in anger, excessive burden, or addiction; it also arises through another corruption of the blood. It is produced by Vata, Pitta, or Kapha—either individually, in pairs, or by the combination of all three humors (*doṣa*)—after they have agitated the flesh and dispersed the blood.

Even a malignant ulcer (duṣṭavraṇa) is terrible; the aggravated humors (doṣas), having vitiated the skin, blood, and fat, and taking refuge in the bone, gradually produce a severe and formidable swelling. An ulcer arising from Vāta should be recognized as being accompanied by blood, pain, throbbing, and tremors, and it is rough and painful. An ulcer born of Pitta is characterized by a burning sensation, a hissing sound, and the emission of pus; it tolerates touch, feels cold, provides relief, and undergoes quick suppuration. One that is hard, circular in shape, and terrible—[is known as a Kaphaja ulcer].

A Kaphaja ulcer is yellowish, associated with mild pain, tolerant of heat, very unctuous, and slow to heal (7). One should recognize an ulcer arising from the combination of all three humors (Sannipāta) by the presence of all these symptoms; in those born of two humors (Dvandvaja), the characteristics of two humors are observed (8). Those ulcers arising from trauma (Abhighāta) are to be known as fourfold; others are sinus ulcers (Nāḍīvrana), which are accompanied by wind and pain (9). But others occur within the channels (Srotas); hear now their treatment: first is the draining of Mandavi, and second is fomentation (Svedana) is prescribed (10). Third...

Maturation (pācana) is prescribed for a ripened [abscess]; likewise, incision (pāṭana), purification (śodhana), and healing (rohaṇa) should be applied. Subsequently, the same sequence should be followed, as it is beneficial for wounds.
