Rāsnā, vacā, and śuṇṭhī, along with the juice of mātuluṅga and sour gruel (kāñjika), used together for washing, are for a wind-dominant (vātika) wound. Yaṣṭīmadhuka, mañjiṣṭhā, paṭola, and nimba leaves, boiled in milk and cooled, are for washing a bile-dominant (paittika) wound. Triphalā, kadamba, and jambu [are also used].

A decoction of *kapittha* is excellent for washing a wound arising from *kapha* when it is accompanied by heat. (15) The roots of *mātuluṅga* and *agnimantha*, or likewise *suradāru* and *śuṇṭhī*, applied as a paste with *kāñjika* vinegar, are beneficial for a wind-born (*vāta*) wound. (16) *Nala*, *mūrvā*, *madhuka*, *candana*, and *raktacandana*, ground with rice-water, destroy wounds caused by *pitta*. (17) Having ground *aṅkolaka*, *rodhra*, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, *vetasa*, and the leaves of *pāribhadra*, one should apply them as a plaster to the wound. (18) [This is to be done] once the wound has reached suppuration.

In a deep ulcer, one that is painful, or one with cavities, purification (śodhana) and washing (dhāvana) should be performed by the best of physicians. (19) Washing for deep ulcers should be done with a decoction of *karañja*, *dhava*, *nimba*, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and *vetasa*, boiled down to one-quarter of its original volume. (20) *Mañjiṣṭhā*, lac-resin (*lākṣā-rasa*), realgar (*manaḥśilā*), and the two types of turmeric (*niśā-yuga*) should be ground together, strained through cloth, and mixed with honey; this is a purifier of ulcers and beneficial for them. Crushed *nimba* leaves mixed with honey also serve to purify ulcers. (21–22)

22. Nimba leaves, sesame, honey, along with dārvī and madhuka, as well as a paste of sesame seeds, are used for the purification of wounds. 23. A decoction of nimba, śītaka, leaves of sumanā, and [other ingredients] is beneficial for the cleansing of wounds. 24. Having recognized that the wound is purified, one should then smear the wound with fresh butter (navanīta), which is excellent; by this means, the wound does not burn. 25. Jātī, karañja, picumanda, paṭola, yaṣṭīmadhu, rajanī, and kaṭurohiṇī [are also used].

Equal parts of mañjiṣṭhā, utpala, muśīra, karañja seeds, sārivā, trivṛt, and māgadhikā [should be prepared]; this cooked ghee is indeed beneficial for wounds, highly recommended for those that have become sinus-like (nāḍī), painful, or accompanied by blood; it destroys spider-poison and erysipelas (visarpa), and causes even deep, burning, and hard wounds to heal. Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Wounds," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya, concerning the *Jātyādi-ghṛta*.

Chapter Thirty-Six. Ātreya said: Ślīpada (elephantiasis) arises from the same treatments prescribed for ulcers; by Vāta it appears cracked, dry, and dark. By Pitta it is seen with burning, suppuration, and fever. By Kapha it is produced as smooth, dense, and accompanied by swelling. By Sannipāta (the combination of all three), O best of physicians, all these symptoms arise. When located in the fat tissue, it is called Vālmīka (anthrax-like) and appears like an anthill. One should recognize its signs as being similar to those arising from Vāta.

One should cause the treatments prescribed for wounds to be performed upon that [condition] according to the rules. Ghee prepared with *jāti* and other [herbs] is recommended, as are various ointments. Furthermore, an application should be made using *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba*. Having ground the root of *girikarṇikā* and also *vṛkṣādanī*, an application should be made for elephantiasis (*vālmīka-ślīpada*). Having ground *sūraṇa* tubers with honey and ghee, this application is beneficial and removes elephantiasis caused by anthills (*vālmīka-ślīpada*). Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Elephantiasis," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Thirty-Seven. Ātreya said: Furthermore, due to injury from wind, exposure to drafts, or even from a wound, blood-carrying channels (raktanaḍīs) sprout and likewise become obstructed. By that, the passage of the blood is blocked, and because of that obstruction, a very large tumor (arbuda) arises. The wise should recognize that it is soft and rough from Vāta, dense and cold from Kapha, and characterized by burning, suppuration, and so forth from Pitta. From the combination of all three (Sannipāta), it becomes hard, dense, and resembles a stone.

O best of physicians, a *gaḍuka* that has increased in size is incurable. At the outset, one should perform incision while avoiding the vital points (*marmasthāna*); one should also apply an ointment of rock salt (*saindhava*) and ghee. O best of physicians, having burnt the *sūraṇa* tuber with ghee and molasses, its application is the destroyer of tumors (*arbuda*). The remaining treatments for wounds are prescribed as beneficial for the pacification of tumors; furthermore, wind-destroying (*vātaghna*), wholesome, and sweet foods are recommended. Thus ends the section spoken by Ātreya in the *Hārītottara*.

In the third section, the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Arbuda. The thirty-eighth chapter. Ātreya said: "O best of physicians, thus has the treatment of ulcers been described in brief; one should apply the remedy correctly after understanding the appropriate course of action. A cluster of glandular swellings (*gaṇḍamālā*) arises from drinking contaminated water and consuming unwholesome food, occurring when wind (*vāta*), phlegm (*kapha*), and bile (*pitta*) are deranged. Furthermore, the host of defects produced by worms spreads from the glands. Due to *vāta*, the symptoms resemble those of wind disorders; due to *pitta*, there is burning, pain, ulceration, wasting, and heat; and due to *śleṣman* (phlegm), [there is heaviness and numbness]."

From the combination [of these factors], there arises a cold-dense swelling caused by the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*), characterized by all their symptoms. O son, listen as I shall describe its remedy: *rohiṇī*, *viśadā*, *vijayā*, *vibhedinī*, *kāntārī*, *vajrapuṣpā*, and likewise another called *indrāyudhā*—these are the seven types of *lūtā* (spider-bites); listen now to each one individually. *Rohiṇī* is red and appears on a red spot; *viśadā* is white in color and occurs on a fleshy part of the body. And *vijayā*...

In the center of the head is the yellow-colored *yavaprabhā* (7). At the site of the fat (*medas*), there is the *bhedinī*, which is white with a blue streak (8). In the middle of the bladder (*basti*) is the *kāntārī*; the *śvetāṅgā* and *raktamuṇḍikā* are also located there. In the middle of the bones is the *vajrapuṣpā*, considered to be white and black in its vessels (*śirā*) (9). At the end of the head is the *indrāyudhā* vessel, and the *dhūmrā* vessel is considered to be black (10). The *rohiṇī* is the size of a finger; the *viśadā* is uniform with urine; the *vijayā* is shaped like a barley grain, and the *vartulā* is likewise a *vijayā* (11). Others among men should be known as resembling the thorns of the *taṇḍulī* plant.

Rohiṇī, Vijayā, and Viṃśā are located in the region of the flesh; Bhedinī is seen at the ankle or at the joints of the bones in a man. Know, O son, that Kāntārī is in the belly, between the ears, and at the outer corner of the eye. Vajrapuṣpā is in the head, and Indrāyudhā is considered to be at the end of the head. Therefore, I shall speak of the medical treatment; listen, my son, with diligence. They know a wound to be deep, exuding thick pus, and malodorous; another is painful and has the luster of a ripe jambū fruit. [These are the characteristics] of spider-bites (lūtā).

One should avoid these [lesions] as long as they appear unripe, as well as spiders located at joints or vital points (*marmasthāna*); once that wound has been treated, a cauterization with heated oil should be performed immediately. (16) A plaster made of *aṅkola*, liquors, leaves of the *pāribhadra*, house-soot, and black cumin (*kṛṣṇajīra*), ground together with cow’s urine, is highly recommended as a supreme remedy for the destruction of spiders. (17) One should apply a paste of *piṇḍītaka*, *viḍaṅga*, the root of the *iṅguda* tree, and the roots of the *bījapūraka* to treat *gaṇḍamālā*.

Likewise, it quickly destroys the terrible *prakaṇṭakas*. One should apply the milky sap of *snuhī* and the milky sap of *arka* into the opening of the spider; by that means, the insect dies within it—of this there is no doubt. Having ground *girikarṇī*, sandalwood, and [other ingredients] in equal parts, one should apply a paste from the mouth [of the wound]; it destroys even the most dreadful spider-bite. One should cook *karavīra*, the milky sap of *arka*, as well as *kaṭutumbikā*, the two types of *niśā*, and *jāṅgalikā* in sesame oil; by anointing with this, it destroys the spider-bite.

One should also apply ghee and substances such as *jātyādi* for severe *gaṇḍamālā*, as well as other treatments prescribed according to rule for wounds. Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Lūtā and Gaṇḍamālā," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Thirty-nine. Ātreya said: Consuming incompatible drinks, heavy foods, sour substances, and alkaline water, as well as excessive bathing, sleeping during the day, and staying awake at night—these cause the Pitta, residing in the blood, to become aggravated. When that morbid humor reaches the skin, it spreads; the wise declare this disease by the name Kuṣṭha (leprosy). O knower of the rules, these diseases arise from sin and manifest intensely in the bodies of men who greatly provoke the humors. They say there are eighteen types of Kuṣṭha; I shall describe their characteristics individually.

These [diseases] are incurable or curable, born of karma, arising from the humors (*doṣa*), or innate; they consist of compassion, roughness, itching, horripilation, exhilaration, numbness, piercing pain, and aching within the body—these are the signs when *kuṣṭha* resides in the skin. (3–4) Furthermore, there are *kapālaka*, *udumbara*, *dadru*, circular patches (*maṇḍala*), erysipelas (*visarpaka*), *hastibala*, *kiṇa*, *gojihvaka*, red circular patches (*lohitamaṇḍala*), *vaipādika*, *carmadala*, and others. (5)

Now, eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*), multiple ulcers (*bahuvraṇa*), itching (*kaṇḍū*), and eczema (*vicarcī*) are described; likewise, other skin diseases established through the differentiation of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are as follows. That which resembles a skull and is white in color is called *kapālya* by those who know the rules. That which is oily, spreads over the entire body, and is itchy is called *udumbara* by the wise. That which resembles ringworm is *dadrū*; they call that circular patch *maṇḍalaka*. That which creeps along is *visarpa*, and another type, which is like an elephant’s hide, is called *gajacarma*.

That which is rough, harsh, and as tough as a cow’s tongue, which is prone to splitting, and characterized by yellowish-red circular patches accompanied by itching and ulcers—this should be known as *lohita-maṇḍala*, arising from blood and located in the blood; it is intensely painful and clearly manifest. That condition is called *vipādikā* and should be treated accordingly. Arising from wind aggravated by blood, appearing like small eruptions (*visphoṭaka*), or otherwise known as *bahuvraṇa*, it is characterized by minute cracks. It is well understood [as such].

In a man, itching and scabies are well-known in this world; when white, subtle, and pale-red eruptions spread over a man's body, and his blood [is affected], no youth can ever be cured [of it]. (12) The Śirīṣa flowers, the Śirīṣa fruits, the loss of natural luster, and a subtle person—pricking pain as well as trembling are the signs of Vāta; by Pitta come emaciation, vertigo, burning sensations, and thirst. (13) When arising from Kapha, there is hardness, coldness, and paleness in the eyes, nails, and body, as well as a lack of desire for food; in the case of a combination [of humors], these symptoms appear mixed.

That which arises from the combination of all three humors (sānnipātika) possesses many symptoms. 14. One should know that which is located in the skin (tvak-stha) as dry, itchy, soft, and cold; that which is located in the blood (rakta-ga) has a discharge that is burning and red-tinged. 15. One should designate that which is located in the flesh (māṃsa-ga) as very unctuous, characterized by pricking pain (toda), and deep-seated; that which is located in the fat (medas-stha) is characterized by aching and a sense of constriction, is very unctuous, and causes redness of the eyes. 16. That which is located in the bone (asthi-stha) is deep-seated and causes discharge through the nose and mouth in the case of visarpa; and that which is located in the marrow (majja-stha) renders the patient incapacitated.

A discharge of marrow occurs and the entire body becomes shattered; this is likewise known as the stage involving the semen (śukragata). 17. Therefore, O best of physicians, I shall describe the remedial treatments in brief. 18. When [the disease] resides in the skin, fomentation and ointments are used; when it resides in the blood, bloodletting is prescribed. For its presence in the flesh, purgation is declared, and for its presence in the fat, the drinking of decoctions and digestive treatments is advised. 19. Now, these three [treatments] are likewise applied when it has reached the bone and marrow. Fomentation is beneficial in the Vātika type, while cooling measures are for the Pittaja type. 20. This [Vātika] is said to be difficult to cure, whereas the Sānnipātika type is incurable.

Having considered the cause of the disease, one should then commence the treatment. For leprosy (kuṣṭha), one should perform purification (śodhana) and digestive processing (pācana) fortnightly, induce purgation (recana) monthly, and for the sake of thorough cleansing, bloodletting (asṛgmokṣaṇa) every sixth month. One should quickly drink a decoction of vāsā, paṭola, phalinī, lavaṇa, vacā, and nimba bark; this induces emesis in cases of leprosy when combined with madana. In emetic treatments involving madana, a decoction of pathyā (harītakī) is used. Triphalā, trivṛt, and dantī constitute a purgative.

O best of physicians, the decoction should be drunk with warm water; O supreme physician, for one suffering from labored inhalation and exhalation, if a vein in the head is to be pierced, then a meal consisting of decoction and unctuous substances should be administered. A decoction prepared with ginger, long pepper, khadira, pāṭalī, paṭolī, mañjiṣṭhā, kṣura, viṣa, bilva, yavānikā, vāsā, and triphalā, when taken with water, destroys the disorder of leprosy in a person.

A decoction of vāsā, viḍaṅga, picumanda, paṭola, pāṭhā, śuṇṭhī, surendrataru, the roots of the five trees (pañcataru), and pathyā destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) born of wind (marut); this great medicine should be administered for twenty-one days. (27) The powder of chinnodbhavā taken daily along with its decoction, or milk mixed with ghee taken when the previous meal is digested, destroys all types of kuṣṭha, even those that have reached the seven bodily constituents (dhātus). (28–29) [Kuṣṭha] made from kāśmarya, darada, ghana, kuṣṭha, and the two types of niśā... [is effective]. (30)

This *kāñjikakuṣṭha* is recommended for external application; it destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), as well as *vicarcikā* and the affliction of *visarpa*. (30) In that case, these [herbs] should be ground and applied as a paste with *madhuka*, *kāñjika*, and urine; this cures even malignant *kuṣṭha* and *vicarcikā*. (31) For the affliction of *visarpa*, one should perform washes as prescribed; a wash with the juice of *sauvīraka* or with *triphalā* water is also effective. (32) For *kuṣṭha* caused by Vāta, a wash with a decoction of *nimba* leaves mixed with the paste of *yaṣṭīmadhuka* and milk is praised by the wise. (33)

Even with a cold decoction of *vidārī*, one destroys most terrible skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*); however, washing [the area] is not recommended. (34) A decoction of *agnimantha*, *paṭola*, the leaves of *mātuluṅga*, *śaṭhī*, and *parpaṭaka* is used for washing those suffering from phlegm-related diseases (*śleṣmaroga*). (35) O best of the wise, having washed *vipādikā* with fresh butter (*navanīta*) and having applied fomentation (*sveda*) with the milks of the *arka* plant, an ointment should be applied using honey and oil. (36) [Kaṣāyas are made from] *khadira*, *nimba*, *kadambaka*, as well as *kakubha*, *pāṭalika*, *śirīṣaka*, *kuṭaja*, *kiṃśuka*, *vāsa*, and *samoraṭa*.

Vaṭa, kuṭaja, naṭa, pippali, pīlu (37), dhava, mudga, rambha, and vetasa—when boiled together and taken with ghee according to the prescribed method, this acts as a destroyer of all types of skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), and the man’s body becomes equal to the moon in luster. (38) Āragvadha, dhātakī, karṇikāra, dhava, arjuna, sajjaka, kiṃśuka, kadamba, nimba, kuṭaja, aṭarūṣa, and likewise khadira and mūrvā—(39) having properly collected the roots of these, a decoction is prepared until one-eighth remains; this is mixed with an equal amount of ghee.

It destroys all skin diseases born of the body. It quickly cures all types of leprosy (kuṣṭha), erysipelas (visarpa), ringworm (dadru), and eczema (vicarcikā) in a person. The roots of khadira, kadara, mūrvā, and vālaka, along with karṇikāra, kuṭaja, saparibhadra, and āragvadha—these being ground and boiled, this medicated ghee (ghṛta), when drunk in the maximum dose, destroys all forms of leprosy, erysipelas, and prideful afflictions. Bhallātaka, trikaṭu, powdered akṣa, kuṣṭha, guñjā, the five salts, and the three fruits (triphalā)—[these are used for the preparation].

Oil cooked with these ingredients, when used as an ointment, destroys ringworm and leprosy (43). A paste made from the roots of *aśvaghna*, *malinī*, *samaṅgā*, the two types of *niśā* (turmeric), mustard, *citraka*, *bhṛṅgarāja*, *kuhatumbikā*, *kuṣṭha*, *viḍaṅga*, and *magadhā* (44)—this oil of sesame seeds, cooked with the milks of *snuhī* and *arka*, when fully prepared and applied as an ointment, will surely destroy ringworm and itching in a person (45). [Also included are] *haridrā*, *samaṅgā*, *surāhva*, *citraka*, and *viḍaṅga*.

Kṛṣṇā, viśālā, ambu, kuṣṭha, as well as lāṅgalī, cakramarda, guñjā, viśālā, and the leaves of ariṣṭa—this powder, once prepared and processed with jaggery, should be cooked in the heat; it is beneficial for application and very quickly destroys kuṣṭha, pāmā, and vicarcī in a person. (46–47) Nimba, paṭola, kirātaka, jātī, viśālā, along with punarnavā, payoda, the juice of lākṣā, vāsā, trāyantikā, bilva, kuṣṭha, and yaṣṭi—these should be finely ground into a powder. (48)

Ghee cooked with milk and curd is beneficial for sprinkling; it destroys leprosy (kuṣṭha), wounds, ringworm (dadru), blood disorders, scabies (pāmā), and eczema (vicarcī), as well as itching (kaṇḍū). When bile (pitta) becomes diseased and is impelled by wind (vāta), and when blood is provoked along with them, it produces a pale complexion. Its symptoms include a stiff mind and deformity; this should be understood by the best of physicians as either incurable or curable leprosy. That which arises from the derangement of all three humors (sannipāta) becomes slightly reddish and pale.

That [disease] which arises with variegated spots on all limbs and is oily is incurable; however, that which has arrived with a yellowish complexion and is pale and rough is known to be most treatable. Purgation, cleansing, emesis, and bloodletting are recommended. (52–53) A paste made from vāsā, guḍūcī, triphalā, karañja, paṭola, nimba, arjuna, vetasa, along with kṛṣṇā and samaṅgā, is beneficial when drunk for the treatment of *citraka-maṇḍala* (vitiligo). (54) [One should also use] khadira, vāsaka, nimba, paṭola, dhava, yavāsa, and the three fruits (*phalatrika*).

It conquers all types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), circular patches (*maṇḍala*), and the pallor of a person. 55 *Pāṭhā*, *viḍaṅga*, *magadhā*, *suradāru*, *citraka*, the two types of *dadrughna*, and *rātri*, as well as *samaṅgā*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, and *madhuka*—ground with *saindhava* salt and sour gruel (*kāñjika*), or else with urine, blood, or meat-broth—when applied as a plaster, this proven remedy destroys variegated leprosy (*citra-kuṣṭha*), ringworm (*vicarcikā*), itching, and quickly eliminates eruptions (*visphoṭa*) and spreading sores (*pratisarpana*). 56–57 *Bhṛṅgarāja*.

Turmeric, *dūrvā* grass, jasmine, *viḍaṅga*, black sesame, *citraka*, and yellow sandalwood (58)—these, ground with urine and applied as an ointment, destroy all types of *dadrū* in one afflicted by variegated leprosy (*citrakuṣṭha*), as well as *kuṣṭha*, *dadrū*, and *vicarcikā*. (59) One should also employ those foods prescribed as wholesome during fever which are not burning-hot, not sour, and likewise not aggravating to *vāta*; these are beneficial for those undergoing treatment for ulcers and the streaks of leprosy. (60) Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Leprosy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 39.

Chapter Forty. Ātreya said: Due to excessive burden or over-exertion, from the state of extreme sharpness and heat, or from coldness due to a lack of oil massage—especially through the aggravation of pitta—a disease of the head arises in men, whether caused by the defect of worms, or by vāta, rakta, kapha, and pitta, with pitta being particularly prominent. These conditions, as well as others born of worms, should be understood as arising from the combination of all three humors (sannipāta). Furthermore, there is the disorder known as Ardhāśīrṣa (hemiplegia of the head), which increases day by day; pain from vāta occurs at night, and the patient's head then suffers great distress.

She may find relief through fomentation and massage, or from pain in the rectum and scrotum caused by Vāta. (4) He whose limbs become hot in the head during the summer heat, whether by day or night, finds relief from smoking or pungent substances in cases of Kapha; or he attains health and comfort at night due to the cold. (5) Or he finds relief from the cold, yet first experiences thirst and intense pain arising from Pitta; or there is vertigo and very intense thirst occurring at sunrise or at the end of the day. (6) And his head becomes cold along with numbness.

If a pair [of symptoms] accompanied by sweating and resembling the eyes occurs, or if there is a desired disorder of the head due to phlegm (kapha); 7. If a web-like membrane emerges from the nostrils due to blood (rakta), and there is thirst in the rest of the mouth, redness of the eyes, and [pain] in the abdomen—he is called one suffering from a head disease born of blood. 8. When the middle [part of the head] is corrupted and spreads, and yellow, watery discharge with feces flows from the nose, and he suffers from numbness, delusion, and labored breathing—due to the obstruction of the three humors (tridoṣa), a headache arises. 9. For whom [the pain] is excessive...

Even when the head is being split apart by a goad, there is a discharge from the nasal cavity mixed with blood and pus, and a headache accompanied by the emergence of worms. Another type of headache arises from anger or grief, as does that caused by excessive physical exertion and over-fatigue; such painful affliction of the head in men is also caused by *vāta*. Furthermore, pain born of *vāta* and *rakta* (blood) occurs from excessive writing or reading, as well as from looking at minute objects or from straining the sight to see distant things. There is pain in one half of the nose, and pain may also occur in the pair of eyebrows, which appear blue or black.

One should observe that pain occurs at the head (13). Bile does not exist without blood, and blood is moved by bile; there would be no headache without bile, for bile is moved by wind (vāta) (14). Therefore, I shall describe the treatment; listen to the characteristics of the medicine: fomentation (sveda), external application (pralepana), nasal medication (nasya), drinking, massage, and rubbing (mardana) (15). Fomentation is indicated in cases born of wind and phlegm (vāta-kaphaja), as well as in injury (abhighāta); however, one should not perform fomentation in those two [types] when they are born of bile or blood (pitta-raktaja) (16). In the case of blood-born [headache], a vein (śirā) should be pierced, and in the case of bile-born, [treatment for bile is required].

Alternatively, in some cases, one should apply a decoction made from the plant called *kokilā*, *tarkārī*, *kaṭukā*, neem leaves (17), and the seeds of *śobhāñjanaka*; one should foment the area with this, or by applying a paste of these, relief will arise for him. (18) For a fever born of *pitta*, there should be cold sprinklings and cold applications using *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, sandalwood, *kesara*, and *mātuluṅga*. (19) O best of physicians, *kadamba*, *arjuna*, and *sindhuvāra* are for the purpose of application; or alternatively, *nāgara* with jaggery, or *pathyā* with jaggery. (20)

Through the application of nasal drops (nasya) using jaggery and the juice of *śobhāñjana* separately, or with goat’s urine as a nasal drop, headache is pacified. O best of physicians, for a severe headache arising from *kapha*, one should administer a nasal drop of black pepper (*marica*), *pathyā*, and *kaṭphala*, mixed with either urine or warm water. For a headache caused by the derangement of all three humors (*sannipāta*), the use of a nasal drop of *vacā*, the essence of *madhuka*, or the root of *girikarṇikā* is prescribed. And for a headache born of worms (*krimija*), one should apply a measured amount of the root of *vandhyākarkaṭakī*, ground with warm water, as a nasal drop.

For diseases located in the head: take one part *mṛṅgarāja-rasa* and two parts of *kāñjika* (sour gruel), and add three parts of *śobhāñjana*; throw all of this into the mixture. Add five parts of *sauvīraka-rasa* (sour barley water) and six parts of *tumbikā-rasa*. Then add ginger, rock salt (*saindhava*), *amlīkā*, *paṭola*, *vāsaka*, and *śivā* (harītakī). Also include *abhayā*, *surasā*, and four parts of oil. Once cooked, this should be administered as a nasal drop (*nasya*) in a dose of six drops. Likewise, it is beneficial for anointing the head and is beneficial when used as ear-drops.

In diseases born of wind (vāta) and the like, as well as in headaches and those caused by worms, O wise one, one should extract oil from *karañja* seeds and *vibhītaka* fruits using a closed vessel (*puṭapāka*), and apply three drops via nasal administration (*nasya*); this destroys skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*) and disorders born of worms. Having taken *kuṣ�ठ* (costus), *yaṣṭīmadhuka* (liquorice), and the juices of *paṭola*, *jātī*, and *surasa*, and having cooked them with fresh butter (*navanītaka*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*), this is certainly for blood-bile (*raktapitta*). This [preparation], combined with sugar, should be administered during the day when the provoked humors (*doṣa*) have increased.

Lac juice, sandalwood, liquorice, *paṭola*, *dhātrī* fruit, sugar, curd, milk, and fresh butter—when boiled together, this is employed as a nasal medication (*nasya*). (31–32) In cases of disorders of the eyebrows, the temples, or depletion of blood, or even when the humors (*doṣas*) increase day by day, one should administer ghee cooked with saffron, liquorice, and costus, mixed with an equal amount of sugar and fresh butter, as a nasal medication. (33–34) Diseases born of *pitta* and disorders of the half-head (*ardhāvabhēda*) are destroyed by the administration of this [nasal oil] for a period increasing by one day at a time. (35)
It subsides quickly. 35. Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Head," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 40.

Chapter Forty-one. Ātreya said: In one who is habitually prone to excessive recitation, or by the observation of subtle objects, or by gazing at distant things, or by heat, the disorder known as *bhrū-doṣa* arises. (1) The morbid humor (*doṣa*), localized in the blood and wind (*vāta*) and intensified by bile (*pitta*), produces pain in the eyebrows and in the vessels originating from the bridge of the nose. (2) It aches during times of heat and especially during cold; moreover, one perceives blue and yellow circles within the center of the eye. (3) For that condition, one should first apply treatment, and the veins (*śirā*) should be diligently venesected.

The previously mentioned sudation (svedana) should be performed; for nasal therapy (nasya), the "six drops" (ṣaḍbinduka) and other formulations are used. (4) Devadāru, rajanī, ghana, śaṭhī, puṣkara, seeds of kuṭaja, māgadhī, kuṣṭha, rodhra, cavikā, and yavāsaka should be boiled and then strained again. (5) To that [decoction], one should add guggulu, along with powdered śuṇṭhī, saindhava salt, and the three fruits (triphalā), which is beneficial. This is mixed with curd and milk, cooked, and turned into fresh butter (navanītaka). (6) Once prepared, it should be administered cold and mixed with sugar; this is a beneficial nasal medication (nasya).

Nasal therapy (*nasyakarma*) applied to the region of the eyebrows, forehead, arms, and the base of the temples removes pain from the head; even when administered solely as a simple massage, it wards off diseases of the head, including hemiplegia (*ardhaśīrṣaka*), and oil is likewise a supreme remedy for disorders of the head. (7–8) The juice of betel leaf (*tāmbūlapatra*), combined with *viḍaṅga*, rock salt (*sindhūdbhava*), and asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), ground with jaggery (*guḍa*) and water, when prepared as a nasal treatment, destroys defects of the eyebrows and temples as well as worms. (9) Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Eyebrow Disorders," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 41.

Chapter Forty-two. Ātreya said: O wise one, nasal disease may be caused by worms (*krimija*), by the [humoral] defects (*doṣaja*), or by blood (*raktaja*); O best of physicians, hear from me its symptoms. (1) In the Vata-type, there is headache and swelling; in the Vata-Pitta type, it is accompanied by the [signs of] the defect; in the Kapha-type, it is thick and cold; and in the worm-type, there is the discharge of blood. (2) For nasal inflammation (*nāsāpāka*), in the Vata-type, a nasal drop (*nasya*) prepared with jaggery and ginger should be used; in the Pitta-type, a nasal drop with sugar, ghee, and liquorice should be used. (3) In the Kapha-type, it should be prepared with the juice of *surasā* and *vāsā*.

In cases of worm-infestation, viḍaṅga, hiṅgu, and magadhā are considered beneficial. In diseases of the head arising from blood, bloodletting is the primary treatment. Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Nose," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-three. Ātreya said: Now listen, O Hārīta, to the treatment for hair-destroying diseases (keśaghna). Due to Vāta, it is dry and pale; due to Pitta, it is red and accompanied by a burning sensation; when combined with Kapha, it becomes oily. Due to blood, it undergoes suppuration; when caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta), it arises with symptoms resembling all of them. For hair-destroying disease arising from Vāta, washing the head with jaggery, *surasā*, ginger, and the juice of *mātuluṅga* is recommended. Triphalā, *vacā*, and *rohiṇī*, well-ground together with jaggery, [should also be used].

Washing (dhāvana) is recommended for alopecia (aindralupta) arising from phlegm (kapha). For the pitta-type, milk combined with fresh butter is beneficial; likewise, sugar, the fruit of the āmalaka, and liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu) are considered suitable for washing in the pitta-type. One should take the juice of bhṛṅgarāja as well as the juice of ginger (śṛṅgavera), and having ground sesame seeds with sour gruel (sauvīraka-rasa), an ointment should be applied; thereafter, the person should bathe with warm water. A decoction of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, śirīṣa, and rohitaka should be used for head-dandriff (śirodadrū).

One should pacify *indraluptaka* (alopecia) with the flower of the *kurabaka* and the blossom of the *japā*; once the *indralupta* has been rubbed [with these], its prevention is indeed accomplished. Having observed the symptoms caused by *pitta*, washing with milk should be performed; cooling applications are prescribed for those afflicted by *pitta*. Datura leaves, *māgadhī*, *niśā*, *viśālā*, house-soot, and *kuṣṭha*, mixed with ghee and ground with water, serve as a head-ointment that wards off wounds when applied to a disease associated with the *pitta*-derived disorder.

Having ground either the leaf of *paṭola*, or that of *picumanda* (neem), or likewise the fruit of *malakī*, an application with ghee and sugar removes wounds born on the head; this also destroys headaches and various swellings. Taking the soot of an elephant’s tusk, an application with fresh butter (*navanītaka*) [is effective]. An application with fresh butter of the ash of sesame, *arka*, *bhallātaka*, and burnt beans, as well as the application of the ash of a snake, produces a growth of hair on a bald spot (*khalvāṭaka*).
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Treatment of Indralupta," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-four. Ātreya said: Earache may arise from residual [doshas], or from water remaining in the ear, or from impurities; it may likewise result from the obstruction of breathing, or from the vitiation of Vāta and the other doshas (1). Earache may also be produced by combinations of two doshas, by all three doshas together, by worms, by ulceration, or by other causes; due to this, a person hears many sounds (2)—the sound of silence, the roar of clouds, the clashing of teeth, pain accompanied by burning, headache, and the sound of a flute.

O child, know that when one hears everything due to *pitta*, O best of physicians; likewise, in the case of *kapha*, it spreads faintness and one hears sounds like the roar of clouds. (3) In the disorder of worms (*krimi-doṣa*), O most excellent one, pus mixed with blood flows out; likewise, intense pain arises from injury (*abhighāta*). (4–5) From a wound, pus flows out, and another [type] arises from childhood; that ear-pain also arises from the disorder of *lūti*. (6) In these ear diseases, filling with water and this powder have not been prescribed.

One who knows the procedure should apply beneficial oil and fomentation to the ear; the application of drops of warm tears is also considered beneficial (7). One should prepare a fine powder of rock salt (*saindhava*) and sea-foam (*samudraphena*); this filling of the ear with the juice of *sauvīraka* is recommended for disorders caused by Vāta (8). The juice of fresh *sauvīraka*, along with ginger, rock salt, and *guggulu*, should be cooked with oil and the juice of fermented black gram (*kulmāṣa*); when it has become very hot, it should be retained in the ear, as this is praised for ear diseases (9–10). [Likewise, oil prepared with] liquorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), costus (*kuṣṭha*), the leaves of *ariṣṭa*, and turmeric (*niśā*)...

For earache arising from bile (*paittika*), ghee processed with *viśālā*, *asumanaḥ*, and *pravāla* is recommended; likewise, ghee processed with *brāhmī* juice, rock salt (*saindhava*), *viḍaṅga*, and *bhṛṅgarāja* is beneficial. Similarly, *sauvīra* juice mixed with *pathyā* and strained through cloth is also effective. This is beneficial for filling the auditory canal and destroys pus, blood, and worms. All the aforementioned diseases of the head have been described, along with the oils and ghees; one should employ these or those prepared with *jātī* and other ingredients.

The foremost among those who know the diseases of the head (14); wholesome foods that remove wind and those that are burning and heavy (15). Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, named "The Treatment of Diseases of the Ear," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 44.

The forty-fifth chapter. Ātreya said: The humors (doṣas) arising in the eyes become aggravated by exposure to heat, excessive alkaline or pungent substances, or by injury; even by looking through a fine cloth or a small opening [of the eye]. (1) I shall now describe the characteristics of those congenital disorders that are difficult to conquer; listen. Dryness, itching, pricking pain, and a continuous flow of dry, cold tears—(2) one should recognize that as Vātika. Now hear about the Pittaja type. (3) In the Pittaja type, the eyes are reddish, accompanied by burning, and there is a warm discharge. In the Sannipātika type, there is swelling and itching. In the Kaphaja type, there is coldness and numbness. (4)

In the case of the dual-type (*dvandvaja*) fever, [the treatment] is with all those having mixed characteristics; and in the case of the combined-type (*sānnipātika*), having known these symptoms, hear from me the therapeutic procedure. (5) A wash with ginger, *surāhvā*, and *surasā*, along with warm *kāñjika* (fermented rice water), is recommended for the Pitta-type and the Kapha-born type. Likewise, a paste of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) with cow’s urine is praised by other excellent physicians. (6) Ginger, *saṭhī*, turmeric, the three myrobalans, neem, and *patrā* leaves combined with rock salt and sour gruel (*tuṣāmlaka*) are declared by the wise to be beneficial.

In cases of eye diseases involving the *sannipāta* (combined humors), those arising from blood (*raktodbhava*), and likewise those accompanied by pain, the three fruits (*phalatrika*) along with turmeric (*niśā*) are recommended as a collyrium (*dhūma*). In disorders born of *kapha*, or those associated with *vāta*, an ointment (*pralepana*) made of *vacā*, *varṣābhū*, and rock salt (*saindhava*) is indeed beneficial and highly praised. Alternatively, the root of *apāmārga* or the root of *dhattūra*, rubbed in a copper vessel with ginger (*śuṇṭhī*), rock salt, and buttermilk (*takra*), serves as a beneficial collyrium (*añjana*) that removes eye diseases caused by *vāta*. Fresh butter produced from milk and *yaṣṭīmadhu* [are also recommended].

Nimba and sesame seeds combined with triphalā and jaggery form a plaster that destroys eye diseases caused by kapha. (11) Śuṇṭhī, rock salt, tuttha, and māgadhikā, rubbed together on a copper vessel and mixed with curd and ghee, serve as a collyrium that destroys all eye ailments. (12) The juice of śigru leaves alone, when applied along with honey, instantly removes the great pain arising from the humors of vāta, pitta, and kapha in the eyes. (13) And [it cures] the swelling in the eyes caused by improper diet and lifestyle.

The first [type] arises and is easily curable; the second is difficult to cure (14). The third is treatable by surgery, but the fourth is incurable (15). O best of physicians, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *rodhra*, conch-shell navel, and realgar, ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) and dried in the shade (16), are beneficial when used as an ointment for the wind-disorder (*vātika*), with sour gruel; for the bile-disorder (*paittika*), with milk; for the phlegm-disorder (*śleṣmala*), combined with urine; and for the flower-eye disease (*puṣpāñjanaka*), they are beneficial (17). They are also beneficial for pacifying the three humors (*tridoṣa*) when prepared with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*, along with *harītakī* and *vacā*.

Kuṣṭha, pippalī, and marica (18), or else the marrow of vibhītaka, conch-shell navel, and realgar—these should be ground in equal parts with goat’s milk (19). This destroys timira, itching, pāṭala, and arbuda; it kills puṣpa along with paṭala and cures night-blindness (rātryandhya) (20). It also treats injuries from wounds or blows, those caused by grief, or burns from fire, as well as kāca and nīlikā—these are desired for the successful treatment of the eyes (21), [arising] from childhood, the power of the humors, or the indulgence in corrupted food and drink.

From old age, a film (paṭala) may arise; I shall describe its characteristics: from wind (vāta), it is accompanied by impurities (kaśmala) and is dry; from bile (pitta), it is blue and yellow; from phlegm (kapha), it is white and thick; they know that from blood (rakta), it is reddish. Because of the symptoms of the combination of humors (sannipāta) and so forth, I shall hereafter describe the remedy. A medicinal wick (varti) is prepared from ginger, vacā, turmeric, tuttha, realgar, śobhāñjana, collyrium (añjana), viśālā, jaṭāmāṃsī, conch-shell, vāstūka root, honey, rock salt, and kaṭphala, mixed with sauvīraka. This is for rubbing.

When the eyes are dried by the sun's glare, the application of collyrium is recommended; it brings about the destruction of the multitude of eye diseases such as *paṭala*. (26) Harītakī with *añjana* and *kaṭphala*, along with *manaḥśilā* and *kaṭphala* mixed with jaggery, destroys the *netrapracchada* (the film over the eye). (27) A wick (*varti*) made from the fruit of the great *vibhītaka*, rubbed with conch-shell (*śaṅkhanābhi*), combined with rock salt (*saindhava*), milk, and sour gruel, and applied as an eye-salve with jaggery, is beneficial for the *paṭala* born of bile (*pitta*) and acts as its remedy. (28) [One should avoid] smoke, wind, dryness, heat, and similar [conditions].

Likewise, those suffering from eye diseases should avoid pungent and sour foods, as well as sexual intercourse. (29) Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Eye Diseases," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 45.

The forty-sixth chapter. Ātreya said: If one's lips are cracked due to excessive speaking or from a Vāta disorder, the consumption of ghee is prescribed for the prevention of lip-splitting (1). If there is burning and redness, one should diagnose it as Pittaja (2). Anointing the lips with honey and fresh butter is recommended; likewise, curd mixed with sugar is a plaster for diseases of the lips (3). Upon seeing that a lip disease is accompanied by blood, one should perform bloodletting; an application of Dhava, Arjuna, and Kadamba is conducive to comfort.

4. When a row of black teeth is present and movement is observed at the root of the tooth due to wind (vāta), one should diagnose it as vātika. 5. From pitta, one should diagnose pitta-flowing [discharge] and inflammation of the gums (dantamāṃsa); in the case of a phlegmatic (ślaiṣmika) dental abscess, there is swelling and extreme whiteness. 6. In that born of blood (raktaja), itching arises and a bloody discharge is seen; the gums (dantamāṃsa) fester, and likewise the blood-filled socket (datpuṭa). 7. The root of the tooth has perforations, and there is intense pain with throbbing; the gums (dantamāṃsa) fall away in the case of that born of worms (krimija).

Toothache arises [from these causes]. (8) A paste made of *yavānī*, *vacā*, *sahā*, *citraka*, rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *viśvā*, and *sindhuvāra*, taken with warm water, as well as five hundred mouthfuls of gargles, are beneficial for toothache and oral diseases; this is highly recommended for all ailments of the mouth. (9) Rubbing the roots of the teeth with *vacā*, rock salt, and *śuṇṭhī* is also advised. (10) One should hold *yavānī* and *vacā* at the roots of the teeth at night. For dental diseases born of *pitta*, fresh butter mixed with sugar should be used. (11) It should be rubbed with the fruit of the *dhātrī*.

The prevention of dental diseases: For phlegm-based (ślaiṣmika) dental diseases, rubbing with *harītakī* or with jaggery is recommended, as is [rubbing] combined with a decoction of *triphalā*. Holding a decoction of the root of *ahimāraka* as a gargle [is beneficial]. Likewise, a decoction of *khadira*, a decoction of *yavānī*, and a decoction of the root of *nimba* prevent dental diseases. In cases of blood-born (*raktaja*) disorders, one should rub [the teeth] with salt and mustard seeds and cause the blood to flow; that is desired for the lips as well. *Viḍaṅga*...

One should rub asafoetida and *sindhuvāra* with the powder of *vacā*; this is beneficial and highly recommended for dental diseases caused by worms. (16) If there is a swelling on the tongue, one should diagnose it as glossitis (*jihvāpāka*). In the Vata-type, it is painful and black; in the Pitta-type, it is accompanied by a burning sensation. (17) In the Kapha-type, it is thick and white; indeed, in the Sannipatika-type, all these symptoms are present. (18) For the Vata-type disease of the tongue, one should apply a rubbing paste of *vacā*, *bhayā*, *viḍaṅga*, ginger, *sauvarcala* salt, and *kaṇā*, combined with ghee. (19) [This may be prepared] with sour gruel or buttermilk.

Holding a lukewarm gargle of liquorice (*yaṣṭī*), sandalwood (*candana*), nut-grass (*mustā*), and *māgadhī* mixed with honey (verse 20) is a plaster that prevents the eruption of blisters on the tongue in cases of the Pitta disorder; holding a cold milk gargle also destroys [the disease] (verse 21). This is known to be beneficial for dental diseases as well as inflammation of the tongue. A warm decoction of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* is likewise pleasant and effective (verse 22). When inflammation of the mouth arises from Kapha, holding a gargle is beneficial; in disorders born of blood, one should cause the blood to flow out. (Verse 23)

For a tongue that is red (raktajihvaka), one should apply a plaster made by rubbing the tongue even with a thorn, using *mūrvā*, *mustā*, *abhayā*, *śuṇṭhī*, *māgadhī*, and the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric), combined with jaggery and honey. When a swelling caused by phlegm (*śleṣma*) arises in the tongue, they know that rubbing it with the powder of black pepper, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *harītakī* is beneficial. Furthermore, from the consumption of oily, slimy, and sweet foods, as well as excessive liquids and new water, a disease of the uvula (*ghaṇṭikāgada*) born of phlegm arises at the root of the tongue and the junction of the throat.

From that, dryness of the mouth, numbness, and mild fever arise (27). Headache, loss of appetite, drowsiness, and likewise numbness of the face occur; by pressing the *raktapanthikā* vessel between the index finger and the throat, blood flows out, and then *vimlāpana* (resolution) is beneficial. One should apply the powder of *vacā*, black pepper (*marica*), and long pepper (*kṛṣṇā*) there (28–29). There should be massage in the region of the throat; by this, the glandular swelling (*granthi*) dissolves. *Dhānyaka*, ginger (*nāgara*), *jīmūta*, and *vacā*—these in equal parts (30)—form a decoction for fomentation (*sveda*) of the *ghaṇṭikā*.

The physician should hold a bolus of *vacā* root in the mouth during both day and night; by doing so, the patient will find relief and be freed from diseases of the mouth. (31-32) When a growth caused by disorders of blood and phlegm develops in the throat and the passage of the *ghaṇṭikā*, it is known as *galagaṇḍikā* (uvulitis) in men. (33) It obstructs the oral cavity and nasal passages, discharge from the eyes is observed, there is headache, dyspnea, and cough; it suppurates along with fever itself. (34) The highly wise [physician] should act quickly as one who performs swift remedies.

One should apply a surgical remedy by cutting the uvula; thereafter, one should perform beneficial scarification (vimlāpana). 35 A warm decoction of *māgadhī*, black pepper (*marica*), *pathyā*, *vacā*, coriander (*dhānya*), and *yavānikā* should be used as a fomentation (*sveda*) for the pacification of the throat-tumor (*galashuṇḍī*). 36 Holding *yavānī* in the mouth during both day and night is beneficial; by massaging the region of the throat with it, comfort is attained. 37 An application to the throat of *siddhārthaka*, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, turmeric (*rajanī*), *pāribhadraka*, soot from a house (*grahadhūma*), and salt is also beneficial.

38. O high-minded one, those wholesome foods prescribed for fever should not be consumed; likewise, sweet, slimy substances and oil are strictly forbidden in diseases of the throat. 39. Thus ends the treatment of *galashuṇḍikā* (uvulitis). This concludes the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Diseases of the Mouth," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-Seven. Ātreya said: "Impotence is declared to be of five kinds; hear from me them in brief. (1) From the suppression [of the urge] or from excessive sexual indulgence, even in a man exhausted by age, there occurs a loss of semen and impotence also arises. (2) Impotence is born in three ways: mental, from the depletion of semen, and innate; in a man, impotence arises from dryness or from perspiration. (3) For one whose mind possesses a sense of possessiveness upon seeing the dispassion of women, there is sweating at the touch; that is curable."

Mental impotence is recognized as that condition where, due to aversion toward women, the mind suffers depletion through sexual intercourse; in such a case, there is a rapid failure of the penis due to the loss of semen. Another type, characterized by an equilibrium of the humors (*samaprakṛti*), is considered the most difficult to cure. When the mind is depleted, the mind may become over-excited through union with beautiful women, or it may be restored by passionate, playful conversations and discourses. As the semen is diminished, the mind flourishes; I shall now describe the methods for increasing the semen. [The following are the ingredients: *vidārī*, *gokṣura*, the roots of *mūṣaka*, and the fruit of *dhātrī*.

These same [medicines] may be used with *saindhava* salt, or likewise with those from Magadha; one should drink them mixed with sugar and milk. (8) The two types of *bṛhatī*, *magadhā*, *trikaṇṭā*, as well as *ātmaguptā* and *śatāvarī*, when drunk with cow’s milk, sugar, and ghee, produce virility in men. (9) Having prepared a powder of dehusked barley, wheat, and *māṣa* beans, processed with milk or sugarcane juice and ghee, (10) one should eat this excellent *vaṭaka* pill upon rising in the morning. Over that—

Milk-drinking combined with long pepper (pippalī) and sugar; likewise, barley-alkali (yavakṣāra), vidārī, and powdered black gram (māṣa); and a cake made of barley, black pepper, and abundant sugar mixed with clarified butter—these one should cook and eat in the morning, followed by drinking milk. This bestows virility upon men, and the woman takes great delight in him. Guḍūcī, śatamūlī, svayaṃguptā, and balā; likewise, the powder of śālmalī and the root of musalī, when taken with cow’s milk, is an excellent drink for men that produces semen and strengthens the sense organs.

15. Vidārīkanda, aśumatī, the two types of bṛhatī, kākolikā, bhīru, the two types of punarnavā, śṛṅgāṭaka, māgadhikā, and balā—these should be made into a powder, enriched with sugar, and administered with sugar. 16. When that has been digested, milk or milk-porridge (pāyasa) should be used; this bestows strength and vigor upon men. Even a eunuch may enjoy a thousand women; this is highly recommended when prepared for two months. 17. One should avoid pungent, sour, sharp, hot, burning, or dry foods, as well as sauvīraka, which have been declared to cause the impairment of the senses.

Onion, barley, bulbs, sesame seeds, and black gram in accordance with one's strength, as well as rice of the *viśālī* variety, milk, and sugarcane juice; likewise, *vāstuka* and *cillaka* greens are wholesome even for those suffering from seminal depletion (*śukrakṣaya*). However, one should avoid *sūraṇa* (yam) and ginger, and should not employ them except when combined in a specific medicinal formulation. Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "Vājīkaraṇa" (aphrodisiac therapy), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

Chapter Forty-Eight. Ātreya said: A woman may become barren in six ways: either through childhood [disease], or from the rupture of the womb-cavity, or likewise from the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Sometimes the conception of a fetus does not occur at all; one type is the "crow-barren" (*kākavandhyā*), and the second is the one who has no offspring at all. The third is described by the best of sages as the one who miscarries; the fourth is she whose children die; and the fifth is due to the loss of strength. I shall now describe the treatment for her, by which she may obtain [offspring].

4. If sexual intercourse is performed with women who have not yet reached puberty, by that very act the womb becomes constricted and she attains the state of a *bhaga* (vagina). 5. Because of that, the woman becomes barren (*vandhyā*) and does not conceive at all; even if she becomes pregnant, it is with great difficulty, O physician. 6. Through medicines and therapeutic procedures, success is achieved without a doubt; even a woman without offspring may give birth, O best of physicians. 7. She shall not be a "crow-barren" woman (*kākavandhyā*), and even one who is childless succeeds; she succeeds.

O best of physicians, that [condition] arises from the depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). For a disease born of *pitta*, one should administer a drink consisting of sandalwood, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *paṭola*, *dhanavālaka*, *madhuka*, *madhuyaṣṭī*, red sandalwood, *sārivā*, cumin, *musta*, *padmaka*, and *punarnavā*, mixed with milk and sugar. Having ascertained the purification of the womb (*yoni*), one should there apply the great medicine: sandalwood, *uśīra*, *mañjiṣṭhā*, *girikarṇī*, and sugar, stirred with milk; this will bring about the successful attainment of menstruation (*puṣpasiddhi*) in cases of *pitta*.

12. One should examine the menstrual blood (*rajaḥ*) to determine whether it is of the nature of *vāta*, *pitta*, or *kapha*. A wise physician should recognize that the menstrual flow which is painful, blackish, and resembles a ripe *jambu* fruit is afflicted by *vāta*. 13–15. For this condition, the wise physician should administer for seven days a decoction of *nāgara*, *pippalī*, *mustā*, *dhanvayavāsaka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, and *pāṭalā*, mixed with jaggery and curd, as long as the blood continues to flow. Once the blood has been purified, he should then have her drink milk combined with *śvetā* and *girikarṇī*. *(Note: "śvetā" and "girikarṇī" are repeated at the end of the fragment.)*

Guñjā and Punarnavā—by their application for one month, she obtains a pregnancy. (16) That which resembles the Japā flower or the color of saffron juice, and is accompanied by burning sensations, dryness, and dysuria, is afflicted by Pitta. (17) Candana, Uśīra, Mañjiṣṭhā, Paṭola, Ghana, Vālaka, Madhuka, Yaṣṭimadhuka, and likewise red sandalwood; (18) Padmaka, the two types of Punarnavā, Śārivā, Jīraka, and Ghana—with milk and sugar, this drink is for diseases caused by Pitta. (19) Having understood [this]...

In that case, one should administer the great medicine for the purification of the womb (*yoniviśuddhi*): the root of white *arka*, white *girikarṇikā*, and the root of white *adrikarṇī* drunk with cow’s milk. This brings about conception for barren women, resulting in offspring endowed with auspicious marks. When the menstrual flow (*rajas*) is thick, slimy, cold, and causes obstruction of urine, and is accompanied by laziness, drowsiness, and sleepiness, they know it to be corrupted by phlegm (*kapha*). For women, drinking a decoction of *triphalā*, *girikarṇī*, *āragvadha*, and *vatsaka* with milk [remedies this].

The best of physicians should administer the *garbhakāraṇa* [formulas], as well as the powders beginning with *bala*, *candana*, and *drākṣā*, to women for the purpose of producing conception (23–24). Furthermore, the best of physicians should give the powder beginning with *khaṇḍaka*, or the *punarnavādya* [formula] to women, which bestows pregnancy (25). Now, O son, listen as I describe the wholesome diet (*pathya*) for women: avoid *kañcara*, *sūraṇa*, sour things, and *kāñjika* (sour gruel) (26). Anything that causes burning sensations or is excessively pungent should be kept far away from women.

One should avoid the root of the *vandhyākarkaṭakī*, *lāṅgalī*, bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbikā*), *devadālī*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *sūryavallī*, and *bhīrukā*; likewise, one should avoid temple offerings (*nirmālya*), garlands, clothes [from such sources], and sexual intercourse during the menstrual period. Water from women who have bathed after intercourse with another man is beneficial for women as a therapeutic measure. Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Treatment for Infertility," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The forty-ninth chapter. Ātreya said: In the first month, one should have [the pregnant woman] drink licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), *paruṣaka*, and honey-flowers as available, along with fresh butter, milk, and honey; and she should drink sweet [liquids]. In the second month, one should likewise have her drink *kākolī* and sweet [liquids]. In the third month, *kṛśarā* (rice and sesame) is best; in the fourth, rice prepared with meat-broth (*kṛtaudana*). In the fifth month, one should give *pāyasa* (milk-rice); in the sixth, sweet curd; in the seventh, with sugar-candy and ghee; in the eighth, *ghṛtapūraka* (cakes fried in ghee). In the ninth month, various kinds of cooked foods.

In the tenth month, as well as when the third month has arrived, a longing (*dohada*) arises in the woman. Whatever she desires, that very thing the best of physicians should provide her. One should avoid foods consisting of split pulses, those that cause burning sensations, and heavy foods. For pregnant women, one should strictly avoid sour things, warm milk, and other heavy substances. Earth should not be eaten, nor should *sūraṇa* tubers; garlic and onions must be abandoned by a pregnant woman. However, sweet and flavorful *sūraṇa* tubers should be given, for they are wholesome and beneficial.

The physician should always cause pregnant women to avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, anger, emaciation, and wandering about; by doing so, the prosperity of well-being arises for the pregnant women. Now, even when the [gestation] has reached five or eight months as prescribed by one's own custom, a Brāhmaṇa feast and other auspicious rites should be performed. When the longings (*dohada*) and other requirements are fulfilled, a handsome, brave, wise, and virtuous son is born. Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Care of the Fetus," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.

The fiftieth chapter. Ātreya said: If movement of the embryo is observed in the first month, then Madhuka, Mṛdvīkā, Candana, and Rakta-candana (1), stirred with milk and drunk, will cause the embryo to become stable. (2) If movement occurs in the second month, [one should take] Mṛṇāla and Nāgakeśara. When movement of the embryo is observed in the third month (3), one should drink the excrement of a mouse with sugar and milk. In the fourth month, there is burning sensation, thirst, and even pain (4) due to fever.

If the fetus moves in women, then one should have them drink uśīra, sandalwood, nāgakeśara, dhātakī flowers, sugar, ghee, honey, and curd. If the fetus moves in the fifth month, one should have them drink pomegranate leaves, sandalwood, curd, and honey. In the sixth month, one should drink red ochre, black earth, cow-dung ashes, water strained through a cloth, and cool sandalwood mixed with sugar.

In the seventh month, one should have her drink a sweet decoction of *gokṣura*, *samaṅgā*, *padmaka*, thick *muśīra*, and *nāgakeśara*. In the eighth month, for women whose fetus has moved, comfort is attained by those who have drunk *rodhra*, honey, and *māgadhikā* together with milk. Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Treatment for a Moved Fetus," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 50.

The fifty-first chapter. Ātreya said: Emaciation (śoṣa), nausea, vomiting, swelling, fever, as well as loss of appetite, diarrhea, and discoloration—these eight are the complications of pregnancy. (1) I shall now describe its treatment according to the appropriate method: The sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree, *magadhā*, *uśīra*, and *ghana* (musta), (2) combined with sugar and formed into pills placed in the mouth, are a remedy for emaciation. (3) One should administer *vatsaka*, *magadhā*, ginger, and the fruit of *āmalakī*, ground together with tender *bilva* and curd. (4)

A drink mixed with sugar is always beneficial for women during pregnancy. (5) The paste of *bhūnimba* drunk with sugar, or combined with honey, removes vomiting and moisture in the heart. (6) Fresh ginger, *kaṭuka*, and the filaments (*keśara*) of *mātuluṅga* used for cleaning the teeth and tongue, along with gargling with warm water, (7) alleviate the loss of appetite in all pregnant women; likewise, *vatsaka*, pomegranate, *pāṭhā*, *bilva*, and *balā* (8) as well as the tender leaves of *jambu* and mango [are beneficial], according to the tradition. (9)

O Seventh One, for women suffering from diarrhea, [a preparation] with sugar and curd combined with *lābha* [is recommended]. (9) Harītakī, ginger, or Triphalā decoction taken cold with jaggery destroys constipation and abscesses when drunk by women. (10) For urinary obstruction, one should drink the seeds of *trapusa*, *ervāru*, and *bīja*, along with *māgadhī* and *śilābheda*, mixed with plenty of sugar and rice-water;

this certainly and quickly removes the blockage of urine in pregnant women. (11) [One should take] a paste of *madhuka*, *viṣa*, and lotus stalks (*mṛṇāla*), as well as the thick paste of lotus filaments (*padmakiñjalka*), *ativiṣā*, and *aindra* seeds, with water infused with *uśīra*.

Then, a paste made from equal parts [of the aforementioned drugs] should be administered quickly as a drink; this is beneficial even for young women experiencing displacement of the fetus (garbhacāla), provided it is enriched with sugar. 12. Swellings are complications of pregnancy; one should apply fomentation with warm water, but a wise physician must not administer a severe or drastic purgative. 13. Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Treatment of Complications of Pregnancy," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 51.

The fifty-second chapter. Ātreya said: Due to the consumption of incompatible foods, as well as during the distresses of pregnancy, the child suffers from the pain of excessive pressure on the head. Or, the fetus may be expelled sideways through the vaginal opening or another passage, whereby the offspring dies and the mother encounters great suffering. Alternatively, due to the modesty of women, when the vagina is constricted, one should recognize a "mūḍhagarbha" (malpresented fetus); I shall now describe its symptoms. There is also pain in the bladder.

The birth canal becomes obstructed; her womb roars and distension arises. There is piercing pain, breaking pain in the limbs, and loss of sleep occurs due to Vāta; O best of physicians, this results in the retention of the fetus (4–5). From Pitta, there is colic, fever, the three doṣas, thirst, impairment of the senses, and dizziness; there is difficulty in urination and headache, as well as the obstruction of the embryo (6). From Kapha, there is lassitude, drowsiness, sleep, stupor, distension, trembling, cough, and a bad taste in the mouth (7).

In the case of a dead fetus (mūḍhagarbhaka), one should recognize that which arises from dual combinations (dvandvaja) through their respective pairs [of symptoms], while everything [involving all three doshas] would be of the combined type (sānnipātika). [The signs include] dizziness, fainting, thirst, flatulence, obstruction of wind, and agitation; she suffers from fainting, vomiting, roughness, and reaches a state of dejection. One should know this as a dead fetus, even when occurring in a woman who acts quickly. Therefore, O expert, I shall now describe the medicine for this great delusion (mahāmoha). In the Vātika type, the best of physicians should prescribe massage, anointing, mild sudation, and should have her drink gruel (yavāgū) and the five-spice compound (pañcakola). In the Paittika type...

Cool drinks along with cold foods and side dishes [are beneficial]; likewise, one should drink *yaṣṭika* with milk. (12) Trikaṭu, triphalā, kuṣṭha, rodhra, vatsaka, and dhātukī, boiled together with jaggery (*guḍa*), should be drunk for a case of *mūḍhagarbha* caused by *śleṣman*. (13) A decoction of mūrvā, ciñcā, vāstuka, karṇī, mañjiṣṭhā, rodhra, nīlikā, the root of karkandhu, and saurāṣṭrī, taken with jaggery, is beneficial. (14) In disorders of *rakta-pitta*, purification of the abdomen occurs; now I shall describe the medicine for a dead fetus (*mṛtagarbha*).

O best of physicians (15), having diligently massaged the woman, if the fetus within the womb dies due to lack of nourishment, then listen to me regarding the surgical remedies and medicines: having fashioned a well-curved instrument from the opening of the umbilicus, one should place the woman with the obstructed fetus upon it, extend her knees slightly, support her back with a common prop, and draw [the fetus] down from the abdomen.

If [the fetus] is stuck at the vaginal opening, one should lubricate the hand with sesame oil or water and insert it; then, grasping the neck region of the fetus with the index finger and thumb, one should extract it. Alternatively, using a crescent-shaped surgical instrument, one should sever the pair of arms of the dead fetus and extract the limbs. By applying the root of *lāṅgalī* with warm water as an ointment to the navel of women, the fetus is quickly brought forth and delivered.

One should grind the roots of *balā*, *sūryakānti*, and *somavallī* with collyrium and apply it as an ointment. (18) Having ground the roots of *bhīru*, *bhūnimba*, and *vārttākī*, along with *pippalī*, *yavānī*, *agaru*, and *vacā*, together with warm water, (19) and having applied this ointment below the navel, she will give birth. Furthermore, the roots of *lāṅgalikī*, *devadālī*, and *tumbikā* (20), as well as all [the substances] beginning with *kośātakī*, are prescribed for application; indeed, these are the ointments for women in labor, by which she gives birth easily. (21) [This is found] on the northern side of the Himavat.

On the bank dwells a Rākṣasī named Surasā; by the sound of her anklets, the pregnant Viśalyā shall become free from her pains. Aiṃ Hrīṃ! O Blessed One, Bhagamālinī! Move, move! Cause it to revolve! Make the flower blossom, make it blossom! Svāhā! Oṃ! Salutation to the Blessed One, the one whose banner is the Makara, the one whose bow is flowers, who has stirred the hearts of all gods and asuras, and who dwells in the wombs of young women! Hrīṃ! Move the fetus, move it! Svāhā!

One should have her drink milk consecrated with this [mantra]; by that, there is an easy delivery. (23) Aiṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hroṃ hrauṃ hraḥ. (24) Having written this yantra on the upper side of a birch-bark leaf, one should show it to a woman with a difficult labor and place it beneath her bed; by that, there is an easy delivery. (25) One who dwells alone on the banks of the Gaṅgā and wanders in the Himalayas—by drinking the water from her wing-feathers, [the woman] will then, in an instant, (26) give birth to a son, just as the words of Kākarudra [prophesy]. By this [means]. (27)

The messenger should remain anxious until she has been made to drink [the medicine]; by that, the woman gives birth at home with ease, like a crow. Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Treatment of Mūḍhagarbha (Obstructed Labor)," in the third section of the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-third chapter. Ātreya said: Immediately after delivery, one should administer the seeds of *rodhra*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *devadāru*, and *bījakāhva*, as well as *karkandhū*, according to availability, once the blood has been purified. The birth-canal (*yoni*) should be cleansed with oil, then filled and massaged with it; subsequently, one should apply heat by means of a heated stone. Having observed a fast in this manner, on the second day, one should administer jaggery, ginger, and *harītakī*. After two watches (six hours) have passed, one should cause her to drink either warm *kulattha* soup or hot water.

On the third day, one should administer a gruel of five types of *kola* fruits. One should administer a gruel mixed with the four aromatic spices (*caturjātaka*). On the fifth day, one should feed him boiled rice of *śāli* and *ṣaṣṭika* varieties. Following this sequence, one should provide nourishment for fifteen days. (1) One should grind together long pepper (*pippalī*), long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*), ginger (*nāgara*), *ghanavāluka*, coriander (*kustumburūṇi*), and *mañjiṣṭhā*, along with milk, into a paste. (2) For the purpose of purifying the milk, one consumes the paste immediately after drinking it. (3) Black pepper (*marīca*) and long pepper root (*pippalīmūla*) [are added] to the milk for the sake of increasing the quantity of milk.

Māgadhī, Nāgarī, Pathyā, jaggery, ghee, and milk—this drink produces breast milk in women, even when taken in a dose of one-quarter part milk. Having performed this for women on the twelfth day, the best of physicians should perform auspicious recitations and show [the child] to the woman. Furthermore, on the twelfth day following the birth, once the naming ceremony has been completed, he should perform the piercing of the ears, the tying of the cloth, and the marriage ceremony for the child. Thus it is stated in the Hārītottara spoken by Ātreya.
In the third section, the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Attendants of Childbirth" (Sūtikopacārī).

The fifty-fourth chapter. Ātreya said: The wise have described five defects of breast milk in women: thick milk, hot milk, sour milk, and another; [furthermore,] scant milk, alkaline milk, and soft milk. Of these, soft milk leads to well-being, while the other five are causative of disorders. From the consumption of thick milk, there occurs abdominal distension, obstruction, and the onset of dyspnea, cough, and so forth, as well as a bloated abdomen. [A child born from such milk becomes] one of little vitality, emaciated, and dejected.

Afflicted by dyspnea and diarrhea due to the defect of insufficient milk, a son may become mute; (4) likewise, fever, emaciation, and weakness arise in a child from warm milk, as does fever and diarrhea from warm milk. (5) Through mild milk, a child certainly attains a good disposition, strength, and health, and even becomes handsome. (6) Eye disease, itching, discharge of phlegm from wounds, and a moist nose and mouth occur when alkaline milk is consumed. (7) Therefore, I shall now describe the remedy.

Listen, Hārīta, to my teaching: 8. When the abdomen is distended due to flatulence and the child is afflicted by disorders such as labored breathing, that condition is to be recognized as *utphullikā*, which causes great suffering to children. 9. In the case of *udare* (abdominal swelling), one should first extract blood using leeches and the like; in the disorder of *utphullida*, a remedy that neutralizes the defect of milk (*kṣīradoṣa*) should be administered. 10. A strong fomentation (*sveda*) with fire, or even cauterization with a probe (*śalākā*), may be applied; O best of physicians, eruptions shaped like drops (*bindukākārāḥ*) arise upon the belly. 11. A decoction of the root and fruit of *bilva*, *pāṭhā*, the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), and the two types of *bṛhatī*, combined with jaggery (*guḍa*), [is the remedy].

This is beneficial for the fever of children (12). For women, the drinking of these [decoctions] shall be the destroyer of fever in children (13). A decoction of *parpaṭaka* combined with sugar and honey is beneficial; *kairāta* combined with honey is for the destruction of fever in children (14). Alternatively, a powder of *bhārṅgī*, *rāsnā*, and *karkaṭaka* combined with honey, or a linctus [made from them], prevents asthma and cough even in a child (15). A powder of *pathyā*, *vacā*, *nāgaraka*, *ghana*, and *karkaṭa* mixed with jaggery (*guḍa*) likewise destroys cough in children (16). [The powder of] *palāśabheda*...

Having ground triphalā, trapusī, varī, and māgadhī with rice-water, one should administer it enriched with sugar; this conquers urinary obstruction (17). One should give the powder of nāgarī, abhayā, dantī, and guḍa to children; this will undoubtedly destroy abscesses as well (18). A drink of pāṭhā, bilva, śilādi, vatsaka, and the bark of śālmalī with milk prevents diarrhea in children (19). An ointment of arjuna, kadamba, kuṣṭha, and gairika prevents skin disorders in a child (20). [Also] rodhra...

Rasāñjana, dhātrī, and gairika, combined with honey as a collyrium, prevent eye diseases in children. (21) Vacā, brāhmī, maṇḍūkī, ghanasāra, kuṣṭha, and nāgara, given in the morning with ghee, promotes nourishment in children. (22) Guḍūcī, apāmārga, viḍaṅga, śaṅkhapuṣpī, viṣṇukrāntā, vacā, pathyā, nāgara, and śatāvarī—(23) The powder of these, mixed with ghee, when licked by one, causes intelligence to arise; in three days, [one attains] a thousandfold [intellect]. (24)

One should master these twenty-four verses. A powder made of the three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), coriander (dhanyā), caraway (yavānī), *sālamūlikā*, *vacā*, *brāhmī*, and *bhārṅgī* is beneficial when taken with honey; it bestows eloquence upon children and produces a voice like the sound of a lute. O best of physicians, he who has labored breathing, loss of consciousness, excessive drowsiness, trembling, headache, and fever is incurable. He whose appearance is like saliva, who lacks consciousness, whose eyes are rolling, and whose limbs are stiff and distorted, is said to be suffering from epilepsy (*apasmāra*).

In the case of an infant suffering from epilepsy (apasmāra), one should administer cooling remedies; specifically, a nasal drop (*nasya*) of *vacā*, rock salt (*saindhava*), and long pepper (*pippalī*), or jaggery with ginger (*nāgara*). (28) The juice of *agasti* leaves combined with black pepper (*marica*) should be administered; by this, relief will be found. At that time, gentle swinging is beneficial. (29) One should cauterize the area at the back of the head and the forehead with an iron rod. (30) O best of physicians, [the seizure spirits] transfer [the affliction] even to an infant when it is in an empty house, a temple, a cremation ground, amidst a crowd of gods, at a crossroads, at the confluence of two rivers, or when the child is agitated by fear. (31)

Pūtanā, Lohitā, Revatī, Dhvāṅkṣī, Kumārī, Śākunī, Śivā, and likewise Ūrdhvakeśī and Senā—these eight are proclaimed. (32–33) Now hear from me the names of the others: Rohiṇī, Vijayā, Kālī, Kṛttikā, Ḍākinī, Niśā, Bhūtakeśī, and Kṛśāṅgī; these eight are proclaimed. (34) I shall now describe their characteristics and the sequence of worship and offerings; listen. (35) Immediately after birth, the Pūtanā named Lohitā has a cadaverous smell.

And she weeps blood again and again. (36) I shall describe the offering for her, by which well-being arises: on the second day, a *pūtanā* named Revatī seizes the child. (37) Its symptoms are that it weeps and trembles violently; having made an image out of black clay and anointed it with perfumes, (38) one should cast it at night in the southwest direction, along with *kṛśara*, rice powder, lamps, incense, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), betel leaves, and black threads. (39) When the third day arrives, [the *pūtanā*] named Vāyasī...

As soon as she is seized by Pūtanā, the child weeps and will not suckle at the breast (40). He suffers from fever and diarrhea, and cries out intensely like a crow. For her, one should offer an oblation at midday consisting of curd-rice in a vessel, barley-porridge, and fried cakes (41), along with a banner, a bowstring, black fragrant unguents, incense, lamps, and unbroken grains. On the fourth day, the Pūtanā named Kumārī seizes the child; he is then tormented by fever (43) and the child stares vacantly into her face.

He becomes extremely parched and weeps; hear now the sequence of worship and offerings for her: (44) milk-rice, ghee, sugar, and three lamps of ghee. (45) Having fashioned an earthen image and offered an oblation with flowers, incense, and unbroken rice grains at midday in the direction of Yama, one shall become happy. (46) On the fifth day, the Pūtanā named Śākunī seizes the child; seized by her, the infant does not suckle. (47) Afflicted by fever, he vomits, cries, coughs, and then trembles. (48) Of her...

An offering is made to Śobhanikā with sesame-sweets (tilalaḍḍuka), white perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and incense; one should worship her earthen image. (49) Taking recourse in the northern direction, one should present the oblation (bali) in the forenoon. When the sixth day arrives, a maiden named Śivā cries out, sighs, vomits, and likewise trembles. (50) The child, afflicted by fever and diarrhea, does not take the breast milk. To her, an oblation should be given—a sacrificial porridge (caru) made of seven types of grain—along with milk-rice (pāyasa), curd, and lamps; she is to be worshipped. (51)

One should worship the earthen image with sesame flour, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and incense; then, resorting to the northeast direction, one should offer an oblation in the afternoon. On the seventh day, when the child is seized by Pūtanā Urdhvakeśī, the symptoms appear as before, and one should likewise offer an oblation. When the eighth day arrives, the Pūtanā named Senā seizes the child; he breathes heavily and shakes his hands violently. For her, one should give curd-rice, sesame flour, and fried cakes.

Incense, lamps, perfumes, flowers, betel, and unbroken grains (akṣata)—one should offer this oblation (bali) in the south-eastern direction at dusk. In this manner, the ritual of offering (balikarma) is performed for each month and for the year. Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Pediatrics," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-fifth chapter. Ātreya said: In deserted temples, on cremation grounds, at the base of streets and main roads, on carriage-roads, in empty cities with abandoned pleasure-gardens, in parks, and at crossroads—when the heart is agitated, these minor planetary spirits (*kṣudragraha*) arise in men. These well-known planets are of ten types; I shall now describe them. Ten were proclaimed by the great teachers, though some say there are twenty-one. I shall explain the treatment for the ten planets; listen, my son. [The first two are] Aindra and Āgneya.

Yama, another is Nairṛta, Varuṇa, Graha, the Maruts, Kubera, Aiśānya, and the Graha-graha; there is yet another, the Paiśācika-graha—these ten are the leaders of the grahas. That which occurs in a grove, a monastery, or a temple should be known as the Aindra-graha; by it one exults and sings, both with pride and without pride, and is truly possessed by madness. In a cremation ground or at a crossroads, the evil Āgneya-graha seizes; by that very [graha] one weeps excessively and perceives danger on all sides.
