On the battlefield and in the cremation ground, Yama is also said to be roused; by him a man is overwhelmed and distressed, and he behaves like a hungry ghost (preta). (8) At an anthill, a crossroads, or a sacred shrine (caitya), the Nairṛta spirit seizes him; by that [possession], he acts with hatred, runs about, and even kills. (9) With eyes closed, face discolored, yet possessing great strength and a wicked mind, the Vāruṇa spirit moves along the banks of rivers and lakes. (10) By that [possession], saliva flows from his mouth and the man urinates excessively; swelling of the eyes is observed, and he looks about as if mute.

11. And when it seizes one in the midst of a whirlwind, it is the seizure by Māruta; by that, the wretched person becomes emaciated, or suffers from abdominal pain, or weeps. 12. Agitated and with exhausted eyes, he sits down, afflicted by hunger; and when it seizes one in the midst of joy, pride, or arrogance, it is the seizure by Yakṣarāja. 13. By that, he becomes haughty with pride and likewise very fond of ornaments. 14. In a beautiful temple of the gods, Śivagraha provides deception; he smears his limbs with ashes and wanders about naked. 15. He is constantly devoted to the meditation on Śiva.

He is fond of song and instrumental music. 16. The *grahaka* is named after the planets; afflicted by hunger but not by thirst, he neither speaks nor hears. 17. Whether upon what is left over or what is pure, the *piśāca-graha* seizes him; by that [possession], he dances, cries out, sings, and likewise prattles. 18. He wanders like one intoxicated, naked, with saliva flowing, and suffering from hunger and other such needs. Thus, the characteristics of the ten *grahas* have been described by me. 19. Hereafter, I shall describe the remedy; listen, my son, in brief.

Bathing in water is most excellent, as is the performance of the *bali* offering; through these, one attains the happiness described in the ritual worship. Elā, *jātīphala*, the two types of *madhūka*, *rāsnā*, as well as *khādira*, camphor, *āmalakī*, *jaṭā*, *bahusutā*, *ghoṇṭā*, and *amlasāra*—these likewise [are used].

Lead, mercury, and pomegranate seeds, combined with wines and each mixed equally with curd, milk, and the juice of *laṅgalā*, should be ground into a paste. 21. This should be impregnated with the juice [of *laṅgalā*], and pills prepared from it—known as *Candraprabhā*—conquer severe diseases such as insanity. 22. Ginger, the essence of *madhuka*, *cavī*, and *kiṃśuka*, combined with *vacā* and asafoetida and mixed with goat’s urine, should be administered; it destroys the afflictions caused by planetary spirits and is the supreme destroyer of such spirits. 23.

Cat excrement, snake slough, neem, and peacock feathers, together with mustard seeds, snake slough, piṇḍītaka, and sarja-moca resin—these, smeared with ghee, constitute an incense for the pacification of planetary afflictions (24). The pill known as *cetanā*, as well as *brāhmī-ghṛta*, are prescribed; these should be employed here in cases of epilepsy (25). One should fumigate with guggulu mixed with honey and ghee, using that incense; and by means of that mantra, O Hārīta, one should threaten the afflicted planet (26): *Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of Beings, whose nails are like the Kali age, the Fierce One.*

Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Beings, whose soul is the immortal! You who possess fangs that are terrifying; you whose three eyes on the forehead are tawny and blazing like fire; you whose immeasurable splendor is the fire of intense wrath; you who are adorned with the noose, trident, khaṭvāṅga staff, ḍamaru drum, bow, arrow, mallet, the mudrā of granting fearlessness, the staff, and the trampling pose; you who wear a mass of tawny matted hair and the crescent moon; you whose body is colored by the glow of ashes; you whose throat is adorned by the swelling of the fierce Kālakūṭa poison—show, show your form! Dance, dance!

Move! Move! Bind with the noose! Bind! Terrify with the *huṃ* sound! Terrify! Strike with the vajra-staff! Strike! Cut with the sharpened sword! Cut! Pierce with the tip of the trident! Pierce! Pound with the mallet! Pound! Cause the entry of all seizing spirits (*graha*)! Cause them to enter! *Svāhā!* (27) If an excellent offering (*bali*) is given to one possessed by a seizing spirit, he is liberated from it; of this there is no doubt. (28) Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Science of Spirits" (*Bhūtavidyā*), in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 55.

The fifty-sixth chapter. Ātreya said: The physician has designated poison as being of two kinds: stationary (sthāvara) and mobile (jaṅgama). Śṛṅgika, vatsanābha, and likewise śārṅgaverika; dāraka, kālakūṭa, śaṅkha, sadyaḥsukandaka, and hālāhala—these are the eight species of stationary poison. Śṛṅgika is black in color, vatsanābha is yellow, and that which is the same color as ginger is called śārṅgaverika. Dāraka is the color of a monkey, and kālakūṭa is...

Madhuprabha, Śaṅkha, Ativiṣābhāsa, Pītābha, Satsukanduka, Hālāhala, and Kṛṣṇavarṇa—these are the eight species [of poison]. When yellow poison is seen by a man, it immediately causes excellent vomiting. One should always cause him to vomit as long as the *ativiṣa* has been ingested; one should quickly sprinkle his face with water purified by the mantra. Oṃ hara hara nīlakaṇṭha amṛtaṃ plāvaya hūṃ! By the syllable *hūṃ*, swallow the poison, swallow! By the syllable *klīṃ*, remove it, remove it! By the syllable *hrauṃ*, [swallow] the nectar!

"Plāvaya plāvaya! Hara hara! There is no poison! Ucchire ucchire! (7) "Oṃ, salutations! O Hara, Hara! To the one whose form is the manifestation of the mantra, adorned at the tips of his matted locks by the crescent moon and the white-bodied blue-necked one—withdraw the poison! Hara hara hara! There is no poison! Viṣa viṣa viṣa! Ucchire ucchire ucchire! With this "whisper-in-the-ear" mantra (*karṇejapa-mantra*), one should repeatedly sprinkle cold water on the palate and the mouth. (8) Having ground the roots of the *tāṇḍulīyaka* plant with warm water, drinking it destroys swallowed poison when used for emesis.

Laghava (leadwort) would be effective. 9. The root of *kākajaṅghā*, the root of *sahacarī*, *kadara* from the *aiḍaga* tree, and the bark of *kārmuka*—when drunk with warm water, this undoubtedly destroys even the most terrible poison instantly. 10. The root of *khadira* and likewise the fruits of *nimba*—when drunk with warm water, these would conquer poison at that very moment. 11. Having drunk *vatsāhvā* and *aśvagandhā* with warm water, the poison that has been swallowed is quickly warded off; such is the word of the Vedas for a man. 12. Now, the principal [remedy]...

I shall describe the remedy for blood from a wound and for that [poison] of venom, by which well-being is attained. (13) That which has reached a vital spot (*marman*) is considered incurable; that which resides in the blood is curable, while that residing in the flesh is difficult to cure. (14) O friend, I shall describe the medicine for that which has reached the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), which is incurable. Having recognized a man smeared with poison, one should then apply the countermeasure. (15) Poison [is neutralized] by a plaster made of the two types of *rajanī* (turmeric) and *amlaka*, ground with sour gruel (*kāñjika*).

It destroys [the poison] when applied; there is no doubt in this. (16) Whether with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, or with *kāñjika* sour gruel, or with very cold water, it destroys the poison when applied; there is no doubt in this. (17) O best of physicians, that which is called "mobile poison" (*jaṅgamaviṣa*) is said to be of eight kinds: the *darvīkara* (hooded snakes), the *maṇḍalina* (ringed snakes), the *rājiman* (striped snakes), and the *guṇḍasas*; (18) as well as the scorpion (*vṛścika*), the *goraka*, and the *khaṇḍabinduka*. The poison of the *alarka* (mad dog), the rat (*mūṣa*), and the cat (*mārjāra*) is also said to be of many kinds. (19) It is stated that the poison of all *darvīkara* snakes is of the nature of wind (*vātātmaka*), and so too that of the *maṇḍalina* snakes.

The poison of all [serpents] is said to be of the *paittika* (bilious) nature. Those which are described as having stripes are also poisons of the *kapha* (phlegmatic) nature. That [poison] which causes movement in various directions, extreme and unbearable pain in the head, and distress in the heart, they declare to be incurable. That in which there is discharge of blood from the nose and swelling is seen in the eyes, and the tongue becomes numb—the wise know that to be incurable. That in which the body hairs wither and the body takes on a yellowish appearance, and whose head is not steady, [is also incurable].

Seeing that which is incurable by *tamas* (darkness/ignorance) as being devoid of these [remedies], the best of physicians should perform its counteraction: *Oṃ namo bhagavate sugrīvāya sakalaviṣopadravaśamanāya ugrakālakūṭaviṣakavaline viṣaṃ bandha bandha hara hara bhagavato nīlakaṇṭhasyājñā | Oṃ namo hara hara viṣaṃ saṃhara saṃhara amṛtaṃ plāvaya plāvaya nāsti are re viṣa nīla parvataṃ gaccha gaccha nāsti viṣam oṃ hāhā ūcire ūcire ūcire |* With this mantra, one should frighten the mouth with water.

Oṃ, salutations! O Haṃsa, behold, behold the nectar! (25) A paste of jayakūṭa, vacā, kuṣṭha, saindhava salt, magadhā, and niśā is prescribed for a bite-wound; it destroys even the most dreadful poison. (26) Surasā, rajanī, vyoṣa, yavānī, and pāribhadraka are prescribed as a plaster for a snake-bite wound to pacify the poison. (27) A plaster of kuṣṭha, mustā, ajājī, viḍaṅga, madhuyaṣṭikā, and the root of guñjā, applied with cold water, is beneficial for one bitten by a maṇḍalī snake. (28) For those whose poisons consist of stripes, [the application of] house-soot...

A paste consisting of *vacā*, *ghanam*, mustard seeds, *yavānī*, and the three fruits of the *picumanda* tree, combined with *vraṇataila*, is for application on those afflicted by *rājimat* [venoms]. (29) *Aṭarūṣaka*, *kirātatikta*, the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), *vacā*, *viśālā*, *picumandaka*, *pathyā*, *yavānī*, and the two types of *rajanī* are likewise recommended as a paste for wounds caused by bites. (30) O best of physicians, whether it be stationary (*sthāvara*) or mobile (*jaṅgama*) poison that has been ingested, it quickly causes severe pain; thus it has been declared by the most excellent of men. (31) *Oṃ namo bhagavate*.

Obeisance to the one with the crest upon his head, whose entire body is washed by streams of nectar; O you who are surrounded by jars of nectar, flood me, flood me with nectar! Svāhā! (32). Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Tantra of Poisons," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.

The fifty-seventh chapter. Ātreya said: Cut (*chinna*), pierced (*bhinna*), likewise fractured (*bhagna*), bruised (*ghṛṣṭa*), and similarly crushed (*piṣṭa*), as well as *āsphālita*, *samprahāra*, and *saṅghāta*—these are described by the wise. (1) Upon seeing a man pierced by a weapon, medical treatment must be administered. (2) If the flesh remains attached to the bone but the bone itself is severed, or if it is severed at the primary or secondary branches [of the limbs], that is called *chinna*. (3) That which is completely severed at a non-joint (*asandhi*) should be declared incurable.

It is always taught that a wound severed by a sword, a crescent-headed arrow, or an axe is to be treated as follows: first, the application of *cāraṇā* (rubbing) and *dhāvana* (washing) is prescribed, followed by a rapid fomentation using a cotton pad soaked in sesame oil. As long as blood flows, one should continue to anoint it with oil; indeed, when the blood undergoes a morbid change (*vikṛti*), anointment with oil is considered necessary. If swelling and other complications arise due to excessive discharge from the wound, and seeing a person whose joint has been severed, one should sprinkle him with warm water. [This applies] to the accumulated [blood].

Picu-tailaka is also recommended for a wound; when pus is discharging, leaves of nimba and āragvadha [should be applied]. (8) Having ground pathyā with jaggery, this ointment purifies the pus; once it has been purified after three days, applying that same ointment there is beneficial. (9) Having ground the bark of dhava, arjuna, kadamba, and the two trees udumbara and plakṣa with water, an ointment made from that causes the wound to heal. (10) That which is pierced by spears, arrows, bhalla-missiles, swords, tomara-javelins, or by the sharp edges of razor-blades is called *bhinnam*.

The physician declares that [a fracture] arising in a non-vital spot (amarmaja) is curable, whereas that which resides in a vital spot (marmastha) does not heal. Washing with the juice of *apāmārga* as well as *kūṣmāṇḍaka*, or even with fermented rice-gruel (*kāñjika*), is praised by the wise. Anointing with sesame oil is beneficial for one who has broken a bone while in a healthy state; furthermore, the previously mentioned ointments should be applied, as they bring about welfare. Indeed, if [the fracture occurs] in the chest, the head, the temples, the armpits, the feet, or at the junction of the three channels (*trika*), the abdomen, the tip of the mouth, the eyes, or the ears...

A foreign body (śalya) that is difficult to treat becomes manageable with surgical instruments if it is not deeply embedded; however, if it is located in the branches, sub-branches, or vital points (marmans), it cannot be cured by those medicinal treatments. Therefore, a wise physician should extract the foreign body using mechanical appliances, instruments, and counter-measures. One should prescribe exactly twelve types of appliances (yantras), twelve types of instruments (śastras), and four types of bandages for the removal of foreign bodies. These include the "alligator-mouth" (godhāmukha), the "thunderbolt-mouth" (vajramukha), the "tongs" (saṃdaṃśa), the "wheel-shaped" (cakrākṛti), the "heron-foot" (kaṅkapāda), and the "hook" (ayānaka).

The Śṛṅgaka, Kuṇḍala, Śrīvatsa, Sauvatsika, and Pañcavaktra—these twelve instruments have been described by the best of physicians. Now, the surgical instruments (śastra) are declared, each with its distinct name: the Ardhacandra (half-moon), Vrīhimukha (rice-shaped tip), Kaṅkapatra (heron-feathered), Kuṭhārikā (axe), Karavīrakapatra (oleander-leaf), and Śalākākārapatraka (rod-shaped blade). The Baḍiśa (fish-hook), Gṛdhrapāda (vulture’s claw), Śūlī (spear-headed), and Ghanamudgara (hammer)—these instruments are declared for the extraction of foreign bodies (śalya) individually. And the Atigupta (well-concealed)...

One should extract a splinter with forceps; once it has been pierced, the remedy must be applied by one who is wise. (21) Having recognized a deep-seated splinter, one should determine the remedy: it should be incised with a blade of *kuśa* grass and the [splinter] removed with saffron. (22) The remedy for a pierced [wound] must likewise be applied by one who is wise. (23) Where there is intense swelling, there the splinter perishes; having ascertained that it is accompanied by a splinter, is dense, and is painful, (24) one should apply the appropriate instrument there.

Appropriate instruments and surgical tools should be employed there by those skilled in reasoning and analysis (ūhāpoha). (25) The intense pain arising from the piercing of a foreign body (śalya) that spreads throughout the body of a living being is pacified by bitter ghee, slightly warmed and mixed with liquorice (yaṣṭīmadhu). (26) Sāla, Arjuna, Udumbara, Markaṭī, Rodhra, Samaṅgā, and Surasā—these, ground with water for application as a plaster during the extraction of a foreign body, bring about comfort. (27) Furthermore, the remaining treatments previously mentioned are beneficial when [the wound] has been incised or lanced. (28)

In those cases, sand-sweating (*vālukāsveda*) and pot-sweating (*ghaṭīsveda*) should be performed. Having seen a man with a fractured bone, I shall now declare the remedy for him: fractures of the wrist, the elbow, the knee, as well as the hip, and a completely broken spinal column—these, O best of men, are curable. However, a fracture in the region of the neck, at the *indrabasti*, at *rohiṇī*, below the elbow, between the shoulder and the elbow, in the middle of the *trika* (the sacral region), or in the chest and the abdomen—if it is completely shattered, that is incurable.

Seeing a man whose [limb] is shattered, one should bind it with a section of bamboo; one should rub it with fresh butter and wrap it with castor leaves (32). One should sprinkle it with warm water and bind it gently with a cloth (33). Having ground the bark of *dhava*, *arjuna*, and *kadamba* trees with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), an application of this paste is beneficial, and through it, comfort arises (34). One should foment these parts with heat and then provide a covering once more; when the procedure is thus completed, one should then release the bandage (35), even after an interval of one day.

One should maintain that [treatment] as before until a knot forms; one should not bathe the person until then. (36) Upon seeing the person rubbing [the wound], bathing with *kāñjika* (sour gruel), urine, or cold water is considered beneficial. (37) As long as blood continues to flow, one should sprinkle it with oil; furthermore, various medicinal herbs should be applied here in small quantities. (38) In the case of suppuration and bleeding, fomentation (*svedana*) is prescribed; one should also provide treatment according to the rules, as in the case of a fracture. (39)

When a remedy has been administered, the best of physicians must be consulted; through reasoning and deliberation, one should act so that well-being is attained. (40) The disorder arising from a blow to the head is proclaimed as "head disease" (*śiroroga*); likewise, from a blow to the chest, a liver-tumor (*yakṛdgulma*) is produced. (41) In this manner, one should apply a remedy: bloodletting should be performed, and fomentation (*svedana*) should be employed by the physician for the successful completion of the treatment. (42) Furthermore, oil should not be consumed, nor should anything excessively hot or pungent; likewise, fish and dense meats [should be avoided].

And heavy foods (43); soup made from white *śāli* rice, as well as that from *āḍhakī* beans; rabbit, quail, eggplant, *kakkola*, and *taṇḍulīyaka* (44); *śatapuṣpā* and other such items, provided they are not combined with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*); and salt should not be consumed in excess if one desires one’s own well-being (45). One should avoid physical exercise, sexual intercourse, and sleeping during the day in due order, so that a man may attain happiness and prosperity (46). Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Treatment of Fractures," in the third section of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya. 57.

The fifty-eighth chapter. Ātreya said: Having observed a person burnt by fire, that burning is of four kinds: slightly burnt (*īṣaddagdha*), moderately burnt (*madhyadagdha*), excessively burnt (*atidagdha*), and properly burnt (*samyagdagdha*). O best of physicians, listen to the characteristics, my son. Excessively burnt extends into the flesh and is associated with vāta, pitta, and kapha; properly burnt is free from defects, and thus it should be known as being of four types. That burning by which the skin is sloughed off is born of pitta and is accompanied by blood.

When it is associated with pitta, it appears due to the provocation of pitta; that pitta located in the flesh is black in color and accompanied by intense pain. O best of physicians, I shall describe the treatment for its successful cure: For a slightly burnt area, an application of *kāñjika* (sour gruel) is for the sake of comfort. Nimba leaves, *surasā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *dhātrī* fruits—O best of physicians, these should be used as an application according to availability for a slightly burnt area. For a moderately burnt area, *payasyā* is the soothing application. [An oil] cooked with *madhuka*, *kuṣṭha*, and *mañjiṣṭhā*, along with ghee, [is also beneficial].

Kuṣṭha, yaṣṭīmadhuka, candana, and eraṇḍapatraka are considered beneficial; when applied as a paste ground with milk, it is helpful for burns on the body. (8–9) A powder of ghee, camphor, gairika, and rodhra—applied as a dry powder—removes pus and even promotes the healing of a burnt wound. (10) For burns caused by fire, a plaster of āmalakī, sesame, and kuṣṭha is recommended; likewise, a plaster of rodhra, uśīra, and samaṅgā mixed with cold water is beneficial. (11) Anointing with linseed oil and applying a plaster of madhuyaṣṭī with ghee are both beneficial for healing.

Dagdharohaṇa prevents burning. 12. In the event of injury from smoke, emesis, drinking milk, and likewise swimming in water are excellent for the pacification of the burning caused by smoke. 13. Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, named the Section on Therapeutics, in the Hārīta-uttara spoken by Ātreya. The Third Section is completed.
Chapter One. Ātreya said:
A fourth part of a mustard seed is an *aṇu*;
four mustard seeds make a *māṣa*;
and four *māṣas* make a *valla*.
Four *suvarṇas* of gold make one *karṣa*;
four *karṣas* make one *pala*;
four *palas* make one *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*;
four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*;
and four *āḍhakas* make one *droṇa*.

The measure for dry medicinal substances shall be double that for fresh ones; thus, the method of weighing for all [substances] is to be understood. Seventy-eight hundred barley grains (7,680) constitute one *pala*.
Four *pala*s make one *kuḍava*;
four *kuḍava*s make one *prastha*;
and four *prastha*s make one *āḍhaka*.
Four *āḍhakas* make one *kaṃsa*;
two *palas* make one *prasṛti*. [The same measure applies to] clarified butter, oil, sour gruel, milk, cream, molasses, and sugar.
Honey, liquor, as well as grapes, dates, and guggulu—4; and for garlic and salts, half of half a māna each is prescribed; the term *karṣa* denotes a measure equal to the size of a cat's paw. 5.
They know that a *vaṭodumbara* is equal to one *palam* of *audumbara*;
four *palas* are the measure of a *bilva*, and two *palas* are called an *añjali*.
O Mahāmati, two *añjalis* constitute a *kuḍava*, as will be described further.
One should define a *kuḍava* as being four *aṅgulas* in width and four *aṅgulas* in height, made either of wood or of clay.
Four *kuḍavas* constitute a *prastha*, and likewise, four *prasthas* constitute an *āḍhaka*.
Four āḍhakas constitute a droṇa; this is proclaimed as the standard for measurement.
One should administer an emetic and a purgative in a dose of one karṣa, a nourishing drink (santarpaṇa) in a dose of one pala, and a powder in a dose of one karṣa.
A wise physician should administer half a *pala* of alkali, one *karṣa* of *harītakī*,
one *pala* of garlic paste, one *pala* of *guggulu*,
and one *pala* of *sūraṇa* paste.
One should administer other powdered metals in doses of one karṣa each (verse 12).
Having correctly assessed the strength of the body as superior, inferior, or middling,
the wise physician should administer the linctus, powder, and decoction according to the prescribed rules (verse 13).
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Rules for Weighing and Measuring," in the fourth section (Sūtrasthāna) of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Two.
Ātreya said:
"O son, listen; four types of cooking for oils have been described:
the rough, the smooth, the intermediate, and another which is considered drying."

A decoction of *dugdhāranāla* or curd even dries up [the medicine], yet it does not cause the medicinal substances to lose their moisture; that which is foamless and pure becomes like the juice of *mañjiṣṭhā* when subjected to a "rough cooking" (*kharapāka*).
That too should be known as a subduer of Vata and is beneficial for massage and anointing.
It is foamy, cooked to a medium degree, liquid, and becomes solidified;
one should designate it as "medium-cooked" when it has little foam or no foam at all.
O best of physicians, that which is beneficial for enemas and drinks, which destroys the three doṣas,

and whose liquid portion is frothy, moon-like, and resembles that of a healthy person— such a viscous (cikkaṇaka) preparation is always declared to be beneficial when used as a nasal drop (nasya). 5–6.

That which is smoky, excessively burnt, or has the smell and taste of burnt matter, as well as that which is characterized by wind and dryness, should be known as unfit for all medical procedures. Furthermore, that which becomes rough during massage and sticky when cooked in a vessel should also be avoided.
In a goat-skin bag, cooking occurs within the middle of the day, and it is likewise drying;
oil is perfected in a fortnight, and ghee in seven days.
A decoction is prepared in as little as one watch (prahara), and one should accomplish [the preparation] in half a day.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Cooking of Oils," in the fourth section (Sūtrasthāna) of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Three.
Ātreya said:

Having prepared a bamboo tube four fingers wide and one *lakṣa* long, one should perform the enema treatment with it. This should be done neither in excessively hot weather nor in cold weather, nor when the patient has eaten,
nor when he is sleepy, nor when afflicted by urine, nor when afflicted by feces, nor when suffering from pain.

Having first expelled the feces and urine, and having washed the anus, one should place the patient on a bed that is not too soft; then, having contracted the left foot against the left side of the body and the right foot against the right side, and having placed them upon the calves, one should administer the non-unctuous enema (nirūha) and the enema procedure (bastikarma).
The wise physician should insert a tube measuring two finger-breadths into the interior of the anus.
Then, gradually pressing the enema bag, he should administer a *nirūha* (non-unctuous enema) using two *palas* of oil.
Following the *nirūha*, having slowly laid the patient supine and then raised him up, he should subsequently contract [the anal sphincter].
One should strike the buttocks with the palms five times;
then, having restored the patient to health even in an instant, it awakens the stomach and the seat of waste,
and wards off disorders such as bladder and abdominal wind.
The wise know this to be the Nirūha enema and that procedure of Basti-karma.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Nirūha Enema," in the fourth section on Sūtra-sthāna of the Hārīta-uttara as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Four.

Fomentation (sveda) is said to be of seven types: fomentation with a clod of earth (loṣṭasveda), fomentation with steam (bāṣpasveda), fomentation with a flame (agnijvālāsveda), fomentation with a jar (ghaṭīsveda), fomentation with water (jalasveda), fomentation with fruit (phalasveda), and fomentation with sand (vālukāsveda).
One should never perform fomentation without oil;
one should apply oil before the fomentation, for that makes it effective.

One should not administer sudation in cases of high fever accompanied by burning sensations and emaciation, nor in those afflicted by diarrhea, nor in those suffering from fainting, vertigo, and burning pain caused by poison. Furthermore, it is contraindicated in conditions of colic and swelling associated with Vata, as well as in those afflicted by cold phlegm (Kapha).
For these people, sudation is recommended as it bestows comfort.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Sudation," in the fourth section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna) of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Five.
Bloodletting occurs by four methods:
by venesection, by means of gourds, likewise by smooth horns, and by leeches; thus should the wise physician draw out the blood.
In the forenoon or the afternoon, when it is neither too hot nor too cold,
the physician should let the blood flow from one who has consumed barley gruel;
likewise, in all diseases of the head, [blood should be let] from the middle of the nostril.
The best of physicians should always carefully drain [the blood] from the vein.
Having left a space of two finger-breadths above the middle of the forehead, between the eyebrows, one should drain the vein;
at the middle of the elbow of the arms, one should bind the vein.
At the wrist joint (maṇibandha), one should bind the vein after leaving aside the four roots of the thumb and one finger-breadth (aṅgula).
One should bind the vein at the elbow (nātipārśva) after leaving aside four finger-breadths.
One should bind the vein at the ankle (ghuṇṭikā) on the foot.
Furthermore, other matters have not been stated here for fear of excessive prolixity.
It should be known by all that sprinkling with red [substances] using gourd-horns [is required].
That which is black, frothy, dark, or red is born from the disorder of wind (vātadoṣaja).
That which is endowed with all the [proper] characteristics should be known as arising from the three doshas.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Bloodletting," in the fourth section on General Principles (*sūtrasthāna*) of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Six.
Ātreya said:
Leeches are said to be of four kinds—Indrāyudhā, Ārohiṇī, Kālikā, and Dhūmrā.
The Indrāyudhā is blue in color with red sides, has a sharp mouth, and enters into deep, clear water or into crevices between stones.
By that [wind], it causes complications such as abscesses, burning sensations in the abdomen, swelling, fainting, and poisoning.
2. Blue-colored and yellow at the sides, with a mouth like a spike, it enters the lotus stalk;
by that, it causes complications such as abscesses, erysipelas, and swelling. 3.

A black snake (*kālikā*) found in a fish-pond should be discarded from afar. A smoke-colored or pigeon-colored snake with a yellow belly and a half-moon-shaped head that enters into mud or turbid water is fit for bloodletting and is free from complications.

Having washed the site with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should smear it with fresh butter (*navanīta*) and wash it again with warm water; thereafter, a leech (*jalaukā*) fit for application should be placed there once it has become full of blood and then released.
One should wash her face with salt water or urine;
alternatively, it may be milked out slowly like a cow's udder.
Then, having smeared the face with fresh butter, she should be administered [the treatment].
Once the vitiated blood has been removed, one should wash the bite with sour gruel (kāñjika), anoint it with ghee and honey, and bind it with a cloth.
7. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Application of Leeches," in the fourth section on General Principles (Sūtrasthāna) of the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.
Thus the Sūtrasthāna is completed.
The First Chapter:
On a delightful peak of the Himalayas, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas, [the sage] Atri, the bull among munis, was established there, abiding in the splendor of his asceticism. 1.
And after making an effort regarding the *kalpas*, Hārīta inquires:
"O dear one, this treatment has been understood by me in brief;
now, O observer of noble vows, I wish to hear the section on *kalpa*."
Atri said:
"The Abhayā is the best of the *kalpa* plants; hear now its virtues and qualities.
From it, the immortal nectar was drunk by the Lord of the Gods while he resided in heaven."
Drops fell upon the earth, and from them the *harītakī* was born.
It is endowed with five tastes, yet is devoid of one taste;
it is known to be astringent, sour, pungent, bitter, and sweet.
Listen now to its specific qualities, excluding salt:
pungency resides in the skin, astringency in the fat,
acidity within the fat, and sweetness resides in the bone.
Although it is bitter in its internal nature, it is combined with five tastes;

by its acidity it destroys wind (māruta), by its sweetness and bitterness it destroys bile (pitta), and by its pungency and astringency it destroys phlegm (kapha); thus, the Harītakī fruit is a destroyer of the three humors (tridoṣaghni). 8.
Harītakī is beneficial for those who bear bodies; like a mother, she is a provider of welfare.

A mother may occasionally be angry even when well-behaved, but Harītakī never becomes angry even when not practiced [as prescribed]. (9) O wise one, listen as I shall describe its origin and names. (10)
Vijayā, Rohiṇī, Pūtanā, Amṛtā, Cetakī, Abhayā, and Jīvantī as the seventh;
Vijayā was born on the Vindhya mountains, and Abhayā on the Himalayas.

Rohiṇī was born in Vaidiśa; Pūtanā is recorded as being from Magadha (12). Jīvantikā is from Surāṣṭra, and Cetakī is considered to be from Campā; Amṛtā is from the banks of the Sarayū—these are the seven species (13).

Abhayā is for eye diseases, Kālikā for diseases of the head, Vijayā for all applications, and Rohiṇī for healing wounds; Pūtanā is for the purpose of an ointment, and Amṛtā is likewise considered [to be used] in that way. 14.
Cetakī should be applied everywhere, along with the powder of jīvantī (15).
For the benefit of children, one should observe vijayā;
it is said that tryasrā and rohiṇī are [also used], while amṛtā is thick and fleshy (16).
The *abhayā* is said to have five corners, the *pūtanā* is four-cornered,
the *cetakī* is said to be three-cornered, and the *jīvantī* is long and fleshy.
The physician [should know that] the *vijayā* is blue in color, while the *rohiṇī* is yellow.
The *amṛtā* is black in color and slightly white with a yellowish tint;
a wise man should identify the *amṛtā* as being one and a half finger-breadths in measure.
The *pathyā* is most wholesome for men and instantly destroys all diseases.
Bestowing longevity and great contentment, it extends intelligence, complexion, vigor, luster, and memory.

(20) Eradicating pitta, kapha, and vāta, while properly closing the gates of the intellect, strength, and the senses, and causing the discharge of urine, feces, and impurities, the harītakī removes diseases from men. (21)
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Chapter on Harītakī," in the Section on Pharmaceutics (*Kalpasthāna*) of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Two.
Ātreya said:
The fruits of *harītakī*, *āmalakī*, and *vibhītaka* are called "triphalā" by physicians; I shall now state the determination of their proportions:
one part of *harītakī* and two parts of *vibhītaka*.
One should administer these together with one-third part of *āmalakī*.
Triphalā destroys *kapha* and *pitta*, cures major skin diseases (*mahākuṣṭha*), promotes longevity, stimulates digestion, is beneficial for the eyes, and purifies wounds.
When rubbed, it bestows a healthy complexion, destroys irregular fevers,
grants clear vision, removes itching, and cures vomiting, abdominal tumors, and hemorrhoids;
it is the supreme pacifier of all diseases and the enhancer of intellect and memory.
I shall explain the application of yoga for each individual disease:
in cases of *vāta*, it is combined with ghee and jaggery; in *pitta*, with honey and sugar;
in *śleṣman*, with the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*); and in urinary disorders (*meha*), with honey and water.
Combined with ghee and rock salt, it destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha) and indigestion;
a decoction used for eye-washing prevents eye diseases.
Taken with ghee, it removes itching, and with the juices of citron (mātuluṅga), it cures vomiting.
Combined with jujube and *sūraṇa* roots, it becomes effective against abdominal tumors and hemorrhoids;
when taken with milk, it cures consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), and with jaggery, it cures anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*).
It may also be administered with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja* along with clarified butter.
It is known to destroy wrinkles and gray hair, as well as to produce intelligence.
A decoction with milk and jaggery destroys irregular fever (viṣamajvara),
while a decoction with sugar and ghee removes all chronic fevers (jīrṇajvara).
This Triphalā is known to be beneficial for men in every application;

it is a pacifier of all diseases and instantly bestows vigor and a radiant complexion. Likewise, when combined with urine, it is beneficial in cases of swelling, jaundice, anemia, and abdominal enlargement.
Triphalā taken with buttermilk is beneficial in cases of diarrhea and disorders of the digestive tract (grahaṇī).
It is also beneficial when combined with milk in cases of diminished sensory power, chronic fever, and consumption (yakṣma).
Furthermore, it is useful for eye diseases, ailments of the head, skin diseases (kuṣṭha), itching, and the pain of ulcers.
A paste of Triphala and other ingredients, when drunk with water, cures urinary retention, jaundice, and weak digestion;
it may be taken with jaggery and ginger during the cold season, with sugar and milk during the heat, and with ginger during the rainy season. This Triphala is a remover of all diseases. (15–16)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Decoction of Triphalā," in the Kalpasthāna of the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Three:
Abhayā is said to be *dvy-aṅgulā*, and Pūtanā is *catur-aṅgulā*.
The *jīvantī* is one and a half finger-breadths, while the *cetakī* is six finger-breadths.
The *cetakī* is said to be of two kinds according to its shape and color:
the six-fingered variety is said to be white, and the one-fingered variety is known as pure white.
The black variety is declared to be the best for the purpose of purgation by one who desires victory.
As long as the *cetakī* remains on the branch of the tree, animals, birds, and others break it; what wonder is there in this for human beings? (3-4)

As long as a person holds the *cetakī* plant in their hand, they destroy all diseases through its power; of this there is no doubt. This applies even to kings, those who are delicate, and those who are averse to medicine.
For those who are emaciated, such purgation by easy means would be beneficial. Harītakī is an infallible elixir for the poor;
one should eat it to destroy disease either at the end of a wholesome meal or at its beginning.
For those afflicted by thirst, when there is dryness of the heart and throat, lockjaw, or constriction of the neck,
and in cases of acute fever where strength and the senses are diminished— this [Harītakī] is not recommended for pregnant women; however,
it is said to be excellent when used with jaggery and ginger, or combined with rock salt.
And it destroys the diseases of the stomach and the abdomen, like a rainbow striking trees. Ginger (śuṇṭhī) mixed with sugar should be used in autumn; it may also be used with jaggery in winter.
In the cool season (śiśira), it is beneficial with rock salt and long pepper (pippalī); in spring, the three pungents (trikaṭu) with jaggery are wholesome.
In summer, *pathyā* (harītakī) with sugar and ginger is beneficial; in the rainy season, it is likewise wholesome when combined with rock salt (*sindhūttha*).

Indeed, *pathyā* prepared with ghee instantly destroys all diseases. This paste of *harītakī* should be administered with ghee to a person; it destroys undigested matter (*āmānila*) within a man’s digestive tract.
It removes malignant disorders; having cooked it with castor oil, one should immediately eat this wholesome preparation (pathya).

One should also drink that very oil, which conquers all disorders arising from pitta, kapha, and vāta, including those accompanied by pain and constipation, after it has been kept in buffalo urine for seven days. 12–13.

Five *palas* of *pañcābhayā* with five *palas* of urine [taken] for seven days is highly recommended; likewise, others [may take it] until the milk-sea dries up. This is another application for twenty-one days. (14) This quickly destroys *vātodara*, as well as splenic enlargement, flatulence, and chest constriction.
Harītakī, prepared with water from rice-husk ash, destroys both anemia and worms.

Its powder combined with long pepper and rock salt, when used as a fumigant for eructations, immediately overcomes even severe indigestion and generates hunger. Likewise, its paste taken together with ginger produces the same effect. (15–16)
One abandons fever by licking it with rock salt (*saindhava*), curd, and buttermilk; in cases of diarrhea, it is beneficial;
in consumption (*rājayakṣmā*), one should lick it with honey; and for the destruction of swelling and abdominal enlargement (*śophodara*), it should be taken with urine.
(17) In cases of anemia (*pāṇḍuroga*), it should be taken with sugar; in wasting (*śoṣa*) accompanied by burning sensations, it should be taken with citron (*mātuluṅgī*).
"Endowed with its juice and prepared as a paste (kalka), it is declared by the lords of sages to be extremely unwholesome.
18. Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Specific Description of the Formulation of Harītakī," in the Section on Formulations (Kalpasthāna) of the *Hārītottara* spoken by Ātreya.
Chapter Four.
Born during the churning for the nectar of immortality, that great bird, seized by both gods and asuras,
flew to heaven with his beak;
and when he was overcome by the fatigue of battle and rushed along with the force of his exhaustion, [he was caught].
When [the body] had ascended and reached a state of exhaustion, drops of nectar indeed fell;
once the body was defiled, those drops fell and remained there. Consequently, by the power of time, a twelve-year famine arose.
All the small trees, shrubs, and creepers in the forest were completely withered;
consequently, all the sages had departed for a remote and dense thicket.
In their midst was one seized by old age, devoid of mobility, and utterly decrepit.
With his staff broken and his mouth's row of teeth shattered by chewing sugarcanes,
he was well-known there among the rishis who were emaciated by hunger;
he too, afflicted by hunger, wandered over the entire fertile earth.
Somewhere, by the power of merit, he beheld auspicious tree branches and abundant green grass on the ground resembling dark blue moss;
even while tormented by hunger, he ate them along with their leaves.
After six months, that rishi likewise ate withered branches, and after that, he ate tubers for one month; subsequently,
when a time of plenty arose, they all gathered together in one place.
Having become young again, he went to where they were;
seeing him, they were filled with wonder and asked, "What have you done?
He said nothing at all, but was then cursed by them in anger.
The substance that was consumed by you is unfit to be eaten by the twice-born;
it is foul-smelling and variegated, and from it the garlic (rasonaka) was born.
Furthermore, O high-minded one, I shall describe the potency of garlic.
Garlic (laśuna) is endowed with the five tastes, though it is devoid of the salty taste.
It possesses pungent and sour potencies; it is beneficial, unctuous, heavy, sweet in taste, and strengthening.
Furthermore, it is very sharp, increases intelligence, voice, complexion, and vision, and promotes the healing of fractured bones and joints. 14.

It destroys heart disease, chronic fever, abdominal colic, urinary disorders, hiccup, loss of appetite, gulma, edema, piles, leprosy, and the wind arising from fire; it also subdues asthma and phlegm. Therefore, it is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Rasunaka.
In summer, one should extract [the substance] resembling a hen's egg from a withered leaf;
O Mahāmati, having bound it well-protected in a pouch, one should preserve it, and during the rainy season and the cold season, one should employ it in the proper measure. 16–17.
Asafoetida, the two types of cumin, and ajamoda constitute the "three pungents" (kaṭutraya);
combined with ghee and sauvarcala salt, this is especially indicated for diseases of Vāta. It is also prescribed with the juice of mātuluṅga for colic and abdominal distension.
Garlic (rasona), when combined with curd, is prescribed by the wise as a pacifier of wind and other humors.
O best of sages, having squeezed it and extracted its juice, one should serve the juices of wild game and similar meats for the purpose of food.
A person suffering from bile diseases should drink milk mixed with sugar;

likewise in cases of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman), wasting (kṣaya), anemia (pāṇḍu), jaundice (kāmalā), chlorosis (halīmaka), all types of headaches, internal hemorrhaging (raktapitta), and vertigo (bhrama).
This elixir is beneficial for consumption, fainting, and epilepsy.
Having ground garlic together with an equal amount of trivṛt, one should administer it as a linctus, cooled with jaggery and castor oil. 23–24.

Having prepared this with due care, one should administer it to those suffering from urinary disorders; it is beneficial for edema, abdominal tumors (gulma), wind-diseases of the left side, and hemorrhoids.
[One should also use] the meat of the antelope, rabbit, black buck, partridge, and the *karkara* bird, as well as the essence of peacock and other birds, goat-meat, and so forth. 25.
For humans, rice, wheat, and meat are beneficial when accompanied by ghee and sweet flavors, as are guggulu and garlic (rasuna).
One should avoid physical exercise, exposure to the sun, sexual intercourse, anger, fasting, and indigestion;
one should likewise avoid them during diarrhea, urinary disorders, anemia, and anal diseases.
Garlic should not be administered to pregnant women, nor to children, nor to those afflicted by vertigo, nor to those intoxicated by liquor,
nor to those suffering from internal hemorrhage (raktapitta), nor to those with skin diseases (kuṣṭha), nor to those with blood disorders (raktavāta), nor to those with erysipelas (visarpa).
If it is given out of foolishness, purgation or emesis must be induced.

Neither leprosy nor jaundice can afflict a man [who uses it], for when prepared with excellent medicinal formulations, it acts like nectar; it expands the virility, sense faculties, nourishment, and strength of men.
(29) Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Formulation of Garlic," in the *Hārītottara* section on pharmaceutical preparations (*kalpasthāna*) as spoken by Ātreya. 4.
The fifth chapter. Hārīta said:
"O Blessed One, [tell me] the medicinal power and the qualities of that which is named guggulu."
"You ought to tell me for which diseases it is also recommended.
Thus addressed by the disciple, the one of great asceticism replied.
Ātreya said:
Generally, city-trees grow in desert lands;
they constantly exude guggulu resin when struck by the rays of the sun during the summer.
Alternatively, one should duly collect it from the Himalayas during the winter.
Resembling gold, brilliant, and in some places like a ruby;
in other places, resembling the eye of a buffalo—this is the favorite of the Yakṣas and deities.
Learn from me, as I speak, the ritual procedure for it according to the rules.

Guggulu pacifies the three doṣas, is aphrodisiac, unctuous, nourishing, and digestive; it is pungent in its post-digestive effect and increases complexion and strength. It promotes longevity, brings prosperity, and enhances progeny, memory, and intelligence.

Guggulu is remembered as the most excellent for pacifying sins and for promoting semen and menstrual blood. Endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste, it should be boiled in appropriate quantities with various medicinal drugs, each separately, according to the specific disease to be treated.
Seeing that only a small portion remains,

one who has eaten sparingly and is endowed with patience should move it [to another vessel] on an auspicious lunar day, using a white cloth, into an earthenware, golden, silver, or even crystal vessel.
Having offered oblations into the fire, one should attend upon it with devotion toward the gods and Brahmins.
Then, having entered the temple which is filled with flowers and well-supported,
[one should apply] rāsnā, guḍūcī, eraṇḍa, daśamūla, and prasāriṇī.

One should drink their decoction as appropriate, or with *yavānī*, in cases of Vāta; one afflicted by Pitta disorders should drink it with the *jīvanīya* drugs boiled separately. [The ingredients are:
*vāsā*, *candana*, *hrībera*, *mṛdvīkā*, and *tiktarohiṇī*.

A decoction of sarjūrā, parūṣaka, as well as jīvaka and karṣaka, combined with guggulu, should be used for drinking in cases of diseases involving pitta (13). [Likewise, a decoction] of triphalā, vyoṣa, cow’s urine, nimba, dhānyaka, and puṣkara [is recommended].
One afflicted by phlegm (kapha) should drink a decoction of *amṛtā* and *dīpyaka*, as well as *paṭolī*. One suffering from sinus ulcers, malignant wounds, glandular swellings,
scrofula, or tumors, as well as those with urinary disorders (*mehin*) or ulcers, should likewise drink [the aforementioned] combined with a decoction of *triphalā*.
The physician should administer guggulu mixed with a decoction of kirātatiktaka, amṛtā, nimba, vṛṣa, vyāghrī, and durālabhā for the treatment of gulma,
cough, chest injury, dyspnea, abscess, loss of appetite, and ulcers. (16)
One should drink guggulu combined with a decoction of dārvī and paṭola (17).
Or, for itching, pustules, swelling, and other such conditions, one should drink a Vāta-Kapha-alleviating mixture of pathyā,
punarnavā, dārvī, cow’s urine, and amṛtā (18).

The decoction of these [drugs] is beneficial for those suffering from jaundice, edema, abdominal dropsy, and skin diseases such as kilāsa; the dose should be carefully administered starting from one karṣa up to one pala.
Once it has been digested, one should eat with mung bean soup or with the meat broth of wild animals.

One should consume sixty-day rice with milk and soft boiled *śāli* rice for seven days; the first dose is considered moderate, the middle is double that, and the highest measure is known to be triple by those who contemplate yoga. (20–21)

Indeed, the man who consumes *guggulu* even for a year in due order shall suffer no injury from poison, whether from stationary or mobile sources. Freed from wrinkles and grey hair, even an old man becomes young; his intellect, vision, strength, speed, and virility increase, and he becomes devoid of old age.

It pacifies *gulma*, *aṣṭhīlā*, heart disease, and *āmavāta*; it is beneficial for skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*), urinary disorders (*prameha*), stones (*aśmarī*), colic, abdominal distension, erysipelas, and hemorrhage; and it is wholesome for those possessed by malevolent spirits (*bhūta*).
(23) Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Formulation of Guggulu," in the Section on Formulations (*Kalpasthāna*) of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya. 5.
Thus ends the fifth section on the Kalpas; the first chapter concludes.
Ātreya said:
The wise know the body to consist of the five elements, endowed with the five sense organs, possessed of the qualities of the seven constituents, and composed of the ten vital airs;
likewise, the individual soul (jīva), the mind, and space are each of the nature of the three qualities (guṇas).
O best of physicians, this body, produced from semen and blood, is a vessel for the humors (doṣas) and should be understood as consisting of the five elements.
The body is of four types: infancy, youth, and maturity.
The "Elder" (sthavira) is likewise described as having a small body in childhood;
as long as one is sixteen years of age, that state of childhood persists.
In that regard, the strength of the elements (dhātu) exists, and the body is rooted in those elements.
Through the nourishment of the elements (dhātus), the body increases greatly;
life, however, is rooted in the elements, for death arises from their depletion.
Furthermore, through the deficiency of the elements, one obtains only a short lifespan.
A man is seen to live here even by the strength of his constituent elements (dhātu);
from that sexual union, the formation of the embryo arises correctly.
Therefore, they know that the strength of the elements comes first, from that the vital essence (sattva), and from that the passion (rajas).
From *rajas* (the menstrual flow) desire (*kāma*) is born; from desire comes union in sexual pleasure.
Every month women have their season (*ṛtu*); having seen that women are in their season, O best of physicians, the *ṛtu* lasts for as long as the *rajas* flows for seven days.

Purification of the womb occurs after seven nights; therefore, a woman becomes fertile. And yet, O son, the menses of women are seen even without [sexual] union. But the fruit of women is not seen without union, O son.
Filled with wonder in his heart due to this doubt, Hārīta questioned him again.
Hārīta said:
"O wise one, how is it that an embryo is not produced without sexual union?"
"How could there be a flower or fruit without union?
Why is it that the production of fruit in women is not seen as being like that of trees?
Being thus questioned, the great teacher, the bull among sages, replied: 12.
Ātreya said:
"O son, in the case of incompatible creepers and stationary plants, the seed exists there in accordance with its constituent elements (dhātu), together with their respective associations."
No divided vision is seen in him; listen, my son, for all immobile beings are known to consist of Śiva’s power.
O high-minded one, Śiva should be understood as motionless, yet his power of pervasion is vast.

Therein, the qualities of woman and man exist through their union. (15) Just as with the mango flower and its fruit, they know the seed of women to be composed of *rajas*, while the seed of men is the semen, rich in the vital seed and the organ.
Therefore, O son, through union the birth of the embryo occurs.
On the first day, from the union of the semen, the *kalala* is produced; on the tenth day, it takes the form of a bubble and becomes blood. 16–17.

On the fifteenth day there would be a solid mass; on the twentieth day, a lump of flesh; when the twenty-fifth day arrives, the emergence of the self consisting of the five elements occurs. Within one month, the fivefold nature of the embryo is produced.
When fifty days have passed, the sprouts come into being;
when three months have passed, the hands and feet develop; and when three and a half months have passed, the head becomes substantial.
In the fourth month, the growth of body hair is observed;
in the fifth, there is a good life-force; in the sixth, throbbing occurs;
and when the eighth month has arrived, the connection with fire (the digestive heat) begins to function.
When the ninth month has arrived, his movements arise;
he experiences a sense of detachment due to the cause of dwelling in the womb.
He may be born in the tenth month, or even in the eleventh.
Furthermore, by the force of the humors (*doṣa*), the fetus may either be retained or brought forth;
if the fetus is impelled by the wind (*vāta*) before the days [of gestation] are complete,
it may be delivered, and then the infant is seen within that fetus.
Now, O Great-minded One, I shall explain the knowledge of the body's complexion:
through a predominance of male semen, or likewise through a predominance of female seed, or even through deficient vital fluids and sense organs, one who is predominantly male is born. (25–26)

Due to the predominance of female reproductive essence (retas), even from one with diminished semen and faculties, the birth of a female occurs because of the excess of *rajas*; likewise, when the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*) are equal in strength, there is the natural production of a male through transformation. 27.

O best of men, whatever mental disposition— whether characterized by goodness (sāttvikī), passion (rājasī), or darkness (tāmasī)— arises in women whose menses have appeared during their fertile season, she shall give birth to a child endowed with corresponding qualities.

She who meditates upon a brother, a father, or a man—whichever he may be—in her mind, gives birth to a son resembling him; such a woman is the best of physicians. A dark-complexioned man is one born of a windy (vāta) constitution.
Through pitta one becomes fair-complexioned and possesses a pitta constitution (31). Through śleṣman one is born unctuous, dark-complexioned, and likewise hairy;
he has long hair on his head, is stout, and is endowed with a long constitution (32).
Due to *vātarakta*, the eye becomes black; due to *pittarakta*, it is tawny;
and a person with *pitta* and blood is dry, while one with *kapha* and blood is oily and dark.
Due to *vāta*, the circle of vision has the appearance of the *bhṛṅgarāja* flower or collyrium.

Know that he whose hair is fine, black, and coarse, and whose nails are small and dark-complexioned, is afflicted by Vāta. By Pitta, one becomes yellowish, hairless, with tawny eyes, and hair that is ash-colored and reddish-brown.
One who is hairless, with a yellowish luster of the nails, afflicted by hunger, and lacking heat is "Dṛpta" (35).
One who is hairy, with thick and coarse hair, dark complexion, a haughty body, and large in stature;
one with very glossy teeth, beautiful white eyes, a lustrous glow on the nails, a pale and very long nose—[such a person is "Dṛptakaṭhora"] (36).
Through the predominance of rajas with equal virility, a man may become of feminine nature;
known as a "neuter," he becomes neither woman nor man. (37) Through the specific combination of the humors (doṣas) and constituents (dhātus), the formation of the body occurs upon their union.
When error has been committed in sexual union, the mind flows away due to both [factors].
(38) A simultaneous birth of twins is observed, which causes pleasure to another's mind;
this occurs through the power of equal defects, as well as by nature and even through transformation. (39)
When the semen and blood become dark (śyāmā), the birth of a neuter being occurs.
Then, the seed, having been ripened by the fire of the five elements, is formed into the *kalala* stage. That [embryo], situated within, becomes shaped like a bubble, nourished by the external wind.
Having become the *kalala*, it produces a mass by means of the fire of the five elements.

When that mass has reached maturity and become a solid conglomerate, the pervasive wind (*vyāna-vāyu*) generates the five principles, as well as the hands, feet, head, and other limbs. Although the internal wind is one, by resorting to various locations, it fashions the form of the body.
The *udāna* wind, situated in the throat and heart, illuminates the openings of the body and the mouth. The *apāna* wind, located below, purifies the lower opening.
These internal winds, each occupying its own path, exit by creating their respective apertures.
These very nine gates—the mouth, nose, ears, eyes, anus, and genitals—these gates are brought into being by the wind (*vāta*).
Therein, the wind situated within produces, by means of expansion, the limbs such as the hands and feet; likewise, it generates the layers of skin, flesh, hair, body hair, and bone. 41.1–2.
Taste, blood, saliva, urine, semen, and the fluids;
fire, bile, the eyes, darkness, and the pentad beginning with anger;
hearing, touch, as well as exhalation, perspiration, walking, and so forth—42–43.
For these winds are to be fully understood, as well as the other primary elements (prakṛti), along with mind, intellect, sleep, laziness, and intoxication.
From the Void (śūnya), these five are produced; they are established within every body.
In the body, due to vātarakta, the skin and flesh are considered to be dependent on the skin;
fat arises from semen and phlegm (śleṣman), while plasma (rasa) is produced from bone and blood.
Vātarakta resides in the pitta located in the heart, whereas the liver consists of vātarakta.
The thigh is supported by blood, phlegm, and rasa; it consists of phlegm and blood, as do the spleen and the muscles. The body is composed of the five elements, and space is indeed emptiness.
From space, wind arose; from wind, vital breath (prāṇa) is born;
and that portion of vital breath, thus produced, is established in all living beings. From space, water was produced; from water, the earth was born. 48.
From that, its radiance was thus produced; from radiance, darkness is born.
(49) In the body composed of the five elements and endowed with the five senses, that which is the primary among the elements is designated as space. (50)

From space arises fire; from fire, pride; from pride, valor; from that, egoism; from that, anger; from anger, darkness; and from darkness, evil. From space arises goodness; from goodness, truth; from truth, austerity; from austerity, policy; from policy, discernment; from discernment, peace; and through peace, righteousness. From goodness arises passion; from passion, desire; from desire, fickleness; from fickleness, untruth; and from untruth, evil.

From taste comes desire; from desire, longing; from longing, progeny; from progeny, friendship; from friendship, affection; from affection, delusion; from delusion, deceit; from that, confusion; from confusion, falsehood; from that, ignorance; from ignorance, merit and demerit; and from merit and demerit, rebirth.
Furthermore, from *sattva* arises even *tamas*; it is the master of both waking and sleeping.
Impelled by *tamas*, the embodied soul becomes void through the ether.
Because the body finds rest therein, it is proclaimed as "nidrā" (sleep).
It dissolves within the Inner Self between the nose and the middle of the eyebrows;
therefore, the mind of men becomes sleep and merges there. 53-54.
From *sattva* heat is said to arise, and from heat bile is produced;
wind arises from the mind when it is enveloped by *tamas*.
Due to the conjunction of wind and *tamas*, the state of sleep is proclaimed.
Sattva, tamas, and vāyu likewise function through a single conjunction.
Listen, O Vaideha, as I describe how hunger, sleep, thirst, fear, envy, pride, delusion, anger, desire, pleasure, satisfaction, and tranquility arise for those who sustain their bodies. (56–57)
By the desire for food, the digestive fire moves through the body;
it attains satisfaction from the taste of the essence and from the dross [of waste].
Whenever the fire dries up the impurities, at that time it feels as if it has attained satisfaction.
"And when there is dissatisfaction with that very thing, the mind then expands its craving.
(59) Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Body," in the *Śārīrasthāna* of the *Hārītottara* as spoken by Ātreya.
Hereby the *Śārīrasthāna* is completed.
The chapter known as the *Pariśiṣṭādhyāya* (Supplementary Chapter), which concerns the meaning of the body, is taught here in detail;
having heard this, the highly lustrous Hārīta, the best of sages, [acted accordingly].
Then, having prostrated before the most excellent of gurus with a joyful heart,
he went to the bank of the celestial river, devoted to bathing and meditation.
He who reads this scripture, heard from the words of the great sage—
Freed from all sins and free from disease, one attains happiness.
First it was proclaimed by Brahmā, then by Atri,
then by Dhanvantari, and by the high-souled Aśvins.
Thus, it should be known as equal to the Vedas; it is not considered a cause for contempt.
This has been declared in many ways by others who are experts in various scriptures.
Therefore, one should accept the opinion of these [teachers], for they all know [it] to be the same.
Caraka, Suśruta, and likewise Vāgbhaṭa—
these three principal compendia (saṃhitās) are to be proclaimed in age after age.
Atri is considered the physician in the Kṛta Yuga, and Suśruta in the Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, only the greatness of one named Vāgbhaṭa is seen;
there, the Vaiṣṇavī, Āśvinī, Gārgī, Mādhyāhnikā, Aparā,
and Mārkaṇḍeyā are declared by the wise Yogarāja.
O Lord, this compendium was proclaimed by the sages through various kinds of mantras.
Agniveśa, Bhela, Jātūkarṇya, Parāśara, Hārīta, and Kṣīrapāṇi— these six are indeed those sages.
Just as the lion is among the lords of beasts, as Ananta is among serpents, and as Śambhu is among the gods, so is Ātreya in the science of medicine.
Therefore, with effort, by good physicians whose minds are moistened with respectful devotion, [he should be honored].
"Worthy of worship and to be honored, he will bestow the riches of happiness.
Thus ends the supplementary chapter (Pariśiṣṭādhyāya) in the Hārītottara as spoken by Ātreya.
Herein concludes the Hārītasaṃhitā.
